This game right here people...  THIS LITTLE AMAZING GEM is exactly why I review HUNDREDS of unheard of indie games that launch on Steam each and every year.  This little diamond is why I have nearly 4,000 videos up on my YouTube channel!

These days in the massive bombardment of low effort asset cobbled together trash and asset flips uploaded to Steam every single day, finding a little indie gem where the developer actually cares and shows enough effort to make a polished little gem of a game is a rarity it seems. Welcome my friends to "The Maze Contract".  The game combines retro space shooting goodness of the 1980s with the polish and special effects and responsive controls of modern games.  It's easily one of my favorite indie games this year and probably one of the best retro space shooters that I've ever played on Steam in more than a dozen years!



HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!  If you're a fan of old school retro games like Asteroids or even Pac-Man, then this game is a "MUST BUY!".  It's well worth every penny and should pay for itself ten fold by the time you're done going back and playing it again and again.  Not many indie games score a perfect 100% in my scoring that places bang for your buck value as the highest aspect of my score, but "The Maze Contract" is my definition of an indie game done flawlessly.
Recommended.

A very simplistic and cartoony run game with a lot of charm that'll give anyone a good chuckle. Especially if you're a fan of flavor text. I like to interpret Walrus Run as what a little kid pictures in their imagination if they decided to create their own game, and I feel like that's where the quality of it shines the most.
Gameplay wise, the controls are a bit tricky to get used to but really satisfying when it clicks. I'm personally surprised that implementing the slippery and sliding nature of a walrus in a platformer focused on speed works the way it does. 
Very nice that there's customizations to all of The Walrus' movement to make things easier to handle. Because hhhoo boy... the later levels are soul crushing normally and nigh near impossible to escape D rank.

One small problem that I have with the game though is jumping off ramps does not work properly. The only way to maintain your momentum is at the TOP of the ramp. Anywhere else and you're going straight into the pit. Also The Cat's projectiles are unfair to dodge. The fight itself is fine though.

I recommend this game for anyone who wants a casual and easy-going experience or just likes silly expressions. It will encourage you to... er... fish for higher ranks. It's not at all easy, but it's fun to try.

I honestly feel like Walrus Run has potential.
And it's solo made. Give credit to that.

I put a thumb's up because there is no "thumb's middle". Game is enjoyable but do not expect to spend as much time in this one as you did in PlaCo1 for now. It's noticeable they put a lot of effort in some aspects but others were neglected. Here we go.

Pros
 - Path placement is a huge improvement over PlaCo1. You can place rides directly onto plazas and the ride will effectively be surrounded by path making it lifelike instead of messing around with short curves and avoiding the ride's edge. You can also stamp-erase paths making them very malleable. They even added the option to move the edges and/or vertices of paths making it almost limitlessly customizable. You also have the option to automatically put bins or benches as you put paths. You can chose which, at what interval and on what side of the path. Wish you could but both the bin and the bench but it's already very good.
 - There is now a scenery brush. No more placing trees one at a time or through bluprints. Default burshes are different regions trees and rocks but you can make new brush with any pieces of scenery you want. You could make a statue forest if you want.
 - You can add scenery to rides and their vehicles or seats.
 - There's now a camera mode to walk in your park. No more naming a person Tegidcam.
 - Loans system is more lifelike I'd say. There only one kind if loan now and the maximum you can borrow changes dynamically as your park value raises or decreases. There is interests and sales cut. The more you borrow, the biggest cut on your sales the bank takes repaying itself.
 - Pools and flumes. Very satisfying to build. Just wish they added splash pads or spray park items for shallow pools for kids.
 - Personal music for speakers or videos for billboards. They can watch Die Hard while they eat.

Not really against, more like personal preferences
 - Research dynamic is completely changed. Research tree is shared through all career maps but is at least standalone in sandbox. You can basically put three workshops and assign them three mechanics at the first map, fast-forward while you go shopping and you'll have enough "research points" to research everything from a chapter instantly as you move through the chapters.
 - Power and water management. Nothing bad to say just that I don't like managing those. Each facility, ride or store now use a certain amount of power so if your park is big enough, you need about 2 acres square of power generators to power everything and you have to wire them all up to power distributors.

Not pros (c-o-n-s seems to be censored now)
 - Very few themes and they are boring. Thus, making replayability very low.
 - Some rides from PlaCo1 are absent.
 - Staff is less customizable. In a sense that there is three tiers of wage now. Low, Fair and High each affecting morale differently. No more textbox to put your own wage. Can't put a perk in staff buildings anymore.
 - No more security guards, no more pickpockets and no more cameras.
 - Guests just ride and eat, they do not stop to look at rides or scenery. I know PlaCo1 didn't have that either but RCT did in 1999.
 - Same as PlaCo1, some coasters I make are seemingly "too extreme" to open. I would ride them.
 - Less brands.
 - No hotels. But a Resort Theme???
 - No restaurant like in PlaZoo.

My rant
 - The game is good but becomes boring very fast. You have Aquatic, Resort, Viking, Mythology and Planet Coaster themes. In PlaCo1, we have a giant robot dog in three different contexts, aliens and space rangers shooting, cars exploding, pirates fighting, cannons shooting, a kraken, knights playing together and dragons. Let me break it down to your Frontier, Mythology is not mythologic. It's basically Ancient Greece Architectural Kit. Aside from looping doors, turning gears and a windmill, the only real animatronics are a stone Medusa, a mechanical minotaur and in Aquatic theme a huge fish. Didn't it occur to you that a mythology theme should have more than a few pillars and a Poseidon statue? Where is are the hydras, the chimera, Hercules, Hades, Hares, cyclops, dryads, hippogriff, etc. Or even the god dam Kraken that's already in PlaCo1!
Same goes for Viking. To be fair you called it Viking and not Scandinavian Folklore but still. Architecture and a few runes become boring fast.
You get rid of hotels but give us a Resort Theme??? Better not give the team that designed the themes any bonus this year boys. And don't you dare charge for a Hotels and Restaurants DLC while it was introduced in PlaCo1 in a free update.
Now explain to me how guests don't look at scenery or rides when Chris Sawyer made it via Assembly in 1999 in RCT and you, yes you, did for animals in PlaZoo.
Now on a more serious note, I feel the community is not inherently disappointed because they want themes from the first game. We just want something extraordinary. Something beyond statues and architectures that would make a person go WOW. We do not necessarily want the same one. You could make a dinosaurs theme with about ten dinos, a few nests, broken sheds, a volcano, meteor pieces, etc. Your sales would spike me boi. You already have the modeling experience for that with Jurassic World Evolution 1 and 2.
Add actual mythology to your theme. Cerberus, a gate to Tartarus, manticores, etc. There is so much to harvest from that!

Anyway, games not bad but gets boring.

The game has been plagued with bugs from day 1 as well and Frontier, in my book, became another example of a gaming company that's out there for only 1 thing, money money money. The quality in this game is non-existent because it's just an empty and unfished shell.

Let's be clear: This game should be in early access, because that's basically what the current experience feels like.
While I like there being a bit more on the staff and facility side in this game than the first one, it just doesn't run well right now. Instead of constantly decreasing condition and the mechanics then restoring that, this game has maintenance badges that keep the condition stable until they expire.
However no matter how many mechanics I keep around my different zones (which is all a pain to manage right now, the menus are awful), I constantly get notifications about rides and generators being in poor condition. While I don't want the entire game to play itself (which it actually pretty much does in a lot of areas), this is just tedious to keep up with and to order repairs all the time.
This results in constant notification spam, which is made worse by getting these when not having a research facility (I shut it down after having already unlocked everything) and urgent ones for a ride not having enough energy (it was shut down as I was still working on it).


The new pathing tools are a massive upgrade over the first game's system, but too often it's still a lot of work trying to get things to do what you want. The devs apparently also broke a tool recently that would allow to draw path outlines with either curves or straights. Used to be able to combine both, but right now it's just not the case anymore.

Also the rounding tool works inconsitently. I tried making a welcome desk at my waterpark with the rounded wall pieces as sides. If I leave everything around the wall as path, the peds will just walk through it. Trying to round the path to the table only worked on one side, despite everything being laid out symmetrical the other side just constantly drew a wider curve, which looked awful.


Ride tickets have options for automatic pricing, for some reason visitors will prefer "bargain" over custom pricing, even if the custom one was 5 times cheaper.
Ride attendants now are people as well instead of part of the ride. It's again a good idea in principle, but a lot of micromanagement even in a small zone. I have one zone with 3 rides and either 4 or 5 ride attendants that all have staggered break times and short paths between each other and the break room. I still end up with unattended rides all the time, sometimes those employees are just walking around in completely different areas.

The build mode is just more (or in terms of material options actually less) of the same from the first game. At this point I wish they simplified the building elements by separating the shapes from the textures. Like in the first game it's a massive list of all the different walls, arches, door frames, windows, pillars, roofs, etc in all the different materials (but often with certain combinations missing). Instead of this stupidly long list with the filter options would be much easier to navigate if we could choose the shape of a part separately from its material, and just get all material options for all shapes.

To make things worse there's a lot of decorations that, despite being part of the same building I just constructed, don't adhere to the same grid. There are workarounds to get them into place, but it shouldn't be a problem to begin with. The long promised glass items are also falling into this problem. I was holding off on an indoor swimming area because I wanted actual glass windows and roof elements (instead of the fully opaque stuff), and all we got were a few panels that also don't allign to the grid.

The coasters got a few new tools, which is neat, but again the implementation has problems. I wanted to split my station so people would exit first and then new ones would board. For some reason there needs to be regular track between both stations, in case of my water ride it was a minimum of 12m, so I had to redesign the entire station. In addition to that, no matter how long I make the exit platform, people will only ever get off at the very end.

Adding other rides like gondolas allows to move visitors between different areas of the park, but with these gondolas I found another weird restriction: When you want a second station along the cable line the game will force you to build a straight cable section before that. This makes it really hard to position the station and if you start from that end you can go straight into an in/decline, but you will then have the same problem on the other end.


At least the devs are making updates to improve things and overall it's not as bad as certain other builder sims from the past few years, but the current experience has a lot of points of friction and shouldn't be sold as a finished product for 50 bucks.

There are way too many issues with this game that make it very frustrating/irritating to play in its current state.  I continuously have issues with park paths jamming up even with very wide paths and areas.  This really causes issues with the guests moods. An improvement would be to allow us to have specific entrance and exit gates which could help the congestion.  

Some of the scenarios are broken, although they have been working on fixing them, so I will need to go back and try some.  I have issues with using an unloading and loading station and trying to review the test results heatmap.

As a lifelong theme park sim player - from RCT onward - this game delivers well enough to be the next genre leader. The hours of play time on the negative reviews are the telling part for how to appreciate this game. As a sequel, Planet Coaster 2 faces some issues, like controls not being as refined as in the original (why must I recolor everything all the time in build mode??) and currently very limited scenery themes.

However, on its own, PC 2 has all the amount of content you should expect in a base game, arguably much more in individual themes and foliage than the original, and plenty of base game perks that make it stand out from predecessors in the genre - weather, water parks, lots of scenarios, and unique rides. Like any other management sim, it just takes time to get used to. Sequels are never all inclusive of all the perks the previous games had. With what PC 2 provides at the outset, you can make some pretty incredible creations that leave you feeling proud.

More than anything, the devs clearly pay attention, and if the dedication to its sister game, Planet Zoo, is any sign, Planet Coaster 2 is going to be receiving DLC and free updates for many years to come.

There are definitely issues, the path tool still feels quite clunky at times with weird behaviour for more complex shapes but it's more freeform that the first game so something that affords much more freedom is going to be less predictable.

The DLC thing is to be expected at this point in the industry and frankly the base game verity of rides is okay for now. 

Themes wise while there are only 5 themes, those being Generic, Viking, Ancient Greek, Submarine/Industry and Tropical, those themes actually lend really well to pretty easy variation with a little imagination. Infact, I think the current parts set allow much more creative freedom that all the themes in the first game, with scaling etc, you can make basically any theme you want with few exceptions, combining Viking and Ancient Greek together you can make Medieval, Classical, Roman, etc. Same goes for the Submarine/Industry theme, you can mix that with Viking and make Steampunk Western or Mortal Engines, etc. Where the first game themes were a fair bit harder to mix, it was hard to adapt pieces to make more unique themes. If themes were like colour tools in painting software, this game you've got CMYK sliders, you can easily create more exotic and unusual pallet while the first game was more like playing with Swatches, you've got a lot of prefab colours which lock you into using a specific pallet.

An extremely simple yet extremely fun game. Another entry on the list of speedrun styled fps games that are both cheaper and better than Anger Foot.

In Cruel, you are FORCED to go fast, constantly being chased by a fire that catches up to you if you stand still for more than a few seconds. Dispatching enemies as efficiently as possible so that you can keep running is the name of the game, and while healing is actually very plentiful, enemies chunk your health if you let them, to the point where losing control of the situation for more than a few seconds basically means instant death. You can shoot, use melee weapons, slide, kick, parry bullets with a well timed melee swing, and your healing soda cans can double as room clearing aoe attacks (which isn't explained in game). Guns have extremely limited ammo and melee weapons break in just a few hits, so staying versatile becomes an absolute necessity.

There are only a tiny handful of perks to choose from. Each perk can be upgraded twice if you roll it multiple times, but the game does not explain what exactly about it is being upgraded (duration, effectiveness, etc) and while some are gamechangers, others I find to be mediocre at best and almost useless at worst.

My main complaints are:

*The kick is TERRIBLE. The hitbox is so comically tiny you'd swear your character's legs are two inches long and one inch wide. The fact that you can be standing inside an enemy's model and still miss your kick is nothing short of baffling.

*The head hitboxes on some enemies are extremely inconsistent, and that inconsistency matters when every single second counts.

*Trying to knock enemies out windows is nothing short of a pipe dream a lot of the time. If they aren't standing perfectly parallel with the window at the perfect distance, they'll just slide away along the wall, get right back up and start shooting you again.

*The crows legitimately give you half a second to react to them when they crash through the windows, to the point where they feel completely random and unfair.


But despite these complaints, Cruel is a fun game for a decent price. And I'll gladly pay $10 for another chance to dunk on Anger Foot.

I absolutely LOVE games like this. Games that are simple, but extremely focused in their design. CRUEL is my favorite indie game of the year thus far, reminding me of the fun I've had with games like Downwell & Devil Daggers in the past. I'm no game dev but if I ever were to make a game of my own, I'd look to games like this as inspiration.

CRUEL follows the same design philosophy as games like Post Void and Mullet Mad Jack, you're on a strict time limit to make it to the exit at the end of the current floor, and all that stands in your way is a bunch of enemies and traps. Unlike those games, you don't gain time back for killing enemies. CRUEL is oddly enough a little less cruel than those other two games, but it definitely ramps up in difficulty the further in you go, mostly through enemy placements and enemy counts. It still provides that same adrenaline rush though, and it's addicting as hell.

I love the style of the game, visually. The enemy designs are all great and are very distinct which is important in a game where choosing which enemy you kill first could mean life or death. The game just feels very good to play as far as controls go, it's smooth and responsive so no complaints there. CRUEL doesn't go wild with upgrades or enemy types nor does it have a billion weapons and loadouts like a lot of roguelikes, but that's a strength of the game in my opinion. 

It's simple enough to understand and play, but there's enough here that you do have a learning curve and need to hone your skills in order to beat the game. And generally I do think having good skill is more important in CRUEL rather than having good upgrades, although they will give you an edge. 

Definitely give this a try if any of this sounds intriguing to you, it's a blast.

Cruel is a post-void inspired hallway shooter, I think it takes the formula and adds onto it successfully, while giving it an awesome aesthetic touch on it.

Playing it has a rythm game feel to it, where enemies are notes you have to hit and your tools are the instruments.
Enemy variety supports this, with each enemy having special quirks and a few good ways to deal with them. Cultists have their shots easily parried, policemen dont parry you when you stun them with a kick, the kobolds explode harmlessly if you kick them away instead of shooting them, and so on and so forth.
It plays incredibly smooth because most of your actions are independent from eachother, as far as reasonable. You can be sliding through a doorway, that you are kicking open mid-slide, while drinking a can to heal yourself, whip to the side to nail a cultist in the head near the end of your slide and throw your melee weapon to catch the shotgunner behind him because its slightly faster to do such than to wait for your gun to refire.

There is a surprising amount of depth allowed for such a simple game, kicks throw and stun enemies and are sometimes smarter than shooting, they also throw enemies out of windows killing them at no cost to ammo or melee durability. Melee weapons can be thrown for great damage, which also isn't tied to the swing cooldown. You can blow up a cultist's head and immediately throw your weapon into a melee enemy, without waiting, which ontop of being incredibly cool is smart to do because you can just pick up the melee weapon that that enemy dropped.

At the end of each floor your can sacrifice your healing items to gain a perk, or reroll your choices. Some perks are really good, some are very situational, some are not that good. It's a good mix, making rerolling worth a lot. Not getting hit is rewarded with a stronger run because you can reroll your perks more often. Well designed, nice.

In game you are expected to pace yourself according to how good you are at it. You don't lose health with time like in post-void and the fire chasing you is rather forgiving in almost all rooms, this gives you a window to just slow yourself down a little to not get overwhelmed with enemies, as well as do some rudimentary resource management, with juggling cans while at capacity, replacing your melee weapon with a full durability one, and so on. This is never a bother - it's barely a few seconds whenever it does happen and most of the rooms end with you not even stopping and bursting through the next door anyways. It does make you feel smart when you do take a second to take inventory and the short moments of slowing yourself down feel tactical and never turn frustrating.

The only real criticism i have of the game, is that the unbelievably good soundtrack gets less and less to the good parts of the songs as you get faster, since a new song is started on each floor. It would be cool if you had an option to just have the current track run with a dampened filter on while on your way to the next floor, so the tracks can be enjoyed in full, which they should.

I've been wanting to write a review for this game multiple times now.
However every time I go to my library to press the "go to store page" button I go "... Just one game".
Yes even before writing this i played one run, which takes roughly 30 minutes.

What you ultimately do is this: You put in a name of the person you want to kill (This is the seed), you then go from room to room fighting enemies which takes roughly 10 seconds, kick down the door and head to the next one until you either finish the 10th floor or die trying. 
Once there you can decide if you want to kill the person or spare them. If you decide to kill them, their name gets added to a list and you can't play the seed anymore. So if you like a seed, don't kill them.

There are a lot of small gameplay things like for example vending machines.
You find vending machines standing around in a level and dealing damage to them makes them drop a soda can.
Soda cans however have many uses:
1: Drinking one heals roughly 50% of your health.
2: Drinking one but pressing the shoot button crushes the can, dealing AoE damage around the player.
3: Between levels you can trade them in for upgrades, like more ammo drops, health on headshot kill, faster reloads and more.
They're your health, "oh shit" button and currency! How you use them and what you prioritise is all up to you (and depending on how good you are at not dying)

What about the simple act of murder?
There are guns, melee weapons and windows!
Currently there is a revolver, shotgun and uzi. Pistol has good range, shotgun is for close range obliteration and uzi for dealing with multiple enemies at once. Ammo is scarce, so switching between guns is mandatory.
Melee, well, you can swing at enemies or throw it at them which kills most enemies instantly.

But now we're talking about windows:
Going for headshots is way more ammo efficient, and so is going for the head for melee, however a headshot kill makes enemies drop on the spot.
If you however kill an enemy by bodyshot or melee kill they get thrown backwards. This can knock down enemies and instantly kill others. If you have a upgrade you even get armor for throwing someone out a window. Alternatively you can just kick them instead of unloading a bunch of rounds into them.


tl;dr: Game good.

This feels like if Life Force was all tate which is basically Crisis Force without that ship's special abilities. But then there's bricks on the ground you break a la Star Force. Then the name of the game is Xelan Force. That's why I call it "Force times 4" in a math sense xD (okay, all jokes aside)

There's a nod to Compile where some enemies release tiny pods that you grab to slowly upgrade your regular weapon. Then there's the Gun Nac/PC Engine feel with the secondary power up grabs. And what I mean by that is that secondary weapon & missile grabs will weave back & forth across the screen while changing, so sometimes you have to dodge the power up or else you'll grab the wrong weapon. Another nod is Xevious where it has the square enemies with a flipping animation that blocks your bullets. Just let them flip downward off the screen.

While this is a tate shmup, there is one level of the game where the scrolling changes, but your ship is still pointed upwards. There are some dodging stages with tight corridors and one part that speeds up (sorry if I'm giving too much away).

There's 8 stages total and the ending has a questionable element as well as a hint of a possible sequel. I would say it takes about 40 minutes to play all the way through from start to finish.

You have the choice of two drone types: Follow you around in a trail or stationary beside you. The stationary ones have a dedicated button to change their fire configuration. Otherwise, you're just holding one button the whole time.

Some bosses are impossible to hit with some secondary weapons. You'll need to wait for a drop to change it.

There's not much button configuration and they sometimes feel like you're holding down a turbo button set. So if you pause while holding the shot button down, you might just immediately unpause. If you beat a boss while never releasing fire, you'll have to unrelease it and hold it again when the next level starts or your ship won't fire at all.

The challenge is not too punishing overall and certainly nowhere as hard as Recca, but you can't sleep on anything. You also have to be careful of enemies coming from behind sometimes and without notice. You'll need to memorize the stages to know when they can come out. It's not too often. When there's one wave, you can expect a few more.

All in all, if you want a shmup that has a total NES feel in both graphics, sound, and playability without any flickering, you've come to the right place. The price is quite nice as well. If you like what you see in the screenshots, I highly recommend getting it.

Jack and Jill are summoned to Oklahoma to help the mayor plan for the harvest festival by transporting vegetables and repairing railways.  While helping out several problems arise and it is up to Jack and Jill to determine who the culprit is by finding clues.

Each map has you doing tasks, like collecting resources and building buildings in a specific time frame in order to get a three star rating for each map. Play through 45 main story maps, 5 vegetable stand themed mini game maps, 15 after story maps, and 1 classic shooter mini game.

There is NO replayability on this game as there is no end game mechanics, no map metrics to try to beat, and no engrossing story to return to.

While the fact that the game feels like a once and done kind of game; I do recommend it to anyone that likes casual games or is an achievement hunter.

Time Machine Bronzeville is incredible. If anything here speaks to you, then check it out. I feel that TMB is an example of an untapped mode within the videogame form. TMB mixes history, folklore, the arts, and reenactment to make an enriching and uplifting experience. While books will always be an irreplaceable way to understand black history, the scale of reenactment here is not to be underestimated. 

Time Machine Bronzeville uses props and stand-ins to force you to really reckon with how black people actually lived during the time period, it gives the user a guide on how to imagine what Bronzeville must have been like. I find the effect here very interesting. This game eschews the popular mode of photo-realistic videogame graphics. It offers instead something that appears "dated"—a photo-realism of the past. This choice reminds the viewer of the distance of time. Yet the dioramas could still be "real" by their arrangements and commitment to reenactment. Everything is where it is supposed to be, but the final step is interpretive, it's still up to the viewer and user of this software to try to connect this arrangement to what really happened. 

Time Machine Bronzeville chronicles triumphs, tragedies, bit players, and just people getting by. It's an ideal thick text, as it is a snapshot of the life and times of Bronzeville. The gallery setting gives you time to think about these personal histories at your own pace, so you can make your own connections. It networks these stories in whatever way that jumps out to you and conveys them with a feeling of "here, come and see for yourself." The game is held together by your own curiosity and drive to know how the city looked and how these folks lived.

I'm a massive fan of jazz, so I knew Bronzeville as a footnote. Now I understand it as something more. I feel that it is essential to keep the past alive with us and Time Machine Bronzeville offers a great opportunity to do so.

In a world of amazing deckbuilders, Dice & Fold has a lot going for it. The first is the art style is excellent. The simple art style is fantastic and was a major selling point for me. 

Gameplay is a matter of building a character to beat a run by killing monsters with dice. Some monsters 'HP' slots need specific faces while others need a specific total - Each character has a magical power and you collect items that grant bonuses along the way. It's a great formula and as a pick up and play a few rounds type of game, it is more than worth your money. 

The  downsides are simply that there doesn't seem to be a ton of built in balance to the various skills of the heroes. Some really don't feel like you're playing a round to their power and more playing a round in the hopes to random draw some great items. Once you've completed a few characters you'll recognize the type of numbers you'll need for the final bosses and by Round 20 (out of 30) you're pretty certain whether you have a chance to win or whether its a dead round.  Very rarely will you have a game where you feel like you'll JUST beat it if you get good numbers, although it does happen on occasion. 

For a quick round or two game, it is great and worth the price. For building strategy and optimizing, it sadly is lacking.

The thing with this game is that it's kind of trying to be a roguelike with metaprogression, but it lacks the content to do so. Enemies will drop random powerups that increase aspects of your ship, like the power of your bullets, amount of bullets, amount of missiles, and the speed and area of your bullet-and-enemy clearing field-- basically a rechargable bomb.

Between runs, you can take money you've gotten by defeating enemies and purchase permanent ones that basically have you start with X levels of the upgrade in question. I challenged myself to get every achievement without the use of the health-up one, because I assumed this system, and the lack of downgrading, would quickly cause the game to become too easy.

I mean. I was *kind of* right, I guess.

The thing with this game is that run difficulty swings wildly, entirely dependant on RNG. It's possible to get very few upgrades early on, and then because enemies become tanky quickly, become unable to easily defeat them and get more powerups and oops that's a downward spiral in the making. 

Or, you get fed a million fire rate ups, and suddenly the game stops having any difficulty. My final achivement, for getting to Level 12, was basically just me waiting until the game fed me enough that I didn't really have to try. 

Not like you particuarly need to try anyway. This game has like, 6 enemy types total, maybe 2 of which are actually threatening. The lack of variety and creativity in *everything*, from enemies to music to shot types (there is none, lol) to upgrades to even shot patterns (if it is possible to have "stock bullet patterns," this game has them) makes the game very dull and very repetitive very quickly, which is a death blow to any aspiring roguelike. 

(also you can't rebind controls in-game and there's no autofire button. in *2024*.)

There's good *here*-- there is a certain aspect of mindless fun in becoming a killing machine, even if it never goes very far due to lack of variety in upgrades. Bullet clearing is very satisfying if you can get multiple enemies caught and instantly killed in it. 

But it doesn't last. There's not enough here, not enough polish, for me to even feel like I got 5 dollars worth out of the game.

I really enjoyed the campaign gameplay, story and the flexibility of how I could build my characters. This continued until around level 70 when I finished the last of the campaign and started the mapping grind. Once I started the endgame grind I figured this would be when I started being able to really min/max my character, experiment with builds and really dial things in gear-wise. Sadly this was not the case, instead I started to discover just how many little (and sometimes not so little) time sinks have been designed into the game. Everything, inventory management, UI/UX design, buying/selling items, building up enough currency to buy items, finding citadels on the map, literally every aspect of the game’s design is engineered to hold your time hostage and then for some of it they offer to ransom it back to you for real money. Some will argue that you can play the game without spending a penny and they would be right, you can. However the game is specifically designed to make that choice hamper your gameplay in every respect. 

Beyond the design elements that attempt to ransom your time back to you there are elements that just unapologetically thumb their nose at it. For example player deaths and the 10% XP loss. At level 70 this is no big deal and you won’t think much of it. Once you reach the upper 80s and into the 90s you are going to start losing hours and hours of gameplay and it just gets exponentially worse. For me this was most common when mapping with friends and 9 times out of 10 I wouldn’t even be able to see what killed me and maxing out resists does not guarantee you won’t still get one shot by something you never even saw coming. The level of visual noise is so incredibly high that it just isn’t possible to see everything that could kill you. I can live with it when it is my mistake and I just got lax. When the player is not given the opportunity to try and avoid it then it becomes a design flaw.

Player to player item sales early on were ok, it was quick, efficient and most players were polite enough to let you know if the item you DMed them about was currently being sold so you didn’t waste your time waiting on them to respond. Over time a shift took place and people stopped communicating and the process became a lot of refreshing the page waiting for the market to update so you could see if they sold the item to someone else. Instead of being able to just pay an intermediary system this system requires the player to be online, it requires the player to stop what they are doing to meet up and it requires that you don’t miss a message in your chat log which is very easy to do when mapping. It seems like it was perhaps designed to push players to engage with each other but unfortunately it winds up being just as impersonal as an automated marketplace and far less efficient. It even goes so far as to clash with mapping mechanics. When you generate a map with a waystone you get a limited number of portals to access the map. Every time you leave the map and go back it consumes a portal. Due to limited inventory space it is very easy to consume most or all of your portals just retrieving loot. Leaving a map to meet with a player and sell an item will consume one of these portals making it the wise choice to finish the map first which can often result in a missed opportunity to sell something as the buyer often hedges their bets by DMing multiple sellers with similar items.

Ascension trials are terrible. Period. The honor mechanic in Sekhemas punishes melee classes while making it easy by comparison if you are ranged. Trial of Chaos will often present you with such terrible debuff options that synergize with each other so strongly you can wind up forced into an unbeatable trial. It should always be possible to get through it! This is another place where the game can completely waste your time and provides absolute nothing but frustration in return.

The list of problems this game has goes on but I’ll just conclude by saying that if you value your time and don’t want to invest in a game that has no respect for the limited time we all have on this earth then look elsewhere for your entertainment.

[h2] Path of Exile 2[/h2]

From the very first minutes of the game, I was pleasantly surprised by the physics, movement quality, and combat mechanics in general. You could say that the visuals are no worse than Diablo 4 (and in some situations, even more interesting). 

Of course, the budget difference is colossal - one studio can literally create short films for its story - but for me, that's probably the only area where Diablo has the upper hand. If you want to chill and enjoy a cinematic storyline, that's the game for you.

But Path of Exile truly shines in battles against mobs and bosses - the sheer variety of builds and progression is insane. Almost every boss is unique in its own way, and this is the first Souls-like Diablo-style game I can remember (even though it loses some of that feel in the endgame).

The gameplay is pure excitement, and defeating mobs and bosses gives you a real dopamine rush - unlike the complete indifference I felt in Diablo 4. I want to wait for the full release and finish the remaining unfinished acts before diving into the endgame, but from what I’ve seen so far, I’m more than satisfied!

Unfortunately, after almost 300 hours spent in this game, I've come to the conclusion that I can't really recommend it.

The honey moon phase is FANTASTIC. I've never played any other similar aRPGs, the Diablo games and the like nor the prequel, but despite the slightly overwhelming learning curve of the beginning I quickly became very addicted to this game. The campaign is fantastic and I enjoyed completing it many times with different kinds of builds that felt absolutely riveting to level up. For that experience alone I still hold this game in high regard. Someone somewhere said that learning is ultimately the best part in any videogame, and the amount you get to learn here to make yourself powerful feels really rewarding.

The problem is the endgame, and specifically one particular aspect of it that kills the game for me: loosing XP when dying. Now I get that there's got to be some kind of a consequence and punishment for dying (and playing badly), and there's arguably several here (loosing the Waystone and any items on the floor you didn't pick up), but the loss of the XP is just disrespectful to the player's time. Maybe I'd feel differently if I wasn't in my 30s now and felt like I'd have more time to dispose into gaming, but since that's not the case, this punishment feels horrendously frustrating. And it's not like I didn't try to min-max the heck out of the possibility of dying: I've watched several endgame build tutorials on how to stack defensive stats through leveling and gearing, spent hundreds and hundreds of exalted orbs onto really cracked gear, upgraded everything to the max and stacked resistances etc, but no matter what, sometimes you get deleted in seconds to some silly garbage you can't necessarily even see, which feels even more of a slap to my face. There's no out-learning the mechanics that kill me when sometimes I haven't the faintest clue what got me killed, and ofc you can't learn to avoid dying in something like a Souls-game by memorization since the maps, mobs and their modifiers are randomized etc. The Souls-games, generally considered very "unforgiving" are really nothing in comparison to this: in a Souls-game, you still get the chance to retrieve your potentially lost XP/currency (aside from Sekiro) if you end up messing up and dying, and 99% (if not 100%) of the time you're also able to play evasively and homeward out in order to make use of the souls (XP) in case you want to chicken out and not risk loosing your progress before tackling the new challenge. Slight tangent here comparing the experience to an entirely different kind of game, but the point is that POE 2 is frustratingly unforgiving with your time and effort to level up your character in the endgame, especially when the prospect of managing to get the next defensive or offensive node seems like the possible one that's going to help you survive a lot better in the future.

If they'll end up changing their minds about this and changing what punishment for dying in the endgame looks like, I'll be happy to re-install the game and to continue playing, but as for now, I'm REALLY not up for loosing progress again and again because of some nonsense. And I can't recommend you to play the game that far either; there's just better things to do with the time that you'll loose.

I play with one other player and while there's some parts of it that I enjoy, a lot of the frustrating parts have really outweighed the enjoyable parts. I've noticed the following

1. This is divisive but the game's dodge roll feels awful. As someone who has played a wide variety of genres (plenty of diablo II, POE1, and 300 hours of monster hunter world), the forced usage of rolling in boss fights is done really poorly. It feels incredibly clunky. The general movement in this game feels terrible. Why do all the monsters get to jump and fly around and move faster than me? 

2. The visual clarity is horrible. Maybe this is a settings thing, but I can't tell allied minions apart from enemy minions, and during boss fights, I can't tell what will cause damage (is this fire dangerous or just looks dangerous)? Another things I don't like is that some projectiles track you when you run, so you HAVE to dodge (especially in boss fights).

3. Boss fights can be so frustrating they cause me to not want to play the game anymore. When I play ARPGs, I like being able to go into a fight blind and picking up the boss mechanics later. What really sucks is that fresh into the game, deaths make you have to restart the entire boss fight. I've had it happen multiple times now where in a 30 minute boss fight I die at minute 25 when the fight is the hardest and I have to start all over. It doesn't help that the visual clarity on the boss fights is HORRIBLE so I have to die sometimes twice or three times to the same abilities to figure out what the tells are and how to dodge them. It also doesn't help that some of the boss fights are SUPER glitched with instant kill bugs or can't damage boss bugs. Basically, I don't expect or want to breeze through a boss fight, but I really think that making you start the entire fight over because you didn't understand or could tell that some moves would kill you feels really bad. IMO the bosses legit DO NOT have the quality to be worth fussing over. In a game like monster hunter, every fight is designed and visual clarity is great. I look forward to fighting the monsters (bosses effectively) there. I dread every single boss fight in POE2 because each one feels like I'm going to spend forever just to die near the end and have to start over.

4. The revive mechanic is extremely unfun. If I die, I get to do nothing until my partner resurrects me or dies. If my partner dies, I get screwed over trying to resurrect them because things get interrupted so easily. I genuinely think that revives should NOT be interrupted by damage, or they should simply remove revives. They could also just limit the number of revives and make it easier to revive.

5. I didn't necessarily expect to get far in this game, but I figured I could get through the campaign just clicking around skills the way I thought would work. This completely doesn't work, and really what winds up happening is in practice I have to look up how to play my class and follow some build guide. Right now, I feel like I have to juggle a bunch of skills (just got to act 3) just get to reasonable damage.

6. I'm playing a sorceress, and honor is literally one of the worst mechanics I've seen in a game. It wasn't even clear to me what it was until I failed a trial from getting hit. I cannot imagine how frustrating it would be for a melee character. For a game with so many classes and potential builds, why would you introduce a mechanic that literally wipes out builds? Also, the description on the water made me think I'd lose it on the floor, so I took it early, only to lose it at the very last room where the boss fight was. All my loot sucked, and I couldn't even redo it because I didn't have coins (that I didn't know I would need). I'm pretty sure I would've written a ticket to Steam support if I had a melee character that couldn't ascend lol.

Now, not a single one of these things would be a game-breaker, but when everything is added together the gameplay loop doesn't feel fun and rewarding, it just feels like I'm travelling in the campaign till I get stuck on the next boss fight where I die to something due to lack of visual clarity right before I finish the fight, and have to spend most of my gameplay time redoing the entire boss fight. I'm trying to give the game a fair chance, but I'm honestly not sure I'll make it through to maps.

Path of Exile 2 is a game that brilliantly excels in mechanics but also mercilessly consumes your time and sanity. It’s an ARPG masterpiece with some of the best gameplay mechanics ever designed, yet at the same time, it’s an addictive black hole that can seriously mess with your life—even if you’re a responsible adult with a job and a family.

There’s no denying that Path of Exile 2 is incredibly fun. The combat feels fluid, the skill customization is deep, and the build diversity is nearly limitless. Every small progression in your character feels rewarding, and the feeling of melting through enemies with a well-crafted build is peak dopamine.

The sheer complexity and depth of the game are unmatched in the ARPG genre. Whether it’s the passive skill tree, item crafting, or endgame bosses, everything feels meticulously designed to give you a sense of mastery—if you can put in the hours to figure it all out.

This game, however, does not respect your time. I’ve sunk 230+ hours in two and a half months, and I’m still struggling in the endgame. Why? Because Path of Exile 2 doesn’t just require skill, it requires an absurd amount of time and grinding.

If you don’t have hours every single day to farm, trade, and optimize your build, you’re left behind. The in-game economy is brutal, and the reliance on trading/crafting forces you into a tedious grind just to stay competitive. As someone with a life, a family, and a job, I simply can’t afford to treat this like a full-time commitment—yet that’s what it feels like the game expects.

And here’s the worst part: It’s so addictive that it actually starts harming your life. I’m a grown man, and yet I’ve found myself obsessing over min-maxing, farming currency, and planning builds when I should be doing, you know, actual life stuff. The game pulls you in so deep that it becomes hard to stop—even when you’re exhausted. It’s one thing for a game to be immersive, but Path of Exile 2 feels engineered to be an all-consuming addiction, and that’s genuinely concerning.

Path of Exile 2 is an incredible game, but it’s also a dangerous one. If you have unlimited time to play, you’ll love it. If you don’t, you’ll constantly feel like you’re falling behind while still being hooked. I love the mechanics, but I hate how much it demands from me.
This will be a great game with some time, but if you are looking for a complete experience, give it a few months before you dive in.

Well, it’s definitely not the worst game I’ve ever played, but several design choices make me dislike it overall. Let’s start with the good parts:

- I really enjoyed Act 1 and Act 2. They were fun, had a good sense of progression, and kept me engaged.
- I liked that your build isn’t tied to your gear the way it was in PoE1. That’s a solid improvement.
- Ascent to Power is well-designed and looks like it will be fun to replay.

Now, let’s talk about what I disliked:

- The locations in Act 3 are significantly larger, which makes them feel tedious and frustrating to complete. The mechanics that reset these areas don’t help—they just make the experience more annoying.
- Progression in Act 3 slows down dramatically. You don’t get many useful items, skill gems, or other upgrades. I ended up finishing the act with the gear I got in Act 2 because nothing better dropped.
- The Trial of Chaos is a mess. You’re forced to push through with ridiculous debuffs, only to face a boss at the end with one-shot mechanics. If you fail, you have to redo everything from the start. I can’t even imagine how frustrating it will be at the 10th floor—it already feels absurd.
- Some bosses feel poorly balanced. Take Mektul the Forgemaster, for example—if you don’t have enough DPS, you simply can’t kill him. Defensive builds are basically doomed against this boss.
- The auction system is terrible. Is it really that hard to implement an auction house like in WoW or Throne and Liberty? The current system feels outdated and clunky.
- The build flexibility isn’t as great as the developers claim. Skill modifications are mostly just minor stat boosts. The most unique mechanics you’ll find are things like ricochet or split-shot effects, and that’s it. Compare this to Diablo 4, where Necromancers can make their blood wave reflect off their summons for extra damage. That kind of enhancement is both visually satisfying and mechanically interesting—something PoE2 desperately needs.
- Speaking of builds, the way you have to force certain synergies is frustrating. For example, converting Frenzy Charges into Power Charges just so you can trigger a skill that requires them is not flexibility—it’s a clumsy workaround. The Monk’s access to Power Charges is especially bad.
- There are other issues—like enemies pushing you around, excessive one-shot mechanics, and slow character movements—but despite all that, the game was still enjoyable at first. However, once Act 3 started, the fun completely disappeared for me. I couldn’t find a single enjoyable aspect after that. I really hope Act 4 will be better.

Overall, I can’t recommend this game in its current state. For a new title, it still relies on outdated mechanics (like the auction trading system, which feels like it’s from the early days of online gaming) and makes questionable design choices that don’t improve the experience. That said, I hope these issues will be addressed so that I can eventually recommend it.

I'm afraid that after spending 80 hours into the game I simply can not recommend it. And don't get me wrong the game feels good when you play the campaign but after that it becomes and unbelievable frustrating grind fest. And before you say "but hey this is an ARPG so you should expect it to be grindy" let me assure you that I'm fully aware what type of game this is as I have spend countless hours in POE1, diablo 2-4 and last epoch.

The problem here is not with the "grindiness" of the game itself but rather with how frustrating and random the whole endgame feels. Everything starting from the type of map you are going to run, through the mechanic you may encounter in it ending with the entire crafting system has been for some reason randomised. The whole atlas tree that was previously one of the biggest selling point to me as it was giving you an option to choose which mechanic (or perhaps a combination of different ones) you are going to engage with has now been reduced to a handful of points that does not seem to be too relevant but still require you to clear 10 maps only to get 2 of those. And while I can somewhat understand simplification of the actual skill tree I don't really understand the change behind atlas tree as despite it being quite massive it was a very simple and straight forward concept. You complete the maps and you get the points. You like certain activities in the game, you boost those and engage with them on the map of your choice. But now you instead go into a random map (and we will get to some separate issues with that in a moment) and in order do the content that is fun for you to play you need to find some towers where you can put an item that you may or may not find so that few randomly selected maps on the atlas could be enhanced with it. That simply does not seem like a fun way to progress my character.

Speaking of game design and character progression for different builds I started POE2 as a melee warrior only to very soon realised how stupid decision that was. Because not only every single boss fight turned out to be a "rolling fiesta" with me having to press space bar constantly (even despite my character being technically a tanky one) because the game for whatever reason seem to be now taking inspirations from souls-like games. Which wouldn't be that big of a deal if not for the fact that while I was struggling to find a window when I can walk up to a boss and hit it at the same time range characters were melting those bosses fairly easily from a distance. But what made me quit playing melee and was one of the main reasons why I'm going to quit the game entirely was the mechanic called "Trial of Sekhemas" which is the most frustrating and tidious thing to engage with if you play mele and god forbid a tank. Because imagine that you are building a character designed to be able to take a hit and survive a lot but then you are being put in a long lasting set of mini challanges where you have to avoid being hit by either rande/aoe spamming mobs, range/aoe spamming bosses or you need to go through range/aoe traps. And while this is not a new concept as it was already present in POE1 it was something you may or may not engage with depends on your preferences. But in POE2 for god knows what reason it was made mandatory in order to get your ascendancy points which are vital to your character progression. 

So then I moved to playing a Witch and oh boy it was a night and day when it comes to bossing and early trial of Sekhemas (the cruel version is still absolutely abysmal and should be stripped from the mandatory progression). But what I discovered while playing less tanky mage is the great design of mobs in POE2 which greatest desire is to body block you as soon as possible and make sure that you will not be able to move or cast a spell (as they will be hitting you with a very high speed cancelling your every cast). Even with 30% movement speed half of the mobs can either outrun me (hasted ones will basically hug you and punch to death no matter what you do and how you position yourself) and on top of that there is amazingly high number of mobs that can jump on you, teleport to you, rush on you and what makes all of that even more fun they can actually push you as well. Which makes it so that every single object on the map (including  small objects that you can destroy) becomes a potentially deadly obstacle that you need to be aware of while moving or rolling.

And this is where running "random maps" makes it even more annoying to deal with because most of the time I'm forced to run through a very narrow labyrinth or cave with mobs running at me from every possible direction and nowhere to run. And god forbid I will attempt to make a ritual that spawned on that type of map with a number of additional terrain fragments making it almost impossible to move inside of it.

So all in all if you want to play play through the campaign I guess that will be rather positive experience but this is not a game you play to beat the campaign (its not Elden ring despite it becoming more and more similar to it in certain aspects) but rather to get to the endgame and work on your character progression. But instead of meaningful choices and enjoyable experience you will find yourself at mercy of RNG gods. Which you can trust me when I tell you do not belong to the most merciful ones.....

Mechanically it's fine, but I don't find myself overly engaged in continuing. I'll mindlessly play for a bit but the moments of satisfaction are few and far between. I'm also incredibly tired of the same tired repeating aesthetics of ARPGs...

Act 1: Gothic inspired inspired European-style setting (or Act 1 in Diablo 2)
Act 2: Hey, it's a desert - just like Egypt (or Act 2 in Diablo 2)
Act 3: Rainforest/jungle - just like the Aztecs/Mayans (or Act 3 in Diablo 2)
and so on...

It's boring and predictable, I also just really don't find the setting of Act 2 or 3 nearly as engaging and it feels like a tedious slog - but that's personal preference.

If you're really into the genre or just loved PoE, it's probably worth trying for the price. But I don't really find anything making me want to keep playing. Maybe the endgame content once it's out of early access will be really good, but I shouldn't have to slog through a boring grind of a story I don't care about in a world that doesn't appeal to me just to get to the "good" stuff. I've got better things to do.

The game an appealing premise, unfortunately, its execution is full of tedious mechanics, lackluster storytelling, and baffling design choices.

One of the biggest frustrations with Age of Water is the sheer amount of unnecessary back-and-forth sailing between the same two points for the same mission. It feels like an artificial way to pad gameplay time rather than offering genuinely engaging content. There’s a fine line between creating an immersive world and wasting the player’s time—this game leans heavily into the latter.

The game does an abysmal job of explaining its HUD elements. There’s no built-in tutorial or guide to decipher what each part of the interface means, leaving players to either experiment blindly or scour forums for answers. The lack of accessible explanations extends to part stats as well—you have to build an item (which consumes a ridiculous amount of resources), install it on your ship, and then drive out into open waters just to hover over its icon and see its stats. This is an inexcusable design flaw that turns what should be simple decision-making into an annoying trial-and-error process.

The writing is borderline embarrassing. It feels as if it was written by someone terrified of including anything even remotely engaging or controversial. The result? A dull, flavorless narrative that does nothing to enhance the experience. Good storytelling is supposed to make a game’s world feel alive—this one feels lifeless and uninspired.

Another major pain point is the inability to preview how an item will fit on your ship. Instead, you’re forced to use a clunky build mode window where you can maybe see the width and length squares, and then you have to count them manually. A simple preview function would solve this problem, but instead, the game leaves players frustrated, hoping they didn’t just waste valuable resources on a part that won’t fit.

Basic inventory management  is a mess. You can’t break down items directly from your warehouse. Instead, you need to manually load them onto your ship, set sail and then break them down, adding another unnecessary layer of tedium. And if you’re hoping to compare stats between two items of the same type? Good luck. The game doesn’t offer an easy way to do this, forcing players to constantly switch between menus just to see minor differences.

A fake multiplayer experience. Yes, technically you can party or group up with your friends. But you can't do missions together (unless you start the same mission at the same time with someone. You can't trade items with one another. You're just in a lobby and can see them sail around. There is no aspect whatsoever of a co-op experience. This completely defeats the purpose of multiplayer functionality and makes the feature feel hollow and pointless.

Missions frequently get bugged, preventing players from turning them in and leaving them completely stuck. This can be a game-breaking issue that halts progress entirely. However, the developers are actively working on fixing these problems.

The online servers are terrible, with constant latency issues. I frequently get ping warnings despite having a 1GB Up/Down connection. The connection problems are so severe that it feels like the servers must be located in Antarctica. This makes the online experience even more frustrating and unreliable.

This Game Was Not Ready to Leave Early Access. It feels like it wasn’t properly playtested, as the simplest oversights—many of which greatly hinder the overall experience—should have been caught and fixed before release. The game is riddled with issues that make it feel unfinished and frustrating rather than polished and enjoyable.

The game has potential, but it’s currently bogged down by frustrating mechanics, poor UI design, and uninspired writing. The tedious sailing, lack of useful in-game information, and infuriating inventory management make it a chore to play rather than an adventure to enjoy. Unless major improvements are made, this is one is best avoided.

Like a Kevin Costner fever-dream, you'll find yourself acting as a postman in a water-world. And hoarding resources... sweet, sweet resources.

The boat-builder gives you full-freedom to arrange things above-deck, while the hulls- which are less configurable- provide most of your baseline stats. The differences between a tugboat and speedboat feel properly immense.

I do wish the placement of things on deck mattered more, because installed weapons are able to shoot through other items placed on deck. Expect an arcade-style approach to gameplay, rather than being anything like a simulator.

PvE is the heart of the game. The questlines do their job of pulling you through dangerous places instead of meandering aimlessly. It seems like the variety of weapons available could be more useful, because - other than lack of resources - there's hardly any reason to craft lower-level weapons, nor weapons different from the ones you're using... I suppose cannons and machine-guns are classic weapons for a reason.

I feel there's definitely enough fun and content in the existing questlines to justify its price tag, while more content & fixes continue to be added.

Начну с того, что игра достаточно кривовата. Её явно делала очень маленькая команда разработчиков с очень скромным бюджетом. Часто встречаются баги, камера очень странно себя ведёт, управление крайне неотзывчиво. В одной сцене я погиб во время эффекта замедления времени и после загрузки с контрольной точки героиня продолжила двигаться очень медленно. Хорошо, что через пару минут это прошло. Также игра крайне короткая. Я не самый быстрый в мире геймер, но на прохождение у меня ушло меньше 100 минут. В прочем, чего стоило ожидать за 42 рубля в стиме. 
Что касается геймплея, здесь всё несколько интереснее. Игра сочетает в себе несколько жанров: платформер, головоломка и бродилка от первого лица. Лучше всего, на мой взгляд, реализованы головоломки. Не то чтобы они очень интересные, просто на фоне остальных элементов смотрятся неплохо. В целом, паззлы очевидные, понятно, что делать. Иногда их портит выше упомянутая кривость, из-за которой триггер может не сработать и начнутся проблемы. Платформер сделан достаточно странно. Героиня плохо чувствуется, глубина также плохо ощущается, да и вызова в них никакого нет. Как будто просто решили потянуть время. Бродилка же является худшей частью данной игры. Персонаж ходит очень медленно, действия, которые нужно предпринять для продвижения дальше неочевидны. Ну и по классике главная героиня ничего не может сделать бабайке, от неё нужно просто отворачиваться, как от слэндермена. Это, кстати, тоже работает криво через раз. Ещё у главной героини есть какие-то непонятные мистические силы, но они в геймплее представлены только QTE. 
Ещё в игре есть какой-то сюжет, но он подаётся через записки, поэтому я его не понял.

The description is a little vague so to succinctly reiterate, this is not a game. It is neither a tool nor a toy. Interactivity and reactivity is nil. One chinese reviewer described it as a wallpaper, which fits honestly.

Upon first launch you will be asked who to bless and your wish. You cannot change these later nor can you view the wish. You get the one and that's it which was a bit disappointing to me as I assumed "wishes" were actually singular tasks you set which you could focus on while enjoying the atmosphere of the program then you could report back to the dog with your success and be allowed to enter another one. But no, this isn't exactly like whispering into the hollow of a tree.

As time progresses in the program, the dog will provide text "guidance." This will be some nonsense. Not mindfulness nonsense, not even machine translated nonsense, just nonsense. You can hotswap languages from the settings and nothing the dog ever said made sense in any language I could understand. Elsewhere, the devs say that these things must be read with your heart. Well, my heart doesn't know why the weather is good and if my mom can turn on the oven either.

It's difficult to tell if this was some kind of jaded cash grab shovelware thing. This was crowdfunded but it's something you could whip up in UE in less than a day barring the art and music assets. It actually feels like it took a great deal of restraint not to add anything useful, like, say, a nonintrusive session timer, task based wishes, any kind of animation or alternate art of the dog in the center, better environmental stars that aren't one pixel dust particles rendered invisible by most of the color palettes, a better method of seeing the art you've acquired like a stamp book instead of the fiddly TV you get no direction on how to use, etc.

I'm recommending this despite everything I've typed because sometimes it's nice to have something just take over my entire monitor and distract me from the distractions. I do find the little dog art you unlock to be cute and the music is nice. If you have steam overlay activated, you can set a timer using that though it's a bit disruptive when it goes off. There's probably an infinite amount of better "relax" applications out there but here we are. Look at that dog.

As a remote play together game, this was incredibly fun for me. 

[h1]The Pros:[/h1]
(+) It’s wacky, chaotic, and everything I didn’t know I needed. Think: goblins, power-ups, and general mayhem wrapped in pixelated chaos.
(+) Remote Play Together? Works like a charm. No glitches, no lag, just pure fun with friends who can't dodge to save their lives (literally).
(+) Graphics are actually solid, if you can spare enough time between the chaos to notice.
(+) Progression overload. Store, crystals, characters, you name it. You’ll be swimming in unlocks, and it feels like a never-ending hill. But this could be a bad thing depending on which side of the hill you start rolling the snowball.
(+) The game strikes a balance between competitive but friendly. You can laugh at your friend’s failings, get more points, and still feel like you’re progressing with the help of the team. That’s a win, win, win as Michael Scott would say.
(+) see the mids, below.

[h1]The Mids:[/h1]
(+/-) The pickups are interesting but lack the 'wow' factor. They don’t exactly make me shout, 'Wow, I need this!' More like, 'Eh, I guess that’s fine.'
(+/-) Character upgrades tied to leveling are okay, but I’d love more base stats or upgrades thrown into rooms/crates for variety.
(+/-) The game is like a friend who almost makes sense. On the one hand, enemies are color-coded so you know who can hit what (nice!). On the other, I have no idea what the heck I’m buying with these crystals. 'Teleporter?' Sure, but to where? Mars? Another room? The mystery is real.
(+/-) Room rewards were a bit 'meh'. We fought mini-bosses/event rooms and got power-ups like '+0.25 range'... barely enough to tickle goblins from a distance. I was hoping for more zany or powerful upgrades. Maybe they get better the farther you go, but we didn’t make it that far yet to confirm.

[h1]The Cons:[/h1]
(-) The first boss is like trying to solo a raid. My friends kept dying, so soloing the boss was brutal.
(-) No in-game resolution settings. I play on an ultrawide (5120x1440), and adjusting for Remote Play Together was an adventure. There's no easy way to set custom resolutions,
(-) Reloading takes approximately forreeeeevvvverrrr. You’ve got the Sheriff with 6 bullets, and it feels like you’re waiting for your whole life to pass by before you can shoot again. Compared to the Businesswoman’s 30 bullets, it’s tragic.
(-) see the mids, above.

[h1]Overall:[/h1]
If you love wacky chaos and don’t mind a few rough edges, this game will keep you and your friends having a great time... just don’t play solo unless you’re a glutton for punishment. That being said, if you need a friend(s) to play with, feel free to find me (:

Starlight Legacy – A Timeless JRPG Adventure

Starlight Legacy is a masterfully crafted turn-based RPG that blends nostalgic 16-bit aesthetics with modern mechanics, offering a deeply engaging experience for both classic JRPG fans and newcomers. Developed with inspiration from genre-defining titles, it delivers a heartfelt journey filled with adventure, mystery, and strategic battles.

Gameplay & Mechanics
The game follows Ignus, Frida, and Teryl—three warriors tasked with retrieving relics to restore the Eternity Tree. Unlike traditional RPGs with a fixed progression, Starlight Legacy embraces non-linear exploration, allowing players to forge their own path. As more relics are collected, the world dynamically adjusts in difficulty, ensuring a balanced and evolving challenge.

Combat is accessible yet deep, offering intuitive turn-based battles with customizable control schemes. Players can strategically use items like rafts and magic carpets to unlock new areas, making backtracking rewarding rather than tedious.

Story & World-Building
The narrative is straightforward yet rich, with each province designed to reflect its own culture, history, and secrets. While the main quest is clear-cut, deeper lore and character interactions add layers of immersion. NPCs provide meaningful dialogue, and hidden treasures reward exploration.

Visuals & Soundtrack
The pixel art style is vibrant, bringing life to diverse environments with stunning detail. Each location feels unique, enhanced by a dynamic soundtrack that perfectly captures the mood—whether it’s serene exploration or high-stakes battles.

Final Verdict
Starlight Legacy successfully modernizes the classic JRPG formula while maintaining the nostalgic charm of its inspirations. Its engaging world, well-designed mechanics, and rewarding exploration make it a must-play for fans of the genre.

[i]Will It Steam Deck? Yes![/i]

As a massive SaGa fan, “non-linear” is a word that immediately grabs me. The turn-based, retro-inspired JRPG [i]Starlight Legacy[/i] delivers on this promise, allowing you to tackle its four main regions in any order. But the impact of it all is unfortunately a bit superficial and disappointing. With a weak, predictable narrative, a short runtime, and little replay incentive, [i]Starlight Legacy[/i] struggles to leave a lasting impression.

[h3]What I Liked[/h3]

[b]Aesthetics: [/b] Visually, [i]Starlight Legacy[/i] blends its inspiration between early Pokemon and Final Fantasy games, accompanied by a catchy, era-appropriate soundtrack. While there are no monsters to tame or trainers to fight, the seamless world with no loading screens, a la the Game Boy Pokemon titles, makes the Evaria Kingdom feel structurally adjacent to the famed Kanto region. The pixel art is solid, though it often feels derivative rather than distinctive (more on this later).

[b]Non-Linear Exploration And Design: [/b] While not particularly deep, the non-linear structure offers some engaging exploration. Each region also introduces a traversal upgrade, like a magic carpet for crossing obstacles on top of improved speed, while increasingly-complex locked chests (that unlock as additional zones are cleared) scattered about the world provide incentive to return periodically.

The high encounter rate and frequent grinding could be frustrating, but adjustable settings - like EXP modifiers and encounter toggles - will help mitigate this should you so choose. Enemies and bosses also scale with story progress, which helps keep up some semblance of challenge during most of the journey.

[h3]What I Disliked[/h3]

[b]Copy-Paste Everywhere: [/b] There is a clear lack of variety across the board. Interiors of shops and homes are almost completely identical to one another, the majority of equipment lack any textual nuance, with mere “super” and “hyper” affixes separating each tier. Similarly, enemies have a limited sprite pool, usually marked with X-Y-Z variants, and often only feature subtle visual differences from their weaker counterparts.

These bland differences unfortunately extend to the player’s party of three, with only some subtle stat differences that can easily be offset by gearing them accordingly. Each party member will eventually have access to pretty much everything the others do, eliminating any real differences or depth beyond their outward appearance. 

The copy-paste formula extends to region-specific quests also, as each one has their own struggles based on the fallout of a main plot point. While not inherently an issue, the lack of compelling characters supporting it (and really no side content at all) makes each zone, despite visual differences, feel a bit samey.

[b]Status Effects: [/b] Almost every ability and element type has an associated status effect. Although none of these are truly bothersome, virtually all of them persist through combat which requires a lot of unnecessary menu navigation to cure without any form of “quick heal” option from the main menu. 

[b]Length: [/b] With 19/21 achievements completed and no EXP modifiers, I finished the game in under seven hours - far too short for the price tag, especially when there’s very little incentive from both a narrative and gameplay standpoint to warrant multiple playthroughs. Length is almost never a critique of mine…but it’s hard not to without some part of the experience truly excelling.

[h3]Consider Buying This If…[/h3]

You're simply out of retro-inspired, turn-based JRPGs to play and don’t mind a short experience with very little replay value. Similarly priced games, like Ara Fell, Rise of the Third Power, Shadows of Adam, and even some KEMCO RPGs offer far more compelling narratives and mechanics despite the lack of non-linear exploration. With updates, additional polish, and/or a deep discount, [i]Starlight Legacy[/i] might be easier to recommend.

You can also rotate the shards, then go hunting their place, which gets easier as the puzzle progresses.
Its unfair to compare it to Glass Masquerade, as there are not the themes or the music, but the puzzles are certainly pretty enough in their own right and you get a wide variety of puzzles to choose from. When you exit, you save your place and you can either go back to the puzzle you were doing or start a new one. Its definitely easier to leave this game!

A great piece of software which makes rendering out seamlessly looping audio for your game development so much easier. If you have a piece of music without clearly set loop points, VGMP's search algorithm will find loopable areas in the music for you, which you can test out by listening to the loop areas it has discovered. You can then choose to export the loop information, or render out the intro, loop area and outro as separate files. 
The loop points it finds aren't all very accurate, but for the most part it does a stellar job. 
Highly recommended if you have a large library of purchased or free licensed music you would like to use in your games, but have not been set up for looping playback.

I would say it's worth supporting the developer: with much better visual design, the solid ideas behind this game could make for a very compelling sequel.
