I'm not going to give this game a negative review because the hours I’ve played have been really enjoyable. However, the further you progress, the buggier the game becomes.

Not only that, but the in-game economy is unbalanced. Building a huge house that takes 8+ hours to fully construct and decorate earns less profit than building a small house. It makes no sense. It completely takes away the incentive to go big. You’d expect that higher-value land and larger properties would yield more money, but that’s not the case. The auction cost is much higher, meaning you only make around 80-100k max on a full day’s build, whereas a small build with less cost and less effort nets you 100k plus and can be completed three times over in the same timeframe. It’s really a deal-breaker for us.

On top of that, the more you play, the more you realize that the furniture is way out of proportion, and some assets make no sense. The way fencing and garden paths are placed is terrible, and you can’t decorate or add flooring to your office. You can place items in it, but you can’t paint or floor it, which is disappointing. The game had potential.

They are borderline taking things too far with how detailed some job mechanics are, laying brick by brick and everything else, but honestly, that’s part of what makes the reward loop so satisfying. It takes time, and I like that aspect.

That said, I’d say this game would be extremely boring solo, especially if you’ve just built a massive house only to make next to nothing in return. We’re pretty much at the endgame with no more drive to continue. So for me, I’ve put the game down. It is great fun with friends, especially at the start, but once you’ve made a million and bought some good land, it starts to feel pointless to carry on.

The game has a strong foundation with its in-depth building system, but there are several areas that could use improvement. The inability to merge floors makes designing multi-story homes frustrating, as each tile is treated as a separate room, requiring individual painting and decoration. A more advanced building planner would help streamline the process, allowing for seamless floor transitions and better customization.

Character customization is also lacking, particularly in terms of female representation. My partner feels a bit neglected by the lack of female voices, as the current options all sound male. Adding proper female voice choices and businesswear for women would make the game more inclusive and enjoyable for female players. Additionally, there is a bug preventing players from placing wall-mounted items like paintings and shelves in office spaces, making them feel barren. Fixing this issue would help improve decoration options and allow for more detailed interior designs.

House flipping and building from scratch should also be more rewarding. The time, effort, and cost of constructing a house don’t currently justify the final payout, making it feel disappointing. In contrast, demolishing houses is a much faster and more profitable way to earn money, which discourages players from engaging in the more creative aspects of the game. Increasing the financial reward for building and flipping homes would balance this and make the experience more satisfying.

Despite these issues, the game shows great potential, and refining these mechanics would elevate the experience, making home design more creative and enjoyable.

The one thing that bothered me the most was the Ubisoft overlay on the game screen, the (Press Shift + F2) overlay was covering my game credits, and when opening the main overlay I couldn't get rid of it.
Well, Problem solved !.... Do the following easy fix ......

For starters, all links and stuff for daily challenges and to collect your rewards etc is on the Ubisoft overlay.
These links and rewards and daily challenges can be accessed through the Ubisoft launcher that launches the game.

We can turn off the in game Ubisoft overlay, removing the problems it causes, and just get your bonuses and stuff through the Ubisoft launcher later, or alt+tab in and out of the launcher and game.

To disable the overlay....
1. Open the 'Ubisoft Connect' launcher.
2. Click on your profile (top left corner).
3. Click on 'Settings.
4. Click on 'Interface'. 2nd icon down on the top left (looks like a PC screen).
5. UNTICK the box that says 'Enable in-game overlay for supported games'.

That's it, done.
When you launch the game again it will say overlays are disabled and may effect the game, and advises you not to continue, click ok (A) to continue anyway.

The game will now launch without the Ubisoft overlay screwing everything up.
Enjoy, Cheers.

I'd like to start my review by pointing out that it is NOT geared towards casuals, people who are going to play races once or twice, do some free roaming then never touch the game again, as they'll most likely not care about the majority of the issues i'll be pointing out later on, as they're only apparent if you're someone who'll be playing this on a regular basis for months to come. (It is a live service game after all.)

Now that that's out of the way, did you ever hear the phrase "It gets better after *insert an arbitrary number here* hours of gameplay"?
In the case of The Crew Motorfest; it gets better after at least 200h of grind (i'd honestly say more like 400-500h but i'm trying to keep this somewhat believable to you), and that's not meant as a joke, i wish it was but unfortunately it is the sad reality of the game as it stands right now..

Lets start with some positives:

+ Free roaming here is possibly one of the best experiences in a racing game period, especially with randoms (unfortunately, the online part is completely broken and only works like 20% of the time, more on that later), this is the first racing game that made me fall in love with endlessly cruising around its map for hours on end, never getting bored, always finding new stuff to explore, an easy 8/10 in this aspect.

+ A great selection of various types of vehicles, decently modeled & handle differently enough from each other. (there are currently 751 vehicles, not all of them are unique with multiple being repeats, so more like 500ish)

+ The graphics are beautiful, even stunning at times, a huge improvement over TC2.

+ A bigger & better selection of songs compared to the previous game. (still not that great or memorable though)

+ The playlists (a set of around 8 races with different vehicles set under a united theme, mini-events if you'd like) are very fun to play, there are way too few of them though.. more of that please!

+ The devs were kind enough to allow people to import their cars & vanities (aka under-glows, special tires, boosts.. etc) from the previous game, a big ++ considering the grind i mentioned earlier could easily triple had you been forced to re-earn everything again.

+ The gameplay itself is very fun & addictive, the handling is also vastly improved over TC2.

+ One of the best maps i've ever experienced in a racing game period, although it is way smaller than the previous one it's much more dense & fun to explore.

+ Very extensive car tuning, great car customization for the most part, countless gameplay sliders & assists to play with.

The meh:

+ They added a new weekly car show where you customize your own vehicle & compete against others, this is the first game that made me give a damn about creating cool looking cars and showing them off so it's a major ++, but i'm putting it here because it's ruined by a group of losers who team up each week to mass vote for each other so they ruined the whole thing for everyone pretty much since launch, and yet IVT doesn't seem to give a damn, oh well 🤷‍♂️

The Bad:

- Cars are extremely expensive here, it can & will take you days if not longer to get a "single" expensive hyper car, i have 484h in TC2, and 367h in this one, 851h combined! and i've yet to own all buyable vehicles, let that sink in. (They also made races pay less money & removed the dynamic discounts you used to get in TC2)

- To be competitive you need full sets of parts that give you various advantages ranging from outright doubling your score in Summits (weekly end-game content) to giving you 50% more NOS (along with other bonuses), this system sucks, and is why you need to waste hundreds of hours for the game to get good, this along with getting vehicles are the one major hurdle you need to get over before you can start to actually have fun.

There are 15 disciplines in this game, and there are 6-7 types of gold sets you need for each of them, they made gold drops a lot rarer here compared to TC2, so now to get these sets the optimal way you pretty much NEED to farm a single 1-2min race for close to 200h non stop, and it's all luck based, it could easily take you more than that, let that sink in too..

- Summits are the end-game content you'll pretty much be doing week after week, in TC2, you needed to be top 4k on PC, top 11k on PlayStation & top 8k(?) on Xbox to get the highest rewards, here they combined all platforms & reduced the number from a combined ~23k people to a meager 10k, they took away over half, and for what? to give less free vanities & encourage more spending? making what was already a massive sweat-fest an even sweatier pile of shit? (and just to be clear, i haven't missed a single plat ever since i started competing in both games, so save your "git gud")

- In a game that has the word "crew" in its title, you'd expect to be able to play with others, oh you sweet summer child, that was the previous game, we don't do that here. joining races with others only works like a 1/3 of the time, randoms will constantly disappear a few minutes after you see them, sometimes you won't even see any for days, what a joke of a game!

Head my warning, IF YOU'RE BUYING THIS TO PLAY WITH FRIENDS THEN DON'T EVEN BOTHER, IT DOES NOT WORK MOST OF THE TIME AND THE DEVS DON'T GIVE A FUCK!

- Way too many disconnects, scrapping parts too fast? disconnect! randomly changing liveries? DC! switching too many affixes? DC! taking photos to finish challenges? DC! you get the point.

- Only 2! multiplayer modes, demolition royal (battleroyale with demo cars) that nobody plays and grand races (28 people races) which are very fun to play as long as you're fine with the toxic rammers you'll surely be facing almost every race (that's an issue with the racing community in general so i don't hold it against the game), after all those years, this is the best you can come up with? really?

- Bugs, bugs & even more bugs, the devs will literally push a patch overnight to fix any money glitches & then proceed to ignore well known game-breaking bugs for months if not longer..

- Very slow updates, meanwhile they'll happily flood you with countless overpriced vanities any chance they get, in a 70-120$ game..

- Very few races compared to the previous title (probably less than a 1/3, if even that), the solution they came up with? add a custom mode where you can replay older races with other types of vehicles, instantly inflating the number of races while doing 0 work, genius.. even worse, if you want any of the previous summit rewards you might've missed (including exclusive cars that are often better than the base model) you'll be forced to grind this "new" mode endlessly (it takes over 100h to finish them all btw).

- If you're here for motorcycles then forget it, unless you love being last they're not viable here.

- No real cross-play either (only in leaderboards).

- Terrible Ubisoft Connect overlay that gets stuck any time someone adds you or invites you to a crew. (after months i finally figured out a fix, disable & re-enable V-Sync and it'll go away.)

- The traffic AI is braindead, it's been broken ever since the last big update & they'll constantly go out of their way to ruin your day. (they even added them to feats in summits, making the "competitive mode" less about skill & more about RNG)

- Your AI assistant gets old & annoying way too fast.

There are more negatives about the game but i'm running out of space, sorry folks.


All in All, the core of the game IS good & extremely fun, but the rest of it is less of a game & more of a mindless/endless grind that only aims to waste your time & keep you playing long enough for them to trick you into wasting your hard earned money on all the flashy but pointless overpriced microtransactions. i really love this franchise, and will probably keep playing both games as i already invested way too much time and efforts into them, but for 70$ minimum this ain't it chief. 4/10, only worth it on a deep deep sale.

An absolutely wonderful remake of a classic game!  The quality of life improvements, class adjustments, graphics, and music make this something to behold.  As a long-time fan of the original (played on the GBC) I can tell you this is the kind of thing I want out of a remake.  It's true to the original, but wasn't afraid to shore up some mechanics.  10/10

After finishing the story, I can say I really enjoyed my time experiencing the story, enjoying the enhanced visuals. Loved the sound, voice acting, and music. The class variety is fair for one of the earlier DQ games, and I do like a lot of the added features that help with the direction of the game (Finding out where you need to go).

What I DID NOT like and I think needs some serious revamping is the difficulty. I played on Dragon Quest difficulty (Normal Difficulty) for a majority of the game. The game starts out easy (which it should), It was manageable for a large portion of the game, but about 80% of the way through the game, the difficulty just spirals ridiculously out of control and becomes overwhelmingly difficult. 

Unlike most other later DQ games where you get spell resistance by leveling up, DQ 3 does not have this. Gear that offers up resistances to spells is the ONLY way to get these bonuses and therefore are necessary to succeed in the late game. This really takes away from the variety of play. Without gear for fire/ice resistance, these spells do a whopping 200+ damage a hit. Considering most enemies get two attacks, that's two casts of Kacrackle or Kasizz from an enemy and you're dead.

There is an easier difficulty (Dracky Quest), but the ONLY difference between it and the normal difficulty is the inability to die on easy. (Enemies knock you down to 1 HP but cannot kill you). Difficulties need better balancing in regards to enemy health and damage. Your health, resistances, damage, etc.

I still recommend the game nonetheless, but it needs work.

I really wanted to like Dragon Quest 3 HD but the more I played it, the less I wound up having fun. Ultimately, it ends up being a poorly balanced game with a lot of weird design decisions which is a shame because I actually really enjoyed the story. The top offender was the job switching system. While a great idea, Metaphor did this really well, resetting experience was detrimental and set your character's progress back to 0 for little gain. This ended up making them under-leveled for the rest of the game and an extreme handicap unless you subject yourself to mindless grinding which was slow and at a point in the game where you can teleport to virtually everywhere, so random encounters drop significantly. Combat encounters also had a ridiculous amount of status effects in the later half of the game; it was comical especially when enemies were given sometimes 2-3 attacks per monster before you could get one in. It really was deflating when I was hunting treasure chests in a dungeon filled with mimics and the mimic combat encounter was just it spamming an insta-kill ability on every party member 2-3 times a turn. At the end of the day, the gameplay was the real offender here and made the game a lot less fun than it could've been; this coming from someone who had an absolute blast with FF1 Pixel Remaster. Luckily the story was simple but great, the visuals second to none, the voice acting and soundtrack great, and it really helped invigorate my curiosity for the rest of the series including the original release of 3 which I heard was better. Will definitely still check out the 1 and 2 remakes and play through the both of them.

First impressions & gameplay up to final wave: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ILBvIUPWE6Q

This game, in short, is fast-paced, addicting, and really quite good. The description of "smooth and expressive movement" is on point, and though you don't have a whole lot of offensive abilities (two guns and throwable daggers), their simplicity and versatility works well as you run circles and "kite" around the endless hordes of oncoming cacodemons. Eventually, you need to start using your explosive daggers as vertical movement tech (think rocket-jumping) to escape the cascade of enemy attacks thrust your way, alongside granting you access to the additional higher-up reload points around the map.

It's almost deceptively difficult - you start off thinking that the challenge is babycakes and then by the time you hit wave 8 or 9 you succumb to your first death and need to actually start strategizing. Every demon you kill drops a health pick-up, and you need to weave through the map and continually grab those while balancing not getting hit in the first place. You will get hit. The difficulty only ramps up as you go along, and my time at review includes getting up to the last wave but not yet having the stones to fully beat it (despite repeated attempts).

Each wave is sequential - that is to say, the creatures and their order aren't randomized, so you can try to adjust strategies dependent on the level. One of the things I appreciate is that, in every wave, you need to re-acquire gear - the first couple mobs you defeat will drop your second gun and additional daggers until you've maxed out. While this may seem a little frustrating, it really takes like 15 - 30 seconds and can "set the stage" for however the run is going. 

It feels good, looks good, sounds good, and it's worth the price of admission. Boomer shooters aren't generally my thing and I found this hard to put down. My only slight critique is that I think the slime damage scaling needs to be tuned down a bit - I think they're the only creatures with "splash" damage and it generally seemed out of line w/ other mobs - but maybe I'm just sour at them in particular. Really very good for a solo dev's first outing, looking forward to what's cooked up next!

I really like this game just to relax and drive for awhile collecting stuff and killing enemies. There's a surprising variety of things to find, and you can do a lot with them from sticking decorations (and useful things like containers) onto your car and they'll stick to it, to finding a little red button on most buildings that lets you take the whole thing with you as an item (including everything inside of it, which can also include containers full of items).

I actually like to call this little niche genre the [i]Longroam[/i], a mix of The Long Drive and this game's name. I would actually include games like Raft in this genre as well, since my criteria for it is just having a vehicle and traveling endlessly with it while doing stuff along the way, so it doesn't necessarily have to be a car or a road.

It does use the Synty assets, but it really tries to make an actual game using them that's fun and unique instead of just a lazy asset flip, which this game definitely isn't. There's a variety of biomes with unique NPCs to find (that can do various things for you), bosses to encounter, and different structures and decorations, and you even have a home area that appears every time the biome changes which saves everything in it.

Whereas The Long Drive is more of a "haha funni jankfest" game, Polyroam goes for more of an actual gameplay-oriented approach with actual mechanics such as actual inventories instead of janky physics-based items, and lots of fun stuff that I'd love to see in other games too like the ability to just take entire buildings with you as a single item. You can even keep entire spare cars as compressed items just like buildings, or use this to build up a big collection of vehicles just for the fun of it. There are upgrades, items that give you different boosts by keeping them in your hotbar, and a variety of weapons to use against the zombies you'll encounter as you go.

I've had a lot of fun looking for interesting buildings to carry along and decorate with the tons of different items I've found and just driving along while listening to the custom radio channels, and the game is definitely worth the asking price in my experience.

44 The Jail is an interesting narrative-driven adventure game with its pros and cons. It has inventory items and dialog trees but essentially no puzzles, at least until the last chapter. Mostly we just need to figure out where to go next or which NPC to talk to. We do a bit of exploration, participate in some simple activities and engage in dialogs with NPCs, where we can make some small changes to how the story unfolds or select a backstory we like for a character. Which I think works great because this kind of simple gameplay can be very immersive, giving us the feeling of participation in the story.

The game has a very small number of locations, and the location design is quite simple, but the graphics, animations and lighting effects are pretty good for a pixel art game. Large detailed sprites give more personality to the characters.

A game of this kind can be rushed through in a very short time, but, for a normal playthrough, the 2 hours of playtime mentioned on the store page is certainly an underestimate.

There are some instances where the event-driven gameplay could have been implemented a little better so as to give the player an indication of what the next objective is or to make it clearer whether or not there are some optional objectives left.

The last chapter suddenly introduces some very contrived puzzles, very unnecessary pop culture references and in-jokes and quite a few objects which I wasn't able to do anything with. At the same time, I was carrying too many items which turned out to have no use. It seems that too much stuff was made optional, with many easy-to-miss interactions. So it's possible that I missed some important connections, but I found most of the story implausible and the motivations for most of the characters' actions unconvincing.

The last thing I expected this morning was an Adventure Quest inspired by 8-bit Zelda and Simon's Quest, and for context, I have not touched anything from the developer in about 10 years (apparently it came out on NES a few years ago). I have some history with the series, I would play those games religiously back when Flash was around, many good laughs from just pure randomness in the narrative, and many nights of mindless grinding as well - as I understand you can still play them using their launcher, which I didn't even know was a thing until recently. I have this wonderful memory of finding some undead armor in the store and it wanted me to kill some things in the swamp, I don't remember exactly how long it took me but nobody else had it for like at least a month. That and I always loved running into new Zard species, the way it works, take a Zard, pick a random object like cheese, combine them, and you have a new enemy type.

I want to emphasize that this is a very basic and faithful retro game, it's not very modern or complex, you will be smashing things with 1 button, occasionally using a power-up like deflection or dog launcher. It's very much like the original Zelda, with the exception of platforming sections that reminded me of the early Castlevania gameplay. At first, the game may seem somewhat linear, but after about 90 minutes you will realize it has a limited open world, with a metroid-like progression. 

The story can be completed in 6 to 7 hours, give or take, it's not a very difficult game, but you can occasionally get lost if you not paying attention, and sometimes it's just not clear what you should do. Essentially you have this small open-world and you have to collect 13 power-ups, if I am not mistaken all of them had a dedicated area and a boss associated with them, or most of them at least. Overall the gameplay can get pretty stale which is expected with a retro-themed game, even though you get a bunch of power-ups, most of them will not change how you approach the combat, I pretty much only used the deflection and healing. Aside from the main story, there are a bunch of hidden rooms for health/capacity upgrades, as well as chests that give some gold. The gold itself only has very limited purpose, and the game does not have that signature loot collection for which Adventure Quest is known.

Obviously, the biggest thing here is the Adventure Quest jokes, and if you are a fan there are a lot of silly references which I enjoyed, however, I felt like a lot of the narrative was recycled from the other games, and it does not hit as hard without the flash animation. I did get some laughs out of the "bonus material", I love how the game comes with the manual book and the Pretendo Empower magazine.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) For the most part, I got this game for that Adventure Quest humor, and I got some laughs out of it, especially from the Manual and the Magazine. There are a lot of enjoyable references if you are familiar with the world, although the narrative felt too recycled, and it didn't bring much originality.

(+) After the first 90 minutes, the game becomes more of a metroidvania which I liked, and it can be somewhat thought-provoking with backtracking and figuring out where to go. The main problem I have is that most of the secrets were not very exciting, and I wish finding secrets was more rewarding than just getting more health or capacity.

(+) Other than that, I thought the game played decently and it had a good variety of biomes, as well as just recreating some of the familiar zones in 8-bit which I thought was hilarious.

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] Possible Improvements [/u] - you may want to put a checkpoint at the second pyramid before the double rocks, that is the only part of the game where I felt a bit frustrated with RNG on the insta kills. I felt like the hitbox for the destructible rocks was weird, sometimes you just can't hit them for some reason. You may want to highlight the dark caves and doors a bit better, maybe with a unique tile under them, I got stuck several times because I thought the path looked like a black background.

The game was freezing for me after exiting the magazine pages, showing I was stuck in the pause, and could not click anything. The Start did not work for me on the controller by default, and it would not work consistently in the game menu. 

Adding achievements would probably improve the exploration aspect.

[u] Some nitpick I have with overall experience [/u] - even though the game had a lot of hidden rooms and such, they were not rewarding because the gold had very niche purpose, and other secrets were health or capacity. Adventure Quest is known for loot, and you didn't give us much loot or different weapons if that makes sense, even if the game is simple, at least a few other melee weapons with unique range or speed would have improved it.

I get it's a simple game and it's fine to keep bosses primitive, but even the last boss was pretty limited, so I wish you gave them at least one more attack to force you to move.

[b] Overall Thoughts: 7/10 [/b]

It's not bad or anything, just a hard sell at $18, I personally have so many good memories associated with the series, I still got some enjoyment out of the references, and hey no tokens! As a faithful retro game it was solid, but not super impressive at the same time, it got a little stale in my opinion. I am a little surprised that the developer didn't put much effort into promoting the Steam version*, I would think that $18 release would justify a bit more energy. Hopefully they will make this version more appealing for those returning players so they have a reason to get it again.

The soundtrack is pretty nice and varied. There's some guitar, some synths and chiptune. One thing I picked up on is that some of the music sounds like old Minecraft music disk tracks which was cool to me. There's nothing that truly sticks out as amazing but it's certainly good music.

A good game with some slight complaints.

The cons:

1. It's a bit short. For five dollars, it's probably not a bad run-time. And technically, you can still go to endless mode and see how high of a wave you can conquer, but...it's a bit short. I'll lump in content with this as well; I've 100%'d the game in the amount of time it took to beat the game. Which is not always bad, but I wish I actually had to do something to actually 100% more than 5-6 grind-outs and an equal amount of pushing for the final level, which didn't even have a real boss. 
2. Procedural generated RNG heaven. It's not that bad here, but it is here. One map can be absolute prime turkey sandwiches for straight-shot turrets, others heavily dependent on the machine turrets for most of the map. It favors a particular setup, which is a barrack with some sort of explosive payload constantly dumping on it (your character, or a grenade turret), and clean-up turrets for everything that gets through. Yes, I get that it makes the game "unique on every run," but still. It's a bit annoying, when sometimes what you really need just...never shows up in the spinner.

The pros:
1. It has good music. Boppin' time.
2. Its fundamental gameplay loop is surprisingly good. You have to strike a balance between your income, your character's power, and tower placement/upgrades. It's a pretty good gameplay loop.
3. It's a nice pixelated game. I like the aesthetic, all the better if the game is actually fun to play.

I'd recommend this game, if you have the spare cash. It's a decent seven hours.

Overall I enjoy playing Orbius, its a decent game that you can sink a few hours to kill time. Not every run is the same despite the spell system being a bit limited at the moment. Spell system could be fleshed out more and enhanced. Looking forward what the future holds for Orbius.

[h1]A really fun and novel GBA game experience in the modern day.[/h1] 
Not without it's flaws but a stellar entry that would definitely have been considered one of the greats of it's time, if it came out back then. I gave it a 100% run and had pretty solid fun throughout, with only probably the last hour of it being a bit irritating.

[h2]What I like about it[/h2]
[list]
	[*] The art is really wonderful, it's a lot of big, chunky drill-dozer style sprites (or even Tak 2, which I maintain has nice art despite being a horrendous game).
	[*] The soundtrack is great and catchy, and you don't get tired of hearing it loop, which I think is essential for any platformer game. Both the GBA and the PC soundtracks are really nice.
	[*] The puzzles are fun and not too tricky, and the general atmosphere of the game is tons of fun. I love all of the dog jokes and puns throughout.
[/list]
  
[h2]Stuff I'm lukewarm on[/h2]
[list]
	[*] Sometimes you can feel like you are stuck, or notice a secret that you really want to get, that might be obtainable, but you're not sure about. The solution to this is almost always "come back later"; I think that's fine, but there should be a reminder early on in the game to go and find places with the little exclamation mark to go and do something new. I had some occasions where I'd get frustrated looking for something I just couldn't get at yet, and after I started going with the flow of the game and checking back for stuff which was marked, I had a much better time with the game.
	[*] To do with that, I found the map a bit frustrating. I think it's by and large a pretty solid map, but it scrolls infinitely and loops upon itself. I think this is cool in theory, but in practice it would kind of confuse me about where I was headed and which of the paths the area I was looking for was on. 
	[*] Spoilers: The side quest about [spoiler]Capturing all of the types of monsters[/spoiler] was fun, and I found it to be a pretty good trip throughout all of the worlds, however I really struggled to get all of them, because there were a few which were really unintuitive. [spoiler]The bouncy worms in particular, I had to go back to several times before it would glow that it could be captured and I was really confused as to whether there was a particular worm I needed to do it to, or if I was just doing it wrong. By the end of it, I really didn't have an answer one way or another on that. The Xenolith monster guys were cool, and I figured I would have to capture them, but it was a bit of a finicky and weird operation and I had to look it up to figure out how.[/spoiler]
[/list]

Altogether, it was a wonderful time through and I really enjoyed it. I am looking forward to whatever comes next and I will probably go back and give this game a run through again sometime.

Get to Work, A Grindset CEO's Memoir.

A game so immersive, so painstakingly detailed, that at times I found myself questioning whether I was still playing or simply living. The developers have truly outdone themselves in their ability to simulate the mundane grind of corporate existence, complete with soul-draining commutes, a relentless flood of emails, and the occasional existential crisis by the breakroom Keurig.

Gameplay
The mechanics are as complex as they are depressingly familiar. Players begin as a bright-eyed, hopeful new hire, eager to climb the corporate ladder, but starting as a lowly,unemployed, BALD man. You land the job but not the job you were hoping for, you spend your first few years in what seems to be an unrelenting torment, only to quickly realize that promotions are not awarded for innovation but for one’s ability to master the art of looking busy(and knowing people(fuck you Ted)). Clicking furiously between spreadsheets, responding to passive-aggressive emails, and attending meetings that could have been summarized in a three-sentence memo—it’s all here, and it’s hauntingly accurate.

The game’s difficulty ramps up exponentially, especially with the Middle Management level, where you gain new responsibilities but no additional resources to execute them. It’s here that you begin to master the delicate art of delegating without authority while perfecting the thousand-yard stare that signals both engagement and quiet desperation. You spend your days hurling yourself off metaphorical ramps, sprinting toward that ever-distant light at the end of the tunnel—a light that, upon closer inspection, is just the flickering glow of a malfunctioning office copier.

But it doesn’t stop there. Oh no, Get to Work is a game with levels so intricately designed that Dante himself would have thrown in the towel.

Senior Management: Congratulations! You’ve climbed the corporate ladder just high enough to experience both the expectations of leadership and the constraints of still having to answer to someone else. Your days are now consumed by endless strategy meetings, where buzzwords like synergy and scalability are used in place of actual solutions. You begin to realize that your true role is not to lead but to absorb blame—a human firewall between upper executives and the chaos below.

Executive Level: Welcome to the C-suite, where the game transforms into an anxiety simulator cleverly disguised as prestige. You’ve finally made it to the inner sanctum, only to discover that instead of freedom, you now have visibility—which is just a corporate euphemism for constant scrutiny. You no longer work in the business, you work on the business, which mostly consists of pretending to read reports while secretly Googling “how to appear visionary in meetings.” The light at the end of the tunnel? Turns out, it’s just the harsh LED glow of another last-minute investor call.

Final Boss: The CEO Throne: You’ve done it. You’ve reached the pinnacle. You sit upon the gilded chair of power… only to find that it’s more of a precarious balancing act than a throne. The game’s final twist? You are now the villain. Employees whisper about your extravagant bonuses while you stress over why the stock dipped 0.3% last quarter. Every decision is both crucial and meaningless, a paradox wrapped in an expense report. The only true way to win Get to Work is to exit gracefully—either through an overpriced consultant gig or the elusive Retirement DLC, which remains locked behind an insurmountable paywall. (just a joke but it would be nice to see)

Graphics & Sound
Visually, the game captures the washed-out fluorescent glow of the modern office perfectly. Every cubicle is an homage to monotony, every colleague’s face a portrait of thinly veiled despair. The sound design is equally impressive, from the soft hum of an overworked HVAC system to the soul-shattering “ping” of an incoming Slack message at 4:59 PM on a Friday.
Note: There is a Music audio slider but i think we had to cut staff for that to please the investors.

Realism
Perhaps the most frustratingly brilliant aspect of Get to Work is its uncanny realism. There’s the Annual Performance Review, in which you are given vague, conflicting feedback that somehow doesn’t align with the goals you were originally assigned. There’s the Mandatory Team-Building Retreat, a weekend getaway that no one enjoys but everyone pretends was “really productive.” And let’s not forget the Office Politics Mini-Game, where one wrong reply in the company group chat can determine whether you’re invited to the exclusive after-hours executive happy hour.

Final Verdict
As a CEO, I can’t help but respect the level of effort that went into this cruel, hyper-realistic experience. It’s a ruthless commentary on the modern workplace, and the developers clearly have a deep, borderline sadistic understanding of corporate culture.

Would I recommend it? Well, that depends. If you enjoy stress-induced hair loss and the thrill of watching your youthful optimism erode in real-time, then yes, Get to Work is the game for you. If, however, you value happiness, sanity, or a sense of personal fulfillment, you may want to consider alternative titles—perhaps Early Retirement Simulator or Win the Lottery 2: Powerball Edition.

Final Score: 10/10 in execution, 2/10 in morale boost. A masterpiece of capitalist despair.

The Frequency of Falls
The first time I experienced a fall in Get to Work, I brushed it off as a simple accident, something that would only happen occasionally. After all, accidents happen in real life, so it didn’t seem unreasonable for the game to include such a mechanic. But when the falls kept happening, I realized something was wrong. It wasn’t just an occasional slip-up—it felt like an inevitable event, something that was going to happen no matter what I did. Every level, every new challenge, I would inevitably end up falling in some way. It began to feel less like part of the game’s natural progression and more like an artificial, frustrating obstacle designed to impede my progress.

Each time I tried to recover, there was a sense of helplessness. The game didn’t offer any way to mitigate the falls or avoid them altogether. There wasn’t even a clear reason why they were happening. It often felt random, as though the game itself was determined to throw me off balance for no discernible purpose. I would try to strategize, plan my moves carefully, and avoid situations where a fall might happen, but it felt like I had no control. My hard work and careful attention to detail were constantly being undone by an issue I couldn’t predict or prevent.

The Psychological Toll
The constant falling also had a deeper psychological effect on my enjoyment of the game. As someone who values progression and accomplishment in gaming, the repeated failures created a sense of stagnation. Every time I made headway, I felt as though I had to start all over again after falling. Rather than feeling empowered and motivated, I began to dread the inevitable setbacks that I knew were coming. Instead of a feeling of accomplishment when overcoming obstacles, I was left with a sense of frustration and disappointment. The game stopped feeling like an adventure and started feeling like an exercise in futility.

It’s not just the falls themselves, but the way they interrupt the flow of gameplay. In a game that should be exciting and fast-paced, being constantly set back by the same issue breaks the immersion. What should have been a thrilling experience became a tedious cycle of trying to get back on track, only to be knocked off again by yet another fall. It made me question the game’s design choices—why include a mechanic that frustrates players instead of engaging them?

The Lack of Explanation
Another aspect that adds to my frustration is the lack of explanation behind the falling mechanic. If the falls were incorporated into the narrative or gameplay as part of a larger story arc or challenge, they might have made sense. Instead, they feel like an arbitrary design choice that disrupts the flow without any real justification. There’s no clear reason why falling is such a persistent issue in the game, and this lack of context only deepens my annoyance. In a game where you’re supposed to have agency and control, the feeling of being helpless in the face of random falls detracts from the overall experience. I want to feel like I can master the game’s challenges—not that I’m constantly battling against an unwinnable force.

Conclusion
Get to Work had the potential to be an enjoyable game, filled with excitement and engaging mechanics. Unfortunately, my experience has been overshadowed by one persistent issue: I keep falling. This constant setback has made the gameplay feel more like a frustrating exercise in patience than an immersive adventure. The frequency of the falls, the psychological toll they take, and the lack of any meaningful explanation behind them all contribute to a gameplay experience that is more aggravating than fun. As much as I wanted to enjoy this game, the repeated falls have made it nearly impossible to do so. Until something is done to address this issue, Get to Work remains a game that I can’t bring myself to continue playing.

All in all, despite the frustrations I’ve faced, Get to Work is still worth buying and playing for its unique gameplay, immersive world-building, and the overall sense of accomplishment it offers once you push past the challenges.

Hallways is in many aspects a spiritual successor to Stranger. Confined to an intersection between dark hallways, you're tasked with managing flashlight power to reveal and deter a murderous rabbit. Limited power sources require you to play short mini games on a laptop to recharge your flashlight and silence an occasional siren that seems to aggravate the killer. Especially on higher difficulties (later nights), the tension that builds in this otherwise simplistic gameplay loop is really special, and consistent across the developer's other titles. As an added bonus, the "Custom Killer" feature from Stranger returns, allowing players to swap Whiskers for other characters, making for hilarious gameplay twists.

One detail I really love about the Underground Facility is that the killer can sometimes block an ambient light in one of the hallways, giving you environmental cues of his whereabouts. The Bunker map opts for a more straightforward and challenging design, removing ambient lights and placing focus on the core flashlight mechanic. No matter which you choose, there are ample options for increased difficulty and higher tension. If you're looking for a simple, easy to learn, and tense horror game, consider giving this a try!

I preface this review by saying I LOVE FMV games. This one is technically sound enough...  but EXTREMELY disappointing. 

Like other low level FMV investigation games you enter search terms to find video clips, and from those you discover new search terms to keep the investigation going until you figure out what happened.

However, almost every video is the character complaining about paying bills, being inept at their job, or other 'on the nose' information that is spoken out loud in a clearly ad-libbed performance. The amount of repetition from this style of performance was painful, as nothing is succinct or nuanced. The character talks out loud ALL of their thoughts as though they were vlogging, even though they're meant to be alone. It's difficult to buy into this premise - but was very enjoyable to have a giggle at. Who talks out loud all of their thoughts like this?

To make matters worse, most clips take place in the character's bedroom, which is messy, distracting and overall - confusing. Is this the bedroom of someone with a girlfriend? We thought the many items may offer clues to the mystery, but they are just ill thought out set dressing. 

Upon completing the game we thought 'is that is?'. The plot is shallow, cliched and basic. If you want something thought provoking then look elsewhere! 

The 'Extras' in the game offered insight into the developers clear hatred for the project - Complaining about the idea of the game and the process of creating it. Is this really something you want to include in your game? I understand that developing something like this is difficult, time consuming and stressful, but why have all of the 'Extras' consist of complaining about it? Not very fun extras...

Overall my friend and I had fun, because it was funny - but for the wrong reasons. If you want an FMV game like that then this may be for you. Buddy up and have a laugh. 

I hope the developer learns from the experience of this game, as they certainly have it in them to make an FMV. I don't regret my purchase, I had a great time. I hope you do more. Take this on board and make something else, and I'll be there.

I'd like to state i've only played an hour or so and it quickly became tedious. Due to this, my review will be based on the first tank. (4? levels) I will revisit this again and update my review when I've gone through more of it.

First of all, gameplay is in general way slower than Insaniquarium. You need to feed less, Shells (which are coins) drop less, Critters (Larry the snail) moves way way way way slower.  One of the strong things to Insaniquarium was that the aquarium, quickly became insane. Thisone however does not become insane in the slightest.

You can buy a substantial amount of critters (These are what you'd get at the end of beating a stage in Insaniquarium) but there is no logic to them. While Larry would move around the bottom of the tank, trying to get the most expensive item in the tank at that point, these critters just are there moving around at random. This means that even tho you might have spend your shells on 5 critters, those critters can randomly walk the same path and stick together. In practice this means you might only have two critters catching stuff instead of five. It doesn't feel like there is any logic to them as there was in insaniquarium.

The fish are on a rather exact timer and you can deffo feel it. When you buy new fish in bulk, you better be able to feed those fish in bulk at the same time as well. Tho these are things that were the case with the original insaniquarium as well, those were different less complex days and I would have loved to see more variation between individual fish of the same species. 

There are some balance issues to me especially with the tiniest fish. They drop shells worth "15" and over the course of time, upgrade to fish dropping the same amount as lvl 2 fish, namely shells worth "50". I think the dev went with this because that is how the original game did it, however the speed of the original game was way, way higher and critters were way way more intelligent. These amounts would work for a game that has the same overal gamespeed as Insaniquarium, but that isn't this game. There is never a single reason to buy expensive fish because you have grinded too many cheap fish early on.

The game actively forbids you to build and INSANE Aquarium. it does this by limiting your use of food. There is this whole mechanic that you have to clean your tank. Food that drops to the bottom becomes stale and starts to filthy up your tank. Worse is that if a fish eats stale food from the bottom, they instantly die. If you want to have lots of fish you'll be unable to manage this perfectly and instantly lose quite some due to "food poisoning". If you even start to spiral out of control more, you'll have to chose between letting your fish die by lack of food or having your entire tank wiped due to its cleanliness falling to 0 (and this can go very véry quickly.)

Instead of aliens, there are now bacteria. I'd say they aren't announced great. The music doesn't pause iirc, there is no alarm sound, there is a red warning text at the bottom of the screen but if you happen to play on a rather big screen and you're trying to feed the fish at the top, you're screwed. Next to that, the bacteria are not that obvious. They kind of mask with the tank due to the decoration. So far there isn't a real click battle you have to perform but just click on the bacteria to get them out. I guess it's now more a skill on eyesight instead of a skill on how fast you can click. I rather test dexterity than play spot the differences.

To buy your fish, you have to fold out a pane. The whole mechanic of buying fish is kind of required to play through adventure mode so I don't see why it shouldn't be open. This is why I always leave the pane open. However, every time after you've successfully removed the bacteria from your tank, the pane closes. Especially when you have a lot of fish to take care of, when every click counts, this is incredibly annoying.

It's clear that a lot of love has gone in this game tho. I do believe this is a one guy making this game and I respect that. This might be a game close to the insaniquarium experience but to me it falls short a lot on certain key aspects of the original game. I hope there will come rebalances in future updates and that maybe other tanks are more fun. It didn't feel like fun anymore after an hour, while insaniquarium is a game i'd play for hours straight.

I have a weird obsession with bird games. Like most addictions, [i]it all started out innocently enough[/i]; I got [b]Untitled Goose Game[/b] on sale, played it, and was like [b]heeey this is really neat![/b] So I beat it 100%, but that wasn't enough. The following month, I got [b]Duck Detective[/b], and [b]Just Crow Things[/b], and I've already wishlisted [b]Duck Detective 2[/b]; but [i]I just made everything worse[/i]. [b]The more I consumed, the more I craved; and I don't think I'll ever be satisfied[/b]. So when I tell you that I saw [b]Birds Organized Neatly[/b] on sale for [i]cheap[/i] the other day, [b]you know exactly what happened.....[/b] [i]please don't judge me.[/i]


As you can probably already tell from the screenshots and stuff, [b]Birds Organized Neatly[/b] is a puzzle game where you stuff a bunch of birds ([i]neatly[/i]) in a box and hope they all fit. The concept is identical to countless other box moving puzzles and such, but it's all wrapped up in a cute bird aesthetic! [i]Isn't that nice?[/i] The gameplay couldn't be any simpler: [b]grab the bird with the mouse. rotate the bird with the mouse. put the bird in the box. repeat that for eighty levels.[/b] The game is at its best in short spurts, and is an excellent little casual game if you've got ten minutes to kill or just want something easy to play while doing other things. I said “easy” just now, but I only [i]kinda[/i] mean that; as the levels really jump in difficulty after the first fifteen or so. [spoiler]I spent nearly forty minutes on Level 17. why was that one so hard??[/spoiler] Now, maybe that's just a personal issue, and proof that I'm just not very smart ([b]so sad[/b]); or maybe you'll have no trouble on the levels I found confusing and get stuck on the ones [u]I[/u] breezed through. I don't know. I will say this, though; playing with a friend might be a good idea. I had my brother being [i]a backseat bird stuffer[/i] for a bit, and it was pretty fun; got through a lot of tricky levels. 


You know those [b]100 (thing) Cats[/b] games that suddenly showed up and took over Steam for a while?  [b]Birds Organized Neatly[/b]'s production values remind me a lot of that series, [i]minus the crypto scams[/i] [spoiler](I read it on the internet, so it must be true!)[/spoiler]. The hand drawn art style is [i]adorable[/i], with so many silly looking birds; including [i]ducks, geese, pheasants, chickens, kiwis, and quail![/i]....[spoiler]oh, hold up, I was just reading the menu. ha ha.[/spoiler] Every bird is animated, and gives out a little [b]chirp[/b] or [b]tweet[/b] when clicked on, [i]which is epic[/i]. [b]I love bird games with dedicated noise buttons[/b]. Not only that, but the game goes the extra mile and gives every single bird a unique name; PLUS, a little blurb highlighting their personality! Dino the Parrot loves singing Popcorn Popping! [b]isn't he wonderful??[/b] Sam the Seagull walked into a grocery store and stole a bag of chips, and someone got a video of that and it went viral! [b]that's already more compelling than half of this year's Oscar nominations!![/b] Eugene the Duck loves mysteries and solving crimes!....[i]there's something real familiar about that[/i]. The soundtrack -while brief- keeps up with the standards; all fun and goofy, but still simple at heart; and [b]I wouldn't have it any other way.[/b]


This is usually the part of the review where I'm like [b]I wholeheartedly recommend this game you have to buy this RIGHT NOW[/b].....[i]buuuuuuuuut[/i] here's a couple of problems I had; but I'm not doing that this time, because [b]Birds Organized Neatly is absolutely perfect!![/b] [i]good day, sir![/i]..........you're still here?........[i]okay[/i], I guess there's one thing. It'd be really nice if there was an outline around every bird you get. As much as I love all the silly poses and things, it can be [b]kinda[/b] hard to tell what shape the bird is actually supposed to be (this is especially apparent with Bingo the Flamingo and Elmza the Eagle), and just having a straightforward wire outline would be a lot more convenient. [i]Heck[/i], if you really want to, you could have it where the player chooses to turn it on or not.[b]it's their choice[/b]. anyway, that's about it.....[spoiler]why was Level 17 so hard? It was late and I had homework, but I spent my time on birds. shame.[/spoiler]


[b]Birds Organized Neatly[/b] is about as perfect as you could get for a [b]two dollar block puzzle game with birds!![/b] It's not much, but if you're interested, you REALLY couldn't ask for anything more for the price.

This is an interesting idea but it ultimately is just mostly boring. Using your score from previous run to invest into the next, and snowballing like that, is interesting, but it can also lead to going backwards if you're swapping characters around and pick a bad one or just have super bad luck with shop choices during the run.

On top of that, there is no way (that I can see) to speed up the early parts of the run, nor is there ever any difference in it. This is true of a number of bullet heavens, but it's especially egregious here as you end up spending 5+ minutes every run just doing nothing but running in a circle picking up the money. 

When you aren't "too powerful" for a section, it's pretty typical of other bullet heaven games, although it's made a little bit worse by the scrolling screen. You basically do the same "circle around" movement you do in all the other games, except you have to made sure to do it only in the top part of the screen, so you have time to grab the money (xp) before it drops off the screen and is forever gone. If that happens too much you lose the stat check of the game even faster, so it really limits what your choices are.

Overall, it's an OK concept but I just don't see anything worth your time. It's so restrictive and so repetitive in a genre that is always trying to overcome the repetitive nature of short, repeated runs with novel gimmicks, here there's just nothing to make it more dynamic, and a lot of the other designs make it less interesting than Vamp Survivors or any of the others like it. 

My constructive feedback points would be:

The scrolling screen is unique, but the money / xp going into the void makes the player movement very limited. Find a more interesting alternative so players can feel free to use the whole screen instead.

The repetitiveness of starting completely trivial 5+ minutes of gameplay runs over and over needs a fix. A game speed multiplier makes the most sense to me, but there are other ways to handle it (like "checkpoints" you could start at further in which give you an approximate score and upgrades to choose from if you've reached them before).

A lot of the weapon and character balance just seems awful. I personally think "character facing" instead of "mouse facing" weapons are always too weak to justify the downsides, and here that seems especially true - every one I tried was just worse than basically every other normal weapon. Maybe they're designed around "optimal" upgrades or synergies but in that case they're just always going to be the worst choice anyway.

This is a themed roguelike-deckbuilder which has a lot of charm and a lot of style I hope future updates will bring out more themed decks. Its mechanics are based upon the order you put cards on the table (or are on the table already) making for a very unique style of play. It comes with 6 decks each of which has its own distinct style and theme and each game you need to pick 3 of those to draw cards from and beat a score threshold that increases each round... with the increasing point-threshold and traits of each deck this becomes a challenge whether you truly understand how the 3 decks interact with eachother. Afterall a deck based upon timed delay effects REALLY doesn't mesh well with a deck that discards cards in play, killing off cards on delay before they have the time to activate.

Currently the themes of the decks are:
Stay (space-time style)- Timed delay decks that usually have an initial negative point cost only to be worth big points after they've been on the table for a couple of turns
Flip (warfare style)- Cards that either activate the first or last card put on the table each turn but aren't worth a lot (if any) points by themselves
Retain (bookclub style)- Cards that, when placed on the table, boost the value of cards that are (or stayed) in the hand
Chaos (Revolution style)- Cards that are worth big points but usually also put cards on the table that have a negative point value and stay there for multiple turns
Recycle (vampire style)- Cards that have effects when OTHER cards enter or leave play
Discard (wasteland style)- Cards that remove other cards on the table from play
Mutate (mist style)- an unpickable deck of which you can get cards at various points that revolve around cards that turn into better versions of cards after a set amount of times being played.

The beauty of this game is in its balance. Each deck is made in such a way that it could win the game on its own but by being forced to pick 3 you need to find a delicate balance on which cards you want to add to your deck after each round, which cards you want to play each round and in which order. However, combined those 3 picked decks can make for some hilarious chainreactions which could win you the game too... it's up to you to find these horribly broken synergies and make it through a set amount of games, each time with an increasing difficulty.

Ofcourse all the wellknown tropes of other roguelike deckbuilders are present too such as seals that apply a permanent effect to cards or augment them for that turn of play as well as artifacts (called symbols in this game) which can drastically alter your style of play on their own but also game-challenges that can award you various rewards if only you're willing to up the difficulty of that round.

All this combined together makes for a game that is a refreshing take on the roguelike deckbuilder

The downside is that the tooltips for card effects are OBVIOUSLY translated and sometimes don't exactly do what you would expect them to do OR that certain card-effects don't quite do what you would expect them to... once you start to understand what these effects do, though, or how the translation is a bit lacking each game can become a true joy to play with you searching for that broken synergy in this deck combinations.

Don't miss out on this game; it's definitely one of those underrated gems.

- Relatively high replayability: each level has a "par" and a "dev" score, that give you a number of moves that you have to beat the level in, in order to get a little icon on the level select screen and unlock some achievements. The "dev" score is often the fewest number of moves possible, or close to it, and the "par" score is a bit higher than that. Beating the "par" score on some levels is really challenging, and I have no idea how to beat the "dev" score on most levels.
- Some levels have an extra object you can collect that unlocks a bonus level.
- The levels are challenging without being too challenging, and there are a lot of them (66 total, much more than Blockdude). The first few levels are really easy, but they quickly get more challenging, and trying to beat the "par" and "dev" scores is fun.
- There is a level editor with the ability to share levels with others. I haven't messed with the level editor at all yet.

Cons:
- The only negative I can think of is that it's the same background music and graphics for every level. Some variety would have been nice, but it's not that big of a deal for me.

Overall, this is a simple but challenging puzzle game. Recommended if you like puzzle games.

The first row of levels does a good job of introducing the gameplay mechanics without having to resort to outright telling you what to do. The difficulty ramps up pretty quickly after that. I almost walked away when I saw that the game had hints added, but luckily they are not as hand-holdy as I thought they would  be. Essentially, they provide end-states for the boxes, similar to how a sokoban game plays. Even when turned on, the more difficult puzzles are still challenging, but I am leaving it off unless I get absolutely stuck.
The level editor is nice, and I'm looking forward to come up with some ideas to upload, but the sheer number of custom level slots is overkill. It's nice to have plenty of slots, but I can't imagine any individual person making that many levels in the editor, and keeping track of that many would not be trivial. Also, while this game plays great with a controller, the level editor lends itself better to a mouse. Honestly, I'm surprised but appreciative that you implemented gamepad controls in the editor at all, though I think I will stick to mouse for level making.
I think the bonus levels are my favorite part of the game. Hopefully the dev is listening and will add more bonus levels in an update, or even a DLC level pack. In the meantime, I'll keep an eye on the community shared levels and try to make some of my own.
Overall, this game is fantastic for oldschool puzzle gamers like me who enjoy thinky games. I remember playing something similar on my TI-84 in my college days, and this plays a lot smoother than that while not looking like a mobile game. I look forward to seeing what else this dev comes up with in the future.

This game is an eh for me. It's alright, I finished it, I had some fun, but I'm not excited about it. A lot of the problems I had with it are potentially fixable though, so maybe in future updates the game will be more enjoyable.

The pros:

- Fun story
- Fairly complex in that it's not super short and many of the puzzles have a LOT of steps
- A fair number of locations

The cons:

- Buggy UI that often drops the labels of objects or mislabels them. This makes it a real pain to spend time in some of the locations.

- Cumbersome UI choices that hinder gameplay. For example, the default action is always "Look", even for doors. You can't "Use" a door to open it, must always use "Open". If you want to uncombine combined items it's also "Open". The order of using one item on another can matter. There is an action you have to take every time you enter specific locations that honestly the game should do for you automatically once you figure it out the first time.

- You can end up with a lot of useless items (as in, you won't use them in the game), and the inventory gets really cluttered. That plus the Use X on Y action being a little laggy and finicky makes it a pain to navigate the inventory after a while.  

- The puzzles are a varying degree of fairness. Some of them are nice classic moon logic, but others feel like artificially padded difficulty. For example at some point a character appears in a dark area of a dark screen that you almost never have to visit, and this character has something you need. Okay? And other such examples.

- There is a character of an Indian shopkeeper that currently comes off as a racist caricature. 

Overall, if these issues aren't addressed in future patches I would say this game is okay if you are bored and it's on sale. If the UI issues are fixed and the shopkeeper is rewritten this game would move into the solid recommendation category for me.

Okay let's see...  I've definitely never came across a game like this.  It's uniquely weird.  Not in a bad way mind you, I say, as the game itself keeps your interest.  The ones who wrote/developed it definitely knew a good deal about the topics presented and it's written rather well.

Everything that you can read about the game on the Steam page -> That is it.  They tell you ALL you need to know.  And yes, its kinetic.  You just read and at times click on the map.  Click on the rainbow/shiny things and you will be taken to the next location.  Or click the circle/sun/moon thingy on the left (when shiny) and it will advance day/night.

Obviously this is also based around music and as a tone deaf person myself...  I did like the soundtracks provided.

There are also topics of war, but it's direct and isn't heavily focused on it.  What I am saying is...  You will understand everything you read and if you don't...  There is a glossary.

This IS a BL story and yet...  It isn't like other BL stuff I am used to.  So if you are here for "characters slowly falling in love" or think this is a "kinetic dating sim"...  No, no, no.  Nope.

I WOULD tell you what it is, but that would spoil the message that the Developer(s) are trying to get across.

Oh and there are other characters too.  You get to learn a bit about them.

The artwork...  I am assuming it's supposed to be artistic?  I don't know.  I am also art deaf too...  I will say that it's a bit spooky to have characters with such eyes, but then again...  I think its on purpose and to set the mood.  After all, it DOES match the world they live in.

Even if my review can't help you make a decision, I can tell you this: it's certainly different.  And different...  Bad or good...  Can make you think.

Thank you and I look forward to your future projects!!!  :D :>

Oh, boy... I feel that a negative review is unfair, because overall I enjoyed the game. However it is important to provide some constructive criticism. This is a good game, but a clear step back from the original. Specifically:

1) The mystery. Original game (including DLCs) did a great job of concealing the plot until the very last scenario and keeping you intrigued, while leaving some tiny hints along the way, making it fun too look back at all of the things you missed. This game makes it way too straightforward with huge hints making last few scenarios a chore. 

2) Words and boxes. I spent most of my time not solving the puzzles, but trying to phrase the solution in the exact way the game wanted me to. There was one particularly egregious case (Idol rules) when I had to swap words for no reason whatsoever, because the the game wanted me to say "X or Y" and was rejecting "Y or X" as the correct answer. And there is always an obligatory naming puzzle which rarely serves as a way to actually solve the scenario. 

3) Puzzles and Length. One of the great things about the original game is that all puzzles served a particular purpose - introduce important recurrent characters, advance the plot, provide vital information. This created a great feeling when a bunch of events that felt unrelated on a first glance suddenly connected and the whole picture became clear. In this game probably a third of the puzzles could be cut completely with hardly any negative consequences - they are just puzzles for the sake of puzzles. Don't get me wrong, I love puzzles - thats why I play games like this one! But there are just too many moving pieces and random characters making one-off appearances. It dilutes the main plot.

Was it worth my money? Yes, absolutely. But I know that Color Gray Games can do much better and I do hope they will hit it out of the park with DLCs.

I was hesitant about this game when I noticed a less-than-stellar reception from the fans of the original, writing reviews saying it didn't capture the magic that Case of the Golden Idol produced. After playing both games to completion, I have to say, I have no idea what those reviewers' damage was.
First off, I love mysteries. The Knives Out movies, Poirot shows and books and most iterations of Sherlock Holmes have always shown great appeal, as I'm sure most of you can relate. I've noticed that mystery games have a little bit more trouble replicating this appeal in various ways. In my opinion, the best part of a mystery is being able to follow the story, but not quite so easily so as to accurately guess the end, at least not completely. Few mystery-themed games seem to be able to do this, either being so convoluted and confusing that it's impossible to follow, let alone guess who dunnit, or being so mind-numbingly boring and straightforward that you're so certain of the ending you lose interest half-way through the game.
Color Gray Games has achieved Knives Out-level storytelling and intrigue while having a VASTLY improved point-and-click style gameplay which leaves the player engaged, but not overwhelmed; fascinated by every detail, but still starving for the next clue and what it entails. Case of the Golden Idol is by far the best mystery game I've played, at least until it's sequel was released. What I didn't even realize could be improved upon was improved, what I thought was lightning in a jar was recaptured for my amusement. My love for these games can't be oversold, and the only reason I didn't spend twice as much time playing these games was their enticement, I NEEDED to know what happens next, what it all meant!
The best part about these games is something I'd rather not spoil, because the worst part of them is the same as any other great mystery; once you know the ending it tends to lose 30-70% of it's potency. I'd still replay either again, but not for awhile, and even when I do, the best part will already be known to me. Maybe that's what we all crave, the new and the unknown. Frightening, alien and foreign elements always seem to have negative connotations, and yet we are strangely drawn to them, like gnats to a bright light, so beautiful, so dangerous. The ancient terrors that live beneath the earth are still worshiped by a select few, and the dark will consume us all. You might as well join us now.

The Rise of the Golden Idol is a bit of a strange experience for anyone who really loved the first, I think, but is overall a strong and enjoyable sequel that I think will still find its way onto some people's GOTY lists once they eventually get around to playing it.

Taking place in the same universe as the Golden Idol around 200 years later in the 1970s, the game unfolds almost exactly in the same way as the first, with you clicking around environments for clues and slotting them into a kind of madlibs fill-in-the-blanks where you describe the insane and fantastical events of the scenario you're in. The setting initially seemed much less interesting than the first game's to me, and I wasn't sure how I would feel about it when I first heard, but by the end I was applauding (most of ) their creative choices.

The previous game had a weird mix of wry humor and horrifying high stakes fantasy horror, and this is not different, with a winding, loopy story taking place over years in which apocalyptic disaster rears its ugly head. Here, though, the goofball factor is dialed up a notch, and not all the odious or evil characters really get their just desserts in the way you might like, but there's a strong degree of "art imitates life."

Unavoidably, as it is with all safe sequels, the joy of discovery is gone a bit, since you're doing essentially the exact same thing as you were previously, and if you've played the first (and you should!) you immediately know what to expect once that gold statue shows up. The developer's solution to preventing this from feeling like a really big DLC is to ratchet up the complexity... fast. So not only do they get harder much faster than in the first game, at the end of each chapter there is often a larger "meta puzzle" that requires you to have knowledge of all the scenarios and do some clever thinking. To help you, just as in the previous game the "puzzles" you solve are neatly separated into categories displayed at the bottom of your "task bar," often in sequential order of easiest to solve to hardest.

While I enjoyed really using my noodle (including cases where I straight up got stuck and decided to come back to the puzzle later), I found myself doing a lot of clicking through loading screens that were NOT short (without exaggeration, switching between chapters was comparable in wait time to loading a Cyberpunk 2077 save file), and I often found myself toying with the idea of a pen and paper, which I never felt was necessary in the previous game. This is especially jarring in cases where you can completely understand the scenario and fill out an entirely correct and consistent set of facts that wasn't quite what they were expecting, which happened rather a lot. Possibly this was a skill issue, but I really couldn't help but feel like the developers just didn't anticipate some alternate and IMO equally good solutions to puzzles, whereas the simplicity of the first game made the intended solution easier to arrive at. I noticed this especially in the fifth chapter, in which a few of the scenarios I thought were straight up in need of an extra pass from the devs (though it also contained my favorite scenario in the entire game, so a bit of a case of lows and highs). 

Another criticism I've seen is that the visuals are "flattened" and kind of matte, instead of the more observably pixelated visuals of the first game, and this calls attention away from the actual clues you need to complete the scenarios. This is certainly true, and candidly sometimes the visuals gave me vaguely "AI-generated vibes." So to really get the most out of this game, you'll have to play with the highlights enabled (which, thankfully, they are by default). Otherwise it still has all the verve and visual style of the previous game.

Overall, while I don't think I will publicly gush to people about how great this game is like I did with the first, this is a solid puzzle game that I would recommend to most people.
