First and foremost, I'd like to congratulate Keep the Engine Games on their debut. It's always a joy to see new indie studios take the leap of faith, and bring us new experiences with their craft. I sincerely wish them the best of luck on their future endeavors.

Now, Gems of Evolution is a direct jab at Vampire Survivors. Telling us the player that while unlocking all those powerful shiny skills is fun, yes, and literally annihilating waves upon waves of foes with flashing colors causes your brain to release dopamine; it's all a bit dull since the game kinda... plays itself? GoE takes that concept and says, look we know it's fun, but how about a little more challenge? And to that I say yes.

And challenging it is. All those skills, you have to cast them yourself. There's no autoplay nor handholding. Running around the map you have to keep an eye on your cooldowns as each second a skill is unused is wasted. It is up to you to create a valid build on the fly too, as the merchant has a time limit. 

There are a lot of things to consider in a build. Your character, the starting perks, skills that you chose each time you level up, and the vendor you buy useful items from in between each wave. Lots of numbers, lots of reading. Which can be daunting. For me it definitely was. But not because it's difficult, but because the game falls a bit short on the UI/UX department.

And with this comes the bad. As you probably have noticed from the broken English on the game trailer already ("can you survive 30 wave"), broken English is common throughout the game. It's not a deal breaker in most up and coming indie titles, but here it kinda is. Because the game quite literally bombards you with paragraphs of text. The concept of "show don't tell" is nonexistent, which makes picking up the game for the first time a dreadful experience. And parsing through text written in poor English makes things all the more tedious. I believe the UI, by which I mean the way things are presented to players, needs a rework. And some proofreading would be very much expected before the game leaves Early Access. 

There are other, smaller things that are not huge issues themselves, but would be great to have worked on. Such as;
- Walking animations don't make much sense. Characters feel like they're just gliding on or hovering over the map. Most of the animations actually are quite robotic.
- The cursor during gameplay is hard to see. It's tiny, and bears 4 different colors representing each main element. The concept is nice, but this makes aiming somewhat difficult, which is important on heroes like Eywriis as the primary attack spawns an elemental attack on exactly where you click on the map.
- The enemies get stronger and take more hits to die as time goes on, while having the exact same appearance. It'd be great to at least have a visual cue that it'll take more hits to kill the same enemy, which is needed to assess where to move to on the map. A good example would be aforementioned Vampire Survivors, which solves this problem by having a lot of different enemy types, or sometimes by simply changing their size alone.
- The music is repetitive and constantly loops over the same melody every few seconds. Can't imagine playing the game without muting it and playing something else in the background.

BUT! I write all this because I see potential here. The game has a very cool concept. With some further touches here and there, it can be much more enjoyable. All this gets a pass after all, mainly because of 2 things. First, this is an Early Access title, and small issues like the ones I mentioned are always expected before a v1.0. And second, this is Keep the Engine's first title, so they deserve to be given some slack. 

Once again, I wish Keep the Engine the best of luck out there. They seem really eager and enthusiastic and I love it. I'll be keeping an eye on their future work for sure, on how they'll fine-tune GoE over time, and of course on what their future titles are going to be.

"Oh no i missed the block cycle, now i need to keep listening to this looped part of the song until i catch the next one". It literally makes you dislike the song, which I don't think is the point of an album game. The beat should move you forward, not hold you back in my opinion.

This one had some world-building detail that was good, such as the newspapers and the cassette tapes.  The music was great, I liked the jukebox aspect.  Voice acting was mediocre, which I can overlook.

But the game is not good.  It starts out ok, until after the initial escape room puzzle.
Then it turns into an open-world game with no map, no direction, no threat, no real indication of what you're supposed to be doing.

A huge problem I had was there was no indication to "check for a package at the front door", much less where the front door was.  The house is the size of a county civic center and I'm supposed to just know where the front door is and that I'm supposed to go there?

That was my biggest problem, there is no real indication of what your "mission" is or clue to what you're supposed to be doing after you leave the bedroom.

I couldn't finish it, it was just boring and went nowhere.

I thought there was no way the company that put out one of best games I've played this decade could be that bad.  Obviously everyone is just mad about the AI voice acting -- a new hot button issue.  I was very very wrong.  I would have been embarrassed to have my name attached to this.  This really felt like a cash grab, like maybe the project was falling apart so they put it out just to make some of the money back.

The writing is terrible.  Everything reads like it was run through a translation twice.  MAYBE this is on purpose and you later find out you're an alien or something, but I'll never find out as I'm refunding this.  They also decide to just lock you in your room and let you bumble around angrily as though to snub your nose at the fact the game is doodoo.  I then wondered around the house for 5 minutes trying to locate a ringing phone which I couldn't see due to the colors.

The graphics look like something from the PS3 or PS4 era, yet somehow it still ran at abysmal framerates (I ran Elden Ring at at least Very High so it ain't my card).

The controls are horrible.  I tried to play with a controller, and apparently the game has built-in controller support which binds joystick-left and joystick-right to both movement AND jumping?  So I couldn't even use Steam's built-in WASD template unless I wanted to jump around constantly.  And then even with mouse & keyboard it controls weird.

The sound was ok, then you turn on the radio in your room and get a single guitar strumming mindlessly, as radios are wont to play.  As far as the AI voice acting, yes I think it's a gross thing to do, but I figured, "whatever, let's give it a shot". I soft-locked the game once in my 0.3 hours just using the menus.

This game is free-on-Itch-tier, and even then I'd be annoyed that someone decided to released it.  This is simply unacceptable for a studio to put out without a disclaimer of some kind.

Grade: F.  Please see me after class.  :(

Only played the extraction mode, not the BR. It's really good, considering it's in Alpha. Keep an eye on this one.

The battle royale mode is extremely mid and not worth buying this for at all.

As for the ExfilZone (EZ) gamemode, it is extremely fun. I've played tabor quite a bit and while that game has more polish in terms of questing, controls, and the hideout, EZ is immensely better in terms of gunplay, QoL, and (lack of) jankiness. 

Playing Tabor feels like a chore and I get a headache every single time from what should be extremely basic things such as picking an item up. Dropping a gun on the floor on accident and trying to pick it up is actually awful in Tabor. Virtual crouching not even being an option unless you pick Seated mode make it genuinely a chore to do anything. Picking anything up in Tabor is awful in general. In EZ with force-grab it's literally so easy and painless. The weapon smoothing is awful in Tabor. The gunplay in EZ is infinitely better as well. Scav raids are actually perfection in this. (I hope that a scav rep feature gets added). The scopes in EZ are SO SO SO SO MUCH BETTER and are actually usable as well. The variable zoom scope is LITERALLY perfection. The tasks are also so much more fun in EZ than Tabor imo.
Everything that Tabor and EZ does, EZ does it so much better.

That being said, there is quite a bit of jank and missing essential features.

In tabor, you can snap the neck of a scav to take their gun, or, bring in a knife to kill a scav. If you run out of ammo in EZ, you have 0 offense or defense until you find a weapon and ammo in a crate (or ig a grenade). Maybe, certain items like a screwdriver, or other items like that you can actually use as weapons for stabbing as well. 

Things you are holding in your hands will randomly drop for no reason with no indication in EZ. Combined with this, most items clip through the floor 80% of the time. It is a complete gamble if you drop something if it will just clip through and you lose an item. 

Attaching webbing to your backpack is cool but being able to grab stuff attached to your backpack without having it out leads to so many problems. It's a really cool feature though, maybe it should be able to be turned off so that you can only take stuff out of the webbing if you hold the backpack?

Taking attachments off a gun or putting them on is extremely tedious in EZ. It just doesn't work 80% of the time. One thing that i do miss from tabor is being able to put a gun into safety. So many times in the hide out I am trying to Grip+Trigger an attachment and I end up grabbing the gun with my other hand and wasting a bullet. I love the feature of being able to grab the gun with your other hand without having to drop it first though, it's actually so nice.

There needs to be a way to check hydration, energy, weight, and time left in raid on a watch on your wrist or something. Or, maybe just when you look at your wrist it pops up on there. Opening a menu every time to check a basic thing is very tedious, especially when food and water goes down way too fast in EZ. 
Also, the map constantly re-centering itself while moving is annoying af. Oh, and also also, pings on a map randomly disappear, it is very frustrating lmao.

Another thing I like in Tabor is going to the market, you can test the weapons with ammo and a magazine on the wall. Maybe there could be a feature where if you click an item to buy in the market in EZ, it shows up and you can interact with it before buying it to see how it works/looks.

The graphics options in EZ are awful. Resolution set to "ultra" and it looks like im playing 720p and weapon fire mode writings are impossible to read. Anti Aliasing seems to do literally nothing. There NEEDS to be an option to upscale (FSR, DLSS, XeSS idc just anything) and proper AA (not TAA or FXAA). Tabor's and Into the Radius's graphics settings are mind numbingly in depth. Maybe there should be a basic tab which is what it is now and an advanced tab that is like Tabor's or ITR's. 

All in all, EZ is actually super good, and is so much more fun than Tabor. I don't ever see myself going back to Tabor unless this game dies. The battle royale mode is really bad tbh but EZ alone is worth $20.

At first the game was amazing. There is a learning curve in which I didn't mind. Not new to extract shooters but am new to VR extract shooters. Here are my pros and cons

4) Easy to learn but hard to master

Cons:
1) Scavs seem a little to over the top as far as being sponges
2) to me it seems like armor rating doesn't mean anything since you could have top gear and still get one shot by a scav
3) I think players spawn a little to close to one another
4) EAC is worthless. Updated windows and now I can't play the game no matter what I do (error code 1275)

There's people that wish you could que into single raids but that's not really the point of extract shooters. This game will test to see how much can you adapt to the situation you've been given. I have encountered multiple duos and 3 man groups but if you play smart, you don't even have to deal with them. 

I saw some others saying there's cheaters, I haven't witnessed any on my end but doesn't mean there isn't. I've had some questionable "deaths" but I can't say for certain if it was due to a cheater or not. 

Right now, as much as I'd like to recommend this game, I can't for the purpose of if you're on PCVR and do a windows update, you have a high chance that the games EAC will permanently lock you out until the devs do something about their EAC or if you decide to roll back the update if you can

Edit:
I gave the game a thumbs up now since I was able to troubleshoot my 1275 error code. So I am able to get back in and play.

old review:
If you like Tarkov, you will probably like this game. Many people compares this game to tabor, so i would to. However, I think 'Ghost of Tabor' moves this genre in the right direction, because playing solo weren't much fun at all.

Compared to Tabor, this game is very polished and very interesting. After playing this game, Tabor felt like a junky mess. I really hope that the developers of Tabor can look at this game and fix Tabor's issues.

After a very long time, I unlocked all the shops to the max level and collected almost all the rare items (except for the elephant and golden figurine). So, I feel ready to criticize the game.

First, this game felt like a job. The amount of time you need to invest is too high. If I were employed, I wouldn't be able to afford the time to play this game. It's true that I had some nice gunfights, but they only happened when I had access to good ammo. Tabor didn't have this problem. In Tabor, the starting ammo was good enough. In this game, even if you steal or get a good kit, it's pretty much useless without good ammo, and to get good ammo, you have to invest time in quests.

Also, in Tabor, you could pre-build your kits in the shop and buy them in a few seconds after dying in a raid. You didn't even need to load your magazines.

And, in Tabor, you don't need to run to the second floor to get healed every time. Who even thought that placing the healing station on the second floor in this type of game was a good idea? Tabor doesn't have that problem.

Second, you probably want to have a headset with a DisplayPort (DP) connection to get a clearer, higher-resolution picture. On a Wi-Fi connection, you can't see very far away, and the delay is noticeable. You probably also want a real gunstock. Sniping is a big part of this game because the maps are very large. For some strange reason, Tabor also doesn't have any problems in this area (probably because the maps are smaller and clearer, with less visual clutter, and the optics in Tabor just didn't work properly). Getting a headshot from 300 meters in this game is normal.

The GPU farm is also useless; just get one GPU inside and forget about it. Also, loading the generator with gas is a waste of time that I wish I didn't have to do, especially after opening the GPU farm. Some bunker upgrades are useless. In Tabor GPU farm can support your end game without any problem.

About the guns: I don't like them. I just don't like how they sound or shoot. Maybe the Scorpion is a nice one.

Conclusion:

As a solo player, I mostly experienced annoyance rather than fun in this game. I wish the developers had copied Tabor's game design more than Tarkov's. At this price point, you definitely could try this game (it's a lot cheaper and in a much better state than Tabor). But make sure that you have friends with VR to play it together. As a solo player, you're better off not even touching this game.

This is a slapper! Really nice to just have a short survival horror where you shoot zombies with powerful, satisfying to use weapons in linear levels. It sounds generic, but it's really uncommon. Most zombie shooters just want to be the next COD zombies. 

It gets intense when you get closer to the end, I really liked that. Just a few flaws all of them minor (keep in mind that I only played Story Mode):

1) Shotgun ammo is too rare. Shotgun ammo spawns in one shell at a time, so you never have much.

2) The Hunting Rifle badly needs to be buffed. It has terrible accuracy and body damage.

3) Zombies need to have more audio cues. Especially crawlers, who can hit you without you even hearing them beforehand. Crawlers in general need to be fixed, they can spawn right on top of the player.

4) Syringes, in my opinion, should spawn inside of drawers or drop from crates to synchronize features and remove potential for errors, because they glitched out and were invisible for me.

5) When you get hit, the blood effect is too excessive and blocks the camera. I think toning it down a little would improve the playing experience.

6) The crate drop mechanic needs to be overhauled. Sometimes it would drop arrows, and I think that there might have been a bow that was removed. It also drops what is likely old names of each ammo type (for example, M1911 ammo is called .45 ACP). In my opinion, it should also occasionally drop syringes.

7) The AKM is OP. It completely shreds the strongest enemy type and easily deals with every other enemy. Ammo for it drops like candy on the later stages, too, so there is no reason not to just stick to using it.

Some recommendations:

1) I think that better response mechanics, such as some gore, bigger blood effects,explosive barrels, or semi-destructible environments would improve the playing experience; however this is of course up to the dev. Adding in any of these features may be more time-consuming than it's worth.

2) I think that the game could really use more music. The main ambient loop gets overplayed in the story mode, and just a few other tracks would dramatically improve the playing experience. This is, of course, far easier to suggest than it is to implement. 

The game was very fun. That shotgun and the revolver were very enjoyable to use. Like I said before, it gets more intense as you get closer to the end because, as far as I'm aware, you have to restart the entire story mode if you die or quit the game. [h3][i]Final.[/i][/h3]

I'm not religious at all, but the puzzles and clutter games looked interesting enough to take a chance on this, never mind that it only costs a few bucks.  25 chapters of assorted slider puzzles, nonograms, pick 2 clutter games, variations of jigsaw puzzles, spot the difference games, and a click on pieces until you get a finished picture puzzle.  There is a hidden angel somewhere in each chapter which if you find, goes into a Christmas scene collection.

After each puzzle, there's a Scripture quote taken from the King James Bible describing some aspect of Jesus' life; the biography starts with Jesus' birth and continues through the Resurrection.  I don't enjoy being openly preached to in real life or in games, and there are definitely parts of the story which come off as proselytizing.  But I played with an open mind, and found myself enjoying the challenges of the puzzles.  I'm terrible at the slide-tiles-around-a-grid type slider puzzles, and some were fiendishly hard for me; had to skip one out of frustration but persevered through the others.  The move tokens around the lines slider puzzles were easier.  The other puzzles were considerably less frazzling, but many still took a fair bit of concentration to solve.

There were some things which could have been done much better.  Windowed mode doesn't really work with an older monitor as the window overflows off the screen.  The jigsaws have a clunky mechanic where moving and rotating pieces are both done with the left mouse button, which often leads to the game getting "confused" as to what you want to do.  Would have been better if moving was done with the left mouse button and rotation of pieces with the right mouse button.  The nonograms only have a toggle function with left clicking to either fill or unfill a square.  There is no way to mark unused squares as unused, multiple squares cannot be filled in by dragging over the row/column, and worst of all, I found myself having to guess quite a bit, which is a major nonogram no-no!  At least there's no mistake counter, but still, that's annoying.  Two angels appear to be missing from a couple of chapters as I looked and looked, but never did spot them, which means the in-game achievements can't ever be completed.  It's too bad the in-game achievements weren't made into Steam Achievements too, because some of them are seriously tough to get and you'd have to play the game through more than once to 100% it, assuming the missing angels aren't actually "missing".

Not a bad effort for the price though, and if the developer makes more games like this with different themes, I'd be game to try more.

Positive Aspects:

- Unique Style and Aesthetics: The game stands out with its distinctive visual style and aesthetics. The creative design choices make it memorable and intriguing.
- Interesting Premise and Implementation: The concept behind the game is captivating, and the way it’s executed adds depth and complexity. Players can explore unexpected mechanics, which keeps the experience fresh.
- Journey Experience: The game takes players on a real journey, allowing them to dynamically grow and shrink their party. This sense of progression and transformation enhances the overall adventure.

Areas for Improvement:

-Skeleton Interaction: When clicking on a spot, the skeleton character consistently looks away this feels like a bug. It would be more engaging if this behavior extended froo arrow key movement to mouse as well.
-Tutorial: A tutorial would greatly benefit new players. Providing clear instructions on gameplay mechanics and controls ensures a smoother learning curve.
- Rebinding Options: Customizable key bindings would enhance accessibility and cater to individual preferences.
- Sound Options: The sound volume increments at intervals of 20, which might be too coarse. Fine-tuning the sound levels would be appreciated.
- Auto-Battling Feature: Implementing an auto-battle option or allowing players to repeat their last action would streamline combat and reduce repetition.
- Music Balance: While the music adds ambiance, consider incorporating more background tracks or exploring different genres beyond electro. A soothing, lo-fi soundtrack could enhance the overall experience.
- Transitions: Smoother transitions between scenes or actions contribute to immersion. Improving these transitions would elevate the game’s polish.
- Enemy Information: Providing a place where players can access enemy stats or review previously fought enemies would empower strategic decision-making.
- Combat Visuals: Adding more color and visual flair to combat sequences would make battles more engaging and visually appealing.
- Sleep Mechanic: Address the issue where a player’s lobby can be put to sleep in a single attack, preventing further engagement.
- Quest Clarity: Ensure that quest objectives are clear and intuitive. Players shouldn’t feel lost or frustrated due to unclear instructions.
- Communication: Consider in-game notifications when other players join a lobby to enhance social interaction.
- Reading Preferences: Recognize that some players prefer minimal reading. Balancing text-heavy content with visual cues can cater to different playstyles.

This is a match-three game where you need to decide what is your highest priority before you match the three or more three items. You have to survive the attack of enemies such as snakes, spiders, scorpions etc. At the same time, you have to collect resources to craft potions and arrows and complete the required tasks on each level. Fortunately, if you couldn't get all the stars on the first play, you can replay the level to get the three stars.

There are a few clothing shops to be unlocked as you progress further in the game. Please do not click on the item in the shop if you're not buying what you intended to buy because clicking the item doesn't give you a preview of how your character looks with the item. Also, the clothes and accessories do not offer additional skills or abilities in the fight. 

Overall, it's not a bad game to kill time. Sometimes, the level can be challenging because you probably have to sacrifice your health to deal with the attack when you want to finish the level or gather more important resources. There are 150 levels and the 150th level is the toughest. The levels are getting more difficult as more attacks need to be handled. Then, there are another additional 50 levels which are more difficult than the first 150 levels. Some players probably feel it's repetitive or boring, but I couldn't find what else to look for in a match-three game besides matching items? Anyway, if you love match-three games and want to challenge yourself with survival mode, this would be a great game for you.

This game has a pretty smooth combat system and that's the main reason I'm giving it a thumbs up. Here are some thoughts.

- There's a distinct lack of content including enemy variety and weapons/power-ups. 
- Most of the power-ups are boring stat increases and while they do lead you to feel more powerful over time, they just aren't very interesting.
- Aside from the issue of variety, most enemies only require that you circle-strafe around the outside of the map. 30 levels of that isn't very interesting.
- Feedback from taking damage is minimal and it can be easy to lose half your health or more suddenly to a stream of bullets.

[b]Game #22: Dice of God[/b]

This is not a full game, it's just a demo. There are only three levels, and the first level is something of a mindless tutorial. Even for a $0.99 game, it's shockingly short. You can beat it in 10-20 minutes depending on how long it takes you to understand the rules. 

Level 1: You have to defeat two enemies and one boss. Each turn, you can roll a D6, using the result to either attack the enemy or defend yourself. If you roll a 6, you get a "blessing", which can be used to enchant a random face of your D6 so that it is doubly effective. 

Level 2: You have to defeat a single boss, that's it. Your D6 is now blank, and can't be used to attack or defend. Instead, you have to roll your blank D6 to summon paper dice (The summoning roll is deducted from your HP, but this has no effect until level 3, since your dice is blank on level 2). Here we see the game's main gimmick: you have to cut out origami paper dice from a 4x4 grid of paper with random numbers on it. You try to cut your dice to have the best possible numbers on them. Each paper die you create can be used only once. This level is dreadfully slow and RNG-dependent, unless you happen to know the trick to cutting out two origami cubes from a 4x4 grid.

Level 3: You have to defeat three enemies and one boss. Your D6 is no longer blank, but now has the values -3 through 3. The paper you cut the dice from is now 5x5, allowing you to cut out 3 dice at a time if you want. Occasionally you will get lucky and your paper will be enchanted, and the dice made from it will either be doubly effective, or cast shields on yourself when used.

There are also about 6 perks that can make each playthrough a bit different, but you can only select 2 of them every run.

So, the main gimmick of the game is pretty clever. It also has some interesting achievements to encourage multiple playthroughs, requiring very clever use and understanding of the game's mechanics and random perks. And ultimately, the achievements are why I'm giving the game a thumbs-up, since the game does get more fun when you know what you're doing, and achievements turn the game from a 10-20 minute proof-of-concept into an interesting 2-3 hour puzzle game. Still, its blatant lack of content leaves a lot to be desired, so it gets a low score. It really deserves to be expanded into a full RPG, since this concept has got a lot of potential. 

3 / 10.

[h1]A Great Sequel To A Beloved Metroidvania[/h1]

One of my favorite types of sequel: improving the shortcomings of the first game, while adding more stuff to the established formula. Ender Magnolia is such a sequel. I always appreciate developers taking players' feedback to heart and delivering an amazing experience. Although personally I still have some issues regarding certain aspects of the game, there is nothing stopping this game from being one of the most fantastic metroidvania of all time.

[h1]Things I Like About Ender Magnolia:[/h1]

[b]1. Abilities Improvement[/b]
Hands down the best change, and more.
[list]
[*]The ability charges are gone, and in exchange we have a cool-down system. This is a much-needed improvement. Players are no longer handicapped by the number of usage during exploration.
[*]Ender Magnolia also introduce ability types based on how they perform: Primary(normal attack), Pressure(continuous attack), Cool-down(more impactful attack), and Autonomous(set-and-forget).
[*]All homunculus has three ability variations to unlock. They all have different attack patterns and damage value. Also, each homunculus also has an ultimate attack, offering lots of combos and build variety. 
[*]Pressure abilities are really powerful and my favorite. Using two of them can trivialize any things, and that satisfying hit sound is just wonderful.
[/list]

[b]2. Build Variety[/b]
Way, way more options than the first game.
[list]
[*]Other than choosing four homunculus, the game introduces more ways to improve the character as well: Relics, Carapaces, Bracelets, and Totems.
[*]Relics return with significant stat boosts. Now players can upgrade them using a special currency.
[*]Carapaces grant players parry and trigger additional effect with successful parry. I find the SP recharging one the most useful.
[*]Bracelets are simple stat boosts. Players can equip up to two at once.
[*]Totems provide various benefits, from passive regeneration, emergency heal, to attack boost while healing. My favorite so far is the one that fully restore your health and SP bar when near death.
[*]Interestingly, should players not want to interact with those systems, both Carapace and Totem have items that do nothing but stat boosts. 
[/list]

[b]3. Early Traversal Abilities[/b]
Here are your mandatory double jump and air dash, now can we finally get to the fun part? (says the game, maybe...
[list]
[*]As much as I like to see how far a metroidvania can go without giving you the mandatory traversal upgrades, it is equally satisfying to see them offered right away.
[*]Having both double jump and air dash early is wonderful for exploration. This opens up a lot of places to go and secrets to discover. It's refreshing.
[*]Plus, the game still has attack momentum(every time you attack mid-air Lilac will move forward a little). Using attack momentum along with double jump resetting air dash, you can cover a significant amount of ground early on.
[/list]

[b]4. Other Compliments[/b]
[list]
[*]Map now clearly outlines where you are and how the level looks like.
[*]The character animation seems more fluid than the first game.
[*]Dialogue between homunculus when resting is a nice addition.
[*]Checkpoints are still wonderful wallpaper materials.
[/list]

[h1]Things I Dislike About Ender Magnolia:[/h1]

[b]1. Less Desirable Difficulty[/b]
Both the enemies and the platforming feel underwhelming.
[list]
[*]Maybe it's true or maybe it's my memory playing tricks on me, I feel like Ender Magnolia is significantly easier than its predecessor.
[*]Lack of contact damage(I can't believe I am saying this) or anything to keep players from safely going through. The issue here is that most of the enemies have to first turn around, and then attack. Since players can freely move pass them, it naturally creates a lot of attack windows and looping shenanigans.
[*]Most bosses are less challenging. Their move sets don't reflect players' progression, second phases don't add something more threatening, and of course the issue I mentioned above. 
[*]To be fair, platforming challenges wasn't the strongest suit in the first game, so I was hoping the sequel could have some. I am pretty disappointed at how the game handles them: more poisonous water, sprinkle problematic enemies around the platforms, one-way-portals, and more empty space.
[/list]

[b]2. Other Traversal Abilities[/b]
The first game had no problem about them, so why changing them in the sequel?
[list]
[*]I wish Garm, Hati, Motley, and Lars have their own sets of like the rest of the homunculus instead of just being a metroidvania gating-abilities. Garm could be a second defensive cool-down ability like Shackled Beasts; Hati could be like No.7 with tons of movements; Motley could be an autonomous ability that focus on debuff and defensive buff; Lars would be hard to design, but I wish he could be more than just wall-climbing and super dash.
[*]Motley's grapple hook is really lacking. Snapping from points to points is just not interesting. It needs to have some swinging mechanic.
[/list]

[b]3. Other Complaints[/b]
[list]
[*]The overall art style and soundtracks are less impressive. The color saturation feels watered down. Less hazy, and less atmospheric.
[*]Maybe it's because I am a really pessimistic guy, but this game feels way too hopeful for my taste.
[*]Areas are way too open-ended. Wish they were more interconnected.
[*]Again, what the hell were all those one-way portals and the whole Crimson Forest??
[*]Loadout slots would be nice.
[/list]

Superior in almost every way from the first game. Visuals are stunningly beautiful, music is as good, exploration is very satisfying and combat feels right.

This is also the metroidvania game I've played that respects your time the most. It features one of the most detailed minimaps I've seen, marking whether an specific area has been fully explored, as well as tons of details that will save you from unnecessary backtracking. Moreover, pretty early into the game you will already unlock fast travel across Respites (savepoints).

Even with all those timesaves, the game provides of ~20h of content, with lots of areas easily identifiable and new enemies on each of them. 

It has less companions to unlock than in the previous title, but they have greater depth, with more lore and variants to give them extra options for combat. There are more equippable items as well, making almost every collectible in the game worthy.

The storyline is a bit difficult to follow and in some aspects I felt it suffered from being as interesting as the gameplay, but overall it gives extra context for dialogues and how areas are connected one to another.

Boss fights were probably my least favorite part of the game. Most of them felt much easier than navigating the areas before them, and overall their design wasn't that remarkable for most of them. They weren't terrible but simply worse than the rest of the game.

Still, overall this is a great sequel and aside from some annoying areas, I've had a great time with it and it is well worth the full price. A very solid title on an extremely competitive genre.

A pretty good metroidvania, although I personally prefer the previous entry, Ender Lillies. Although, that is not to say this one is bad, obviously. This review will mostly be comparing Magnolia to Lillies, so it's probably most useful to people who played the latter first.

First, gameplay.
I appreciate the inclusion of a hard difficulty option, firstly because for 2/3rds of the game I felt like Normal was too easy compared to Lillies, and secondly because playing on Hard does actually give you an extrinsic reward - you gain more xp and currencies for defeating enemies.

The lack of dmg-on-touch isn't really complete - there are enemies later on who do deal dmg when you touch them (bcs the're on fire or smth similar visually communicated to the player), so I don't really mind that change - when the developers thought contact dmg was needed, they added it. I'm fine with that.

The more limited roster of companions/abilities this time was smth that had me quite worried initially, but seeing as each homunculus companion gets 3 abilities it isn't that much of a quantity problem - instead of having a jump-and-pound summon and a forward dash attack summon, those are just two abilities Lito can do. That does, however, mean that you can't have both of them equipped at once. Additionally, you can now equip 4 abilities at a time - 1 more than in Lillies. However, you don't have two loadouts to switch between with a button, which gave Lillies effectively 6 abilities that were slightly clunkier to use than Magnolia's 4. A lot more of the homunculi function like Lillies' Faden, or Gerrod's ground slam, giving you 1 or 2 traversal abilities that you can use without needing to equip them.
This basically means you only get what would be the "major" summons in Lillies (Gerrod, Ulv and so on) and not "minor ones" (Hamlet Youth, Travelling Merchant and many more). What this means gameplay-wise is the annoying limited-use-per-respite system for minor summons (and Eleine), which in Lillies made me feel like it was a waste to use them outside of boss fights, especially since I could instead just whack the enemy with Gerrod a few times and then finish it off with the Knight when they were recovering, is gone and replaced with individual cooldowns.

Visually the game is solid, just like Lillies, but the enemy designs are less varied, I suppose since they are actual homunculi created for a purpose as opposed to the mutated-into-monsters blighted. I feel like there was less visual variety in areas you explore, but honestly I think this might just be due to me forgetting how many grey castle areas there were in Lillies. Then again at least the underground crypts were yellow instead of grey. Point is, game's overall still pretty.

Performance on steam deck was fine, no problems spotted, 60FPS all-around. Some crackling audio issues after putting the deck to sleep with the game on, but that's a deck/SteamOS issue since it happens in other games as well.
 
And finally the bit that has me saying I prefer Ender Lillies: the story and atmosphere.
The tone and atmosphere of Lillies, contrasted with the main characters of the little girl protected by the undead knight REALLY worked for me. The fact that you could see the toll purifying Blight took on her (nothing similar is going on in Magnolia) added to all of these Muh Themes of sacrifice, losing innocence and so on (this isn't a breadtube video essay I'll leave it at that). Additionally, since almost everyone in Land's End was already gone, the story didn't have to juggle too many characters and so never became confusing as long as you actually read the various notes ("findings") along your way.
In comparison, Magnolia has quite a few more characters in its story. Besides the homunculi companions actually speaking and being characters outside of their memories unlike the blighted, we now have bosses who aren't all mad/dark souls-style hollow, as well as actual friendly NPCs in towns (or more like shelters) and occasionally in the combat areas. Simply put, I found all the findings and talked to all the friendly NPCs every time there was a new story development and I feel some of them don't have a proper/satisfying conclusion to their arcs/stories/whatever you wanna call it.
Don't be discouraged, this isn't so bad it would make me not recommend the game. What I'm getting at is I preferred Lillies' simplicity and small (alive) character roster than Magnolia's more ambitious storytelling approach (or rather its execution). Plus in Lillies this added to the lonely, sombre tone. 
The fact that you can obtain some of the information abt the characters out of order or hours apart depending on which areas you explore in what order (duh, it is a metroidvania after all) left me simply confused on certain things. After finishing the game 100%, I sat there wondering about some characters' backstories or motivations.

In conclusion: game overall good, get if you like Ender Lillies or 2D metroidvanias in general. Price-wise I suppose it is a bit steeper compared to similar games like Hollow Knight (or even Ender Lillies), but I didn't regret my purchase - make of that what you will.

Here's hoping we get more good metroidvanias from this team (I would obv prefer more sequels in the uhhh "Ender series(?)" since I am a le fan). If they work out the kinks in their execution of a more populated story or deliver us another simpler and lonely narrative like Lillies I'll be a happy fella.

I will start getting the main question out of the way: yes, this game is an ABSOLUTE MASTERPIECE. It is a direct improvement from Ender Lilies in almost every way. Inevitably, I'll be making some comparisons to Ender Lilies. ( without spoilers )
 
-- Story/Characters - A story of rancor, war, forgiveness and of people that fight to their last breaths for a brighter future. The plot unfolds in the same universe from Ender Lilies a couple of decades after its events but it the feels much more expositive and dynamic than the first one, the characters have much more lines and participation. All of them have a clear reason to there and a pretty godd amount of character development. Now sometimes you get an option to talk with them in the respites, where Lilac ( the main character ) talk to the homunculi ( the equivalent of the spirits from EL ) about what's happening at that moment. This gives much more depth to the relationship between Lilac and the homunculi.

-- Presentation/Soundtrack - It is exactly what you could expect from an Ender Lilies sequel. The visuals are beyond gorgeous and the soundtrack is SPECTACULAR, created by the same people that made the Ender Lilies OST. You have that same aesthetic contrast between innocence and tragedy, athough I would say that Ender Lilies is more dramatic, melancholic and carry more sadness. Lily felt more innocent and weak compared to Lilac which behaves more confident and plays more a lead role in the story than Lily. The game also have several different enviroments and it feels less repetitive than EL. All of this will make the game touch your heart.

-- Level design/Exploration - Another big improvment. By any means EL has a bad level design, but here they made even better. The maps are bigger and more complex and each one feels unique. I fell in love with some of them for being challenging with complex pathings that will demand your attention and focus.
  The exploration is very well made and it is what you can expect from a good metroidvania. The overall map is bigger this time and the game rewards you a lot the more you explore, with many important collectables and currencies used to upgrade your equipments, making exploration directly attatched to your overall combat experience

 --Enemies/Bosses - This is for me the bigger improvement from Lilies. In the first game some of the bosses felt like enldess hit sponges that created long and frustrating fights. They completely evolved here, where every single boss feels fair and fun, without any of the frustrating EL bosses mechanics. And don't get the wrong ideia, they're still very hard and challenging, but here you feel you have more creative ways to play against them, since the game has several different builds, attacks and equips for you to customize your experience. Many of the bosses made me change my biuld to adapt, which made the game feels more dynamic and rewarding. The commom enemies are pretty good as well, and will also make you consider change your build to adapt to each area emeny type.

-- Progression/Mechanics - You still have the same relic system from EL but now with the addition of a proper equipment system that allows you equip acessories to improve your atributes and grant some bonus effects like more healing charges, a regen effect and more. Also the collectables that increases your HP and your relic slot size are back, pretty much the same way it was done in EL. Another new addition are two currencies, one used to upgrade the relics and another one to buy equipments and itens from a permanent shop.

-- Combat - Similar to EL, you equip specific spirits/homunculi in four button slots that will attack in your stead, each one corresponding to a different move. Here the combat feels more fluid and fast paced than the first game and everything works perfectly good. You will find different homunculi more effective in some especific combat situations, stimulating you to change your build often, although not 100% necessary. There's melee combat, ranged attacks, automatic attacks, coordenated moves and even two different parry systems that works very well. One very cool addtion to Ender Magnolia is the new status effects, burn, shock and freeze, each one giving you or the enemy different debuffs that both you and the enemies can infflict, creating even more depth to the combat possibilites

In a more personal note, I love video games and together with Ender Lilies, Ender Magnolia is one of the games that changed my life, it has everything I ever expect from a game and a metroidvania. In an age that video games became products, with generic formulas just to make profits, seeing a pure and sublime work of art like Ender Magnolia is revigorating.

ENDER MAGNOLIA is the Sequel to ENDER LILIES the same way Nier: Automata is the sequel to NIER. A shared world separated by hundreds of years, you need no previous knowledge to enjoy this game, though knowing does give some well deserved "oooo" moments. 

Gameplay consist of standard metroidvania powerups, difficult bosses, exploration, and build-building all refined to the razor's edge of perfection. The non-linear map makes getting a new skill or tool an absolute joy, searching for hidden paths rewarding, and fighting bosses, although tough (Most kill in 2-3 swipes) challenging,  but can be made easier by experimenting with your loadout. 
The map is well tuned to exploration, with custom pins, easy to read connectors, and fully explored indicators, 100%ing the game was actually enjoyable!

The story itself gradually unfolds as you "Attune" to the memories of various "Homunculi" who become your allies. Questions like, where is the line between homunculi and human? What constitutes as sentient? Where is the corruption coming from? Who is this sassy, lost child? Are all answered in time. 

All in all, if you enjoy Metroidvania's, you WILL like this game

A sequel that iterated upon everything great about the first game while improving on its shortcomings. 

Pros:
• Distinct art style with good use of color.
• OST is amazing from start to finish. Some songs have Nier Automata vibes, one is guitar-driven jazz rock, and the use of leitmotifs is really poignant.
• Certain attack animations change as you upgrade abilities.
• Almost all the abilities feel distinct and useful, significantly altering how gameplay feels (but always feeling good).
• The basic plot is serviceable, but knowing the first game's lore and reading ALL the flavor text is where it really shines.
• Characters are really good. Making your equipment / bosses separate characters with their own conversations was genius. It takes a less is more approach here and succeeds.
• Map is decent, though some levels have some terribly difficult rooms.
• Incredibly satisfying parries.
• Secret areas are a little easy to find, but still rewarding and satisfying.

Cons:
• Although the abilities are all really satisfying, I didn't feel encouraged to use my late-game skills. The alternate basic attack you get is right before the last area, for example, comes too late.
• Like Dark Souls 3 and Dark Souls 1, this game's lore is vastly improved if you play the first one. 

I would still give it a 9.5/10.

[h3] Headline [/h3]
Already excellent potentially top-tier Slay-the-Spire like, with some very compelling and notable improvements over the classic Slay template, such as far more generous opportunities to build your deck and tableau.

Visually beautiful and super slick playing deck-building turn-based card battler roguelite.

[h3] Highlights? [/h3]

[u] Gorgeous Visuals [/u]
This is some of the most beautiful 2d art seen within a deckbuilding roguelite, and the animations are wonderfully slick and pretty BUT they do not get in the way of gameplay i.e., you are not trapped watching fancy animations or cutscenes. Your time is respected here.

[u] Compelling and rich but unobtrusive lore and narrative [/u]
Unusually for the genre, your runs have a specific, defined purpose, and they take place in a *world* involving characters with a backstory, fighting against bosses with their own stories. You *can* ignore it, but you can also tap into it whenever you like.

[u] Highly rewarding run progression [/u]
This is *better* than in Slay. At every choice of encounter within a regular run you are offered a choice of 3, and each alternative will offer a different set of rewards e.g., cards, relics, max HP, HP recovery. So you have a LOT of control over how you evolve your tableau and deck. Also, whenever you decline a new card you get a small gold reward instead, so you are always getting something positive from a successful battle.

[u] Highly promising escalating difficulty & build varieties [/u]
There is an Ascension system in place, called “Feat of Glory”. This looks very likely to have the potential to provide, along with the 4 playable characters with highly varied powers and cards, lots and lots of enjoyable playtime. I am already at 50 hours and expecting at least double if not far more than that.

[u] Meta Progression [/u]
Offers the usual – new cards – but also unlocks story elements which are quite incredibly well written and interesting to review whenever you like to. For example, each time you fight a given boss, you will get a new page of their story, up to 5 in total. These tell you what those bosses are trying to do in the wider background story, and how they ended up fighting you. Some are rather funny, but in a highbrow fantasy way, rather than slapstick.

[h3] Caveats? [/h3]

[u] Initial Difficulty / Balance [/u]

Feels absolutely fine to me, but for less experienced players in the genre the current final boss might be a really, really tough challenge. Developers are already considering options for adjustments.

[u] Steam Deck UI / Text [/u]
I have not played on Steam Deck, but others that have report that the text in particular is just too small to comfortably play with. It seems very likely – given developer engagement and responsiveness – that this will be changed

Thunder Striker is a vertical scrolling shoot 'em up in the style of a Game Boy game.  It's a simple, classic shmup that despite a few gripes and glitches is fun.

The player's ship is equipped with a basic main forward attack.  There are two weapon upgrade that can be applied to the ship at the same time via pick ups.  The first adds a secondary attack of additional forward shot, homing missiles and spread shot.  Each with their pros and cons depending on the enemy types the player encounters.  The second modifies the primary shot or adds more bombs.  Both weapon systems can be powered up with additional pick ups.

The player also has limited use bombs at their disposal.   These work like most shooters, fire the bomb and gain invincibility for a few seconds.  I haven't played enough, but it also seems the bomb's effect is not the entire screen.  They also seem to be meant for use as defensive weapons.  I tried to spam bombs on the enemy, and it would allow it until the invincibility wore off or something.  

The game play is inspired by shooters of the late 80s/early 90s, but there are far more sprites without slow down or flickering than I believe an actual Game Boy could handle.  But only just barely.  Enemy patterns are simple, but still makes the game fun to play.  The only enemies I'm not a fan of are the ones that come from behind.  There's no shot capping, so even if your ship is flying over these enemies to hit them, that are still vulnerable.  More than a few times I've tired dashing over these enemies to destroy them before they can fire.  Only to be hit with projectiles as the enemy barely makes it on screen.

I'm not sure if it is a bug or a feature, but the player does not lose any bombs they had in their inventory upon losing a ship.  Speaking of glitches the game still seems to have a few.  Mostly just with sound, but the game currently feels a little buggy.  However, the bugginess doesn't really affect game play from what I have seen.  Just lessens the experience.

Thunder Striker is a good attempt at creating a modern black & white (well, green) handheld STG.  I'd like to see the program cleaned up a little more or the price a little lower.  However, it's a decent little game all the same.

Tested using Valve Index, oc RTX 3090, i9 10900K (10 cores/20 threads, 5.3 GHz), 32GB 3200 MHz, Win10 Pro. 

The game works fine with the Valve Index, but there is no finger tracking (like Maze Theory provided in Peaky Blinders). The game uses teleportation, there is no full locomotion. Also there is only snap turning. Generally you have no options but seated or room scale - this is a 1:1 Quest port explaining the lack of graphics settings. There is no MR content in the SteamVR version. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3287679709
Due to being a Quest port, performance is awesome - you can probably play this using an old GTX 970 just fine - and there may be some value for some users in that. I'm using an oc'ed RTX 3090 (40 tflops), about 20 times faster than Quest 3's phone gpu (Adreno 740 with about 2 tflops, also reduced by Meta to save battery). This means I'm getting solid 90 fps using an insane Index res 500% - that's 45 million pixels per frame combining both eyes (remember, 4K tv uses 8 mill pixels per frame, 8K tv uses 32 mill - to put 45 mill into perspective). 
Extreme res does come in handy to reduce jaggies, as this game has no settings for antialiasing. So do turn up res as much as possible, and PCVR will provide a sharp image quality with no jaggies - far beyond any Quest version, where jaggies are a great issue, here according to UploadVR: "It’s immediately apparent when playing on Quest 3 that its beautiful graphics are being impacted by some serious aliasing. This game has some hard angles as part of its architecture and a lot of contrast between light and dark areas, so the aliasing really shows through in most scenes".
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3287663844
Graphics are neither good nor bad - the game is cleverly designed to hide the low-poly environments. Textures are fine, some are high-res. There are no dynamic shadows, but some simple real-time lighting can be found. 

A npc made in 3D is your guide and helps communicate some story elements - but this is more or less a dead world. A voice-over instead of a mute npc guide would have been much better - much of what the guide is trying to communicate is lost, I still wonder exactly what devs tried to say with the ending of the game, lol. 

The puzzles are fun, and the game is rather easy - so coming from Riven VR, this is a walk in the park - but a cosy walk, and provides some nice relaxation. The 5 small chapters are not amazing, but repetitive - especially the last chapter 5 is way too easy and feels like made in a hurry just for the sake of making more content. The game generally is so easy, kids can play it too.

Controls work fine, but after having finished a level in seated mode, I have to move some small statue from one postion to another. This was not possible due to bad centering - the devs should fix this. A solution is to recenter using SteamVR, and that worked.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3287672384
In general the game is nicely polished, at least more than many other VR games, but controls could be slightly improved. I do not see why this game cannot support full locomotion with some added ability to teleport - and smooth turning. Some places you need to teleport from one side to another, but using a combo of full locomotion and teleport like in Alyx, controls could be improved. Graphics are not enhanced for PCVR - you get phoneVR graphics, but it works ok for this puzzle game when using tons of supersampling. 

For the game's current low price, I'd rate the game 6/10 overall, the best level (chapter 4) is 7/10. Many will probably be able to finish the game in 2 - 3 hours. Knowing the puzzles, the replayvalue might be very low. The game needs many more levels, and it feels like a small tech demo.

This review contains no story spoilers, or gameplay spoilers beyond the demo and an extended but tagged discussion of a mechanic in the first third of the game. 
TLDR: The opposite direction of adapting MMBN from OSFE, taking speed in terms of turn count rather than reactions. Try it out! Its demo lets you try out about 2-4 hours worth of the game for free, with save transfer. It's a top-notch game with plentiful difficulty options and lots to do, as well as great music and one of my favorite gimmicks in the genres!

Completed all of the base-game content, as well as a decent portion of post-release stuff. Despite what many reviewers might tell you, this game does actually take its Battle Network inspiration somewhat seriously, adopting a much faster pace than most other roguelike deckbuilders, but still having a turn based system. Don't expect the frantic nature of One Step From Eden, since you have all the time in the world to plan out your moves, meaning strategy is 100% the name of the game. However, just like Battle Network, your goal isn't just survival, it's blitzing foes down quickly as well.

To help you accomplish this goal, Card-en-Ciel has 4 systems in place that work together quite well.

1: Wild Cards. Ever pulled a dud hand in Battle Network or OSFE and wished you had that one extremely overpowered card just this once? Well, now you can! You can bring in a deck of Wild Cards and forge a single copy of one of your choice per turn in battle, letting you tip the scales of luck quite drastically, or even gain access to cards that you normally wouldn't be able to in that area! Keep in mind, though, Wild Cards are disposable per dungeon visit. Later on, you'll be able to carry enough Wild Cards to summon one every turn of combat, making them very reliable! I like this system a whole lot, and if you've played Wizard101, it might feel familiar to you, as it's very similar to Treasure Cards. Do keep in mind, however, that you can't forge a Wild Card if your hand's full, and that can be a recurring issue!

2: Card archetypes. Every roguelike deckbuilder's gotta have 'em. In Card-en-Ciel, they're built with interplay in mind. For an example, Banish does what you'd expect, removing a card from play for the rest of the fight. However, if the target card has Suspend, it'll ignore the Banish, allowing you to use Banish cards without risk. Alternatively, if the target card has Reboot and isn't a forged copy of a card, it'll both ignore the Banish and activate Reboot, which will create a duplicate of the Reboot card! You can hover over a card at any time to see very exact explanations of what each card's keywords do to other cards, and there were very few times where jank interactions really confused me.

3: Cheat Codes. Similarly to OSFE, CeC takes a modular approach to upgrading cards, where each card has a list of possible perks it can provide. These vary from boosting their damage or break, to reducing the cost, to reducing the cost while damaging you (this can be a benefit), to forging other cards, to boosting the damage or break of your next damage or break card, to adding entirely new keywords to the card! You need to keep the cheats on your cards in mind, as oftentimes they completely change how a card functions! Heck, there's even an archetype that lets you add cheats onto your cards in the middle of battle! All copies of a card in play will continue to have the same cheats for the whole fight, whether they're in the discard or draw piles, or even if you forge another copy! You can get more permanent cheats on cards by either winning fights, or getting additional copies of the card that have cheats.

4: Muses. Ever since Mega Man Zero and Azure Striker Gunvolt released, Inti Creates has locked in on their specialty being "mecha and girls". And given this game's timely release on Lumen singer Megu Sakuragawa's 36th birthday, it's quite clear from the onset that they were aiming for a LOT of the latter. When you touch down in a dungeon, you're greeted with a Muse, labelled with an activation condition and an effect. These replace your Artifacts from OSFE or Relics from StS, your primary source of passive effects. Unlike those, [b]ALL[/b] Muses have an activation condition. Whether that be as simple as "Use 4 0-cost cards." or as specific as "Use 2 different sets of identical cards in one turn.", they all have varying degrees of reward for their difficulty of activation. With over 40 to collect, as well as cheats for them, you'll be hearing new tunes for a long time, and several of them will get stuck in your head. In addition to their built-in perks, they also give you a Skill Point to temporarily ramp up the power a single card.

Speaking of, turns work in a subturn system, where each action ticks a counter down on all enemies before they take their next action, whether it be attacking, assisting other enemies, placing down hazardous terrain, messing with your hand, or otherwise hindering you. Enemies can run out of actions, just like you can. However, as mentioned earlier, you're scored at the end of each dungeon based on how many full turns you took to complete the dungeon, as well how many high-erosion panels you cleared out, and whether you fought the optional superboss in each one. This incentivizes you to take on more difficult foes and rush into more complicated fights to get a higher rank, and you want higher ranks, as getting higher ranks means access to higher difficulties in the same dungeon which means you can go for higher ranks in those difficulties to eventually go for the 3 Medal score in Hard +9 Difficulty. As you scale up in difficulty, however, each dungeon introduces more and more mechanics, meaning you won't get too bored of the same place too quickly. And if you're good enough, you can clear out each dungeon in 4 trips: One for Normal, one for Hard +3, one for +6, and one for +9. Good luck with that, as some of these dungeons really require that you step outside your comfort zone and strategize to come out on top (or get really lucky).

Minor gameplay-only spoilers: [spoiler]Grand Battle Dungeons are one of the highlights of the game for me, though. They take most of the above and kick it all up to 11 by introducing 3 important rules. 
Rule 1: You bring in a deck consisting of every single card in your stock, meaning every card you've encountered on your journey, ever. This makes it dangerously inconsistent, but also considering the archetypes are all built around each other, this is also dangerously powerful.
Rule 2: You bring in every muse you've ever encountered as well, and can activate all of them. This also means you have a steady stream of Skill Points to wreak havok with.
Rule 3: Your cards are your HP. Every time you take damage, you drop cards. Every time you restore HP, you regain them. Your HP cap is your total card count. There's a limit to how many of each card you can bring in, so you don't end up with a deck of 600 Blade cards.
This all culminates in a chaotic storm of strategizing around what each and every tool you've encountered is capable of at all times, which gets more and more satisfying as you gain more and more muses and cool cards and learn new card interactions. Overall, a massive highlight of the game, and a gimmick I wouldn't mind seeing parroted in other games.[/spoiler]

As a wrap-up, quickfire notes:
PvP: Cool idea, seems like a fun thing to do with friends who know the game about as much as you do, I don't exactly have that. Also dominated by 0 Cost.
Daily Dungeons: Handled quite well, incorporating the difficulty options to encourages you to weigh your options on whether you want to go all in on a +9 gambit and risk getting blown away, or lower the challenge for a surefire path to victory?
Update content: From what I've done, the update content is REALLY good.

Pretty fun! A roguelike deckbuilder with a 3x3 Battle Network-like grid,  but rather than the expected MMBN reflex test it's fully turn-based and about carefully planning your moves.  Fulfilling certain conditions in battle will summon a "Muse" that provides a vocal track(and there's like 20+ of them, some even in English) and sends whatever mechanic you're currently abusing into overdrive, and with good deckbuilding you can end up with some infinitely handlooping monstrosity that never runs out of gas(the higher difficulties are actually balanced around this)

The cards you have to pick from tend to naturally synergize with whatever Muses are available in the current dungeon, not that it's brainless but just in the sense that the random selection isn't clogged up with completely unusuable crap, something I wish more roguelikes did. there's a LOT of cards within each archetype and there's usually 2-3 keywords to choose from(and they sometimes synergize into each-other) so there's still a lot of strategy involved.  

You can technically fight battles endlessly to make an uber deck but you're scored/rewarded on how many turns you take so you have to find a balance between fighting to build your deck(your initial deck is not going to do crap for long) and hoofing it to the end, and making sure your deck is as degenerate as possible on every step so you're ending fights as quickly as possible.

The story is a bunch of nothing but it's a fairly neat grand tour of a frankly insane(and like 70%ish fictional with a mix of completely original ideas, references and stand-ins for what the director has worked on before) development history. You enter dungeon, discuss the game and flirt with your cyber-gf, then fight whoever the protagonist is. The database function is interesting though, providing info about the real games and what is essentially design documents for the fake ones. Some cool ideas there.

Anyway it was a good time, I recommend it.

Quester: Osaka is a followup to Quester both of which are fast-paced turn-based Dungeon Crawlers that have you lead a team of the titular Questers through the post-apocalyptic underground ruins of various Japanese cities. Last time it was Tokyo, this time it's Osaka! So, how does this journey fare?

Short Answer: If you liked Quester in Tokyo, you'll find much to love in Osaka and then some.

Long Answer: Osaka builds on top of what worked in Tokyo but also demands more of the player.

You are given more starting options in Osaka with 5 themed teams each with different strengths and weaknesses. Many of the Questers return from the previous game but are joined a few Osaka denizens as well. Most of the gear returns from base Quester with a few tweaks such as Party-Wide Barriers costing Fuel. The tight gameplay loop from the first is largely unchanged with a few tweaks made to accommodate Osaka's new feature: water traversal. You can go onto the water via Piers and use it to travel across rivers and onto islands. Sometimes this is the best way to escape from being chased down by a pack of enemies, other times you'll get to the pier and find it crowded by aquatic enemies from all sides (enemy density seems a lot higher in Osaka). The small difference of water travel costing 1 more fuel makes a huge impact in late game and I was pleasantly surprised to see it come up while moving through those last couple areas.

I really enjoyed the map design of Osaka. It's a lot more organic and willing to let the player take different paths than its predecessor. There seems to be a design pillar of almost never obligating a player to have to find a key to open a Gate as there are usually enough paths around them. Keys exist mostly to open up shortcuts letting you use your Fuel more effectively on dungeon excursions. Boss monsters serve as the actual hard gates both in terms of party level (as you need to beat bosses to increase your level cap) and in terms of traversal (they are often blocking the passage between you and the next area). I was less enthusiastic about some of the new enemy additions in Osaka which while adding more variety to combat do tend to have moves that either ignore Hate priority and beeline for whoever has lowest HP or drain HP on hit or keep healing their allies out of range. They are more taxing and can cause a bit of frustration by stretching out fights you already thought were in the bag. The new bosses were quite enjoyable with the Minami Emperor being among my favourite fights in the game.

Osaka tries to have more narrative beats by including a familiar looking Navigator character on your phone. These are mostly welcome as they give more context to the USB lore entries that you find and also serve as a nice sandwich for each boss fight (going up to the boss you are given some hints on its capabilities and after the boss you get some details on how to cook them and yes, the Dungeon Meshi influence is clear). The Navigator did grow on me over time and so I was surprised with where the game went with the ending. Definitely more memorable than its predecessor and hopefully a sign that they want to build on this aspect with each game.

Overall, I really enjoyed playing Quester: Osaka. It felt like it reasonably builds on top of the experience of the base Quester game and has teeth which pressure the player in different ways. I really look forward to where Quester goes next from here. Would be happy to play through the metro dungeons of more cities if the devs are also looking to change up how map traversal and how classes and gear works with each one (if we are still in Japan: Kyoto, Nagoya, and Fukuoka come to mind and if the devs want to venture outside: New York, London, Berlin, Moscow, Shanghai could be great too).

If I had a few points of criticism they would be:

- Its clear that the game was machine-translated for English and while that doesn't hinder your experience in a major way you will often run into gear and skill descriptions that are a bit off. For example, some items have the Strength+ trait but there is no attribute called Strength (maybe they meant Vitality or Melee?) and others that have the Defense+ trait but there is no matching attribute (there is one called Guard). There are also multiple message boxes where you see colour tags which have not been closed which might be a result of running a JSON file through a machine translator and importing it back into the game. You do eventually get the hang of how everything works but it is clear that a better localisation is necessary.

- The UI while stylish in its presentation does fail a bit when it comes to Inventory menus. They give you sort options, however, Weapons of all types have the same icons and colour (despite a rarity system being in place) can only be distinguished by their name which gets a little cumbersome at endgame when you have 16 pages of items to shift through. It would also be nice to be able to mark equipment as Favorites or Junk so you can disassemble multiple items at once and not risk disassembling something your party uses. Also for Level Ups, the ability to do multiple level ups on one UI window by using a bar to let the player determine how many Levels they want to boost a character and the estimated Material Cost.

Hope this review was helpful and leads you to check out this awesome little game :)

Gameplay-wise, the modern series can roughly be divided into three kinds of games: the original duology with the bump combat system, the early games with sprite art and some platforming elements (Napishtim, Origins and Fhelgana), and then the modern fully 3D games with a three-character-party system which may or may not have some platforming elements.

This one is the first entry since Ys Seven that changes the gameplay enough that it no longer quite fits with the previous games. Now instead of a three character party, it's just a duo and sailing is a big part of the game so that, instead of a village like in Ys VIII or an inn like in Ys IX, your "home base" is the ship itself.

Fishing, crafting, cooking, upgrading gear, recruiting NPC's to offer services in your home base, side quests, reporting mapping and other exploration-related stuff, and other familiar mechanics from the immediate prequels are present here with a few tweaks. 

As for the story, this one goes back to Adol's early days adventuring with Dogi just after the events of Ys I & II as they sail along with Dr. Flair in search of new adventures and find themselves stranded in an unfamiliar island, though not because of the usual shipwreck. This time, it's due to a pirate raid. And of course, Adol almost immediately finds himself in the middle of some "chosen one" B.S. when a mysterious voice talking to him through a sea shell apparently bestows upon him the ability to wield mana, which allows him to kill the strange undead monsters that soon start attacking the settlements.

If you liked Ys VIII and Ys IX, you'll probably like this one because it resembles them a lot. My only complaint is that, at least before you manage to upgrade it a bit, your ship is slow AF and the map of the region is huge. Once the story picked up some steam I really liked it. It felt like familiar without being a re-tread of a previous game, and the new co-protagonist Karja grew on me a lot as her character arc unfolded, so that by the end of the game I liked her just as much as I like my boys Adol and Dogi.

I enjoyed the game and I really like that there are no romantic undertones in the relationship between the 2 main characters. Adol having a sister is way more interesting than having a romantic interest.

From the developer of the acclaimed adventures “Blood Nova” and “Twilight Oracle”, comes a new (or in fact renewed) retro-adventure in text-parser style. “Tachyon Dreams” puts you in the shoes of a space dishwasher named Dodger, who finds himself in the midst of an adventure that will decide the future (and past, even) of entire civilizations – though despite the epic scope of the story, the game itself is short and rather minimalistic. It is most resembling to the early Sierra adventures, particularly the first three Space Quests, except here the atmosphere is not that much humorous, rather I had a feeling of light melancholy from it. Game is done in EGA graphics that is traditional for this subgenre, with well-designed scenes, and also according to tradition there is almost no music with the exception of title screen and end credits. Text parser is quite clever and recognizes wide range of synonyms, so you shouldn’t have any trouble with getting stuck on trying to figure the right commands. “Tachyon Dreams” feels like an excursion back into the time where games like this were pinnacle of adventure gaming, and manages to convey the atmosphere and fun that gamers at that time had with these.

There's also an arena that you can arm gladiators with your creations to see how they fare in combat.  It's still early access so there are still some issues, but nothing game breaking.  The developer is very responsive in the discussion forum on steam, and they are actively working on bug fixes and improvements.

The biggest complaint I've seen is there is a part of the game where you can make a choice, that will result in you dying the next time you sleep, and some very unlucky people didn't have a save from before making that choice which required them to start over.  Also, there is a heavy weapon design that is extremely overpowered in the arena to the point where it doesn't feel intended by the developers.

But as is, the game is great, and I'm really looking forward to future updates.

I had a bad experience and requested a refund but that doesn't mean everyone will. The core gameplay of making weapons at the smithy is pretty satisfying. It's fun to go from ores all the way to a fully functioning weapon. Where the game fell apart for me was really just everything else which I will list below in pros/cons:

Pros:
- Weapon smithing is very satisfying
- There is a small mine you can go to to get ores which was kind of cool

Cons:
- Typos everywhere
- Shop signs are written in gibberish and you need to rely on logos to tell what's what
- Relationship bonuses are repeatable over and over in the same conversations. Can you even check how good your relationship with an npc is? Does it even matter?
- Dialog seems like an after-thought and feels really thin. NPCs have very weird reactions to dialog choices sometimes and there's a ton of swearing for no reason
- Your character cannot jump
- If you don't pay the landlord in the beginning as a dialog option, it can just end the game and make you start over entirely which is what happened to me. I thought it was like an "edgy" dialog option because she was a real jerk and other npcs were making fun of me for saying I would pay rent like she asked, so I decided to say I wouldn't pay and the game just ended and made me restart from the beginning. What?

Summary:
The core mechanic of blacksmithing is a lot of fun. It is very satisfying to make a weapon as high quality as you can get it and to then sell it for profit. Everything else in this game seems very thin, like they were trying to just add anything and everything to the game once the blacksmithing mechanic was completed. Everything else just seems like it was randomly dropped in there later on in some update or something and sometimes can seem out of place.

TLDR;
Get the game for the blacksmithing, everything else you'll either really enjoy or just be annoyed by.

A Unique and Challenging Psychological Horror Puzzle Game!

If you’re a fan of psychological horror puzzles, this game is definitely worth checking out! It’s got such a unique concept compared to other games in the genre. Instead of simply going from point A to point B, you’ll be on the lookout for anomalies, and your next move depends on whether or not you spot them. The key mechanic of choosing the right elevator based on the anomalies you encounter is a brilliant twist that keeps you on edge throughout the game.

What really stands out is how challenging it is. It’s definitely one of the more difficult ones I’ve played in the genre, and that just makes the sense of accomplishment after solving a puzzle even better. It’s not just about surviving – it’s about thinking critically and carefully observing your environment.

I love how the game keeps things fresh with its different styles and puzzles. It’s one of those games where each new challenge feels unique, and that really helps it stand out in a sea of horror puzzle games. Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys a psychological twist with their puzzles!
