[b]Grub Truck[/b] isn't a great game, but it is arguably the best food truck-themed management sim available on Steam as of November 2024.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
You start by selecting one of several premade characters (each with their own goals, backstories, and unlockable perks), taking out a loan, kitting out your first food truck with secondhand appliances, and buying supplies.  From there, you [strike]take over the city[/strike] launch your food truck empire!

During the day, you serve customers by moving food from the fridge to your limited-slot tray, then placing the food in the correct appliance, waiting until it cooks, and moving to the window to fill orders. Successful orders increase your reputation, which then unlocks new menu items and neighborhoods.  After hours, you can expand your fleet of food trucks, set them up, hire managers, purchase supplies, etc.

[h3]Review[/h3]
[b]Grub Truck[/b]'s gameplay loop is repetitive but all chill vibes, and the decorating mechanics are surprisingly flexible.  I've spent more time than I care to admit lining up salt and pepper shakers [i]just so[/i], and have yet to turn down the music.

That said, the game is rough around the edges.  The UI looks like it was created in Microsoft Paint; the world, characters, and customers are all Synty Studios Polygons (which is fine, but I'm personally tired of seeing these same assets everywhere); and the mechanics are pretty bare-bones.  Cooking is more about inventory management than anything that feels like cooking in a food truck, and the camera moves strangely between appliances. Everything from hiring managers to ordering supplies is extremely simple, which likely appeals to more relaxed gamers but - as a stress junkie who has been playing management sims for 20-odd years - I feel that I've seen everything this game has to offer in ~2 hours total playtime.  

[h3]Recommendation[/h3]
I recommend this if you're looking for an easy business simulation game to kick back with for a few hours, or really want to run a food truck.  I don't recommend this if you were particularly interested in decorating or cooking, if you want a crunchy-ish business sim, or if you're looking for an artsty indie game.

I understand it's not supposed to be an action game where you're mowing down enemies, but its not horror-survival either. There is no healing or inventory management as far as I can tell. This game has been consistently updated since release in Early Access, plus it's from Charm Games, a VR dev with a history of not missing (Form, Twilight Path, Burn it with Fire VR). The good news is that the price was reduced to $11.99 USD and I bought this game and I think the price matches the value currently with the latest build (update 15). I had fun playing this game. It's a rogue-like arena combat game with a SUPERHOT time slow mechanic. Basically, whenever you move, enemies move. 

This game is melee and magic based. So you'll be swinging your magic wand which turns into a sword when swinging, as well as casting spells and ultimates. Currently, you have fire, lighting, and ice spell variations available. You pick different paths on a board with varying degrees of difficulties, as well as different objectives. 

Game is running on the Unreal Engine 5.1. On my RTX 3080, I was getting mostly 90 fps, but I did notice some frame rate drops, and my game did crash once during my 1.4 hours on record. I'm not sure what I can say about this game that others won't have beaten me to. Praise for the art style, the gameplay, the writing, the soundtrack - every aspect here [i]is[/i] great, but just ranting about that is insufficient. This game is more than the sum of its parts. It comes together beautifully; Ace Attorney's flow with Danganronpa's flare into a downright beautiful crossbread.

But that's all kinda rote still. Just buzz and hype. And having just played Ep 1, I want to try and make this review something more sincere. So I'm going to praise something specific, and I personally really like. Morgan's dedication to her job.

I'm used to works that star a defence attorney going out of their way to stress their 'heroic' attributes. They're a defender of the innocent! A champion for what's right! And while that's flattering, it kinda occludes the necessity of the profession. We just see them defending clearly innocent people. They're 'guardians of the truth', right?

It feels like in these works, 'defense attorney' has become divorced from the actual job, and is substituted for 'hero'. If one of these attorneys used dishonourable tactics, fans would be shocked! If they represented someone who might be a criminal, they'd be scandalized. The representation's moved away from the actual career and showing why it's so important.

After works like that, it's refreshing to see an attorney of an older, truer nature. Someone who bloody well defends their client, and doesn't need to pontificate about the truth or righteousness of that. Calling Morgan 'a cyberpunk Horace Rumpole' is a *crippling* simplification of her character, but I see in her some of what I saw in him. Determination. Bloody mindedness. (Perhaps even principle? We'll see) Drawing that analogy is the highest mark of respect I can give, both to her as a character, and to this game's writing in general. 

Eagerly awaiting more. If I'm ever in London with my Steam Deck, I'll try to take a picture of the title screen from the Old Bailey.

this has definitely scratched the itch of mystery writing that I've been looking for for a while, and while some lines of logic did trip me up a bit (the blind system could be a little more present on how much you could be penalized), overall it's tight enough to follow through with some very good cases. excited for the future!

there is no character quite like Morgan, i fell in love immediately in ep 0, and episode 1 had me falling in love with her every single scene.

i could write a dissertation on how astonishingly talented and passionate this team is in every project they put out, and i'm at the ready for what's next.

thank you, nth Circle

Though, even describing it as such feels reductive. This is a smart, prescient story with oodles of charming character writing. The commentary about our post-truth world feels like a bullseye hit, and Serra might be my favourite assistant in any of these games, and the hints at her and Morgan's shared history, and its implications, like a shot to the heart. Of the Devil is a genuinely great mystery game. Morgan is such a fun and unique protagonist, and a really interesting lens through which to present the world. The game has such a strong sense of style, which is used really smartly to feed back into the narrative. The cut-ins, cut-aways, fade-outs, etc. all contribute to building the atmosphere, show how Morgan is thinking at a given moment, or just add emphasis to individual lines. It's all really cohesive, but more importantly it's really fun. I truly was never bored while watching things play out.

The setting and genre combination (ace attorney-like cyberpunk) make for a really interesting combination for a story, and a lot of that is due to the fact the team clearly did a lot of research into the legal system (IIRC the main writer came up with the concept while studying for some sort of law exam). That and the fact it's murder mystery results in a very grounded noir-style take on cyberpunk that adds a lot to the story. 

Plus the cast is stacked with terrible awful evil women who are nasty little freaks.

This game absolutely charmed me, I fell in love with the demo and couldn't wait for episode 1 to come out when it was teased that playtesting was happening.
It's nothing short of an amazing visual novel created in unity with 3d spaces and 2d character sprites, but even with the distinction between the two, you'd think they clash, but they fit together very well in a Danganronpa type of style.

Something this game perfected within my tastes is ANATOMICAL ACCURACY, it was subtle, but being a med student in training I picked up on a lot of things my friends didn't pick up on since they don't know a lick of anatomy; but the grey matter (myelinated neurons) lobotomy reference at the end of episode 1? loved it, the neuron diagram? loved it, the referencing of the 3 layers of spine meninges cracking like a soda can? Peak. You could tell every single anatomical thing in this game was researched and fact checked, along with all the legal ploys. The game doesn't hide how well made and well researched it is at any point. From the chemical compositions to the world building, this game will not hesitate to make you fall in love with each and every character and it's very strikingly funny humor. Other games have the "character we made solely for you to hate and be happy you beat them because they're the bad guy we want you to hate", but all the villains in this game are well written, have actual character and reasoning in them.
Even the ADDS and androids are well explored, in the game you find out what's in their blood, how they function, what their muscles and hair are made of; it's the little details of this game you come to love and appreciate.

The additional content and concept art is nothing short of amazing (specifically the MS paint concept map art, I see you devs, they're kind of funny to look at seeing the full 3d maps now, especially Evan Dawes industrial room and Morgan's apartment)

But all in all, the game is worth the $10, even though I got it on sale for $8.99, I highly recommend buying this game and playing it for yourself, you really get a feel for the dialogue, the characters, and how they interact. It really puts the player into the moment and makes them feel like Morgan.

Review through Episode 0 and Episode 1:  

As other reviewers have said, game is very stylish, has ace attorney adjacent gameplay mechanics, set in engaging sci-fi/cyberpunk setting.  Highly recommend.

Additional notes:  Episode 0 should be played before episode 1.  Episodes 0+1 combined feel like a relatively complete story, so even if episode 2 never releases episodes 0+1 are still fully worth experiencing.  
Relative to most Ace Attorney games, I think more time is spent in the "investigation" segments and less time in drawn out courtroom sequences, at least if you engage with fully searching areas and reading glossary/articles.  In episode 1 I personally enjoyed the investigation segments (great dialogue and world building) more than the courtroom segments so that wasn't a problem.

Genuinely, this is an incredibly written and styled game.

The world building is very in depth, but in a way that always loops back into the themes and story beats the game wants you to pay attention to. On top of that, it is a very well researched game. Both in terms of the functions of a cyberpunk society it imagines, and also just the act of looking up things like toxicology and the court system. The story knows how to twist these things to make an exciting story, but also keep it grounded and reasonable within the setting itself. It earns its flair if that's the kinda thing you're concerned about. The cast has a ton of character and charm; even characters I thought would be one note generally had more going on to them, then you'd first expect.

And speaking of flair, the art is awesome too. The 3D style merging with the 2D sprites looks great, and the entire thing just has a very bright, dirty neon feel to it. Its really foreboding sometimes when you look at a megs HQ to a dark alley. Its got a ton of visual influences and reference to other games in it's genre and other media, but it wears all those influences so nonchalantly and re-imagines them so well it always feels like its own thing. Lots of quirky references, the game knows what inspired it and wears it with pride.

I played on Highroller mode and it was a good amount of fun. Theres enough little tricks and traps to keep you on your toes, and while I didn't end up losing throughout the run, there were definitely moments where I could've. It really adds more weight to the trials, and I'd highly recommend it. Just make sure you click all the lore for chips, you dirty bird.

Over all, great game. If you like detective games, you'll like it. If you like stylistic anime games, you'll like it. If you like good cyberpunk story writing, you'll like this. If you like all of these things, you're about to feast. Buy it now its cheap as hell even off sale.

I’m giving this game a thumbs up since it’s still in early access, but it does have some issues. The concept could be cool if the game gets more polish in the areas listed below. A game set in a procedural city where you shoot zombie hordes could be a lot of fun, but in its current launch version, it feels very basic.

As far as I can tell, zombies spawn sporadically, you have a single gun (a pistol), and the gameplay revolves around shooting them and picking up ammo and health scattered on the ground. In its current state, I think the price should be around $3–$5, but I understand charging a bit more due to Steam taking 30–50% of the revenue.

Things That Need Updates the Most:
Sound Design
This needs a complete revamp. Please add city sounds, improved zombie sounds, and more detailed shooting effects—for example, shooting glass should sound like shattering glass. Add footsteps and other environmental effects for better immersion.

Gunplay/Combat
Add more guns and make pickups easier to spot by highlighting them, similar to what Apex Legends does. Implement "physical materials" (the technical term) to enable different effects and sounds when shooting various surfaces. Please include a melee option—I ran out of ammo at one point and died. Additionally, the player falls through the floor when they die, which needs fixing.

Quests
I found one NPC, but she didn’t give me a quest. Please add objective text and markers, along with a tutorial and more guidance on how to progress in the game. All I could figure out intuitively was shooting zombies and running around the procedural map.

Performance
Performance is actually really good. Usually, games like this are unoptimized since they’re often a developer’s first attempt. If you add more content, please try to maintain the current frame rates.

Graphics

Menus

Monsters of Mican is what you get when you take the gameplay and character building of Might and Magic 6-7, marinade it in Diablo-like loot gathering and then drown it in an ocean of endaringly silly humour with exceptionally mismatched graphics and music.

The resulting game looks like a joke. And it is - pretty much every monster is based on a stupid pun: a flying sandwich with magical abilities is called a Sandwitch. A brigand with a porcine face is called a Pigand. Many a time you will roll your eyes at the stupidity of the puns.

Of particular note are the sound effects. Most are spoken word. Meaning that when you swing a sword, the sound it makes is the developer shouting SWISH, throw a fireball he yells FROOOSH! It is absolutely and astoundingly silly.

And I love it. Despite all of this, the game is shockingly good, even for a very old-school RPG player such as myself. The monsters may be silly, but there is a completely crazy number of different enemy types, each with different abilities ranging from attacks to buffs, heals and debuffs, with many encounters requiring much preparation and strategy to beat. Character building is also very enjoyable. Unlike the older MM titles, loot is mostly randomised and equipment can spawn with different properties, allowing you to bring a highly diverse crew into the dungeon. Leveling up is fast and enjoyable as well, making improving your party feel very rewarding.

I highly recommend Monsters of Mican for fans of the old-school Might and Magic games, although you may need a somewhat silly sense of humour to get the most out of it.

"Mom, look at this 3D baguette with a hat."

I’m only an hour into Shadowgate 2, and I’ve already encountered game-breaking bugs and graphical issues. While I expect these to be patched eventually and can overlook them to some extent, my bigger concern is that this game simply doesn’t feel like Shadowgate.

I loved what they did with the remake of the original Shadowgate, but this sequel is nothing like that. Instead, it feels more like a mobile game—something I’d expect to play on my iPad—rather than a proper continuation of the series. It seems to be attempting a blend of Legend of Grimrock and Wizardry, but it executes that style poorly.

The interface is both overly simplistic and frustratingly clumsy, making interactions feel tedious rather than intuitive. The biggest issue, however, is the combat. Battles are frustrating, even when you know exactly what to do. The difficulty feels poorly balanced—why even have hit points if I’m reduced to 5/100 after every fight? Most games ramp up difficulty gradually, but Shadowgate 2 throws players into punishing encounters right from the start. This will likely turn off newcomers to the series.

That said, I don’t want to be entirely negative. One thing I do appreciate so far is the puzzles. While they aren’t on the same level as Shadowgate, they are at least decent.

Overall, this isn’t what I was expecting or hoping for in a Shadowgate sequel. Even if the bugs and graphical issues are fixed, the core game play choices may still leave longtime fans disappointed.

Due to the low price and the reasonably stable performance, I would give it a slight recommendation for fans. Be careful: there are supposed to be some serious bugs. If the game was actually polished-- even in its current state-- mostly free of bugs, egregious typos, and careless mistakes, I would be able to recommend the game. But it's not, so I can't.

Pros:
-Very different from SG 1; similar to Mines of Mythrok.
-Dragon Quest style combat.
-Music is solid, but it's not inspired the way SG64's was, and it's basically just 2 tracks through the entire game.
-Return of some bits of lore from Shadowgate series (not much....) and an attempt at Shadowgate Rising (another bad one).

Cons:
-MULTIPLE GAME BREAKING BUGS-- so far I was softlocked at [spoiler]the Djinn's first riddle solution[/spoiler] and broken save/load bugs. HUGE list of bugs-- was stymied and locked out of progression multiple times, including in the last stage. It's a bad look for a puzzle game to leave you more puzzled by broken mechanics than its actual puzzles.

-Very different from SG 1; similar to Mines of Mythrok, but also uninspired. The environments never feel like Shadowgate. Even the closest we see to any reference to the Circle of Twelve looks like some generic Unity asset.

-Outsourced devs-- if you look at their recent works it's all mid. It shows here, too.

-Turn based RPG combat that becomes a passionless recital of telegraphed moves, which is a weird step back, even if interesting at times.

-Simplified actions-- you can take and use items, but that's all.

-I didn't know SG64 was a stylistic choice we'd have to live with in every 3-D Shadowgate-- these assets look terrible. Did you think a game in 2025 would be released with a bones texture pasted on a geometric shape? I sure didn't see that in my 2025 bingo.

-No explanation of changing targeting on bosses when it's crucial by your second fight. 

-UI elements are missing or just omnipresent to annoyance. No need to see Raven all the time or one of TWO equipable items. Similar, it'd been nice to know, being that the graphics don't necessarily indicate, if you're in the present with your chrono orb or another timeline.

-The game fights you playing it the entire way-- whether it's trying to scroll through your list of spells or slowly walk amongst the mostly empty environment in which you must be 3 feet tall.

-The way the devs try to build in storytelling lore is immersion-breaking at best and insipid at worst; SG64, Beyond Shadowgate, and Shadowgate would never let you walk through a library without the capability to read a book. This feels extra silly being that your character just suddenly remembers random tales relevant to upcoming fights. In past SG, you'd read a library, and the correct answer was in the pile of books in the library along with 20 world-building red herrings. Instead, the tales are basically word salads to telegraph fights, and that's all it comes down to.

-The possibility of any actual ambiance this game could have given is ruined by static monsters standing around, which especially ruins immersion at the end of the game.
-Actually engaging with Yorick makes the game a chore, as he simply tells you what to do without any further inspiration. But the game is so featureless you feel starved for content if you don't engage with Yorick. Yorick's best voice lines are for when you die, because playing this game makes you want to kill yourself.

-Which leads me to my final issue, the castle is not actually deadly until the final stage, and even then, it's a few pitfall traps. This is a shallow rendition of the allure the Shadowgate franchise holds over players, and a travesty. Most all of the memes this franchise hold are in the deaths you can face. But nothing in these environments feels living in the first place at all. Not the monsters, not the characters, not the castle, especially. And the whole point of this franchise is that you're in a LIVING castle.

Ancient evils are stirring again in the castle Shadowgate. Sorceress Raven, the great, great  granddaughter of wizard Lakmir, enters the ancient castle the see if she can fix the situation.

Shadowgate 2 is, at heart, a puzzle game, just like the original was and the 2014 remake and the rather fantastic 2024 Beyond Shadowgate. But unlike the previous entries to the series, Shadowgate 2 adds turn based combat into the mix. The combat is, however, more of a puzzle rather than test of raw strength.

During her stroll through the castle, Raven is at times recalling stories she has heard in the past. These stories are not mere flavor text, they are clues on how you should best proceed in the various battles on her way. 

Besides monsters, Raven's exploration is halted by other dilemmas as well. Generally, these puzzles are pretty easy.  Solving some of these puzzles do require her to travel in past on an occasion, luckily she can do it with her grandfathers magical orb. And it's not only the puzzles that need time travelling, some monsters need a little time warp as well.

Magic is also important part of the story. In the beginning, Raven knows only a handful of spells, but after every battle her powers grow a bit more, unlocking new magic. Then there's the Djinn, who gives her riddles to solve in for exchange of new powers. 

Another huge difference in between the previous games and Shadowgate 2 are the graphics and game play. Shadowgate 2 is a real time 3D title, played from 1st person perspective.  This does cause some issues in some locations, which just feel a bit empty and at times even a bit boring and bland.

The music is just as good as it has been on the previous games. The voice acting is decent as well. 

Shadowgate 2 might not be as good of a game as the previous entries in the series, it is relatively flawed in terms of game play and puzzles. but it's still fun enough of a puzzle adventure with some okay battle scenes in the mix, if you keep your expectations in check.

I'm going with a solid yes on this one. It adds something unique when compared to Factorio/DSP/Satisfactory. Quick, intuitive controls for building lines and loops. It becomes a bit more of the programming side of things where you are going to need to configure gates to control/automate worker production/movement/job assignment. I was really worried about the worker death aspect when I read that. i want to automate things and increase the network, not worry about attrition, so I was thrilled when I realized that automating the movement with gates was the primary focus of the network, and when setup properly, your worker population maintains a nice balance.

I found the implementation of QoL (Quality of Life) features to be insufficient.
One major issue is the lack of clarity regarding the unlock progression. It is unclear which unlock leads to the next, and at the very least, a visual representation of the unlock tree along with its costs would be helpful. Many times, I attempted to unlock a specific feature only to realize that the branches were not connected or that I needed a different unlock currency than I currently had.

Another frustrating aspect is the automatic snapping of lines. This often results in unintended connections, and the only way to fix it is to redraw the lines manually. While snapping can be convenient, unintended snapping is more of a hindrance than a help.

Additionally, the statistical data is difficult to interpret, making it challenging to identify problems when encountering issues. This contributes to the game’s overall difficulty in an unintentional way. Most problems arise when a resource deposit is depleted, causing resource acquisition to drop to zero. Allowing lines to pass through resource deposits could mitigate this issue to some extent.

Another problem is the scattering of resources when an ant carrying them dies. Other ants may pick them up unintentionally, causing congestion near facilities as they stop unexpectedly, blocking others from moving. While this can be managed using gates or trash bins, setting up multiple of these structures is tedious. Furthermore, the game lacks both a blueprint feature and a copy-and-paste function, making it even more cumbersome to build efficiently.

Screen navigation with WASD is also very slow. Since moving between islands is a frequent necessity, the sluggish camera movement quickly becomes tedious.

The game's main missions have an inconsistent level of granularity, with some phases being extremely detailed while others are quite broad. This inconsistency stands out.

At its core, this game is more about resource management than automation. Compared to games that require strict resource management, it feels slightly more forgiving, but if you approach it as an automation game, the difficulty will likely take you by surprise.

One major difficulty early on is the scarcity of glass and fiber. Fiber becomes more abundant as you unlock more islands, but depending on your progression, you might struggle to obtain it in time. Glass, however, is an even bigger problem—it is required in significant quantities, yet the available supply is surprisingly low. I believe that increasing resource availability by at least two to three times would result in a more balanced difficulty.

Another surprising aspect is how resource nodes are outright destroyed when placing buildings. This leads to pure resource loss, serving only to make the game harder. Let me give a little context about the writer here: Factorio, or more specifically heavily modded Factorio, is by far and away my GOAT game. But I have bounced off of every other factory game I have tried, including Satisfactory, Foundry, and Final Factory. I also bounced off of Oxygen Not Included (debatable whether that one is a factory game), although it took dozens of hours for that one. The point is that I like factory games in general, and am generally interested in finding another one that I like, but I am picky about them, so there is a good chance that I am pickier than you.

The basic gameplay here is mostly ordinary factory builder fare: collect materials to build structures and research technologies that open up new materials, structures, and technologies. There are two main gimmicks. The first gimmick is that tasks that in a game like Factorio would be handled by the player character, a belt, an inserter, or a robot, are handeld by your little robot ants moving around on trails. Various "logic gates" then allow them to choose a different path when they reach a given location. Oddly, there are two big exceptions to this "workers do everything" motif. First, construction materials just teleport to construction sites from stockpiles, provided the building is on the same island. Second, you can build "dispensers" from stockpiles (for free) anywhere on the same island, so the only "long haul trucking" to be done is between islands.

The second gimmick is that your workers, besides your four starters, die after 10 minutes or so. Workers are renewable, because the input to make new workers is a renewable resource, but you still have to manage allocating them between your various tasks, and there are a lot of those right from the start. 

The basic problem here is jank. Mostly this is not the underlying game being jank, though there is a bit of that. In particular, configuring trails feels fussier than it seems like it should be, and the freeform placement generally feels awkward. At least grid floors are unlocked early, so you're not stuck in freeform life for as long as you are in something like Satisfactory. Anyway, the main problem is that your base is gonna feel like jank, and there's very little you can do about that. Foraging paths are inevitably a tangled mess in order to tap into as many flowers as you can. Same for mining routes. But you can't just set up that mess and then ignore it. You have to fiddle with it, so as to bring more flowers into the foraging routes gradually as your population grows. Between that and the choice to make relocating anything (even your queen!) entirely free, nothing feels like it can be or even should be permanent in the early game. I can't count on anything to keep functioning for the next hour while I think about something else. Not even my basic worker production.

I am also disappointed in the difficulty in extracting numbers from the game. There's no analytics screen, no option to hover over recipes to see their numbers, etc. This makes a lot of decisions that you actually do need to make, like how many ants to allocate to a given trail, feel full of guesswork.

Overall, building and maintaining an orderly factory like in the promotional images for the game sounds really fun, but it's not really clear to me how long you're gonna be stuck fiddling with a janky starter base before you get there. Also, what I am hearing in other reviews about needing to rebuild most of your old infrastructure again on each new island is sounding very plausible and not very pleasant. But I am not there yet myself.

Side note: I played the demo before the full release came out. I hesitated to even try the full game but ultimately relented. My hesitation was based on there being core functionality for basic automation inside the tech tree, and gated by more than just a tiny bit of playtime. A little bit of this stuff was made available from the start, such as the Counter Gate. This is a good call, but I still feel like they underdid it. For example, the Old Gate is still in the tech tree, but you could make use of it as soon as you have started reproducing, and it is fiddly to retrofit it into an existing base.

Followup after ~2 more hours: the trail snapping is still annoying before you have grid floors in place. But what is bothering me is that some basic tools seem like they should just be available to begin with, instead of needing to struggle without them for a few hours. You can gate them behind a longer tutorial if you like, but they seem like they should already be there in the standard mode. For example, why shouldn't the Null Trail be available from the start? It doesn't even do anything, it just makes ants not get distracted as they go from A to B. For another example, you need the Old Gate and Caste Gate to properly set up the basic early game loop: small worker working -> old small worker becomes big worker -> big worker working -> old big worker becomes inventor. Ideally you have the Elder Trail as well, but you can retrofit that painlessly enough. But before you have those gates, your worker production just...sucks, for seemingly no reason. Similarly, something as basic as a smelter array can't really be automated properly until you have a Counter End gate, which is needed to just tell ants "I only want one ant waiting in front of the smelter while it's working". Again, before you get that, a bunch of your different kinds of material processing just...sucks, for seemingly no reason.

[h1] Microtopia: The Ant Colony Automation Game We Didn’t Know We Needed [/h1]

If you’re a fan of automation games but fancy something a little different from conveyor belts and factory lines, Microtopia is an absolute treat. This game takes the intricate world of an ant colony and turns it into a deeply satisfying, yet refreshingly relaxing, automation experience. With its stunning visuals, thoughtful mechanics, and a community-driven development team, Microtopia has all the makings of a modern classic in the genre.

[h2] A Relaxing Yet Engaging Challenge [/h2]

At its core, Microtopia captures the hypnotic satisfaction of watching a well-oiled system run itself. From laying trails to managing food stores and expanding your colony to differing biomed island, everything feels intuitive and rewarding. Unlike some automation games that can feel overwhelming with their complexity, Microtopia strikes a perfect balance—offering deep strategy without ever feeling like a spreadsheet simulator.

One of the most intriguing mechanics is the fact that your ants have lifespans. This small but significant detail keeps things dynamic and prevents the classic automation pitfall of setting up a perfect system and then watching it run indefinitely. You’ll need to constantly adapt, ensuring a steady stream of new workers while keeping food and resources flowing. It’s a mechanic that adds just the right amount of challenge without ever tipping into frustration.

[h2] Visuals and Atmosphere [/h2]

Let’s take a moment to talk about the visuals—because they’re fantastic. The cutesy bio-tech styled ants, the soft glow of bio-luminescent energy nodes—it all creates an atmosphere that feels alive. The animations are fluid, the interface is clean, and every tiny detail feels lovingly crafted. Watching your ants scurry about their tasks is an oddly mesmerising experience, reinforcing the game’s relaxed but engaging vibe.

[h2] A Game That Listens to Its Players [/h2]

Another standout feature of Microtopia is its development team. They’re highly responsive, engaging with the community, taking feedback on board, and rolling out thoughtful updates at a steady pace throughout the demo and pre-release. It’s always a great sign when a game has developers who genuinely care about its long-term growth, and Microtopia has that in spades.

Speaking of community, the player base is shaping up to be one of the game’s strongest assets. There’s already a wealth of discussions floating around, with players sharing clever colony designs and strategies. If you ever get stuck or just want to optimise your setup, you’ll find plenty of friendly advice.

[h2]A Future Giant in Automation? [/h2]

With the right support, Microtopia has the potential to stand alongside heavyweights like Shapez 2 and Factorio. Its unique twist on automation, combined with its beautiful presentation and well-balanced mechanics, makes it an incredibly strong contender in the genre. It’s a game that respects your time, challenges your planning skills, and—most importantly—makes you want to keep coming back for “just one more tweak.”

If you love automation games but want something fresh, Microtopia is well worth your time. With its strong foundations and an active dev team behind it, this tiny world of ants might just become the next big thing.

It's EXTREMELY fresh.  The twist on the factory game recipe, where it's not your power or space but your LABOR that limits you, is really intriguing.  It has two innovative mechanics: all your logistics share a single common root- your queen; and EVERYTHING must be done in loops and roundabouts, from the very beginning.

It's been frustrating to play, because it really is MUCH different than your typical conveyor-belt game.  But it succeeded in stumping me many times, leading me to stare and prototype and re-design over and over as I struggle to adapt my modes of thinking.  (Manifolds are dubious in this scheme.)  It has its teeth in me, and feels "unsolved" in a great way.

Some of the tech tree progression feels out of order or strained- some key logistics pieces are gated behind quite a bit, which has felt a little artificial.  You'll be forced to make some janky designs that will inevitably be replaced.  (Looking at you, Stockpile Gate.)  This has been the source of most of my frustration.  You can expect to have to demolish and rebuild large sections of your base to take advantage of new abilities as you unlock them, more frequently than feels great to me.  But this is a learning process, so I'm not sure this is exactly a straight criticism.

If you're a devotee of the factory genre, this is a must-buy, just for its strangeness and the surprisingly nuanced places it takes your designs.

Aesthetically great.  Cute and strange, with a sort of micro-pikmin vibe.

My single true complaint is the soundtrack.  Perhaps the soundtrack is supposed to become more upbeat as you progress through game stages, but I play slow enough that I've been stuck with a mopey ambient wail for hours and hours, and I hate it.  Otherwise the sound design is quite excellent, the sound effects and filters give a nice tactile feel to the gameplay.  But come armed with your own factory music, because what you'll hear for a long while is soporific, verging on depressing.  (Seriously, this is begging for industrial, mechanistic techno-marches, but I'm stuck with Aquatic Ambience for 10+ hours?)

OK, I feel kind of bad leaving a negative review, because this is a pretty good game with a neat aesthetic and some fun concepts for the first 3ish hours. Shortly after that, the design kind of falls apart and it gets a lot worse. You don't get the kind of tools you need to keep things running well across multiple islands without consistent manual intervention. Maybe that's supposed to be a puzzle, or there's an intended way of playing that avoids that issue, but I didn't figure it out before it stopped being fun, so here we are.

Nonexistent graphical options, which means the game simply runs so ridiculously high on FPS that it runs your video card at max for a game that should take a fraction of that memory. The game will happily run up to and including thermal shutdown, it doesn't care, it just sucks resources at maximum. You have to MANUALLY go to your GPU tools and force the program to have a framerate limit.

The logical aspect is great, very much like designing circuits. The total lack of quality-of-life tools is insane. No blueprints and you have to first UNLOCK and then also expend resources to have grids. The alternative is an unreadable mass of lines. If I want to set up a production line of, say, five factories, I have to MANUALLY lay down every single freaking instruction for every part of the line for every building, then link all of that together in a loop, then link THAT loop to my main population loop. If you burn up a set of resource deposits, you can't just move the collection operation and instead have to delete the whole thing and start over at the new spot with a whole new mess of lines. Just setting up a factory can be a dozen lines of logic. Now do that dozens and dozens of times, even when repeating structures or functions. It's an incredibly absurd waste of my time to make me keep laying down the same logic lines over and over and over again when I should be able to just copy and paste layouts like any other modern game in this genre. I can't even mass-select logic points so I can move them en masse, only ants can be selected as a group.

I don't inherently mind that ants have limited lifespans, but that strongly pressures you to have efficient logic which requires efficient spacing which, again, requires grids and you have to burn resources to build grids. Aaaand then when you start needing more complex products and need more complex production, there's simply no good way to clear things and rebuild. You can't even move sections, it's either lay waste and start from scratch or fight with what you already have.

Basically zero documentation, in-game or otherwise. What resources does a building take to build? Don't know until you try to build it. What the heck is the SECOND type of research point blocking several important structures? No idea, no explanation anywhere. Overall a very irritating research tree because you are constantly blocked from useful structures by annoying objectives and resource demands, constantly forcing you to do things the most tedious, manual way first even when you can see a much better solution waiting behind an annoying lock.

Dealing with the different islands is SLOW and FRUSTRATING. All resources are stored per island and transporting resources between islands is incredibly tedious and time-consuming. You literally have to move resources blocks a single block at a time. Walk it, fly it, throw it, doesn't matter. One. At. A. Time. Need to move ten screws from one island to another? That is ten round trips across a costly bridge (oh, and the basic bridges are expensive and ONE-WAY, so you have to build TWO for any actual traffic flow... and the traffic can't be monitored with counters). Additionally, you can't make counters work across islands which means either micromanaging bugs from one island to another or setting something up and hoping it doesn't suck up your main population onto a secondary objective.

Speaking of resources, even the basic resource handling WITHIN islands is tedious and annoying. Say you want two resource piles to feed a third pile because of space issues. Well, short of a congo line of transport ants, there's no way to directly transfer the resources to the third pile, which consumes ant population and time. You can get around this by outright deleting resource storage so it will "dump" to another storage spot on the island (which defaults to selecting a random empty pile, if available) but this means, again, annoying and tedious micromanaging requiring you to periodically delete and rebuild resource storage buildings to get the resources where you want. Then if you want a resource facility to feed resources for construction, you have to manually select a given resource point, place the outgoing pipe as needed, and repeat this EVERY TIME you need a resource pipe. And there's no overhead indicator of what is doing what, so you end up with abandoned pipes and resource points all over the place because you're expanding.

Overall, it's a game about using logic to automate things but has none of the tools of a full, polished game to not be incredibly tedious. Maybe they'll fix this stuff at some point, but this feels to me like an Early Access game just left unfinished and slapped down as a release game. It's practically designed to eat time pointlessly.

I definitely regret the purchase.

People need to be quiet about: "It's just Factorio with extra steps". Factorio was not the first automation game, but it's the one a lot of us played first. And if anything, if someone plays this game and thinks of factorio... that's kind of a compliment right?

Regardless, onto the game.

This game replaces the conveyor belts model of most factory games, and instead all transport and gathering is done by workers.  Your workers have a timed life, and this presents some additional challenges. 

Potential spoiler: Early in the game you unlock the ability to combine worker ants into a longer life worker ant. This creates the opportunity to simulate a "natural life" for your workers. 

Example: In my colony I birth the basic small ant, these small ants with their very limited life, move to a field for collecting food for the queen to birth more. If they get "old" they automatically route out of the food gathering cycle, and proceed to go to a combiner, or other machine, to turn into a new ant with a renewed life span. Of which, my more skilled newer ants will then proceed to handle more complex jobs, so instead of hauling food, I make miners, transporters, plant cutters, manufacturers, etc. 
Once these workers near the end of their life, they automatically move out and get repurposed into an end of life unit that does other things of which I don't want to spoil.

This timed life aspect of workers adds a nice complexity to the automation process. I AM worried about potentially soft locking myself on my main area, but Im sure theres a research down the road that will solve my issue. 

I'd say the technology is pretty well timed in the beginning of the game. In fact, when you reach an issue with your colony, you genuinely tend to get a technology that will solve that issue pretty soon. 

Overall, I'm enjoying this game during my lunch breaks. Very fun, would recommend for the price that it is.

Brilliant little game. 

People keep comparing it to Factorio, which fair in the sense they're both automation games but there are plenty of fundamental differences that make Microtopia its own beast. 

In Microtopia you don't have a little avatar to awkwardly move around, so you can instantly access and change any part of your empire, which also means the game can be comfortably played with just a mouse, Redesigning and optimising stuff is so very, very much easier than Factorio, which is good as the game has more of a focus on it. 

Microtopia is more goal focused, many parts of the tech tree unlock off of achievements instead of simply build numbers, making you engage with systems as they unlock. Further to this, the game feels less open than Factorio and more puzzle and goal focused, but that's a deliberate design choice I personally prefer.

Microtopia has no time pressure so you can play at your own pace. You can pause and make sweeping changes to your empire whenever you want. No biters are going to swarm your walls, no pollution spreading making the difficulty continually tick up, the only thing that will screw you up is you, which is inevitable as the size, complexity and tools available all continually grow. 

Factorio is a great game and so is Microtopia, and I, for one, welcome our new insect overlords.

Very lazy development. I love "in the hole" games, but this is one of the worst versions. VERY VERY VERY disappointing
good game. wish there was more stuff to do.

Astro Miner is the first game I tried from the QubicGames bundle that pops up during the big sales. If you’re into grindy games, this one’s right up your alley—but if not, you might want to skip it.

In this short, grind-heavy title, you mine in a small area, collect resources, and use your earnings to upgrade your character and purchase helpers to gather gems. There’s even a range of skins available, though chasing every single one can make 100% completion nearly impossible. For that elusive achievement, you'll need to buy all the anvil power-ups and most jetpacks—even if many of those jetpacks end up being mostly useless. I ended up having to revisit several planets to fully complete the game, which got a bit monotonous.

The money balancing leaves much to be desired: early and late levels both dish out the same cash rewards (200 cash for 2 stars), even though your upgrade costs can skyrocket to 30k by the time you're on the later planets. And don’t get me started on the auto miner—it eventually becomes so underwhelming that its gem drops hardly add up to anything compared to the richer finds later on.

6/10 – A grindy, incremental experience that may satisfy enthusiasts but is let down by balance issues and repetitive gameplay.
a chill game for achievements

This app would be great if it wasn't linked to steam, I have this issue where whenever I open another steam game it closes the app and I cant use it, not sure if there's a way to stop this from happening, I followed the instructions from the top comments response but this still happens, if there's a fix for this please let me know :)
Nothing special, not particularly well designed, no real choices, no fun

BALATRO meets YAHTZEE with endlessly customizable dice.

If you love Balatro, I don't need to say another word. You need this game. The same goes for 'Luck be a Landlord' & 'Bing Bing'.

All 3 are Balatro-likes with different mechanics. Cards, slot machine, and roullette... again with Balatro infusion.

In this game, as mentioned earlier, Balatro meets Yahtzee. You will quickly see the influence.

Works great on SteamDeck.

It is a easy game with a simple mechanic system

i'm a huge detective/investigative game fan, and this is among the best out there, if not the very best. while it doesn't have the unique art appeal of obra dinn or the golden idol series, it more than makes up for it with the amount of breadcrumbs to follow and an incredibly satisfying gameplay loop and storyline. i welcome the roottrees to the detective game scene with open arms and have high hopes for what the creators have planned going forward.

I never post reviews...But dudes. This game was unbelievably wonderful. If you're looking for a game that has an interesting story and thinking process, I highly recommend. 

If you’re especially looking for one that doesn't easily give to answers but rather pushes your own deductive skills, this is a good one.

A solid geneological Dinn-clone (Obra-like?). It lacks polish, but the core gameplay is good. If you like Obra Dinn (or Case/Rise of The Golden Idol) and need "moar" then this will satisfy your insatiable detective lust.

The primary gameplay of sleuthing around, deducing the facts, then having them confirmed in the Obra-match-3 style is great and works well on the family corkboard. However the game itself needed a tiny bit longer in the oven. It lacks a bit of polish, especially in terms of UI and textual errors. It's nothing major but it does make the whole experience feel a bit budget.

Also, nothing really tells you this, but it's actually two game scenarios in one. The first game is a snazzed-up version of the old itch.io one, where you deduce the existing family tree. Once you've completed that you get to play a second scenario involving new additions to the family tree, and this time around the deduction is "harder", as not only are these potential matches, rather than existing solid ones, but now there's a lot of extraneous data you have to dig through to find the facts.

(Actually, the Steam webpage does talk about the second scenario, but it's like one line, which is somewhat amusing as the entire game is basically spent pouring over text looking for a single line to spark your next clue.)

Some unorganised praise:

* The photo scrambling is interesting and novel
* The artist has done a fantastic job on the concept of "family resemblance".


Things I'd like to see improve, either for this or for any future games:

* The game needs a bug report form.
* Another copy editing pass needs to happen. Especially on that newspaper, which is the very first thing you see. There's some small typos and oddities hanging around.
* Why does the evidence icon look like SEARCH THE INTERNET icon? After 15 hours of gameplay I was still clicking the wrong damn icon.
* Why is my notebook limited??!!? I WANT MORE TABS.
* If you're going to use free music, try not to use some completely overplayed stuff like that Kevin Macleod piece used in the Kerbal rocket editor. 
* Throughout both games it seemed that birth years, and establishing the chronology in general, was important. But it gave us no tools to track this, and I'll be damned if I'm busting out a pen and paper. It would have been nice to have date of birth as a piece of information to fill in.
* I'd like to be able to tick off or cross out notes, rather than deleting them. I accidentally deleting some information I had yet to process at one point.
* The pedantic nature of searching for a city in Roottreemania is some American nonsense that the rest of the world doesn't need to know about. 
* I'd like some hotkeys, especially for changing to different screens.
* I'd like some way to organise or label the evidence.
* I think there should be MORE information to sift through. Right now if felt like every single non-joke web page was directly relevant in some way.

This game was made specifically for me, a librarian with an interest in genealogy. It brought the same sense of accomplishment I get from putting together a physical puzzle -- each little piece fitting together until suddenly I have the whole picture. It made me want to create my own mystery game in the same way reading a good book makes me want to write my own. 

TL;DR: This game engaged my intellect, sparked my creativity, and watered my plants.

Great game!!!! Play if you liked Return of the Obra Dinn!! Includes a great hint system that helps without giving too much away. I bought this on a whim and I am extremely impressed. This is the type of game I would make if I knew how to make games and also was not lazy. Note: buying this gives you access to two games in one, "The Roottrees are Dead" and a sequel "Roottreemania."

A fantastic puzzle game of rooting through a late-90s internet and logicing out details of an extended family who are not quite what they seem. Solid writing, fun characters (mostly the family antics), and very good difficulty overall. The Extra chapter turns everything up to 11, which required me to grab some hints, but luckily there's a really good gradual hint system that nudges you before giving more explicit direction.

The premise and gameplay have potential , but the story is just not compelling enough to make you want to engage with it. I did finish the game so I could feel like I gave it a fair chance. In the beginning , it feels like a scavenger hunt , but by the end you're reading walls of texts about people you're not given a reason to care about.  Finding pieces of information often feels intentionally obtuse rather than clever , and there is no good way to keep track of anything. 

The core gameplay has potential to be something much better with some minor QoL improvements and most importantly a more compelling story.

Great deduction/mystery game! I love these types of games, one of the best along with Golden Idol & Obra Dinn. Honestly this game has one of the most fluid search systems, and considering how much physical evidence and texts you gather- it doesn't feel overwhelming due to it being amazingly thought out.

Stellar. Right up there with Obra Dinn and Golden Idol for me. The main beats of the story are interesting enough to make it hard to put down and it's enhanced by a ton of interesting flavor and context to discover around the edges. The music is also so fitting and complementary to the whole experience. Buy it.

Should note I played on Steam Deck. There's a lot of typing and the touchpad can be finicky when highlighting text / clicking things, but it's totally playable and was still a good experience imo.

Absolutely love this style of game. It's really neat being able to use a "search engine" within the game to look for various books, articles, and more to determine who the family members are. I found myself playing for hours without realizing how much time had gone by, which is a sign of a good game to me.

A phenomenal game for those looking to scratch the itch of Return of the Obra Dihn.

The Roottrees are Dead is a game about uncovering the truth and identifying familial connections. The puzzles it provides are both incredibly engaging and well-thought out. This game is very user friendly, though the massive amount of information can be a bit overwhelming at times. It isn't particularly easy, but the reward for finishing the game is immense.
Love love this game. I saw Gab Smolders playing it and had to pause the video to come buy it lol

Possibly the closest that anyone has come to recreating the magic of Obra Dinn, the first part of the game is fantastic - and while the second part is a nice addition, it jumps up massively in difficulty if you're up for that - absolutely give it a try.

Very fun puzzle. Occasionally, it can be hard to figure out where to go next (in my case, usually from forgetting to search a name and then losing it), but the hints are helpful and the plot is interesting, so any issues I had with progression were quickly swept away. Overall, very fun!
SUCH a good puzzle game, holy hell. Ended up 100%ing it in one sitting and accidentally pulling an all nighter lmao. Big recommend.

It was a really nice game where you had to gather information and try to figure out how people are related and what their names are. 

I really recommend this if you like games like The return of Obra Dinn or The Case of the Golden Idol.

Deductive games are likely super challenging to make.  You need them to feel smart but be accessible.  I also prefer them not feature ridiculous leaps in logic.  To be fair, the game allows leaps here and there but it's done in a clever way: for the initial case the question is can *you* put the facts together, the case has already been solved so some leaps come from simple elimination.  This gives that cheeky feeling of 'cheating' the system, even though I'm pretty sure it's the intended path most of the time.  Even so, all of the important evidence is 100% verifiable.  I'd put it as about a medium level sudoku puzzle.

I really only got stuck at the very end and it turned out to be fairly obvious: I missed a search because the 1998 internet is limited and I assumed this wouldn't turn up results: I was wrong.  It was the only time I used a hint and the hint was quite helpful because it was like, "Hey, did you search for *everybody*" and I was like, "No, I didn't."  And voila, finished the game.  The second case, which I haven't finished, is clearly the harder puzzle so I can't say if it's quite as well-structured as the first.  I can say if that's the mission statement I wouldn't be upset: first prove you can use the tools and deduce the clues, then hand out the hard level puzzle.  That's just good design.

So yeah, I liked this game a lot and felt it did a great job of presenting a puzzle to solve.  The tools were slightly frustrating as some searches felt like they really should've turned up *something*, but I was able to correctly guess the final puzzle (it wasn't that hard to be honest, I had my suspicions basically from the start) and never felt like I was being asked to interpret some clue in an absurd way to reveal a detail.  Methodical searching and analysis wins the day and for that I recommend it heartily.

EDIT: After completing the second case, I am quite pleased.  I literally tried to put the game down but ended up going until I solved the whole thing.  If the developers make more games like this I do hope they'll improve some of the note taking tools.  The second case I ended up with quite a lot of notes, awesome, but there were bugs in the interface and being able to, for example, pin search results would have been really, really welcomed.  Nevertheless, the second case was really good.  I got all of the major plot points and questions right and the ones I wasn't sure of turned out to be because I missed a really obvious piece of evidence that felt so silly to miss.  The game even deliberately slaps you in the face with it at one point, so I didn't feel cheated, I just didn't notice the very obvious clue staring me in the face.

Excellent work, highly recommended.
i really enjoyed this! its super easy to lose track of time while playing bc of how much you get drawn into the mystery and vibe and i super want more things like this now lol

Good but frustrating (if you’re stupid).

It’s a genealogical deduction game where you scour over a sudo internet to retrieve relevant information about a mystery. This ever growing breadcrumb trail provides the information to fill in the detailed history of multiple generations of a family, all without leaving your house. Similar to Obra Dinn and Golden Idol, you are confirmed correct when a certain amount of deductions are all correct and it feels fantastic looking up a source, following a trail, doing some logical deduction, and seeing that your guess is correct. The hint system especially is great because it guides you to where you should look at first which sends you down rabbit holes that you spend hours trying to dig your way out of. If you’re into other deduction games, you’re gonna love that aspect.

That being said, unless you’re a turbo nerd (non-derogatory) who is prepared to physically write notes for every minor detail and follow up, getting the most out of the mystery is going to be hard. There are no keywords like Golden Idol since everything is freeform text. This is great because it really does feel like sleuthing and detective work. However, it REALLY feels like grindy detective work when you have hundreds of individual pieces of evidence and you forget where you got a detail from just to backtrack through your entire logical tree to get back to some article. You’re going to need to write detailed notes of how you got where since the UI is early internet and doesn’t store much outside of page history and a highlighting notebook. You miss one little proper noun and entire swaths of evidence could be blocked off. The ending takes the kiddie gloves off and just says “go deduct”. You have to read in between clues, look at dates, and match every scrap of evidence to another to get the actual final answer. Luckily the game does still allow dumb people like me to wrap up the story without getting it 100% right.

For some turbo nerds (again not derogatory), this is fantastic and will scratch that deduction itch after you speedrun Obra Dinn, thought it was too easy, and gave Her Story GOTY. For smooth brained puzzle lovers who need constant dopamine hits and don’t have the journaling skills of a tik tok mom, it can get frustrating not being able to figure it out. Skill issue I know.

They say that you recognize a good book if you are sad that it is over.

This game definitely caused the same feelings as a good book. A masterpiece!

It's not quite as polished as Obra Dinn, but fun-wise on the same level. Obra Dinn had its outstanding momento-mori idea, and Roottree has its Wikipedia-rabbithole charme. Both give the absolute satisfaction if your guesses are verified.

Can I buy those shirts anywhere? :)

I got this game after watching Secret Sleepover Society play the first part. The game feels like going down the Wikipedia rabbit hole: going from page to page, finding new information, and connecting the dots.
