Beating this game at 4am is a spiritual experience
I was expecting to play for an hour, ended up playing for about 8 hours..my brain hurts a lot....10/10 recommend!

Decent game up to a point. It's super annoying when I need to use hints because my internet searches for, without spoiling anything, Alexander Roottree yield no hits and I should have used an abbreviated Alex Roottree instead. Why? That's not how googling works. When you have 50 characters that you can search for in 7 directories, and hundreds of seemingly insignificant things that turn out to be super important, so that you have to search for every other noun in all directories, it's simply not acceptable for the actual name of characters not getting hits.

My biggest gripe: The big final conclusion of the game makes no sense.

[Spoiler] I can see, with a few reasonable leaps of reasoning, that E.C. was estranged from his family for some reason. I got there myself, there were plenty of decent hints. I find it questionable the family successfully just erased him from history (despite him obviously being publicly known) whilst also employing him and him not even trying to get to the fund that should rightfully pay him millions. There were public ads talking about his 5 children before the 6th was born and then they went back to claiming it was 5 again. But sure, whatever, maybe everyone was ashamed, suspension of disbelief.

But the fact that he had a gay lover was never, ever a reasonable conclusion. The closest we got to evidence was that he lived with a roommate. Yes, I get it, Uncle Bill lived with a room mate and we don't talk much, ha ha, that's a stereotype we've all heard. But he was a farm hand in the early 20th century. It is completely reasonable for farm hands to sleep in the same building or, y'know, people did actually have room mates. That doesn't automatically make them gay. If that's what Sam wants to use in court, I dunno man, that's not even close to evidence, that's just guessing. E.C. could have just been a drug addict, adulterer, war criminal. I realize people got to the conclusion, and I reluctantly did, too, because it's a stereotype and there was only one character left, but not because it's in any way logical. It felt like we needed a twist and that's the best and somewhat zeitgeist-y thing they could come up with.

I would have much preferred figuring something out about the tons of strange deaths, especially the titular tragedy.[/spoiler]

By the way, from the other reviews, all these issues are even more prevalent in Roottreemania.

Despite all this the writing of the game is pretty good and made me laugh at times. The art style is more miss than hit, the music was pretty well chosen, but not nearly enough tracks in rotation. If the websites were not just text and had some clickable links, that would have been a huge improvement.  The way the game works right now is like pixel hunting but with words and 'use everything on everything' if you're stuck. Still there's promise there with these developers. I'm sure they can cook up something nice next time. I would liked to give a mixed review, but with the game being at overwhelmingly positive right now (congrats), I'll go with a negative.
Best game I've played in a while! It definitely scratches that detective itch. Excellent storyline, and the gameplay reminds me of Her Story.

This was a really fun mystery-solving/puzzle game!! It is quite literally if going down Wikipedia rabbit holes was made into a game. I also Loved the built-in note-taking system in this. I played with a few friends and we had a great time!
Edit: I just played the extra campaign, Roottree Mania, and it was also such a blast!
5 hours for the base game, 5 hours for the expansion (but I did make liberal use of the hint feature for the expansion). Very good game, get it.

Really well written, engaging, and in my opinion fairly balanced difficulty that manages to create a wide gamut of challenges out of its seemingly simple gameplay. Detective games can sometimes have a disconnect between the player's character being a good sleuth and having experience, vs the player themselves not necessarily being that savvy but wanting to feel as smart as the character. The summaries of article/webpage information, as filtered through the detective's understanding of what is relevant or not, is a really good way to bridge that gap and help the player feel a little less overwhelmed. I'm definitely looking forward to more games in this vein if the developers make more, the formula is very solid and they're already  making great updates to some of the less polished parts of the interface.

Fantastic detective game that really hooks you in. Great if you like games like the Golden Idol games or Consortium. Really enjoyed learning more about the family and unfolding their story through deductions.

An excellent puzzle game with a surprisingly good soundtrack. The feeling when you finally find the birth name of that one spouse of the third cousin from the first dude you found is indescribable. The setting in the late 90s is a great touch and completes a well rounded experience. If you enjoy puzzle/logic games, I wholeheartedly recommend this game for you.

I loved this game!!! I felt like a true detective. All the research and reading of articles and photos made it feel real. Along with finding the clues and solving puzzles.... Chefs Kiss. Seriously!!  I binge played this game and I reallyyyyy hope a similar game like this comes out!! It was a challenge and reward. Thanks! : }

Really fun deduction game in the style of Obra Dinn (which it's inspired by) and A Hand With Many Fingers where you guess identities of people based on evidence found in internet pages and periodicals. Actually made me stretch to figure out search threads at many points, and to think laterally. The articles are all really well written with a lot of funny tangents if you dig deep enough. I've been on the lookout for similar games to OD ever since I fell in love with it and this really scratched the itch. The sequel (included here)- Roottreemania- was also really good, and definitely challenged me to dig even deeper with my deductions. A really great puzzle game!

Highly recommended for fans of games like Return of the Obra Dinn , The Case of the Golden Idol and Chants of Sennaar. Scratches that detective game itch perfectly. My only gripe is some of the ambiguity in the very last puzzle but other than that it's solid deduction game.

Absolutely wonderful game. I played all of it, both the main section and Roottreemania in one sitting! 

I found the first part excellent and it felt wonderful anytime something was proved right, the hint system was excellent for near the very end when I had forgotten little pieces of evidence, just the right kind of nudge.

I found Roottreemania a lot harder, part of that I think may be due to the sometimes subjective nature of the final answers but that might just be my way of thinking. My main problem arose with not knowing anything about American geography and so struggling with which periodical was the correct one for what I wanted to search for but again the hint system is really helpful in this regard. 

Instantly have started looking for similar games to play because I loved it so much!

A true detective game in the same vein as Return to Obra Dinn and Hypnospace Outlaw, a fantastic experience that you shouldn't miss if you enjoy mystery games.

Filled with witty and funny easter eggs, an intriguing plot and very satisfying 'aha!' moments, the Roottrees are Dead is one of those games that not many people may know about, but more definitely should.

This is a really great game! If you're a fan of games with search systems (e.g. Her Story) and deductive reasoning, and have a penchant for genealogy, then this will likely be right up your alley. I personally found the nostalgic vibes, jazzy music, search mechanic, and note taking system to be immersive and captivating. I would highly recommend giving this game a try if you get the chance! Fingers crossed that they make more games like this in the future!  :)
Delivers all the the high highs of actual genealogy research without the crushing hours of real research.

Excellent detective game. It's deceptively simple at first, but towards the end of the main game and *especially* in Roottreemania, it gets quite challenging but even more satisfying. There's no guess and check needed, though towards the end I relied a bit on process of elimination. Even still, once I confirmed my answers via PoE, I still went back and picked up on clues that made me want to smack myself for missing the first time around.

An absolute must-play for anyone who liked Obra Dinn or the Golden Idol games

Great game.  This game is for people who like to read and figure out clues.  The game is in two parts.  Once you finish the main Roottree story, there is a second situation.  I found the second part to be more difficult, but still much fun.  This game requires a lot of reading and rereading to dig out subtle clues.  So, if you don't like to read and research all sorts of topics, then this is probably not for you.

I had a great time finding little snippets of information that turned into larger revelations.  Enjoyed the music and the story lines.

There is nothing like a Wikipedia deep dive to soothe the soul, and The Roottrees are Dead satisfied a need for this type of game that I didn't even know I had. Every clack of the '90s keyboard as I copied and pasted things into '90s Google gave me a strange sense of purpose.

Only complaint? Wish there were more library books. God I love a library search.

If you like mystery games and especially The Return of the Obra Dinn, you'll enjoy this game very much. There's also more than 1 mystery to solve, which adds playtime and depth to the story. Overall and very fun and quirky game. Easter eggs are silly :)

I really enjoyed The Roottrees are dead. The story had plenty of twists and turns as you'd expect from a detective/mystery game. The puzzles were logical and I had a fun time trying to link the various family members using the clues available. The second part of the game was a bit tougher than the first, but still enjoyable!
Really, really good. My only criticism, which is minor, is that some of the documentary evidence you are looking through is not totally plausible. But most of it is really good.

This game is awesome! My daughter and I had a blast sifting through evidence and researching. The family drama was so interesting and the unexpected expansion at the end was a great addition. Took us a while to get through the game , however the duck hints were a welcome help :)

An excellent game, entertaining and engrossing. It can get hard toward the end — we definitively solved a few cases through despair and hope — yet it never felt unfair; I could always see how I could have reached such or such conclusion.

Not the game for me, sadly, though I wanted to love it. The 90s nostalgia is great, as was researching and tracking down leads to build the family tree in the first case. But the story is too much about exposing scandals/unpleasant behavior of all sorts (especially once you move on to the second case) for me to enjoy it. If it makes me a "prude" to say that, so be it, I own it. I don't play video games to be reminded how awful people can be — I see enough of that in real life. 

And back to the second case, I didn't find the gameplay to be nearly as enjoyable as it was for the first case. It felt unnecessarily difficult and tedious to track down information and make deductions.

Very good detective game in the vein of Obra Dinn, the Golden Idol games, and in particular, Hypnospace Outlaw.  The first campaign is a bit weaker in that it basically requires you to use the process of elimination on the list of names you're given to lock in certain people rather than actually finding conclusive information about them in your investigation.  The second campaign is much better in my opinion, though I do think the final puzzle has some strange choices in what it considers definitive evidence which leaves the game on a bit of a sour note.  Overall excellent though, strongly recommend it.

This is the best puzzle game I have played in a very long time. Full of humor and easter eggs, this game was challenging enough that I stalled out, but I never got stuck so badly I couldn't proceed. If you like puzzles and internet sleuthing, this is a must play!

We loved this game! Amazing level of detail and true to the 1990s. It was pretty hard, especially the later stages. We did a high-five each time we uncovered a new periodical! It was very satisfying to get to the end. Thanks for a well-spent 17 hours!

One of the best detective games I've every played! I'm always on the lookout for puzzle games that don't involve a lot of walking around (I have zero sense of direction). This one blew me away. Everything about it is great. I usually mute games but the clicking of that mechanical keyboard was just too divine.

My laptop broke in the middle of my first playthrough and I swear I thought about the Roottrees nonstop until it came back from the repair shop and I could finish the game. So much fun, perfect level of challenge, I wish I could wipe my brain and start it all over again.

The comparisons to Obra Dinn are pretty misleading (and not fair to either game) as while there are core mechanical similarities in deduction but the games are otherwise *very* different. It's a bit more like Orwell, for example. No kraken here.

At first, paying attention to the nuances of the documents on display is enough to get through the game.
And it feels great to progress through the board.

However, later in the game, you have to take some wild logical leaps that I do not care for ([spoiler]for exemple, deducing a job out of "green thumb"[/spoiler]).

Still, I do think it deserves some love.

10 / 10 game.

When it leaves you wanting more (spoilers), it gives you more.
Right when you think you've had enough, it sucks you back one final time.

The DUCK ends up being the GOAT.

Incredible game! I'm an avid watcher of game playthroughs and saw someone playing this game. It's not very often I get 10 minutes into a video and become so invested, I have to buy the game myself. This is exactly what happened with The Roottrees are Dead. It's challenging, but not too much. I enjoy a "thinky" game every once in a while and this scratched the right itch. The hint system is also great, gives you directions to follow without giving you answers right off the bat. The art style is also very cool. Highly recommend!!!

The Roottrees are Dead is a great little game. If you like solving mysteries and googling while listening to jazz, you will like this. It does not take 34 hours to play, I played through it twice and left it up and idle while cooking dinner etc. over a few days to get that time. It's probably about a 4-5 hour game if you just sit down and play it all the way through. The duck gives good hints if you get stuck.
Music is great, mystery is great. Really scratches the Obra Dinn, Golden Idol itch

An excellent little investigation game! Mechanically somewhat similar to Obra Dinn, this game brings a charming 90's vibe and lets you peruse through websites, articles and various historical paraphernalia to cobble together a family tree! Genealogy just got a lot more exciting!

I 100% loved this game. It’s games like this that make me hate myself for playing them soon after they come out because I already want a second game even though they give you a second game with in the game. If you love logic games where you have to be attentive, this game is for you. This game was amazingly written and clever in the context and hidden clues. Loved!

Incredible game rivalling if not surpassing the best of its genre. I personally enjoyed this even more than Obra Dinn. Where Obra Dinn had me taking shots in the dark toward the end of the game, Roottrees had me seeking out hidden paths to the evidence I needed. Really scratched the itch I had after blowing through Rise of the Golden Idol (and the fact that the new Idol didn't let you turn off clue markers and did away with the key word hunting made Roottrees's hint hunting system that much more satisfying and challenging). The story is great and the gameplay and pacing is perfect. A+++++ game, maybe one of my all time faves.

An unconventional and very clever puzzle game. Sometimes the conclusions were a bit to strained in my opinion, but I enjoyed the hell out of this. Give it a try if you want to play something unique and don't be to shy to use the hint feature if you get stuck.

I bought this game on a whim, and absolutely loved it. If you like mystery games that are low stakes and casual, this is the game for you. Deduce who are actually part of the family tree, and after you finish the game, surprise! There's another game! The Roottrees Are Dead has a surprising amount of substance for the price and gives you hints when you are stuck. Highly recommend.
Great game! All puzzles feel great to solve. One you have finished the main game, Roottreemania opens up and that is and extra challenge that is just as enjoyable. Wish the was more!!!

Yet another solid addition to the burgeoning category of indie detective games. The Roottrees Are Dead isn't subtle about its influences, clearly drawing on the mechanics of Return of the Obra Dinn and Her Story, but it comes to a really different conclusion than those works and, while I don't think its story is as strong as a detective game's should be, the game is mechanically tuned to near-perfection.

The general pitch is that you're tasked with filling out the genealogical tree for a famous candy production family after the death of the CEO's family. It's a strong hook that's met with the challenge that all you have to go on are a few clues as to who is in the family tree and access to an old computer on a dial-up modem in the late 90s. You have to scour documents and search results for potential threads to further pull on and this can lead down countless rabbit holes.

I frankly loved how this game engages the player. The player quickly finds themselves in a rat's nest of information that they have to sort through for valuable details and it's just enough info to overwhelm the player but not so much that it's impossible to know what to do. Clues and hints always stick out just enough that you're able find another to chase down, but don't feel like the game is treating you like an idiot. The Obra Dinn threshold system requiring multiple correct lock-ins prior to confirmation ensures that progress is challenging, but moves at a good pace. I played through practically the entire work while using like zero guides/hints. I used guides to hunt down a few pieces of evidence when I was so far wrapped up that it didn't affect my ability to solve the cases. So that's a pretty good indication that the game has tuned its logic incredibly well.

All that being said, I definitely think there are some weak points that could use work in a future outing. First, the artstyle is pretty bland. It's a lot of semi-realistic art, and a 3D room with super primitive texturing. It just lacks flavour or flare, which can really enhance an experience like this. Second, the finale of Roottreemania is rough. I ended up just using a guide to explain the logic, as there was no way I was going to be able to sus out some of it. It demands a lot of thought by the player with no lock-in system nor much of an effect on the ending. It also requires some big stretches in logic that I wouldn't have considered since it starts to degrade into conspiracy theories.

Finally, and most critically, the story isn't great. Piecing together the story is awesome and I had a lot of fun in the moment, but when I take a step back and view the work as a whole, the story is just utterly uninteresting. Plot twists don't really have much impact and the drama just feels kind of low-stakes. I think this kind of game could use a really crazy conspiracy or murder mystery to make it shine.

Overall though, I had a really good time with The Roottrees Are Dead. Its stylistic and narrative issues aside, the gameplay is some of the strongest in its genre and the difficulty is pitch perfect, showcasing the talents of the people involved. At this point, all I could hope for is to transplant these systems into a game with more flashy presentation and a more compelling and memorable plot.

I'd score it 8/10.

I picked this one up after hearing positive comparisons to Return of the Obra Dinn.  And while its not exactly the same, if you enjoyed one you'll enjoy the other.

After a tragic plane crash kills the current head of the Roottree company and his family, you are approached to research the Roottree family tree, using internet searches to dig up clues, you'll have to find names, photographs and professions of all the members of the extended clan, while also finding the legal framework that oversees the distribution of the vast fortunes of the families companies to its members as well as hints of a secret hidden away in the Roottree lineage.

Theres a great deal of satisfaction as you chase clues across web pages multiple clues can send you chasing down book from the library or old newspaper articles and gossip magazines, there are often multiple lines of inquiry so the clues will flow from the start allowing you to get hooked quite quickly. That initial pace will leave you feeling good about you detective skills, but the interconnected nature of the clues means that as you get down to the final missing faces it can be hard to figure out where the clues leading to them are. I got stuck as the missing family members I needed were hinted at by a single clue on a search for branch of the family I had already completed hours ago. But rejoice as there is a pretty robust hint system for just such an occasion, and I do wish I hadn't been so avid in avoiding it. Hints a layered so if you happen to be missing a section of the family tree the first hint might just say to research family member A, this being the first link in the chain that leads to the place you want, with the hints becoming more specific as you go. 

And then theres that one last secret,  no spoilers, but theres a something going on with the family, its hinted at throughout your research but never spelled out. Once you complete the tree, you'll be given the chance to fill in the final secret section, and unlike the rest of the game where you pick details out of drop down menu's, you'll  instead have to fill this one in by hand. I like this sort of thing, whereas its possible to brute force other parts of the game, here you'll only be rewarded if you were paying attention, it makes you feel like you really solved this thing once you get it (you can skip this if you like, put in any old answer, the game will reveal what the correct answer was along with the clues that lead to it, if thats all you want).

If this was all the game had to offer I'd already be pretty happy, but the game comes packed with a free expansion. After solving the games first mystery, its revealed that a bunch of people have out of the woodwork claiming to be illegitimate children of the Roottree line and looking to get a fat payday as a result. This time you'll have to research a series of affairs and the children that resulted before ultimately deciding which of these people are really related to the family. Unlike the previous mystery this one is separated into distinct sections, this means no parts where you can't figure out where the clues are because you missed a tangent in a section that is now complete and you have no reason to go back to. This does however mean that you won't get that easy flow going and it takes more time with far more digging before you start locking things in. It can be a little annoying but that makes it way more satisfying when it starts to click and once again you'll have that final write in section at the end to check if you were paying attention.

I had a great time with Roottrees and I hoping to see more games like this going forward, definitely worth a try.

If you're a Millennial, this game is a time capsule of your own memories, an actual drive down memory lane. It took me a couple playthroughs to understand why the setting is so vague - the currency symbol is fake, the town names are an amalgamation of Northern and Western Europe, so you could be anywhere from the west coast of Canada to England to Germany to Scandinavia - no setting is defined. Even the names of the people you meet are not names but descriptions, eg. The Kid, The Bride, etc. I found this clever little obfuscation allowing me to imprint my own experiences onto the game, with memories people and places I haven't thought of in 20 years all flooding back. The generality of everything allows a huge audience with a common lived experience to connect with the game on an extremely personal level. 

As for gameplay, nothing is groundbreaking and you've likely seen most of the mechanics before, but the game exists as a canvas for you to paint your own memories onto. It's really an extraordinary masterpiece. The strongest piece of the design is the freedom afforded to the player - you are given goals, but you don't need to complete them. You set off originally to get to a festival within a month, but the game lasts for 3 months and if you don't want to go to the festival then you don't have to. Nothing is forced, everything is at your discretion. Do drugs, or don't. Buy guns, or don't. Pick up hitchhikers, or don't. You won't be punished for anything except careless driving - but maybe don't get pulled over by the cops when you're drunk, that's a pretty tricky combat. 

Special mention for the soundtrack, absolutely incredible. Honestly the price of the game is worth it for the music, I have no idea how to developers found all this great obscure music, most of the songs in this game have less than 10,000 plays on Spotify. Cruising around in your car listening to this soundtrack is a distinct pleasure. 

Overall, 10/10. Even 11/10. If you get the vibes in this game you will have an extraordinary experience.

Example: When this girl takes a pee break for the 90th time, I hover over to the cigarettes, and have to wait a full 8 seconds before I can drag them to use, and if I click the item prematurely, the game will glitch out and prevent me from using anything in my glove box. A wonderful story engine type game with an amazing and unique setting. Generally it is easier to do games set in sci-fi or fantasy worlds, but if you are like me, you usually crave for system-based games that utilize the underrepresented realistic/urban setting (funnily it is the other way around in the movies, realistic scripts are easier to do there). 

Keep Driving absolutely nails and satisfies that crave there - it is an RPG centered around upgrading your janky car and building up a party of hitchhikers in a world of 00s coming-of-age hipster Sundance road movie. And the combat is you encountering various obstacles on the road to deal with, like entering vague lines or going behind a tractor or having a flat tire, which is neat and unique idea!

Speaking of mechanics, it is very captivating how the game awards you rewards for trying out new stuff, which is an on-spot narrative fit for a coming-of-age story centered about protagonist trying stuff for the first time in their life (getting their first car, going to their first movie festival, and everything that happens in-between that you choose). There's a hidden traits system, like if you eat mostly junkfood, you get addicted to it, and if you prefer to escape the battles by excessively hitting gas pedal, then you get a trait that buffs you for doing that etc. So you keep encouraged for experimenting, and at the same time your habits also shape the personality of your character in countless ways.

The hitchhikers cast is diverse and colorful, and each has unique mechanics attached to him. As they level up, their stories unfold and they also get new traits that can affect in both positive and negative ways, like a gambling addicted creepo prevents all females for getting any exp points, and a hiker who's a hippie nature lover makes you numb at some point to being inspired by anything other than the nature. And they have those little fun dialogue interactions between each other which adds to the experience!

Room for improvement: the combat mechanics are pretty fun at the beginning, but getting very repetitive, as you acquire more and more skills, it becomes too easy you can mostly deal with anything. I wish there was an auto-battle mechanics or at least a possibility to speed it up. Or ideally if there were more dangers that could be a real late-game challenge. Driving up the mountain (a 36 hour drive that depletes all your resources) was the only real late-game challenge to get one of the endings. I also wish there were more distinction between cities and villages and the assortment in the stores, then coming to each new city would've been times more exciting. 

Get this game so those talented developers would have the resources to work on those in the future sequel! And by no means those flaws make the game not enjoyable, so you'll have a good time as long as you vibe with its setting.

This game would be an easy recommend were it not for a massive issue. I don't find the core gameplay loop fun. The bulk of the gameplay is these little pseudo-combat minigames you have to do numerous times on every road segment. The minigame is matching skill types and consumable types to threat types until they're gone in a turn system. It is intensely basic, I don't find it fun, and it slows the game down tremendously, taking away from the actual fun parts.

The aesthetic here is great. The world is small but filled with charm. The sound design is pretty solid. This is all weighed down by the matching game bits (the bulk of the play experience) not being terribly engaging and that's a huge issue to me.

If the concept and charm really draw you in, there is some fun to be had here, just take caution that there is loads of tedium to be dealt with as well.

It's alright. Fun little cozy game that seems to be in the same genre as Darkest Dungeon and games like it. In Keep Driving - your enemies are "threats" during your roadtrip such as road kill, potholes, insect swarms, cyclists, etc. It's fun but it gets pretty played out and you'll encounter the same threats a dozen times over. The last hour of my playthrough had me itching to just cross it off my list of completed games.

In total I played for 4 hours. My first hour was bad. I didn't really understand the game very well but the second time around I beat the game in under 3 hours. No I did not speed run it. You are given a certain amount of days to make it to the festival. I think it was something like "be there by June 28th" and I made it the morning of the 27th. So just barely.

There isn't a ton to do and watching your vehicle auto drive toward 'threats' in the road starts to feel like a slog. There aren't enough food options that provide buffs. You get chewing gum, cigarettes, duct tape, and I think a lottery ticket as glovebox items that you can use as defense against threats. It's pretty limited.

Vehicle upgrades are pretty bare. There aren't like... rare versions of the upgrades so every shop in every town has about the same stuff and they all provide the same bonuses. It becomes a snoozefest and defeats the purpose of even visiting.

I was originally thinking this would play more into hitchhikers but in my first playthrough I ran into one. On my second playthrough I ran into two and their buff-to-debuff ratio isn't really worth bringing anyone along for the ride besides one that I found. I forget her name. It was something silly like The Champion or The Warrior. She leaves trash in your vehicle as her debuff but her bonuses are great. She steals 1 item from every shop that you visit for the first time and you get to pick that item. Then she also has the ability to destroy several threats at once if shes intoxicated or high. I was always high because weed was accessible and the cops don't seem to bother you for it. Alcohol is not worth it. You can get arrested and you can lose your game. You also get a ton of extra debuffs during fights when you are drunk... So it's literally pointless. 

Hitchhiker bonuses should far outweigh the downside of having them but then again, finding them is nearly impossible.

Once you make it to your final destination "The Festival", the game ends. I think it should give you the option to keep driving or start over versus it forcing the game credits and making you start over. The benefit here is that when you do finish the game and start over, you get to keep your vehicle and the modifications you put on it. Everything else gets erased.

I judge a game by hours played. I think it should parallel the dollar value. Considering I only got 4 hours out of this game, I don't think its worth $18. I do however think a $10 price tag would be fair because everyone is different and some people may get a little more enjoyment out of it.

But it just wasn't for me. I do think it's unique and I enjoyed the style so I do recommend it for others to try. Just be warned.

Some beverages spilling when driving.  Picking up hitchhikers that are part helping, part annoying.  The consequences of eating unhealthy food for days.  Customise your car.  Unlock skills.  Get traits depending on what you do in game.  I could go on forever.  All those small things add up and make the game the gem it is.

The roguelite aspect of the game is there, but it's not a game where you need to lose 5 runs to finally get a chance to finish one.  The things you unlock change things a bit, but they are never needed to get good results.  Example? New vehicles.  They play a bit differently but that's it.  Or you'll unlock different starting conditions, to keep things interesting.  A very interesting thing is the music, you find/buy cd's now and then, they get added to your playlist, and you keep them from one run to the other.  The music fits the game perfectly by the way.

The game gives enough info to know what you are doing, but some elements keep a mystery to them, you are left guessing what an item does.  It's not a bad thing honestly.  After all this time, I can only kind of guess what some of the bobbleheads really do.  And it does not matter.  The game is about the atmosphere.  Min maxing everything is not needed, so who cares if my guesses on bobbleheads' effects are wrong?

Runs last 3-5 hours roughly, there are 9 different possible endings to record in your journal (this is not a spoiler, you see that journal with all possible entries right on the welcome screen), with a lot of side quests you can do, it is far from over after your first run.

I checked and most negative reviews are about the fight/road events system.  I have no idea what those people were expecting.  It's a simple system and it fits the game perfectly.  It's there in part to keep you busy while travelling; simply clicking on the destination and being warped there would be silly.  It's also to keep an element of surprise, you never know what you'll encounter: a hitchhiker, a random suitcase full of goodies, sheep blocking the road, construction zone?  It's also much needed to keep you using resources.  Upgrading your car would be pointless without those road events.

Now, my personal only negative critique of the game.
It's a turn based game, [i]mostly[/i].  I say mostly because there's alcohol in the game, you can drink and get drunk, and then the game does not stop you from driving if you want to.  Fine.  My problem is, while drunk driving, you now have a clock to play each of your turn during road events.  It makes the game a lot tougher, I'm fine with that, but it was very unexpected from me at least.  Why break the turn based chill aspect of the game like that, the game could be tougher while remaining turn based?  Yes, there are ways to make drunk driving a lot easier, with a great car, good skills interactions and such but still, I feel like it breaks something.

On the bright side, you can totally avoid drunk driving and keep the game turn based if you want to.  The only 2 exceptions are:[spoiler]one ending that can't be reached unless you drink and drive, to unlock the final stage of a story line[/spoiler] and [spoiler]another ending that does not involve getting drunk but breaks the turn based aspect anyway.[/spoiler]  So those exceptions are not the end of the world, the game can be enjoyed as a turn based game.  I just personally wish I knew that was a thing before I started playing.  I was that close to refunding, with 30 minute played, because of how unexpected that was.

Overall great game, can't wait for updates/DLC/Keep Driving 2 if those ever materialise.

[h1][b]You're young, you have time.[/b][/h1]
[b]Pack your bags, we're going on a roadtrip![/b]

Keep Driving is an early 2000's take on roadtrip games such as Oregon Trail and Death Road to Canada, where the journey itself is more important than the destination. 

You'll explore a wide range of incredibly well made pixellated environments, ranging from beautifully lavish countrysides, to bustling and busy cities. All set to the hum of your car of choice and the CD of your burning.

[h1]Keep Driving has stunning visuals[/h1]

Before anything else, the visuals of this game are beautiful. If you're one to admire environments, you can easily get lost in the beauty of it. Whether you're cruising at high speeds on the motorway, or stopped in a nearby town for a quick respite, this game has phenomenal pixel art, no matter where you are. Alot of passion has been put into making this world feel lively, and it feels like you can even breathe it in. 

[b]It really grips and immerses you into its world, and complimenting that aesthetic would be it's music.[/b]

[h1]Music that enhances the experience[/h1]

The music of Keep Driving is, to put into simple words, extremely fitting. All of it's diagetic, coming from your cars CD player. If you want some music, you can burn your favourites into a playlist and hit play. Or shuffle you don't wanna spend the time. 

Either way, you'll be greeted with fantastic and fitting music from small swedish bands such as Westkust, Holy Now, The Honeydrips, etc. Genres vary a bit but they're all great. So good infact, when the demo released, I bought a vinyl of Westkust's album, Last Forever. 

[b]It's easily gotta be an early contender for best soundtrack this year, it's that good.[/b]

[h1]You've discussed the game but not gameplay[/h1]

The gameplay of Keep Driving consists of plotting a route on your map, and driving down roads to destinations. Whilst doing this, you must manage your resources, consisting of your Energy, Money, Gas and Car Durability. Lose enough of these with no backup, it's game over. You may occasionally receive Skill Points to put into skills for this games 'fights', and Buffs and Debuffs that may affect you on the road. 

On the road, you'll be intermittently interrupted by different things, from Introspections, short little thoughts that vary in outcome, Hitchhikers, which you may pickup that act as party members with upsides and downsides, and Road Events, small little 'fights' against things such as Potholes, Speed Cameras, Flocks of Sheep, Biker Gangs, etc. Road Events are the main threat of the game.

During Road Events, you'll be targeted by 4 different threats, corresponding to your resources. Fail to remove the ones with a red exclamation mark and you'll lose some of that resource. You use both your's and your Hitchhiker's Skills to clear these events by performing different combinations of 'attacks'. Clearing these without taking damage is incentivised by giving you buffs and potential permanent traits.

Outside of events on the road, you'll be given small little character interactions between you and your Hitchhikers, or even between themselves. It really helps to sell the world. 

One of the only gripes I actually have with this game is during these downtimes, nothing really happens when events aren't happening. On one hand, you get to gauk at stunning vistas and environments, on the other, if the trips long enough, it can feel tedious akin to the slog you'd feel in Desert Bus. There's also a small issue with item's not being very clear on their use, and there are a few bugs I've experienced that have soiled the experience, but not enough to leave a huge impression.

But either way, reaching a town allows you a bit of respite, whether it be buying food and supplies from a gas station, working a short job at a job agency for some money, sleeping in the car for a bit of energy, etc. You can also find garages and auto-shops, that allow you to upgrade your vehicle with new parts, helping with Road Events, amongst other things.

Your ultimate end-point of your journey can range from going to a music festival with a friend, to participating in a race for first place, to summiting a giant and lengthy mountain trek. You'll be given more options as you play.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

[b]Keep Driving is a beautifully immersive game, comprising of stunning pixellated vistas, moments that feel real and grounded, characters with little tid-bits to learn and experiences to forge into never-ending memories. It hits a very strong chord and specific niche while having a wholely unique, but ultimately 'relatable' feel.

It feels 'subjectively' good. You may like it, you may not, but it will deliver an experience that compares to no other when it hits. When it doesn't hit, it can feel a little dazed and confused however, such as some of it's bugs and description eligibility.[/b]

Give the game a go though. It truly feels unique in the market and incomparable to much else I've played.

[h1][b]The trip has a bittersweet feel to it, knowing it will close in on an end soon enough, but the journey is fantastic and definitely worth your time.[/b][/h1]

A fun faux MMO game that is reminiscent of massively multiplayer online games of the early 2000s -- with furries. This game is currently in early access as I write this so this may not reflect the finished product. I also didn't use public lobbies so my review doesn't reflect that aspect of the game.

I discovered this via one of Iron Pineapple's 'souls-like games' videos. What drew me in immediately was how cute and fun the character creation is and that's when I wishlisted it on Steam and played it upon release.

The art direction and sound design is true to what it is inspired by - the clunky loud computer-esque SFX with ominous distorted portal effects and a funky bopping OST. Even the low-poly graphics are reminiscent of the time, and I really think the developers did a great job of mimicking these elements while also adding their own personal style to the characters. I also loved how unique all the enemy designs were, my favourite being the boars.

The combat was more confusing if anything for me at first. I played a lot with my partner and fights in the dungeons would end up being one of us being chased by monsters waiting for abilities to recharge while the other would be chasing them with their attacks. I even whipped out my MMO mouse to see if it would help but, again, it always felt like enemies were a lot stronger than us. Even when we would grind for over an hour we still felt like we were puny in some dungeon rooms.

I really liked the class system, particularly that your character was locked in on their class once selected (also very reminiscent of older MMOs). Rogue ended up being the most fun to play, followed by mage, followed by warrior. As an extension to the classes I also loved the weapon designs, my personal go-to being the massive bells.

Armour sets in the game were risque, impractical, and looked so so so cute. I loved the "glamour" system in play for being able to equip ugly or mismatched armour underneath what I wanted to be presented wearing. My only gripe with the armour sets is that I wish there were more dye options. The green, red, and blue dyes are all so saturated and bright to match the three classes which I do understand, but I do wish a game like this where the character customisation is so creative had a matching armour customisation system that wasn't limited to the palette it currently has.

Overall I am really routing for this game. I'm excited to see what it will be like once it leaves early access and I'm hoping that what I have mentioned above is improved upon alongside more features being added to the finished product.

Low-effort horny jokes aside, Atlyss is genuinely a very fun ARPG to play, and I'm eager to follow its development! And it is still being actively worked on, which is excellent news. The movement feels so zippy and smooth, each class feels like a cohesive unit while being versatile enough for multiple possible builds, and dungeon delving is engaging and challenging right through to the end of the currently released content. My favorite class is Mystic, followed closely by Bandit, but the Fighter class is really enjoyable too, especially with its ability to reflect damage when parrying. I've also been tempted lately to try a run of the game where I never spec out of the Novice class and just use the scroll skills the whole way through...

Aside from the horny stuff (I'll get around to that by the end of this review, I promise), the aesthetic style of this game is excellent. I've seen a lot of people say the graphics remind them of Sega Dreamcast, and the enemy creature design in particular reminds me of the classic Spyro the Dragon trilogy for the PlayStation 1. The soundtrack is phenomenal, too! 

If you're willing to delve into multiplayer (not all of the lobbies are just ERP lobbies, there's usually a few that are explicitly labeled as SFW PvE lobbies), the multiplayer is fun, too! I haven't touched PvP because it's not something I usually enjoy, so I don't know how good (or not) PvP is in this game, but in PvE you can have a party of up to four players, and multiple parties within a lobby (the vanilla cap for lobby size is 16, but I've seen people who've modded the game for bigger lobbies). One important thing about multiplayer--loot is instanced per player, not per party, so there's no need to fight over loot. If one player gets a boss drop that another player's been looking for, people are generally perfectly willing to swap loot, which is nice! Though given that the way to do that is just "drop the item on the ground and wait for the other player to pick it up" it's kind of just down to an honor system to keep other players from swiping something another player dropped that was meant for you to take. So far, though, the multiplayer community seems to have few issues with people doing that.

The hints of story that are in the game so far have me intrigued, as well! The basic gist of it as explained in the very beginning of the game is, the world has been shattered and you've been brought back from the dead to reconnect the pieces. The bookshelves in Angela's tower contain lore tidbits hinting at some great apocalyptic event and the possible departure of a god. Exciting stuff!

Now for the elephant in the room. Yes, the game has some horny character design choices. There ARE settings in the game that let you turn that down, though. That's something I'm very glad about, actually! When I first encountered this game, it looked like something I'd enjoy, but I was hesitant to get it until I was told you could turn down the horny stuff, because that's just something I personally have no interest in. You can disable suggestive jiggle bones, clamp the body sliders to less exaggerated proportions, and there's an underwear toggle (labeled as "clear clothing" in the settings menu). Even with the underwear toggled off, there are no genitals in the game, just big boobs, big butts, and scanty clothes. There is a hidden achievement for slapping a particular character's butt and "annoying" said character, but it's a hidden achievement and no one is going to make you do it if you don't want to. Honestly, the most suggestive thing in the game that can't be turned off is a single attack animation used by a single miniboss that you only ever have to fight once (one of the Slime Diva's attacks fires dual beams of tiny slime bunny enemies out of her boobs).

So that's Atlyss! Genuinely a really fun game regardless of whether you're here for the actual gameplay or just for the jiggle physics. As I said earlier, I'm eager to follow its development. I really think this game is going to go places, and it's already got me hooked!

I kinda like this game! I've only played mystic so far and the skills and possible gameplay combinations are varied enough to feel fun to experiment with at least for that class; it should be possible for most people to find a playstyle they feel comfortable with. The movement is really satisfying and one of my favorite parts of the game. It gives you enough agency to have a fighting chance in more intense areas and to slip away when you need to heal, but it never feels too op.
I feel like it's a general rule in games that movement should come at the cost of damage and vice versa, and finding that balance for different types and amounts of enemies is the bulk of what engages me in the combat. The leniency of the parry and the fact that it can override/interrupt basically any ability also helps a [b] lot [/b] in making it less frustrating than FromSoft or other parry-heavy games. Speaking of FromSoft, the lack of a real punishment for dying is also something I heavily prefer over the opposite, though me having spent 400 hours in Celeste might've indicated that already.
The knockback on some enemies makes it easy to get stunlocked especially in small rooms, and this is where you can start to feel a bit powerless. It's entirely possible to push through those kinds of moments where you're hanging on for dear life, but if you're well and truly stuck the game always presents opportunities for improvement without making it feel like too much of a grind; I find the combat engaging even against lower level enemies.
I think the artstyle is a big reason why I keep wanting to spend more and more time with this game. I'm not even particularly nostalgic for ps1-esque graphics. It's just really pretty and pleasant to look at, and I will [b] always [/b] prefer a game with clear artistic vision and great performance over a hyper-realistic, 120GB game that I can't break 60fps in even if I play on medium. Also character design is super cute, can't wait for more customisation options to be added (though the jiggle physics are maybe a bit egregious).
All in all, I'm really enjoying this game and I'm really excited to see where it goes in the future!

The amount of customization in this game is just nuts. You would think that makes a few loopholes, or some sort of crazy cheese strategy ... but no. My glass cannon sage is insanely powerful, but the cost is that he often goes last and has some ailment vulnerabilities (on top of the physical weakness). A buffed up knight can hit hard and keep aggro well, but when a spell comes through that reduces his aggro to 0 ... things get wild. That's one of the things I loved about this game. You may have some strategies ready, but creative enemy and boss encounters will throw a wrench in the mix. 

Similar to the Megaten games, ailments in this game REALLY matter, and boy do the enemies love to use them. I like games that make you consider this. You don't always need to stack offense. If you fight a boss that is charming your team, you need to find a relic to stop that. A late game boss was just chewing through my tank's HP, but I saw that he had a fire vulnerability, so I added a few relics to counter that and fared much better. Again, that's what is so brilliant about this game. There's always something you can do to help the encounter (if you explore and find the equipment or build up your skills to do so), yet the encounters are STILL interesting, because they will often throw in an ability or spell that nukes your strategy. Yes, that sometimes causes a wipe, but you have to dust yourself off and try again.

I'll say this ... I've definitely played easier games. You can't just blindly wander through later encounters in this game, especially in the post game. A KO vulnerability will spell (quite literally) instant death for your team, and a surprise by the wrong group of enemies could be a rough time. Even after saying all this ... I don't think the game is TOO challenging. It can be challenging at times, yes, but it's still fair. If something is not working for you, it's almost always because your build needs addressing, though I guess it IS possible to be severely under-leveled or not have the proper team.

Needless to say, I would recommend playing this if you enjoy interesting combat mechanics, amazing party and equipment customization, and fun exploration, all in a retro style. The music is pretty great, too. I couldn't believe how many cools music tracks were stuffed into this one. 

The only complaint I have with this game is that I feel like I robbed the development team by only paying $13 for it. The amount of content and enjoyment I got out of it was surely worth more, but I thank the team regardless for such a good game.

I'm not one for long-winded reviews, but: level design is easily digestible. World is mostly linear except for the few open-world sections, and those are limited enough that there's no worry about getting overwhelmed or lost. 

What really shines about this game is character customizability. You start out picking 4 of 16 classes, but don't worry about it - you can spec your existing characters into the other classes as you go along, leading to infinite permutations of abilities. Your mage too squishy? Give them a knight subclass and equip heavy armor. Your mage too weak? Give them a sage subclass and get AoE magic + 25% magic damage up. 

Past classes, there's the wide variety of equipment. Most equipment in the mid-late game isn't strictly better or worse than other gear as far as damage or defense goes - rather, what you're looking at are extra attributes like counter percentage, evasion percentage, status effects, and so on. Keep everything you find, because you might find yourself needing to change up your strategy for a tough boss, and you'll need the perfect set of equipment to do it.

Blood Bar Tycoon is a relatively simple management game (on the casual, not hard difficulty) and whilst it can be fun it is plagued with plenty of bugs. Positives:
+ Unique take on tycoon games (vampires, blood bars)
+ Catchy ambient music that fits
+ Colorful cast of characters that you can interact with (there are consequences for annoying them)
+ Good range of themes
+ Having a casual and a harder difficulty
+ Just kind of quirky and fun

Negatives:
- UI is a bit jank, there is no way to determine keywords or customer types on humans. They should add an option to hover over text to explain or show these details.
- The campaign is a bit loose with no real story or clear end to it. 
- The campaign map has clear sections where districts would go, clearly these were left empty for DLC when there are only 6 or 7 levels so its a bit disappointing to be planning for paid levels. 
- The "Crazy Vampire Girl" District is a horribly laid out map.
- Lack of variety on some themes decorations. Some are unlocked way too late.
- Having to complete later stages before going back and 3 starring earlier stages.
- Feels like there are missing research upgrades, I was constantly on 999 points and needed 0 money.
- The BUGS. There are a lot. I'll make a list of what i found. Customers get stuck at tables, Staff get stuck at tables (possibly fixed), everyone gets stuck on doors (some possibly fixed), customers wont use the toilets, humans getting stuck at the exit point meaning no more humans will spawn, investigators "investigating" the entire outskirt of the map, staff getting stuck on bars, staff outfits corrupting, staff being stuck there after firing them, some staff/customers are unclickable, achievements are bugged by either not progressing or not unlocking when conditions are met, some customer types never spawn even with the correct themes (didn't see a single pirate). Honestly cannot remember more so I'll end that list here. AGAIN they said they would fix these but this game released as a v1.0 so it should have been ready, even if they are a small team.

A Bloody Good Time... With a Few Bumps in the Night

I sunk my teeth into Blood Bar Tycoon expecting a fang-tastic management sim, and while it definitely delivers a unique and entertaining experience, it also left me feeling a bit… drained.

The Good Stuff:
🩸 A Killer Concept: Running a vampire bar? Count me in! The theme is refreshingly original, and the dark humor adds a delightfully macabre charm.

🩸 Addictive Gameplay Loop: Managing blood supplies, customizing the bar, and keeping customers (both living and undead) satisfied is surprisingly engaging. I kept telling myself, just one more night... and suddenly hours had vanished.

🩸 Delightfully Dark Humor: The game leans into its spooky aesthetic with clever puns and witty dialogue. If you love wordplay as much as I do, you’ll get a kick out of it.

The Not-So-Good:
🦇 Gameplay Balancing is a Little... Anemic: At times, it feels like I’m running a black-market organ farm rather than a vampire bar. Most of my income comes from research, making the game feel more like Anatomical Research Tycoon than Blood Bar Tycoon. And don’t even get me started on the murder mechanics—there’s almost no incentive to be sneaky. I can go full Jack the Ripper, toss the bodies in the sewer like it’s trash day, and nobody bats an eye. Where’s the tension? The thrill of the hunt? The paranoia of getting caught? If the game pushed me to actually keep my bar’s true nature a secret, it would be so much more immersive. Let’s get those VIP rooms dripping with mystery (and, well... blood). Secret blood raves, off-the-record torture chambers—that’s the kind of exclusivity I’d expect from an establishment catering to the undead elite.

🩸 Where’s My Blade-Style Blood Rave?!: Look, I get it—licensing and all that. But come on. If I can run an underground vampire bar, I should absolutely be able to throw a blood shower rave. The fact that I can’t is the real crime here. Let me drench my guests in a crimson downpour while techno blasts in the background, and I promise you, I’ll never complain about game balance again.

🦇 Bugs That Bite: Unfortunately, I ran into a fair share of glitches. Customers and staff sometimes got stuck, and there were moments when the controls just didn’t respond. While patches are rolling out, it’s still a bit of a pain in the neck.

🦇 A UI That Needs a Little... Life: The interface feels clunky at times, and certain mechanics could use better explanations. I spent way too much time trying to figure out how to optimize staff (the meaning of passive traits is still in the shadow) and understand customer needs. I keep accidentally closing the bar because the close button is poorly located.

🦇 No Reason to Get Crafty with Bar Design: Right now, the layout of my bar doesn’t really matter. Traps just magically teleport victims to their cages like some kind of supernatural Uber. Where’s the fun in that? I want to design my bar with actual strategy—hidden passages, secret backrooms, labyrinthine corridors that make The Shining look like a straight shot to the exit. If the game forced me to cleverly place my cages behind walls and route victims through my own personal haunted house of horrors, it would make base-building way more satisfying.

Right now, I don’t feel like a sinister baron of the undead—I feel like I’ve got some glitchy teleportation spell that does all the work for me. Give me a reason to craft a truly deceptive layout, and I’ll happily turn my establishment into a real house of horrors.

🦇 A Repetitive Grind: Once I got the hang of things, the challenge sort of plateaued. There wasn’t much to shake up the routine, and after a while, I found myself going through the motions rather than strategizing.

Final Verdict:
Blood Bar Tycoon is a fun, quirky take on the tycoon genre, and I had a blast running my own undead establishment. But as much as I loved the concept, the bugs and UI frustrations sucked some of the fun out of the experience. If the devs keep polishing it, this could easily become a cult classic.

For now, I’d recommend it to anyone who loves vampires, management sims, and a good pun—but maybe wait for a few more updates before taking the plunge. 🦇🍷

The research tree just *looks* like it was meant to have more to it. In fact, I think I saw mention of an "incinerator" as another machine for disposing corpses, so I feel like all of the intended content did not make it to release. 

I also wish that some things were more impactful. For example, I didn't notice too big of a difference with the minions' stats. I definitely paid attention to the minion skills but their actual stats didn't seem to affect my bar's performance very much. The patrons themselves also seem to have features that I largely ignored simply because I didn't need to pay attention to them in order to get 3 stars. For example, humans have a stat that indicates how much they'll affect the Awareness stat but I would kill indiscriminately and never had trouble there. Also, vampires seem to have different levels of prestige? There were commoners and aristrocrats. I wish that the impact of these traits were more obvious.

So there's plenty that can be done to flesh out the game more. I honestly do recommend it at its current state though. Go into it expecting a simple game with a fun aesthetic and I think you could have fun with this. I hope it gets more content as I would love to come back and play it even more!

T/L-D/R: Game is a grind for upgrade resources/gear check based shooter, bosses are basic "kill the adds before boss spawns more, dont stand in fire and dodge slow, big, moving projectiles" type bosses, except for the mech bosses in the final area, they are more of a gear check/los them until either your shield dude is good to fight again or your heal items are ready to use again. Game took me 73 hours and 30 mins to complete once you take out afk time.

Long version:

Finally beat the game. It's as alot of other reviews say, its very grindy. The whole reason why only 3.8% of people that have bought this game have beaten it, is because of how grindy it is, not due to difficulty. The story is nothing special but its not bad either (most of it is told via the characters you find, once they get back to base after having saved them, you talk to them and then question them for info). Most people get burnt out of the game with in the first 10-20 hours of game play it seems judging by the reviews since it is all very "samey/reptitive".

The bosses are nothing new, they are pretty much gear checks, although you could kite them to a rock if you wanted too, wait for their clip to run out, then pop out and hit them for the 2/3 seconds it takes to reload, but that would make them take a VERY long time, and as i said, most spawn enemies, about 6 each time and if you dont burn them down fast enough, the boss will spawn more and you will be overwhelmed by mobs and die. Plus they have 3 "phases" each which seems to transition every 30% hp or so (just gain another attack or spawn harder to kill mobs or spawn an extra mini boss).

Their is lots of upgrading to do, can lvl up your character, base, gear and so on. Speaking of your base, the one negative review that has gotten a chunk of upvotes, the dude says something along the lines of "I got to the korean base and gave up and choose to cheat and give myself all the mats to upgrade the shit out of my self, since it would take me another 60 hours to grind for it"..... yeah..... the korean base and your starting base are almost one in the same. Your upgrade's from your first base transfer over 100%. The only difference is that you get access to a food stash that has an upgrade cap of lvl 3 (so unlock it, then upgrade it twice) and it does not require alot of mats. 

Plus he had 60 hours clocked in, so im guessing, about, ill say, 55ish hours clocked in before he cheated (which he admits to) to upgrade himself to all hell and made a B line for the last boss as fast as possible and finished the game at 60 hours played. As i said above, i beat the game in 73 and a half. so no, it would not have taken him another 60 hours to grind out what would be needed to beat the game. (looking back on it, i could have beaten the last boss with less upgrade's then what i had, so even sooner). Still, as i said above, the game is grindy, so i can understand that part 100%.

Then it gives you 2 goliaths and access to the ability to upgrade your goliaths (they are not needed to beat the game, hell, i found them kinda useless personally and never bothered to use them, and yes, i did upgrade them, still did not find them useful). Past the extra food storage (which again, is a small amount to cap) and the golaiths, the base is the exact same as your first. The only other thing the korean base has past this, is "end game" content via challenges. 

These challenges can be done any time and provide rewards for finishing them. Its really just fighting multiple bosses at once or fighting 1 boss with only 2 or 3 squad members rather then 4, or fighting multiple bosses with only 2-3 squad members. Sometime's they let you use goliath's and some times not. The npc will let you know if you can take the mech into the fight or not when you try to do it.

As for bugs, i encountered a sound bug that was very odd and seemed to be restricted to certain area's. When i would aim/shoot to the left, the sound would be normal volume then when i would aim to the right and fire, the sound would be very quiet as if the volume lvl dropped to only 20% of what it should be. Not game breaking, but annoying none the less. Past that, the game ran just fine.

Also, in the youtube vids, almost all are for the mobile version, in this game (the steam version), in the last area, all the mobs including the last boss, are lvl 11, not lvl 12. Thats pretty much it for this review. Overall i found the game to be decently enjoyable. That being said, be prepared to grind cause again, dont forget, only 3.8% of ppl that have bought this game have bothered to finish it due to how grindy it is. 

I got by without spending mats on gear for a long while (i focused on just upgrading the base early game, crafted VERY VERY little gear early game and NEVER upgraded my gear until i had end game gear). I almost made a B line for things like storage units/bigfoot cores ect after i had cleared out all lvl 1-4 area's. i did not do full clear's for any of the lvl 5-8 areas. I did all the world missions and about 9 (maybe 10/11) challenges. I fully cleared the last area as well (and i only lightly dabbled in fishing and that was early game only). That  ended up being a bit more then enough to beat the last boss.

Thats all i got for you for tips. But yeah, personally, over all, as i said, i found this game to be decently enjoyable. Not insanely fun, but i enjoyed it enough to beat it where most ppl just got bored/burnt out of it since as i said above, this game is not about skill, its about the grind. If you like this game enough to grind for 67-70 hours, then you will see the end, if you cant see yourself spending 67-70+ hours on it or close to that, then chance's are you wont see the end.

Over all, i think this is a decent game to kill time with (even more so since it saves a ton). Thats all i have to say about this game, i bid ye good day.

Huge rail shooter fan and a huge shmup fan. A fan of arcade in general. This game seems to be a blend of everything I love. The atmosphere, the visceral feeling of moving at high speeds and shooting, it feels great. I especially like the sheer scale and presence of the bosses. I just finished the main story and still have many other modes to dive into, but I'm going to go ahead and say I already got my moneys worth.

I have one big nitpick, however. Hot take, but I think the stages need to be much shorter and much denser. They were all pretty long, but the tunnel stage especially drags. I know the mainstream audience would cry about it and say it's too short, but they don't know what true replay value means. If I were to set out to master this game and replay it hundreds of times, there would be so much accumulated time that I'm just mindlessly fighting small popcorn. So, if that were condensed down to where the moment-to-moment gameplay matched the intensity this game is exuding, you'd have a 10/10 on your hands. 

But like I said there are other modes I haven't played. I know there is a caravan mode, and that will probably be closer to what I'm looking for. But my criticisms for story mode still stand because the short, snappy rounds would go so well with the escalating narrative. 

Overall great game. The industry needs more of this and I look forward to what you put out in the future.

The bosses could use stages with varied attacks at each stage. Hidden routes in levels or hidden objectives would have been a great feature. That said, this game does a combo meter incredibly well. When you start getting high 50's combo, you get that feeling like in Tony Hawk during a long combo where you momentarily consider playing it safe by breaking your combo...but you think to yourself "Fuck it, we ball" and you keep going. Overall, this is an excellent 7/10 game, well worth the price of admission.

I had been bouncing from one cozy game to another feeling burnt out and unsatisfied. This game is such a refreshing palette cleanser from the typical farming/crafting sims. 
The aesthetic is deliciously delightful! From the vibrant, dynamic environment to the utterly charming stop-motion effect on your character’s movements (Aardman Animations, anyone??), it’s a feast for the eyes!
I have a blast just reading all the cute and quirky names of every single NPC. (Apricot needs a raise, btw). The world is alive, bustling with charm. It’s such a joy compared to the often sparse worlds of other cozy games. The dialog and personalities are an absolute treat.
And the mini games! They are so unique and adorable. Plus the music is so chill. And let’s be honest, the beat that drops when you start driving your caravan …. It just, HITS in the best way <3 
I even love that my poor bee is a bit of a (honey)drunk driver…. by user error, of course. I promise Rigby, I’ll get better! 
There’s zero pressure, no racing against the clock—just a leisurely pace where you get to chill and enjoy all the wonderful little details. Every corner has something delightful to discover.
The character creation has so many adorable options, colors, and outfits it was seriously hard to choose. You’re telling me I can play as an opossum?? YES, PLEASE. A turtle? A gecko?? A deer? The cutest cow you’ve ever seen? Omfg. I could keep going for all of them. 
The crafting mechanics and animations are so cozy and delightful. I love cooking/sewing by candlelight in my little pajamas. If it’s a multi-step recipe you can pin the recipe and turn your brain off while the game guides you through each step - genius. I love changing my outfit into something “fancy” on market days. I’m also weirdly obsessed with running and jumping through dandelion puffballs & mushrooms! 
I’m truly amazed at how extensive  this game is for the price, especially being in early access. No regrets - Just pure love and excitement for this gem. I could seriously live in this little world, in my cozy caravan, just vibing, exploring new places, and helping critters along the way forever. This game is a love letter to my inner child that I didn’t know I needed. Huge thanks to the devs for putting a sparkle back into my gaming experience! 

Also, I play on steam deck and runs great.

At this time I cannot recommend anyone buying this game for anywhere near this price.  I see alot of potential for a good $20 game at best.

You can view my gameplay & early impressions here: https://youtu.be/sk8rxwQoIjk

Quite simply, I had fun. This is a budget-priced arcade kart racer where you push yourself forward like you're on a wheelchair in this open-world obstacle course. You can boost, double-jump, or glide in the air as you try to get to your location to complete quests. It's closer to a platforming game than an actual racing game, but you can definitely race against your friends online.

The controls are quite easy to learn, but can be challenging to master, especially when you try to go up an incline with the wind trying to blow you off. I do think the game can use a better tutorial, especially for the more advanced tricks you have to learn to get around some obstacles. There is usually a ghost (AI player) you can sort of follow to learn how to do it though.

Pushing yourself around is actually pretty easy so it's not an intense workout. The challenge is mostly trying to figure out the obstacle course. I wasn't sure about the content, but after about an hour, I'm still no where close to finishing the race just due to the challenge. It's a really huge map.

Game is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting a steady 72 fps (Q3 default). I did not experience any serious issues or bugs. You can play comfortable seated, as long as you can move your hands backwards to forward from your side. You can easily re-center as well in-game. The game uses an automatic tunnel (vignette) and helmet, you can turn those off in the settings to get a clearer view.

My biggest complaint is that the scales are a bit off. It just feels like the world is big and you are small. Also, it seems like the game automatically shows your IP address in the main hub area. There is no off-line mode. The game could use some graphical settings as well. It does need a better tutorial for the more advanced techniques. However, all in all, the game is fun and is off to a good start in Early Access. It just needs more people (and possibly a more secure connection).

[b]What is it:[/b] A grid-based sliding/sokoban puzzler, in which you have to slide ice cubes into holes. Split into 8 chapters, the first 7 introducing a new mechanic, and the last one putting them all together in some very hard puzzles, the game gets quite hard and interesting.

There are many things the game does really well. The mechanics are good. Unlimited undo even across restarts. Good achievements. Good level select. All levels in a chapter are unlocked at once. Unlocking the next chapter requires only 5 out of 10 to be solved, plus a puzzle inside the level selector itself! Good difficulty progression in a chapter, and across chapters. A good hidden puzzle that requires thinking outside the box. Overall, an excellent game!

However, the implementation is terrible. Only one resolution (700x430), which can be doubled. Control is mouse only, and moving the non-sliding pieces across the level one click and drag at a time is soooo tedious. Almost no settings. UI both in English and Japanese at the same time.

[b]How hard is it:[/b] Easy to hard, a good spectrum. Each new mechanic is gently introduced, but the last 2-4 puzzles in a chapter are quite hard.

[b]How long is it:[/b] 88 levels split in 8 chapters, for about 5-10 hours. All levels in a chapter are unlocked from the start, and half of them must be done to unlock the next one.

[b]Level design:[/b] Very good. Varied levels, with non-trivial solutions, and no obvious mistakes.

[b]Quality:[/b] Mixed. See above for more details.

[b]Worth the price:[/b] Yes.

[b]Most positive aspect for me:[/b] Good and varied mechanics, good puzzles.

[b]Most negative aspect for me:[/b] Mouse only control.

[b]What would make it better:[/b] Keyboard controls. Better support for resolutions and fullscreen. Better support for the steam deck or controllers.
