This is a solid start to the Early Access launch, but I wouldn't currently recommend buying the game unless you think 15-20 hours of monotonous shallow gameplay is worth $15 to you. I’ll keep updating this review as the developers make changes. 

The art is impressive, and there’s a solid foundation, but the gameplay itself feels like it was made for a very dumb robot.

1) Brew basic beer to earn money and improve town relations.
2) Complete repetitive quests with ale recipes you’d never make otherwise.
3) Repeat the cycle.

Optionally brew some higher-quality beers for special orders, though this feature feels like a chore, requiring you to constantly make random mid-tier beers for a little extra cash.

Yes, that's the entire gameplay loop.

Here are some key areas I think could use improvement:

Raising Funds: You can brew any kind of beer to make money, but ironically, the cheapest beer often brings in the most profit, which takes away any fun or strategic element from the game's secondary mechanics. So, you just throw in the bare requirements for each ingredient to make the beer you wanna sell and you're done.

Boring Tasks/Quests/Missions: NPCs will request specific brews with unique characteristics, which can be fun at first, but the problem is that these beers rarely yield a good profit. You end up making them once, feeding them to your staff, and repeating it endlessly. This repetition makes the game feel more like a grind, especially after the 400th time you’re tasked with the same thing. It's made even worse because there doesn't appear to be a way to delete recipes so you'll end up with hundreds of recipes to scroll through that you'll never use again. If I'm wrong and they can be deleted, please comment and let me know how,

Shallow Building Mechanics: Early on, you’ll spend time carefully choosing which rooms to build and where to invest resources. But by mid-game, most players’ abbeys look the same because the number of rooms and staff is so limited. With a cap of just 16 employees, you'll likely end up with 2 dorms, 2 cafeterias, one of each other room type, and a bunch of breweries. There are no interesting bonuses for positioning rooms (like +10% brewing speed next to a dorm), so there’s no real strategy to it. All you need to focus on is making sure your staff has food and sleep nearby to minimize wasted time.

No Fail States: The game allows you to go bankrupt without any consequences. You can run negative cash flow, take out a one-year loan of 800G (with no interest or penalty for non-payment), and just keep playing indefinitely. You can essentially start a new game, have 2 people do research and acquire all the techs up to phase 2 of the monastery with no risks of failing then start the game with 60% of the techs in the game.

Shallow Interior Decorating: There are plenty of decorative items to unlock through quests or research, but most of them are completely pointless. You’d be better off sticking to a single high-quality decoration, as that’s far more effective than using any of the less useful ones. It would be nice if there were more incentive to use a variety of decor, like making the first item you place have increased benefits to encourage diversity.

Lack of Meaningful Choices: Progression feels too linear. You unlock the same things in the same order as everyone else. It would be more interesting if completing tasks gave you meaningful choices, like unlocking a new brew, decor, staff member with a unique perk, or even a special room with unique features (like a luxury dorm that reduces sleep time by 20%).

No Interesting Ingredient Acquisition: There’s no real variety in how you acquire ingredients—no farms, herb gardens, or orchards to make the process more dynamic. The merchant is there, but they don’t add much excitement to the gameplay. If you rely on the merchant in the late game, you’ll need a lot of storage rooms, but it’s generally more profitable to add another brewer instead. The same issue applies with cellars, although one cellar is fairly necessary.

I know this game has received mostly positive reviews, but I suspect many of them come from players who haven’t reached the endgame content yet. I’m curious to see what the community thinks once they hit the grind wall and curious how the developers respond. I’m excited to see what updates they’ll bring, but for now I would just wait if I were you. I can't get my $15 back, but you can save yours. If it goes on sale for like $7, that would be a buy with the current content and gameplay loop.

Ale Abbey is a great simulation game with a strong gameplay loop and satisfying progression system. There are some rough spots still in the game design, but overall the game is already fun even if it needs a little more intuitive design.

Pros

The music is a lovely old style, it really captures that monastery feeling without being too bold to be off putting.

The recipe system is extremely dynamic! You can stick with genre perfect beers, or you can make a Fruited Hefe, or a Coffee Lager. Creating new recipes with distinct differences is rewarding because of the Unique Trait system which provides bonus' for unusual combinations. Once I made a honey herbal ale, and it gained the trait of Bribery which made it more cost effective to bribe the local thugs with.

The art style is cute and just works. Not much more to say. The game is plenty pleasing to look at.

This game also educates you in beer, what makes a Old Ale different from an Amber Ale? There is a lot to learn, and of course it isn't 100% true to life. But as someone who works in the beer industry it is plenty impressive how much knowledge can be gleaned from this game.

Cons

There are some systems which need to be added to make this game play better. Currently if you want to remodel your monastery, you have to remove ALL furniture from a room, which means you have to sell it for a low price, demolish that room AND repeat for any rooms built out from this room either on top or going across. This means if you make one mistake in the early game, you cannot fix that until you have basically beaten the game and have an excess of money because of how prohibitive that is.
I'd suggest that instead of Demolish a room, it should be "Make Room Blank." If there was a Blank Room type, which allowed any kind of furniture so you don't have to sell it and buy it back later, I think that would mostly fix this issue.  And then you can change the Blank room into any other type of room you'd like.

Some of the brewing mechanics are not intuitive at all. Aging ale can only happen if a brew has 5 or more strength, but the game never tells you that. It does ask you to age an ale, but it never mentions how to do this (I had to ask on discord how this works.) Additionally the transition from 100 liter brewing to 300 liter brewing is bumpy to say the least. Once you upgrade your Abbey to level 2, you are flooded with requests for 110+ liters of beer, at first you may think you can brew 2 batches of beer and combine them to meet the request, but you cannot. You have to brew at least the amount the request is for, which requires you to upgrade to 300 liter brewing capacity. You can research a Brewing Stove upgrade, and the game currently lets you upgrade your Brewing Stove, which sounds great at first. But if you didn't research and upgrade your Fermentation Barrel as well so that it can HOLD 300 liters of beer, you just wasted money. In my situation this resulted in a game over, since the new stove cooks slower than the old one and I wasted nearly all my money on this one upgrade without knowing I needed to upgrade both.

There are currently a few game breaking bugs in the game. I was able to go 9 hours without encountering one, but this is Early Access. If you buy it right now, you have to expect this sort of thing.

Overall the game is WELL worth putting on your radar, or just purchasing now. The dev team is active on their discord and is constantly working with players to fix issues, and help with problems understanding the game. I firmly believe this game is going to be a hit once completed.

I appreciate that Ale Abbey is in Early Access, because it needs to be.  I found the game to be a slow, monotonous crawl with little reward for your time invested.  This isn't to say it's an overall bad game, there is a good game here; it's just neither balanced well nor is it captivating.

Your humble beginnings, you are walked through the setup of your Abbey, preparing some basic Light Ale's to sell to a local town.  The start of the game is engaging and as you take each step, there are actively things to do, and it's very easy to get hooked - in fact, this period is mirrored in the demo, and is what sold me on purchasing Ale Abbey.  However, once the reigns come off, and you're left to your own devices, it very quickly becomes a slog.  The game just becomes a exercise in repetition, with little player feedback required - especially once you research the Custodian Closet, and you now have cleaning and candle resetting done automatically (which, I'm thankful for, but once those chores were gone, that's when my eyes opened and I realized how little there is here).

As you research and expand your Abbey, you get little sub-quests to unlock new Ale varieties for a town, and you're tasked with coming up with recipes that match certain requirements.  This requires a little bit of playing around to get exactly what you need, and making a brew for the first time (or rather, the first time a specific individual makes a brew), creates the template for what you'll sell going forward.  However, that's kind of all you really do.  Now you just brew a batch, sell it to a town.  Brew a batch, submit some to an order.  Brew a batch, put it in a cask.  You ... aren't really doing anything else, except playing on the fastest game speed, waiting for a brew to finish, and clicking something, then you're done.  Your residents run around and do their own thing with no need to get involved in their business, at all.

Ale Abbey is also plagued with the whole "Reinvent the Wheel" style research tree, which I loathe.  Once you upgrade your Abbey to Level 2, you unlock more researches, one being: Storage.  Yes, my dear reader, you invent the idea of putting stuff in a room.  You needed to research this very basic concept.  I do understand from a gameplay mechanic why it's there, because Storage allows you to buy ingredients at discounted price and have them stockpiled, to save money (rather than buying ingredients at full price when you go to create an ale).  However, this is where poor balance comes into play: the storage, this massive room that's the same dimensions as every other room (such as a bedroom that fits 8, or a flippin' library) can store a whopping ONE HUNDRED ingredients.  Yes, let me emphasize: a library with four bookshelves takes up the same volume as a room that possesses... one hundred tiny hops.  Something that should take up no more than a 1'x1' box, for some reason, uses the entire Storage room.  So yea, balance.  Storage room is locked behind some hefty research requirements and then you're expected to build twenty of them.

Nevertheless, the lack of anything to do in Ale Abbey is really where my crux is.  All joy increasingly declined once past the tutorial.  It was just throw as much ale at each town as possible, whenever possible, because if you don't you'll go bankrupt anyway - the profit margins are quite slim.  So Ale Abbey is more of an idle game than a real game at this point, unfortunately.

However, I do have high hopes for future updates.  At least there's a core gameplay loop prepared, and there's absolutely room for so much more!  I am excited to see what's next, but for now, I've had my fill of clicking exactly two buttons in sequence.

P.S.: I recommend changing the look of when research is complete versus unlocked-yet-incomplete.  The tiny green border, I feel, is insufficient.  I consistently thought I had unlocked researches when I did not, and vice versa.

There are quite a few UI issues, which for this kind of game is critical. It took me a long time to understand that I could add more than one ingredient of each. After that point, it's nice to mix them to settle on the qualities you want to reach. However, this is clearly too complex for the start. Another similar issue, is what to do with the beer you just brewed. The result buttons are too small or unclear, especially when answering an order, where you have to click and hold. That's not explained anywhere. You see the market from the get go, but cannot use it at all. Why do that?

Parallel to that, placing furniture in the rooms is a bit frustrating. More often than not, it means closing a window. I'm not sure if it influences the room lighting, but it's a pain. Improving the room quality is also not very visible, apart from a small popup. The setup inside of a room seems to have no gameplay effect.

Managing your people is too complex from the get go. There are many parameters, they all start depressed, and it's a drag to try and improve that. And at the start, you can't even do anything about it, which is worse. Also, they seem to drink whenever they want, you have no control over it. They also gain levels without any signalling about it.

Some gating is very unclear. I was looking to add one brewing post, but could not. No idea why, but it was a clear and frustrating limit. Also not possible to have a third research post, why? I was left with a fourth, idle worker at all times. Why I could not build rooms on top of other rooms is also unclear. At the very start, it took me some time to find where to create a new room.

As for the central gameplay of brewing beers, the resulting quality seems to be very much random. It's a pain, a drag, especially with only one brewing station. It's unclear how to improve, and if you even improve over time. It seems there's no way to modify an existing recipe at start - even if the choice is already present.

The mini gameplays of cleaning and changing candles are strange. Why would the player have to do that manually? I guess it gets automated later.

I'm sure the team can fix most of these issues, and improve the game. I'll revisit later.

Ale Abbey: A Delightful Early Access Experience
After 8 hours of game play, I'm thoroughly enjoying the game. Rather than rehashing known issues already acknowledged by the developers, I'd like to focus on the game's strengths and potential improvements.

What Makes This Game Special

The visual presentation immediately draws you in with its charming art style, well-designed models, and cohesive aesthetic that perfectly captures the monastery brewing theme. The user interface deserves special praise for its intuitive design that makes managing your brewing operation a pleasure rather than a chore.

The atmospheric soundtrack complements the medieval setting wonderfully adding to the brewing experience without becoming repetitive or distracting.
Quest design shows careful thought, with missions that not only guide new players through the brewing mechanics but also provide meaningful goals that deepen your engagement with the game world. I particularly appreciate how these quests help focus your brewing experiments while teaching core concepts.
One of the most innovative features is the market system with its specialised traits and interests. Different regions prefer distinct flavour profiles and characteristics in their ales, which adds a additional layer of strategy to your brewing decisions. 

This regional variation transforms what could have been a straightforward production simulator into something with much richer game play possibilities.
As this is an Early Access title, I'll not comment on content length and the research progression. The brewing modification system also shows promise, and I look forward to seeing how these elements evolve through development.

Opportunities for Enhancement
While already enjoyable, several additions could elevate the experience further:

Brewery Management Flexibility: The ability to remove or relocate rooms would significantly improve facility planning and adaptation as your brewery evolves.

Order Fulfilment Mechanics: Currently, order fulfilment feels unnecessarily restricted. For example, despite having 400L of storage capacity across multiple barrels, I couldn't fulfil a 180L order because my brewing equipment was limited to 100L 
batches. Allowing combined deliveries from multiple barrels would create more strategic options while accommodating early-game limitations.

Enhanced Delivery Challenges: Introduce multi-product orders requiring several ale types in a single contract. This would create meaningful endgame complexity while building upon the existing market license mechanics, encouraging players to maintain diverse brewing capabilities rather than specialising in only a few profitable recipes.

Streamlined Order Management: The ability to fulfil orders directly from the market screen would improve workflow efficiency compared to the current requirement of interacting with brewing vessels.

Expanded Abbot Role: The Abbot character could become more integral to game play through morale effects or special abilities like blessing brews, purifying infected barrels, or accelerating ageing processes.

Deeper Bandit Interactions: The existing bandit system could evolve into a more complex faction mechanic, where allegiances influence market prices in different cities or provide benefits like protected deliveries.

Ingredient Cultivation: Vertical expansion of the monastery could enable external farmland for growing brewing ingredients, adding a production element to the supply chain.

Research Expansion: A second research station in the library would allow simultaneous recipe development and modification.

Diversified Income Streams: Historically, monasteries produced various goods beyond beer. Optional side ventures like cheese-making could provide supplementary income without overshadowing the brewing focus.

Recipe Recovery System: A mechanism to rediscover deleted recipes through extended research would prevent permanent loss of valuable formulations.

Ageing Mechanics: Long-term brewing could impart special bonuses to beers, creating an incentive for preserving "ancient" recipes and developing specialised brewing techniques.

Steam deck Compatibility: Adding support for Valve's portable device would perfectly complement the game's relaxed brewing simulation. The ability to manage your monastery while travelling would enhance the game's accessibility for players preferring flexible gaming sessions.

Conclusion

Ale Abbey has already established itself as a thoroughly enjoyable simulation with distinctive charm and engaging mechanics. The developers have created a solid foundation that balances accessibility with depth, and the game's Early Access state shows tremendous promise for future development. Highly recommended for fans of management sims, brewing enthusiasts, or anyone looking for a uniquely relaxing gaming experience.

I look forward to sharing additional thoughts as I continue exploring the game and discovering new aspects of the monastery brewing experience.

Ale Abbey is a medieval-monastry themed tycoon game where you manage monks to design, brew and market a wide variety of beers. In general, the artstyle and concept were very fun and I think its off to a promising start.

That being said, the game is still fresh in early access, so you can't actually reach the planned 'end' yet which appears to be reaching the capital (i imagine this will be called 'Hopsburg', all cities in the game have such clever titles). I played through the available content in about 8 hours, which is fair imo for the price tag plus the fact the game will be much larger on full release.

The recipe designing is fun in itself; its a game of balancing four 'virtues' of the beer to within the acceptable range for that beer type. When it comes time to unlock the next, more populous (and therefore profitable) town, the lord may also request a beer with a specific style, ingredient and virtue level. 
Once you design your beer, you choose what price to sell it at within a range. With unlockable technology, you can also forecast demand/sales for the beer at that price. Selling beer to a town gives you money to buy new ingredients and expand your operation, but it also gives you reputation to unlock new beer styles and towns. Generally, the best policy I found is to sell beer as high a price as possible while still garnering ~100lt sales per week. Plebians have higher demand for higher quality beer, which comes from having a good recipe and having it brewed by talented fermintines.

If I had one principle complaint, I feel the gameplay loop is a bit flat at the moment. From the beginning, it is 
1. Prepare recipe for new ale type
2. Have your ferminines brew it and send it to a town
3. Unlock the town's new ale type
4. Eventually unlock the next town and focus on it instead
5. Repeat.

The game doesn't greatly incentivize you to focus on the unique beer trait mechanics or the reputation system, because making money and reputation is not challenging and the demand recovery of villages is quite forgiving. As is, there is not a huge incentive to expand the monastary to greater sizes because you'll progress through the game just fine by only selling the best beer to the most recently unlocked villages, thus you never really need more than 2 fermintines brewing, 2 for maintenance and 2 for research.  There are also manual beer orders villages will send you, but even with the ability to negotiate a greater fee (typically +40%), its not worth the money in the later stages of the game.

All in all, if you like tycoon games, this is a good one to chill with for a day. In the future, it may become a more long-term enriching experience

Great game, knows what it is and executes it well. You can play it at whatever pace you like, you can just play it like and idle game and pump out basic, cost-effective ales to make number go up, or you can invest more time and money into trying to develop the best possible recipes and brews, or a mix of both. 

Currently, I have three brewers making whatever the market is demanding, to fund the experimentation of my two most experienced brewers. Last night I procced a relatively cheap, profitable ale that managed to get 5 bonus traits, and it felt like breeding a shiny in PokeMon or getting some rare loot in an RPG -- that brew is now a prized accolade that I keep stocked in my cellars to buff my staff. My cellars are stocked with (1) aging ales that need time to reach their max value, (2) special brews that provide buffs to my workers, I always keep a few barrels of high quality ale for them to enjoy, I like thinking they keep some of the best stuff as a reward for all their hard work, and (3) brews with seasonal bonuses to sell once the season changes. I haven't even unlocked cold cellars yet, which I think is where the true aging rotation kicks in.

Overall the game is very engaging and has enjoyable progression loop, fun experimentation mechanics, and charming vibe. I'm looking forward to future improvements, specifically in developing more detailed UI interfaces and tool tips that provide more clarity on bonuses and traits, as well as smoothing out some of the mechanical friction in re-designing your room layouts. There are some other things I think can be improved, but I submitted my input through the in-game report function and received an acknowledgement from the dev only a few hours later, so they're clearly listening to players on where friction points are while maintaining their own vision for the game, which is a difficult balance to strike.

The core experience is very strong as it is and well worth the asking price. It's easy to find yourself playing one more in-game month, and then another, and another, and before you know it you have multiple cellars, multiple brewers, and seasonal brews or regional brews, you're rotating client orders, experimenting with new ingredients, rearranging your rooms layout, unlocking tech, and all the overlapping systems that keep the player wanting more. I don't recommend, but please don't take that to mean this isn't a good, interesting, somewhat fun, and vastly novel/creative game. It is definitely all of those things, and I congratulate the makers on developing a puzzle that tries things I haven't seen in games before.

Unfortunately, for all its creativity and genuine challenge, the game just doesn't quite come together cleanly enough to be a widely appealing experience. I am not sure I knew what I was buying when Epigraph went on special, but I think I was expecting a set of cryptogram puzzles where the aim was to unravel various letter-substitution ciphers. 

When I started the game, I realised I was looking at something quite different, and I was excited. After half an hour of poking back and forth, this looked like it was going to be amazing - a test to unravel a genuinely new language from limited clues. After an hour I'd made great progress on getting started. And then the game showed its design flaws, as I spent the next hour achieving practically nothing new, making educated guesses (as the game seemed to want me to do) only to have to keep undoing them when they didn't work. As someone who is usually great at word puzzles, this was hugely frustrating to me - and yes, some of that can be put down to just a reaction of my hurt pride, but at the same time, the lack of any sort of positive/negative player feedback is also to blame, as Epigraph throws you into a lake and says "Swim!" and then gives you NOTHING to confirm if you're on the right track or not.

I absolutely LOVED the sensation of being in the shoes of a real historian and seeing what it must have been like for anthropologists and linguists throughout history who have had to tackle this task of interpreting lost languages for real. But for all that, the game designers seem to have forgotten that they needed to balance that experience (with all of its stress, dead ends, frustration and feelings of isolation) with some degree of gameplay mechanics that allowed the player to feel a sense of genuine progress, or, at the very least, a way to determine what they were doing right or wrong at certain key points. Instead, all you get is a flawed "completion" indicator on the menu screen, which is useless for tracking progress as it only shows you what percentage of the text fields you have written in, but not what percentage of your input is actually correct.

There is an excellent hints walkthrough on the Steam forums, and even as a huge fan of word puzzles and codes, I wouldn't have got past the first obvious "chapter" of the game without that guide. It got me on track to be able to reason my way through a bit further, but then the game just kept dropping me back into darkness and feeling of being lost. It was one of the rare times when I literally gave up on a puzzle game, choosing to stop at what might have been the half-way point and just find and read through someone else's solution online. I just stopped caring. 

So I'm torn - as I said, I really like the feeling of "realness" of being thrown into something almost entirely on your own, with no help, no hints. The player IS the expert, and can't call on outside help. But after circling blindly for too long, it stops being a game. I can see where the designers tried to incorporate certain deliberately confounding elements or ideas, and sure, these provide a couple of enjoyable "aha!" moments, but because you get a couple of these early on, it means that when you get stuck later you can't help wondering if you're just lost because the designers decided to deliberately throw in more unnecessary confounders. The balance just didn't work for me.

Long blah blah blah review. 
Tl;dr is Good concept, good feeling of what this kind of work would be like in real life. But insufficiently gamified for the average player, with assumption and guesswork being core mechanics in the mid- and end-game phases but no system to confirm your guesses, so there's a LONG period of blindness that I personally couldn't push through.

I'm a typing game enthusiast (100~ wpm 💪🤓), and for the longest time I thought that no typing game could compare to Typing of the Dead until I gave Blood Typers a try. It really innovates on a genre that's long been flooded by "Mavis Beacon"-likes by uniquely blending beloved mechanics from different genres! 

Movement, inventory management, combat, and environmental mechanics are all handled by the keyboard alone. You switch between exploration and combat contexts and move your character tank-controls style. While awkward at first (especially the combat/exploration context switching), the whole system grows on you quickly, and the first mission gives you ample opportunity to learn the ropes before tossing you into a horde of zombies. 

It's hard to put into text how well Outer Brain Studios executes on this fusion until you give it a try yourself, so do yourself a favor and give the demo a try! Unfortunately the demo doesn't let you play online, but I think your friends will be convinced if you stream yourself fumbling the keyboard.

As an online co-op game, it's very competent in delivering on the horror w/ friends gameplay that Lethal Company and others have popularized, and as others have said, there's good fun to be had solving puzzles, managing your inventory, and fighting zombies Resident Evil-style while yelling at your friends over VOIP. 
Disclaimer: I had some trouble getting VOIP to work (2 of us had it working immediately, I had to switch to a different mic to get anything, another friend couldn't get through at all) so for my time playing we just used Discord.

There's multiple difficulty options, 8 unique characters, and 4 playable scenarios (levels) w/ more on the way so there's a good bit of content to sink your fingers into. Enemy variety is a little lacking at the moment (or maybe I haven't seen them all just yet), but the varied weapons keep combat encounters interesting.

I've only tried the first scenario so far, but I look forward to playing this game with the boys well into the future! (This is me granting permission to release paid DLC for additional content.)

I'm a little let down that the game doesn't have you typing proper sentences, especially in the computer segments where you type long strings of texts. I think it's a missed opportunity to feed the player interesting passages to type/read through, though their word bank at least includes many keywords relevant to the game's context.

Finally, my one request would be for the devs to let us add custom word-lists, something like what Typing of the Dead: Overkill did.

[h1]Game of the decade in regard to originality and genre of game(Coop).[/h1]
In this boring, horribly optimized, and mediocre era of "modern" games, this game saves gaming.

Don't take the sentence too seriously; it is a small game, but it keeps its fun factor even while replaying. A mini L4D2, if you will. I do feel the game is a bit on demo scale to me. If it had 50% more mission and content, but that's off-topic and it doesn't affect my score.  Still, I understand why it is right now.
It is Typing Of The Dead and Resident Evil combined. That means, quick typing fingers, having a good positioning, knowing when to fight and when to run. And on hard and above, you really need to know when to move and when to fight. [b]Because those 2 settings, really have a huge difficulty spike[/b][i](between normal and hard, and hard to torment)[/i].  I am not sure if that(torment)difficulty was play-tested fully.

[b]Don't let it fool you, this game is accessible to anyone, regardless if they think they can't type.[/b] However, to get the feeling of the game, [b]you must play it on Casual(Easy); [/b]that's where I started. Because of its “stressing” gameplay in typing, you really need to understand its fundamental design. If you don't and have low patience, [i]you're going to give up the game.[/i] Why? Because there are some things not fully explained to you, and you need to have a keen eye. And playing it on non-Easy will just stress you out. 

[h1]The reason to play it[/h1]
[b]For an even more obvious reason, this is a coop game.[/b]  Solo can be fun for a bit, but you really need to play COOP. Thankfully, there is a discord group of the game and the developers, so that's enough.
The game will test your cooperation and attention, as you really don't need to fight everyone and certainly not the same target. It is really possible to avoid any damage, but you need to be attentive and strategic. 
Things will be added in the future; we all got to be patient and, especially, not stress the developers.   The game gets improved often, a worthwhile purchase.

At least, it is a coop game that keeps its fun and lets you replay it, [b]like EDF 4 and L4D[/b]. The replay factor in a game is very much ignored today and in the past.

This game is brilliant.  I absolutely mean it when I say this is the single best typing game I've ever played.  You type for EVERYTHING, it's not an on rails shooter. They have multiple difficulty levels, one set for typing speed, one set for general gameplay.  This is fantastic, as a fast typer can really get a challenge, and a slow typer can still have a good time with the lower setting.  And this is separate from making the enemies stronger or the game more punishing.  Wonderful addition, that.

Last but not least, the game is co-op!  It even has proximity based chat.  I have not played with this myself, but I'm trying to get some friends to join me.  People say that really adds to the experience.

Whether you play with friends or alone, I think there's a great time to be had here if you enjoy a solid typing game with horror themes.  Music isn't bad, either.  There's a rave in the game that does something that I think is very clever and awesome with the music.  But I won't spoil that.

I love it. 
It's Resident Evil Outbreak and Typing of the Dead in one package.

It's silly good fun, and we're on a shortage of typing games. There's enough here for this type of game to be really enjoyable, with characters that are distinct from one another and survival horror elements. With a handful of levels with more to come, and layouts that change each time you play, I can't really complain about what this game is going for. I really just want more.

However, there is one MAIN thing I dislike about this game and it is that every mission's primary objective is the same. Given its strong parallels to Resident Evil Outbreak, I just can't understand the choice to only ever collect red tapes to fix the elevator. It would make the levels more exciting and interesting/unique, while I'd also imagine that it'd make developing levels easier since there would be more freedom to create diverse themes and objectives.

The few remaining complaints that I have about the game are the character designs being a little weird, and the fact that the characters don't seem to have unique roles in the story.

Drawing the comparison to Outbreak, I'd like to see characters getting unique roles to play in specific scenarios and actual cutscenes that pertain to those characters. It can feel a little bland not having more context on who these characters are, and Outbreak did a great job at that with special events and scenario ending cutscenes for each character. 

Really, I think that more cutscenes in general would make this game really special. It would help further sell the fact that we're playing through a horror movie together.

I really hope this game continues to develop and grow, because co-op survival horror with a twist is something I didn't expect to see but always wanted. I really can't overstate how much better this game would be with disjointed scenarios instead of this strict tape and elevator theme.

An amazing horror game where you don't ever need to use a mouse. Play the demo.

The game play is centered around the player having to type words in order to do actions, for instance, to move, there might be a three letter word or string of letters on the ground. Typing them causes your character to move there. When you're in combat against enemies, you have to type words to damage them. Some enemies vary by having Longer words but fewer overall, where as some enemies have more. There's one enemy which requires about 12 words typed to kill it, but they're all very short. 

The atmosphere is very creepy and the art style perfectly compliments it. Each of the playable characters (8 at the time of writing, yes, it does list their [b]blood type[/b]) are crew members of a film company. They each have different stats and a unique perk which significantly change how they play. Each level is themed around a fictional VHS Horror Movie and the scattered lore throughout the game shows that you're following the footsteps of the company who made those VHS tapes, and you discover [spoiler] how everything went wrong...! [/spoiler] [i] dun dun dunnnnnnnnn! [/i]

The maps are semi-randomly generated, they all have their consistent amount/types of rooms but they'll be distributed differently each time you play them. The game features survival horror aspects and resource management. If that's really not your thing, you might struggle to enjoy the game, but then again, there's a free demo, so don't knock it until you've tried it.

The game is extremely engaging, I found myself totally immersed in it. You don't have to be a court stenographer to play the game, either. The game features two adjustable difficulty sliders, one which affects the difficulty and complexity of the words you must type, where as the other affects enemy density and item scarcity, so if you enjoy the typing aspect but you don't really want to get into the survival horror aspect, there's something for you, too.

The game features checkpoints, but these only function when you die. There is no save system as each level is designed to be able to be completed in a single sitting. There is up to 4 player Co-Op but the game doesn't feature split-screen.

Very little is explained to you, but the first level (available in the demo) is designed so that you figure things out on your own. I recommend joining the official Discord server if you're ever stuck.

Personal Feedback:

- Sometimes there can be some really wonky camera angles when fighting multiple enemies, or doing certain actions near walls.

- Difficulty: I don't necessarily find this game 'hard' however I don't think most people are well skilled 'typers' being able to hit 70+ WPM (Words Per Minute) on average. I do understand that there are 2 different difficulty adjustments for WPM and Game Difficulty, to be able to scale them differently to provide different challenging experiences (I think this is genius for a typer game). But I feel that just playing on the base difficulty for both might be a little too challenging for most players.

I believe I am a fairly fast typer, I am usually around 65-85 WPM depending on how I am feeling and on some occasions being able to hit up to 100+ and just playing on the normal difficulty in this game can feel very stressful with my type speed, I can only imagine what higher WPM and Difficulty would be. 

I believe you would benefit from slightly tweaking the difficulty scaling, and I highly consider adjusting the WPM scaling as well, maybe to this: 01-30, 30-50, 50-70, 70-100, and 100+ or something similar. This way is allows for more slower typers to enjoy this game, and if they want to learn from this and grow in typing speed they can just increase the difficulty over time to better their typing speed!

- Enemy Spawner: I feel this enemy has too many words for how fast it produces enemies, I believe it should have less words in general or at least for the lower difficulties. Alternatives: Slow down spawn production speed.

There's the fundamental basics of a good game here, but there are some key elements missing.

Information about the characters, their abilities and what they do is only presented at the start of a run. If I have questions about the intricacies of "Darkness vampire stream", I can't find the answers once the game has started.

I'm not sure I ever learned what leveling does for my character. A way to view my stats would be helpful.

There's a distinct lack of sound effects (especially on hit, both for my character or the enemies). The extremely limited variety of enemies make few noises. The sounds that are there are very muffled. A general audio balancing pass would go a long way.

Similarly, there's nothing to break up the very few music tracks which play on repeat. When I exited one floor and the music faded, I thought I was about to get a new track - and instead it was the same song I'd already heard on repeat for 10+ minutes.

The lack of "greebles" - details meant to break up the surface of objects - means that every dungeon feels the same. They're also especially small and you encounter dead-end halls fairly often, and they always have no reward other than the enemy or gems you can find everywhere.

There are "taming items" you can find (seemingly just two at the moment) which can be used to tame creatures you may find in the dungeon. Thus far, I've found multiple taming items but only one creature to use them on. The taming items themselves often get stuck on dungeon walls or just disappear instantly once thrown. When it did work, I received an allied animal which began to follow me until about 30 seconds later it became stuck on a wall. It also has limited energy and seemed to give up shortly after attacking a few enemies. I don't know that I saw it actually defeat a foe.

There are no options, nothing to configure, and no way to rebind keys in-game.

The core gameplay is decent enough, but the absence of these elements really makes it feel pretty shallow. As it is (and at this price point) I can't really recommend the game. I love Tales of Alethrion, but I have zero desire to revisit this title as it stands. It doesn't do anything you can't find better elsewhere. I respect that its a "work in progress" but its also being billed as a full release, so I can't even give it the Early Access pass.

This game is mostly a vehicle to support Tales of Alethrion, an incredible fantasy YouTube series featuring fluid animation, wordless storytelling, and visual worldbuilding. Those familiar with Skjald know that new seasons are often accompanied by side projects like this.

As a fan of Alethrion and the roguelike genre, this was an easy purchase, and I'm glad to keep it to support one of my favorite animators. But as a standalone purchase I feel like neither the setting or the game genre shine here.

The bones are there; I like the fluid animation of the pixel sprites, the character's attacks and specials feel feel distinct, there's a core loop that features the dungeons mentioned in the game description. Unfortunately the game isn't very interactive:

- I imagine leveling up increases primary stats, but it's such an understated change I would often level up without realizing it; no choices or mechanical changes. I would almost rather start as a weak Vito/Wilhelm without a secondary ability, just to make room for some progression that feels more like The Reward.

- Because of the lack of character progression, it doesn't feel very roguelike; there aren't different decisions to be made, just a reconfigured map.

- The environment, which is one of the most impressive aspects of Tales of Alethrion, needs some life breathed into it.

I know that Skjald plays a long game, and I'm interested to see how this game expands as time goes on. I'm also interested in people's experiences with the local co-op. But it feels like an Early Access title, and if we look at the promise of additional levels/characters, it clearly is.

I can't recommend for purchase based on its current gameplay. But if you want to support an awesome animator and get a little dopamine from seeing beloved characters pixelated, go for it, or check out their patreon/kickstarter.

Herein comes the main problem that I have with this game: the price.  While there are more levels than normal, the average level would take a player 5-10 minutes to solve, and even at the higher end of the spectrum, it would still only take 500 minutes to solve every artwork in this installment.  That's just 9 hours, 40 minutes of content.  The metric I always use when playing certain types of games is this:  $1 per hour of game time spent in a game. On multiple occasions I got dinged for a doll having missing fingers even though I'm quite sure they had them all during visual inspection. Also, the odd sentence structures and grammatical errors in the spoken dialogue make it obvious that English isn't the developer's first language, and that they didn't bother to have an editor look the dialogue over.

Even with these minor foibles, I'd still recommend Dollmare if you're in the mood for a smaller, self-contained horror experience that can be finished in a sitting or two. Metroidvanias with hard rock music have a history of being very bad.

Metroidvanias with anthropomorphic mice also have history of being very bad.

This has both. My hope is that two very negative trends would cancel each other out to produce a good game. Unfortunately that didn't happen but it was not for the reasons I expected. It turns out the reasons this is bad are as follows:

- The map is completely useless
- The game decided to try out a unique 2.75D style. How should I explain this... do you remember those old arcade beat em ups how you had to move into lanes and could only attack baddies in the lane that you are in? well, this game has that, its the first metroidvania ever made to feature that. Unfortunately, it doesn't work out at all in practice. The reason why is that it is usually very hard to see which lane the enemies are in, enemies can shoot at you from any lane but you can only attack them on their lane. It's too bad this doesn't work really, this could have been a really fun originaly metroid like
- The performance is too poor when there are too many entities nearby, which is weird because my CPU was recently adjusted to be able to handle lots of stuff thrown at it... so why didn't it?
- The game is too unpolished and the menu feels really unfinished and primitive.
- The lighting is too poor, the devs clearly didn't follow the guides for how to use lighting to subtly guide the player either....

I've been looking for a cute, cozy sim game that I could play couch co op with my 8yo daughter and this is finally it! Marking this "Not Recommended" over the structure of the "couch co-op" to serve as a buyer beware for anyone looking for an actual co-op experience. The split screen featured in the ad and "couch co-op" declared in the product description definitely made us think we were getting one.

Wife and I were excited to have another game we could play together, having logged hundreds of hours on the likes of Stardew Valley. The game is exactly as we hoped---cozy, cute, and scratching the itch of a peaceful farm/craft sort of game. However the co-op mode is excruciating because of a major design flaw: entering or exiting any house or different area transfers both players to that zone. This mean no one gets to play the game because separating from each other at all just results in you being tethered back to where the other is at all times. The game works in day cycles where you go to sleep at night. So say you start the day--you head to the post office to do a mission there, you're almost at the door, but alas! Your co-op partner entered the Tavern, so now you're both in the tavern. The only thing to do there is to talk to an NPC, and as all progress is shared in co-op (resources etc.), you get identical dialogue boxes, so there's absolutely no point for you to be there to talk to that NPC as well. Rinse and repeat with everything you can do.

We loved the vibe and what the game is going for (I'm certain it achieves it in a single player experience), but this tethering mechanic makes it unplayable as a two player experience. We REALLY hope the dev decides to patch in a true co-op experience, as you might as well play single player and pass the controller back and forth as that functionally mimics almost exactly what is going on currently. Kills me to leave a thumbs down as this is exactly the sort of game I want to be made!


Also---Honorable mention to bugs in co-op. The dev seems good natured and I think they'll patch this stuff as fast as they can so I wouldn't mention it save for their decision to release early with a confident statement that the game was fully functional. Purchasing/furniture placement are major parts of the game. They either weren't tested in co-op or deliberately ignored.

1) HUD popup around interactables is bugged in co-op to stay on screen when the tethering mechanic is triggered while displayed.
2) Player 2 cannot see the HUD for purchasing market goods. The pop-up instead appears on player 1's screen, but only if you rotate the camera to a specific angle that it seems to spawn in.
3) Moving furniture in your bakery often goes berserk in co-op. I think it's if player 2 touches the lifted furniture object while being moved. It tweaks out, clips all over the place and you have to spam click accept to try and get it to place in a legal placement area to try again.

Ahh, cute bunnies living in a cozy *shire*, what's not to like.

As advertised, you own a bakery, you grow and harvest your crops to then bake goods to sell (or gift).

The game is pretty simple and straight to the point, and the systems work fairly well as expected.

It is a very solid foundation, although a bit bare bones in it's current stage, which is kind of worrying as I understand this is a full release and not an early access. It's not clear if the dev will continue adding features to the game.

It could use a better tutorial or UI. As it is right now, it doesn't really hold your hand. It takes some trial and error to know how things work and what is actually interactable and what not. For instance, if you don't go to bed by midnight your bunny will just fall asleep on the spot wherever it is and allegedly not be properly rested by morning, but whether or not this affects you in any way is not properly communicated (it doesn't seem like it affects you at all... I think?). There are also beds on sale which promise you better sleep but it's not clear exactly what the benefits are. Tracking other bunnies for an errand also involves some exploration as well as learning what their daily routines are (which is not necessarily a bad thing). How long will community projects take to finish is also unclear, and it is frustrating that a couple days after paying for the project, that mine and forest are still unaccessible and no hints whatsoever on how longer I still have to wait.

Your bread also goes from well made straight to completely burnt, maybe adding some inbetween levels of burning could leverage the punishment for leaving your bread a little too long in the oven. Maybe add a "slightly burnt" tier with half the price drop?

While you can customize your bunny and your house, there are not that many options. This is kind of a major letdown as customization is usually the "endgame" of lifesim games. Could start by adding more layers of customization, as for instance right now a moustache, glasses and a tophat all 3 of them share the "Hat" layer so you cannot wear them at the same time. Fur pattern is also tied to the fur color, as well as eye colors are tied to their shapes, so could separate them as well and let the player pick whatever color they like (even if they end up with some sparkle rainbow bunny abomination, but hey more power to the player if that's what they want). Since the bunnies are more on the feral side it's understandable they don't wear pants, but could still add shirts or vests or other accesories like jewelry or backpacks.

The sale value of goods doesn't seem to be properly balanced either. For instance, a Loaf of Bread sells for 2x the price of Flatbread, but takes 2x as long to bake and 3x the Flour and Water. There doesn't seem to be ANY scenario in which it's ever better to bake a Loaf of Bread over Flatbread, other than maybe just checking the oven half as often, I guess.

Also, the best way to earn money (carrots) in the game, specially early on, is NOT by baking bread or by collecting goodies in the wilderness... but by drawing water from the well... which is the most boring and mind numbing activity in the game. So, you can plant the wheat seeds, spend the 6~ in-game hours that it takes for them to grow roaming around collecting 30 carrots worth of mushrooms, spend ~30 in-game minutes grounding the wheat and shaping it, then put it in the oven for another ~6 hours to then sell it for 30-100 carrots depending on your skill... OR you can hold a button at the Well for ~12 in-game hours straight just drawing water and sell it for ~400 carrots. 

Quite frankly. my biggest gripe with this game is by far the price. I'd recommend waiting for a sale, as there's many alternatives in the same price range for this genre which are much more feature-rich.

I should be the prime target audience for this game: I was looking for a nice Animal Crossing-ish game, and I am absolutely obsessed with bunnies!

Unfortunately, the game falls flat in almost every regard for me.

In the order from most to least frustrating:

- The first bread I baked on my own after the tutorial, which I waited for six in-game hours, straight up despawned into nothingness after I took it out of the oven for no apparent reason; seems to be a glitch. For a game about baking bread where the progression is seemingly entirely dependent on you baking bread, this is unacceptable and it made me quit the game. The entire first day's progression just despawned.

- There is no easy way to tell apart the other rabbits, and they all look same-y. They're all "just" normal rabbits – a bit of visual identity and character would have gone a long way to make me care about them a little more. They do all have some kind of unique personality traits when you talk to them, but since they all look like the same generic rabbit with different ear models, fur colors and slightly different faces, I cannot tell at a glance who is who, and they don't particularly look "interesting" enough for me to want to meet and get to know them. Why not put some accessoiries on them? Little hats, bows, clothes, fancier colors? The game should lean into the cartoonish art style a bit more. 

- Dialogue feels pointless and stale a lot of the time. In Animal Crossing or Stardew Valley, you would often get asked a question, told a joke, or got some other kind of setup that made you glad you interacted with the character. In Cinnabunny, most of the dialogue seems to be one-line throwaway lines like "I am glad my daughter helps around the house" or "I like making the world a better place". There is barely any interactivity, nothing to surprise you, nothing that prompts you to answer something that you feel would come up later, nothing. I assume this will get better over time as you build relationships, but right now it feels less like a social experience and more like talking to those random Pokémon NPCs that say things like "My mom always cooks the best pasta!" 

- The entire game feels like it's a bit devoid of attention to detail and love. It's the little things. The environments are largely empty fields of featureless grass, there are no flowers around or anything. Empty plots are just a brown flat platform. My bakery doesn't have a chimney from the outside even though the oven inside it looks like it does. There are very few landmarks, none of which are particularly interesting. The whole game world is very oversized, reminding me of an MMO; stretches of land between every house, no hidden nooks or crannies, it just feels like you're tiny on a large featureless stretch of grass. Other bunnies are just hopping around in circles endlessly without any animations or things to do; at least as far as I got in the game, which isn't very much due to the bread glitch.

- The voice sounds are *jarring*. They're going for the same kind of fast high-pitched phoneme chains like Animal Crossing, but the snippets are so choppy that it's painful to listen to.

- The animations and movement are very unsatisfying; between every hop there's a noticeable little pause, which makes moving around feel more like jumping than running.

- There have been some instances even in the very beginning of the game of uninspired and clearly not properly proofread dialogue. My own dialogue choices don't feature punctuation, which looks unclean ("How are you" instead of "How are you?"). Some dialogue is written in a pretty forced way as clear author tokenism inserts to talk about topics to you, the player, instead of the character. A bunny giving you a Wikipedia copy/paste lecture on their medical issues (e. g. eyesight) once you meet them without any personality or reason to talk about it is just odd, and many characters are like this. It feels like they designed some characters with a single personality trait in mind that they felt needed representation, that needs to feature in every one of their lines henceforth because they're the xyz character.

Overall, it isn't worth 25€ to me, no matter how much content there would have been after this. Playing the rest of the game with this frustrating movement, empty uninspired world and generic characters (in a narrative character-focused genre, no less) does not sound appealing.

Cinnabunny: A Cozy but Repetitive Baking Adventure

Cinnabunny is an irresistibly cute and cozy game where you get to live life as an adorable bunny baker. The art style is charming, and the bunny characters add a delightful touch that makes the experience feel warm and inviting.

However, while the game excels in aesthetics, the game play can feel a bit slow. Baking—arguably the heart of the game—takes quite a while, which often leaves me wondering how to fill the time between batches. Though there are areas like the forest and the mine to explore, their primary purpose is to gather ingredients for more baking, reinforcing the game’s singular focus rather than providing meaningful variety.

There are goals to work toward, and the cozy atmosphere is undeniably appealing, but the game play loop starts to feel repetitive after a while. If you love relaxing games centered around baking, this might be a perfect fit. However, if you’re looking for more diverse activities beyond the kitchen, Cinnabunny may leave you craving something extra.

Cinnabunny! Be the bestest bunny. Bake the bestest breads! 
I've played for 12 hours and I can't get enough. The graphics are easy on the eyes and whimsically pleasing to the imagination. Aesthetically, Cinnabunny is cottage core, meets Studio Ghibli, meets Wind in the Willows. The 3D environment makes this game more immersive than it's 2D brethren.
Collecting ingredients keeps me busy for hours. I'm able to just let my mind wander as my bun runs around collecting ingredients to make better and better baked goods. I really love how there is a piece of equipment for everything. There is a cave for you to collect extra ingredients in, but I haven't seen any mobs which is really nice if you want a break from all the fighting you see in other games.
I LOVE how there is a function to take notes on what a bun does and does not like. It makes finding their favorites so interesting! I would really like to have the ability to log the bunny's favorites though. (Maybe it's already there and I'm just not seeing it.)
Most of the movement is perfect. If you hit shift, it will make you faster- only by a small amount but that small amount is good enough as you don't have to run away from anything. (I would like to see the speed function explained somewhere, I came across it by accident.) There are little paw prints in the ground by the community stage that allow you to dance on Friday evenings or stretch on Wednesday mornings. That's rather fun! I don't understand why, as bunnies, we can't jump. I fall in to the water often when bird watching and it would be lovely to be able to just jump out of the river instead of having to swim until I find an accessible bank to get out at. 
I love, love, love the color scheme! I love how every blade of grass moves and how the rain actually makes the ground appear wet. The blowing leaves and whirling wind are amazing touches! The singular thing I'm not fond of is the field of view. You can only see a short distance in front of you and you can't look up unless you're using the birdnoculars. Perhaps this is to save on rendering as you can see the whole scene through the birdnoculars.
The quests are pretty straight forward and you can pin one to your display so you can keep track of what to do next. You can have 3 quests at a time from the community board and then your system quests. None of the quests I've come across are time sensitive- which is nice! I would like to remove a couple of the quests I picked up though as they are bird picture quests and I'm not far enough along in bird watching to see those birds. I haven't found a way to remove an accepted quest yet. 
The cave is so much fun to run around in! You can collect all kinds of ingredients in there! There are so many different types of mushrooms in there and I'd say it's the most lucrative place to explore. Just remember to sell the mushrooms you collect! There are these glowing orbs that I haven't figured out what to do with yet, and what looks like some kind of shrine which I also haven't figured out what to do with. I'm only 12 hours in though so that may become apparent later. There are all kinds of bugs and lizards in that cave too! I hope we get to collect them! The flutterby is my FAVORITE! I love that no matter where in the cave I am, I can still get out, just by talking to my flutterby. 
The forest is pretty cool, I really enjoy hunting for eggs and the different types of birds available in there. The deer feeder has just come available at the post office so that's what I'm going to work on next. I love how you have to use the handcart to get to the forest. It adds a fun little mechanic to the game. The mushrooms in the forest are much easier to find after you get to level 10 in mushroom collecting.
Character customization is super fun, I love how you can buy "hats" from the market. You can find a mirror in the house with the stone roof, I don't remember off the top of my head who lives there, but it's the only house with a stone roof. It seems like your bun is a guy and there is no way to change the gender- though that doesn't really affect anything in the grand scheme of things. You can still put on bows or flower crowns as you please. It only becomes apparent when interacting with other buns.
One thing to note is that the story progression is slow. It can take several days for things to be built, to complete quests and objectives, and to level up your skills. For some, this might detract from how much they enjoy this game. For me, once I figured this out, it made me love it even more! I'm not going to be "done" in a month or two (real time) and feel like I haven't gotten my money's worth.
A note to the developer: You have done an absolutely fantastic job with this game! I never would have guessed that you are a solo indie developer! For a brand new release this game is more put together than many games I've played that have been out for years! Thank you so much for this little gem of peace in a market flooded with chaos.
A note to those lamenting the cost: The cost for this game is not out of the scope of realistic. Years of learning how to program, learning graphic design, color theory, marketing (just to name a few of the things the developer had to learn)- probably having to pay for much of that schooling, all while having to hold down a normal- soul sucking day job to afford things like rent, bills, food, medical bills etc. Then years implementing all that knowledge- [u] all by themselves.[/u] The cost- less than $40 CAD wont even begin to cover a single day of school.

If you are looking for a calming game, this is it. The pace of the bunnies hopping around is slow and steady, the music chill, and the vibe is peaceful. The gentle sprinkled puns in the text is cute and not overdone. The tutorial phase is short and sweet so you can just get on with the main game, especially as the mechanics follow the standard garden/cooking sims so everything is intuitive. I really enjoyed the realistic feel of the day: not every bunny arrives/leaves the open air market at the same time, each bunny has their own routes/schedules that are well timed as to not be predictable and boring, that type of thing. The community stage is charming- what an adorable surprise when I just accidentally stumbled on an open air music concert! Each bun house reflects the bun owner and there is a decent variety of body types that makes it easier to spot who you need from a distance. 

The map is small enough that you can do several tasks in a day, including tasks that are for you the player to find relaxing (such as bunny yoga) and not just grind grind grind. The environmental effects are very pretty. The waves of the wind blowing through the grass is probably my favorite so far. I found myself having my bunny hop through open fields just because I loved the effect so much. 

The notebook feature allows you to work your own way through the likes/dislikes of the individual bunnies. As you complete it on your own, you get a sense of accomplishment with figuring out the best (and worst) gifts rather than just being told what to do. 

Recipes can be found from other buns as gifts, but once you have the general recipe you can explore mix-ins on your own. For example, you start with "flat bread" and can add in herbs, nuts, or any number of items that you find or buy without needing to find "rosemary flat bread" or "spicy flat bread" recipes. It's a good balance between finding recipes and creation/exploration of your own. 

Any negatives I have are mostly just minor pet peeves. The letter "l" is so much taller than the other letters that it becomes abrasive to read words like "milk." Your bunny is always in the middle of the screen which means half of your viewing field is behind you, not in front, and you can't tilt the camera to adjust for this when you are in the zoomed in mode (or at least I can't find where the camera tilt is). The map is small and I can't find a way to zoom in (is there even a way?) so it's only good for a general "you are here" and not for navigating. The game price feels steep at $25. If I had a choice between this and another cheaper cozy game, in all honesty I would rule this one out for personal budget reasons, as the appeal wouldn't be strong enough to overcome the cost difference.

In general, the vibe of this game is relaxing with just enough cooking/relationship building to keep one's mind engaged enough to not be tedious- but not so much engaged that it becomes a task rather than a way to unwind and escape after a long IRL day. I would recommend it to a friend (and in fact already have!) In the cozy game sim world, this looks to be a perfect fit.

Moto Knight is a callback to the mid 2000s and 2010s web and mobile game era of games along with a unique style derived from a challenge of restricting all game art to a single post-it note. Moto Knight is a charming game that did manage to entertain me for the hour it took me to complete it, for a game made in just a month by a solo developer there's not much more to ask for. 

I do want to offer some criticisms however for the developer as someone who has been doing game development myself for nearly a decade now. The level design is the biggest weakness of the game by a decent margin. The player movement is very responsive and intuitive after a short while (though a break button would really be nice) of playing around but the levels often don't take advantage of it's full potential. The third world is the biggest offender of this in my opinion. Most of the levels are very very short and gimmicky. I personally feel more stunt oriented levels that allow the player to really go max speed and spin in midair more would have made the game more enjoyable. I feel like Moto Knight is more of a precision platformer on a bike instead of something akin to moto X3M and other classic flash/mobile games.

Overall I really applaud the work here and think the developer should be very proud of what he has made here. Looking forward to whatever he publishes next!

Having played through the game a few times, I can recommend this game to other puzzle lovers. It's not without its problems so let's start with those. 
Cubic can be confusing and I understand what the developers are trying to do, they want you to work out how the puzzles are figured out and then work them out. It's the how part that's frustrating and after a bit of back and forth from the developer (I love developers who are active with the community) the puzzles were a breeze, almost too easy. So the hardest part is figuring out how to solve the puzzles and it felt like that side of it could of done with a bit of work. Definitely playtested more from people not involved in the development. There are other issues like performance and easily breaking out he map and bypassing puzzles. I don't see bypassing puzzles as an issue though, it's typical with SVG games and it's up to you if you want to cheat yourself. I do enjoy finding these areas to break out though so that's why I probably giving it some slack.

Having said that, it is great. Most zones are fun to work out. Just one super confusing zone. The map is small and condensed but looks great. A nice variety of puzzles and a good learning curve. 

For anybody about to play, here are some things that might make you less confused. Don't try and solve the platform zone puzzles. They can't be solved in the way you expect, just make platforms to jump from one side to the other. Zone 5 I had the most issues with but if you pay attention to what rule is applied first, you should have more fun with it (a patch has added the ability to see the starting and completed state after you have completed the puzzles which makes it much easier to work it out).
When you come across the black block, it's all there to work it out. The best example in the game of how to introduce a new block. 

A fun, short, and unique puzzle game. I hope SVG does a sequel because this could be something really special. I love how they improved the Door series with each new release with Insignia being one of my favourite open-world puzzle games and I would love to see similar improvements to Cubic. Also, play Door3 Insignia after you played this :)

Cubic Enigma is a puzzle game based around grids of coloured blocks. It's set in a slightly mysterious world with a loose narrative that provides the backdrop to the game.

Similar to games like The Witness, it works on introducing puzzle mechanics incrementally, steadily building up complexity into the later puzzles.

Pros:
- [b]Simple concept[/b]: May take a bit of head scratching at first. But once you get your head around the base mechanics the game is pretty straight forward to figure out.
- [b]Beautiful setting[/b]: Using the Unreal Engine the game looks very nice.

Cons:
Although I do recommend giving this game a try, there are a few downsides (to be fair, some of which are bugs which are likely to be fixed soon).

- [b]Inconsistent voice over[/b]: Almost certainly a bug that will be fixed, but during my play through the voice over suddenly switched from English to Russian and didn't come back (though the subtitles staying in English).
- [b]Short once you've figured it out[/b]: With a few exceptions, once you've figured out each block mechanic you can pretty much zip through the rest of the game. Would have been nice to have had a few more wrinkles, or some expansion on other mechanics that turned out to be one-shot rules.

The last con is really my biggest downside. Once I was into the game and figuring through its puzzles it was a shame it was over so soon. I did enjoy my time with Cubic Enigma and just wish there was more. Hopefully there will be a longer follow up as the concept is generally a fun one.

Edit: Updated to review to clarify a couple of my original issues (invert Y option and separate music volume) have now been fixed. Good work on the quick update devs!

Kinda bummed to give this a Not Recommended, because I loved everything apart from the combat, but since that's the main attraction to an FPS, I believe it falls short of expectations.

I really dig the whole aesthetic and the original (or, at least, not-very-exploited) idea of an FPS controlled with only a mouse, I loved the cinematics and the not-in-you-face humor the game has sometimes. I loled at the sudden loud table hit in the first cutscene.

However, even though the gimmick of the game is to control everything only with the mouse, the controls are terrible for my taste, specifically the shooting mechanic. In close quarters combat (most of the encounters), enemies move a lot, so you're constantly aiming and moving. This makes the cursor move, so every time you want to shoot, you have to move the cursor to the weapon and click, then move it to "reload" (can't say the actual word on Steam) on another part of the weapon, then move your character again and aim, and then move the cursor again to shoot. I played in easy mode and while it totally is a skill issue, I kept dying because of this.

There's a simple fix for this though, make it so that when the player moves the character (holding RMB), the cursor is fixed to the last position you left it at. This way you can move, aim and shoot at the same time if you left the cursor on top of the weapon. The manual "reloading" mechanic I dislike specifically for the revolver, as it's not as strong of a weapon as the shotgun so it doesn't need that kind of nerfing, but because of that my entire run has been SMG-dependant, which sucks because the other weapons are interesting too. Also, allowing the players to use the mousewheel to change the item being held would be much apprecitated.

Health in the game is integrated in a fun way (I really like the whole feeding and patching up animations and mechanic), but the health these items give you is insanely low. I've had to repeat entire segments more than 5 times because I was left with 5% of health and the only health item I had near only gave me 5% more, and then I'd have to survive 6 enemies with only 10% of health.

Speaking of enemies, hate that red guy, but most importantly, I was left wanting more types, or at least skins. There's a beautiful snow level after the first one but the enemies still wear the green and red suits from the first level. These guys must have never heard of camouflage.

The game also fails to communicate when you take damage, which makes for funny but frustrating situations where you're reading a note, hear a dog bark somewhere near, and then realize it's been attacking you for the last couple of seconds because there is no feedback to tell you "Hey, you're getting mauled, maybe stop reading or something". A simple red screen would do the trick. Also, the same thing can be said for "reloading" or out-of-ammo. There's no sound to indicate your weapon hasn't bugged because it's not shooting, but rather you have to "reload" it or find more ammo. I think a simple "click" sound effect when trying to shoot and the ammo text flashing yellow when out could go a long way.

Overall, I really want to give the game a go again because I left at the space station level frustrated with the shooting controls but it looked interesting and it had me hooked. Dev, if you're reading and are up to fixing the issues I commented, especially the cursor locking when moving, I'd love to finish the game and change the review into a Recommended.

Cheers.

I'm going to preface this with a "THIS IS EARLY ACCESS" warning (It was released on the 13th of May, so VERY new)

This is a very fun "pick up for a round or two" game, and I was sucked in for a good 2 hours going run after run.

I love the art style, I've always been a sucker for low poly, particle effects and cool lighting, and sure enough this game has that.

At the moment there only seems to be 2 types of dungeon; the wood floor and the stone floor dungeons. In future I would hope to see some more variety with the levels, and a better sense of progression via cues from the environment, but for a game that has only just released, from a solo developer, it's a cute and spooky style that I really dig. The procedural generation does a lot to offset this however, and I never truly feel like "I've seen this before" as the snaking corridors and open areas all blend to make every run feel unique.

The gameplay is more of the same story, really satisfying. The movement is direct, dodging feels super snappy, and enemies are really easy to distinguish with easy to projectiles and attack animations. This means you never feel as if the game has screwed you over when you get hit, it's all down to your skill. At present there are a few 'classes' of enemies, with several variations, modified attacks and additional armour to keep things feeling fresh and challenging as you progress deeper through the dungeons of Algoduul!

Though it can get very tense when the game decides to spawn you next to 20 enemies just waiting for you to move. I keep trying to run and I end up running into more of them! The dodging feels great, especially since you can shove enemies and furniture with it! You can actually hurt them by doing this and allows for some great gameplay trying to yeet the explodey bois into a crowd for maximum collateral.

Some of the abilities you can get are really cool, and the idea of an ability "consuming" some of your max HP really makes your thought processes in those fast-paced, fight or flight situations carry more weight. "Do I use this ability to give myself some breathing room? Knowing that in the long run it's going to put me at a disadvantage?

Some things I'd like to see added is more variety in general, with the environment, enemies and abilities, as after a few hours of playing you tend to do the same thing against the same foes. And while it's actually surprisingly fun to play again and again, it would be nice to have that further progression to turn this from a fun little time passer, into a real fleshed out VIDYA GAEM

Overall this is a really promising start for a dungeon crawler, and I hope to see it updated as time passes into a feature rich time sink!

Things to improve: Maybe scale down the arenas just a little bit.  The levels were a bit too big, especially the base. It kind of overstayed its welcome and was a bit too easy to get lost in.
