It might also be useful to work on the pacing in places.  I started to get a little bored during the base, which for a climax to a story is kind of the opposite of what you want.  Making it a bit smaller, a bit more focused, could be way, way better to building that tension you need at the climax of a game.  

Keep making games.  Please.  You've genuinely got something here.  I may go back and finish this, I may not - but regardless, you've got something fun here and I see the hard work.  I look forward to seeing whatever you make next.  Keep sharpening the iron and you'll make something pretty brilliant.

Secrets of the Shore is a dating simulator and visual romance novel for all ages. The game is visually impressive, with high-quality renderings. However, it is quite linear, limiting the player's choices to deciding which of the female characters to develop a relationship with.

[h3]Story and Characters[/h3]
The story begins with the protagonist on a short vacation trip to some islands, intending to relax and escape daily worries. During excursions on the islands, the player meets Ashley, a young woman fascinated by artifacts and ancient architecture.

In addition to Ashley, the player also meets Evelyn, a local guide who works on the island. She seems to be a character more connected to a simple life and nature. Between these two characters, the player must choose who to invest in emotionally, shaping the course of the romance.

[h3]Mystery and Exploration[/h3]
Although the protagonist is initially focused on relaxing, the game introduces a small mystery that the player needs to solve. One of the islands has a museum full of interesting discoveries, suggesting that there is more to the story than meets the eye.

[h3]Interactivity and Gameplay[/h3]
Secrets of the Shore is quite straightforward and, despite its beautiful renderings and intriguing premise, lacks greater interactivity and a variety of choices. The game is quite short and can be completed in less than 30 minutes, which can be seen as an advantage for those looking for a quick experience or a downside for those who want a longer and more engaging narrative.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
Secrets of the Shore is a visual novel that attracts with its visual charm and the simplicity of its narrative. Despite its short duration and limited interaction options, the game offers a pleasant experience for those who enjoy quick, romance-focused stories.

Seems like actual quantum computing in a video game, though run through a simulator of course. Not everyone has an IBM Heron processor lying around at home.

The explanations are a bit math heavy, but the game will step you through what each of the types of gate does, and expects you to match some final end-state that you want to morph your qubit state into. The visuals are fairly intuitive so even if you don't understand the math, you could probably experiment with what each gate does to understand how to use them.

I got into the game because I just wanted to learn more about quantum computing, but I was surprised how compelling some of the puzzles were, and it's been fun comparing myself to other people on the leaderboards and trying to figure out the clever optimizations that they did. A small part of me also likes that I'm able to play around with logic in this game that might have otherwise taken me 2-3 months to learn to do on paper in a college class.

Several reviews mention Zachtronics-like but I don't think this game really falls under that umbrella as it is not very gamified and is a direct match of real-life quantum computing instead of being an alternate programming environment where extra restrictions are a core aspect of the game. This is not a criticism and the game delivers on its promises, just be aware that the game falls closer to the educational end of the spectrum than even a game like TIS-100.

The game is still in Early Access but is polished and with plenty of content, including community content, and I am looking forward to seeing how the game will evolve with further development.

I'm a big fan of Zachtronics games and I thought I'd give this a try as someone who has never really thought about quantum computing. The early puzzles eased me in pretty well, though some of the text explanations have a bit of the "draw the rest of the owl" quality to them. I was able to use some outside resources and the game's own built-in encyclopedia to fill in some gaps. I'm about 5.5 hours in to the game so far and definitely had to replay some sections to solidify the concepts (phase and interference earlier, and now trying to wrap my head around phase kickback), but things have sunk in.

That all said, this game did inspire me to install Qiskit (a quantum computing library for Python) and the concepts I learned in the game mapped pretty cleanly on to Qiskit and that's the best kind of praise you can give for a game like this.

[b] TLDR: [/b]
Elevator Warp is a short unique puzzle/exploration experience with a modest price. It has simple but well thought out mechanics. Like Geodepths, it has very satisfying visuals that give it a unique feeling.

[b] more detail: [/b] 
I was a big fan of Geodepths, I got it a few days after it was released. I wanted to support the creator, so I tried this game too. This game is much different than Geodepths and is not the same type of experience but that isn't a bad thing. It’s good to see the creator branching out and trying to create something that feels unique to them along with all players experiencing the game. 

If you are trying to scratch that 2012-2015 narrative puzzle indie game itch (Stanley parable) this game does a good job of that. For me, playing this game has provided not only a pleasant experience but also a sense of nostalgia for an era of thought and passion-filled titles that are hard to come by these days. I love that this game provides a sense of "what is this thing" or "does this do anything?" when trying to interact with or explore the environment.

[b] Desired changes (constructive criticism): [/b]
from a quality-of-life perspective, the one change I would recommend is that the settings in the menu can have direct numerical input, such as the FPS limit or volume percentage. Alternatively, make the sliders easier to snap using KBM. Positive note: For a game this inexpensive from this small of a developer, the settings offered are simple yet robust. This developer seems to be aware of things people want in the settings that even some large titles miss.

[b] Regarding the direction of A Little More Games: [/b] 
I enjoy the unique approach that both Geodepths and Elevator Warp have taken. The design choices of both games are noteworthy for how they have the potential to preserve assets, reduce rendering cost, and provide a more unique experience. With Geodepths, some people may have an issue with the drill-release system being a more "simulated" experience that leaves you with something to be desired. My argument in defense of systems like this is that they are used in a unique way to provide a new, potentially more immersive experience, not as a crutch for lack of content or development ability. I was excited to see that in Elevator Warp, this rendering or loading system was very appropriate given the context of the game. It seems that A Little More Games is exploring this niche game structure and I'm excited to see what other experiences they have to offer in the future.

This game is actually a hidden gem. Reasoning below.

Mechanics is simple, it's pretty casual. You place stuff, you click battle, battle plays out and you get mana to place more stuff. You can refresh the shop and synergize items, there's Plant builds, Wand builds, Crystal builds - healer build, poison build or direct damage build.

Stay Alive My Son is unlike any VR game I have played before. The settings are well thought out, and the pacing allows you to absorb the story while tying in the different themes that the environment brings. VR Interactions with the surroundings also feel very natural, and do not distract or take away from the core message of the game. Alternatively, they add depth and understanding. Being both immersive, but never intrusive, I have found stay alive my son to be a triumph in interactive storytelling.

Caught it at the Annecy Festival this year and bought it on Steam during the sale for my family to experience. I was blown away - educational, touching, powerful, and grounded in history. This VR experience is next-level, with stunning graphics making every moment real and multi-layered sound design that pulls you right into this man’s world, thoughts, and emotions.
For those who are sensitive: this story is a rollercoaster ride of deep emotions that keeps you wanting more despite wanting to stop many times. I felt this deep need to wanting to find out what happens to this man’s family. 
My kids saw it - a 9 and 13 year old - and they loved it! They were not scared, if anything they asked me a million questions and we even googled things afterwards about this man, child, and history. 
I am more faint at heart and a parent so this experience struck a deeper cord of realization and intensity so often seen even in modern news stories from Ukraine, Israel, and Palestine. I couldn't imagine leaving my child with a stranger. But the circumstances surrounding this decision were explained as harrowing, giving you chilling moments that make your heart race and palms sweat until you escape. If you make it this far - and you must because the most beautiful experience follows as  you fly to this gorgeous temple of salvation. Your heart calms and you see the strength and love of this parent versus the loss. 
By the end, you'll be weeping when you realize this is a true story and this parent is still alive and searching for his son. Absolutely unforgettable—10+/10!

Supporting a project like Stay Alive My Son, in my view, is supporting a project in medium that sends this message discretely yet undiluted for those that want something more than a conventional game or film. Schools that study genocide should install SAMS to truly help the next generations learn and understand more deeply. Then, just maybe, our future will be brighter and peaceful.

I like the concept behind this game and since I've never played an Anno game, Worshippers of Cthulhu seemed like a good way to jump into that genre.  

The First chapter plays like a tutorial and was generally a good experience, but in Chapter 2 you have to manage six different islands and that's when the mechanics became tedious.  

The early game is very slow paced since you have to wait for materials, followers and ritual cooldowns to become available.  You can speed up the game but you're still waiting.  It's not like other games I've played where you always have something that you could be doing. 

The midgame and endgame is where you spend a lot of time managing followers.  Homeless followers are only a number until you give them a house, and then they spawn with a random profession.  A lot of the time, it's a profession  you can't use yet or might not want on that particular island, but to swap you have to flip through all of the islands you occupy to find the person you want (if available) or hope that you can carve a new profession into them.  It would be nice if there were an easier way to move followers and see how many of each profession specialization you have available.  

The problem gets worse when you have to deal with higher tier followers.  They can't be swapped with anyone from a different tier, so you either make that follower homeless (and have to tier them up again with fungus) or you hope that there is a follower of the same tier on a different island that you want to swap.  

Getting a follower to the third tier requires four buildings.  I can understand the need for some of them, but why do we have to spam re-education centers everywhere?  You will find that that nearly all of your space is going to be used up by housing and these required buildings.  There is an edict that gives increased range to one of the buildings, but at the cost of it not being able to generate fanaticism.  

The carving minigame is a cool idea but some of the carvings are too similar to each other and I made the wrong carving about 3-4 times during my playthrough.  You can't redo it once it's done and it has a ten minute cooldown so that's frustrating.  I don't think the carving has to be automatic, but it would be better if it were more precise.  Technically, you can carve whatever symbol you want for fun, but I found myself not wanting to take any risks of messing it up so I went with boring circles and rectangles.  

The horrors you can summon are also a bit of a letdown.  In Chapter 2 you can summon three different ones.  The first is fairly weak and can only handle a couple of ships or towers, but it's fairly easy to summon.  The second horror is the real powerhouse.  Not only is it a lot faster, but its health lasts for awhile and it can do more damage.  The third horror disappointed me the most.  Not only is it expensive to summon (you need 30 god nails from a blacksmith and several high level followers) but its health goes down very fast compared to the others and it moves slower than horror #2.  When I was trying to achieve one of the Dreamspire quests in Chapter 2, for instance, the creature died on me before I could finish summoning the other two and I wasted followers/materials as a result.  It just wasn't worth summoning so I stuck with the second horror to finish wiping out enemy bases even after it started requiring higher tier sacrifices.  Also, I don't see why you can't have some kind of scouting boat to pick up salvage.  It doesn't have to do any damage, but having to summon a horror just to pick up some stuff in the water seems like a waste.

Overall, I do think it's a cool idea for a city building game, but the mechanics need some polish.  I'm setting this game aside for now, but I'll give it another shot once it gets out of Early Access.

Very retro (in a good way) pathfinding puzzle with a touch of Snake.

[b]What is it:[/b] A puzzle game in which you have to gather all the ducklings and reach the exit. Whenever you go near a duckling, it joins the queue, forming a long “snake”, so most of the puzzles are about managing your snake length: don’t get too long when you still need to get into tight rooms, get long enough to have a tail to stop you from sliding, keep your length odd to flip a switch, trim your tail and reattach it later…

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3317951249

There are four worlds. The first one (park) has just ducks, buttons, switches and gates. The second one (icy) introduces ice patches on which you slide until you hit something. The third one (factory) introduces conveyor belts that push you in a certain direction. And the fourth one (moon) introduces portals. The levels are good, mostly easy, but a few are a bit challenging. The presentation is very retro, pixel graphics with options to make it look like an original green and darker green GameBoy screen, or black and beige dot matrix, or low-bit colors, and primitive (in a good way!) chirpy sounds.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3317951919

Overall, the game looks and feels like something you’d find on a GameBoy back in the early nineties, and is a nice retro puzzle to enjoy for a couple of hours. The few blocker issues at the time of the release have been quickly fixed by the developers. There’s no undo, and it could really use it. [strike]The last 5 levels don’t unlock properly and can’t be played. The Linux/SteamDeck build is completely broken. The input scheme is very awkward and hard to discover.[/strike] 

[b]How hard is it:[/b] Mostly easy, with a few more mildly challenging levels.

[b]How long is it:[/b] 60 levels, 1-3 hours. Each world has 10 normal levels you can play in any order, and 5 bonus levels that unlock when solving all the normal levels. The next world also requires solving just the 10 normal levels.

[b]Level design:[/b] Decent. Very easy levels at the start of every world, showing how the new mechanics work. Decent mechanics. Fairly distinct levels.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3317947494

[b]Quality:[/b] The awkward controls and some missing QoL bring down the quality a bit but the idea is great. No undo. Decent level select, [strike]except that after finishing a level you always go back to level 1 and need to navigate to what you want to play next[/strike]. Works with a keyboard or a controller, and the keys are configurable. The mouse can be used to click on menu entries, but not for playing levels. No input caching. Decent audio and video settings, including emulating the horrible graphics of the first generation LCDs, and a dark mode. Retro pixel graphics, but sometimes it’s very hard to see ducklings. Good retro music and sound effects. No cloud saving. Progress achievements. Fast and responsive.

[b]Worth the price:[/b] A bit expensive, wait for a discount.

[b]Most positive aspect for me:[/b] Good retro gaming experience.

[b]Most negative aspect for me:[/b] No undo!

[b]What would make it better:[/b] Undo! Cloud saving. [strike]Level select screen should put me in the last level I played, not the first one.[/strike] Even better, automatically open next level when finishing the current one. [strike]Fix the bug that causes the last 5 levels to not stay unlocked. Fix the Linux build.[/strike] [strike]Add a white on black (dark mode) palette.[/strike] Make Space and Esc work better. [strike]Esc in a level should open up the menu instead of resetting.[/strike] Space in the in-level Reset/Quit menu should push the selected button instead of closing the menu. [strike]Space should start the selected world/level, it’s called “start” in the keyboard config screen but it doesn’t actually start anything.[/strike] (actually Enter is for selecting). Add a highlight button that highlights all the ducklings, sometimes it’s hard to see them. Add input caching.

DeTechtive 2112 is a cyberpunk-themed co-op shooter developed through the collaboration of M11 Studio and 5Deniz published by indie io. Set in the year 2112, the game blends detective elements with intense action, offering an engaging experience for fans of the genre like Ruin and Ascent.

Pros
✅ Visual Atmosphere & Art Design: DeTechtive 2112 does an excellent job of capturing the cyberpunk aesthetic. Neon-lit streets, detailed cityscapes, and a retro-futuristic design make the world feel immersive and visually striking.

✅ Story & Atmosphere: The game's setting is inspired by classic cyberpunk and detective narratives. Players are drawn into a mystery-filled world as they work to solve a case, which enhances the overall immersion.

✅ Co-op Gameplay: One of the strongest aspects of the game is its four-player co-op experience. Playing with a friend makes the game significantly more enjoyable, and the tactical cooperation required for missions keeps the gameplay engaging.

✅ Fluid & Satisfying Combat Mechanics: Gunplay feels smooth and responsive, with a solid cover system and a variety of weapons allowing for different combat strategies. Enemy AI also provides a fair challenge.

✅ Optimization & Technical Performance: The game runs smoothly, demonstrating that the developers prioritized optimization. It performs well even on lower-end systems without sacrificing visual quality.

✅ Commitment to Post-Launch Support: The developers have expressed plans to support the game with additional content and updates, which increases its long-term appeal.

Cons
❌ Mission Variety Could Be Improved: While the story is intriguing, some missions follow a repetitive loop. More diverse objectives would enhance the gameplay experience.

DeTechtive 2112 delivers a satisfying experience for co-op shooter fans. Its cyberpunk atmosphere, fluid gameplay, and cooperative mechanics make it a strong entry in the genre. Interesting to play as its a mix of simulation game and puzzle solving trap.  At first it looks like you are supposed to be in charge of the gym, but instead your job is to build the facilities and then hire staff.  The only real engagement you have with the gym part is to set up each camper's gym workout and meal plan.  And the meal plan part only starts once you have achieved level 4 and built the dining hall.

And I think that's where the game has flaws.  The UI is quirky and counter-intuitive at times.  Worse, when you register a camper you have to take their picture, but then you will need to exit their profile to get the game to continue, but to put together their gym workout and meal plans you have to go back into their profile.  Worse, the gym workout pages will be set to whatever page you last viewed, which is likely to be the activities you want the camper to do last as you want them to warm up a bit before doing high risk good exp exercises.

I also found that once I had a level 7 camp the campers suddenly needed a lot more exp in order to achieve their weight goals.  Often as much as 50 exp in a day when a maximum risk gym program with 5 high exp tasks won't give more than 30-32 exp.  You can gain a bit more with meals (maximum of 9 per day), but getting someone the required exp quickly becomes far more difficult than it had been.  Its not game-breaking, but it was frustration creating as all my campers after I reached level 7 were constantly demanding refunds because they failed to achieve their goals.   (and don't get me started on the fact that you can have a full camp and yet campers continue to show up and will score the camp 0/10 because you didn't admit them, despite the fact that you couldn't.)

Its just a lot of little things that make the game UI far more complicated than it should be along with a game-play loop that was not easy to define and which seemed to constantly shift without clear warning.  Its possible to work through it, but I would say this is definitely a "buyer beware" situation.  Make sure you love this kind of simulation.

**Great visual style, unique card expiring upon use gimmick, elemental blocks/attacks/strength/weakness, dark and light alignments, and huge array of characters to play as. I thought I found a gem here.**

Can't recommend now though.. The game doesn't utilize these to it's full potential. Here's the bad.

-12 characters! Well.. not really. They all share the same card pool. All of them. 
The only difference is they have a unique buff, but the buff isn't game changing really. It's just like +1 water defense to water cards, or 2X gold on combat wins. 

-Light and Dark alignments! Sadly this doesn't effect events, nor are the alignments permanent. You can't go down a dark path or one of good and have altered events on the game map or requirements for special items/cards based on alignment. Nothing cool like that, it's literally just an extra effect that's only in battles upon card use; it changes how strong/weak a card or enemy is. It goes down every turn like a buff/debuff.

-Elemental cards and plain cards. I did like this gimmick but it's half baked. For example, if you have a fire shield of 10, and get attacked by a normal attack of 5, you have 5 shield left. If you get attacked by water with 5 it has a 200% buff and breaks the shield. If you attack fire with nature it'll do half damage. Sadly, that's about it. There are card synergies as well but with so few cards it gets old fast.

-Narrative. It has a cool narrative for each characters motivation and why they traverse the map. You can even fight the other 12 characters on the map! As cool as this is, it's not that deep. Every enemy fights you for a reason if you read the encounter, but you ALWAYS have to fight. There is no dark/light alignment, factions, race, or RPG stats that enable you a chance to alter the battle encounter. 

-No relics or perm progression. The game is just, beat the bosses with each character. That's it. No meta game or unlockable aside from the characters. You can't have a unique run with relics or stats, it's always the same. Including the map. You'll find the best route and then rinse and repeat. Not enough RNG imo.

I have just passed 20 hours of playing this game so far, and I am having a blast. I wanted to write a detailed review as I almost gave up on it an hour or two in. Overall, I would give this game an 8 out of 10--as long as one goes in knowing that one has to actively select just two main abilities/spells per character to use at a time. They can be slotted in-and-out at will, as can items, even during combat. But it takes significantly more effort to play this way, just know that in advance. (More on that below.)

It is a reasonably straight forward grid-based very old school RPG. You start with one character, and gather up three more along the way in your adventure. It is real time, which some people may not prefer. For those, like me actually, who enjoy standing there just ‘tanking’ the fights out, you are better serviced by sliding in anticipation of the opponents blows, for example. But I’m finding that it’s not critical to one’s success; I can stand still enough and just use more potions or rest breaks (mana and hps naturally regen over time) and it’s not an issue thus far into the game at least.

The graphics and music are plenty good, but nothing amazing. I play on a UHD+ monitor with high-end graphics card, and I’ve still had to drop the resolution a full slot to get better frame-rates – so there’s room for optimization there. The automap function works well, but no notes can be made on them. (This was not an issue for me though as it didn't feel necessary.) The screenshots on the store page are pretty representative of the game.

I am finding the story thus far quite good!! But though I’ve been an avid reader of fantasy/sci fi since the late 70s – and /very/ much appreciate a great story – I sometimes feel that reviewers are too hard on [especially the small] developers saying that the stories aren’t creative or good enough. (If you’re expected Steven Erikson, GRRM, Tolkien, Simmons, Sanderson or pick a dozen other authors here, then no it’s not close to that level haha! But it’s been more than good enough for me for the type of game this is; I’d give the story an 8.5 out of 10 at least to halfway through the game.

The game has really good balance and progression. Foes were neither too weak nor too hard; just the right amount of challenge. And going up levels does feel quite meaningful, both with the stat increases per level as well as a new path skill/spell every two levels. The puzzles and riddles are pretty good and stand their ground with others in this genre, and there is help on the Steam forums (including from the developer themselves) available. There are also a bunch of extra ‘secrets’ to also go after – but I don’t know how to tell how many you have at any time, which is an area for improvement for sure. (To my knowledge, you don’t find that out until you finish the game.) The good news is that there are people who’ve played through multiple times looking to get them all, so that does say something positive about the games replayability. That said, I expect for many of us it’s a one-time through type of game. And there is more than enough game to justify its full price.

A weakness is that though the items you do find (with slots for rings, amulets, weapons, armour, etc.) have tangible benefits and trade-offs for using, the game would benefit from having more items and choice available. (Opponents don’t drop items, just chests and items strewn about that you have to keep an eye out for.) Most of us who play grid-based RPGs are probably used to having to go carefully and not miss things; but here it is even more important as you can miss out on a really good item if you don’t go carefully. 

The major caveat with this game is that it only allows each character to have two slots of abilities. And this includes weapons! So you have to select which two- including weapon(s), active abilities, and spells -- you want active at any time for each character. Each is hot-keyed to the keyboard, and can be tailored. (I play mouse and keyboard so I can’t comment on controllers etc.) For that reason, I would either give this game a 4 or 5 out of 10 for those strongly wanting a bunch of active abilities to choose at any given time. Normally that would be me--and it’s almost why I almost gave up on the game early. But I gave it a second chance after a post from the Dev clarified that the game is balanced for characters only having the two slots -- and am very glad that I did. (Note that you -can- slot in other weapons/spells/abilities on the fly. It means taking the time to open the inventory screen and so on: It’s not -that- bad to do on occasion, but it would be tedious imo on an ongoing basis in every fight.) Most of my focus is on passive abilities, which are limitless and stack--and really  impact game-play in meaningful ways. Overall, going in with seeing this game as a more straight-forward RPG I am really enjoying it, and would give it an 7.5 to 8 out of 10.

A few tips for newer players – I recommend giving the weapon from the first other character you meet to your ‘main’ if you make any kind of warrior. It’s a very good weapon, and will have more ‘bang for your buck’ in their hands in the front row. (You party is a 2 by 2 formation, which you can change at any time.) I also recommend throwing a few points into constitution to get their hps up – I did this with my entire party and it made the early stages much easier. As well, pay very close attention to those passives. There are some really great ones in those Path lines that each character can choose from. You can select multiple paths, so don’t feel that you only have to limit yourself to one or two paths. Finally, Personality stat increases in particular add a bonus to -all- party member’s damage, which is pretty cool.

I hope this helps.

This is terribly made asset flip type of game, no two ways about it.

Let's talk about presentation first and lack of overall cohesion. The main character, fox lady, is quite detailed and well animated 3d model. And then, NPC models and the maps are very low poly 3d - clearly there is a disconnect here. 

I did some research and found some of the original models: "Kyoko - Game Ready Character" (the fox lady) on cgtrader website, and "POLYGON - Ancient Empire" map (called Empire in game) on syntystore website. That's where I ended my quick search, but I am pretty certain that all levels in this game were store bought, as well as the music.

Look, I have no issues with pre-made assets, so long as are used creatively (as opposed to mindless copy-paste) and there is consistency in terms of style. Last but not least, the end product has be functional, which is not really the case here.

Yes, this game barely works because it is riddled with bugs, collision detection issues, etc. Here are some examples: you will hit invisible barriers often, fall through the map and die, die just standing there doing nothing, die by getting stuck in a wall, getting stuck on the floor, clipping through objects. Another sign that we are dealing with poorly cobbled together assets.

In case you are not familiar with this type of games, it is a 3d platformer that has you go up from start to finish (Only Up clone). It feels like climbing a huge tower essentially, without the walls. Each section or map is represented by a different theme: feudal Japan, western, viking map, roman empire (very original stuff). 

To spice things up, enemies are scattered throughout the various levels. There is a combat system, but it's so badly made and unsatisfying that I would just run past brain dead AI altogether. No point in fighting them since they don't drop any loot or XP. Avoid combat at all costs in the platforming sections because it will only lead to you fall to the beginning of the level and start over again - don't say I did not warn you! 

Then you have what I think are "pal" npcs, which the game is partially named after. These oversized and brightly coloured npcs don't look like they belong in this game at all in terms of the design/model, and you cannot interact with them. They serve no purpose in the game itself, but I will get back to those in the conclusion.

Platforming is the core of this game - it works for the most part, but it will get frustrating fast because of the previously mentioned collision problems, annoying enemies -with throwing weapons- and the fact that the wall bouncing is inconsistent. In some sections you need to jump off the side of a wall to reach higher places, but on many occasions the game won't register the input for the 2nd jump. As a result: you will fall to the beginning of the area and this is very annoying.

And then there is the last level...Remember that Crystal Cave section in Dark Souls 1, that has you walk on an invisible path? Well, imagine that section in this game, 3 times as long, looking ugly as sin and with just a finite number of consumables to show you the way. In fact, I don't think that section is possible and I will soon post a video on community hub to illustrate the problem.

This is probably one of the best (if not the best) "action rogue-like" I've played. It also does an excellent job with both visual and audio cues for stuff like dash cooldowns or other in game timers.  Everything about this game seems designed thoughtfully and well executed.  Each ship functions in a different way and forces a different playstyle; I had one ship with a strong recoil on its shot that I would use to help me maneuver and one that would lay mines behind you which required serious mental adjustment (especially when most enemies come at you head on).  I've played Vampire Survivors, Boneraiser Minions, Slime 3k, and probably more I can't remember right now.  Cellfish and Halls of Torment are on top in terms of enemy design and to me that makes for more engaging gameplay.

Graphics: Graphically the game looks great.

Sound: The music and SE are very good, simple but effective

Narrative: I like the story's approach, you know it's there in the background in everything you're doing, but the game doesn't beat you over the head with it.

Combat: Turn-based fun, can't go wrong.

Enemies: There's a pretty decent variety, the build up to what I'd consider the first major "boss" is pretty good, and if you're not ready it's devastating.

So far my only critique lies in character creation and some weapon calculations.

You can't name your characters, or at least I didn't clearly see a way to, instead you have to pick from a list of what I'm assuming are Lore appropriate names. They're the typical Medieval Fantasy, Tolkien-esque names so they're fine overall, but it is kind of a bummer that you're forced to choose from them.

Also ALL melee is calculated through the "Power" Stat, which equates to the traditional Strength Stat, which is fine for a lot of larger weapons like long swords, clubs, mauls, etc. but it also handles traditionally Dexterity weapons such as daggers and some short swords.

Technique, this game's version of Dexterity, handles only ranged weapons, although certain skills required to utilize specific weapons such as the "Short Blade" skill require Technique to unlock short blades only use power, and if you don't have enough power stat, you'll "Miss" nearly every attack. 

This makes characters like Thieves more useful if you think of them as fighters instead when rolling their stats.
Speaking of Stats, it's all a roll system, no point buy option or even the classic D&D roll 4d6 drop the lowest and assign so you could potentially sit there for a little bit crafting your perfect character.

Short and sweet vania that gets a lot of mileage out of only 2 types of hazards (there is danger, but no combat). 

You begin with even less mobility than one might expect, and over the course of the game you unlock a few useful upgrades. The map is peppered with checkpoint/respawn bells and optional gold coins (which must be banked at a bell), and the game rarely asks you to pass through more than a few screens of danger between bells.

The map is divided into a few regions that each prominently feature a particular mechanic. Each region houses one of the upgrades along with a challenging trial that tests your mastery over that upgrade.

A basic clear can be achieved with a relatively small portion of the map explored, so a hefty portion of the game is optional. I chose to complete the trial gauntlets and collect all the coins, but I'm satisfied not trying for a deathless clear.

I did find that some aspects of the movement felt a bit hard to get used-to --
• when you jump to a vine or ladder and try to grab on, there's nothing damping the horizontal movement and it's very easy to slip right off until you get used to releasing your directional input at the right moment.
• the mobility features rely on "snapping" your character into a specific row of tiles, and even with practice it seems to require a tremendous amount of precision to reliably snap to the row you want.
• when you gain the ability to have controlled descent, anything more than a brief tap will send you plummeting into the bottom of the screen, which likely means a death in most of the areas where you'd use this ability.

The game is very charming overall. There are a few cheeky gotchas to make sure you're paying attention, but it never feels hostile. The map is also just small enough that I didn't dread backtracking for missed coins.

I played this game in its entirety, but I wouldn't play it again. This is mostly due to how frustrating it can be. Yeah, this is one of those platforming games that make you want to smash your controller against the wall. You attack enemies with music notes by pressing a precise sequence of controller buttons. I often found this mechanic unresponsive with what seems like a slight delay, which means you will often have to keep trying over and over again to get these attacks right. This is nothing though compared to when you are forced to make perfectly timed speed runs over spikes, numerous lengthy wall runs, and freeze water at the top of pipes with split second timing in the later levels. These sections are a big reason why I stopped enjoying the game. Another major issue is how LONG the levels seemed to drag on doing the same thing over and over again. There are only six chapters in this game. However, each area that you are in seems to go on forever and ever with seemingly no end in sight performing the same jumps and wall runs and battling the same enemies over and over again. There is also a highly annoying and frustrating boss section where a fire boss keeps killing you over and over again. This boss battle is divided into three phases and the game does not save in between phases, meaning you will have to start the entire battle over when you die. 

Voice acting in this game is atrociously bad and there are also some fairly harsh frame rate drops when entering new areas or when an event is triggered that cannot be fixed by changing the graphic options. There is also no inventory to manage nor any way to improve your character. You just keep making the same jumps, wall runs, and battling the same enemies until the game ends. The developer clearly designed this game to get more challenging as it goes on, but this only made for a more frustrating than enjoyable experience in my opinion. The way the levels drag on though doing the same thing over and over again is what really ruined it for me. Overall, this game is worth the price. However, I cannot recommend it as something to be played more than once.

Yaoling: Mythical Journey – A Fresh Take on the Monster-Capturing Genre

Yaoling: Mythical Journey offers a new experience for fans of the monster-catching genre with its unique capturing and breeding mechanics. Despite being in early access, the game already stands out with its solid mechanics and entertaining gameplay.

Strengths: Mechanics and Variety
The game's monster-catching and yaoling-breeding systems are highly satisfying in terms of strategy and variety. Each yaoling has unique abilities and combination potential, making team-building an exciting process. Additionally, the auto-battle system provides a more comfortable experience for those long grinding sessions. These mechanics make the game accessible to both newcomers and seasoned players of the genre.

Visuals and Atmosphere
The world of Yaoling offers an eye-catching atmosphere with its vibrant color palette and creative yaoling designs. Exploring different regions to discover new yaoling types adds depth to the open-world experience. Moreover, the visuals and user-friendly interface make the gameplay smoother and more enjoyable.

Story: Room for Improvement
The game's weakest link is its story. Considering the potential of the Yaoling universe, a deeper and more compelling narrative could have been delivered. However, as the game is still in early access, I’m optimistic that the developers will take big steps in this area. By the time it reaches its 1.0 release, the story could become richer and more meaningful, elevating the overall experience.

Early Access and Hope for the Future
As an early access title, Yaoling: Mythical Journey continues to surprise players with big updates. It's encouraging to see that the developers are paying attention to community feedback and working diligently to improve the game. The yaoling variety and mechanics are already among the best I’ve seen in the genre. I hope they maintain this level of quality when it comes to storytelling and world-building as well.

Conclusion: A Promising Start
Yaoling: Mythical Journey is a must-try for anyone interested in the monster-catching genre. Its mechanics and yaoling designs have already placed it among the top games in the category. If the developers manage to strengthen the story and world design, this game could become a masterpiece remembered for years to come. Even in early access, it’s already a highly enjoyable experience, and I’m excited to see what the future holds for it!

Being Slovak, I was pretty excited when seeing this game on the store page, as the game was made by Slovak developers. Unfortunatelly, in its current state, this game is not far from being unplayable.

I´ll start with the good, because there´s not much. The art style is pretty appealing. The almost retro-style graphics are pleasing to the eye. The second positive being the music. It does fit the creepy and depressing setting of the game. Unfortunately, those are all the positives I´ve  been able to salvage from this, so now I´ll move on to the negatives.

The first, but least problematic would be the lack of enemy variety. There are only 2 enemy types, but it´s more like 1 enemy type, because they behave exactly the same. One is a zombie soldier with a stahlhelm, the other a zombie with an officer´s cap. Both behave exactly the same and die from 1 bullet to the head. The second problem would be in the guns. I´ve been able to find 4 in the 2 levels of this game that I´ve played. Problem is, there´s not much point in using the remaining 3, because the starter pistol does the job just as well. Now, we move on to the bigger problems. A really jarring one is the wrong description of some important items in the inventory. For example, towards the end of the first level, you get a key. In the inventory, it says it´s a drawer key, yet you use it to open a door to exit the level. This may mislead some players, and result in them wandering in circles in the trenches wondering what to do, like I initially did. Some objectives can also be incredibly vague. The first level is a clear example. Your first objective in the game is to ´´read a note.´´ There are several notes at the start of the level, yet none of those are the actual objective. The actual note is on the other side of the trench, on the wall with a knife sticking out of it. Once interacted with, it will bring out a totem out of the ground, that you HAVE TO interact with to open a gate to progress. You can also just clip through this gate, because it has no collision, but then the level script will screw up, and you won´t be able to complete it. The game is very specific like that on what you have to do. The second level is particularly bad in this regard, because the first one at least shows you cutscenes of stuff happening, so you know what to look for. But the second level is very subtle like and area previously blocked by a tank now being open after completing an objective. And also one of the objectives is to literally just LOOK AT something instead of actually interacting with it, which can also confuse. 

But this brings me to the worst offense of this game so far. As I´m writing this review, The second level of this game is broken to the point of being unbeatable. At the end there is a bridge with a locked ramp and a gate/door behind it. This is clearly meant to be the end of the level, since I got an achievement once I reached it. Problem is, you clip straight through the door. behind is a broken bridge with a river underneath,that you can cross, but upon reaching the other side, there´s nothing but a flat wasteland, essentially the end of the road.

I don´t rightly know if this will ever be fixed. It may since the game is early access, and it hasn´t been out for all that long yet. But right now, iin its current state, I wouldn´t recommend this game to anybody.

Meh, a not very good TD game, mildly interesting. I will probably play it a gain, so I am going to give it a tepid one thumb up. 
The game does lack most of the bells and whistles you expect from a TD game.
No way to speed things up.
No tower upgrades at all.
No tactical options.
No Strategic upgrades of any kind. 
No fluff.I know that doesn't bother everyone, but it seems such a simple thing. 
No pathing, again, not a big deal, but some people want to know.
The assets are fine, so small it is hard to really see what is going on. Some of them look far too much alike. (Looking at you, assassins and bombers) The monsters look pretty good though. 
The game starts with only one tower for you to pick. This is every level, the same tower. As you gain experience new towers are automatically unlocked. The first level has five that you eventually unlock. The levels I have tried so far have one more for each. No clue what the max will be yet. 
Perhaps the best aspect is the variety of monsters. Some are fliers which ignore the path, some spawn little versions of themselves when they die. There are a lot of different looks. Again, no index of them, an easy addition.
A pet peeve, this is one of those games that makes you collect the coins. Not a huge deal. At least so far the towers seem immune from dying. On the down side, they also can't be sold if you want to upgrade a position.
Another pet peeve is that it lies to you on occasion. Before each wave a few arrows show when monsters will spawn. Maybe, LOL. Most of the time it is right, so I assume this must be a glitch.
All in all, a lackluster edition to the genre, but mildly interesting.

The Gravedigger is another solid horror game from Authogin.

Graphics are, as usual with this dev, pretty stunning. But it’s not without a cost: my 8GB VRAM was almost maxed out, and the game was barely running. DLSS saved the day, though, boosting me from a miserable 25fps to a smooth 70fps on Quality setting at 3440x1440. Weird thing: I think the DLSS settings are mixed up. Balanced gave me worse frames than Quality, and Performance was even lower. Also, some animations are missing, like "fade to black" skips that feel cheap and break the mood. And the priest has no facial animation when speaking, which feels odd.
Jumpscares are still top-notch, though. Authogin nails those, popping them in when you least expect it. 

A few nitpicks: I would have love jumpscares using the cadavers, maybe some earrings to collect, better weather (like drizzle is audible but not visible, maybe a moody rainstorm), and more cadaver variety. Just small stuff, really.
Now, the real downsides: it’s crazy short, 2 to 4 hours to beat the game. There’s this annoying lighting bug too when in the coffin room, and the lights go out, turning them back on doesn’t fix the coffin lighting which is frustrating.
Also, it feels like there’s a hidden third ending, but it’s either cut or not there yet, which is a bummer.

-----
Still, The Gravedigger is a fun game with well done jumpscares and top-tier visuals, a classic Authogin game. But with how short it is and some rough spots, you might wanna wait for a sale instead of jumping in at full price.

This game is great and well worth the price. I think it's an excellent intro game to Foddian-style/masocore games and has replay value via speedrunning. If you've played Jump King, your skills will carry over to this. It's not as punishing or difficult as JK, but still offers plenty of challenge the first playthrough. If you haven't finished JK, I'd guess an initial playthrough would take about 5-8 hours. If you have finished JK, you can probably beat this one in roughly 2 hours.

The movement in this game is like a mix of JK's deep snow/Giant Boots + ice/Snake Ring, i.e. you can only jump and can't walk, and your character has a bit of slide on landing. The double-jump opens up a lot of movement potential, and it’s genuinely a blast using it in different ways. There's seemingly no delay between landing and you're jump count resetting, which lets you schmoove all over. Mixing double jump, slides, and short hops makes for overall movement that is very satisfying and snappy. The collision detection - in particular when you're just clearing a platform's corner into a slide - feels extremely fair and perfectly matches what my eyes are able to process in the moment. The developer added a speedrunner quick restart just prior to the Steam release, which is an excellent thing to have built-in rather than having to mod it in.

I love the music in The Tower, and the visuals/atmosphere throughout are very well done. The leaves on the trees and shrubs have this beautiful effect where they look painted, and in my first playthrough I really enjoyed spending time soaking in the artwork. The spider's animations look great, and the heartbeat sound + zoom-in on the camera when the spider's near you are very nice touches.

The spider is an interesting mechanic, and I imagine it'll be fun watching streamers interact with it. As a heads up if you have grinded JK: you may not find the spider super threatening after the first couple encounters with it. I don't see this as a negative, as I feel like the spider's inclusion is intended for a different audience than speedrunners. The developer mentioned they may be able to make the spider more aggressive for speedrunners if the game has a committed group of runners that would benefit from this type of update.

Difficult, rewarding, and spooky as hell. I love this game.

Every platform has been precision-engineered to make you sweat. You will fall, and fall again, and fall for a third and fourth and fifth time ad infinitum trying to get to each new area.

The double-hopping movement mechanics are unusual and hard to master, but over time, they become really fluid and satisfying. Once you get the hang of it, you can fly through parts of the map that you struggled with at first, and that feels good. But the challenge never goes away, and in fact really just increases into some insane leaps of faith farther up the map.

The spider has made me literally throw myself off a cliff trying to get away from it so many times I can't count. The way it moves and lunges at you is unreal. Absolutely hate that thing. It's fantastic.

For people who will never make it to the top (read: me), there are a ton of details and bits of lore scattered around like bread tabs that still absolutely make it worth playing and exploring. The atmosphere is beautifully crafted, from the chilling music to the weirdly menacing little moth-centric fables you find throughout the map. It's ominous, but it also has a sense of humor, and I enjoy that immensely.

Thank you to the devs and their twisted minds. You've put evil into the world, and I hope you're enjoying watching us suffer :D

After playing for around 10 hours, I have to say the game just doesn’t feel fun. Here are the main issues I’ve noticed:

Skill Imbalance: Some skills seem much stronger than others, making about half the skills in a class useless on Insane difficulty. For example, wolves on the Revenant and status effects don’t work well at all in higher difficulties, forcing me to focus on cooldown reductions instead.

Excessive Grind: The game pushes you to run easier difficulties over and over again just to collect gold and soulstones for unlocking stronger passives. This repetitive process quickly becomes tedious. I don’t want to spend an hour grinding lower levels just to make progress.

Limited Build Variety: It’s rare to achieve a “non-moving” build unless you’re on an easier difficulty setting.

[b]TL; DR[/b] a short but enjoyable title, it has a fun gimmick, some cool enemy designs, but is otherwise simply serviceable. If you are interested in run-based games with turn-based combat, then this might be for you.

[h1] Story [/h1]
Darkness is ascendant and it will consume the light.

There is little narrative to [i]Revelatio[/i], you get the premise and a couple of cutscenes to set up the chapters and the bosses. That is pretty much everything besides some short flavour texts. 
There is so little of it that it is hardly worth talking about, I would not say that the writing is especially evocative or atmospheric it mostly feels serviceable and that is fine for a short game that does not focus on its narrative.

[h1] Presentation [/h1]
What first got me interested in [i]Revelatio[/i] was the visuals, it has some very inspired enemies, and a couple of great screens during dialogue, even the basic foot soldiers of the forces of light look good, albeit generic. However, you can convert them to your side, you see them consumed by darkness and their shapes twist and malform into one of your loyal servants, that looks cool, and the recognisable but corrupted designs make for a nice contrast, though they still look a bit generic. 
On the other hand, we have the bosses, some of them are very much archetypical paladins, but the majority feel inspired, like King Phanuel or Appaim, and yes, you can convert them too, everyone can join your side, and they all get unique looks, it is really neat. 
You can even get a closer look at the bosses during the cutscenes, which is always something I appreciate, they are simple but sweet, the faded colours make it seem like it was recorded on ancient parchments, or as if darkness had drained the world of its vibrancy, which is very appropriate.

Something that bothered me from early on was the UI, it mostly works fine enough but it is boring, and can be used in literally any game, there is no identity to it, which is really something they should have had when the game is so short and simple. 
A good UI can do wonders for immersion and can help reinforce a title’s character, while a generic UI is, at best, forgettable. 
It is also jarring when a game uses different words to describe the same thing in different menus.
‘Back’ and ‘quit’ are different words, they mean different things, and as you start playing you have no idea if they are different on purpose or just because, does ‘quitting’ mean I forgo my justly earned reward, or does it mean ‘go back’, who knows? 
I do! It is neither, ‘quit’ is used when viewing a unit card from your roster!
It is objectively a minor issue, but it is also something a player will see numerous times during the course of their playthrough.

There is also music, fairly ominous, pretty generic, it is not bad, but it is what you would expect from a game where you play as the dark lord, however, it only takes up a small portion of the soundscape so it never gets grating.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
[i]Revelatio[/i] is a simple turn-based game with one gimmick, corruption, as you fight you can reduce a unit’s faith, and once it hits zero, they will switch sides and are put at your disposal.
This works both ways, if the forces of light redeem one of your powerful servants you will be put in a bad spot, and might outright lose the entire run, so you should be aware of your enemies and the situation that you find yourself in. Focusing on faith-reducing enemies is key, because it is difficult to recover faith once you have lost it, nothing sucks more than having a boss convert several units in a single attack just because that one archer seven battles ago happened to get a few good hits in.
Manage the faith of your roster and prioritize breaking your enemies’, snowball to victory!

They also draw some inspiration from rogue-like deckbuilders, [i]Revelatio[/i] does not have a card deck, but you do have a unit roster, and only three creatures will ever be selectable at a time. So, in a way, you do draw a “hand”, and new “cards” each time you play a monster. 
This does encourage smaller rosters because it guarantees that you can start with something good every turn, this together with the fact that you can save one monster per run incrementally results in a strong start, but again, there is the faith concern, you do not want your most powerful servants to turn traitor, so filling out your “deck” with fodder is a good idea, and they can also be quite useful to drown enemies in bodies, as sacrifices or to buy time.

With all that said, most battles are quite easy and straightforward, and they start to get a bit repetitive after a couple of runs because they are never really all that different. 
Enemies look different and have different attack ranges, but they do not have enough mannerisms to differentiate one from another, so, it gets repetitive, unless you are talking about the bosses. 
[i]Revelatio[/i] has some really fun bosses, they typically get some adds, and each of them has a unique mechanic, so they all feel very distinct and fun to master. 
The Saviour is one of my favourites, just a horde of adds swarming you to defend the last bastion of heaven, he demands map control, ceding a tile gives you less manoeuvrability and that makes it more likely for him to redeem your units and use them against you. He is not the most challenging fight, provided you can deal with the adds, but he is one of the coolest, and if you manage to convert him... all those mechanics are now on your side.
This is where the [i]real[/i] fun of [i]Revelatio[/i] comes in, using bosses, and their mechanics to crush unsuspecting enemies, it turns the repetitive encounters into something enjoyable and is not that wonderful?

[b] Overview [/b]

Pretty enjoyable and challenging roguelike game that requires some planning and strategy. You have mana and dark essence to use for summoning your units and corrupting your enemies. After completing each run, whether successful or not, you can save one unit. You can bring along saved units in your squad of 4 units for subsequent runs. I spent about an hour getting accustomed to the game mechanics and building my units and sanctum, but at approx 6 hrs in, I completed Act 2.


[b] Positives [/b]

1. Very captivating visual appearance. I appreciate the visual difference between your own units and your enemies, especially the animation when units are corrupted or edified.
2. The combat and overall gameplay is pretty straightforward. The unit skills itself feel pretty thought out and it is interesting seeing the balance between attack, speed, range, etc.
3. The overall level of difficulty so far feels fair, it's not impossible and it's not too easy.
4. I appreciate being able to hover over different icons and the description box appearing.
5. I like the visual progression of some things as your progress further into the game as well.
6. Each round feels pretty fresh, even if you take the same units due to the rng nature of roguelikes. The enemies you encounter can vary.


[b] Initial Criticisms as of Oct 5, 2024[/b]

1. There is no way to view the instructions/mechanics presented at the very start of the game again. It would be helpful to have the option to view it in the menu, as this would make it more accessible for both new and returning players (if someone were to stop playing for a while)
2. There is no way to effectively end your run immediately. Other roguelikes (eg, Dead Cells, Othercide, etc) have a button to end the current run/start the next one. In Revelatio, you must either wait until you lose your lives, or go to the main menu and start a "new game", but the latter means you cannot save a unit from the run. I can understand the stylistic choice behind this, but gameplay-wise, it feels slow if you know a run is done for.
3. No beastiary or library to view units that you have encountered but are not in your Divine Hall.

Game style spectrum: Domekeeper<-- -- Wall World -- -- -- -- -->Drill Core
[b]This game is about building up, both during a run and outside them.[/b]
This is much more casual than domekeeper and wall world.
It's more about the mining and building upgrades vs heavy combat focus.

[b]mining:[/b] for that focus, this gets a lot of good attention. Instead of you/single person mining everything, instead you mark blocks for mining, priority mining, cancel (important strategically), send soldiers, etc. There is a good tension between using your resources to upgrade miners' abilities, buying needed buildings, and needed defense turrets (for the wave). In the mine, you have blocks that can fall/crush enemies, nests that spawn enemies in nearby blocks (break it quick before it  hatches), flame spewing blocks that both help and hurt, earthquakes that drop blocks, buildings that add special abilities, and risk/reward of pushing how late to flee the mine. A+

{b}Combat:[/b] unlike the hyperactive domekeeper/wall world is instead a tower defense with a good selection of abilities that can drastically improve things. What towers you find in a run, what other buildings you find, etc = variety/not playing the same towers every time (though some do seem like always good to pick choices). The fact that you might get quite a few towers down before finding one of those means it's worth getting a booster for those instead of your go-to. B to B+ 

Mid run also has perks that can be quite significant, such as: extra workers, X-Type weapon fire rate, turret range increase, faster mining, faster movement, longer day time, cheaper (tower, worker, building), etc. What you choose really depends on the run. A+

[b]Meta/outside the run permanent upgrades:[/b] There is a regular upgrade section with things like worker bonuses and rerolls etc, as well as platform upgrades (accessed where picking what run to start) with very powerful upgrades (generally better than the regular upgrade section), and there are technologies per difficulty level that pick to try to unlock by completing objectives (eg reach 350m depth, kill 1st boss, etc)
Also, there is currently a second dwarf platform to unlock that plays very differently and has its own platform upgrades. (so it benefits from the general upgrades section, but not your human platform upgrades).

Run selection consists of: difficulty level, biome (currently 2), platform (currently 2), tech to try to unlock, platform configuration (what tech to start with and platform perks).
There is intentionally limited slots to fill, because they make a big difference. For instance, being able to start with expensive rocket turrets (and your first 2 turrets are free) plus a perk to extend turret range or make buildings 1 iron cheaper are huge boosts to the run.

I have probably tried too much to see how deep I can go, because it actually rewards you per mission with quite a few upgrade resources. The game is setup to encourage you to get in do the stuff and get out (which I've kinda not done). So I have a lot of permanent upgrades, but have been slow to unlock the new technologies (eg Mark2 versions of turrets).
Also [b]very happy they included "recycle" button that allows you to swap upgrade resources into others you need[/b]

Despite 100% it, I do have a few irks to share
#21 Rainbow ball : all balls Bonus when hitting pegs, but at that point, it's better to have carpet bomb instant-clear of boards
#20 Star ball : spawns more star balls like the auto drop when hitting pegs, makes making a clear board to farm the bucket difficult, then doesn't seem to do much when carpet bombing
#19 Ghost ball : goes through obstacles and pegs and gives a bonus to all balls, so it's a great ball for the bucket grinding, but it comes up so late that it doesn't matter much and the bonus for having ghosts on screens only really works when manually throwing balls as the auto-drop cap feels quite low for those

The purchase/info menu can be locked to stay visible on the selected ball but it's either covering the side of the board or the other balls, stopping you from switching selection in some situations.

I finally decided it was time to put myself through the task of getting 2 hours into this slop. Hopefully this review serves as a warning to people who saw videos and thought this game was going to be enjoyable.

First issue is the meta progression system. After every run, you gain enhancements that will make subsequent runs different, if you've played roguelikes before, this should not be news to you. What SHOULD come as a surprise to you is how atrocious this system is in this game. It actively gives you too little to make a noticeable impact on gameplay without hours of work. At which point it becomes less about fun and more about work.

The primary combat mechanic in this game is tiles, which can merge. Cool in concept, very cool in fact. However, this game seems to actively try to screw you over on your tile merges. I will use 2 tiles as an example here.

3 shields make a level 2 shield, every run, I have about 8 shields in my inventory,. and can never get them to merge to level 2. A level 2 shield providing 3 armor instead of 1, you trade 3 separate tiles for 1 tile and get the same amount of shield.

3 water mages make a level 2 water mage. Water mage reduces enemy HP by 1%. You would think, in following the trend, a level 2 water mage should reduce by 3% right? WRONG. Oh and if the horrible merging mechanics got your hopes up, you screwed up, because the second you have 3 of these guys, it's going to merge so you lose 1% of the reduction.

The entire combat system in this game is flawed in that it's all about making combat take way too long with way too little payoff. Very rarely do you get a reward from an enemy that makes the health you lost feel worth it.

The balance in general is just as terrible as the meta progression system. You start with soldiers, which are generally pretty useless, but the second you beat your first  run, you can get ninjas, who are all you will ever need. And even then, have fun trying to kill anything because everything just becomes way too tanky after like the fourth level in a playthrough. Have fun with bosses you can't counter. Bosses that just get to deal damage no matter what, bosses that cut your shield amount in half, you know, because the game even provided you sufficient defense to begin with.

This game is not worth your money, nor is it worth your time. It's another one for the trend of putting minimal effort into a game and just going "It's a roguelike." rather than putting the time in to balance it.

Whether you enjoy this collection depends on whether you know what you're getting into. It's not all that great when judged just on the quality of its games, though that's not to say there's nothing good here. [i]Don't Look Back[/i] and [i]Mr. Platformer[/i] are really cool little platformers with some creative twists, and I love how inventive [i]At a Distance[/i] and [i]Naya's Quest[/i] still are after all this time. But as many other reviews will likely point out, the highlight is definitely [i]Grab Them by the Eyes[/i], which is just a really funny concept brought to life.

With that being said though, "fun concepts" is really all most of these games amount to. Even at their best, the games in this collection don't amount to more than 30-minute-long novelties, and many are incredibly basic or just straight-up gag games that won't even last 5 minutes. There's a few very simple arcadey games that might get you hooked, but otherwise a 5-hour play session will show you pretty much everything. And yeah, the fact that the majority of these games are readily available freeware doesn't help things; I could bring up the debut inclusion of one of Terry's oldest games and an unfinished game, but these are easily the worst games in the package because... well, they're old and unfinished. Bottom line is that if you're getting this collection just to see how good the games are then you'll probably come out disappointed.

The real value of this collection comes as a historical piece to showcase Terry's craft. You get a pretty wide variety of games spanning from his early years to just last year, and I think it's valuable for historians or even other indie developers to have this whole timeline of Terry's career at their fingertips, or just to see a bunch of really cool concepts that could inspire future works. And good lord would I like to see [i]At a Distance[/i] be fully realized into something.

Also, kudos has to go to the work that went into porting all of these games. It seems all too easy nowadays to just throw a bunch of Flash games into an aging Adobe AIR launcher and call it a day, but with this collection you can feel so much of the respect and passion that Terry has for his own history. Here we've got Flash games, Unity games, HTML5 games, and a QBasic game compiled and playable together with controller support, localization, no display issues (that I could find), and compatibility with all devices. Even the minute-long gag games feel like so much work was put into getting them to work properly. It's an unprecedented level of care for a collection of web games.

So if you're viewing this collection like any other game collection then it's a bit of a tough sell. If you're the kind of guy who likes particularly experimental games or just indie game history in general then you'll probably love it. And if you've played all these games before then now you get to do it with a controller, in pixel-perfect fullscreen, or from the comfort of your Steam Deck. As for me, I may have gotten myself addicted to [i]Maverick Bird[/i].

A very pretty game with not much going on under the surface. On the plus side - it's cheap, it's quick, and the cyber-deco-noir style is really beautiful. I wish more games looked like this. On the minus side - the story is basically non-existent, the city building is simple, and the achievement design is bad. 

The gameplay consists of being dealt a small hand of three cards that represent buildings you can put down and trying to keep four factions above water points-wise by building stuff that gives them more resources, making their buildings more efficient at generating resources, and balancing events so that nobody drops below zero. Every week everything gets more expensive and eventually you'll fail. At the end you get xp with the four factions and get more stuff added to your deck of buildings. None of this is bad, it's not particularly great either. I found myself wishing I was just playing a game like [i]Reus 2[/i], which takes this same idea and does it so much better. 

It took me about two hours to finish the "story" and another two hours to get all but one achievement. The final achievement requires you to get random events that let you give influence to the fifth faction that isn't represented on the board and only comes up every so often. I get the feeling I'll be playing as long again trying to get a run where I get the choice to give this faction enough influence for the achievements as it took me to do everything else put together at least. 

My other main criticism of the game is that for as simple as it is, it explains almost nothing. What is coming next in the faction level ups, why I get certain events and not others, what exactly all the game terms mean, the game just doesn't want to let you know (you can guess a lot of it, but it's annoying to have to). The sort of advanced planning that more interesting builders take advantage of to keep you engaged isn't really possible here given how little you know about what's coming and how much of what you can do is based on what you draw and what flips as you expand the map.

It's cheap and pretty and will keep you entertained for a few hours, so if you're looking for that it's a good choice. If you're looking for anything more than that I would look elsewhere.

Overall Review:
A fantastic productivity app that keeps me focused on tasks without the temptation of opening a browser and getting distracted. The built-in Pomodoro timer is a great addition, and for just $5, it's a solid deal. It also features a nice selection of chill music and a few extra features to make short breaks more enjoyable.

Pros:
✅ Relaxing music – Great for staying in the zone
✅ Pomodoro timer + alarm – Helps manage focus sessions
✅ Delivers on its promises – Simple yet effective
✅ Affordable – Only $5 for a productivity boost
✅ Customizable to-do lists – Keep track of tasks easily

Cons:
❌ Fish tank is too small – Feels like digital animal cruelty 🐠💔
❌ Music gets repetitive – More variety would be great
❌ Alarm volume issues – Not loud enough compared to the music, and there's no way to adjust it

Final Thoughts:
This app is a great tool for productivity, especially if you struggle with browser distractions. While the music and alarm system could use some tweaks, it's still a solid, budget-friendly choice for anyone looking to improve focus with the Pomodoro technique.

⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (4/5) – Would love some updates, but definitely worth it!

- I wished you could change the gender of the person you're studying with (though it'd kill the idea of Lofi Girl so I understand). 
- It'd be nice to have a bit more freedom when setting the time (you're locked at 90mins max) and have tasks over the week and not just daily. 
- I know there is only one 'activity' which is reading/writing at the table, and it would be awesome to have maybe a second one especially since you have so many other scenes available and of such variety (steampunk, ancient China, spaceship etc.) but again, I know it requires a lot of work.

Overall, a very great app that doesn't require anything from your PC, is perfect if you want to have a way to focus on your studying and gets you motivated to actually finish them, all for a fairly cheap price!
