[h3][i]NOTE: I’m writing this review while listening to the tracks from the app in question. It’s quite helpful, seeing that this is my first proper text in a long time.[/i][/h3] 

I came across [b]Chill Pulse[/b] by pure accident – it was recommended to me while I was considering the purchase of a similar tool called Spirit City: Lofi Sessions. What solidified my choice was the nice discount on the former, so, I clicked the Buy button and gave this new app a try. 

It’s worth mentioning that [b]Chill Pulse[/b] is my first experience with tools for focus and relaxation. I do use sounds of rain during some naps, but that’s a different thing, imho. I can’t honestly compare [b]Chill Pulse[/b] to other similar games/apps/tools due to the mentioned lack of experience, so my opinion in this review is based solely on what I got from introducing this one title to my daily life. Please, keep this in mind. 

Well, now, all the technicalities and boring stuff aside, let’s dive right into the review itself!

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3426204099

[h1]WHO IS IT FOR?[/h1]

Based on my research, focus-improving games and apps are an amazing tool for not only students, but also artists, stressed out office workers (and other people under the daily pressure of adulting), and even people who suffer from insomnia. In my case, I was looking for something to improve my time while drawing and working. Recently, it has been increasingly difficult to focus on either, and my usual methods – squishy stress toys, gallons of tea, motivational speeches in front of the mirror, crying under the blanket, and philosophical debates with my inner voice [i](a nasty little bugger)[/i] – didn’t really help, sadly.

I have tried using Lo-Fi channels on Youtube too, of course, but they grew stale at some point. I needed more motivation; something that would really make me focus while also not getting too distracting. Surprisingly, at least for me, [b]Chill Pulse[/b] turned out to be exactly what I was looking for. 

You see, this game-tool has one very nice feature: collecting things. And boy oh boy am I a hoarder by both nature and whatever those obsessions of mine can be called! So, an incentive to focus in the form of cute animals and clothes? Yes, please!

[b]Chill Pulse[/b] doesn’t offer a lot of stuff right now, which is a small downside, but what it already has is really good. If the developer continues updating their game, it will certainly continue shining like the little gem it is in the future. Plus, it’s inexpensive enough to justify the purchase to your inner miser.

[h1]WHY DO YOU NEED IT?[/h1]

If you’re struggling with focusing on stuff, just want something nice and relaxing to listen to in the background or need a personal diary, [b]Chill Pulse[/b] is a good solution. It offers several useful tools, including: 

[list]
[*] Pomodoro Timer;

[*] a To-Do list that you can fill in with tasks every day;

[*] a personal diary (actually, you can make several of them);

[*] a basic calendar;

[*] a collection of tracks in various genres (jazz, oriental music, vaporwave, lo-fi, classics, etc.), plus the ability to add your own music;

[*] an assortment of natural sounds – wind, rain, thunder, etc.;

[*] several scenes to use as background for your virtual girl;

[*] an opportunity to exchange messages with the said girl via inside phone tool – there is even a love story in the Chinese setting!

[*] a chat (can be disabled and doesn’t bother you with constant notifications) where you can talk with like-minded people;

[*] a letter exchange service that lets you write inspirational and kind messages to other users and receives some from them; 

[*] a bunch of items to collect (clothes, accessories, pets); 

[*] a little aquarium that provides you with not only adorable fish but also diamonds (the local currency);

[*] and some drinks to boost your leveling up and collecting. Drink terrifying amounts of tea together with your virtual buddy and get addicted together! 
[/list]

I think that’s all worth mentioning for now. If the developer adds anything interesting in the future, I’ll update this section.
Oh, and on a bit of sidenote: I also used [b]Chill Pulse[/b] during lessons with my students. They all loved the addition of background music and sounds of rain to our usual routine. Plus, it is very useful for aviation students specifically as they need extra noises to emulate their usual work places – the “extra difficulty mode”, as I call it :)  

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3426203874

[h1]WHAT DOES IT LOOK LIKE INSIDE?[/h1]

Chill Pulse is very easy to navigate and doesn’t overwhelm you with billions of buttons and menus. Everything is neat, the user interface is uncluttered and functional, and the overall design is very pleasing to the eye. I like the color palettes the most as every scene is vivid enough to be unique and memorable – perfect for setting the mood every day. 

There are no fancy looking elements like in some mode advanced games/tools/apps, but the generally simplistic design choices are actually a huge boon and not a downgrade. They make [b]Chill Pulse[/b] feel and look cozy, welcoming. It’s always pleasant to open this game and just look at it for several moments to unwind after a stressful moment.

Plus, there are no bugs*, freezes or anything that would distract you from focusing on what’s important. 

[i]* Hm, though, I still haven’t found a way to take screenshots in the game properly, and it seems that it is indeed some sort of a bug(-ish thingy), but at least it’s a miscellaneous one, so, yeah, not much of a bother (for me at least).[/i]

[h1]WHAT I’D LIKE TO SEE IN THE FUTURE[/h1]

Perhaps the ability to add radio stations or YouTube channels like Lo-Fi Girl? Or maybe an assortment of texts/audio books, too – maybe even ones written or recorded by the users themselves! I’m always eager to read a good story. 

I’d also like to see more music tracks and genres for the audio player. It’s easy to run out of things to listen to during long working and drawing hours, and my own music collection has honestly already become boring – I have been listening to most of it for years on a daily basis [i](plus, a big chunk of my stuff now is pretty heavy and dark…)[/i].  

[h1]WORTH IT?[/h1]

Being greeted by the stunning pixel art is motivation enough to fire up ChillPulse and begin a productivity session. The game presents the player with scenes to choose between, set in different locations and time periods, which allows the art to shine and makes sure the setting doesn't get samey or claustrophobic. The player can add their own personalisation by selecting an outfit and accessories for the protagonist as well as choosing a pet companion ^_^ New items are added pretty often in updates, the latest of which was snake-themed for the Lunar New Year!

Of course, being a focus tool, the productivity features are important. The essentials are here. ChillPulse provides a pomodoro timer and to-do list, along with the 'hub' that records your focus time each day and which tasks you completed. There are also post-it notes for quick scribbles and a journal. Sadly, the journal needs some attention from the developer. I haven't used it since I realised the formatting gets messed up for saved entries and the only way to scroll is using the arrow keys. This may well get fixed though! The developer is still actively working on ChillPulse.

The music and ambient sounds are also important in productivity tools. This game has a few sound effects, like a fireplace, plus weather effects that add both the corresponding audio and visuals. The selection of tracks on offer is also better than I realised! It took me far too long to notice that there are several genres to choose between, not just lofi. You have to expand the track listing and then click on the music note to see all the available genres. There is a playlist to match each scene <3

There are two extra features that I absolutely adore: the drink making and the love stories. Each setting has its own collection of drinks and the player has the joy of mixing together the available ingredients to discover the full menu. Each setting also has its own romance that plays out between the protagonist and Her. Gradually learning more about their developing relationship is the most cute, heartwarming little reward to keep you motivated between timers.

ChillPulse pretty much has it all! You'll find gorgeous visuals, an excellent variety of music, solid productivity features and enough character to keep you coming back.

Interactive fiction / walking simulators / strollplayers appeal to a certain type of person; if you enjoy games in that particular niche, I think you'll find [i]The Haunting of Joni Evers[/i] to be a worthwhile journey.  I certainly did.

Games like this succeed when they invite you into a believable, well-crafted world, then immerse you in that world with strong characters and a story that entertains and satisfies throughout.  Joni's story is thoughtfully crafted, features solid writing (performed [i]note-perfectly[/i] by its voice cast), and is supported by lots of specific details throughout the house and the atmosphere created by the audio design.  Getting to know her and her history was a delight as an understanding of her relationships with other characters unfolded and developed greater depth right when it felt like they should.

Certain supernatural elements appear early on (which might initially challenge your immersion in the story), but the ways they appear and the reasons for those choices start to make sense as the story builds toward its climax in a satisfying sequence where the player's involvement [i]feels important[/i] and your emotional investment in the characters pays off nicely.

With the amount of careful attention Causeway Studios has given to realizing its characters, their relationships, and the story they have to tell, I can't wait to see what story the team tells next!

I LOVE THIS GAME!  The atmosphere and the game play just feel unique and I find myself returning to it constantly.  I typically loathe games that have a grind to them.  However, this game is all about the grind, and because of that, the mechanics fit.  You're not the hero.  You're just trying to survive and help your small underground community survive.

So Why Don't I Recommend It (Yet)?
You may be thinking that it's the water death system.  Most everyone points this out as the big culprit of why the game just isn't good.  But the truth is, there are ways to work around the water death system.  If you don't mind doing one water run a day (that takes 5 minutes of your time) then it's not a factor.  Don't let the water death discussions push you off of this game.  It's not that bad.

The Real Reason I Can't Recommend It.
Spawns.  The game has a certain rogue like element, especially with weapon attachments which greatly enhance your survival but are often hard to find.  Because leveling up weapons takes a great deal of grind, the best way to gain attachments is through exploring the world, but the good attachments drop rarely.  When you die, you lose the gun and its attachments.  Considering the game is designed to be hard with a "high risk/high reward" design, I find this to be fair.  What I don't find fair is the spawning system.  Imagine you turn right to see down a corridor and confirm it's clear of enemies.  You turn around to find a Euruskan patrol is about to pass you by, so you move slightly to cover.  Suddenly you're being shot in the back.  Not ten feet away from you is a patrol of ten Eurasian cyborgs in that corridor you cleared moments earlier.  What happened?  Well, they spawned on top of you.  But now you have two sets of enemies to deal with and no escape.  You're dead, and you just lost all of your loot.  This scenario has happened more than once to me and is infuriating.  You can also see it happen to YouTubers so it's a confirmed issue.  Losing your hard work and rare attachments because you got spawn blasted just sours the game.  I'll keep playing it, but it's hard to recommend in this state.

Conclusion?
Once they fix the spawn issue, this is a definite recommendation!  But until then, I think most people will find it more frustrating than it's worth.  I know the game is still in development, so I look forward to this fix so I can change my recommendation to a YES.

It should be said right off the start that this game does not and will not respect your time, especially if you are an adult and have responsibilities. This is reference to the Water System, which depletes in real-time regardless of anything. Failure to keep your water reserves filled results a wipe of all of your progress, which is frustrating to say the least for someone who would love to enjoy this game casually and an absolute deal-breaker at worst for anyone who remotely wants to play other games or take breaks.

And this game is hard. You WILL die, and quickly if you're lucky. Anything you take with you will be lost to the wastes.

I should say that The Forever Winter reminds me so much of Escape from Tarkov both in game style and scope that I don't particularly mind the more difficult aspects of the game. At least Fun Dog Studios is open about what they want and make clear videos about the direction they want to go for. I don't blame them for the Water System being hard. Some games are and should be difficult - they just haven't found the balance yet. If you're interested in the game but on the fence, at least subscribe to their YT channel. I had before buying this game just because their candid attitude is refreshing in the current gaming age.

That being said... I really like this game. It is janky to say the least right now but the scale of the depressive nature of the environment makes the 40k fan in me giggle in delight. I've held my breath as AI gods of war have duked it out less than 200 feet from me, praying that I can make it out with my precious water. This game doesn't just drip theme. It let's it out in an unending monsoon of uncaring, dystopian warfare and bleak existence. There is something so beautifully horrifying about watching robotic bombers drop their payloads of cyborgs into trenches so full of blood, oil, and detritus that my mind literally can't call it water. And everything fights each other. The maps are either alive with roaring gunfire or the soft whisper of the dead on ashen winds. Silence is a rarity and when it is quiet is when the game is sometimes at its most dreadful. To me, the world is the best part of the entire game. On that alone I think TFW deserves a comic or animated series.

And it is violently punishing to say the least. I've died in hails of explosive gunfire before my brain can pick a point to flee to. The gunplay is okay, not overly enjoyable but I suppose it isn't designed to be. Guns are tools meant to aid the acquisition of things to take from the dead to give to the living. Our characters are rats in the grand scheme of things, nothing more. Our armor is our wits and the best weapon is knowing what and when to fight something while 20+ enemies duke it out all around you. Seeing soldiers fight in the distance is great but very clearly needs some work. I've watched AI driven combat tanks fly through the air like Tony Hawk before landing on a bunker to become the King of Turrets or watched enemy patrols walk into each other for a good few moments before realizing who is who. 

But that's okay. 
It is A LOT and that Fun Dog Studios got it to where it is now with this game is impressive to say the least. It's a big game at 104gb and the maps reflect that. I hope this game gets to a 1.0 where the AI is more fleshed out and new, horrifying creatures of war prowl the trenches or streets of dead landscapes.

In the end, if you are NOT willing to put time in at least a few hours a week, don't think a punishing game is worth it, or just don't like jank - hold off or just don't buy the game. If you are a fan of Trench Crusade, the worst parts of Warhammer 40k, or simply love a punishing scavenger sim that makes you wonder why anyone would try to continue to exist in an apocalyptic world locked in never-ending war, give it a go. This may be the game for you.

Finally an extraction shooter with no PVP! In The Forever Winter you play the roll of a Scav trying to eek out the necessities in a war torn world with a fantastic aesthetic. Though currently in early access the game has several maps to explore and re-explore, with encounters being different between each run. Like other extraction shooters, you loose your loot and whatever you brought into a run if you die -  however the mechanics are not as punishing as Tarkov or similar games. 

Now - the water system, which has turned off many prospective players, has been updated in late 2024 to be more forgiving. You must collect water to survive, and it drains in real time, whether you log on or not. If you run out of water you must fight a battle to save your base and your stash. If you loose, your base and stash are reset. You do not however lose character progression however, as some have claimed. You can insure some of your gear and cash against this even by using a special secret stash in your base to preserve your most prized gear in the event of a water wipe. 

Though still in early access this game is a lot of fun and very promising. The biggest parts that need work are the water system - which could benefit from doping the real-time drain, and the enemy AI which is unpredictable and very janky.

Good game even though it is in early early access. 
the gameplay loop is very satisfying, the risk to reward ratio makes it worth it. The game is sufficiently difficult that it feels like an achievement everytime you have a good run. But not too difficult that you get frustrated. And given that we are in early early access the gameplay will only get better. And as of right now the gameplay is better than most completed games i have played.
Maps are very well designed, and beautiful in a grim dark way. This is what  warhammer would look like if the world was dead broke and recovering from doomsday, while the major global powers continue to wage war against each other and the rest of humanity are refugees. 
An innovation that i have not seen in other games that i have played is that the warring factions, actually prioritize fighting each other over you. In fact a common escape tactic is to lead your pursuers to their enemies and let them duke it out. 
Moreover every time you enter the same map the run is not the same. 
Enemy patrols most of the time follow the same routes until they shock you and don't. For example i had figured out a safe route in the Ashen Mesa map and used it a dozen times with no hiccups. Then yesterday as i was approaching the final bridge leading to the exit what did i find? 
A 12 foot tall exo-skeleton guarding the bridge. I spent a nail biting 5 minutes trying to get past it. Phew!

Another aspect that makes each run different is that even if the patrol routes are the same, the opponents change. Sometimes you will run into light infantry fighting cyborgs, the next time a 40 meter tall mech fighting drones, or the next time a squadron of tanks taking on Exo-skeletons. And there is a lot of variety amongst the enemies.
Thirdly, items are also different each run, in the sense that spawn for containers will change, and spawns for items within those containers are different every time. Sometimes water spawns, other times explosives spawn.
The result is that no two runs are alike.

The mission you get have sufficient variety, although i am sure there will be more. Missions might require you to assassinate a certain target, recover components from certain enemy types, recover certain items in certain areas, extract from certain maps, or kill certain types of enemies, access particular parts of a base and do something there like deliver repair parts of a mech. 
The  rewards are varrying rewards.  But bear in mind Mission rewards are not great, think of them as a bonus for your run, but understand that  most of the money you will make will be through scavenging. Which makes sense since you are a scavenger.
The game does involve base building, you have a hideout, and you can spend credits and water to upgrade them. From building crafting tables to turrets to protect your base from thieves that will steal your water. The options for base building are at present limited. But once again this is an early early access game so expect that to change. 
The result of all the above mentioned gameplay mechanics  is that you genuinely feel like life is a struggle in this post apocalyptic world. 
This is not a game for people searching for Power Fantasies, this is a game for people yearning for a true taste of how difficult life will be in a post apocalytpic world.
Neverthlees, I would recommend that you wait for a few more updates before buying, not because of any issue. But all the maps in the game are not yet accessible, and certain maps balances are still being implemented. Thus some are easy while others are a nightmare. I believe this is the case because they are still determining what enemy types to put in which places.
So put it on your wish list, and wait till may. By then the issues i pointed out above should be resolved.

The Forever Winter – We Are the Buried

Some games entertain. Some challenge. The Forever Winter devours you.

You are small. Insignificant. The world belongs to giants—war machines locked in an endless struggle, oblivious to your desperate existence. You scurry through the ruins, like the first mammals darting between the towering legs of dinosaurs, hoping they are too busy killing each other to notice you stealing scraps from their war.

The game does not explain itself. It is not here to comfort you. It leaves you with questions—Who fights this war? How long has it lasted? What are we, in the eyes of the titans? Like all great science fiction, The Forever Winter does not hand you answers. It forces you to wonder.

Stealth is not just an option. It is law. You crawl, you hold your breath, you listen to the distant roar of machines, praying their sensors do not sweep your way. Confrontation is a death sentence. You are not a soldier. You are a scavenger, a survivor, a shadow among gods.

Some complain about water. They miss the point. The war does not care about their comfort. The war does not care about you at all.

The lore is a whisper, the details meticulous. The world feels real in a way few games ever achieve. There is no safety, only the illusion of it. Every step into the unknown is a gamble. Every moment of survival is earned. And somehow, you keep coming back.

This is not just a game. This is a vision—one that echoes our own uncertain future, where survival is not a right, but a fleeting privilege.

Play it. If you dare.

An interesting blend of legally-distinct beyblade, platforming and a collectathon. The tone is charming and the world is quaint and full of secrets to find. There's a variety of gear and customization items to acquire. The music and sound help fill out the mysterious setting, and the writing is pretty humorous too.

If I had one complaint, its that the platforming has several quirks to it. Your overworld movement is grid based. You can jump after moving to carry your momentum forward. Which is fine, but sometimes you need to jump up to a block you should be able to reach, so you have to jump and then move, or wall-kick - techniques which become increasingly more demanding as the floors grow in complexity. I wish these controls were a bit more refined, or the jumps a bit more forgiving, but there seems to be no penalty for falling into a pit so its not too punishing.

I imagine this is the sort of game that would be immensely fun in group or co-operative play. I can't speak to that yet, but I can recommend it to folks looking for thrilling combat and a quaint albeit mysterious world to explore.

While I got hooked into both the biggest hurdle is definitely the platforming, which involves understanding how to take advantage of the fact that wall-kicking resets coyote time and fighting some fairly narrow input windows to make those tricks work. But ultimately I found it satisfying once it clicked for me what each challenge was demanding.

My only disappointment is that I would loved to have seen more experimentation with the combat. It's the kind of fun that makes me wish it had absurd optional challenges in the same way the platforming does.

This is a full recommendation if both modes of gameplay sound appealing to you.

As Fleximan, you take on the role of a vigilante superhero who has one mission: to take down all the traffic devices that make life harder for drivers. Armed with only your trusty hose, you'll mercilessly saw off speed cameras, road cameras, parking meters, and even speed humps. The gameplay is absurdly simple, but oddly satisfying as you destroy these everyday road annoyances.

However, there's a catch. The traffic police are out there, watching for any signs of rebellion, and they won’t hesitate to chase you down and throw you in jail. The squad car, which patrols the area, makes no sound, so it can sneak up on you when you least expect it, adding a bit of tension to the otherwise chaotic action. One moment, you’re happily sawing away, and the next, you’re running for your life, hoping you can escape before getting caught.

It’s a short, fun game that doesn’t take itself too seriously, and while it’s not a long-lasting experience, it’s definitely a bizarre and amusing one. If you're looking for something that’s quirky, silly, and doesn’t demand too much thought, "Fleximan" fits the bill perfectly.

The premise is straightforward: You take care of an unknown, seemingly amnestic girl whom you stop from committing suicide. Depending on her attitude towards you, the living conditions in your apartment or her stress levels, she may try to take her life again. The game revolves around you trying to discover her background while keeping her from harming herself. You do this by buying food and books for her, purchasing furniture for your room, interacting with her either by talking about what she is currently doing or playing a console game with her. 

The world map has several locations, though most serve only their purpose in few specific routes – your trips will mainly be to the convenience store, the pawn shop and the aquarium. 

You enter a route by choosing specific options in the context menu (such as selecting 'investigate' at the police department), exploring the mountain, purchasing a specific piece of furniture or a set of furniture, having her stats above a certain level or a combination of the above. 

Now, some routes can be obvious in regards what to do next, as they disable interactions that were previously available (like at the aforementioned police department), or explicitly tell you what you should do next. Others, on the other hand, might require a little bit of experimentation to reach and complete.

The game has around 20 endings. Completing at least one unlocks NG+ options that can either increase the difficulty or make the game easier. This also adds the credit CG for that ending to the gallery. The gallery also serves the purpose of giving a hint on how to reach each ending. However, as I already mentioned, some routes are not as straightforward as others, and the hint may not be enough to reach an ending.

One of my gripes is that the locations on the map feel underused. There are locations like the park or the creek, but they serve no purpose except in an ending or two. Why can’t we go on a picnic, or take a hike to the top of the mountain? Options like these would make the game feel more open.

I really enjoy the visuals and the style this game went with. The music, while simple, complements the overall PC-98 aesthetic that the game aims to emulate. Each ending that I reached was interesting, though it was obvious that some had more effort put into them than others.

[i]Hidden in my Paradise[/i] is a unique take on hidden object games. It includes decorating, completing missions and creating your own hidden object maps for others to play. 

[h2][u]Gameplay & Features[/u][/h2]

Settings include; audio controls, language, cursor speed and an explanation of the controls for keyboard & mouse. 

If you wish to put your game into windowed mode, put [i]-screen-width 1920 -screen-height 1080[/i] (or a resolution of your choice) under properties in the games Steam library page under launch options and relaunch the game. Then after relaunch just hit alt+enter for it to resize. 

Gameplay is divided up into three parts per level. Recreating snapshots (items can be dragged and moved around to create each picture), a hidden object component and finding hidden fairies. Hidden fairies will show sparkles around certain objects, moving the object will reveal the fairy. 

[u]Highlights[/u]

* Earn coins by playing and rating online levels. 
* Buy decorations in the in-game shop with your earned coins to decorate and create your own hidden object levels. 
* Decorations for every theme; forest, city, beach and farm. Plus seasonal decor. 
* Earn tickets in each level (called paradises) to play the Gacha machine in the shop-one ball gives you lots of cool decorations. There is a gacha machine full of prizes for each theme. 
* You can change the time of day at any time (day, night or sunset). 
* You can change filters of each level by clicking the colour wheel icon on the top left. Choose between a variety of filters including black and white, solid colour, contrast and much more. 
* Search around for treasure chests to open for coins and pet all the animals in each level for coins too! 
* When you're finished playing the main levels go into “extra levels”, here you will find seasonal levels for Halloween and Christmas. 

[h2][u]Overall Experience[/u][/h2]

This game is unique and offers so much more than just your standard hidden object game. Everything is interactive and can be moved (which is necessary to recreate the snapshots). The art is hand-drawn with some cute cartoon characters. What also sets it apart is the sandbox mode where you can create your own levels and share them for others to play. You can rate others' levels too (which you need to do for an achievement). 

There is a bit of a grind element to this game however to earn enough coins and tickets to buy all the decor from the store and get all the gacha prizes for each theme. 

This game offers hours of wholesome fun for everyone to enjoy. And a lot of other players have uploaded some really nice levels (I especially enjoy the winter ones)! 💗

**[i] At the time of my review I have not finished the game, only the first theme (forest). There is so much content in this game I wanted to get my review out so if others were interested they could nab it for the Winter Sale price! [/i] **

It's really nice passive life, reminds me of interactive screensavers in the 90s. TL:DR, it's charming but it has some really odd design decisions that make building  and planning more of a pain in the a** than it needs to be.

Some issues that I initially thought were bugs that the developer pointed out to be some counter intuitive zoning rules. You can zone an entire house for your little dudes, or try zoning bedrooms for a 'roomate' setup.

The problem is alot of furniture REQUIRES a zone by default. If you want to build a roommate house you have to choose specific furniture that doesn't require a zone, and it looks like most of the zoning agnostic furniture is low tier stuff that won't fill your dude's needs as efficiently.

Some other design features I don't agree with is you'd expect a painter career and a painter easel to be placeable outside, but alot of the career items like paint cans can only be placed indoors, these kinds of weird design decisions make planning a satisfying living space more complicated than it needs to be.

Tl;dr:
This game is an instant classic, and I highly recommend it, especially at the $5.99 price tag.


[h1]Full Review:[/h1]
I'll be honest, I "borrowed" the game first because I've been burnt by these types of "Micro-games" before that just don't feel complete, or they aren't as interactive as you expected, or they just don't work as they should, etc.
After only a couple of hours passively playing, I knew this was not the case with this game, and immediately bought it. 

It's charming, extremely aesthetically pleasing, genuinely fun, and a GREAT second monitor game. 
Honestly, it's a breath of fresh air compared to some of these other idle, casual, passive type games. 

The developer has been releasing updates like a mad-man, and I'm super excited to see the improvements to come!

All of that being said, there are some improvements I'd love to see:
[list]
[*]Foreground Items - Like chairs and stuff, I'd love to be able to place a desk chair in front of a desk, pet beds and bowls would be nice too, they take up a lot of floor space. 
[*]Customize Characters - Change the looks and clothes of the people
[*]A Fullscreen Mode - It could be a combination of the vertical and horizontal modes currently available, allowing expansion in both directions!
[*]Pomodoro Technique Timer?? - A built in timer for work/break schedules. Most people use 25 minute intervals, but a custom timer would be awesome! It could be night during work time, and day during a break. 
[*]Workshop Support! - For custom items, professions, etc.
[/list]

love it.. its perfect... 10/10.. great for running while working on things or doing something mundane or even to overlay next to online games, has worked perfectly so far and yeah is just great <3 and its super cute :3

Different well thought out modes and camera options so you can put the overlay pretty much where ever it works best for you inc a small camera window thats really awesome.. and hotkeys to quickly switch views.
The Play modes; city or the regular one so you can either build and view it in landscape across the screen or in City mode (the one i've been using) building up like a tower or apartment block so it takes up the edge of your screen.. 
Ability to click on and off the game as it works as an overlay so you can seamlessly go between whatever your working on and Little Life, yet your still able to alt tab if needs be.. and it even has quick press buttons to smoosh the games display so u can see more of your screen at the press of a button and then back to the normal view by pressing it again (This is top notch, well thought out and fantastically useful)..

Pros: A simple game that you can either play actively or just let happen in the background or at the bottom of your screen. It is a game where you recruit/invite tiny people to live on your screen and your goal is to help them fulfill their dreams and live their tiny lives to the fullest. It is easy to play, just buy stuff for your tiny inhabitants, build living quarters, and make them happy.

Cons: (Note: This game was just released, and is being worked upon so what I say here may hopefully be irrelevant in the future.) The interface is a bit wonky for me, and the main menu has some sort of standard setting that meant that I couldn't even see what stuff was. After clicking around a bit I mamaged to get a zoomed in view where I could see/read, but then in some submenus some info was obscured by the UI due to (I guess) scaling issues. Sidescrolling is done (at the point in time when I'm writing this) with arrow keys or by grabbing and sliding with the mouse, and not by WASD as I would have liked. A largely mouse operated game where you have to use the arrow keys would work OK if you are lefthanded. I am not lefthanded. Not being able to (again, when I write this) rebind keys is kinda low level frustrating, BUT it IS a game still being worked on so I have hopes about that.

If you like RPGs and fishing minigames, you'll love [i]Sea Fantasy[/i]: [b]Easy 9/10[/b]

[h3]General Play[/h3]

I'm a sucker for fishing mechanics in games, so I've seen quite a few different versions implemented across genres. This is by FAR my favorite. There are enough varying gimmicks to keep it from getting stale, but they're never frustrating or so complicated that you can't figure them out after seeing them once or twice. On the contrary, it's great every time I encounter a new way for fish to fight back, iand so is catching them after I understand what they're doing. Whenever I think I've seen everything, the next sea monster throws something new at me that's always a pleasant surprise. It's interesting enough to keep pulling me forward, but forgiving enough to strike that balance between challenging and chill.

The game is very charitable with the ability to reseed spawns by quickly casting and cancelling, so it's easy to farm for a specific target if you want to. Losing combat also just causes you to respawn close to the same spot with partial health, so the only real penalty is losing whatever spawn you were battling and having to try and fish it up again. I'm never annoyed when it happens and it has yet to interfere with my fun.

[h3]Primary Mechanics[/h3]

The variety of creatures has more depth than you might expect (no pun intended); the game does a fair job of tracking valuable info when you encounter them, although there's some room for improvement. Spawn times and primary locations are recorded the first time you hook something, whether you successfully catch it or not, along with the materials it drops, your record for largest caught, and a short blurb about the creature itself. I'd personally like to see one or two other details (like HP so you can recognize the spawn more easily, since any given mob always has the same stats), but you do get more than enough to help you relocate targets later or know what you should be fishing up for crafting.

The crafting system is simple and straightforward, but effective, and money isn't really a problem after you get going past the prologue (especially if, like me, you're insistently fishing to catch a king-sized version of every local beastie before moving on to the next area). I'd say there's a little more randomness than I usually like when making your own hooks, but honestly it's not really an obstacle; you'll do enough fishing in the course of regular play to have plenty of materials on hand so you can spam crafting when you need an upgrade.

Speaking of upgrades, this is definitely one of those games where it feels like every point matters—not in the sense that you need to min-max your build to succeed, but rather that you'll immediately feel a positive difference each time you improve a stat. In turn, that means it's great whenever you find or make a new rod, hook, or outfit and when you level up, since a couple of points can suddenly mean that one stubborn mob you previously couldn't catch is now within reach.

Probably my favorite thing the game has thrown at me is the unexpected variety of play modes, jumping from simple fishing to fishing against mobs with fun special abilities, then two-stage boss battles with actual combat before the fishing, and then side-scrolling sections with monsters and puzzles and nothing to even do with fishing. There aren't many dungeons like that, but it's also a fairly small game, and they're rewarding because you get a new ability (like the [i]Zelda[/i]-style power to lift heavy objects) at the conclusion of each one. I absolutely did not go into [i]Sea Fantasy[/i] thinking I'd be platforming or dodging obstacles on a race course, and I love it.

[h3]Plot/Story[/h3]

The story is uncomplicated and holds the game together as much as it needs to, giving you a chance to feel like you're accomplishing something heroic without being overbearing. This is where the RPG stuff most visibly takes a backseat to the fishing mechanics, but I don't mind one bit; I'm allowed to fish as much as I want, whenever and wherever I want, and the plot is there when I choose to get back to it without feeling like I've lost the thread or forgotten some crucial bit of lore. In this sense, I think it's very much like a classic [i]Pokemon[/i] title in the best way: The focus is appropriately on the collectathon, and everything else is mostly there to prop up those elements and help explain why you're doing so much fishing. When I finally get around to the next boss fight, it feels rewarding to win and the game kindly reminds me of why I just did that and where I'm supposed to go next, then lets me have my way again.

[h3]Quality of Life[/h3]

The devs obviously have a lot of love for this game and have been working nonstop to address bugs and add quality of life improvements since release: Translation errors, little things like camera movement and targeting control, etc. Honestly, the only criticism I have is that, outside the main story, the individual sea creatures don't feel like they have enough impact or presence except for the joy of filling out your bestiary. That's perfectly fine on its own, but in addition to materials having stat ranges when used in crafting, I'd love to see a couple of things like unique hooks or bait with special abilities that can only be made from the drops of certain mobs, giving you a second reason to seek them out besides checking them off your list. Catching the king-sized version of each creature feels like an achievement, but it would be really cool if perhaps, in addition to the common and rare materials already present, there were extra-rare drops that only came from king-sized specimens of a given species. That would add more purpose to hunting for them beyond prestige, and help to balance out the fact that "rare" drops don't really feel that uncommon, even with relatively low Luck.

The various fishing rods already do a decent job of diversifying your arsenal, but most of them only feature varying stat configurations versus the handful with an ability that actually alters gameplay (like slowing down your targeting bar or negating certain opponent gimmicks). That's not a criticism by itself, but rather to demonstrate how there's room left for additional content and new mechanics in an already-good game—tacking a little something extra onto concepts that are already present would add a lot of value to those concepts and better highlight them as things that can be fun if the player chooses to prioritize them or make them important.

In a way, this is already done with sidequests: Exploration is absolutely rewarded, with little prizes and encounters waiting for you in out-of-the-way places, randomized pickups and new tools (like a creature detector) providing at least some incentive to revisit prior locations, and some metroidvania/[i]Zelda[/i]-style doubling back when you unlock new abilities. There's a more than reasonable number of things to do in a game this size that aren't required for progression, which is nice.

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]

If you made it this far, I'll wrap by saying that it's a steal at full price ($15USD) and easily worth at least $5USD more than they're charging for it, given the content and the amount of fun I've had already. The soundtrack is limited but charming, the gameplay is entertaining and more challenging than you'd think without being obtuse or overly complex, and the world has a lot of color and personality even without extensive lore dumps. There's room for [i]growth[/i], but not too terribly much room for [i]improvement[/i], if that makes sense. I'm already hoping for a sequel, or at least another game that takes what [i]Sea Fantasy[/i] is doing right and builds onto it.

Not sure if it qualifies as the currently-going definition of a "cozy" game, but it's certainly my kind of chill and an easy recommend.

[h3]Verdict[/h3]

9/10, please support the devs and give it a try!

A friend and I raced this game blind and we both loved it! My experience is with the harder ‘kaizo’ difficulty as we did not play the normal mode.

The game had great music, great visuals and very nice linear difficulty. It was tough, but a fun tough that felt fair (except a sneaky surprise on the final platforming level, hehehe). Some of the ‘whomp’ esque enemies felt a little unreadable first play through, but the quick respawning makes this not an issue. The first phase of the final boss had unintuitively designed animations with regards to when they were lethal, but otherwise there were no graphical quirks.

The game does, unfortunately, suffer from a few glaring faults that for some people might be deal breakers, I’ll list them in order of most egregious to least egregious.

1) There is an incredibly confusing, and definitely unintended, “feature” where holding slightly up/down when moving the stick left or right makes you go in the opposite direction. We tested a few controllers before realising it was the game, and not a ‘Snap Back’ issue of the stick. Given this game is essentially a kaizo it would spell out death to suddenly go the wrong way. This probably cost me about 15–20 deaths in total, so not substantial but it was annoying whenever it happened. Although this number is probably much lower due to us solving the root cause (the angled directions). Might be some sort of dead zone issue that the dev fixed but for the wrong directions. (This is probably worsen by the fact that dpad outright does not work for the game)

2) The controls in game do not match any of the graphical guides for them. It tells you jump is lower face button, but it is side. It tells you spin is side face button, but is top. Once this is worked out it isn’t an issue, but still a rather weird bug.

3) The main menu is outright broken. If you use a dpad it inverts your directional input, and keyboard seems to function weirdly. Keyboard as a whole didn’t seem to meld well for the game so my friend ended up playing with controller when he never usually does.

I had a blast even with these issues, but the first is definitely gonna be a deal breaker for many.

Buckshot Roulette... or as I like to call it, Backshot Roulette. That’s exactly how you’ll feel when your entire friend group takes turns unloading shotgun blasts into you, one after another, while they skip your turn six times in a row. But hey, I’m not jaded, you are! It’s all part of the chaotic fun, right?

Singleplayer – While it's a short experience, the singleplayer mode is surprisingly sweet and satisfying. I won’t dive into "Double or Nothing" just yet, but the gameplay is engaging. The items offer some intriguing mechanics, from enhancing yourself with questionable substances to receiving cryptic calls from your unsettling Uncle Roger, who hints at which round is live or a blank. It all adds a layer of fun and unpredictability.

OST – The soundtrack is absolutely fantastic. Even if there weren't an achievement to "soak it in," I’d still relish the chance to immerse myself in the club’s electrifying music. It’s just that good.

Double or Nothing – After finishing the main story, you unlock "Double or Nothing," which is essentially an endless mode. True to its name, it’s a high-stakes challenge where you can lose it all or double your winnings. That said, once you’ve completed the story, there’s not much reason to return to it outside of achievements. The core gameplay is largely the same, with the main difference being the added difficulty from reduced health.

Multiplayer – The multiplayer mode really stands out. Connection issues are rare, and global matchmaking is a nice feature. However, don’t expect to always have a full game with random players—many tend to leave early, whether after a quick death or losing a round. For the best experience, it’s definitely recommended to play with friends.

Overall – It’s a fun game with a unique novelty and an enjoyable experience, but ultimately, it doesn’t offer much long-term engagement for me. It’s definitely worth playing through at least once, but after that, it may not hold your attention for too long.

Introducing...the single most nerve-racking game you'll likely ever play. 

Have you ever wondered what it would be like to appear in that classic scene from The Deer Hunter where DeNiro and Walken are forced into a game of death against one another? No? Well, too bad for you because that is EXACTLY what Buckshot Roulette is all about. 

Those looking for a story need not apply. The premise is simple: You randomly wake up on the floor of a night club toilet. Upon exit, you discover that the door at the end of the catwalk opens out into a windowless room where a hideous Dealer coerces you into gambling with the ultimate prize...your life. 

The game itself is a pretty straight-forward affair. You and your host take turns to point and click with the....equipment...until one of you has lost all of their lives. There are a selection of debuffs and perks available as well to spice things up, though ultimately that is what is on offer here. Not the most complex game in the world but definitely one that will keep you on the edge of your seat. In terms of duration, the main game seems a little brief, albeit with infinite replay value, though the possibility of multiplayer should add an interesting extra dynamic as well. 

That's all there really is to say about Buck Shot Roulette really. Not the best game in the world but it should give you a thrilling experience if you'd like a break from the norm. Care to give it a shot? - 3/5 stars

TL;DR: a relaxing puzzle game, with the caveat that some of the rules on on placing rail pieces is not always clear or logically consistent. 

This is a one of the most laid back games I ever played, while still being mentally engaging. The pastel colors and light, ambient soundtrack make for an enjoyable game, especially at the end of a stressful day. So far, all but the first couple puzzles add additional inhabitants after connecting the first inhabitant, so the goals can shift within any given puzzle. Controls are simple, and the game is tiny. It boots almost instantly and runs well on even my most low-powered computer, a 4th gen i5 Dell laptop with integrated graphics. My everyday/everything-not-work-or-graphics computer is an 8th gen i9, and the performance monitor doesn't even register any noticeable resource consumption. 

My only complaint is that the rules for placing rail pieces don't always seem logically consistent. There seems to be a continual learning curve on how players can apply rails in any given puzzle. I am going to give Polygon Matter the benefit of the doubt here and assume that dynamic rules are an intentional part of the puzzles. Regardless, I still enjoy this game very much and think it is an excellent value.

[h2]I'm sorry but you get a BIG VOXEL NO from me[/h2]
This game had it EASY in my eyes. You take the voxel style and slap it onto a sort of reverse bullet hell shooter a la Vampire Survivors. Then shove as much rogue lite/like elements and abilities into it as you can! Do it well and it should be PRINTING you money.

Voxel Hunters does not do this well. THIS FULLY RELEASED GAME has so little to show.
It's lacking so much style outside of the Voxel Hunters themselves and their Voxel Enemies.
There are more details on the SHIP that players might never see than there is in the PLANET MAP. Which is actually just a small Square.

See Time Warpers on how to use Voxel in a more interesting and varied way.

"Assemble your squad. Calibrate your gear."
There is no one to play with in a squad. There is nothing to "Calibrate" for my gear. All these little taglines on the store page are nonsense.

[h3]The Menus?[/h3]
They're basic and plane. No style or anything Voxel to look at. It's a see through box on top of pixel style of outer space.
The game name is in some sort of weird font that gives it a slight style but ultimately is just as bland as everything else.

Starting a Session dumps you into what seems like a Planet selection menu with no real knowledge of what to do next or why it looks so barren. You have 2 Planets to choose from and the first one in the center of the screen is Sol Invictus which... Does nothing. Is this a Planet or a Star? It's got heavy "That's no moon!" vibes to it. Your REAL option is to choose the other planet on the left, Aeagrus. Which is a neatly animated pixel planet but is also... not Voxel like the floating Voxel Hunter next to it.

After selecting Aeagrus as your planet of NO CHOICE... you're greeted by this new Menu screen which is your everything screen as it's your Hunter Selection, Character Customization, Character Upgrades, Character Info. Weapon Selection, Weapon Customization AND Details (Of which is actually PLANET DETAILS or MISSION BRIEFING)

The UPGRADES Menu has a damn SCROLL BAR for it. YOU HAVE SO MUCH SCREEN REAL ESTATE and made all the info as if my monitor is 600x900. Why is everything so HUGE? Why is everything contained in large boxes If it's just a +10%? Look at how Vampire Survivors did the Upgrade menu, it's a Box with an Icon on it, you click it and information is displayed within another area. This method allows you to fit MORE onto the screen at one time. It also limits the need for scroll bars until you have enough upgrades to spend into.

OPENING THE PAUSE MENU when playing in SOLO PLAYER MODE does absolutely NOTHING to pause the action. So you can die while trying to adjust volume settings.

Things like Character Information and Stats are in either different selectable menus or a weird toggle and they literally just could've been shown on the same screen.

Being able to Color your Voxel Hunters and their Weaponry in whatever choice of colors you want is a great addition. However, the way rotating them around is with the Mouse seems to boarder on the insanely annoying as it they can be rotated in any direction or axis with no reset even if you switch characters. I had my Voxel Hunter stuck at a weird angle which made it annoying to color.

[h3]The Enemies?[/h3]
They either rush head first towards you at insane speeds or attack you from a distance with a Wildstar style grey attack outline. Every enemy from 1 second in to 4+ minutes in are basically the same AI wise. They are constantly winding up for attacks to the point where they overlap each other and with your limited Dodge Rolling, Movement Speed and Fire Rate... you just end up getting hit.

Why do they not slowly come into frame and make their way towards the Hunter? Like, seriously, WHY are they so aggressively fast from the get go?
Why are they not really animated at all? They have a sort of wiggle or squish effect visually but they don't really do anything other than that for the most part.

I honestly can't even tell you if there are Elite enemy types or bosses as everything I've seen besides the Insta-Kill Tremor guy are just more of the same with a different appearance on them.

[h3]The UI?[/h3]
These are just a series of boxes that either scream PLACEHOLDER or are so Minimalist it hurts.
I do not like how the 100/100 sits at the left of the HP Bar instead of the Center. Nor do I like how there is no animation to the bar itself. It doesn't even have shading! It's just a plane red bar.
The EXP bar does not show how much XP you need to level, which is fine but... WHY BOTHER HAVING every enemy I kill say +XP on them then? It doesn't even tell me HOW MUCH XP. Is this here because there are no XP ORBS or something like that to pick up?
What's the Cooldown time remaining on my Plasma Genade? I dunno, it's slowly filling back to white it doesn't even have a secs timer on the VERY LARGE ICON. And said ICON does not properly represent a GRENADE in the slightest. It looks like a wannabe Blockchain icon.
There is no retical of any kind. Not even a Rockstar DOT!
There is No PROPER indicator for how many shots I have in or left for my gun. A large Orange bar does not tell me how many before reloading. It, infact looks more like a Stamina Bar for Dodge rolling. If you had a retical you could've place the ammo count within it.
The Choose Weapon or Hunter Upgrade screen is so boring and the placement of the options are weird. Why not just do it the standard 1, 2 ,3 instead of have 1 and 2 standing on top of 3 like an upside down 3 block pyramid.
Why does the game not tell me to BREAK ROCKS FOR UPGRADE CURRENCY? I literally didn't get anything from killing waves of creatures besides XP. I had to go the the store page and happen to notice the gif towards the bottom.
Why is the Mini Map populated with a Black Box which is my "Ship" and a Green Box, which is me... and NOTHING ELSE?! Is this supposed to be useful for Co-op Play?

[h3]The Upgrades?[/h3] 
They're the EXACT bog standard type of ones you'd expect. There is nothing really cool or interesting here. Even the upgrades your select while battling it out on a Planet are the same bog standard X does Y +25% style things. But since all the enemies do the exact same things and there isn't a tiering up mechanic, it's pretty pointless. These Rogue Lite/like options just exist to check the box not to make for interesting gameplay.

If I had to rate this game... I'd give it a 2/10 and it's entirely because I like the Voxel Visuals.
I'd love it if the dev could continuing making some improvements to actually flesh out the game they expect people to pay for. Until then, [b]The Cosmos Needs Hunters; but there is are challengers[/b]

I originally got this elsewhere, but decided to buy it again because this is one of my favorite games of the Spellarium series.  There are a bunch of these games now, and even more in the other 2 series this developer does (Laruaville, Cursed House) in which you must remove obstacles in some pattern to obtain all the coins.  If you enjoy more challenging puzzles with your M3 games, this one rivals some of the hardest Cursed House games because it's possible to make solving a level far more difficult if you do things in the wrong order.  This was also the first game to introduce the toggle gates, which close off sections of the board.  Later games have a more sophisticated gate mechanic, but in this game, the cascades can be as much a pain as pleasure with tripping the gates.

You have 110 M3-puzzle levels in which the goal is always to obtain all the coins, and tons of minigames (mahjong, solitaire, spot the difference scenes, and hidden object scenes) of which one appears about every 3 levels.  The newer feature of being able to replay levels on demand wasn't introduced yet, so beware of skipping any levels if you're a completionist.

I also get a chuckle out of the scene to build, with light emerging from the oddest places.

I'm going to preface this by saying most reviews here seem to have very little playtime and almost no playtime in higher difficulties. 
I've played for 16+ hours at the time of writing this, primarily to unlock every character, finish a run at Max difficulty, and max out the roguelite elements. (Ex: +10% dmg +5% Intrest, etc). 

Additionally, before I begin, I'd like to say I'm going to be pointing out a LOT of flaws with the game and I hope this can act as a feedback to the developers to fix some of what I feel are issues and some of the bugs. The game is fine for the price point, in early access, and I am very much asking for probably more than is considerably FAIR for those facts. I am doing most of my comparing to Brotato as it is a very similar game and this game could use a few things to help it stand out (Which I will talk about) and things that Brotato does better which I hope the devs can take some inspiration from if they haven't had the chance already. 

This will act as the pros section as there really isn't anything about this game that's unique or interesting from other similar entries:

The game IS worth 5$. That's about it. You'll get 5-8 hours of entertainment from it. I say entertainment because anything more really does just feel like pointless same old same old. It's a game worth playing for a few days if you're bored and got nothing better to do.

Let the cons section begin...

-Most of the characters are nothing characters. This means they either have the same abilities as another character with minor stat changes that might as well not even be there or they basically don't do anything or in some cases, work at all.

- The leveling your inventory every run is slow and painful. I imagine most players enjoy this kind of game through upgrading and getting more powerful as they go deeper into the dungeons or whatever the game has to offer. However, you need three (3) of an item to level it to tier 2. In most games, this would be fine. However, Sleep stream does NOT have anything but tier 1 in the shop. This means as you go deeper with your limited gold, you have to buy three (3) Tier 1 items to make a tier 2. Now you need three (3) tier 2 items to make the final Tier 3. However, this means you need the shop to OFFER and PURCHASE nine (9) tier 1 of an item. The implementation of offering higher tiers of items as you level the shop would do wonders for this game.

-Synergies are mostly JUST weapon dmg % bonus. Only a very few like Devil (1HP recov for every killed enemy +50% dmg taken and -50% lifesteal), Bloody (Lifesteal %), and Rampage (Attack speed %) change anything that isn't just do more dmg. Some synergies don't even work such as the RICH trait. You'll see more about why it doesn't a bit later as it gives Interest 10%

-Leveling up the shop and your character each run is exceptionally odd at times. ALL characters get X number of weapon slots and Y number of armor slots. However,  almost every character starts with 1 weapon slot active. You're expected to spend gold on both upgrades and leveling the shop to both unlock higher quality items AND unlock active slots. This would be fine, however in 20 floors (The max amount), you do not get very much XP passively and are forced to spend a large amount of gold on unlocking active slots. Most of the armor in the game is pretty much useless so you're mainly going for weapons until some of the very end game armor items (Which also means its nearly impossible to upgrade both a few weapons and armor to tier 3 before run end). Sadly, a lot of the earlier levels unlock mainly armor slots. So you'll be spending a lot of your early levels in the run just buying worthless slots and falling behind on gold due to getting weaker every floor. 

-Some of the stats in the game just flat out do NOT work. Ex: Interest (Gain % of remaining gold per floor). As far as I can tell through testing, this just doesn't work. I've not once gained a single extra gold upon starting a floor or finishing one(Other than income) from this stat. This makes amassing gold that much harder.

-Some of the character abilities are just straight up do NOT use or you die. Ex: Berserker puts you to half life, gives life steal and you take 30% more dmg. Not dmg buff, no attack speed, movement speed, or anything. I see what the dev was trying to do here, and while I cannot recommend it I will be constructive and point out the positives as well as the problems. Who knows, perhaps other players will get more out of this than I could. 

Overall, it is an extremely simplistic 2D explore hack 'n slash with a story. So simplistic that it is effectively just left, right, jump and slash. And your slash only has one move, with no enemy context. 

The charm is in the large sprites, especially the main character which have an old-school arcade feel, and the effort with the story which tries to offer lore, background and atmosphere. The delivery, via a ghostly 'friend', is text-based, and can get a bit annoying but somehow I found it kind of cute. 

There is a lot of running around doing nothing followed by either easy fights or fights where it's hard to avoid damage because your one slash isn't useful until you get to the best position against some of the enemies. There are some jumping platform sections which are well implemented and fairly decent exploration / pathfinding for a 2D side scroller, but the respawn points can take you far backwards meaning a lot more walking and repetitive fights. There are a few bugs and glitches too, but not game-breaking ones that I saw.

I'd guess that this is a first-time proper project which, if so, will have proved some code theory and game design for the dev, and I very much wish them well in learning from this early attempt and reaching for higher complexity and satisfaction for future endeavours. For most Steam gamers, this is by no means a $5 game but if you want to support a dev, it's not completely awful on a sale.

Story is fun, but it drags a bit towards the end. The penultimate chapter felt somewhat shallow: progression was linear, there wasn't much to explore, and stakes felt underwhelming. The story was wrapping up in a very predictable way, and I just wanted to get on with it already. That being said, Chapter 2 was fantastic. Cobigail was super fun, the mystery was interesting and suspenseful, Saul was a great mini-antagonist, and the resolution was wholesome as heck.  

The central mechanic of re-using other people's words is neat, but it gets very shallow towards the middle of the game. In the first chapter, you get access to a bunch of general phrases that are flexible and can get a varied reaction out of characters. As the game progresses, the phrases became more and more specific, to the point there was barely any point to playing with them. They just felt like keys to take from point A to point B rather than a new tool to try out on everything around you. This is noticeable in the limited inventory: in chapter 1 your want to collect as many phrases as possible because they all do something. But in chapter 3+ you rarely feel the need to 'hold onto' phrases because they're only used in 1-2 places. Obviously keeping this mechanic deep is challenging and would require more time and resources to develop, but since it's the central mechanic of the game I would've hoped to see more from it.

One thing I think was missing in this game compared to 'Smile for me' is the connection to the characters. This game has a lot more characters, and most of them are limited to a single chapter. The only characters you get to bond with are the busyboys, which is why they stand out. As such, the world and the characters felt less 'personal' than in 'Smile for me'.

Overall, a neat, cozy little game that's not afraid to talk about feelings. Worth it for the art design alone, but the story and game are pretty darn good as well.

For what on the surface may seem like a silly little game about helping a community overcome their differences, it truly is so much more than that. GGG is a game about love, history, art, community and communication, and their importance. It is about radical self acceptance, about loving thy neighbor, about doing the right thing even when the circumstances are dire. It is about resistance when the world is coming down on you. It is about insecurity. It is about being afraid and doing it anyways.

Each character, regardless of their screen time, is charming in their own way. LimboLane really has a penchant for making unique and loveable characters and it shows through every detail, down to the distinct voice of each individual. Some made me laugh, some made me cry, some surprised me, but one thing they all have in common is I was totally captivated by each and every one. I would also touch more on the vast cast of openly queer characters, but I'm not good with my words and we'd be here all day, so I'll leave it at this: Even with the larger than life atmosphere of the grove, the inner relationships of it's citizens are very much based in reality. If you take away the funny accents and bright colors, these are just people, like you and I.

Blending strong, memorable characters, an amazing soundtrack, and a message on the importance of proper communication, LimboLane presents a guide to the effects of misinformation and censorship. At the heart of GGG is the need for community, the need to create in the name of passion and love, but also how easy it is to fall into working against that.

Most, if not all, of us feel out of place, like we need to fit in, like we need to meet a particular standard set by general society. Because of this, it's easy to give into despair, and give into more selfish tactics in order to feel "Normal" or "In Control". Without getting into spoilers, GGG displays how easy this is, and how even the best of us can succumb to the pressure, and fall into doing things we wouldn't normally do, hurting others in the process. 

LimboLane has delivered another heartfelt piece of art that will stick in my brain for years to come, and I can't wait to see what comes next from the quirky sensibilities I've come to enjoy.

TLDR: It's okay but it shows potential
Before writing this, I wanted to 100% the game but in its current state, it was easier said then done. Overall, I think the game has an okay experience for its price, it just needs a lot more work before its really something to be considered amazing.

The story is simple. It doesn't do anything too far fetched and voice acting suffices. You can tell the VA's try hard and it shows but some lines delivery aren't the best. For the story, it's not hard to invest yourself into your own character or the other characters. You have a job to do so you naturally want to do it. To leave the apartment, you have to help a spirit which anyone would agree to to be free. Unraveling what happened was kind of fun and interesting and you'd could sympathize for the characters a bit. Setting the first spirit free isn't hard to do but the second spirit, I couldn't figure it out. I hope I'm not outing myself for making a bad decision but I've tried replaying a few times and I could never figure it out despite listening to him before leaving.

Gameplay is a walking simulator and the locations is just the apartment, stairway, and laundry room. I know the building is suppose to be run down but some areas are over detailed with garbage and trash while others are just empty. The mechanics werent hard to figure out but going through the game for the first time, it took me a minute or two with some things.

The glitches in this game are outright game breaking. A common one which I dont actually consider a glitch but poor programming is if you try to speed through certain parts or do an action too early, youre stuck. It's very obvious when you have to close your eyes. My first play through, I sat with my eyes closed for about 5 minutes just to open them and die. Second time getting to that part, I waited to the last second before closing my eyes for everything to play out as normal. This isnt the only part like that. Sometimes of you open a door to early or interact with something in your journal/inventory, you'll be locked in place unable to move which requires a restart. Sometimes, it felt like an entire save was plagued by that so I had to restart the game entirely.

I hope what I said doesn't come off crass because like I said, I can really see the potential and if this is a part 1, I am excited for the part 2. I just believe that there's a lot of work to be done.
To rehash my critiques in a more constructive way, story and VA are done well, level detailing could be polished more, and the game has a bit of quirks to work out but it is an overall decent experience.

I own A LOT of games. I play A LOT of games. It's not that I don't like Avatar: Frontiers, I do. But I can't recommend it, especially at full price. Here is the deal. The only issue I have had, besides spending some considerable time messing with the graphics, is the "pop-ins" (especially while flying) Some of it I understand but it can be an INCREDIBLE eye-sore in certain areas, ruining the immersion (at least for me)

 I waited for awhile to buy the game on sale after reading all the issues people were having early on. I can't believe they release these games sometimes so unoptimized then expect gamers to "deal" with it. Which gamers do! Shout out to all my gamers out there making games playable after developers drop the ball! Because of all the gamers though, by the time I decided to play it the game was playable. 

For some peoples reference I am playing on a RTX 3070 8GB VRAM, Intel I7 7700K 4.2GHz, Windows 10 (because 11 won't allow chipset), 4TB NVMe SSD running 1080p on mostly HIGH settings. Game looks great and runs smooth besides the pop ins but I really hate the pop-ins. I've also watched a lot of videos and those people have them as well. I have also saw many, many posts about it so it is an obvious issue across many different set ups.

Then, there is the "Penance mission" bug that cannot be completed. This bug has been known for months now by the developers and still there is no fix. This one for me is unacceptable and the MAIN reason I will not recommend this game, even on sale. I paid $45 for the Deluxe on sale and I am disappointed. I'm not even a completionist and this bothers me. The game has been out for a while now and this should of be taken care of, especially when people are paying upwards of $120. I count on the gamers finding a work around before the developers. 

With all of that being said, I have 82.5 hours in this game at the time of writing this review, with 82 of those hours messing with the graphics settings (LOL) I actually enjoy playing the game most of the time but I tend to agree with those that say the is a Far Cry clone with Avatar dressing (albeit good dressing) I love the Avatar movies so I obviously think that helps. I love the Far Cry series (especially 3) and that helps me enjoy the game as well. Maybe the game is worth 25$ at this time, at most. So if you can get it for that, why not? (wait a year)

In closing I would like to take a little jab at Ubisoft (You Be Soft) Since joining the PC gaming community 8 years ago I have noticed many issues with this company. Especially performance and optimization issues. Then there was the shutting down of The Crew with no offline option. Ubisoft is "ON NOTICE" with the gaming community and it is only a matter of time before they suffer the consequences of shady business practices. I like many of the Ubisoft games but as a consumer the only vote I have is with my wallet. I will stop buying their products if this continues.

For context: 
When the game came out originaly on Ubisoft Connect, I played the game for about 60 hours without much issue.
Now, after it's DLC updates and release on Steam I can no longer play it. The game crashes my entire system constantly. Is it a performance issue? Poor optimization from the games side? Faulty hardware from my side? I don't know! And after hours of troubleshooting I've given up. This is the first game that as ever given me trouble like that. How do you even manage to code your game worse after it's release? 

And it makes me sad honestly. I really enjoyed playing the game on it's release. The open world is designed beautifully and some of the wildlife has become my favorite in the Avatar franchise. 
The movement is fun! And the gathering mechanic to craft new armor and weapons has some neat ideas.

Other stuff tho... the story is alright, combat becomes repetative (at least with the human enemies) and the systems to level up your character are infuriating. Health ups and Skill points (yes, there is a skill tree) are scattered across the map, so If you want to unlock new skills you basically have to do a fetch quest. Exploring the world is fun, but only really becomes viable once you reach a certain point in the story.

The games biggest problem is obviously the performance issues, so if you're not a fan of the games visuals to begin with, there are better games out there to spend your money on.

I basically have thrown 40$ in the void now because I can no longer refund the game and have to wait for performance updates that who knows when come out. 

tldr:
Like Avatar? Fan of open world games? Have a PC that matches the recommended (yes the recommened, not the minimum) requirements? 
Cool, buy the game on sale if it looks promising to you.

And if not... save that money, wait another year or so If you want to buy it eventually. Or don't.

The map is massive and traversing it is unlike any other game I've played, there's not some set path you navigate through like in Red Dead Redemption. You navigate through the forest -- and the forest is confusing. The crafting seems intimidating at first. The missions don't tell you 100% where to go. But I think those qualities are a part of the satisfaction because you WILL get better at those things. I've played for ~15 hours now and I feel like I'm starting to get the hang of it. I'm glad it wasn't some immediately understandable thing because the learning curve makes it 100% more satisfying. I'm making my own routes throughout the map. I've finally got the hang on crafting, and I'm starting to blow through the missions, despite their sometimes lack of instruction.

I understand why people are upset because it's just another Far Cry disguised as Avatar, but as someone who has never played Far Cry, i'm enjoying it.

Good luck facing those suckers with a bow and arrow. Also, the freaking "weakspots" are one of the buggiest things i have ever seen. Makes it impossible to go full stealth mode.

"Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora" offers an immersive experience that truly brings the breathtaking world of Pandora to life. Set in the same universe as the beloved films, this game allows players to explore lush landscapes, engage with unique creatures, and delve into the rich lore of the Na'vi people. 

One of the standout features is the stunning visual fidelity. The graphics are nothing short of spectacular, with vibrant colors and detailed environments that make it feel as if you’ve stepped right into the movie. The attention to detail is impressive, from the dense foliage to the bioluminescent flora that lights up at night, creating a truly magical atmosphere.

The gameplay mechanics are engaging, allowing for a mix of exploration and combat. The controls feel intuitive, making it easy to navigate the environment and interact with various elements of the world. Whether you're gliding through the air on a banshee or stealthily maneuvering through enemy territory, the action is fluid and exciting.

Story-wise, "Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora" weaves in themes of environmentalism and the conflict between technology and nature, staying true to the essence of the films. Players find themselves invested in the narrative as they take on missions that reflect these themes, adding a layer of depth to the gameplay.

However, there are moments where the game feels a bit derivative of other open-world titles. Some quests can feel repetitive, and the AI of certain enemies may not always provide the challenge that players might expect. 

Overall, "Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora" is a visually stunning and entertaining experience that fans of the franchise will appreciate. While it may have its flaws, the captivating world and engaging narrative make it a worthy addition to any gamer's collection. If you're looking to escape into a beautifully crafted universe, this game is worth exploring.

I have progressed pretty far in this game and for the most part it runs extremely smoothly.
