It's also frustrating since the spawn rate for mature direhorses seems to be pretty low in my game or there's always predators or RDA near their locations so they disperse.
Combat is a nice mix of easy and difficult especially since the game encourages stealth or speed to gain better rewards from attacking bigger RDA facilities. The gear levels are honestly confusing and frustrating since you can have something with perks that would overall make it seem a better choice, but once equipped will lower your combat level...so it's nice the game shows you beforehand how it impacts your level before equipping, but overall seems a little janky. Going off of weapons, hunting is difficult to get "clean kills" even with high level equipment which makes me feel terrible however it could also be a skill issue on my part.
For the story I will admit I'm more into exploration and just flying or riding around so I don't really have much to say about it. Price wise this game can be pretty expensive for some people, especially when compared to the possibility it may not work, however when it goes on sale it's really decently priced (I bought base and DLCs for about half price) unless you don't mind spending the full amount. Otherwise I'd wishlist and watch out for sales.
Overall I have not experienced issues or bugs (outside of the normal for just about any game) and if you have a computer able to support this game, love amazing graphics and soundtracks, enjoy exploring, combat, nature, and a lot of content, I would highly recommend checking this game out and giving it a shot :)

Having tapped out of the Far Cry franchise several iterations ago I found I didn't mind returning to the familiar mechanics, albeit with some fresh and unexpectedly artful new additions. Even the repeated encampment raiding is varied enough, and there's a satisfying learning curve in developing tactics to deal with them efficiently, a process which is meaningfully rewarded when successful. 

And just as I was I getting a little numb off over-exposure to magnificent glowing rainforests filled with an astounding variety of flora and fauna, the game branched out into an entirely new area with a whole new array of plants and animals, expanding upon the world beyond what is found in the movies, and I just found myself saying "wow". 

This game may be a repeated installment of an old formula in some ways, but the environment and visual experience available here is a groundbreaking milestone in gaming evolution. Awe and Wonder become increasingly hard to come by as we go through life, but I've found myself feeling both at multiple moments in this game.

Don't miss this because of that Mixed rating. Check the system requirements, upgrade your rig if necessary, and discover the awe and wonder that await you in the Frontiers of Pandora. (Gag-worthy tagline there, I know, but legit.)

"Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora" transports players into the lush, vibrant world of James Cameron's cinematic universe, offering an experience that's visually stunning but mechanically familiar. Developed by Ubisoft Massive, this game captures the essence of Pandora with breathtaking landscapes, from dense jungles to floating mountains, all rendered with impressive detail that's sure to awe even those not particularly enamored with the films.

The gameplay is a blend of exploration, combat, and environmental interaction, echoing Ubisoft's well-trodden open-world formula seen in games like "Far Cry." You play as a Na'vi, raised by humans, who must reconnect with their native culture while combating human colonization. This narrative framework is rich with themes of environmentalism and resistance, though the storytelling often lacks the depth to fully engage with these ideas beyond the surface level.

Combat in "Frontiers of Pandora" is a mix of archery, stealth, and the use of human weapons, providing a decent variety but lacking innovation. The parkour and flight mechanics, however, are where the game shines, offering exhilarating ways to navigate Pandora's vast terrain. The connection with nature, through linking with plants and animals, adds a unique layer to exploration, though it can sometimes feel more like a checklist than a profound experience.

The game's world is expansive, filled with side quests that, while adding depth to the Na'vi culture and the ecosystem of Pandora, can become repetitive. The main campaign, while engaging at times, is criticized for its length and the padding with generic open-world activities. Technical issues at launch, including performance problems and bugs, have also been a notable downside.

Visually, "Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora" is a triumph, arguably one of the best-looking open worlds in gaming, with environments that encourage exploration purely for the beauty they offer. The sound design complements this, creating an immersive auditory experience that captures the wonder of Pandora.

In summary, while "Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora" excels in its visual presentation and the joy of exploration, it stumbles with a lack of innovation in gameplay and narrative depth. It's a game that feels like a missed opportunity to push boundaries in both storytelling and mechanics, instead resting comfortably within Ubisoft's established open-world paradigm. For fans of the "Avatar" universe or those who appreciate breathtaking game worlds, it's definitely worth exploring, but perhaps not at full price.

Let's address the cosmic catastrophe head-on: my descent into ruin because of Escape from Andromeda. My existence became a tattered tapestry of shattered dreams and broken promises, each thread unraveling as I plunged further into the void. I sacrificed everything—my family, my friends, my very soul—all in pursuit of the next level, the next upgrade, the next fleeting moment of digital euphoria.

The toll it took was staggering. I stand here now, a mere husk of my former self, stripped of dignity and drowning in debt. My wife left with the children, taking with her any semblance of stability or hope for the future. I sold my possessions, pawned my memories, and gambled away my last shreds of dignity—all for the sake of a virtual thrill among the stars.

And yet, even as I teetered on the brink of oblivion, Escape from Andromeda beckoned me with its siren song. Who needs shoes on their feet when they can soar through the cosmos on the wings of imagination? Who needs money in their pocket when they can trade their earthly woes for a digital escape among the stars?

But the debts... oh, the debts. I owe money to three different mafias, each more menacing than the last, their shadows looming over me like dark clouds in a storm. They demand payment, they demand retribution, and yet all I can offer them is the hollow promise of tomorrow's winnings in the game that has become my only lifeline.

In conclusion, Escape from Andromeda isn't just a game; it's a cosmic roulette wheel that spins the wheel of fate with reckless abandon. It's a cautionary tale of obsession and addiction, a cautionary tale of a man who lost everything in pursuit of a fleeting dream among the stars. So, if you dare to venture into its unforgiving void, tread carefully, for the price of admission may be more than you're willing to pay.

This is an interesting game that offers something that no other game that I know of has done. A trivia game like Who Wants to be a Millionaire where if you fail, the game turns into a platformer where you have to go through an obstacle course as punishment. 

[b]PROS[/b]

• The concept of this game is unique as mentioned above and it works
• Week 1 & 2's questions offer great variety without being too much of a brain scratcher
• The art is wholesome and reminds me of 90's Nickelodeon
• The extra options you get after game completion are great. Though I wish there was a way to select which platforming segment you can jump to so you can practice speedrun strats more effectively
• This game has the potential to pave the way of the future for these types of games

[b]CONS[/b]

• The story while simple is weak. However the message it's trying to convey is good.
• The game is very short. You'll likely have it beat in 2 hours.
• The questions take a sharp turn on week 3 where it seems the questions stop being generalized for everything. The last week specifically asked questions that were so far from week 1 and 2 that it became something else and 90% of the questions were related to Soccer (EU Football) and it's not that popular in my country. So the question nor the answers are well known here so you're forced into guessing.
• The hit boxes on the spinning blade traps aren't properly aligned, so you will die at times when jumping over them or without them even touching your character model
• The jumping with your character during the platforming section is jank. You can expect to clip through platforms and double jump sometimes without your character's feet touching the ground.
• The testing for the game seems to have had some questions slip through the cracks while fact checking. I streamed this game on Twitch and here's a clip I got from tonight where the game says I gave the wrong answer when in fact it was correct - https://clips.twitch.tv/PlausibleGloriousKoalaBleedPurple-acgqzLqATMHW9rMJ

[b]CONCLUSION[/b]

The game in concept is amazing and I want to see more done with this kind of genre. I honestly think it has promise and this being the first one of the kind that I have personally seen. I can see this getting bigger in the future and I am so down for it. I could easily see the implementation of choosing your own categories, more questions, different punishments like being turned into a fighting game instead of a platformer. The possibilities are endless.

Star Wars Outlaws – A Galaxy Far, Far Away… Bogged Down by Bad Design

As a lifelong Star Wars fan, I was excited to dive into Star Wars Outlaws, expecting a thrilling open-world adventure set in the criminal underbelly of the galaxy. The game nails the immersive Star Wars feel, with stunning environments, solid voice acting, and plenty of opportunities to explore the Outer Rim. Unfortunately, that's where the praise stops—because everything else is bogged down by frustrating design choices that turn what should have been an exciting journey into a tedious grind.  

Wasted Potential in Mission & Game Design  
The biggest issue with Outlaws is how repetitive and time-wasting the core gameplay loop becomes. Missions are uninspired and formulaic—you go to a location, track down a contact, get double-crossed (because, of course, you do), deal with a surprise twist, and then repeat. It’s predictable to the point of boredom, and rather than feeling like an outlaw making their own path, it feels like you’re just running through the same checklist over and over.  

And then there’s the tedious mission markers—too many objectives force you to search for some tiny item in a massive search area, dragging out what should have been a quick, engaging task into a frustrating scavenger hunt. These mechanics feel like artificial padding rather than genuine gameplay.  

Forced Minigames & Unskippable Scenes 
Why on earth is Sabacc (the card game) a mandatory part of main story missions? A side activity? Sure, that would have been fine. But making it required for story progression feels completely unnecessary—especially for those who just want to focus on the action and adventure. Star Wars has a ton of side games in-universe, but forcing this one into the critical path is baffling.  

Adding insult to injury, the game doesn’t let you skip a ton of slow-paced dialogue and cutscenes—but ironically, the scenes you would want to skip (like ship landings and takeoffs) don’t let you bypass them immediately. Instead, you’re stuck waiting on animations that get old fast, which disrupts the pacing. For an outlaw constantly on the move, this game sure loves to slow you down.  

Lack of True Freedom – One-Sided War  
Perhaps the biggest letdown is that, despite being a supposed outlaw, the game forces you to take a side in the Galactic Civil War. Where is the choice? Where is the opportunity to manipulate both sides, profit off the chaos, or even double-cross both factions for a true lone wolf ending? Instead, the game railroads you into a predetermined allegiance, robbing players of what should have been an exciting element of freedom in an open-world Star Wars game.  

Traversal Frustrations – Exploration Has Limits  
While the environments are beautiful, the level design frequently forces players into needlessly complicated routes just to reach their objectives. Sometimes the correct path is either unclear, poorly marked, or absurdly convoluted, leading to wasted time wandering around instead of enjoying the adventure. Even with environmental interactions enabled, the game loves to funnel you into slow, linear pathways that kill the sense of freedom that the open-world setup originally promised.  

Final Verdict – A Missed Opportunity  
At its best, Star Wars Outlaws captures the immersive world of Star Wars in a way that few games have. The graphics, world-building, and exploration are fantastic, but they’re overshadowed by a repetitive mission structure, frustrating design decisions, and a lack of true player choice. The game constantly slows you down with time-wasting mechanics, forces you into unnecessary minigames, and takes away the very agency an outlaw should have in the galaxy.  

I expected more from this. Fans deserved more.

Star Wars Outlaws, set in the criminal underbelly of the Star Wars universe, offers an ambitious open-world experience where players navigate a galaxy rife with danger and opportunity. The game captures the essence of being a rogue on the run, blending space travel, smuggling, and high-stakes heists. While the setting and premise are exciting, the narrative struggles to provide the depth needed to make its characters truly compelling. Despite its potential, the game falls short in delivering a truly transformative character arc for various characters, which affects the emotional impact of the story.
The story follows Kay Vess and Nix, a rag-tag duo trying to carve out their own path in a galaxy ruled by criminal syndicates. While the premise is engaging, the execution leaves something to be desired, particularly in Kay's development. Other story narratives typically show characters growing and changing due to their experiences, yet characters feels largely the same at the end of the game as they do when they are introduced. This lack of progression diminishes the stakes of the journey, making major story beats feel less impactful than they should be.
Gameplay in Star Wars Outlaws provides a mix of third-person combat, exploration, and spaceflight, offering a variety of activities for players to engage in. Gunplay is serviceable but lacks the weight and fluidity of the best shooters, making combat encounters feel somewhat standard. The open-world elements introduce an impressive amount of freedom, yet the missions often rely on familiar tropes and repetitive objectives. While the ability to interact with different syndicates and choose how to approach missions is a highlight, it doesn't always lead to meaningful changes in the story.
Visually, the game is a stunning recreation of the Star Wars universe, featuring beautifully detailed environments, immersive lighting, and well-designed character models. The various planets feel distinct and lived-in, creating an authentic and rich sci-fi world for players to explore. Animations and facial expressions are solid, but some cutscenes suffer from stiffness, occasionally breaking immersion. Despite minor inconsistencies, the overall presentation does justice to the grandeur and grit of the Star Wars galaxy.
Overall, Star Wars Outlaws delivers an exciting adventure with engaging gameplay and breathtaking visuals but falls short in its storytelling and character development. Kay's journey, while full of action and intrigue, lacks the emotional depth needed to make her arc truly memorable. The gameplay offers a variety of experiences, though some aspects feel underwhelming or repetitive over time. Despite its narrative shortcomings, the game's attention to detail and immersive world-building make it an enjoyable experience for Star Wars fans.
Star Wars Outlaws gets a 6/10.

I really wanted to like this game, as I'm a big Star Wars fan, but it's hard to recommend. From my experience, the majority of the bugs have been rectified, but I believe this game has fundamental game play faults. 

The gunplay was fun at first, but I soon realized the sheer lack of options in combat. you're stuck with your blaster the whole game, and get to do a few upgrades that feel shallow, and mostly used as a way to advance the story line. You're able to pickup weapons, but it was an intentional design choice to make them temporary and clearly stronger than the main blaster you use. As a game that focus on it's open world aspect, (such is Ubisofts style), it greatly lacked enjoyment. I got pretty bored of the combat after the first few hours. The ship combat was a little more interesting, but still greatly lacked diversity. Everything felt more like a chore. From the contracts, to all the codes and collectibles which were used to upgrade the already overused blaster. 

The story was... meh. I wasn't a big fan of Kay. She didn't learn from almost any of her mistakes. I didn't grow attached to any of the crew, and the relationship with her and ND-5 felt shallow, and underdeveloped. There were some twits here and there, but it was hard for me to get invested when the characters felt unimportant. The Dialogue was all pretty rough around the edges, even cringe at times. *SMALL SPOILER* The ending mission just had Kay end up exactly where she started, but with a ND-5, a ship, and none of her original goals achieved. 

The graphics were pretty decent though, no real complaints there with most the bugs fixed. Although, the game did crash my PC a couple times.

This is one of the better Star Wars games I've played in a long time.

It doesn't have a lot of deep depth, like this isn't a Star Wars simulator, you're not going to need to memorize the key combination to turn on the ship's bathroom, but it does a great job of giving the feeling of making your way through the Star Wars universe.  The feel is there, the details are solid, it feels right.

Gameplay is solid too.  It's a reasonable sneak-er game, although shooting your way out of trouble happens sometimes.  As you progress you'll unlock new abilities and some of them are pretty fun and change gameplay approaches.  Your little pet minion guy is fun too and opens some fun options.

The only "real" downsides as I saw it:
-Some of the animation sync is marginal.  If you approach someone from a weird angle while doing a takedown, it might not sync right, like you'll still do the takedown, just the character models might not convincingly connect.

-Early game you're really fragile and a lot of the skills that let you skate later are not unlocked yet.  Its basically a much harder game at the start, by the end you're nigh unstoppable. 

-There's a couple of spots in the campaign that are hard, or don't telegraph the specific thing you need to do as well as I'd like.  Not the end of the world, just you might need to google "okay so why can't I do this?" and it'll be fine.
-Some of the open worlds are actually pretty small, from tiny space stations to one major hub that's a single city (that said there's also expansive open worlds so...)

That said I really really liked this game.  I got it cheap on sale as a "well hell why not?" and it bumped most of my other games off my play list until I was done.  The characters are fun, the story is neat, the setting is engaging and you feel like a Han Solo-like character in all the right ways.  

Compared to Jedi Survivor, another great game, Outlaws feels much more grounded (less places built more or less like jungle gyms, more places you can traverse without laser fast reflexes) and it was a lot less frustrating and reliant on timing and laser fast reflexes.  It also had more story and points to engage with that story, and the open worlds have quite a lot to do.

Basically by the end of the game I had pretty warm feelings.  Kay and Nix are fun, the game may frustrate at times but I forgave it quite quickly, and this was just the best Star Wars game to come around in a long time.  It isn't without flaws, but I would suggest this game to anyone looking for an action platformer with sneaking, or anyone who enjoys a good Star Wars game.

For an incremental management sim, it's really quite good. 

The core gameplay loop is that when you collect two fruit, they merge into a higher tier. This might sound basic, but a tier 10 fruit is made of 2x2x2x2x2x2x2x2x2x2 fruit. That's 1024 tier 0 fruit needed for tier 10, or 1048576 tier 0 fruit needed for tier 20. The goal is to get to tier 48. 

To do this, you hire an army of naked people to work your plantation, while they shit themselves silly for fertiliser. You use these little people's turds to upgrade your saplings, which give you better fruits to merge. When you hit milestones, you get coins to spend on a roguelite system of cards, which completely modify the gameplay mechanics. 

The dev's mind must be a busy place to live.

It's arkanoid but in VR. It ticks a lot of boxes, but has fatal flaws.

There are bricks. You hit them with your ball. You hit the ball with your gun, and you have a way of dragging the ball to kind of where you want to move it. If you miss the ball you are rekt.

As a game it has all the most essential features: a scoreboard, a scoring system which rewards precise play, a reasonable progression that encourages you to keep playing, and enough of a skill ceiling that you don't feel completely shut out of competition on the leaderboards for that reason. If you're casually playing this game, then that's really all you need. It even has all of the various things that a competitive player would love: daily and seasonal challenges and global leaderboards. To be blunt, it's clearly marketed at a certain group of people who look a lot like me.

The scoring system is extremely good. Every brick you break gives you a set number of points. However, every brick releases a multiplier, which you need to collect with your ball before it disappears. Hitting the ball gives you the multiplier the ball's collected, and it fills a gauge which gives you more balls. Each ball in play multiplies your multiplier, and you can have up to 4 balls in play. Because there's a set number of bricks on the board, a serious player is going to try to hit as few blocks as possible in one shot while collecting as much multiplier as he can - this is how you maximize your score. There's a lot of thought that you have to put into trying to do this, and it's quite enjoyable.

However, there is also a powerup system: some bricks attach powerups to your ball, which impact how you play. These range in usefulness from the excellent "putting all the multiplier on the board on one ball,"  to the mediocre "making your ball pierce through bricks," to the absolutely abhorrent "putting a bouncy wall around all the bricks for your balls to bounce off of." The first unambiguously helps, the second is situational, and the last just completely destroys the run because you break a lot of the bricks without collecting the multiplier. The powerups seem to be randomized, which functionally randomizes your score. There doesn't seem to be a way to selectively avoid powerups, so the end result is that you can have a good run ended by picking up a bad powerup. It's extremely disappointing, because the game is otherwise pretty good.

This is an example of a well-crafted game with a single severe flaw that hurts it badly. It's very sad.

[b]Fantasian Neo Dimension[/b], [i]or personally my Final Fantasy XVII[/i]

Even after 20 years later, Hironobu Sakaguchi, father of Final Fantasy, was still able to create games that make an impact in player's lives. Innovating concepts in the industry even to this day. Wow.

Fantasian is everything you love about PS1-era Final Fantasy with the character-writing of FFVI, the rich world & twisting story of FFVII, the masterclass dialogue of FFIX, and turn-order combat of FFX. Fantasian is undeniably the most "classical" modern Final Fantasy you could get your hands on right now. You won't regret it.

Bread-and-butter of Fantasian is its gameplay. [b]God it's fun.[/b] It adds this really well-crafted core mechanic of curving your magic and abilities, lining them up for a more efficient cast that can absolutely change the tide of battle. The loop is so fun and addictive that in each battle I would patiently set up the perfect line for my ability for a satisfying return.

Additionally a new gameplay feature called the Dimengeon, another innovative piece from Sakaguchi. The dimengeon basically allows you to collect the monsters from your random encounters into a single entity space, and battle them manually or when the entity reaches full limit. This is honestly [b]life-changing[/b] to RPGS that I hope other games take note off. Quality-of-life in exploring dungeons by not having to battle every few steps, efficient farming and satisfaction of killing hordes of enemies, an an option to even empty the damn thing and not battle at all! Amazing.

Without a doubt, Fantasian is also one of (if not) the most challenging RPG I have played in modern times. Would even call it the Dark Souls of turn-based RPG. The game's 2nd part unlocks A LOT of stuff that was fun story & gameplay-wise. You get to really unlock the full potential of your party members. However, this is where things get [b]uniquely tricky.[/b] I say uniquely tricky because when you step into the game's Disc 2, the mini bosses and bosses also unlock their potentials and will brutally murder your party if you do not efficiently grasp the core of the gameplay itself and strengths of your own party & equipment. Having a clear understanding of your party & gear is key to surviving Fantasian's Disc 2. [b]But the satisfaction of beating a Fantasian boss is unlike any other RPG, ever.[/b]

Haven't even told you the best part of Fantasian yet. [b]Classic pre-rendered backgrounds made up entirely of hand-crafted dioramas.[/b] It's a work of art. The sheer creativity & artistic direction of Sakaguchi for Fantasian shows his freedom of love & real genuine care for the game. Every single time I enter a new screen, I'm awestruck on how beautiful every set-piece is. I just stand there and look at the view. It's these types of games that keep me going.

Of course we can't talk about a Final Fantasy-like game without our grand composer Nobuo Uematsu. Many lives were saved and cancer was cured when people heard Sakaguchi and Uematsu were teaming up again for a new game. Battle themes were not as strong as Uematsu's previous pieces (I'd even argue it's one of his weakest) however every track outside battles is a real delight. My definite favorites are Gravity, Owen's Theme, and Kina (Destiny). Really really sad that [b]Fantasian's OST is Uematsu's last ever role as the leading music composer of a game.[/b] Your music has brought joy and life to us, thank you Uematsu-san.

Hironobu Sakaguchi made wonders on this game with developers Mistwalker that reignited classic RPG fans. Sakaguchi also said he's cooking up a successor to FFVI before he retires. We will be there when it releases. I hope to see you there. Thank you Sakaguchi for an amazing game once again.

[i]PS: played with no character voices for classic FF immersion. it was a nostalgic experience voicing them yourself again[/i]

A pleasant JRPG which I would call a "Final Fantasy Lite". It shares elements with the classics yet has its own identity. The hand-crafted diorama locations are the most unique aspect of the game and it is fun to look at them, appreciating the craftmanship.

The game also has a brilliant workaround about random encounters where you can put enemies into a pocket dimension and fight them in a big group fight when you please. No more frustration having a random encounter an inch away from a treasure chest.

All the playable characters are nice with recognizable designs, though the game doesn't go too deep into some after their arc is done.

Nobuo Uematsu's soundtrack also didn't disappoint. It is more experimental from what people might be used to, but it's apparent that he had a blast doing the songs.

While the game is good, it is also too long and stretched out. I'm aware the game was originally released in two parts, but the pacing slows down during the second part until it kicks up again towards the endgame.

One other gripe I have are some of the boss fights, which require you to die once or twice to understand their gimmick, think your strategies and equipments before the fight rather than in the middle of them. I'm aware that's how the fights are designed, but I wasn't a big fan of how some leaned into trial & error.
Luckily retrying the fights never was an ordeal itself, and there's always a save point near them with minimal pre-dialogue and story before the fights.

In short, good game for those who crave more classical JRPG with some modern quality of life improvements. I'm appreciative it was finally released from the Apple Arcade jail, thanks!!
I also never want to hear another "PAPIPAPII! PAPPA PAPPA, PAPIPIPAPIPAPI!!" in my entire life, thanks again!!

Fantasian Neo Dimension - 2025 Review - Chaos or Order? All that matters is this gem is freed!

Sometimes after legends create their legacy, they decide to go off into the sunset. Sometimes they try go build more of their legacy, yet fall into the darkness. Sometimes they prove why they were called legends all over again, and for that reason is why we are talking about Fantasian by Hironobu Sakaguchi.

Hironobu Sakaguchi, the godfather of Final Fantasy, had left to create his own studio Mistwalker which developed games such as Lost Odyssey, Blue Dragon, and The Last Story. In 2018, after replaying Final Fantasy VI, Sakaguchi felt the passion burning again to create an emotional role-playing narrative. Bringing in longtime partners, such as Manabu Kusunoki (The Last Story) as the artist and composer Nobuo Uematsu (Final Fantasy), this project began to be developed. Both Sakaguchi and Uematsu had the same mindset that this the game may be their last large-scale project due to health issues at their age. Apple quickly made a deal for the project knowing this could bring business to their apple arcade platform. Outside the game needing to run on Apple operating systems and platforms, Mistwalker was given complete creative freedom. Eventually the game was released on April 2021 (Part 1, then Part 2 released on August 2021). Then comes December 2024 for the release of the high definition port on consoles and PC. This was the first time that Sakaguchi had worked with Square Enix since leaving the company in 2003.

Art Style:
The environments were created using real-world dioramas, including designs by veterans of the tokusatsu industry. Tokusatsu is known for the use of miniature sets. Miniatures are placed from the camera's perspective to create the illusion that the characters are larger than they are.

This game is an absolute work of art. The way these dioramas were created and even just the angles of the pictures taken were clearly carefully considered. The world is vibrant and definitely has a Chrono Cross vibe to it while also at times giving off NieR world. Somehow while not being a prerendered background, this game gives off immense nostalgia for Playstation 1 lovers. It brought me back to the PSX Final Fantasy games while taking it a step further and more detailed. Truly something special that I hope is used again in the future.

Cast of Characters:
This cast felt very Final Fantasy like, in both pros and cons. Clearly Sakaguchi brought a part of Lost Odyssey into this game with the way of short stories. Each character had their own smaller story, and I felt like they were quite enjoyable. Definitely had my favorites like Zinikr and Valrika, but each one had a special part with some more screen time than others. Leo was your typical amnesiac main character, but I am glad that it wasn't the main focus of the plot. Clearly when this game was getting advertised it seemed that it would be the main plot point, and while for the first half it was, it didn't take over. I felt like this game did a great job highlighted other characters over the main character which is a breath of fresh air. So many games like to prey on the amnesiac who actually is someone more important then they realize.

Gameplay:
Fantasian is a turn based combat that has random encounters for enemies. The creative thing is after you start you get an item called a Dimengeon, a space capable of holding up to thirty enemies. After it fills up you fight all 30 enemies in a space that spawns special bonuses and attack boosts. It is a very creative addition to battles that makes your standard random encounters a lot less annoying. There is also a growth system based on a grid similar to Final Fantasy X, yet one for each individual character. Now every game is not perfect, and my biggest issue comes here in gameplay. I believe there is a fix in the works but as it stands there is an issue where everytime the camera changes, your joystick does not adjust and your character moves in the direction you were going before the camera angle changed. This can cause some janky movements that you then need to release the joystick and move again. While not a big deal, it did pull you out from the experience which is an issue. The other "issue" which isn't nearly as much of a big deal for me was the difficulty spike. The original game was made in two parts, and its pretty clear as the second half of this game is MUCH much harder than the first. What I did appreciate about this game is the jewel system. These are accessories that have stat bonuses, resistances, and special attributes. I'll be honest, in most games I never, I mean NEVER use resistant equipment.....except for this game. It truly did make a difference and changed the battlefield against some bosses. I will mention that being as this game was originally on mobile, most scenes that were being shown that happened at other times besides the present were done in a storybook type manner. The artistic work was fantastic, but I do know this bothered some as there was a large amount of them and it pulled them from the story. Personally I didn't have a huge issue with this but I do see where they are coming from. It does make sense though as this was a mobile game and it would be quite difficult to make everything active sequences.

Story:
A short synopsis would say this story "revolves around Leo, a young man who becomes amnesiac after entering an alternate universe known as the Machine Realm. Various characters join him in his quest to recover his memory and discover who he is, while also confronting the mysterious Vam the Malevolent along the way."....and while there needs to be some sort of explanation while staying away from any deeper details, this is not what this games story is really about. This story is about decision making, choices we make for ourselves that could affect loved ones which are then followed by decisions for those same loved ones. Its about what we would do for those we have lost, how do we remember them? Do we hold on tight to all the joy we had with them, or do we carry forever the burden of what we did or didn't do to them. I won't go into spoilers, but this game is such a more in depth story than what the actual plot is. Its utter brilliance, and through each character story and plot point it starts showing itself more and more. Love is not always found where we think it is, and what will we do when that love is lost? There were moments after playing this game that I just wanted to hold my wife and kids close, call my parents and tell them I love them, and think about memories of my grandmother who is no longer on this earth. Clearly I felt something from this game, and I hope this review gives you the desire to play it and feel it too.

Soundtrack:
Well after all that what else is there to say........except HOLY UEMATSU! If this was going to be his finale, boy did he put an orchestra together! I've seen some reviews saying this OST is "decent but nothing like his older stuff" and I think, that's just cray cray (yes I said cray cray - fancy for saying "that's wackadoo"). Some of these boss battle themes are unbelievable and hit so so hard. Then boom you get the opera chants and vocals, its so intense! The last couple fights were just unbelievable and I'd say you will stay in the end game boss battle longer to hear the music (but I can guarantee you that you won't have to because that battle is no 5 minutes in heaven).

In closing, this game was everything I could have asked for. It made me feel like a teenager playing Final Fantasy IX all over again (actually oddly exactly like that even with the settings both quite different). This game was so clearly a passion project, as Sakaguchi put his whole heart and soul into this game. If those janky controls get fixed, this game is an absolute masterpiece.

This game takes me back to the late 90's and early 2000's Final Fantasy series, specifically 7, 8 & 9.  If you liked those games then there is a good chance you will like this one.  3d generated character models moving around on pre-rendered backdrops.  Goofy movement controls that have a nostalgia factor that is difficult to explain, and despite sometimes being annoying, I still really enjoy them.  

This game does not do anything innovative that I've seen so far, nor do I need or want it to.  

 Combat is random encounters using a turn based system. It has a small qualify of life feature with random encounters that makes them slightly more interesting, but it just barely counts as an improvement.  You have fairly high random encounter rates, not the worst I've seen by far, but you won't be moving around on the map for long before a battle starts up.  Early in the game you get the ability to delay those battles, at least for a short period of time: This does not allow you avoid them, but rather save them up to 30 opponents and then fight them all at one time.  This makes it sound like it should make those encounters much more challenging, but so far I haven't found that to be case.   They give you special bonuses you can obtain during these large battles, bonuses that I don't actually think you need (at least not on Normal mode) that perhaps make fighting a large group even easier than stopping to fight each group individually. 

 Finding treasure chests and secret item points littered around the maps and over world (when that is available) works just like in the classic rpgs of yesteryear.  

 The characters are serviceable and mostly likeable, even though they come right out of the tropes handbook for jrpgs, complete with your main protagonist having to deal with a budding love triangle.   The dialogue is well written in most places, and I find that I am enjoying the voice acting even though I'm listening to it in English.  I didn't realize I could change the voice to Japanese until after I had already spent quite a bit time with the  English voices.  The Japanese voice actors are, without a doubt, superior, so I would suggest starting with them if you aren't dense like me!

 From what I can tell there is virtually no real life political ideas being presented in this game, for better or worse, the ideas being presented exist on a more fantastical level than acting as commentary for what is happening in the real world.  I imagine this could come off as refreshing for some or infuriating to others.  

This is a fun game for people who have been looking for a perfectly nostalgic creation from the early 3D days of squire rpgs.    For most younger gamers I don't think I could recommend it, the action in the game is far too slow for anyone who grew up with action rpgs, and the graphics are nowhere near "good", although I am enjoying them.   This is EXACTLY the type of game I've been looking to find for the last 10 years.  

 I have read that the second half of the game is a brutal slog, but I haven't reached that point yet, and I am that old school type of gamer that grinded every one of my characters to maximum level before beating the game, so I don't think I'll be as turned off from it as many seem to be. 

It's a real shame that this game seems to be getting virtually no coverage, and of course not the most stellar reviews.  I don't expect to see another game like this one ever again.  I give it an 8.5/10, although if this had come out during the early 2000s I would likely have rated it a 6.5 or 7 at best.

I am writing this review to counter these new "Mixed" reviews.

This game is incredible. It is a love letter to turn based RPGs. The combat is a mix of Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy X. That sound good to you? Yeah, it is

Ever say "Gods, the encounter rate in this place is insane" Because you get into a battle every 5-10 steps? Well, this game has a system where you can stockpile battles, then use the chrono trigger esque combat system to curve your shots, force enemies to group up, and AOE down your enemies, all while getting exp and items in these giant 3 vs 30/40 brawls

"You get basically no experience and have to grind like crazy" is a common criticism. Literally get good? I am almost level 50, just playing the game normally, and I have not had to grind one. single. time. Not once. There has been exactly one boss that I fought and decided to come back at a higher level, and that is because you encounter it at around level 20 and it's level 48, it's meant to be an end game fight.

The story is linear in the first part, and the second part it opens up and presents as almost open world, but there's an order to it. What is that order, you ask? Check the quest log dudes, it tells you the recommended level.

This is a very casual hidden object type game. The cats are the objects you must find.  I thought the graphics were charming and reminiscent of some of the buildings and scenery I remember seeing in Turkey.  It doesn't have a story, and it isn't timed which makes it good for very casual game play.  It is however very short.  I wasn't trying very hard and finished it in about half an hour.  I liked that you could view the backgrounds in either black & white or in color.  You could easily switch between the two options.  While the somewhat cartoonish line art was fun and a little whimsical, it did lead to cat-like shapes that don't always resemble cats.  Those cat-like shapes are the ones that tend to be a little harder to find.  Being a free to play game I can't complain too much, it was a quick and enjoyable way to reduce stress for me for one afternoon.

I did enjoy that there are achievements and while 100 may seem like a lot for such a little game, you should keep in mind that all of these are progression unlocked (normally I'd say story unlocked ,but again, no story).  You cannot miss any because each cat you find unlocks an achievement for that cat.  If you complete the game you will get all the achievements.  I actually dislike that because I like my achievements to provide a mix of easily obtained and challenging achievements.  There are no additional types of achievements, no secrets, no recognition for completion, nothing for any special actions.  If you just want an easy game to 100% this is great for that but if you want a challenge in any way this isn't it.

Overall, I'd recommend it to anyone that likes cats, appreciates the art style, and/or has a passing interest in the Middle East or Turkey who is just looking for a quick casual game to relax with.

I can't recall ever playing a game with such a clear divide between the good and the bad. Sadly the bad far (far)  outweighs the good, and I cannot give this a positive review.
For starters, it is a very basic tower defense game. There is a minor strategic set of upgrades that you choose randomly, and no tactical attacks. There is no fluff, and no pathing. There is a speed up button, but no ability to pick your towers targets. 
In addition there is a tower cap that you can buy upgrades too, but it never goes over ten.
There are a wide variety of towers, and you can merge same-type gems to upgrade them, 3-1. I have only gotten a few towers to level three, but it seems like there are only twenty levels so there isn't really time to do more. You can continue after level twenty as a form of endless mode. 
There is only one foe, and it is cute, but aside from a little run animation, no effort was made to make things look decent. They only have one angle, running to the right, so they run backwards (?!?) when moving to the left. This seems such a minor thing, but it speaks volumes to how the developer didn't put much effort into this. It almost feels more like a proof-of-concept than a game. 
There is a boss, but he looks exactly like the regular unit, having only a bit more health. 
There seems to be only six maps, and they are all really short. You can play any of them right from the start, so there is no progression of any kind. Blah. 
That said, it is fun to putz with, and I suspect I will get a few hours of fun out of it, so it isn't refund material, and at the current price, it isn't a bad thing, it's just not good enough to recommend. 
I rather hope the developer will put some more effort into this, I love changing negative reviews to positive when a game gets better, but from their comments I have seen elsewhere, it seems really unlikely. 
One thumb down.

Meaning it is not quite perfect. Real-life arguments, like the examples used in the game, rely not just on logic, but also on a body of facts and on preferences.

Depending on the context, a statement may be guilty of the Slippery Slope fallacy or an Appeal to Consequences, or it may be grounded on established facts. Moreover, some statements are border or edge cases, overlapping the fallacy types. It does not help that some of them overlap, such as the Appeal to Motive and the Genetic Fallacy (the difference is to a large extent/often in the subjective issue of how relevant motivation of the allegedly disreputable source is).

The most  glaring imperfection in my opinion is that claiming that something should be done (and not simply tested) because it has never been done before is a fallacy (Appeal to Novelty?) not a logically valid statement. It should be considered a fallacy just like doing things in a certain way only because it is the established way is an Appeal to Tradition.

Having said that, once you learn how to embrace the author's factual and preference standpoints (who are by all means reasonable and open-minded), the game shines. It is not just educational, it manages to be entertaining and challenging and is graphically impressive, You can get at least a couple of hours of good game play (plus the time possibly necessary to take notes and revise the fallacies). And then it can be used to regularly refresh your memory and achieve long term learning.

It is amazingly good and especially entertaining for a solid educational game (despite the limitations above, which are probably less annoying and frustrating than in most logic teachers). And, as a "real game" it is a cute little filler gem to enjoy and to come back to from time to time.

[h1]Things?! What things?!?![/h1]
[b]This review contains no story spoilers[/b]

[h3]Intro[/h3]
Step into the exciting world of a Risk Assessment Data Processor for Terebro, Inc as you 
Take the night shift examining the file of a case sent to you by a supervisor who you only communicate with
Via intercom. As you pour over the details of the case, you uncover a sinister plot at the heart of the companies
Past. One they'd very much like to be kept buried. 

[h3]Visuals and Art Style[/h3]
Visually the game is basic, there's a desk with some crap on it and a nice, nighttime cityscape to look at. Other than that the whole game is confined to this office desk. As the game is set in 1986 it has a nice retro feel to the computer and the radio. It reminds me a lot of Stories Untold (a game you should check out if you enjoyed this). The documents you examine are a mixture of handwritten notes, typed redacted reports and photographs which are unsettling at times and, overall, add to the gradually building tension in the game.

[h3]Sound and Music[/h3]
Sound plays a large role in setting up the atmosphere because, let's face it, there's not a whole lot else going on that'll help. You have two radio stations to listen to for music and another for a solution and that's pretty much it as far as the music goes. Good thing the two stations are quite well done, mixing the ambient music in with the usual banal radio announcements and adverts. What's not well done is the lack of variety in them, over the course of even an hour long playthrough, you'll hear one of the DJ's stories about her car breaking down around seven times. But the radio does fade into the background and doesn't intrude on the gameplay.

[h3]Storyline[/h3]
There's not much of a storyline in Things too Ugly. In part, because it's so short and in part because there's so much left unsaid. As such, I'm going to have to try quite hard not to state any spoilers because it's so easy to ruin whole tracts of the story with a few stray lines.  The story has a lot of vague inferences, shadowy motives and hidden agendas. These two things work against each other to leave the game a but of a hollow experience. You aren't left with much left to mull over after the game ends and what is left could really do with some additional texture. I'm not saying that everything needs to be spelled out but there's so much you're left totally in the dark about. For stories that have as much, if not more, of the narrative left to the players imagination then you have to leave enough explanation in for the imagination to gain traction on. Confusion and bafflement do not inspire any further thinking. The creepyness progresses throughout the cases builds nicely, a bit too quickly, and it could've done with a few more to really nail it. The denouement is both anti-climactic and yet perfectly fitting with the rest of the game due to it's brief nature and lack of any explanation.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The gameplay is basic. You use the arrow keys to look around, and use a mouse and keyboard to examine the files and type in the answers. The puzzles are more complex than your usual standard but aren't anything too taxing. The solutions are made easier to determine as the form the answers take is provided to you. For example, a question asking 
About how to extract an object using a wave generator will ask the verb, the waveform and the frequency stated in the report. A big decision on the gameplay side is the lack of any saving, you fire up Things too Ugly, you've to finish it or redo the whole thing at a later date. This mechanism, for me, didn't ruin anything because the game is so short and has no replay value at all, there would be no need to sit through the whole thing again after you're done.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
In  conclusion, It's difficult to assign any sort of conclusive opinion on a game that's this short. It's, at most a two hour playthrough, I've heard that it's supposed to be a 2 to 5 hour experience but I couldn't imagine anyone spending 5 hours on what little content is here. That said, that little content is really good and definetly left me wanting a lot more. But the unsatisfying ending somewhat spoils what could've been a nice short creepy adventure.

[h2]Quick Review[/h2]
Kingdom Rush 5: Alliance TD uses the same Kingdom Rush formula with a few changes as part of the new alliance system. It’s a cool idea, but honestly, it doesn’t make much of a difference compared to the previous games. It scratches my tower defense itch, but that’s about it. It feels like the series is playing it too safe to make any real changes.
[h2]Key Points[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]What’s New?:[/b] The alliance system lets you team up with Kingdom and Veznan's factions and allows two heroes at the same time, which is neat. But it’s more of a small twist than a big leap forward.
[*][b]The Experience:[/b] Classic Kingdom Rush. Great visuals, smooth gameplay, and all the charm you’d expect. Still, it’s starting to feel a little too familiar.
[*][b]Biggest Letdown:[/b] They didn’t take any risks. The alliance mechanic is nice, but it’s not enough to make this feel fresh or exciting.
[/list]
[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
If you love Kingdom Rush, you’ll have a good time, but don’t expect to be blown away. For newcomers, it’s a fun game, but maybe check out the earlier titles first—they feel just as good, if not better.

[h3] Kingdom Rush franchise falls back on outdated mechanics and relies on nostalgic callbacks and beautiful artwork that makes for a fun and nostalgic, but overall underwhelming experience akin to replaying a reskinned, QOL improved Kingdomrush 2. [/h3] 

I will draw some side to side comparisons to Bloons TD 6, not only because it's a massively successful classic tower defence game with mainstream appeal, but also there was a time where kingdom rush revolutionised the tower defence genre with the melee troops, and for a period of time the "bloons" games seemed old and outdated and "kingdom rush" was the modernised epic tower defence entry, and while bloons seemingly kept improving and adding mechanics both to towers and enemies, kingdomrush seemed to have stagnated, adding variations in enemies only in terms of visual style and movement quirks - to the point the roles have been reversed and BTD6, a game from 6 years ago is way more abundant in modern mechanics and tower defence innovations and near infinitely replayable (I have near 1000 hours on BTD6), while the latest entry of Kingdom rush feels samey, empty and at times frustrating - which feels acceptable as it provides a break to the monotonous moment to moment plays (I have played through the main campaign and will most likely not return.)

 [h3] Lack of fun... [/h3]
 This is not merely a nonconstructive jab at the devs, but it genuinely feels like the Kingdom Rush team is not fully aware of what makes Kingdomrush fun and why fans are drawn to it, let alone the draw of the tower defence genre as a whole. The draw of the tower defence genre is not the micro gameplay of clicking on multiple things and keeping track of various elements on screen and maxing out your apm - there are game genres that do that better - namely MOBAs and RTS games. The draw isn't the character design and visual aesthetic. The draw isn't the story (though i have to say I have a soft spot for ironhide's signature quirkiness and sense of humour). The draw isn't even the victory screen at the end of the game. 
 The main reason people play tower defence games is building up towards an overpowered defence and the dopamine rush of a maxed out Dwarven Artillery tower oneshotting hordes of goblins. 
 Which brings me to probably my biggest complaint about the kingdom rush games is that the games are too short. I find that by the time I've fully upgraded my towers and am just getting ready to enjoy the fun part of the game, the game ends abruptly as if snatching away my reward from the hard work of economy managing and micro-ing. 

 Speaking of Dwarven artillery, one of the main fun-elements the KR games struggle with is the FEEL of towers. The first game was quite good at this, but as the games went on they seemed to struggle to make the towers feel impactful. For example, one of the enemy vaiants they rely heavily on is the "big-hulky-armored-enemy" that will mow down your barrack troops and you require high single-target damage towers (ie. not artillery) of their opposite resistance type to take them down. This is NOT fun. And if you've played any of the KR games, you know i've basically described ALL of their "mini-bosses" as well. Psychologically speaking - ONE artillery tower taking out groups of dozens or hundreds of smaller enemies feels way more powerful and impactful and rewarding rather than 10 towers lasering down a massive chungus, and the healthbar barely moving. 

 BTD6 understands this well. The towers at max upgrade feel POWERFUL, and almost unstoppable, and is fun and rewarding to watch. Some towers are so strong to the point a whole mini-fanbase has spawned around an unofficial community gamemode called 2TC, where you try to beat a map on the hardest difficulty using only 2 towers. 

 This either lack of awareness of or lack of willingness to give the players what is fun to play is maybe the biggest frustration in the franchise and is reflected throughout many of the design choices such as boss battle designs, enemy designs, map designs, etc..

 [h3] Enemy variations [/h3]
 Kingdom rush has 3 main enemy qualities that you can counter using different towers: 
 1. Armored
 2. Magic Resistance
 3. Flying
 This is the same system that the FIRST kingdom rush game from 14 YEARS ago. The other variations boil down to gimmicky movement enemies, super tanky enemies, and varied anti-troop enemies from long ranged assassins to evolving-after-kill monster type enemies (which is incredibly frustrating and undermines one of the main strengths of KR which is the barracks tower and heroes, which contributes to the anti-fun-ness). Although across the 5 games there are probably HUNDREDS of enemy variations combined - as you can probably tell from the way i'm describing them, none of these enemies are memorable because of the way they just blend into generic "types" with separates them that requires meaningful counter strategy.
  Compared to BTD6 enemy immunities - qualities that require unique counter strategies:
  Lead (explosion), Camo (invis), White (Freeze immune), Black (Explosion immune}, Purple (Magic immune), MOAB (Super tanky earlygame, but easily 1-shot by specialised towers in the late game) 
 A game where your enemy is a wave of sentient BALLOONS feels like it has more complexity despite having exponentially less enemy variations simply by having more damage resistance types and tower types. Which is the biggest take away here. KR HAS experimented with and still utilise unique resistance types such as invisibility, explosion resistance, etc. But cannot commit to it and reserve it as a one off portion of the campaign because of an outdated core tower design philosophy of 4 tower types - magic, sharpshooter, artillery, barracks.

[h3] Tower Limits [/h3] 
 Limiting the player to 5 - previously 4 towers per game. There is literally no reason for this except maybe for simplicity's sake of UI, but having 10+ tower variations and only being able to play 5 at a time is a hefty price to pay for simplicity. 

 [h3] Free tower placement [/h3]
KR has maybe the most restrictive tower defence placement system where they go for preset tower placement slots, as opposed to other games in the genre that opt for free placement or grid placement. As the games go on, it feels like in an attempt to make the game more challenging, these tower spots are more in awkwards positions or have less spots overall.  

[h3] Minor complaints [/h3]
- Heroes and towers unlock too late: Heroes are possibly the coolest parts of KR games that usually fit very well into the setting and with unique personalities, but most of the heroes and towers are locked until extreme late game/until you have beaten the campagin? KR, with its campaign map style, inherently lacks replayability to have heroes and towers locked until so late. 
- No true endless: I know frontiers and possibly one other entry had an endless mode? But with the previous point of only having 5 towers to choose from, it is quite limiting and also the gamemodes seem to get exponentially harder very quickly to the point it feels like it DOESN'T want you to be playing for long, and you rarely get to play until you have lategame towers - just feels pointless as an endless gamemode. 
- No economy: You rarely get to the phase you have fully upgraded towers with fully upgraded abilities, and the fact that there is no economy towers in the any of the KR games adds to this point. Funnily enough there are abilities that provide you gold but it is such a trivial amount that seems like it's there to add flavour and just feel tragic. 

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]
 As it stands, Kingdom Rush 5 feels like a flash game developed a decade ago boxed in a time capsule and released in 2025, and is not worth the price.
 The 6th installment of Bloons Tower Defence feels like their Magnum Opus, and I am holding out hope that Kingdom Rush 6 will be their best.

[h1] PROS :D [/h1]

Game is really fun! Simple, fun, effective. I mean it's a modernisation of 1980s Space Invader formula, and for the price it's [i]extremely[/i] well crafted. Works on my shitty laptop :D

[h1] CONS :( [/h1]

It's really hard though :(
It's so random you can just get pooped on by the game. Random upgrade options, random waves, random enemies that give you huge bonuses.

You can be doing really well and the game will just be like >:D [i] hehe [/i] "[b]NO[/b]"

Like getting the super bonus for not letting anything get to the floor and then it can just send waves of enemies that are very very very difficult (for me) to prevent reaching the floor even with nukes (Curse you Cheval >:(  ). You lose the bonus, which means you lose upgrade points, which means you may as well restart because to get further you're going to really need those early upgrades. So have fun doing the start of the game over and over again.

[h2] It's good tho :) [/h2]

Destructible platforms from OG space invaders that help people that want the Conservation Bonus? Upgrades to make them regen or resist damage? Basically, very good game, hard game, more upgrades please.

This was such a vibe! I've been putting off getting this one, because it seemed too generic. Minutes in, however, I saw a game that's closer to "Fears to Fathom" or "Chilla's Art" than "Slender" or "Granny".

Yes, of course: it's a budget title and it shows. The models are stiff, some design choices aren't optimal, the sound mixing needs more time in the oven and the controls are a tad awkward. But there's so much care put into this regardless: choices made with QA in mind, a ton of overdesigned, little things that are obviously born from passion and some little details that serve as great, albeit basic worldbuilding.

The game, vibin', explorin' and geting both endings, takes about 4 hours, which I find is pretty fair for the asked price. What's more: I'd totally play it again for the fun of it. Because it's not stressful. Spooky? Sure! But the player is allowed to earn moments of safety, which let me play this at my own pace and that I truly appreciated.

Honestly at this point it checks almost every box I look for in a survival game:

Responsive fun gameplay

Good graphics

High difficulty but nothing to crazy. There are settings to make it easier and harder. I'm on normal across all settings and the game feels generally balanced.

Horde nights

Fitting music. You have your fantasy exploration stuff, battle tracks, and the gloomier horror tracks that play at night that gets your skin crawling.

Light to medium grinding but nothing ridiculous

Punishing death but nothing to extreme. Losing my magic bar hurts a lot but it's something I can recover from while at the same time it really makes me try to avoid death as much as possible.

Tons and tons of exploration without areas feeling like empty wastelands 

Enemy variety

Gear checking (rings, amulets, armors, weapon and weapon variety, potions) it goes a bit light. There is only one armor path but there are multiple weapon archetypes and their paths. Weapons, potions,powders, food balancing,rings, and amulets will be where the bulk of building your setup is. Each weapon archetype has its built in magic attack and your usual slashing, piercing, and blunt damage. 

Fantasy setting

Every area has its own unique set of enemies with each having their own varied attacks that separate them from the others in the game

Changing world(s)

Farming

Smithing

Crafting

Leatherworking

Mining

Animal husbandry goes pretty light here but it's something you can still interact with that requires your attention

Tons of cooking - for real though, the amount of recipes here are pretty crazy. They're needed though as variety in food is how you get your permanent stat upgrades. Food functions as both to fill your food meter and to balance traits. The food bar is almost never a issue so it's mostly about building your permanent stats up while managing hunger on the side.

Tons of combat

A level up system i've never seen done before like this and I wish other games adopted the trait food leveling system in this game.

Good design in general really

Less bugs than starship troopers - I experienced 2 or 3 bugs but they fixed them within 20 minutes to a few short days.

A developer that really seems to actually care about what they put out. They're tinkering with the game lately but nothing that negatively impacts the fun. if anything they've strived to build some great quality of life features onto the systems the game shipped with. Larger item stacks, bug fixes, audio fixes, etc.

The only negative thing I can say at this point is I just want more content but I shouldn't get to greedy since i'm 20+ hours in (I'm expecting to get at least 6 more hours based on still having at least one more world to unlock that'll have its own set of gear, maps, and challenges) and only paid around 5$ for this. Well that and no custom keybindings but at this point i've built some muscle memory with the built in keybindings so that's not really a issue anymore.

This is currently my favourite game (ok, got it recently and have a life, so didn’t clock many hours...yet). It scratches the exact itch I have. You have your base area where you are safe (other than when in nightmare), where you can do you “chores” like building/farming/crafting/fishing etc. You head out to find treasure and challenge. As you progress you take your base area with you and expand with new features. Combat was initially hard for me (I’m not good at it), so I soon started an “easy” save (it’s not trivial though!) - I’m already excited to start over with the default difficulty. Love the cooking/eating/attributes system (read the guide posted by the dev). Farming is “limited” but in a good way (I would cover the whole are with wheat otherwise). The animal handling (bees, rabbits and chickens) has a nice simple system. Storage/inventory system is a perfect balance - you have generous specialised storage (in places you’d expect and you can craft/use items from whenever in your base) and although your inventory isn’t unlimited, it’s not punishing or in your way. I feel that a lot of thought went into balance generally throughout. Nothing feels random but rather meaningful. You don’t have total freedom where things are in your base but it works for me as I’m always struggling with layout. Graphics is of course a matter of taste, but like what I see. UI is very polished, very comfortable to use. Music is great. I generally don’t like “raids” on my base, prefer where I decide where to meet danger but you can scale it down, where it’s not stressful and you know when they’ll happen - so I was surprised that it didn’t bother me. So far the fact that nothing respawns (as far as I could see) isn’t a problem at all (on the contrary - it makes you feel you "completed" an area). It’s not too grindy, but you can make it so if you like it.
I never write reviews but I’m so positively surprised by this gem that I hope more people will notice it and give it a chance.

okay this time i can do a real review
i found this game by sorting by release date for all steam games. i looked through ten pages and most of them looked lame! i ended up only trying two. this was one of them.
it initially got my interest because:
- rpgmaker mv
- weird aspect ratio
- hey thats the omori mechanic
truth be told i was really not expecting too much, in recent years i have seen a ton of people try to do some stuff after playing undertale and omori and things of that sort and i think its hard to escape those comparisons when the inspiration is worn so clearly, and they usually don't do the smaller game well. this is me speaking as someone who has done that as well by the way.
pair that with the amateur-looking art and i think clossure does not advertise itself well, BUT
but,
that was just my assumptions going into it. i did actually play it believe it or not

and here's what i'm feeling out of the gate, two huge things make this game very distinct for me in the first few minutes. first is aku(ma). i'll be real, i don't like the guys name/design very much but he is funny and going to his little website was pretty awesome. always a big fan of those.
second is the first time i got in combat with the guy, hot damn, that collage stuff for the enemies is awesome. aku and the queen in particular, whatever they got going on is super badass but it works very well for the normal enemies too.
speaking of the art, i did knock it a little earlier but there are some other places where it really shines too. i think the tileset, especially in the sanctuary, is really solid. cassey's sprites, both in the overworld and in battle, are really the only thing that bother me. kodi is great though.
there are a pretty good amount of CGs and while they aren't billion dollar illustrations they look nice and are clearly high-effort. whole game is pretty high effort with the large tileset and especially the way the castle music progresses as you go onward, its super cool. it seems to have lyrics in japanese, but there were a lot of words that i couldn't make out or just sounded like gibberish. lyrics somewhere would be cool
the whole ost is pretty neat but that part is the standout for sure.

so about the gameplay
there's a couple things i do like and a couple things i don't like.
to get the simple stuff out of the way first, i don't think it's good when you can grind infinitely, and it really takes the value out of exp and messes with the flow of the game. random encounters go with this, it never feels good to just get stopped and roped into a battle without any way to know it's coming or avoid it. really kills my motivation to explore. i equipped the charm that reduces random encounter chance as soon as i got it, and then only fought like two more random enemies before the game ended, which i don't think is a great solution either. i didn't have any trouble with the queen but i would have liked to get any new moves at all for kodi before the credits rolled!
i'll have some positive things to say but first as for cassey's gimmick, the emotion system, well, sunny had it better.
i already thought that enemies only being locked to the first level of an emotion in omori was missed potential, but here, enemies innately have an immutable emotion. it's much closer to fire/water/grass typed pokemon than anything versatile, except it doesn't seem like kodi can get emotions and cassey can change their emotion as an instant. even the queen that will always try to get type advantage is made ineffective when switching is free.
basically, it's kind of a pointless mechanic that always guarantees that the player will have type advantage, and the only depth to it is the skill changes that come by switching. this is not a bad idea though!
the idea of having a versatile moveset based on state can lead to interesting situations and was something i've explored before, albeit shallowly. i think the emotion system would work a lot better if there was more nuance to how you changed between states, and also maybe if enemies either also could or they just didn't have it at all.
maybe you've got like three bars that fill up when certain things are done (getting hit/dealing damage/healing/using sp/etc), and when one fills, the others deplete and you get that emotion. maybe.
anyway i think the double turn item is great. "s-useless" is the best move in the game by a long shot and i realized that in this chapter there is not much reason to switch off sadness.

and finally i wanted to give a shoutout to the
secret route!?
unfortunately i did not find all the cards i needed for it but hm yes this goes in my book as "awesome". if the gameplay were more compelling i would have easily done a second run to make it happen but alas, i simply opened the game in rpgmaker myself. i'll get a save file with it properly when the next chapter releases i suppose!

Fatal Falls is an indie psychological horror game with a lot of ambition, but unfortunately, its execution falls short in some areas (no pun intended). While it has an intriguing premise and some moments of genuine tension, for instance in the sewers-like chapter, the game has a few issues.

1. Puzzles
Some are well-designed and even embedded in well-written dialogues, but others rely too much on backtracking or finding tiny, hard-to-spot details in dimly lit environments.

2. Inventory
The way items are handled is clunky. Certain objects don’t save correctly across chapters, and using something like a battery for the camcorder feels like it was tacked on rather than a meaningful survival mechanic.

3. Performance
The game runs smoothly in some areas but chugs in others, especially during the later chapters. It feels unoptimized, with occasional stuttering and frame drops despite good hardware.

Fatal Falls has potential, but it feels like a game that’s trying too hard to be deep without refining the core gameplay. The horror elements are undercut by tedious puzzles. However, if you love psychological horror, a decent story and are patient enough to deal with its flaws, you might find something worth experiencing.
Finally a horror game that doesn't rely on cheap jumpscares but actually has an interesting, deeply unsettling story. The puzzles are quite difficult though, I had to use a guide.

As far as idle games go, Astrodle is fine. For a few bucks, I got 14 hours of game out of this, playing through once in each of the active/passive modes, 100%'ing both times, with a couple of hours of idling in the latter playthrough being the only real inflation of my time.

It's strengths lie in its presentation, the fairly flawless execution of its well-tread idea, and it's got some novel ideas, especially in the small differences in how you gather some of the resource types -- a few of these are novel good, one is particularly novel bad.

Personally, my recommendation hinges entirely on how idle vs. incremental you like your games. If you like to set things up and watch number go up, then Astrodle is definitely worth the couple bucks it takes to experience.  From the interface to the gameplay, every inch is a well-polished, shiny delight, with a lot of data available to the player that I wish other incremental games could take cues from. It dips its toes into a combo system, gives shades of player expression, but mostly it's a relatively satisfying and familiar loop of harvest - upgrade - prestige - repeat that we all well know, without any real twists on the formula.

But if you're in this genre for something more interactive and incremental instead of idle, then give Astrodle a skip. It's no Orb of Creation or Crank; what you see is what you will always get.

I feel like this is a good strategy game with very weird choices for the meta structure of moving between fights. There is no time limit on how long you can spend just roaming around clearing fights, the enemies only get stronger. How much stronger? No clue. I have no idea how much easier or harder this game would have been had I spent more (or less time) before the final fight.

 The game is also not particularly challenging. I was able to beat all four stages of the 'balanced' difficulty (the easiest one was reccomended and the last two were locked) first try. The ability to retreat from combat, losing some of the cards in the process is nice and has saved me multiple times from forgetting to bring a card that can damage the enemy boss

I feel like there are probably some interesting pathing options on the map for getting a good deck, someting I did multiple times was to hunt down the boss that  moves the move 1 forward item and combine that with riders. But you don't need those if the game isn't hard, you can just collect everything and then build good decks when you need them.

The game also doesn't do a very good job of explaining itself, combat was initially very confusing,
and the meta structure is more confusing still. If you defeat the king, you start over with a new objective. This time you will have to help a spider queen first, new objectives and cards in new locations are added upon each clear up to the final and fourth clear. That is cool, but I do not know what happens when you die. Initally I thought that you would keep the unlocked things, but the fact that the game seems to treat it as one run (it says new run with no option to continue on the main screen now that I defeated the king a fourth time) makes me think you might start over at ascension 0, losing the run.

The rations never ran out, I think their purpose is to force you to take some combats (you can get cards just by looting graveyards as well).

Being able to adapt the deck to every single combat is an unusual design decision and I like it (for this game). It brings variety into the deck building and allows the devs to add more distinct encounters.

Run lengths are something I can say little about, my run consisting of 4 repetitions (or 1 playthrough and 3 repetitions, words mean whatever you want them to) took about 8 hours in total (had the game open for another 4 hours without playing), but I have no idea whether a more optimized run would take longer (to farm more powerful 1 time use items for strong encounters) or shorter, because you need none of that and beating the king is what matters.

I am still going to reccommend the game, as the game has taken some risks in multiple aspects of its design, overall succeeds in many and that makes for an interesting roguelike to play.
