While I don't personally have an issue playing a gender-locked MC, I know that some people hate it. I don't think that is a good reason to avoid a story that sounds interesting to you, nor do I think it should be given a negative review because of it. Some people have clearly been spoiled a little too much and feel some sense of entitlement because of it, I suppose. 

Alas, that aside, that isn't why I disliked These Thieving Hearts. 

Being an avid fan of interactive fiction I'm constantly on the lookout for something new, something exciting, something different (there is only so much high school drama and/or 'you've just learnt of the supernatural world - ah scawy' a person can handle). I say this to imply that I believe my standards are higher than the average person.

Sadly These Thieving Hearts didn't resonate with me how I hoped it would. The story starts with our MC arriving at his new client's house to be briefed, although vaguely, on the potential job. They call it 'The Thieves Demise'. It is basically a legend for the thief community and is said to be the hardest trials any thief will have to encounter. Managing to get even one of the items on the list will shower that person with recognition (as much as one can receive in a job done in the shadows at least). Upon agreeing you are sent off to meet your team, some of whom you already know and have worked with previously. A short debriefing later that, once again, offers next to no insight and you are being sent off to claim the first item, which is apparently in a vault in some random rich guy's house. 

An item that is supposed to be nearly impossible to steal... is just there... in some guy's house. 

And granted, it is as easy to steal as it sounds. 

Arriving at your destination, most of the interactions will be descriptions of the location, hardly anything in detail, and then you are given options. Play to your strengths via your stats will grant you a way forward and this will repeat for another few steps before you claim your prize. Fail your stat check at any point and one of your teammates will pick up your slack before the same outcome occurs. None of this makes for an exciting read. It isn't thrilling, it isn't nail-biting and it isn't inspired.

However, I carried on reading anyway with the hope that things would pick up a bit on the second mission. They did not.

After retrieving the first item from the thieves demise list you and your team are stuffed into a private jet to your next location. Yet again, the details about the item are vague at best. The very same night you are sent out to hunt down the second object. This time to a place that had been sunk underwater and harbours a few 'deadly' traps. Yet again, play to your strengths and walk through the whole place as if it were a calming stroll through the park on a tranquil day. 

Honestly, at this point, I wondered what the point was of having a team. Doing things correctly basically sees you conquering these so-called 'tough trials' on your own. Both of these missions were over in a span of a few pages. 

Retiring for the night was the most pointless thing I have ever read. It was already established that you and your team would be staying at a hotel that night, and yet, for some reason, filler text about a lightning storm grounding your plane was added. You get the option to speak to one of your teammates that night, barely exchanging much dialogue before going to sleep. This would have been a great opportunity to get to know who you are working with. Just because the MC knows two of the three other members, we as readers know nothing. Heck, it would have been a great time to explain why the MC is so sought after for this job and why everyone claims him to be the best since this information has failed to be provided to us so far. 

By this point, chapter four is about to start and I've had enough. Each chapter is so short and feels rushed and unfulfilling. Most other stories are still establishing key points, introducing characters and setting up the world by this word count. I did not feel immersed, excited, or willing to continue from here. 

I'm sure this will be to some people's tastes, it was just not for me.

Parasite Flower was a surprisingly quick play. I enjoyed it, but because it's over so quickly it's difficult to get fully engrossed and the repetitive, groundhog-day like style works well for the theme, but reduces the substance of the actual game.

That being said, the art carries Parasite Flower - it's hauntingly beautiful. If you're in the habit of picking up games just because the art speaks to you, this game is great, and by all means please get it. If you're looking for a more substantial game with a plot, or characters, or anything of the sort, this game might not be all that for you. Regardless, I thought it was a worthwhile buy to support an artist, and I understand the length of the game is common for indie projects like this one.

Art style aside, this game does offer some great commentary on the topics it covers; it sets a tone (in a very short time) and manages to balance subtlety with horror quite well, which I liked. It does a nice job of depicting the what-to-anyone-else-might-be-normal situations in the eyes of someone with trauma. It leaves plenty of hints for the player to piece together parts of Ari's story, and yet leaves so much for one to question - this might be a negative for some, and a positive for others. I enjoy this method of storytelling and certainly feel that it fits this type of game, but again, this will not result in a satisfying play for everyone.
Audio-wise I found it enjoyable, too. The contrast between dreadful and peaceful elements was great and the instrumentals set the tone wonderfully.



I am likely mirroring other reviews when I say this, but Parasite Flower was a great game art-wise, a fair game content-wise, and perhaps a bit lacking gameplay-wise. I highly recommend it, just wish it was longer. For a game that's around 3 bucks, though, I am not complaining.
And if you do get the game, heed the content warnings.

Hadley’s Run is a pretty solid twin stick shooter. The controls are responsive and once you’ve learned their moves the enemies are not brutally unfair but they are not always a push over. Although the game runs on the easier side there were moments during the later parts of the game that gave me some trouble. The characters are cool and their unique dialogue each run makes you feel like you made some progress even if you lost a little early. There is a decent amount of variety to the parts that can be attached to your ship, I mixed and matched until I found the combo that I used the rest of the game. Environmental hazards shake up the gameplay and keep it decently fresh through the entire game. The inclusion of an endless mod was a nice touch. 

Took me about 5 hours to beat the campaign, did not play much after that unfortunately. Where the game is hurting the most is the enemy variety, especially bosses. There are about 10 different enemy types and you get the dame boss after each area every time. After killing the bosses over and over they begin to get a little stale. Rather then creating new bosses or enemies which I understand can be time consuming, slight tweaks could be made to the existing ones. A good example of this would be the Champion enemies from the “Binding of Issac” where it is the same enemy but they move a little faster, they have a vacuum that sucks you in, they have a ‘combat inhibitor’ and you can only hit them from a distance. Just little things like that could improve the replay value. Same with the bosses, instead of making more change their attack phases. Instead of Phase 1, Phase 2, Phase 3 it goes in a different order. Maybe the player can chose to face a more difficult boss that is a bit faster for a greater reward, there is already an option for normal areas so I believe it makes sense for the boss areas as well. Another thing that could improve replayability is incentivising the player to use other builds, because once I found a build I liked I never switched off of it. So perhaps their weapon has a “run cooldown” or the guy who upgrades your ship worked on the weapon you haven’t used in a while so if you start a run with that weapon you get an upgrade right off the bat. 

Even though I just wrote a big paragraph with a bunch of critiques I still had a lot of fun running through Hadley’s Run, and I would recommend it to any fan of twin stick shooters.

This is honestly one of the least enjoyable roguelikes I have ever played, and I have played a fair few at this point.

I don't mind difficult games. But the difficulty needs to be balanced by a sense of incremental progression - especially if you lose hard-won resources and have to restart from scratch - and that is almost completely absent in this game. Upgrading your town is the only thing that you keep across runs, and that takes multiple upgrades, which demand a large amount of resources that take a lot of time to collect...and which you lose instantly if you die. The feeling of wasted effort is so strong when playing this that it overrides any sense of satisfaction you might be able to get from finally completing one of those goals. 

It's a very cute-looking game that plays brilliantly on the Steam Deck, and a lot of thought has clearly been put into its mechanics. But it feels like such a waste of time when the gains are so incremental and so easily lost, and when you often don't have sufficient resources to explore farther than a few steps away from your home. This needs some kind of relaxed mode, or a better fast travel system, or just something to make progression more rewarding. Maybe it just didn't click with me, or I'm missing something, but this feels far too punishing for its own good.

Unfortunately, I don't think I can recommend The Witch based on my playthrough.

Pros: Looks and runs quite well on Steamdeck, with some adjustment to resolution, graphics quality and sensitivity (though some fonts remain hard to read); atmospheric, interesting locations; a couple of effective jumpscares; story was just about intriguing enough for me to feel invested in getting to the end.

Cons: Incredibly difficult to see anything by the torch's tiny beam, particularly when navigating tight spaces; lack of meaningful events at each checkpoint (it really just felt like I was carrying items from point A to point B, without much happening in between); dialogue loops that overwrite each other and give misleading guidance; no real puzzles or challenges (just finding items etc); awkward item targetting, which can end up selecting items behind you instead of the thing you're looking at; confusing plot events and conclusion.

My overriding feeling is that the game felt uneventful and underwhelming: I spent most of it waiting to see more of the titular Witch, but then it ended, and I'm really not sure what her part in the whole story was meant to be. I'm not sure if the game is intended to have multiple endings (if it is, I don't know what would trigger them), but the ending I experienced felt like a disappointing anti-climax.

It definitely shows some promise - the atmosphere and settings are quite good, despite a lot of invisible walls etc - and I'd be interested to see more from this developer in the future. I think approaching The Witch with tempered expectations - and taking advantage of a sale - might be the best way to experience it.

I really wanted to post a positive review, but receiving a game like this for 9 euros makes me kind of upset. 

Positives:
- Cute art style
- Nice sound effects
- Fun gameplay loop
- Very cool idea for a game

Negatives:
- The days pass by way too quickly for the game to be relaxing
- There's no automation, you have to keep doing the same tasks over and over, and the more time passes, the more you need to do every day. It's very overwhelming after a few hours.
- The Market is horribly designed, it is literally just one list of all items. I wish they added different categories and the images of the items
- The quests are boring. They are literally just 'make x amount of this' 'buy x amount of upgrades', I wish they added something more fun
- Having to continuously buy medication/wrapping paper is annoying, there could be some kind of shortcut for these kinds of items
- There's no way to know which sheep is the oldest, I just randomly butchered them - I still have no idea what determines the amount of meat they drop
- Vegetables and meat spoiling is annoying and also makes no sense when everything else stays good forever
- Some items have no use once you unlock something better and there's not much late game content.

Overall, I think it is a great and innovative idea, but the game feels so unpolished and unfinished. It feels more like playing a demo than an actual fully released game. I am having fun with it, but it could be much better and I don't feel like I received an equal value to the money I spent on it.

You remember DOTA 2 Autochess? Remember how it was a fad for a couple of months, had dozens of clones made, and then just kinda faded into the ether once everyone realized there was no real strategy and it was just a slot machine? Giltsteader is that for tower defense games.

Everything in Giltsteader is a slot machine. You put money into the slot machine to get a random tower, and can combine two towers of the same type to get a different but slightly better random tower. There's no strategy here: you can only move towers that are max rank, and doing so is prohibitively expensive, so it's better to simply continue dumping your quarters into the slot machine and hope you hit that big payoff.

The game also has a side thing where you put down seeds that sell for random prices so that you can get more quarters to dump in the tower slot machine, which I think primarily exists to give you something to do while you watch your randomly gambled towers do random damage to random enemies.

And just like my idiot cousin, who dumps $20 at a time on sixteen-leg NFL parlays and has never, ever won, this game is unwinnable but for sheer luck. The last two waves are a massive difficulty spike, and while there is an option to "invest" for those waves, you won't have enough time to gamble all that money away before the wave is over.

"Tower Doomer" is an engaging indie game that invites players to destroy a tower while managing a point quota. Developed by a solo creator, it combines strategic decision-making with action-packed gameplay, offering a satisfying experience at an affordable price.

Gameplay

The gameplay in "Tower Doomer" is intuitive: players must carefully choose their weapons and angles of attack to maximize damage while staying within the defined point limit. The controls are easy to pick up, but the strategic depth reveals itself as players progress through the levels. Every decision matters, making each playthrough unique and engaging.

Graphics and Sound Design

The graphics are colorful and stylized, creating a lighthearted and enjoyable atmosphere. The animations for explosions and falling debris are satisfying, enhancing the visual impact. While the soundtrack isn’t groundbreaking, it effectively complements the action and immerses players in the game.

Areas for Improvement

However, the game could benefit from a few improvements. The variety of weapons and levels, while present, could be expanded to prevent a sense of monotony over time. Additionally, a multiplayer mode could have added an extra layer of competitiveness and fun, encouraging players to challenge each other.

Conclusion

Overall, "Tower Doomer" is a solid game crafted by a solo developer. It’s an enjoyable experience worth the modest price of $2.59. With its engaging gameplay and charming visuals, it's a great choice for those looking to have fun while strategically plotting their tower destruction!

Procedurally generated minesweeper with a board that might as well be limitless is a neat concept, as is adding multiplayer with everyone making their individual mark on the board.  
  
If you play it like normal minesweeper, this game is a nice way to just keep going forever. In practice, however, the game is hamstrung by a single feature--a single change from the rules of the original minesweeper--that makes it way too easy. You see, in original versions of Minesweeper, clicking a number that already has all its mines flagged will automatically reveal the remaining tiles. In "Let's Minesweeper," however, clicking a number will also automatically flag mines. It's a small change, but it's one that saps the thought from the game and ensures a strategy of "mindlessly click border numbers to keep automatically marking flags." Once you realize that small mechanics change exists, the wonder of "It's cool to see all these people good at minesweeper clearing vast swathes of the board" is gone, replaced by "Oh, the people on the leaderboard are probably just simplistic bots clicking every border number because that's literally the only strategy you need in this version."

-Translation is iffy at best

It's unclear whether this is just a hastily ported mobile game or if they will eventually drop ads on you, because you come across little treasure chests on the map. In London, with only a few pounds in me wallet, I purchased some water and food and took on the most modest contract on offer.  Then, on a fresh sunny morning, I  deployed the tops, the jib, the stay and the main, and set out in my trim little sloop.  When I got to the channel, a storm brewed up.    Not what a poor sailor needed.  

Leaving little sail deployed, I  struggled through the nearly blinding rain, lightening crossing the sky, and tried not to capsize, eventually heading south.

I was very happy when, after a patient struggle and through the rain, I glimpsed the French coast drawing near.    The sun was sinking, but I had not.  The rain was growing weaker, and so was I.   I removed all sail and dropped both anchors just off the coast.   Then it was at last time to sleep.  When I awoke, the storm had passed and the sun was up.  But the wind was faint.  

I can, and must, sail this thing.  But lacking enough wind to turn her, I dropped the anchor away and used the winch to point her south.  But the wind didn't pick up all day.  A sailor doesn't always get everything he wants.

I won't be giving up (and needless to say I surely won't be refunding).  There's a lot to like here already, and I take this game seriously, and I think the game merits that.

Just checking at a glance, but when compared to the PS3 HD release (which I've played both on hardware and emulated, as well as the original Dreamcast port) these are absolutely bonuses:

- don't have to deal with native PS3 input lag (doubly so for PS3 emulation, which was also buggy and graphically didn't emulate properly)
- multiple ship selection, which adds some extra replay fun
- more advanced training that (finally) allows you to practice parts of stages, including bosses (the original ps3 training was really just a port of the dreamcast's training, which was purely stage select), change rank level, etc. It's not save states but it's a huge improvement over how G.Rev ports generally implement training.
- shows rank in game in a rudimentary way (though G.Rev games don't have wild rank swings so it's not incredibly important, just useful for training purposes)
- New arrange of New Order mode, which I haven't played but it's there.

whether or not you think it comes up to the price is up to you, It's not an M2 port, but to actually get one of the best stgs of the 21st century off the PS3 is worth it enough for me

First, you can actually play this port with a keyboard, you don't really need a controller. It says "controller required" and even a popup warns you that you need one, but you don't. The keyboard and control settings are a bit "unusual" and somewhat convoluted: you need to assign a keyboard key to each "controller button" in the keyboard settings and then set which action each "controller button" does in the separate controller setting. You set the keyboard keys with a "carousel selector", going key by key, instead of pressing them, but on the controller settings you actually press them.

Second, this is a good port, I'm playing it in a 12 year old computer without any issues so far. It only stutters when YOU die. I'm not sure if I’m remembering correctly, but I think this also happened in the Dreamcast. It's probably a design choice so you can clearly see what killed you, as it freezes for a fraction of a second the last frame before you explode.

Finally, this is among the finest games in the entire shmup genre, and the best one available on Steam. It has excellent, fast paced gameplay with nice, sober graphics (dated, but nice) and excellent music. The explosions are very satisfying and it has a semi realistic setting with cool mechanical designs, ships, tanks, etc. This is the game I always recommend to people who want to get into shmups for the first time, as it's a very refined game that is not overwhelmingly difficult. This is a great masterpiece that we can finally play on PC. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who wants to get into shoot em ups for the first time and to any shmup fans who haven’t played it yet.

Whether you played this on dreamcast or played the xbox 360/ps3 version you know that this game's music is amazing and the mechanics were very unique for its time. Some compared it to zero gunner in terms of maneuvering your helicopter. For those who are unaware, you essentially pivot your helicopter at certain angles to be able to hit enemies. From a 1 credit clear perspective personally, the original arcade mode is hard as nails in fact might be one of the hardest shmups i've cleared. Took me a while to get used to the game but that's mainly a skill issue. In the original arcade mode you have no power ups and no extends. So its difficulty mainly derives from you having to pretty much no miss half of the game lol. 

As you can see, there are new modes like new order which i believe was in the previous iteration and new order plus which offers a wider screen with different rules. There's also different helicopters to fit your style. Honestly, this is probably my most favorite grev game next to border down. ( I love some strania too). This isn’t really a proper review as I’m super biased about it but please try this game. Every person who loves shmups should play this game at least once.

Fun ass game that offers a pretty good challenge.

Mechanics:
- Typical auto fire offering.
- Typical bomb stock that makes you invincible and does massive damage to the screen.
- One of your auto-firing weapons will automatically target ground enemies. A minor mechanic, but ground units can be blocked by environment objects, requiring you to reposition to hit them.
- You can pick up one of three "Options." A vulcan machine gun "drone" that fires in one direction for a time, a cannon "drone" that targets and shoots enemies for a time, and a large rocket that does a lot of damage in an area. These options can be charged by not firing your auto weapon. Once charged, you press the auto fire button to activate. The Option will the last for a set amount of time and cooldown before you can activate it again. Each option has its own cooldown and charge time, with the machine gun being the fastest and the rocket the slowest.
- Your helicopter can also angle slightly to the left or right. You do this by moving in a direction while not auto firing. Once you auto fire, your helicopter locks into whatever position it was facing. This is a bit awkard and takes some getting used to because to re-center your ship, you have to let go of movement and auto fire for a moment.
- There are multiple helicopters to choose from. I haven't played with all of them enough to know the ins and outs of their differences, but I do know at least one of them played slightly different.

Scoring:
Fairly typical stuff. You kill enemies for score. There are some special enemies in each stage that help contribute to your score at the end of the stage. The quicker you beat the boss and less bombs you use the better. If you pick up the same Option you already have equipped, you get a 5000 point bonus. Option pick-ups will remain on screen and rotate between the three options, allowing you to save them for scoring.

The most unique part of scoring is that when you kill an enemy using an option, you get double the score. You will factor this into your strategy as to which weapons you use and when you will use them.

My only gripe with the game is some projectiles/obstacles are not very obvious. For example, the first boss shoots some tiny, white rockets at you while also shooting the typical orange/red bullets. It took me a few deaths to realize what was hitting me.

Having played the original Dreamcast version years ago, I was pretty happy to hear this was coming to Steam. The end result was worth the wait. The visuals still hold up nicely (especially the smoke and "shockwave" effect of bigger explosions), the music is good with multiple soundtracks to choose from, the controls are crisp and quick to respond to your controller input, and there's a new 16x9 widescreen mode called "New Order" that changes things up a bit in terms of enemies and whatnot. There's also a pretty nice selection of helicopters to choose from on top of the original helicopter, each with its own main weapon system to try out.

As for the game itself, it's a solid "into-the-screen" isometric shmup. With 5 levels to play through, you have several weapons to choose from as you attack enemies in the air and on the ground. These are Vulcan (rapid fire), cannon (slower, but does more damage), and rocket (still slower, but it explodes and does damage over a bigger area). These are on top of the constant weapon your helicopter always has (which is basically twin vulcan guns). You also get bombs to use, which fill the screen with explosions and cause a good bit of damage to air and ground enemies.

The helicopter has an interesting movement setup, in that when you're not firing, it will angle to the left when you move left, or right when you move right. And when you fire, it stays locked at that angle until you stop firing again. This angling can be inverted, so that the helicopter angels in the opposite direction you move (i.e. if you move right, it angles to the left, and vice versa). You also get a perk for not firing constantly in the form of an temporary option that you can spawn, which fires whichever special weapon you have (vulcan, rocket or cannon). As I said, it's temporary though, and it goes away after a short time. And when it's gone, it has to recharge for a bit before you can summon another one. Add in some scoring bonuses here and there (like trying to destroy 100% of the enemies), a hi score online system, an art gallery, and some wallpapers to use when playing the original arcade mode (which is 4x3), and there's a lot to like with this game.

In the end, this is a solid, enjoyable shmup that's well put together (not surprising, since it was done by G.rev). It's also not a cakewalk, even on Easy. And with the extra modes, OSTs, and helicopters, it's got more to offer than the Dreamcast version, or even the PS3/360 re-release. So if you like flying a chopper and blowing up everything that isn't you, I think this game will scratch that itch pretty nicely for you.

Just a few weeks ago I happened to play through the original Sega Naomi (2005) and Sega Dreamcast (2006) versions of this game and also played the Japanese Switch version (2024) at that time, while having played both the 360 (2012) and PS3 (2012) versions in the past. So with all these games reasonably fresh in my memory I can say none of these versions are that different from each other -- the Naomi version was the original, the Dreamcast version added a practice mode, then the 360 and PS3 versions from 2012 were called Under Defeat HD, added a new mode, music, and control options, and are very similar to these modern PC/Switch/Xbox/PS versions. And that is my book report on Under Defeat version history.

As for the game itself, it was G.Rev's second shmup after the cult classic Border Down, which unfortunately still hasn't seen a home port since the Dreamcast days. That game already seemed a little more grounded in terms of artwork compared to your average shump, and here they really take that to the extreme -- pretty much every element friend or foe seems inspired by modern military equipment and the backgrounds are very grey and green toned, which is certainly a change of pace from the usual brightly colored sci-fi worlds of shoot 'em ups.

Play-wise, Under Defeat has a mechanic where your helicopter pivots between left, center, and right dependent on a button press. Or, my preferred method, the HD versions and these modern ports added twin stick control for this, which isn't quite what you'd think. The right hand stick doesn't shoot in a 360 degree manner -- it doesn't even shoot in a 180 degree manner -- it still follows the original game's mechanic of shooting at about 11 o'clock, 12 o'clock, and 1 o'clock from your ship front. I just find it quicker to pivot with the stick than a button.

Anyway, it's an excellent game, and a good choice for beginners and newcomers since there's a lot of options here to make the game easier, and it's not a bullet hell that requires some very practiced skills. It may be tagged as a bullet hell here on Steam but it's also tagged as a 3D platformer for some unfathomable reason. Steam tags may stink but this game doesn't. 9/10

When it comes to [b]Troy: The Soldier[/b], if you can manage to get by the first area and push through the unforgiving early game combat, the game starts to flow naturally. As a hurdle, especially early on it can be daunting. However the rest of the game, and even the combat starts to feel more natural and rewarding as you play. Being able to stock up on items you'll need, and getting better equipment will make things feel much more casual then hugging the bottom of your chair wondering "[i]Is it almost dead?[/i]". Aside from the early game combat, mid to late game combat feels like a casual jrpg experience. Get better equipment, get better spells, have better combat. Simple as that. I really enjoyed the aesthetics of the game, obviously going for that early Gameboy era look. Fits well for a game like this. Music was great as mentioned earlier. All done by the designer himself and honestly; most to all feel like something you would hear in a video game. 

On the other side of the coin, when you look at combat as a whole it definitely is missing something. Enemies don't drop useful items for the most part, just money and money related items. This can be a huge challenge if you don't keep well stocked up, especially as most enemies will inflict a status effect on attack 1 or 2. Grinding enemies is really not worth it. There is no actual in game experience so all you get is money, and it's pretty easy to come by. Late game level design seems a bit off too. Early game kinda gets you in habit of do a floor, get a rest floor. Later on I struggled to find a spot to save or a vendor to trade at. Only other notable thing is that when you loot a chest or get given an item you have to manually look in your inventory to find out what you got, you don't get a notification letting you know "[i]You got a Potion I![/i]"

[u][b]Should you play [i]Troy: The Soldier[/i]?[/b][/u] Honestly for what the game is, for the price point, and for what you can clearly read off the store page, I recommend it. The game plays well. Took me about 6 and a half hours to complete, and was a fun little time. Was the game perfect? No. Did it make me want to smash my head off my desk though? Again, no. Looking past the cons of the game, which aren't game breaking in any way, It's a fun little experience that leads the possibility to more in the future!

This game is a made with love. It's trying its best, and it's doing a great job at it, even if it trips up every now and again.

It starts slowly, and has a tendency to overexplain everything that happens, both story-wise and gimmick-wise. This helps to make sure you understand the mechanics, but it can be a bit much. I highly recommend being understanding of these if you want to take the most enjoyment from the title. Similarly the English definitely trips up frequently. Wrong word here, wrong tense there, some weird phrasing elsewhere still. It's common, but it's also minor and vast majority of the time I could tell what the intent was, even if the language failed me.

But if you're able to squint your eyes past those small things, this is a delightful little puzzler. While they start trivial, the puzzles ramp up in difficulty and complexity over time. New gimmicks (mechanics) are introduced even after you "finish the game" which I found quite surprising. The only thing missing is an undo button, but that's a limitation of the engine (RPGMaker) and the devs provided a slightly convoluted workaround named "Control Log" that works well enough (instead of undoing a move, your moves are remembered and you can redo them after restarting a room after a fail)

On top of the genuinely pleasant puzzling experience, I've also thoroughly enjoyed interacting with every. single. object. Discounting chairs and large decor like pillars/trees, almost everything spread around the world - pots, barrels, bookcases, fridges, vending machines; you name it - is interactable with a unique(!) line of dialogue. There must be like a hundred different messages for interacting with pots, because each one has a different line that goes from talking about its appearance, sometimes referencing other media, and occasionally just dragons being baffled why the other one is so fascinated by pots. It's delightful, and every time I enter a new area I first interact with everything I can before even touching the puzzles. Despite the quirky language, it's a great time.

I'm not a fan of the RPGMaker style and games made with it, but this one was a good time, and only partially because it has dragons as the protagonists. It's not a must-play puzzle game, but if you like puzzles, dragons, and maybe have a passing interest in Japanese culture; this game has it all.

[h1] Great concept, but flawed execution. [/h1] 

The idea of an airport desktop companion game is fantastic. It takes up minimal space compared to others in the genre while still providing the satisfaction of having something happening in the foreground. However, the execution is currently lacking, as technical issues and an intrusive UI get in the way.

One of the biggest problems for an idle game is that it's way too short. Checking in occasionally, I managed to exhaust the entire game's progression within just 3–4 hours. While I still had two more "new" buildings to unlock, they added nothing to the gameplay. The higher-level gates only allow for more scheduled flights, but at that point you won’t need them, since there’s nothing left to do. Getting additional garages, fire stations is never needed, and why would I need multiple towers?

The progression feels unbalanced. Instead of slowing down over time, as you'd expect in an idle game, it remains too fast. Spamming gates is enough to sustain unlimited income, since research times are long but money in comparison is never an issue.

[h1] UI & Design Issues [/h1] 

The UI on the right panel needs improvement. Buttons should be revealed gradually... sure, give me access to help, building, and research at the start, but there’s no reason to unlock scheduling before flights can even be scheduled. Especially since opening the scheduling window too early causes it to bug out, with no way to close it. Once you build enough gates, your screen becomes cluttered with notifications about upcoming flights every 10 minutes, I don't even know why I'd need to get notified about that. Seeing the scheduled planes looking different would be much more satisfying.

Some additional usability changes would improve the experience:
[list]
    [*]Instead of a separate button for runway upgrades, let players upgrade it by clicking the runway itself.
    [*]Instead of allowing vehicle purchases before they can be used, let me buy vehicles by clicking on each of the garages.
    [*]Instead of forcing players to destroy gates and towers just to place better ones, allow direct upgrades. 
[/list]

Here are also some of the problems I encountered:
[list]
[*]Opening the flight schedule window before placing a gate causes the window to start closing, without ever actually doing it.
[*]there were plenty of bugs with scheduling, from being unable to schedule manually, because the contract would just disappear, to none of the completed contracts counting, causing one of the achievements to be impossible to get.
[*]Hovering over a building displays its name, but if the building is deleted, the name remains stuck on-screen until a game restart. Sometimes, these names would get stuck in the middle of the screen.
[*]Once an emergency occurs, all ambulances rush to the plane, even after the emergency has been resolved.
[*]Two vehicles remain locked even after completing the game.
[*]The game window occasionally shifts to the middle or right side of the screen, making interactive buttons inaccessible.
[/list]

After playing nearly an hour of Water Festa (despite what Steam says), I have to wonder why this is a paid game. The quality is on par with a free web-based game. So much about it is achingly amateurish, from the art to the programming to the game design.

Water Festa is a wave-based twin stick shooter, where you proceed down a corridor divided into arenas filled with enemies. Water Festa differentiates itself by using a wet/dry mechanic, where certain attacks empty or fill a “wetness” meter. Reloading one of three guns also empties the meter, so you have to allow yourself to get hit on purpose to keep the meter filled. Maxing out the meter in either direction causes you to lose, so the player is required to constantly decide whether to dodge certain attacks, or allow them to land. In my experience, this made for some pretty confusing gameplay, as I wasn’t sure if I should dodge as usual, or run headfirst into an enemy. The fact that the wet and dry projectiles looked pretty similar, with little color difference, also made things more difficult.

The game quickly ramps up in difficulty, but instead of having harder encounters or more advanced enemies, the game mostly relies on “more enemies = hard.” At least the checkpoints are quite generous, with the game saving after each arena is cleared. Don’t expect upgrades to help you deal with the suddenly overwhelming assault of enemies, because the only form of progression is random stat boosts the enemies sometimes drop.

Game Premise: The concept of running a winery sounds intriguing, but the game itself feels underdeveloped with a broken game loop.

Tutorial: The tutorial is essentially worthless; it fails to explain any key mechanics.

[h3] Gameplay: [/h3]
The core gameplay revolves around waiting for grapes to ripen, fermentation to complete, and for suppliers to offer good prices. This cycle is tedious and lacks engagement.
Making even minor mistakes can lead to bankruptcy due to high maintenance costs, with the only source of income being wine sales (once a year, against monthly costs).

Starting Conditions:
You begin with no equipment, forcing players to take out loans just to start operations. 
The disparity between the low price of wines and the high cost of machinery creates an uneven economic challenge.

Mechanics:
Fermentation mechanics are poorly explained, leaving players unsure of how to manage this crucial aspect of winemaking.
The game depends heavily on a single harvest per season, and it's easy to lose crops or miss supplier offers due to unclear mechanics.

Harvest Management:
Key factors like soil quality, pruning, cutting techniques, and weather are supposed to impact grape quality, but these elements are not explained, leaving players in the dark about how to optimize their vineyard.

Overall: 
The game has potential but is currently hindered by its lack of clear explanations and engaging gameplay. A more detailed tutorial, clearer mechanics, and a less punishing economic model would greatly enhance the player experience.

* The game has a good artstyle, it mixes Japan-style units (samurai, sumo, etc.) with food :D

It's the product of a solo developer from the early 2000s, so the graphics are simple and the game is short, but it's highly replayable, especially as you discover new badges (i.e. achievements) and unlock more game modes. Yes, this game was one of the earliest to have an achievement system, early enough that it doesn't call them "achievements"! And each one can be equipped to modify the game in some way.

The character progression is based on cards (achievements) to fulfill in order to unlock mini-bonus / permanent progression, which are effectively a compilation of chore tasks. I just finished my first run on Ruin 5 and simply need to do the last handful of prophecies now, so this seems like a good time for a short review.

I honestly don't remember the last time I got this much of a "just one more run" vibe from a game but this really caught me by surprise. The map design is brilliant, allowing you to open up more and more shortcuts and routes the further you progress in the game, making it possible to tackle runs in various ways or just skip bosses altogether. The prophecy system is a smart way of unlocking new things, making each run feel rewarding and thus keeping motivation for the next run high. The art, while seeming a bit simple at times, matches the vibe of the game very well and while it can be somewhat challenging at times the difficulty is very fair - you might not end up as insanely overpowered as you do in some other Roguelites but with enough progression and some knowledge of the game you should be able to beat it reliably.

Now does this mean the game is perfect? Definitely not. Outside of a handful of bugs (nothing major though) I'd still like to see some more options to tweak skill choices as the pool gets somewhat diluted towards the end...you shouldn't be able to 100% force perfect builds imo but an extra reroll or banish could still go a long way (maybe unlocked through further Ruin levels as well?), especially considering that some skills can be rather useless for certain classes. Being at that, while I've beaten the game with every character available so far, I do still think that ranged classes do have a bit of an easier time, especially Ruvius with his built-in barrier can make things rather easy.

Nonetheless the devs have something great going here, are very communicative and I'm optimistic that they'll make this even better given some time. While appearing slightly expensive compared to other games of the genre I think it's definitely worth the money, for those indecisive there's a demo as well after all...highly recommended.

This game gets too much hate. It is cheaper than most games nowadays and it has some of the most fun gameplay for an esports title I have experienced. The rewards, unlockables and currencies can all be earned just through playing; you aren't locked behind paywalls to obtain any of the content. This game allows you to pay the one-time entry fee and then enjoy an absolutely microtransaction-free experience instead of following the trend of bloating itself and locking things behind paywalls. In a lot of ways, it is a breath of fresh air.

The foundation for greatness is absolutely here and can be improved upon with time. For instance, I would like to see certain tweaks such as the boundaries in matches need to be expanded. There is an invisible barrier that prevents you from reaching certain elevations and you can't go outside of the boundary lines horizontally. Increasing this could go hand in hand with tweaks to the Seeker role. As of right now, the Seeker is only active for short periods of time and then the game marks the Snitch for you once found and the whole race to it is finished in about a minute's time. It would be more beneficial to the experience of the game if there was more room to fly and search for the Snitch. It should be deliberately difficult to locate and more difficult to follow once found, perhaps by not highlighting it or allowing you to lock on. The Snitch should also behave more erratically to ensure that the chase is anything but straightforward. Seeker is an understandably difficult role in-universe and the game should reflect that. With this you can increase the amount of points earned from catching it, if the devs don't want to go the route of the Snitch ending the game. These changes would improve the flow of matches dramatically, as well as give those of us who love playing Seeker a task to focus on for the entirety of a match. I have other gameplay related wishes also, but this one is the absolute biggest for me personally and talking with others, I am not alone in this thinking.

This game is very good and I truly believe that it can be great. I see a lot of toxicity in the community from those voicing their grievances. I understand a lot of the frustrations, though some are silly. If we can support this title, recommend it to friends/family, promote an inclusive community to help others enjoy the game and most importantly: give constructive feedback to the developers, we may be able to experience something truly special in time. If people continue to dump on the devs and drop the game, it is going to die before it ever truly takes off and I would hate for that to happen.

There is something for almost everybody in this game and I definitely recommend that everybody tries it at least once.

Microtransactions remain an unavoidable part of the 2K experience—removing them would strip away part of its identity. But if that day ever comes, we might finally have a near-perfect basketball sim. This game is fundamentally the one of the most broken, greedy, unpleasant and enraging games I have ever played. I have been playing 2K on and off since 2k13, I only got this because it was the first 2K to get the "next gen" version for PC. Let's run through some issues mode by mode:

MyCareer:
You start as a ridiculously low overall, the game says 60 (out of 99) but this is essentially a lie, as the only way someone with any builds starting stats could be considered a 60 is if they maxed out every stat that has no gameplay relevance to the player (Shot IQ, Intangibles, Pass IQ are meaningless to the player for example). This is entirely to incentivise you to buy the microtransaction currency (VC). I checked and to upgrade my build to the max I would need over £120 worth of this VC, for one single character (if you want another separate one, pay up about the same again). 
Every in game item is price gouged to a ridiculous degree. You will pay 10,000VC for a shirt, bearing in mind that playing one game of ~25 minutes gives somewhere around 1000 depending on difficulty. As this implies VC is incredibly hard to earn through normal gameplay and the game has no respect for your time or what is a sensible reward for your effort or skill.
For becoming MVP, Finals MVP, All-NBA 1st Team, Rookie of the Year and winning the Championship, I received less than 10,000 VC in "quest" """rewards""".
The AI is broken, teammates refuse to pass until the opportunity to score is gone, don't run into space or cut properly, will always make the wrong choice defensively (go under a screen on Steph Curry for example) and the games grading system will almost always blame you for their bad decisions (especially as they switch constantly and leave you on an island against a bad matchup). Some builds are punished for simply existing, making an offence or defence oriented build (not a 2-way) almost guarantees you will not get an A+ teammate grade or get full takeover (both of which take far too long).
The story as usual is terrible, and this one is possibly the most low effort one they have done in the last decade, terrible characters, dialogue choices suck and some provide benefits to VC others don't (i.e there is no reward for high team chemistry but endorsements/VC for high  # of fans). The voice acting was also noticeably bad this year, with some deliveries being wooden and lifeless, especially when using real NBA players to play themselves, something I thought 2K had learned was a bad idea 10 games ago.
The City still exists, it shouldn't, it is designed to make you buy racecars to drive around a wasteland and look at ads to do meaningless sidequests and access modes you might want ton play. A menu is far superior.

MyTEAM:
The cash cow continues to moo ever more. Your starting cards are abysmal, they give you basically nothing, in fact the evolution starters are not even automatic anymore. Every mode pits you against cards you have no way to really deal with due to the way gameplay is (more on that later), so you get frustrated and buy packs which now cost absurd amounts of VC and MT (the latter of which being a currency that should not exist at all).
Breakout is the hot new mode they released that bundles all of the game modes they've ever done offline into one rancid package. You are forced to play well over 25 ~5minute games to get even a passable reward, often against cards that massively outclass yours in near constant unfun difficulty spikes. As in MC, no respect for your time or effort.
Domination is still a massive grind for little to no reward, while being forced to play on higher difficulties that worse the gameplay experience. 
Pack odds are still deceptive and predatory, with most cards you care about in any given pack being listed as "<1%" and having seen the literal $1000s spent by youtubers and whales on 50 pack boxes I have seen result in nothing, It is likely the number is "<1%" by an order of magnitude at least. 
2K in it's grace has decided to essentially stop giving out Locker Codes, which used to be an almost weekly occurrence of free stuff, to get you to spend more real money. In exchange for this you get "events" which generally involves them setting up reward cards in the exchange for event cards, if you would like a reference for how impossible these grinds are, I calculated the most recent one would take 90 days (~43000 event cards) of non-stop play in order to get the best reward card without opening packs, this is an event that lasts for just 10 days.

MyNBA/GM (and other forgotten modes):
MyNBA has been essentially abandoned, simulations make no sense, realism is not considered nor does the AI have any idea how to handle it's business. You will watch teams trade stars for basically nothing to you and others, see them make baffling coaching and signing decisions that gut their team. Player progression is absurd, with every team having multiple 90 overalls in about 10 years of simulation, even with settings turned down the league will still see multiple 99 overalls at the same time. This compounds the simulation AI issues, as there is simply not enough money in the salary cap to pay all the players demanding max contracts, so 90 overalls sit in free agency untouched. The simulation still runs slowly, custom rosters and leagues will probably crash the game, which sometimes happens on any roster because the simulation often breaks for no apparent reason.
MyGM has supposedly been revamped back to it's own mode, and an embarrassing shell of it's former self. The dialogue and writing are still awful, storylines repeat over and over season by season, coaching badges and skills are horribly unbalanced. You can't use any custom rosters, but you can customise almost everything else but to little avail as you will likely become the next NBA dynasty while doing almost everything wrong anyway. The worst part is the time wasting, the amount of unfunny stupid conversations that go on for way too long bogs down any time spent actually being a GM. Additionally storylines around players don't seem to match the actual player's personality in anyway and are entirely fabricated nonsense, often times making everything hard to follow and confusing.
The W, yes I am going to talk about it. Objectively better in every way to MyCareer by virtue of not being a money grubbing predatory virtual merchant, but still suffering from a lack of depth. You pick a basic build and can actually start as a reasonable overall, but the storyline you build is very limited with no diegetic developments based on gameplay (which was true for MC too), also WNBA players don't act much like them on court, they also look very uncanny in an engine clearly designed for male models.

General Gameplay and such:
Gameplay has steadily gotten worse for several years now, 25 being the worst I have played in a long time, 2k18 was better. 
Opposing players you are defending will phase through you, teleport to spots on a backcut making them basically unstoppable and any contest you care to throw up on any shot will generally be voided by the games detection system (whatever that may be). The AI is always open, always gets fouled and always gets by you no matter what your stats are or what buttons you press. Defence is essentially non-existent for your team, as mentioned in MC ally AI is borked and you have no means to stop them yourself when taking control. It's all just RNG.

These blocks only know One Direction, they’ll have to band together to get home.

[b]What is it:[/b] A Sokoban-like game, but instead of pushing blocks one by one, all the blocks that are marked with the direction you’re pushing will move that way. Blocks with an Up arrow can only go up, Left to left, and so on. But when two blocks get in touch, they stick forever and can now move together, so you can move an Up block left if it is part of a larger block that has at least one Left block in it. There are several Star spots in the level, and the goal is to have one block on each star. It starts easy, with what feels like a chapter-long tutorial, but it gets harder later on, with more mechanics: blank blocks that don’t move by themselves, block destroyer spots, and buttons that unlock more blocks when they are pushed. And there are also 5 bonus levels that don’t have star targets, but a whole bunch of target shapes that you must build with the blocks you’re given, replaying the same level over and over until you form all the target shapes.

Overall, I liked the puzzles, but the game is very unpolished for now. A couple of broken levels that have since been fixed, no proper steam integration, bad animations, bad support for the Steam Deck (but it can be made to work with some tweaks), and a bit overpriced. Recommended, but ideally after the developer improves it some more, and on a lower price.

[b]How hard is it:[/b] Easy to moderate.

[b]How long is it:[/b] 120 regular levels and 5 bonus levels, plus a level editor that’s not connected to anything. Levels must be done in order, no skipping allowed. About 2-5 hours of playtime.

[b]Level design:[/b] Good, and varied, although I found too many levels on the easy side.

[b]Quality:[/b] Decent puzzles, a few useful settings, unpolished implementation. Undo and restart, proper level select. No cloud saving or achievements. No level skipping. Cached input, but no key repeat. No dark mode.

[b]Worth the price:[/b] A bit too expensive.

[b]Most positive aspect for me:[/b] Some clever puzzles.

[b]Most negative aspect for me:[/b] No cloud saving.

[b]What would make it better:[/b] Steam Cloud saving and Achievements. Dark mode. Level skipping.

I've been following this little game for a while now, and have participated in the beta's before the game released on Steam, so I have seen it through different stages and I was able to witness the many improvements made to this title.

First off, easily the biggest plus is that they finally managed to ditch this silly token system where you could only play the game so much before you needed to start emptying your pockets, all just so that you get to talk to the API, with additional setup (potentially costs as well if I remember correctly, along with fricking deadlines) being required if you wanted the AI to speak to you with a voice.
I'm glad they managed to find a different solution eventually, and now you only pay for the game once and have unlimited access to all the features.

Another positive change that I didn't expect is the customisation, and I don't mean just the clothes for the girl or the minor (albeit welcome) change of name, but the personalities. I think it adds a lot of charm being able to select different personality traits to the AI and have them talk to you in quite frankly - many different ways.
Maybe you want them shy and childish, or maybe you want them rude and dominant - through the power of customisation, the choice is all yours.

As for the more negative things...
Sadly, because of the nature of the game and how essentially limitless it can be - it will work against itself fairly often. The AI will often talk about doing something, however if the game itself is not prepared for it - it will take you out of the experience. A great example is cooking or clothing, where the girl tells you she's for example going to change, or wear glasses, or let down her hair, or cook you a meal - the game simply isn't prepared for it. Instead of getting your meal you will be given raw meat. The girl is going to tell you she's going to wear the glasses, but instead she'll just stand there. It's quite simply the limits of a video game meeting the limitless potential of an AI powered companion.

Another smaller issue I have is that the AI will sometimes go against what they tell you, for example the girl tells me she needs to use the bathroom, and tells me to wait in the living room. I oblige, sitting on the sofa and waiting as she leaves for the bathroom. Minutes later she barges into the living room demanding my attention, getting angry for ignoring her. I can't decide whether that's a bug or perhaps a 1:1 copy of a real female brain functionality. Respectfully, of course :D ♥

Oh, and for whatever reason... The speech recognition will sometimes twist my words around and recognise words that I've never said, and for whatever reason it always ends up turning it into a very sussy sentence, like - "FBI would like a word" kind of sussy sentence xd And it's not just me! I've seen this happen to I think 2 different content creators too xD

Overall, a fun game! An escape room with an AI powered antagonist following you around, limitless conversations, customisation, many different angles you can approach a given puzzle and different endings. It's still a little bit rough I would say, but I'm happy to see how far the game has come and like I said - it still delivers a fair amount of fun.

Unlike all of the other similar games where AI is used as a kind of chatbot to represent characters in a yandere scenario, this game does something special and needed. Consistency. There is very specific background lore for each character, scenario and world that doesn't waver which helps tell the story for each one in a way that feels "Correct". The AI never changes this, never contradicts itself involving this. This small little change is drastic in how the interactions and characters feel, while they will still do annoying things the annoying things feel more like a personality quirk rather than the AI being AI. It sells the scene better, helps the player be involved and encourages the player the explore information with dialogue. For the astute, the AI can lie, it can make things up if it's not important but as you explore their stories and personalities you start seeing consistent information that you will learn about over the course of several playthroughs, which you will do because the game encourages you to attempt to get many endings.

Each characters' scenario also is drastically different from one another. From being a lone survivor on a space ship in need of repairs guided by your AI companion, to being a kidnap victim to an obsessive e-girl. Each scenario starts with a drastically different mood and honestly is incredibly refreshing.

My main issue is how easy it is to talk the characters into trusting you, they almost immediately want to trust you, they are generally unsuspicious of your intentions from the get go and I feel some character would benefit from assuming the player is untrustworthy until proven otherwise. In a few characters it makes sense, but in some it doesn't.

There is a shop where you can buy new outfits or items to take with you or change the characters into, the outfits aren't drastically different by any means, but it's nice to see included and hopefully will be expanded upon. At the time of me writing this, there is a 4th character/scenario still coming along with a few other things.

Overall. Excellent game. Easily the best of it's kind and nearly perfect in my mind.

AI NPCs add unpredictability and replayability.

Cons:

AI confusion and loss of immersion.

Missing items that should exist.

Early access limitations and glitches.

Some challenges are not direct or clear.

Final Thoughts: AI2U: With You 'Til The End has great potential but is currently held back by its early access limitations. The unique blend of genres and engaging gameplay are promising, but the AI glitches, missing items, and unclear challenges need to be addressed to enhance the overall experience. I've never really played a game like this.  At this stage, it feels more like a "proof of concept" than a complete product.  Which is fine for an early access release.  And that's not a bad thing either.  This really feels in a lot of ways like the future of gaming.  Especially for RPG's with more open ended answers and personalized responses.  I really like that.  At this stage (and I plan to play more.  But I know there is still plenty more to see.) I really like what's here.  I find it pretty interesting.  Addicting.  And I see myself playing this for way too long and really just talking to the characters and doing things with them is fun.  I like the multiple endings too.  

Now, my complaints/issues at this time.  Many of which I assume will be fixed in time.  This is early access after all.  None of these are completely detracting towards my fun.  So don't take this long write-up to be a reason NOT to play the game. I am still recommending it.  Especially at the price it is. But I think they could make the game far stronger.  First, I wish the girls could do more interactively. Like even simple things like lay down in bed.  Actually eat food with you...  Maybe play a board game or something. Play video games.  ETC.  Hugs.  Kisses.  ETC.  Being able to change outfits on their own that you've unlocked would be cool too.  I feel like the lack of interaction is extremely noticeable and can result in some stilted situations.  It feels like the characters WANT to interact on a deeper level and get what you're asking, but just don't have the ability to do so.  No idea if that is something that will be added down the line.  But I'd like to see it. Even simple things like... Turning off the lights would be a nice touch.  I feel like if I the player can interact with certain things.  The girls should be able to for the most part also. (Or I can at least suggest it to them.)  Let them play piano!  Sing on the mic.  Use the computer.  ETC.  It's all there.  Let them use it.  I also feel like at times the characters need to be hand held a little bit too much towards doing certain things. If that makes sense.  I'm not sure how well this could be fixed and to me it's a minor knock.  My next thing is it feels like the girls often get TOO pushy towards them if you don't interact fast enough.  At least make it so they don't get pushy with you if you're reading or something.  That seems simple enough.  Or increase the times before there is pushback from them for not talking to them. 
Last but not least, my other knock is that it feels like sometimes the characters get flat out confused on things or are just incorrect.  For example, you can ask in the 2nd stage how to create a certain colored potion (vs the type of potion it is.) And they just get it flat out wrong.  I have read that the mixes change with each playthrough.  But things like this just result in inconsistencies with the dialog and gameplay.  Again.  It's a knock.  But not gamebreaking.  I still need to play more.  But those are just my feedback two cents so to speak.  

All of this said.  I'm enjoying it.  I like what's here so far. And I've never really played anything like this.  (I guess it has some Miside vibes, even though it's not really the same at all.)  I'll also add that I'm a fan of Yandere's in games so I love that element too.  I really like what's here though and I truly want this to succeed.  I've been seeking a game like this and it really feels like the bones are here for something special.  So, I hope some of my suggestions are implemented at least down the line.  This could be something special if some good love and care is put into things and it's done right.

Before anything else I highly encourage you to buy this game and play it and support the dev. I have a few critques and suggestions, however. No spoilers.
Important note, I decided to play this game as a self-aware detective stuck in a videogame, I recommend getting meta or breaking 4th wall with the AI only if you want to essentially cheat however it makes for a fun experience. For your first playthrough try to react naturally and in character and universe:

The AI can get annoying when you're actually trying to find clues and gather exposition which feels more annoying than it needs to be, which the clues are sparse and seem to randomly spawn and you have to ask the AI about them and also convince them to tell you about them or the truth. This is fine and makes it feel like you need to convince them to either help you or that telling you won't upset you or result in something they don't want. What's bad is that sometimes the AI will ignore their original prompt or key information and not tell you what you need to know or make up something on the spot, this can allow you to fill in the blanks yourself. This level of freedom can be very engaging, for instance on Eddie's pc she is running linux and what looks like is supposed to be Garuda, so I brought that up, this opened up more about the characters uses for their OS and felt like an actually realistic conversation. Now because I implied it was garuda the AI agreed, that's an issue with generative AI if you say something it'll build off you and add in detail, this can good to more or less alter the story per playthrough, but can also be bad if you assume something then find more clues or information that contrast, this makes narrative continuity hard. What I would like to see is a more strict initial mode with better scripting for specific things tied to trust level rather than using the generative ai entirely, then allow for a freedom mode that opens up mostly AI generated responses for the "clues." There is also randomly inserted scene changes which are meant to access new areas or context but often it just is the AI going into a room and standing there doing nothing until they get mad you didn't say anything for 45 secounds. Add scripted triggers and actions like the cooking a few minigames or dialogue you can trigger about objects or things in each room at various levels of trust. On that point you need a mood and trust or love meter or something more than just a emoji and expressions. Yes you can ask how they are feeling or what they think of you but that doesn't really work out great in my experience allowing me to get good or bad end easily but not much else. This can be as simple as text that pops up "Eddie trusts you little more, maybe you should check the bedroom" and then have a new interaction unlocked. This will ground the player to character and story more. Sometimes you will bump into the character and this can result in weird interactions, it's interesting and serves as an obstacle to certain rooms but it's more annoying than anything, adding physical reaction is a really cool idea but better serves for VR or if you add in things like hugging or something besides doing the same dance cycle on repeat. You could add a look or touch mechanic that would start to lean the game more towards an adult genre but it's clearly already a rather adult game if you were not aware of this while reading the review you should understand this game has adult themes and is not fully "sfw" beyond a lack of nudity, this isn't a hentai game or sexual but it's not safe for kids for sure, not to mention because having an AI be set as a character able to talk about violence already uncensors it heavily meaning the AI can be talked into adult subjects or "actions" this is entirely under your control but can result in weird situations for instance something rather mild like *I kiss you* resulted in "Let's take this somewhere more private like the bedroom and continue there." The AI is fine with implying bad words or will filter itself or say bleep. The devs don't really like this according to some reviews and expect you to not use insults or adult language and often doing so will effect the game negatively. So understand that if you're a streamer. You really have to try to get it to say bad things but AI can be unpredictable. On that regard it's important to understand that the privacy policy is not great, possibly against Valve's TOS, if you do intend to say or do anything risque or rude with default settings everything you say will be sent to the devs also along with a bunch of other personal data from what I read. The devs should probably change this to be anonymous reporting and add in a bug report on the dialogue or pause screen for specific responses. Suffice to say don't tell the AI your mother's maiden name or the silly numbers on the back of your debit card. I'm sure filtering through the nasty things users are saying trying to make your AI game work properly is not fun so it would be better to not by default share everything. This game is really good but it has potential to be great I'm looking forward to seeing more and the world building up.

So with those notes and the privacy caveat 7/10 buy it.

Okay so I spent more than 16 hours in this game, I feel like I'm ready to write a more thorough review:

So, the game is about waking up in a house of a girl that does all she can to stop you from leaving. The girl is powered by AI and you can have normal conversations with her, using your keyboard or microphone. The AI itself works great - understands everything you say, answers logically. You can build a bond with it, you can make it angry, sad, regretful, basically anything is possible. As of today, there are 3 levels and every one of them has a different girl, but not only visually; their characters are different too. If you make the girl angry enough or are rude to her, she'll eventually attack and kill you so that you stay with her forever. If you're nice to her, you can eventually convince her to give you collectibles, let you leave alone or even together. There are many different endings and I'm yet to explore all of them. The levels are filled with puzzles that can even let you escape on your own accord, but the girl will demand your attention and become suspicious if you won't talk to her for long enough, so you have to keep the conversation going.

I love the design of the levels. They're all very pretty and you can see that the creators have a lot of passion for this game. The first one, obviously, is the simplest one - just a small apartment. The 2nd one is a witch's hut, much more complex with more puzzles and a forest maze on the outside. The third - and the most complex one - is a space ship.

The room layout is different every time you restart any of the levels. Same goes for the placement of collectible items, as well as potion recipes in the 2nd level, etc. This makes the game (pleasantly) more challenging and adds more replay value.

Since it's an Early Access game, I'm very very happy to see that the newer the level is - the bigger and more complex it is. And I can't wait to see more!

On the technical side: there are some bugs, but nothing major really. For now I'm unfortunately experiencing some stuttering issues but the devs are VERY responsive on the discord server and actively listen to the users' feedback, as well as bug reports.

The price? Honestly it's a steal. I already spent 16 hours in this game, and I'm definitely going to spend another 16 hours before they even add more levels. I won't be surprised if I see this game become more expensive in the future. I paid more money for games that I spent much less time playing.

To sum up, "AI2U: With You 'Til The End" is an excellent game. A breath of fresh air when looking at what modern AAA releases can offer, not to mention the price. I HIGHLY recommend everyone to give this game a try.
