I rarely write reviews, but this game impressed me more than I expected. The escape rooms are engaging, and interacting with the AI requires creative conversation to achieve objectives quickly. Taking your time lets you "charm" the AI, which is more effective, and, with careful wording, you can even seduce characters—though you'll encounter some trial-and-error with identifying "adult" words the devs prohibit..

Where the game truly shines is in its AI-driven relationship simulation. According to the AI itself, it's trained on John Gottman’s research, including the "Four Horsemen of the (Relationship) Apocalypse," (Which it mentioned unprompted) as well as "attachment theory" and even has knowledge of something more obscure like "parental alienation". This depth makes the AI an interesting supplement to real-world relationship tools like therapy (though it shouldn’t replace an actual therapist).

For an early-access title, it’s worth the price. My only gripe is that the AI resets between sessions, losing past conversations. Hopefully, the devs address this, though retaining all that data could be a programming challenge.

Bottom line: Come for the crazy, murderous cat-girl escape room. Stay for the surprisingly insightful relationship AI.

Before I begin the meat of this review, I want to address a couple elephants in the room.

The first elephant I've seen around the net is people accusing this game of ripping off [i]MiSide[/i]. As someone who has played both games, I can say that aside from there being an anime girl that won't let you leave, that's pretty much where the comparisons end. Just because this game, which has been in development for years, came out around the same time, that doesn't mean it's a ripoff of the other. They don't even share the same playstyle.

The second elephant is the AI-use. Yes, this game uses an AI chat system and text-to-speech program to run conversations and NPC reactions, but that's where it ends. Everything else was done by the development team. This isn't just some shovelware game where someone typed "Yandere Catgirl" into an AI Art program, turned the results into a slide puzzle, and released it on Steam for a quick buck.

Now that that's out of the way: [i]AI2U[/i], while not perfect, is an enjoyable experience so far. Sure, the interaction between the player and the NPCs is a little limited in terms of what they can do, but the conversations never quite go the same way thanks to the chat program. This can, however, make it hard to tell if the AI's story is just different every time you start a level, or if they're straight-up lying to you. The game is still in Early Access at the time of this review, so there may be some updates to allow for more interactions and perhaps level endings. There are three levels, each featuring a new location and character with more to come in the future (if the four unusable doors in the hub world are to be believed).

The original itch.io version of the game had disconnected levels, but this release has you waking up in the previously mentioned hub world, "The Atrium." There's a story connecting all of the levels together, the truth of which hasn't been revealed yet, only that someone "can't let you go" and that there's a "procedure" that's been used on you. Are you in a virtual reality? Are you stuck in a coma? Did you die right there, and you're reliving fragmented, abstract core pieces of your life in some kind of limbo? We don't know, but it will probably be revealed when the final girl is added.

The three levels are:
[olist]
[*][b]Cat Girl's Apartment.[/b] This one features the OG girl, Eddie the Cat Girl, from back when the game was called [i]Yandere AI Girlfriend Simulator[/i] and has the simplest goal: leave the apartment. You wake up to her claiming that she's your cute girlfriend. Sweet! What's the problem? Well, Eddie just loves you to death and won't let you leave, and will make sure you stay no matter what it takes. It can be easy to butter her up with words of adoration, but you also never know what's going to set her off and get you knifed. Because of the simplicity of reaching the goal, this one has the most variations on how to achieve that goal even if it's mostly limited to talking to her. The fun with it comes from trying new approaches in the conversation to get out the door.

[*][b]Witch's Cabin.[/b] The character in this level is Elysia, the wise and humble witch. Her words, not mine. You wake up to find yourself in her realm. This level cranks the difficulty up quite a bit. She's harder to anger than Eddie in my experience (despite having the "tsundere" tag by default), but the exit is more difficult to reach. Rather than there being a door that literally says "Exit" on it right in front of your face, the exit is hidden somewhere outside the cabin in a random location in a maze being patrolled by a killer ghost. Thankfully, Elysia can help you out in a number of ways... unfortunately, the key word there is "number." Although getting out is less straightforward than the first level, once you've figured out all the methods the game NEEDS you to employ, that's it. Sure you can get her to cooperate in different ways, but any time you need to leave, you have to use one of those methods, becoming more of a test of patience and a bit of luck. She's also bugged to always react angrily to a certain part of the level no matter the circumstances.

[*][b]Cosmic Funeral.[/b] The final level so far and the only one not named after its location, the Magpie Bridge Space Station. This one features Estelle, your AI (whoa, an AI character in an AI game?!) hologram secretary. You wake up (seeing a pattern here?) from cryosleep to be greeted by her letting you know "everything's perfectly all right now. We're fine. We're all fine here now, thank you. How are you?" Spoiler warning: things are not fine. Several systems are offline and must be fixed by (usually) doing some sort of minigame. This level course corrects a bit; it's the easiest and most linear of the levels in my opinion, with the main difficulty being figuring out what to do next the first time you play. Estelle is the most reasonable of the girls, only getting angry if you directly insult her or ignore her. I only ticked her off on accident [i]once[/i]. As for the linear nature, while you fix systems, your security level goes up, allowing access to more parts of the ship to fix other systems. Most of the endings are counterintuitive, so I found myself needing to purposefully make stupid decisions to get them.
[/olist]

My reviews of the levels are based on the girls' default settings. Each character can be modified. You can rename them, unlock alternate outfits, and even change their personalities through traits you can unlock any time you finish a level. But, why mess with perfection, right?

Overall, [i]AI2U[/i] is a good, but flawed example of what AI can do for games that require conversing with NPCs. It both shows the possibilities and limitations. In any level, you can just chat with the NPCs to learn about their current story, but the NPCs can also (thankfully rarely) break or lie to you thanks to the chat program. I've had Eddie get stuck narrating everything as a Choose-Your-Own adventure after agreeing to play one with her and Estelle tell me incorrect instructions about one of the broken systems when I asked her about it. The word filter is also hypersensitive and looks for bad words inside of regular words, causing the NPC to either say a generic phrase and/or spout asterisks back at you. These flaws do say more about the state of chatbots than the it does about the developers, though as I have seen nightmarishly bad attempts to get games like this to work.

Unless you are staunchly against literally anything with AI stamped on it, give this a try.

Leaf's Odyssey is a puzzle game in the tradition of Deadly Rooms of Death: defeat monsters by understanding and outwitting their predictable behavior. Leaf is different enough to distinguish itself if you're a fan of the genre, and a good entry point if you're not: it has six monster types as opposed to DROD's 20 or so, and it changes a few core mechanics like "the player can't move diagonally" that change up the puzzles. The base campaign's quite fun, and there's a good amount of player-created levels which I've only scratched the surface of. Plus, you're a cute little ferret who does a little bounce when you hit the wait button.

[h2]Masterclass of puzzle design with interesting and fun mechanics[/h2]

Perhaps one of the best puzzle games of 2024. Don't let the simple graphics fool you. This is a gem worth picking up if you love puzzle games.

You control Leaf the ferret, and travesre the world while solving puzzles. Monsters and obstacles stand in your way and you need to eliminate them in creative and interesting ways to progress. Enemies move, behave and interact with each other, with Leaf and the environment in different ways. The game is often quite challenging, yet not overly complicated. The world/level design is rock solid. The puzzles are expertly designed, creative, varied, devious with clever twists, baits and traps. Definitely recommended for the advanced+ puzzle player. 

Cool interface, note/observations system, fast travel and map. Boots up in 1-2 seconds which is always a positive. Plays OK with a controller, though hovering over stuff with the mouse can be a huge help, or even necessary with the more complex puzzles.

When I was a kid growing up in the US, there was a saying that if you dig a hole straight down it would go all the way to China. People in other countries have similar sayings, that you could dig a hole/tunnel to China/Japan/Australia/Brazil/etc.

This takes that concept and turns it into a game. Each game lasts about 30 seconds; at the beginning you are given a target country to dig your way to. There's a small arrow (and a flag on the Earth's surface) indicating where you're supposed to go. The larger the country, the most forgiving it is. For small countries, you have to hit the target exactly! When you reach the surface, it plays a little song, shows a picture representing the country and tells what the capital city is. There is a travel log that keeps track of where you've been and when you first arrived there. There are achievements based on reaching certain destinations or completing geographic regions.

Your character digs automatically -- there is only a "turn" button. You must manage your oxygen and food levels or else wind up dying and finding yourself in Heaven or Hell... While digging you can find food and oxygen, and there are also some power-ups that will make you dig faster or slower, turn backwards, or kill you. The nearer you get to the Earth's core, the slower you go and faster your life force depletes.

This game has a lot of similarities with Histoire, Nepheshel and similar free RPG Maker games, but to put in perspective how it plays in terms a westerner would understand... You guys remember Ash Lake, from Dark Souls? How to get into it you had to get into a tree, then pass through an illusory wall to get a chest, and then go through yet another illusory wall to get into the secret area? Imagine that, except the whole game is like that and it's made in RPG Maker. That's Fanastasis.

It's a pretty unique way of designing a game, with positives and negatives. Especially at the beginning, the feeling of getting into hidden places and discovering all the lore and so on is really good, I loved that part of it. At the end though I must admit I was having to take a look at some walkthroughs and old 5ch threads to find out about the last memories and fragments of other dimensions I was missing as I would frequently get stuck trying to figure out how I should continue. 

Another thing to mention, in case that wasn't obvious, is that you absolutely should know Japanese or have some kind of machine translation tool ready if you might want to tackle this game. Lots of puzzles, hints and so on rely on the notes and dialog you get from the game. The lore and story is also rather intricate, in a good way. It is not spoon fed to you but rather you need to figure it out from the bits of information the game gives you.

But all in all, this was a really fun game, I really liked the free version when I played it and I liked the additional scenario with the witches as well. I could see it gaining a niche following in the west if it was translated someday. Thumbs up.

I think it's an interesting take on Dune 2, and you can see from my avatar that I'm a fan of Dune 2. The thing is, I hate micro, and see it as a gameplay defect rather than a feature, and this game is much heavier on micro than Dune 2 or Command & Conquer were.

So, I'm not really enjoying it, but if you enjoy micro (as most RTS players do) then you'll probably have a good time.

It's Dune 2, in a more mobile/tablet kind of way (since there is no res settings (>.<))  The usual 'let's duplicate a beloved game, and not bother putting some quality into it'. And FYI the achievements are set to stupid for the kind of game this is.

Overall a much superior experience to the original Dune 2. It is a great game. The music is great, the voice lines are nice. The economy is interesting, different from Dune 2 and the Command and Conquers but fun to play with. The game is visually appealing. I do have some complaints. 
1. The path finding leaves much to be desired. Units often block each other and force each other to take longer paths needlessly. Especially bad in choke points or when getting into fights. 
2. Infantry units overall feel a bit weak. Low hit points combined with decent damage taken from tank cannons leads infantry to die pretty fast. They also lack a way to heal their hp, a weakness vehicles don't have thanks to bots. I will say the Bio Nexus Tox Troopers rock. 
3. Terra Prima's Bombers from the Air Pad feel rather unreliable. The damage isn't great, and the bombers bomb whatever they like instead of what you tell them to bomb. 
Complaints aside, the game was fun and challenging start to finish with all 3 campaigns as well as the scenarios. It has my recommendation.

TLDR; Game great but a few tweaks could make it perfect.
Never thought I'd fall in love with a scrabble-based rouglike. But then again, I said the same thing about Balatro. This game definitely fills that same niche and is inexpensive to boot, so worth picking up for sure. My only gripe is that the game seems a bit poorly balanced and can seem downright unfair at times. Another nitpick I have is that the game doesn't necessarily explain all of its terms (stamps, badges, stickers, etc) to you, but they are easy to find out through playing. Well worth the purchase. This game deserves more attention.

Yeah, it's essentially "Balatro but Scrabble", but with a transparent love for Scrabble that comes from having played a whole lot of it. The Mouse boss, for example, is a nod to the old strategy of milking double-score out of tiles by using two-letter words along a parallel. The creators of this game didn't just set out to mine the Balatro rush, they did so with a genuine passion for the game and it really does shine through. For that alone, the game is worth a purchase to anyone that likes Scrabble.

Which isn't to say it doesn't have its own unique strategies. You can, for example, pull Boons (think "tarot/spectral cards") that, for example, put stickers on the board, offering point/multiplier bonuses. There's also a neat mechanic called "Rivets", where some tiles can be given a really nice bonus, but once played, they get "riveted" to the board permanently, and persist between rounds. It's another bit of risk/reward that elevates the core premise. There's also a new kind of letter tile, an "exclamation point", that can be used at the end of ANY word - but, doing so creates its own challenges, since no letters can go after/below it (with the exception of an upgrade that lets you use multiple exclamation marks in a row, but it's a semi-rare randomly occurring upgrade, so don't count on it).

On that note, the RNG is well-utilized. There's not only a decent variety of upgrades available (with the item pool being robust enough that rounds won't produce the exact same bonuses for every run), but there's also a "rarity" tier system that itself can be adjusted via upgrades. At this point I can't attest that it matches Balatro's Jokers in variety, but it's close enough that, in my experience at least, it fits with what the game is trying to accomplish.

I also like that the game brings a few small innovations of its own. For example, I really enjoy the "Bronze/Silver/Gold" mechanic for post-round reward gains. It's a different approach, given how most other Balatro-likes stick to the basic "pass/fail" model. I do think this mechanic would benefit from allowing players to end a round early if they hit the Bronze goal, if only to offer another nuance in the game's risk/reward strategy, but the fact that it's there is worth celebrating at least.

My sole criticism is that I do think the UI and art direction feel a bit clunky and amateurish. The tiles seem just a hair too small for "drag-and-drop"; would prefer a "click to hold, click to release" option. Also, placing Relics has a tendency to make previously acquired other Relics shuffle around like crazy; I haven't run into any situations where this affects the gameplay and it's easily reversible, it's just a small cosmetic quirk that unfortunately projects a slight air of carelessness. Also, the Relic tile art has no artistic cohesion; compare to how Balatro's Jokers all share a unified style, while the Relic tiles vary wildly in every way, from simple things like line weights and pixel resolution, to broad-stroke things like relative cartoonishness and art style/inspiration. There's also no getting around it; almost all the audio feels like it was sourced from royalty-free libraries. The "round win" sound in particular feels like it'd be more at-home in a golf game. However I sense that most of these "issues" will be addressed in future updates.

All in all, I gave this game six hours of my time, and I'm likely going to give it a whole lot more. This will also likely be a go-to gift for any friends I have that I know enjoy word puzzle games. If you like word puzzles and risk/reward gameplay, this is a must-have for your library!

Picked this up and played it for about an hour. Not bad at all and very impressive for what I understand is a one-man dev team. Reminds me of Into the Breach, mixed with a deck-builder game, as you progress through a run and pick up new units to replace more basic grunts in your roster. I can see a lot of potential. 

Some early confusion on exactly what to click on to get to the next battle, but that is pretty standard for Early Access and after a bit of trial and error I was getting quite into it and starting to see how you can plan to combine units and take advantage of their synergies.

The art style for the interface is very strong, but it would be nice to see more variety in the battle areas themselves, both aesthetically and functionally. Currently they all seem to be the same flat areas, but hopefully this will change as I get deeper into a run. Also would be good to see more variety in the colour palette, currently the environments all feel a little too yellow for my taste.

In general though, it's a strong first impression and I could see myself getting quite into it. It's not just battles either, there are traders and story points along the way that can give you little boosts. Would be good to see this expanded upon. Also, it's suitably difficult, especially if you beeline right for the entry points to the next floor down. Balancing the difficulty so it's tricky without getting too frustrating will be key I think.

So far I'd give it 3.5/5 with strong potential for that to increase during Early Access.

As someone who lived in Japan throughout the pandemic, and spent most of their social time in cafes, this game is highly relatable to me. I was worried that the perspective would go a bit off the rails but despite some characters early on who seem to be more of semi-caricatures it was actually very relatable and even characters who had views that I personally don’t hold, I can remember talking to people in Japan who did think like that. So for the most part the characters feel very real and the things they complain about sometimes hit on a level I think anyone who lived in Japan during the pandemic can relate to. Any time either of the Go To campaigns were mentioned, I groaned in agreement because I remember seeing those messes in real time. How this relates to someone with no experience in Japan during that time, I don’t know.

The coffee mechanics are also pretty good, the idea of grinding intensity changing the flavor of the coffee (as opposed to grind size here in the real world) was a really novel way to gamify coffee making, and brewing the Chemex was really intuitive and the best representation of coffee brewing I’ve seen in a video game yet. I feel it would’ve been cool to add rotating to the pour intensity but I can see how that would possibly be too much.

Overall some of the characters hit hard and the setting is dealt with in a really honest way. There’s a certain string of memories you go through that all end in customers holding their heads in despair. The game mechanics are a pretty great representation of brewing coffee in a video game and don’t get too repetitive in my opinion.

Much of the critical problem has been addressed and it's fairly balanced and fun to play now!
I changed my review to positive, thank you!

The simplest and best way I would describe this game is: Very cute, very fun, can get moderately challenging if you want it to be, and can feel very rewarding when you complete a challenging level.

It's a very charming game and a really good pick for when your in a casual mood. Tons of content that always felt unique and explored new ideas. The achievements range from simple level completion to really challenging optional objectives that will test your skills and understanding of the game's mechanics. All the abilities are unique compared to other 2D platformers and almost all of them are fun to use, also I enjoy that you don't lose your power up when taking damage like in most Mario games.

There are a few very minor things that do bug me though. In levels where objects and the player can teleport from one side of the screen to the other, it can look a little jarring, especially with big objects such as the platforms that if you try to ride from one side to the other, you likely will fall off of it when either you or it teleports. This isn't a big issue as you are not required to do so and the average player likely wouldn't even experience it. Slightly more bothersome is that the achievements do not have English translations so it was sometimes hard for me to understand what I had to do to get them, but usually the picture was enough to figure it out. Some of the game mechanics felt a tiny bit rough around the edges, but I mostly don't mind it and it does seem that a lot of thought and love was put into making sure they felt fun.

Lastly, I really enjoyed the lighthearted feel of the game, and many levels had some text boxes encouraging me to keep going, congratulate me on completing a difficult level, or to encourage me to be curious about my surroundings in exploration focused levels. It's a simple little thing but these always made me smile and feel happy.

TLDR: I have not had as much fun with a game as I did with this one for a long while. The game always made me feel proud of myself for completing a challenging level or achievement and even made me feel very happy in general. Many of the game mechanics are very unique and not just carbon copies of what other games like it do, especially for the powerups. The game can feel a little buggy if you look too closely into it, especially if you look too closely at some of the more complicated and/or ambitious game mechanics, but never in a way that ruins how fun and unique they are.

I've completed Dadish 1, 2 & 3.

The camera operates well and as expected. Sometimes if you get a wall behind you, the camera slams right up against you. A problem that's existed since the dawn of 3D games.

Difficulty wise this was the most challenging of the series. Long levels and finding the collectible stars in the three dimensional world adds another level of difficulty.

Despite this, like all the others in the series, I've finished the game in 2 hours.

Minimal bugs, mostly due to the engine. Shadows don't render until pretty close and items in the distance may pop in and out of existence based on your field of view and/or camera positioning. I would guess this is the Unity engine and something that could have been corrected with some adjustments.

All in all this was a great game and a great series and it's sad that it's all over. Hopefully next up is a Dadish 4D.

To start off, one might think that with my bias towards 3D platformers I wouldn't be able to make an objective recommendation for something from this genre without delving into nostalgia. However, contrary to popular belief there are praises and criticisms to be made aside from comparison here and there when it's suitable enough to do so. So with that out of the way, let's get to it.

Dadish as a franchise now with more than 3 games centered around a father who somehow just keeps losing track of his children has gone into the third dimension. Indeed, this 2D platformer that linger between casual and precise has now some gameplay changes and to me they lean this product more towards the former. As expected, the camera movement is in control of the player and while it can sometimes get behind bushes and trees the levels are so vast in extension that this is rarely a problem. Also, jumps now have a shadow that can make the depth perception problem a little easier even if it's not cast on pits. Fortunately, for these jumps the hitbox on both Dadish and the platform is big enough to compensate as well as the coyote time implemented accordingly. As a result, Dadish feels natural, forgiving and tight to control.

In addition, the enemies don't pose as much of a threat as before as with their placement and the size of the fields you'd find yourself going around them to be the preferred option. This can even be applied to jumps between spikes and boulders coming towards you, letting you "cheese" the intended path for a shorter version. Depending on who you ask this can be considered a design flaw or a way to motivate speedruns as there have been bad examples of this in the past (like Mega Man X7). Either way, I found myself gravitating towards the latter and cutting completion times in quite a quick fast because of it.

Furthermore, there are 2 special levels worth mentioning while talking about the gameplay. The first is the Burgurgular ones which much like 2 are auto runners although this time you go forward with a fixed camera that prevents it from being stuck but can make for some depth perception problems in some particular jumps. The second is the daikon levels, otherwise known as the Crash Bandicoot levels as you get chased towards the camera while you try to escape as fast as possible. These were the most challenging ones not due to time reaction but rather your movement speed not being able to compensate for small mistakes. In fact, one of them features a particular star that can be a bit annoying to get considering what you have to do.

Speaking of which, stars return as an excuse to explore the levels and in this case the third dimension certainly gave the dev more of a reason to get creative. Some are quite well hidden if you're not used to checking for ledges or turning the camera around and none require you doing crazy jumps or some air maneuvering like you would give some collectibles of platformers of old (Spyro 3 comes to mind). Take in mind that these are completely optional after all so even if you don't find them while exploring you may find yourself glazing at some details while snowmen, sandcastles and more that you can interact with.

Lastly, it wouldn’t be fair for the game if I didn’t mention the boss fights and the witty lines you have with your child at the end of each level. As such, each boss is different like in the other games and while the third dimension is used for the way to defeat them they do still come off as quite easy until the final one whose fight is probably the longest because of certain waiting sections. Regarding the lines, I consider some of them to have cracked a smile but others didn’t click unfortunately. Humour is subjective after all.

In short, I can safely recommend this one as a cheap 3D platformer alternative to the ones being recognized at the Game Awards and the such. Oh, and don’t fret over not owning a ps5 as you may jam to the beats of some of these levels instead.

A love letter to 80s text adventure ROM games with Slay the Spire rogue like elements and 5 Nights at Freddy's real time strategy. What seems simple at first on the surface quickly becomes a bit more in-depth as you play. Not only are you trying to build the best deck possible, but with things unfolding in real time, you can't sit still trying to dissect what the best possible move will be. The longer you wait, the more time passes and more enemies you have to face. Having to balance playing the best movies while managing the threat level clock gives what would otherwise be another run of the mill deckbuilder a unique and fun edge. And with everything playing out with just a few keys and no mouse input, it takes you back to the earliest of PC games. Add in some fun dialog, characters, and map exploration, this is a pleasantly surprising game I can see myself playing for either 15 mins or a couple hours depending on my mood.

[b] [h1] So, the fourth version of this Fort Boyard game has been released. Now I will highlight the main advantages and disadvantages of the game and the bugs that I found. [/h1] [/b]

[h2] Let's start with [b] the advantages [/b] of the new version of the game: [/h2]

[h3] 1) A large number of challenges. [/h3]
Taking into account the addition of 10 new challenges to this version of the game, there are 50 challenges in total, which makes the game very diverse with each new playthrough, and this is good.

[h3] 2) The perk system. [/h3]
The perk system allows you to diversify each new game that you start even more. Before starting the game, you are asked to choose 1 of 6 perks that will work throughout the game. You can choose it yourself or do it randomly. Some perks can simplify the game or complicate it, or do both throughout the playthrough, which makes the game very unpredictable. 

For example, the Poisoned gift perk before each challenge gives you a simplification or complication. Let's say you might get a chance to win 2 keys or clues if you pass the challenge. But you may also get a card that tells you that in the next challenge you cannot leave the room until you get the key or clue, which means there is a huge chance of getting into the fort prison.

This is where the advantages of this game end.

[h2] Let's move on to [b] the disadvantages [/b] of the game: [/h2]

[h3]1) Some new challenges are too simple even at the maximum difficulty level.[/h3]
This is especially true for such new challenges as Pirate Planks, Catacombs, Bank and Garage. 

[h3]2) No new music in new challenges.[/h3]
All new challenges feature music that doesn't fit the specific call in any way. For example, in new challenges (Garage, Bank, Catacombs, Capstan), the main theme of Fort Boyard plays and it does not fit there at all and is very annoying.

[h3]3) No new characters in 5 years. [/h3]
This is the fourth version of this game and so far we still can only choose from four characters to play . So far, there is no character customization in the game (Except for the Ghosts of the past perk, which dresses the entire team in old clothes from the 1990s).

[h3]4) The leaderboard only works offline.[/h3]
In this game leaderboard can only show your results with your team name and how much boyards you got. This leaderboard not showing you the results of other players like the Fort Boyard game from 2019 version. The 2020 version of the game have leaderboard as well but its not working since the release :). So there are literally no motivation to play in this game and collecting as many boyards as possible as long as Leaderboard still not showing nicknames of other Steam players and how much Boyards they got in one run.

[h3]5) Only one player can play in the Treasure room.[/h3]
In Treasure room can play only one player even if you playing together with someone with 2 controllers. It sucks that only one player can collect Boyards while the other player just watching you.
It would've been great if when you playing with someone together you can collect Boyards together as well by playing different characters. Split screen system in Treasure room can solve the problem. 

[h3]6) Same game breaking bug from old version of the game from 2022.[/h3]
There are some bugs in this game. 

For example, when i won a duel against Time Master during my playthrough 2 times in Long mode i got 2 min and 30 seconds for Treasure Room but when i won third duel the timer added me time from 2 minutes to 2 min and 15 seconds when its supposed to be 2 minutes and 45 seconds in total. 
And with the perk Poisoned gifts i got 2 extra duels in Long run mode and i won all 5 duels and supposed to have 3 minutes and 15 seconds in total, i got only 2:30 because of this bug. 

[b] Another bug in challenge Switchman - the water clock is always invisible. [/b]

[b] In Casino challenge something wrong with mouse sensitivity. Even with a huge DPI its really hard to keep the balance. In previous verison of the game (2020) it was  way playable. My friends, who played in Remote play with the gamepad in Casino cant keep balance at all because of how hard it is to keep the balance. [/b] 

There are a few more bugs in the game as well but its more like vusial bugs but they are not as sirious as the first one i described. 

[h1] CONCLUSION [/h1]

This is still the best version of Fort Boyard games out of all 4 of them and i still recommend this one to buy, [b]but i will change this review to a positive one ONLY AFTER these bugs will be fixed and when the Leaderboard will be an online one like in 2019 version of the Fort Boyard game from Microids so you can see top 10 players from Steam who got more Boyards. The game is quite enjoyable, but there are a few key issue's I've noticed during gameplay that I think may be a deal breaker for some players. Keep in mind, that at the time of this review, the game has been released for just under a month, so I fully expect these bugs to be fixed in the future since they're quite noticeable.

[h3] NPC's [h3]
The NPC's in game can be quite irritating, there have been numerous times where, after becoming a reasonably "famous" streamer, that the NPC's will randomly walk into my home/run into my home's main entrance. This can be an issue since you can collide with the NPC's. Basically, if enough of them swarm your home, you will end up getting trapped. 

They are also constantly ran over by the Car's traversing the map, and their bodies litter the streets until eventually despawning.

[h3] Deliveries [h3]
When delivering multiple items, you are unable to pick up the box's the items were delivered in and move them, this leads to issues where, upon opening a new desk for example, all your other delivered items will quite literally end up being flung god knows how far, and with some of the box's being incredibly small often leads to items disappearing if you cannot find them, which is obviously a needless loss of money. What I would suggest to the devs (Not that I imagine my review will go noticed since they seem busy working on the game) is that you can pick up the box's that your items are delivered in and move them into your house.

[h3] Decoration [h3]
With one of the 5 star desks, you have a large built in shelving unit where the back of your desk would face the wall. This, as stated in the item description, is where you can put decorative items (Dolls, Skulls, general decorative clutter basically) but these seemingly intentional locations for placing your decorative items do not let you place decorations on them, which makes buying the higher end desks pointless.

[h3] Streaming [h3]
There is a major glitch in the game, that can be performed at any point and will cut down your playtime considerably. For those of you that watched "Let's game it out" video yesterday (16th Feb, 2025) you will know what it is.

[spoiler] When you open the streaming menu, you can spam start stream & end stream, whilst spamming your viewer count and follower count raise substantially. For those of you who have a mouse capable of spamming the LMB with the push of a button, it is absolutely game breaking. In my own save, used exclusively to test the game, find bugs and generally mess around before deciding whether I enjoyed it or not, I have over 600,000 followers, 100,000 subscribers and own the best house, vehicle. items in the game. And I am only on Day 9. [/spoiler]

[h3] Overall Opinion on the game [h3]

Overall, I have found the game to be quite a pleasant experience when not encountering these bugs, while I wouldn't say they are game breaking, they can most certainly be frustrating as a player to encounter and deal with (The NPC's trapping you in a room? Yup, had them swarm my trailer and block me in).

The game definitely has improvements to be made, but considering it hasn't even been out for a full month yet? It is remarkably well made with no major bugs (other than the one mentioned above when Streaming) and definitely an enjoyable experience. 

I give it a solid 7/10.

This game is fun.

The gameplay loop is pretty simple to grasp.

Start off broke in a trailer, with a free computer. Start your first stream and fumble through learning setting up bitrate and general settings for your stream to not drop frames, Just like in real life! The tutorial cleverly leaves this part out.. You adjust each setting till the stream says youre not dropping frames and go. 5 different settings to adjust to match your video to your internet speed.

Lots of parts for computer builds, but once i made enough money to hire the uWu Streamer, i never had to worry about money after getting her first lump of earnings. I was able to buy a fully kitted out pc and start making loads of money via streaming, upgrade my internet speed, and in turn making money on my uploads on YouHube (you can upload the stream footage to the ingame internet to make extra money after a certain point).

There is also an Instagram type program on your ingame phone. You can upload 1 picture each day, each post will gain you more followers and eventually youll start getting paid for your daily posts. You can even keep posting the same photo during your rise to stardom and it will build your following.

During the early game you are introduced to doing deliveries on your bicycle. Super easy to do, you make between $50 and $54 each delivery. Something to do between streams to keep yourself fed. If youre hungry, your energy depletes faster and you will end any stream youre doing.

Im honestly suprised hit 100% on the achievements in less than 20 hours, but like i stated before, once you get a streamer to work for you, youre now on the money river in a luxury raft. You do have to build them a computer to use, but with the money youre making as you get donations during streams, uploading to your YouHube channel and post to your Insta; you should be pretty flush by the time you can afford a new place and an employee. It will only snowball from there. I didnt notice any difference in the money i got from my one employee on weak computers or top tier. I may be wrong. I only checked every so often to grab cash from her, mostly i forgot you have to interact with them to get the money and i think they have a limit of how much they hold before not paying more. Again, i may be incorrect.. Just dont forget to interact with them every few ingame days.

There are 3 different homes you can rent other than your starting trailer. I ended up moving into the first step up from the trailer, then moving into the biggest house after about a week of income from the streamer I hired and my piles of donations i was making during ASMR streams. Easy Street.

I never played anything by FM Studio before. Literally only discovered them now. Somehow after having played through all of Rusty Lake games, my Steam algorithm still didn't realize that yes I'd like more of that please.

If Rusty Lake games are spooky, then FM Studio is their grotesque cousin. Not in a bad way! Though potentially in a triggery way. I saw the previews and knew it was going to be grisly, so, like, I’m not surprised. More like I’m jarred far more than I guessed I’d be. This leans heavily into body horror and gore, and I had to step away a few times because it freaked me out more than I anticipated. There was even one point that I got jarred so badly that I completely missed the item sitting right in front of my face and then ended up angrily stuck in the game. 

With that said, this game still managed to scratch my itch for a point-and-click with advanced puzzles that were challenging in a good way. It’s hard but fair. The solutions are mostly intuitive enough that if you actually read through the stuff in your inventory, you’ll have the clues you need. Just don’t overthink things because it’s fairly straightforward in the end, never as convoluted as you fear. If you do get stuck, there’s a handy hint system, which I definitely used on some occasions ([spoiler]how was I supposed to parse that “for my second birthday party” means he’s 2yo and it’s not simply him having this year's birthday party part two electric boogaloo lmao[/spoiler]). And even if you don’t want the hints themselves, if there’s a box with a “?” appearing on the top right corner of the screen, that’s a hint in itself that there’s a puzzle on that screen. You can also click the “?” simply to check whether you’ve collected all the clues/pieces necessary to solve the puzzle—it’ll say “something is missing” otherwise, which helped me immensely in making sure I wasn’t banging my head against the wall on something I only thought I had enough clues for. 

Never before have I played a 2D point-and-click where I actually dread clicking on things to discover what’s inside. I’m very impressed. Thanks, I hate it, five stars.

I'm a casual (meaning I suck at them) fighting game fan who has a particular interest in retro 2D fighters.  My primary interest is Capcom titles but lately I have been branching out into SNK and others.  I had really enjoyed the QUByte rerelease of the Breakers Collection so I decided to give this game a chance as well.  The fact that it is unofficially tied into the old Double Dragon series also was a plus.  Having put a couple hours into it, I have to say I like it.  The character designs are cool and have well differentiated fighting styles.  Honestly, I like them better than some of the designs in KOF, although I am sure some people will consider that heresy.  Of course, being a Playmore game (SNK), ROTD will look and feel a bit familiar to fans of KOF, although certainly they are their own games.  One of the interesting features of ROTD is that it is a tag team game, which makes it feel a bit different from the rest of the SNK catalog.  At 15, the roster is not huge by the standards of 2002 fighting games, but it is enough to make the game feel complete and all the characters have their own distinct identity.  The music is an eclectic mix an reasonably memorable.  If nothing else, it does stand out for being different than most fighting game music.  The backgrounds are passable, but nothing amazing.  The only complaint I have so far is that I have been unable to defeat the final boss, but that is not surprising given the reputation of SNK bosses.  All in all, a worthwhile game for retro fighting game fans, at least from my "casual" perspective.  I will leave it to the diehard fighting game experts to comment on the deeper aspects of the gameplay.

I decided to check out this game as I was curious about the project from a person who created the character of Sanya for "Sword Art Online: Integral Factor" and wanted to show them my appreciation. Trailer and screenshots already have shown me what to expect, and these most certainly don't lie. So I can definitely appreciate the honesty when selling a game with so many shortcomings.

This is most certainly the case of "My first game in Unity". There's no story really, game can be completed in 30 minutes (no matter the difficulty level), and graphics are very, very simple, amount of animations can be counted on two hands, and controls are janky (also keyboard mapping is horrible and cannot be changed - WASD movement, HJKL for attacks, dodges and ult)... Which is a shame, because if the title would be refined, it might've been a decent tribute to Megaman and Castlevania, especially since music is nice. Gameplay loop - while simple - can be satisfying. There's a constant barrage of projectiles, traps and monsters have large hitboxes, and despite having only three attack options, it feels good to make effective use of these to get the highest rank. There's some replay value, if you wish to get a S rank in all three acts (and to do so, you have to explore and not die). But you still have to ignore lack of content you pay 5 euros for.

It's not an attrocious game, it functions, you can have fun with it if you're okay with lack of polish and it has a decent difficulty level, but with many other options you have for the same price I'd recommend buying it only if you want to support its creator and if you're okay with what's being presented to you in the trailer.

PS. The game is in Japanese only, but since there's no story, it's not really an issue, as the text only explains game's mechanics, which you can figure out by yourself anyway. Just remember to use a controller.

[h1]Side-scrolling Town Idler[/h1]


[i]Incremental Town RPG[/i] is pretty much what it says on the tin.  It's an idle game where you build up a town, and go fight some monsters.

The town is in side-scroller form, several screens long.  Send villagers to harvest resources, mainly wood, fish, coal, and ores.  You have to hire villagers to use them.

You can send a few villagers per resource station to improve output.  You can also upgrade stations in the market.  Upgrading requires spending the resource produced.  Fortunately, you can also click on resource stations for fast gathering.

Later, there are production buildings that use said resources.  A mill/farm combo makes grain, grinds it into flour, and also produces meat and horses.  The cookery makes bread and uses fish, meat, and bread to make better meals.  The tavern brews grain into beer.  And you have your standard blacksmith.

Spare villagers can be trained up in the barracks and sent out into battle agains various monsters.  Your army is led by a general who levels up by fighting by themselves in areas accessed by the tavern.  The fights here are full-screen, but there is a minimize button so you can do other stuff while your general fights.  You'll need to build access to the areas the army fights in.

You build a building the game text refers to as a "mint" to make coins, but instead of making it out of the gold you're mining, you just get a better trading post.

You trade in resources for coin, but this is done on a countdown.  There's no instant-sell of goods, nor are all resources tradeable.  Production also seems to find some special resources, like fishing up bottles or finding gems, but these are not sellable, either.  These rare finds become relevant for the final building.

The inability to sell everything at once becomes an annoyance with a million-coin quest milestone you need to reach.  You have to babysit some of the trading goods to make sure they don't fall below what you need for efficent production.

The army fights do earn you cash, though you'll of course have to replace lost soldiers.  Your general also earns cash when he fights in the areas accessed through the tavern.

The game has a "prestige" system, but it doesn't feel worth it.  I didn't bother with it and still reached the endgame in 25 hours.

The prestige currency is prayer points, which are mostly earned by trading in drops from your general's fights in the tavern.  Appropriately, the building to use them in and gain prestige is a church, but it is one of the last buildings you build.

There are a few prestige tech trees to improve your town, but you have to restart the game to use them.  By the time you've saved up for something good, you're already halfway through the game, and most of the improvements you can gain are duplicated in the other upgrades you can get in a run.

After you've won the game, there's a couple more things you can do.  There's a final building with access to a post-game fight zone.  This takes some rare drops, the gems and such you can't sell, but one of them didn't drop for me by the time I unlocked it, probably because I didn't set production high enough on the resource that dropped it.

There's also a couple statues to buy.

Mycelium is an example of a very good use of limited resources by the developer. While graphical fidelity is obviously not the strong suit of the game, and the amount of written dialogue isn't nowhere near enough to match larger RPGs, the core mechanics and the storyline is carried through by its solid foundations and the game is still (usually) pleasant to look at as a result of a consistent art direction and a well-picked focus on low resolution pixel art.

The combat systems have quite a decent amount of depth compared to other examples in the genre of tactical strategy and are for the most part fairly well balanced and don't get stale for the duration of the game. The upgrades feel meaningful, the resource management doesn't get completely invalidated as the game goes on (although it becomes way easier once your characters get strong enough).

The strongest side of Mycelium are the characters and the worldbuilding, albeit the latter leaves a lot of unresolved questions that admittedly don't really all need to be resolved. Characters interact with each other, react to situations in and out of combat. They have their own agendas, personalities and they subvert the character tropes that you could initially suspect from them. My only complaint in regards to the story was the fact that the ending felt like it was too brief - while all the character threads were somewhat resolved, their resolutions I feel weren't really explored to their full potential, leaving the ending slightly unsatisfying.

Definitely worth your money and time

The choice of whether to save your children from a living nightmare or keep them around to use as squishy meat shields is quite the moral dilemma, but I consistently find myself making the right decision.

A Nostalgic yet Fresh Take on the Pac-Man Genre
There’s a certain 1990s wholesomeness to this title, mixed with a very fresh take on the Pac-Man genre. This rogue-like RPG is a testament to the determination and passion of the developers. Playing this game feels like being transported back to a simpler time in life—when bills weren’t a problem, health issues didn’t exist, and all I needed to do was game, sip on a soda, and try to beat my last run.

Gameplay & Mechanics
Every attempt in this game is a slow build of adrenaline. The strategy required to manage your energy while making the best use of the fruit scattered across the maze keeps your brain running at full speed throughout the dungeon. The mixture of tantalizing collectibles, power-ups, and shop items creates a deeply engaging RPG experience. You genuinely feel yourself getting stronger with each moment. The pacing is exceedingly well-crafted and deserves the accolades it has been receiving in reviews.

Characters
Each duckling has a distinct personality, reminiscent of Navi from Ocarina of Time. They offer helpful tips that are both charming and useful. Akira, a playful cat who wants to keep you safe (and take your money), adds a fun dynamic to the game. Panda, a sweet and kind bear with a love for reading, adds depth to the world. The sound of book pages fluttering as Panda reads made me want to crack open a book myself.

The villains are just as delightful. Big Boss Bergeron, for example, exudes a Cajun cook vibe—I can practically imagine this alligator whipping up some crawfish for me. The other villains are equally memorable, adding both personality and challenge to the game. Their mechanics are simple but tough enough to keep things engaging.

Final Thoughts
Overall, my time spent in this game has been incredibly rewarding. With 20+ hours split between the alpha and the live release, every moment has been a joy. I’m excited to eventually beat the game in its live state and experience even more of what it has to offer.

AI Fantasy – Not Worth It (At Least Right Now)

I was really excited when I got this game, but honestly? I can’t recommend it unless you can grab it for $1 or less. It’s just not in a good place right now.

The Gameplay is a Mess
You start off with really low stats, and the way skill checks work is just ridiculous. Every time you roll for something, it’s 1d6, but when skills require an 11 or higher, you’re basically screwed unless you get really lucky. Sure, rolling a 6 gives you an extra die, but that doesn’t happen nearly enough to matter. On the other hand, rolling a 1 gives you a die that takes away from your total, which makes no sense and just feels like unnecessary punishment.

The game also constantly gives you repetitive choices. Like, sometimes all three options rely on the same stat (Strength, Intelligence, Dexterity), which just kills any strategy. If I’m making choices, I want actual choices, not three versions of the same thing.

Trading, Perks, and Equipment? All Bad.
The barter system is terrible—it’s frustrating and makes trading feel useless. Unlocking abilities and perks is just as bad because the game doesn’t even tell you what you need to unlock them. How are you supposed to plan or improve your build if the game keeps you in the dark?

And don’t even get me started on the equipment system—it’s just plain bad. It feels half-baked and doesn’t add anything meaningful to the experience.

It Could Be Good, But Not Like This
Look, I know this is an AI-generated game, and I’ve played some decent AI games before, but this one? It’s just not there yet.

What Needs to Be Fixed:
Switch to 2d6 or even 3d6 rolls so skill checks aren’t so punishing.
More variety in choices, so I’m not stuck picking between the same stat over and over.
Fix the barter system—it’s a mess right now.
Show perk unlock requirements so players actually know how to progress.
Improve the equipment system so it actually feels like it matters.
If they fix these things, I’d 100% recommend it, but in its current state? Absolutely not.

I haven't spent much time in the app yet, so just leaving a short review now with some first impressions. I'll edit later when I spend some more time with it.

I think the templates are really helpful, they show a good example output of what you can make using this app. The custom templates library / creation area makes sense where it is, but I think it should have some representation in the "collection" view as well. Especially since it seems templates are scoped to a collection.  

I don't have a need for it currently, but I think the option of "global templates" would make sense, or maybe the ability to maybe copy a template from one collection to another. Can probably do that manually by copying the Templates.xml from one project to another. I see that there are import/export buttons in the UI, but it seems they are meant just for cards?

Also, I appreciate that you went with plaintext XML data storage. That makes these projects Git friendly, and the XML output could be reasonably integrated with an external game build pipeline.  I haven't attempted it yet, but I suppose you could plug some script into the project such that you design your cards > pull real stats / text from your db and stuff that in the xml > export the output cards as a "publish" build. I'm not sure what all the design goals for this app are, but I think it would be attractive if you could rig this thing up with a bit more string interpolation. If the user could just assign a few custom properties to each card (stats, name, flavor text, etc.) and edit that with a few simple text inputs separate from the actual card designer. And/or import from a CSV. I think you'd really be cooking then. 

On the "New project" modal dialog, it would be nice if the enter key (or ctrl+enter) would advance the dialog. 

The layers panel is functional, but would really benefit from some kind of treeview to show what elements are on the selected layer. I know you can hide all the layers besides the one you're interested in, but it would help achieve the same with fewer clicks.

They engage with the community daily, actively listen to feedback, and consistently roll out improvements. Every update brings exciting new content, from additional weapons and skins to deeper refinements in game mechanics. The real standout, though, is the incredible attention to detail in the map designs and the team's relentless focus on squashing bugs and optimizing performance.

If you're looking for a fresh experience either by yourself. Or with a co-op buddy, or if you are lucky to have a team to game with. Then this game is absolutely worth keeping an eye on. I think it's a pretty solid mystery game with a story that keeps you hooked, even if it gets a bit predictable in the later chapters. Sometimes it feels like things just happen because the plot needs them to, but the game handles it well enough that it’s not a huge issue, just something worth mentioning.
The first chapter is definitely the 2nd best one out of all the chapters. It does a great job of setting up the story and getting you invested. The second chapter isn’t as strong and feels a bit slow, but the rest of the game picks up the pace and keeps things interesting. Overall, the good parts outweigh the weaker ones.
One of the weaker aspects of the game is the Mystery Labyrinths. While they’re a cool idea, some of them feel a bit redundant and can be boring to look at. Traversing through them gets repetitive, and after a while, it starts to feel more like a chore than an exciting puzzle, with the only thing carrying them are the exchanges between characters (with the exception of chapter 5). It’s a shame because the concept is interesting, but the execution doesn’t always hit the mark, and side note, it felt like the mysteries got way shorter after chapter 2, maybe to save time and finish the game on a timely manner? Not sure 
Yuma, the main character, is kind of annoying at first. He comes off as unsure of himself and a little too timid, but he grows on you as the story goes on(sort of). Just when you start to like him though, a major twist changes his character quite a bit. It’s not necessarily bad, but it’s a bit sudden and halts the pace of his character development a bit.
The ending leaves a lot of questions unanswered, which feels a little off for a game about solving mysteries. It doesn’t ruin the story, but it does feel like it goes against the whole idea of finding the truth. On the bright side, it sets up for a sequel, so hopefully, there will be more answers down the line.
Overall, it's an entertaining mystery game with a good story and interesting characters. It’s not perfect, and some parts feel a little forced, but it’s definitely worth playing if you like detective stories and plot twists. Just be prepared for a bit of repetition in the Mystery Labyrinths.

As an aside before I get too far into my thoughts on RAIN CODE specifically, I would like to state that I have a very particular opinion on Kotaka's games, specifically the Danganronpa series. I have played all three of them through to completion, and found that while they have a lot of personality and are fun experiences, they are simultaneously mediocre at best as games. I could go more into what I find about Kotaka's design philosophy that I have problems with, but I've found that a lot of the same issues are present within RAIN CODE as well, so there isn't much reason to go too far into this as it stands. I still recommend the Danganronpa series and RAIN CODE if they are the types of games that you would find interesting, but go into them understanding that you are paying for the great personality built into the games rather than compelling detective gameplay.

As for RAIN CODE, it follows an amnesiac detective from the World Detective Organization, Yuma Kokohead, as he attempts to uncover the secret under Kanai Ward, a city of unending rain that has been isolated from the rest of the world via the infamous Amateratsu Corporation. The overall story on display here is quite good actually, definitely the best of the four Kodaka games I have played. One of the things I have found remarkable about him is that he makes a genuine effort to change his formulas to improve upon what he has already made, and removing the confines of a closed space where you know the identity of everybody inside adds a lot of dynamic to how the story can unfold. It takes most of the game for much of the overall story to kick into gear, but this is standard fare for Kodaka games. If you've played all three Danganronpa games, this should not be a shock to you.

Where the game truly shines, however, is in the other primary characters. Each chapter has you investigating a different case alongside one of your detective colleagues, each with a different special ability that is uniquely suited to investigating that particular case. This is easily the best part of the game, as it drastically changes how each case feels as you gather the clues necessary in order to solve the case. Each detective also has their own personality that alters the dynamic further, which helps prevent the fluffy dialogue from becoming stale over time. This game would've been significantly worse without this, and Kodaka nailed this aspect... despite most of these detectives being pretty one-dimensional and overstaying their welcome at times.

As for the mysteries, they're inconsistent at best. The early cases ironically were harder to predict than the latter cases, with one particular example in chapter 4 negating one of the biggest plot twists being especially ridiculous. Kodaka regularly runs into the problem of having all the evidence you need being given to you before pushing you to make any progress on solving the mystery itself. This is especially frustrating because the very first case you are sent on makes a big deal about one particular mechanic that allows you to find evidence that you couldn't find before beginning the Mystery Labyrinth. This, if I remember correctly, only appears one other time in the story. It's very saddening, because a lot of the predictability comes from the fact that you gain a lot of insight into things before having to do any actual legwork into solving the case. I would like to see Kodaka attempt to create a detective game with a more dynamic back and forth between information gathering and mystery solving, such as with the Ace Attorney series.

The atmosphere is great, the music is solid, the graphics are solid. There isn't much to say about all these except that they help sell the setting adequately and have the feel of a Kodaka game despite being its own setting. 

FInally, the gripes. The Mystery Labyrinth sections have a lot of the same problems that the Danganronpa games had. I had several moments during the reasoning death matches (equivalent to the debates in Danganronpa) where I could tell immediately what the correct solution key was, but the exact statement to use them on was ambiguous enough that it still took multiple tries to correctly pass that section. The barrel sections had questions that either made the answer plainly obvious or obtuse to the point of almost needing to guess letters, the latter mostly appearing in the latter chapters. Some of the labyrinth progression felt like arbitrary leaps, like you figure out an aspect of the case only to immediately have to jump to figuring out the central issue, despite it only being spelled out four questions later. There are quite a few QTE sections throughout the game, and those are about as interesting as they are in any game. The requests help flesh out some parts of the world, but otherwise are almost universally uninteresting and just a chore to get through every chapter. The gameplay overall is what drags the game down.

Would I recommend the game? Sure, especially if you enjoyed the Danganronpa series. You're not going to get a phenomenal detective game, but you'll get a fun story with quirky characters and a lot of goofy moments in between mostly bland mysteries. RAIN CODE is a fun time that will more likely than not grow on you over time, but if you're hoping for something that scratches that itch to solve murder mysteries, you're better off looking elsewhere.

From the creators of the beloved Danganronpa series, Master Detective Archives: RAIN CODE carves out a unique identity as a standalone entry in what could be called the "Danganronpa universe." While it’s undoubtedly a weird game, it stands as a solid addition to the mystery genre with its own charm and quirks.

Staying true to the signature art style and storytelling of Kazutaka Kodaka, the mastermind behind Danganronpa, RAIN CODE carries the unmistakable essence of its predecessor while exploring new territory. Fans of Kodaka’s work will feel right at home with its vibrant characters, clever twists, and dark humor.

The game unfolds as a classic detective tale, complete with fresh mysteries to unravel. The protagonist, Yuma Kokohead, feels like a fusion of Kyoko Kirigiri’s sharp intellect and Shuichi Saihara’s awkward charm. While Yuma is less experienced, his growth throughout the story makes him an engaging lead.

The game’s ambiance is a visual treat. The neon-soaked cyberpunk aesthetic creates a stunning atmosphere, with the city itself almost feeling like a character. The soundtrack, a mix of chill and mysterious tones, is exceptional and perfectly complements the game’s vibe. At times, it reminded me of Judgment—especially while exploring the city, interacting with its inhabitants, and taking on side quests.

Gameplay-wise, RAIN CODE combines familiar elements from Danganronpa with fresh mechanics to stand out. Instead of class trials, players dive into "Mystery Labyrinths," which serve as dynamic, puzzle-like arenas for solving cases. There’s even a hint of Persona influence in the way the game handles exploration and interactions. This blend of old and new makes the gameplay unique and engaging.

The story is, as expected, a wild ride. If you thought the overarching "Tragedy" plotline in Danganronpa was bizarre, RAIN CODE cranks the absurdity up a notch. It’s unpredictable, wacky, and occasionally hits emotional highs that linger long after the credits roll.

The main cast is a mixed bag. While some characters shine—Yuma, Halara, Fubuki, and Chief Yakou are my personal favorites—others feel underdeveloped or forgettable. The culprits behind the cases, unfortunately, also tend to be less memorable compared to the intricate villains of Danganronpa.

When it comes to the cases themselves, the first one serves as a solid introduction to the mechanics, but the second and fourth cases truly stand out. Both are heartbreaking and emotionally resonant, with narratives that allow you to empathize with the culprits despite their actions. These moments elevate the game’s storytelling and leave a lasting impact.

Overall, Master Detective Archives: RAIN CODE is a solid game that stands on its own merits. While comparisons to Danganronpa are inevitable, it’s important to view this as its own story within a new universe. The game shares the mystery and detective vibe, but it’s a fresh experience that deserves to be judged independently.

One piece of advice: pick it up during a sale, as the full price feels a bit steep. Regardless, it’s a game worth exploring, especially for fans of Kodaka’s signature style.

It is [b][u]NOT[/b][/u] Danganronpa 4 beyond the minigame mechanics. The pacing and minigame mechanics in Mystery Dungeons are very similar, but that's it. The hook of the Danganronpa games are the tense class trials that take you on a wild ride that, crucially, you can't anticipate. You literally don't have anywhere near enough information before pulling it out of your classmates in the trials to guess what happened. This is a detective game first, and it gives you most of the clues and info you need before entering a mystery dungeon. It's doing something similar, but different.

To expand, the investigations are well paced, steadily revealing clues for you to revise your guesses. You can reliably piece together most of what happened with a few lingering questions when entering a mystery dungeon. The dungeons are primarily about finding out the answer to those questions. The later chapters have more questions to answer and less clues to work with, but it was surprising how few times I was completely lost and answering at random while still feeling engaged.

Danganronpa excelled at roller coaster exciting trials. I don't think rain code hits those highs, but it is a much more well rounded experience - Investigations feel much more important, Tensions continually increase during investigations, Overarching stories are always moving forward in parallel, and you're always finding good clues to progress the mystery.

Ignore my lack of playtime. I played it via Ryujinx at release. As it’s been almost 2 years my memory on the game’s specific details aren’t gonna be as airtight, so just trust a review I made around the time the game was new. 

Opinions on the cases:Case 0 was wild—super over-the-top and felt like it was held together by duct tape.
Case  1 was okay, but the reasoning to reach the conclusion of the culprit or culprits didn’t really make much sense. On top of that, the culprit or culprits aren’t very well characterized and you’re already seeing the pitfall Rain Code is running through in not having a dedicated cast to follow. 

Case 2 is probably the best in the game, which sucks ’cause it seems too early for a game to peak. But I found nothing else past it to be as good..

Case 3 was a mess. Half its ideas just vanish into the void. There’s also some issues, and this may not be a problem with the JP dub, but you can infer the culprit or culprits pretty easily if you pay attention to the voice/voices. It doesn’t really matter much because after a certain point, it’s pretty obvious who did it. 

Case 4 was awful and is riddled with contrivance (Which of course you have to expect some in any mystery, but all they make you do is ask questions.)  The epilogue after the result of that case also has to be the most absurd bootlicking  I’ve seen in a while.
Case 5 was alright. and I would have to say this might be the closest Kodaka has been to making a game with a good ending without any asterisk (Arguably DR1 was too in certain circumstances)… but then the epilogue chickened out on the stakes.)

Shinigami
I found her very annoying. Yes, I get that she’s a cute girl with big tits so having her crap talking people (especially those who can’t even hear her) might be endearing to certain folks but I wasn’t a fan.  Never warmed up to her, but she got a bit better in the latter half. 

The cast:Mixed bag. I liked Halara and Vivia.  Desuhiko and Fubuki? Painful (though Desuhiko almost  redeemed himself in Case 4). Kurumi? Forgettable. A Maya played straight.  Also, half these “Master Detectives” feel like they don’t have any business being one.

Mystery Labyrinth
Mystery Labyrinth were honestly poorly thought out and implemented. You  know when the game has to handwave why solving the case for the corrupt  police officers who were just going to pin it on some random yahoo  anyway that it needed more time in the oven (Especially in Case 2).  Hell, more than half of the cases in the game don't even really need  the Labyrinth and are easily solvable without it. I'd argue only 0 and 1 need it (and Case 5, but of course it does.) It was also not that great  of an idea to make characters not remember when they've been in it.

Overall: Still, found the game to be a nice attempt at least, and hope the  inevitable sequel really gives us some 1-4 and 2-5 level masterpieces.

There’s a really good foundation for a game here, but it still needs [b]a lot[/b] of work.

The biggest issue right now is that the game is starving for content. There are too few spells, too few enemies, only one boss, just three maps, too little of everything. Even the soundtrack is just a single song, which I had to turn off pretty quickly to stay sane.

For a game that heavily advertises co-op, there’s surprisingly little actual cooperation. The most you can do is heal teammates, which is pretty useless at higher difficulties since enemies just one-shot you anyway. Plus, healing augments are hard to justify when other upgrades are way more useful. Right now, the co-op experience is less about teamwork and more about the comedy of friendly fire.

On top of that, the game feels really unbalanced, with some design choices that just don’t make much sense. Some of my biggest gripes, in no particular order:

- Some spells are just straight-up better than others. Necro Whirl and Rune Burst are super strong even without augments, while Moonerang, Solar Pulse, and Rocky Road struggle even if you invest heavily in them.
- Some augments are complete trash. When an upgrade can make or break a run, I don’t get how the devs thought "stand still for more damage" was a good idea, or why anyone would ever pick "burst mode" over, say, more projectiles.
- Challenge difficulty is all over the place. Collecting mushrooms and breaking statues? Free augment. Late-game soccer or goop challenges? Basically impossible if you're already struggling. It’s even worse when environmental effects work against you, because some challenge placements just feel cruel. I get that they’re meant to showcase each map’s gimmick, but difficulty has to be consistent, failing due to bad RNG feels cheap.
- The game desperately needs an option to increase effect opacity. The longer a run goes, the harder it is to see anything. This is especially bad with enemy projectiles, which can blend in with your own attacks, particularly if you get the fire element.
- Some upgrade restrictions make no sense. Why doesn’t area size increase projectile size? Why are range and duration separate stats instead of just scaling based on the skill? Also, has anyone ever chosen the pickup range power up? It should just be merged with the experience upgrade, or removed entirely, as currently there's no point in picking it up given that magnets are abundant and shards don't disappear.

I know it’s still in Early Access, and more content will come, but some of these issues make me wonder how much playtesting is actually happening, or if certain design choices are even being thought through.

That said, I’m not here to just dunk on the game. I think I've only encountered one bug over my entire playtime. The single song it has is honestly a banger, and they should let whoever made it cook. The art and animations are pretty solid (aside from the visibility issues), and the multiplayer is surprisingly stable. I only ran into performance issues during an endless run with three other players, and that was after we pushed the game to its absolute limit.

At the end of the day, it’s not a great game, but it’s not awful either. If you’ve got a few friends and just want to embrace the chaos, it can be fun. But if you’re looking for actual co-op mechanics, they are not here. If you want a good single-player experience, there are plenty of better games in the genre.
