Shade Silver is an absolute gem that has quickly captured my heart and imagination. From the moment you dive into its beautifully crafted world, it’s clear that every aspect of this game has been meticulously designed with care and passion.

Visuals and Art Style: The game boasts a stunning art style that combines rich colors with intricate details. Each environment feels alive, from lush forests to hauntingly beautiful ruins. The character designs are equally impressive, with unique animations that breathe life into every character you encounter. The visual storytelling is so engaging that it often feels like you’re playing through a living painting.

Puzzle Mechanics: One of the standout features of Shade Silver is its ingenious puzzle design. The puzzles are not just challenges; they’re integral to the storytelling and exploration. Each puzzle you encounter is thoughtfully woven into the environment, encouraging players to interact with the world around them. From environmental puzzles that require keen observation to logic-based challenges that test your problem-solving skills, there’s a delightful variety that keeps you on your toes.

What I particularly appreciate is how the puzzles evolve as you progress. Early on, you’re introduced to simple mechanics that gradually become more complex, allowing you to build your skills and confidence. There are moments of pure eureka joy when you finally crack a particularly tricky puzzle, and the game’s design rewards curiosity—often, exploring the environment leads to unexpected solutions.

Gameplay Mechanics: Shade Silver masterfully blends exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat in a way that feels both fresh and intuitive. The controls are smooth, making even the most complex maneuvers feel effortless. The sense of progression as you unlock new abilities and explore previously inaccessible areas keeps you engaged and eager to discover what lies ahead.

Narrative and Characters: The story is compelling and layered, filled with twists that keep you on the edge of your seat. The writing is top-notch, bringing the characters to life with relatable backstories and engaging dialogue. I found myself genuinely invested in their journeys and emotional struggles. The way the narrative weaves through the gameplay is seamless, enhancing the overall experience and making every moment feel significant.

Sound and Music: The soundtrack is nothing short of enchanting. It perfectly complements the game’s atmosphere, with scores that evoke a range of emotions. The sound design also deserves a mention, as the ambient sounds create an immersive experience that pulls you deeper into the world of Shade Silver.

Overall Experience: Playing Shade Silver feels like embarking on an epic adventure, one filled with wonder and discovery. It’s a game that invites you to lose yourself in its world, offering hours of enjoyment and a story that lingers long after the credits roll. The puzzles stand out as a highlight, blending seamlessly into the narrative and making each victory feel earned.

In summary, Shade Silver is a triumph in game design, delivering a perfect blend of art, storytelling, and engaging puzzles. I can’t recommend it highly enough—this is one adventure you won’t want to miss!

There's unfortunately some work needed between what the game is now, its price point compared to its contemporaries, and my expectations.

TL;DR: Mango 64 is "the Toree3D we have at home". No controller support, wonky controls in general, it being more expensive than both Toree games combined, and a frustrating final boss, make it a title I cannot recommend in its current state.

[b]A few positive notes:[/b]
The level designs are simple but good and varied! The ~8 levels of the game can collectively be completed in around a half hour at the most if you're collecting all of the collectibles, with speedrun timers to motivate you to return. Cosmetics are a fun reward for collectibles as well. While the normal enemies never posed a threat, each level has its own and they are fitting and varied level-by-level. Mango's design is simple but cute.

[b]The rest:[/b]
First and foremost, the game does not support controller. This, for many reasons, is baffling - especially for a 3D platforming game. Being built in the Unreal Engine, I'm fairly sure that the Unreal Character Controller supports Controllers essentially out-of-the-box. Additionally, not only does the game Not Support Controller, it [i]actively breaks[/i] if a controller is plugged in. If it ever detects the right analog stick of a controller moving at all, the camera will start permanently spinning until you close the game.

The KBM controls unfortunately leave a lot to be desired too. Many side areas (thankfully not the main game levels) use fixed camera perspectives, but the WASD controls of the character don't update to reflect the fixed perspective. There are points where holding W moves your character Left relative to the camera, or even Backwards. Additionally, for some reason, holding LMB to use the grappling hook forces your character to walk at a 45 degree angle, whether or not you're tethered to anything. I had to get in the habit of looking 45 degrees left before grappling anything, so that I could travel in a straight line.

Bouncing off of bouncepads does not restore your double jump, leading to many confusing deaths in situations that would otherwise have contributed to a good flow state. The "drop shadow" below the player also confuses more than it helps, as instead of becoming invisible when not above ground, it either sticks to the player or hovers awkwardly in midair, defeating its purpose.

Finishing a level awkwardly plops you back at the start of the hub island, almost like something broke. Additionally, leaving a house in the hub island puts you back outside the starting house, not outside the house you were just in. This felt extremely confusing.

I ragequit the final boss after 6 or so tries. Its attacks are so erratic, hard to see coming, and single-hits sending you back to the start of the fight were too much for me to bother with.

[b]Conclusion:[/b]
At the very least I cannot possibly recommend this game for its current price point of $5, when the far more fun and functional Toree games are available for $1 each. If the game receives update(s) fixing some of the technical issues and adding controller support, I'll revise my review.
Why does a 64-bit-era throwback feel like a precision platformer? Because the controls are no good, and the platforming leaves little room for error... but not in a challenging, fun way.

Mango 64 is a cute, short, fairly fun little platformer that gets a lot of points for its emulation of N64 style and textures. The game comprises 10 total levels and a final boss fight where you must guide Mango, our protagonist flamingo, as he runs, swings, and double jumps through the platforming courses. You're then given a rank depending on how fast you went & how many collectibles you gathered - receive all A's throughout the courses and you get a special reward from someone in the hub world. This incentivizes replaying the levels beyond the initial "plot" clear.

While in the hub world, you can swap out your hat to make Mango look a little drippier; halfway through the game, you can also unlock hats that affect your abilities (such as infinite flight), though this nullifies your ability to get A ranks. Without going back through the levels to get all A's, I completed the game in about an hour.

I would have tried for all A's if the level replayer wasn't broken at the time; a core element of the game is using your mouse (to rotate your camera) and the WASD keys in conjunction to navigate the world. In my experience, I was completely unable to rotate the camera when trying to replay a level, which made the acquisition of A ranks next to impossible. I imagine this core flaw is/will be fixed shortly after release.

While what I played was fun, I also wish there was more depth to the game mechanics. Perhaps more abilities, more varied level designs, or simply doubling the length of the game would go a long ways to extending the enjoyability of it. There could be a whole echelon of particularly difficult levels - or more difficult versions of the levels that already exist - to add onto the relatively easy & charming levels as they are. I also think there was some real potential in adding more things to the hub world - perhaps mini games or other side missions - to flesh things out in the Mangoniverse.

Overall, a decent little first game that does an alright job at emulating N64 aesthetics with a fairly fun and at-times-challenging gameplay loop. Pick it up if you're looking for a bite-sized rank-based platformer with pretty aesthetics to spend an afternoon with.

One Boss One Fight - A Surprisingly Addictive Indie Gem

I love little indie games to kill some time, and I found this one thanks to a friend. The game takes you straight to hell, literally. No warmup, no minions to slice through, just the boss right in front of you from the get-go.

If you've played other games with boss patterns, it's like that but without the  corridors and mobs inbetween. It's just you learning (and hating some of) the patterns and figuring out how not to get obliterated by Death itself.

The progression system is neat, even if it's not perfect. After about 20 hours of gameplay (which is pretty great for a €10 indie game), I've unlocked a bunch of abilities that keep things interesting. The developer is quite active and is constantly fixing issues. I've had some really broken but fun runs, it felt like playing 'The Binding of Isaac' when you get the right items and combinations of constellations!

The "constellations" the system allow the game to be really good, it's like managing your stuff modificator on diablo or death must die. Should you focus on critical chance and damage or maybe lost a little bit of dps to gain more heal potential?

For hardcore fans, there's a hardcore mode that's a real challenge. Maybe a bit too hard, as I can't progress with items anymore. Might be a skill issue on my part (i think so) time to git gud.

Visually, the scenery changes multiple times, and the graphics are nice. The sound is good but can get a bit repetitive after a while.

So yeah, if you love roguelike indie games made with love, go for it! It's at least 20 hours of fun!

However, SRK is really cool arcade game about street racing with many cars, with customization, with great music and vide, with different and interesting events, with enjoyable progression. I recommend to play this game!

I think this game has potential, but in the current state it's in I don't think I can recommend it. There's a good game in there somewhere, but the jank and glitches really impede the experience. Also some mechanics just don't mesh as well as they could. Like, some of the things don't feel like they really belong. Why have an infection mechanic when you just ended up dying by the enemies much faster? Especially since you don't end up really doing anything with that mechanic outside of just being a spectator of your own death and watching your monster self do it's thing.

It's a multiplayer game that doesn't really feel multiplayer. The encouragement of splitting up means some very isolationist experiences.

The gunplay is pretty awful. Have had friends complain the aiming gets glitched, and some of the weapons don't allow you to aim at all. The shotgun is alright, but all the other guns feel unusable.  The vehicles speak for themselves. The complaints about them are valid. There isn't much reason to use a good chunk of them.

Enemies spawning on top of you.

Dying and sitting there for fifty minutes is no fun. The respawn mechanic isn't very effective, I had a friend respawn two times in a row while the rest of us just ended up waiting. A friend died at the start of a match, and never ended up respawning. You don't even get the option of viewing the map or seeing the progress, so you're just left spectating. 

There are no real mechanics to let you be the creature. Unless you like watching your transformed self shuffle around the map endlessly.

Getting trapped in a ravine, or glitched into a spot where I can't move, meant I effectively just had to sit out and wait to freeze to death. My infected friend ended up getting stuck in a door. 

This game crashed the computers of a few of my friends. And their computers are pretty good. The optimization could use some work.

I think the priorities of development should be focused on fixing core mechanics and bug stomping, instead of adding mini-game mechanics like pool, new enemies, or a new map. The current mechanics aren't working properly, the enemies aren't working, and the existing map needs some work.

Please narrow the focus, this game could be something amazing.

The game is obviously a passion project and a successful one. There are two main parts of this game that I believe are sinking the motivation my friends and I had pre-update, which is the lack of reporting system (7 dollar games lets the toxic losers in) and the broken game state post-update. I want to elaborate on the latter point.

The current state of the game is unplayable. The recent update had an enormous amount of bugs that have broken the game state. The roadmap that was made was overly ambitious, and since then, has been addressed by the developer. It's not impossible for anyone to assume the update came out without proper preparation. My issue, however, is not the bugs or broken game. My issue is the lack of any timeline for these fixes. I've seen this in other early access games, where the game has some part of it that's unusual / broken for a game of it's type, only to never fix it in an appropriate time or at all. It has been a couple of days, and there has been no announcement about the bug fixes. The only thing I could find was a pinned comment about no ETA for the list of bugs they have found. 

I think the more appropriate measure would be to set some kind of deadline, so there is some sort of accountability. I understand this is an early access game, but transparency does not require you to have a full-fleshed out game. I think many developers are afraid to make a public announcement about their game state because it usually is followed by some accountable plan, or to answer uncomfortable questions from players about a timeline. I will be returning this game for now, and I will re-buy the game after another big update only after watching response this time around. To end on a good note, this game is unique and has some detail you wouldn't expect from a game of its price. If neither of my cons are bothersome to you, buy the game as you will most likely enjoy it as much as I did. If the developers follow their roadmap, this game is going to have some great content to keep you and your friends motivated to keep playing.

this allegorical non-fiction draws on eclectic influences to tell its esoteric and dangerous tale. one of its intellectual progenitors tells the tale of an arrogant man brought into a world of vampiric intrigue who narcissistically fosters progeny to rule the world, rejecting his condemnation by the authorities in order to pursue kompromat on the Elder God. one of his wayward subordinates eventually returns to the fold to play the role of fateful redeemer, but not before it appears as if he has been betrayed and manipulated by his flawed father-figure.

juglio epstein is called to action by a letter from his gamer buddy Lenny. much like the protagonist of the previous story, he is captured by a tale of intrigue. while his own father-figure (J.E.) is never seen, he is present in spirit at around every corner. Juglio's own origins are hinted at by conspicuous peppering of his last name throughout the game. could 'J.E.' also be an Epstein like Lenny and Juglio? it appears so; but in fear of the powers that be, the game may only hint at this.

[h1]Beautiful non gore oriental horror FMV game [Eng and Pt-BR review][/h1]
Back is a horror game in FMV. The game starts in a very classic way, with the main character arriving at a house and getting trapped there while escaping from a ghost. While this can be considered quite cliché, the game manages to follow a slightly different path.
First, I really liked the house, it's not your typical wooden house in the middle of a storm, it's actually a very modern and spacious house, making the whole game very beautiful. Speaking of beautiful, we come to the second point, the actors are very good-looking and there is no gore in the game, which is an important point for those who are not into gore. Third, I really liked the execution of the first-person footage, for example, when running the camera shakes and you only see the MC's feet and at the same time his hands come out of the corners of the cameras, this creates a very cool immersion, it really is a first-person FMV. And the fourth point, the game's story is good, of course, it could be explored more, but together with the gameplay of gathering clues and short escape room sessions, it works well.
As for the game's negative points. Not exactly a bad point, but the game is quite fast, at least it doesn't force an unnecessary length. Some sound effects are well-known to horror lovers and other sound effects could be used (not necessarily a bad thing either). And perhaps the only real negative point, the game doesn't have subtitles for written text. Sometimes the MC holds a page or newspaper but there are no subtitles translating the text, you can kind of understand from the context of what's happening in the game, but I wish I could read it.
[b][u]In the end, it's a visually interesting game with a cool story, not too long and nice to have fun in one night, especially for lovers of oriental horror.[/u][/b]

[h1]Bonito jogo FMV de terror oriental não gore [Eng and Pt-BR review][/h1]
Back é um jogo de terror em FMV. O jogo começa de um modo bem clássico, do personagem principal chegando numa casa e ficando preso lá enquanto escapa de um fantasma. Enquanto isso pode ser considerado bem cliché, o jogo consegue seguir por um caminho um pouco diferente.
Primeiro, eu gostei bastante da casa, não é a sua típica casa de madeira no meio de uma tempestade, é na verdade uma casa bem moderna e espaçosa, deixando todo o jogo bem bonito. Falando em bonito, chegamos ao segundo ponto, os atores são bem bonitos e não há gore no jogo o que é um ponto importante para quem não é de gore. Um terceiro ponto, eu gostei muito da execução das filmagens em primeira pessoa, por exemplo, ao correr a câmera balança e você vê apenas os pés do MC e ao mesmo tempo as mãos dele saem pelos cantos das câmeras, isso gera uma imersão bem legal, é realmente um FMV em primeira pessoa. E o quarto ponto, a história do jogo é boa, claro, ela poderia ser mais explorada, mas junto do gameplay de reunir pistas e curtas sessões de escape room, funciona bem.
Quantos aos pontos negatios do jogo. Não exatamente um ponto ruim mas o jogo é um tanto rápido, pelo menos não força uma duração desnecessária. Alguns efeitos sonoros são velhos conhecidos dos amantes de terror e poderiam ser usados outros efeitos sonoros (não necessariamente algo ruim também). E talvez o único ponto realmente negativo, o jogo não possui legenda para texto escrito. Algumas vezes o MC segura uma página ou jornal mas não há legendas traduzindo o texto, você meio que pode entender pelo contexto do que está acontecendo jogo, mas eu gostaria de poder ler.

Sokoban, but instead of pushing boxes directly, you grow and shrink plants that push the boxes.

[b]What is it:[/b] A Sokoban-inspired puzzle game in which you don't control a box-pushing worker, but can grow and shrink “plants” along predefined tracks, pushing boxes out of the way as they grow. The goal in each level is to get the boxes on the designated spots. You have two different kinds of boxes, red and yellow, but they behave the same, it’s just that they go on the spots of the same color. You have two kinds of plants as well, one just pushes boxes ahead as it grows, and the other kind can grab one box and drag it along. You only control which plant to grow or shrink, but they always go on predetermined paths, and up to a predefined limit, a plant cannot go off its track.

The first half of the levels are quite easy, I found them rather boring, it’s usually obvious what you need to do, you just have to click your way through the solution. And click you shall, hundreds of times! That’s my biggest dislike in this game, the controls are terrible. It’s all mouse only, and one click at a time, no repeats when growing a plant. Click click click click to grow to the desired length. Fortunately, shrinking does support a turbo mode, if you keep the right mouse button pressed for a bit, it will shrink the plant really quick, and there are keyboard shortcuts for undo and restart (non-repeating, of course). But other than these two keys, the game is really mouse centric.

The second half of the levels does get a bit more challenging, yet I still found most of them unsatisfying. They are challenging just because there’s too much going on, but a jumble of paths, boxes and target spots doesn’t make a clever level, just a mess to sort through. Overall, maybe there were a handful of levels that I enjoyed.

A few more aspects bothered me. The game is slow, with needless pauses inserted. Like I usually complain, I’m an impatient player, I want my “impatient player” settings in a game. When finishing a level, there’s a “Level Completed” message displayed, with nothing to do, and only after a couple of seconds the “Next level” button shows up. Why? What good does it do to not have the Next button displayed right away? Loading and restarting a level is also slowly animated. At least the game is quickly reacting to grow and shrink commands, it keeps up with how fast I click, but it obviously wasn’t designed with that speed in mind, since the animations can’t keep up and look broken, with black spots leading the slowly growing plant.

Overall? A good puzzle idea, but with sub-par levels, terrible controls, and lacking QoL features.

[b]How hard is it:[/b] Trivial to moderate.

[b]How long is it:[/b] 35 levels, usually 3 unlocked at a time. Can be finished in 2-3 hours.

[b]Level design:[/b] Not good enough; simple easy levels with obvious solutions, complex levels just because they’re full of stuff, rarely a clever layout or clever use of the mechanics.

[b]Quality:[/b] Poor. A few volume and screen size settings, unlimited undo, decent level select. No cloud saving, no achievements, very few non rebindable key shortcuts, tedious clicky controls, useless delays. The last level is always locked in the level select screen, the only way to access it is to finish the 34th level and proceed to Next Level from there, and even after finishing it, it still appears locked.

[b]Worth the price:[/b] Not until it gets improved a bit, and even then I’d wait for a discount.

[b]Most positive aspect for me:[/b] Interesting mechanics.

[b]Most negative aspect for me:[/b] Terrible clicky controls.

[b]What would make it better:[/b] Keyboard/controller support. More and better levels. Repeated growth when keeping the mouse button pressed, and repeated Undo when pressing the Z key. Steam cloud saving and achievements. Back button on the level end screen. Progress reset.

Alfred Hitchcock once used the concept of a bomb under the table as a parable for effectively setting up suspense in a story.  If the bomb is under the table and the audience isn't aware about it, it's eventual detonation might surprise them, but they'll be kind of bored up until that point.  If the bomb is under the table and the audience does know about it, suspense builds.  They wonder why the characters at the table are having such an ordinary conversation in the face of certain death.  Tension mounts as the timer on the bomb counts down.

Welcome to Maison Chichigami opens with the main character losing his job for exposing the underhanded practices of his employer.  He did this partly because he lost his lust for life, figuratively and literally.  (It's almost as if someone involved in conceiving this story was a game developer.)  When his favorite girlfriend-for-hire can't summon his enthusiasm, she refers him to a hot springs resort in the mountains.  The main character has little else but time and severance money.  He decides to check it out.

Dude almost dies in the woods.  Some kind of spirit light guides him to a western style mansion.  All the ladies in there have incredibly large... personalities.  I actually mean that, for the record.  Like other eroge, Maison Chichigami relies on well-established archetypes to sell its heroines.  Unlike other games in the genre, they have a lot going on beneath the surface.  In my first playthrough, I felt that more aspects of the characters were hidden than were revealed.  That's probably a big part of why I got the bad ending.

The mansion's only other inhabitant is the disabled wealthy patriarch, who wears a horror movie mask to hide his face and cannot leave his wheelchair.  He cannot hear or interact with the main character.  (As far as I know.)  The matriarch seems to be in control of the situation.  After an, uh, unconventional interview, she asks the main character to tutor her daughters in physical intimacy.

This is where the suspense I mentioned earlier starts to creep in.  This is no lighthearted romp.  When the main character answered this call to adventure, a rift grew between him and me.  This is not a normal arrangement.  As far as I know, this isn't even a normal arrangement for the obscenely wealthy.  This does not deter the main character.  His comfort with the situation caused me considerable anxiety.

After this point in the story, the game opens up.  Compared to other erotic visual novels, Maison Chichigami seems to give an unprecedented level of choice and autonomy.  In the mornings and afternoons, you might choose to explore the mansion and learn more about your environment, peeling away layers of the mystery.  You might instead choose to hang out with one of the women in the house as they go about their daily business.  The nights, though, are reserved for escalating acts of carnal depravity.  You get choices, even in that.

The characters in the game are rendered well enough, but it certainly isn't what the game does best.  I might even go as far as to say that this game doesn't even do what it does in this arena as well as most other erotic visual novels.  A lot of the action has some animation.  For many of those animations, certain things fall out of line.  Tufts of hair move out of time with the body.  The programming neglects to erase the walking maid's profile walk loop and just lays the face-turned walk loop over the top of it.  For me, these kinds of things mostly happened in the game's prologue chapter.   It's almost as if that chapter was added at the end of development to help guard against Steam's refund policy.  (Pure speculation.)  That's fair enough, though, because this game's opening drew me into the game like no opening of any other game, ever.

The prose in this game is fantastic.  I don't know who to credit more:  the localization team or the original author of the scenario.  This is probably the best-written eroge I've ever played.  (What I Mean Every Time I Say This: Not perfect, but exceptional for the genre.)  It's so good that I realized I'm here for the prose more than the lewd images.  If I just wanted the imagery, I could dig through image boards.  If I wanted to sink into a mischievously crafted thriller with erotic elements, it would be hard to do better than Maison Chichigami. 

The writers who worked on Maison Chichigami knew where to point the focus when describing scenes.  Unlike games with poorer translations, I don't think I was ever confused when reading through any of the text.  The pacing kept me hooked on the game all the way through.  Normally, when I play through a game like this once and get a bad ending, I just look up the other endings outside the game in the interest of thoroughness.  I want to hang out with this game and its characters for a while longer.  I even want to hang out with the main character a little more and see how he develops towards the end of some other possible routes.  I want to unravel the mysteries of the mansion on my own.  This is the strength of this game's writing. 

When Hitchcock directed Psycho, even depicting the toilet in the bathroom was a big deal.  The shower stabbing was an extreme spectacle, especially considering that it was Janet Leigh who was stabbed in that scene.  Janet Leigh was the top-billed actress in the movie.  Her character died in the first act.  The hotel and the killer became the table and the bomb, respectively.

After one Bad End playthrough, I want to crawl further beneath the table that is Welcome to Maison Chichigami.  I want to find the bomb.  I want to mess around with it until I defuse it.  I think I'll probably have an okay time doing that.  If any of this interests you, you might also find delight in that endeavor.

A fun large-scale puzzle game, operating with an iteration on Minesweeper rules. Every number on the board details how many white squares should be touching it, expecting you to fill them in to find the one solution to the entire 250x250 square board. The game comes with a good mix of options for how errors are handled to allow some degree of control over the possible frustration of a puzzle this large. With everything off, it is very possible to find yourself too far along to easily find your own mistakes.

I did run into a minor but persistent bug during my time. When finishing a 3x3 section with a number in the center square, the game typically brightens the number, allowing you to see what has been completed at a glance. Sometimes this would not happen and the game would not count a section as complete until the offending square was filled in again.

A small wishlist item would have been some additional tools to make notes or mark square possibilities without locking them in. Due to the size of the puzzle, I rarely ever felt the need to sort through the logic of a small area and would instead just move on to another more obvious area entirely until I would naturally return, sometimes finding that I overlooked something nearly complete as my eyes started glazing over all of the numbers. With all of the hints and error correction off, I feel that this would have been a welcome change to allow some more planning or focusing on an individual section.

After completing it, I do recommend this title, especially if you are looking for something to chill out with in both short bursts or long sessions. It's a very satisfying experience.

Pros:
-Mining
-Becoming more efficient at mining
-A simple but robust customization system with quite a bit of depth
-70-100% completion takes longer than some AAA campaigns I've played

Cons:
-Two audio tracks. Mellow enough to fade into the background, but the repetition over 20 hours may induce madness in some folks. Turn it down and play your own music.

-While there is a fair amount of progression "buildings" to unlock, most of them are fairly linear in their returns. This doesn't bother me, but the "big boy" power spikes are 30% grinding, 20% puzzle solving, and 50% pure RNG, while being tied to a crafting animation. The developer appears to be working ways to mitigate the this. The majority of your upgrades in the early to mid game come from simply playing. Late game "build optimizations" rely on you crafting hundreds of blueprints in search of one that is compatible with the goal you have in mind.

-The textual hints and tooltips are largely accurate easy to understand. That said, some of the wording on things you encounter late in the game are vague, difficult to test, and sometimes leave you scratching your head.

-Early/mid game build choices are all pretty viable and enjoyable if you play around them. Towards the end, several build synergies pull ahead by a large margin, leaving less variety if you value efficiency

Excellent game that brings fresh ideas to the grid-based, first-person dungeon crawler. The real-time aiming/looking combined with the tile-based movement works super well and makes combat feel dynamic and kinetic, which is not something I ever expected to say about a game in this genre. There's a decent variety of weapons, all with different power, speed, and reach - so you can do things like catch enemies on a diagonal with a long spear, or start a swing on a super heavy weapon and then move to the tile adjacent to an enemy just as the swing completes.

The level design and exploration is really satisfying and provides a nice sense of progression. I had a hard time putting the game down once I started. Tower of Mask does some legitimately cool stuff and is really impressive for a solo dev project. The fact that one person made this game is super cool, and I've gotta give em props there. Mask is a grid-based dungeon crawler that brings some meaningful innovations to the genre by virtue of letting you move with a free camera tied to your mouse - which is a massive feels upgrade compared to the WASDQE paradigm that most of the real-time tile-based dungeon crawlers use - and requires you to actually aim and block, rewarding landing headshots on enemies with your weapons by enabling you to barge through them for bonus damage and reposition as a result. This gets around two classic grid-based combat problems - one, the ADADing you do to constantly freak out enemy AI is not as effective here, as some enemies weapons actually do reach multiple squares, and two, if you get pressured into a corner, you can land a clutch headshot and shove the enemy out of the way to break free and give yourself some space.

Mask actually has decent enemy variety, especially for a solo project - it takes about 10 hours to complete, but over those 10 hours you'll run into a handful of different enemies, several of which "break rules" and have unique mechanics, like teleporting behind you, walking through walls, laying down dangerous areas to deny space, et cetera, while also having different weakpoints and weapon types you have to learn and play around. The game uses a durability system ala BOTW, so you're constantly cycling through gear between encounters, which keeps finding loot enjoyable through the game.

But, it's not all great. There is progression - you level up and improve stats - but honestly the stats didn't really speak to a particular playstyle, so I found it pretty flat and ended up just equipping whatever gave me the most net positive stats by the end. There's not great feedback when a weapon breaks, so sometimes you'll get surprised to find your shield's been broken for 2 blocks and you've lost half your health, or your weapon broke and you throw a punch before swapping. The localization is done by AI, which makes some descriptions for puzzles a bit hard to parse. And, at least for me, the first few floors started out pretty tight and engaging to navigate, but the final few floors got pretty convoluted and annoying to keep in my head, to the point where I started just wanting to have the game be done. Sometimes I feel like dungeon crawlers get too invested in being really complicated and weird, and I feel like the first few levels struck a better balance of tension, confusion, and excitement compared to the last few levels, which just got a bit frustratingly heady and circuitous for me.

All in all though, it's really awesome seeing a new tile-based dungeon crawler in 2025 - especially one that takes so much clear inspiration from the OGs, recent contributors like Grimrock, and other heavy hitters like the souls titles. It's impressive for a solo project, and although it's got some definite rough edges, it's still a really cool and unique experience that I'm really glad I played through.

Shallow Sea Roaming offers a mixed experience that shines in some areas but falls short in others. As a survival game, it has its moments of fun, particularly when looting and roaming around the island. The exploration aspect is enjoyable, with a variety of environments to discover and a dynamic weather system that adds immersion to the game.

Pros:

    Enjoyable Exploration: Roaming around the island and discovering new areas is genuinely fun. The variety in landscapes and the challenge of finding resources keep the game engaging.
    Weather System: The weather system is a nice addition, bringing an extra layer of realism and challenge to survival.

Cons:

    Save and Load System: While you can save your progress, loading the game makes you start over from the beginning, which is frustrating and undermines the sense of accomplishment.
    Crafting Issues: Crafting is where the game struggles. Some items don't function as intended—for example, crafting shoes gives you armor instead. The game only allows you to craft one item at a time, which becomes tedious quickly. Additionally, if you switch to the crafting menu too quickly, it defaults to crafting an axe, which can waste your resources.
    Super Oxygen Tank Problem: The super oxygen tank is a cool concept, letting you dive deeper, but it's poorly implemented. It gets you down to the depths, but you'll die trying to return to the surface, causing you to lose all your progress due to the flawed save system.

Conclusion:
Shallow Sea Roaming has potential, particularly with its enjoyable exploration and survival aspects. However, the game's numerous bugs and frustrating mechanics, especially in crafting and saving, hold it back. If you're looking for a survival game with some unique ideas, it might be worth a try, but be prepared for some frustrating moments along the way.

*In response to the developer's request for more info*:
Here are some more exact issues:
-For some reason, you start on day 9, which means that despite being given a bunch of starting resources, if you start trying to build turrets immediately, they get wiped instantly on day 10 (2 minutes into playing). This frustrated me on the first play through. Why wipe towers immediately when the game starts? It doesn't make any sense. So why not wait until Day 10 to build? Because you can't build during an invasion. Okay, whatever, I'll try and fight the Day 10 wave. This wave is actually exceptionally difficult. The only way I could figure how to beat it was to instantly pour all my crystals into stamina regen (You have about a 20 second window to do this btw), and then sprint at the first giant while drawing aggro of half the invasion, and then you MUST cleave multiple enemies every swing or you WILL lose. And in spite of all of this preparation and careful fighting, it is inevitable you will have to pour some of the dropped red crystals into repairing the primary crystal, WHICH DOES NOT REGEN BETWEEN INVASIONS.
-Menus are ugly.
-There is no feedback when you press buttons or open menus. No sound, no jingle, no highlighting when your mouse hovers over things, nothing.
-It is hard to tell when you take damage unless you stare at your tiny health bar in the absolute bottom left of the screen.
-When you do finally figure out the day 10 wave puzzle and beat it, you finally get to build towers. This will make your job much easier won't it? Nope, after waiting all that time and spending all of your very limited resources, towers are destroyed in under 15 seconds. They do almost no damage and get destroyed instantly.
-No time for gathering between waves. I can barely go to one biome and pick up stuff before the game simply progresses forward. You are INCREDIBLY slow in this game. This is supposed to be a survival crafting tower defense game, but you can't even gather resources without letting your main crystal lose half its health, WHICH YOU MUST SPEND RESOURCES TO FIX! It is a Sisyphean task.
-The PVP isn't exciting or fun at all. You have to spend energy to swing. Which isn't a big deal right? Most games have stamina. But this stamina regens incredibly slowly in proportion to the number of mobs you have to fight. The game basically forces you to purchase the stamina regen upgrade, but recall that resources in this game are incredibly limited, so basically that is the *only* skill you can get. Also remember that the towers you build are essentially instantly destroyed, so its not like you can play around the towers either.
-You can't seem to slow things down or stun them, or burn them, or poison them, or anything. You just do damage. The gameplay is incredibly flat.
-No end screen when you die. The second your crystal or you die, the tutorial instantly appears on your screen. If the game wants to be difficult, at least show me a "YOU DIED" screen with some stats or SOMETHING. Everything feels like it has no pay off, imagine how furious I would be if I could make it to like day 30 and then die incidentally to something and then the tutorial pops up in my face. Its almost insulting.

In conclusion:
-Not aesthetically pleasing.
-Mis-mashed assets with very different art styles.
-Overly difficult and not in a satisfying way.
-Zero consideration for the player is thinking or feeling at every single step.

Dale Dawson's Stationary Supplies takes the social deduction genre to new heights, blending the intense gameplay of "Among Us" with the quirky, low-stakes world of office life. As a worker in a seemingly mundane office environment, you're tasked with more than just filling out paperwork or answering emails—you're in a battle of wits, trying to figure out who the slacker is before it's too late!

One person is the designated slacker, and it's up to the manager (and the rest of the office) to deduce who's been slacking off and sabotaging the workplace. The game's real strength lies in its clever take on office life: meetings become intense interrogations, break rooms are full of whispers, and every paper shuffle could be a clue. It feels like you're actually working a 9-to-5 in a suspenseful environment where everyone is a suspect.

The office setting adds a delightful layer of humour and charm, and the dialogue is full of hilarious office tropes and banter. The fast-paced rounds make each game feel like a whirlwind of paranoia and deception, but it never gets too overwhelming—just the right amount of light-hearted tension.

The visuals are simple yet effective, capturing the feel of an office without overwhelming the player. The sound design—ranging from the hum of printers to the office gossip—is spot-on, enhancing the immersion.

As you navigate this workplace drama, you’ll quickly realise that the true fun comes from working together (or against each other) to outsmart your colleagues. Whether you’re trying to prove your innocence or point fingers at the slacker, the game delivers plenty of laughs and tense moments that’ll keep you coming back for more. Perfect for fans of party games and social deduction, Dale Dawson’s Stationary Supplies offers hours of office-themed fun, intrigue, and deception

Fundamentally, Escape Tales is a deceptively simple narrative-driven adventure puzzle game which tasks the player with exploring a set of otherworldly locations. If you are familiar with the idea of an escape room, the formula this game overtly draws a lot of inspiration from, you know the drill. Each subsequent location contains several puzzles of various degree of complexity, which when solved, reward the player with either a key item necessary for solving another puzzle or an item significant to the story. While some of the puzzles are rather simple and are quickly solvable, others are less so and expect the player to slow down and analyse all the clues thoroughly. In case a puzzle turns out to be more complex, the game offers hints that can help you get on the right track. If a puzzle turns out to be difficult even after being provided with hints, you can use the auto-solve feature to avoid getting stuck and progress the story. In overall, the puzzles are distinct and don't lack in originality. What I think could have been a bit expanded on is the methods of solving the puzzles. Ultimately, all require you to deduce a correct sequence of numbers from a set of different clues. As far as I know, the game is based on a physical escape room style card game but since I haven't played it, I cannot really tell how well it reflects the gameplay of the original.

What is the highlight of the game for me personally, is the game's old-school approach to solving puzzles - the game offers  a built-in notebook of sorts, allowing you to write down your own notes as you solve the puzzles. The game actively encourages to use that feature, given the complexity of some of the puzzles. This reminds me of the old days when I used to play video games with a piece of paper to my side, writing down any important info. It's a really nice touch! Keep in mind, though, that the window where you provide the solution to the puzzle is rather large so it may obscure the notes you took while analysing the puzzle. Best to avoid that by writing down the final answer somewhere in the corner of the screen.

As far as the story goes, the game tells the tale of a widower who, driven by desperation to find a cure for a mysterious coma his beloved daughter has fallen into, decides to conduct an occult ritual, hoping it might help him save his daughter. As you progress the story, you will unravel more secrets connected with the main character's past. In overall, I feel the story is engaging - the story is delivered in a way reminiscent of a book. The graphics nice and are serviceable. They low key remind me of the nostalgic era of puzzle games made in Flash. My only concern about the graphics is somewhat low resolution of the cards containing clues. Upon enlarging, they get a bit blurry which sometimes make it difficult to discern some details. Besides that little flaw, together with the great audio consisting of spooky yet catchy tunes and ambience in the form of frantic whispers, the aforementioned aspects make for a great immersive experience. Especially due to the audio, I recommend playing with headphones on! As far as I know, the game has several different endings. The one you receive is based on the choice you make and your performance (I believe), so there is a lot to uncover for those who like to replay their games.

To sum up, Escape Tales: The Awakening was released just in time for those who are keen on indulging in the spooky vibes explicitly associated with Halloween. If you are into puzzle games and are looking for one that will allow you to casually spend a cold autumn evening while cosily enjoying a cup of warm tea, be sure to grab it.

Only completed two runs but wanted to get a review in for this pretty early to help with the exposure. I'm a huge fan of the genre and have around 20+ games in my library in this genre alone.

It's a solid bullet heaven/Survivor-like game with some small twists to make it a bit different.

I'll run down some of the key things the game brings:

You can have up to 4 weapons per run.
They can be upgraded each level, as well as increase stats each level.
At lvl 5, 10 and 15 of the weapon they get big upgrades very similar to Deep Rock Galactic Survivor, with level 15 being the most dramatic change.
Generic Meta upgrades. (Permanent upgrades from currency you collect, like Increased HP, Faster Movement etc)
Quite a lot of Characters to unlock, which is where I see a bulk of the grind is aimed towards
Lots of areas to unlock.
Achievements in-game but not on steam sadly. Maybe one day?
Mid-run events with rewards that you can only get from those events. Chests give you powerups like magnets or speed for X time, Basements give you rare passive upgrades, Rifts give you a free upgrade for a weapon. (Btw, you don't need to stand in the circle to complete rifts. Just activate it and run out, then kill things. You'll get bombarded by suicide monsters if you stay close. I lost my first run because of that.)

Now what does it do different?
It has a building system. It's nothing crazy. But you create mines (By standing in designated spots) and use those mines to gather stones.
Said stones are used to build Traps and other helpful contraptions in other designated areas.
They're also the way to build 'Forges' which is what is used to 'Tier up' your weapons at lvl 5, 10 and 15. They only become available when you're able to tier up a weapon.

It's nothing game changing or anything, but it is kinda cool to get 3 Traps near each other in a triangle and just stand in the middle to watch everything die.

Overall, if you're a fan of the genre you'll get a kick out of it. But I don't currently see it as being something I'll get sucked into for a long time like some others. Definitely worth the price tag for the content it currently has.

TLDR: A soulless, humorless version of a game you've probably already played. There are a few things this game does right, but all in all it's sloppy and uninspired.

Pros: 

-Each character has a unique starting attack and slightly different stats. This does a good job at making each character feel different and most games in this series fail to do this.

-Building structures is ok...you'll have limited stone so can only build so many but basically you'll either build flame or spike traps for a damage circle around you or build a bunch of trojan horses in the corners of the map because you get 5% crit chance for 5 stone, even though their ability is broken and useless. (your reinforcements just move to a random area and attack nothing their whole existence)

-Graphics are better than some of the other games in the genre.

Cons:

-No voices, no indicators when you get hit, no attack animations. Enemies just walk at you and you take damage if they touch you even though they're wielding weapons. Nah, that club stays on that ogre's shoulder and he touches you to attack. Feels like the devs couldn't be bothered to give any personality to the enemies.

-Huge missed opportunity for cool, unique enemies from mythology. Instead, the enemy champions are just giant scorpions and spiders for some reason with horribly small hit boxes that again, just walk towards you to touch you with no attack animations. Some of the bosses are "OK" I guess.

-Each mission is basically the same. Either survive for 20 minutes and automatically win. Survive for 20 minutes and then kill enemies in 3 circles to open a portal and leave (sometimes all 3 circles don't spawn in correctly). Survive for 20 minutes and kill a boss. Also, the 20 minute time limit per level takes away the power fantasy of some of the other games' endless modes or new run +. Just when you get maybe two weapons upgraded to level 15 or so, you'll beat the level and start over.

All in all, I'll keep an eye to see if maybe they'll improve the game but as of now I'd say go buy Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor, Ember Knights, Spell Brigade, or any number of survivor games that do this formula better. No I frames after getting hit so if multiple suicide bomber spiders corner you, you'll just die (stolen right from DRG:Surivor except they don't set off satisfying chain reactions). You'll sometimes get the same two skill choices as a reward for an objective, some skill options don't do what they say they'll do, attacks are unbalanced so you'll probably stick to the same ones, I could probably find more poor design choices but I lost interest playing the game.

Moreover, the game suffers from a lack of clear explanations about the items you pick up. There's no intuitive way to understand what these items do, leaving players guessing rather than strategizing. This not only slows down the gameplay but also diminishes any sense of progression or mastery over the game mechanics.

Overall, Achilles: Survivor left me unimpressed. The combination of a confusing minimap and opaque item descriptions makes for a gameplay experience that feels more frustrating than fun. If you're looking for a well-polished survivor game, you might want to look elsewhere.

Mines of Moira: a striped down re-make with monster spawn cranked to 11, because why interact with stuff when you can kill waves of monsters!

Let me begin by saying this is Moira is one of my favorite games., I started playing as a kid on floppy disks, and I still play once in a while today. This is a re-make of that game and unfortunately is extremely broken. Many features are removed from this game and that's sad considering the game had all the innovations of 1985 floppy disk. However the games real problem is the monster spawn. I'm not sure why the game design became lets spawn a monster every few rooms. The game was not designed to work this way, and it makes doing things other then fighting or playing classes that need to rest often like mages, nearly impossible to play. The removal of a lot of actions and game play just turns the game into constant grind of monster spawn and fight. You no longer have time to search for secret doors, or tunnel for treasure, and haggling for lower prices at stores, closing a door to keep from getting overrun by monsters, bashing/pushing monsters, throwing things, and a lot of other things are just removed. Some parts of the game are just different like identifying items as soon as you reach town, fewer secret doors, and other changes that are different choices but not broken.  The one strong point is the ability to rewind the game in case you died from a mistake or just bad luck. 

This game spawns lots of monsters, and you fight lots of monster. Want to search and tunnel, no fight monsters, want to interact with things in the dungeon, why have some monsters to fight, want to cast spells that do interesting and unique things out side of combat, look more monsters. Need to rest to regenerate mana, look a monster interrupted you better cast a spell, wait no mana? Oh well time to fight. Want to walk through town getting mobbed by so many attackers that you can't walk out of a shop without getting attacked from five different directions! This remake has you covered. 

I may consider recommending the game if the monster spawn is fixed, it should not be sold on PC in this broken state. I will consider changing my review if the developer cares about fixing this crazy spawn rate., but for now this is a hard pass.

Also some reviews mentioned the source code missing, there is a section about the source code on the web site.

I'll give this a pass, but only just for the reasons below. 

A walking simulator / mystery explorer with puzzles in the vein of Gone Home and Edith Finch. It is compact and fairly clever with some tricky puzzles but an intuitive flow to solve them mostly. The graphics are pretty good and it has a suitably creepy atmosphere. Bonus points for a clear UK voice-over with some character. However, there are issues not all players will tolerate despite some recent fixes.

- Stair navigation is broken, you have to jump and then reposition and jump further, No reason for this, just using walk would be fine. 
- The VO is over-used and becomes annoying very quickly. There is only so many times it is worth saying the same thing like "a box, what a good use of your time" so why not just have a shorter version like "just a box" for subsequent examinations, or none at all? Same with the bit using the computer.  This is even more annoying because
- you have to pick up and examine everything you are able to discover what has a useful clue or doesn't (triggering the VO.) There's no rhyme or reason as to what you can pick up pointlessly and what you can't pick up at all. Or why so many assets are re-used (its just silly that Kate has so many piles of the same books for instance!) 
- there are many clues and assets which seem pointless, and that's because the game is unfinished,

Which brings me on to the unforgivable part of this game. It turns out that this is just part 1. There is no mention of this on the store at all which is IMO borderline scammy behaviour and something that a new indie dev should not be doing. Just say on the store page that "the exciting second part will be coming soon" or something. Be clear and honest with your players - read the room - players have had enough of being duped. 

This also means that the game is very short for the price. If the following parts are 'free' add-ons to this purchase then the price is reasonably I suppose. If they are not, and require additional purchase, this review will be changed to 'not recommended.' Again, you must be clear to your customers what they should expect for the price.

Lastly, there is no good reason not to have achievements in a game like this. Even just one, for completion or something. It's low effort not to put one in. 

I'm recommending because I can see effort put into the game, especially some of the puzzle flows, and it is quite enjoyable but there are also red flags to consider at the moment.

Scunners Run has some potential, but makes some crippling control mistakes that need to be fixed.  The cursor is sluggish, moving and accelerating behind the player's input instead of with them, disconnecting you from the game.  This is a surprisingly common dev mistake on controller, but here it affects the mouse too, which is inexplicable.  Sluggish aim is not ok, especially in a fast action shooter, where responsiveness is a fundamental element, not a design question.

For example, let's say your move your controller aim stick from west straight to northeast.  The correct behavior is for the reticle to be at precisely the same screen position as your stick position throughout that motion, from leaving when you leave, to arriving when you arrive.  This connects you to the aim movement, and feels good.  Bad behavior is pretty much anything else.  Here, after you move, the cursor starts accelerating (already losing connection with your position), moseys around the outside of a circle (now taking a different direction/path entirely from your input movement), and finally, as it [i]approaches[/i] the stick position you wanted to aim at and have already reached, it begins to slow down, making its arrival not only that much later, but changing up the timing on you to throw off your anticipation of having your shot lined up.  On mouse, that deceleration leaves the cursor in a different position than where you stopped, and the various issues just leave the mouse feeling like it's in a different place from the reticle.

Does any of that sound like the "fast, twitchy shooting" the store page describes?  Sure, you can call me a picky gamer, but there is right and wrong, and this is simple, basic stuff.  You do not slow down and change the player's input and break their connection with the play.  If a dev ties the camera to the cursor (which, FYI, this one does, and there's no option to disable that if it bothers you, like there's no aim assist option, nor remapping), and they find the aim-look too jerky, the [i]camera[/i] needs damping, not the player.

A twitch action game that gets the action wrong needs to be fixed.  Even more so for a simple action game, that doesn't have much else to go on for the player experience.  Fundamentals are almost the whole game here, and they need to be nailed to pass muster.  Scunners Run does not.

Decided to play this game hoping it was fun. It was recommended to me because it was "similar to other games I have played." The game has some good ideas with being able to use a gun to destroy blocks and being used as a way to help the player move. That is the end of my praise.

This is a platformer game, so the controls and movement should make sense and work well. Jumping is one of the main mechanics and they somehow managed to mess it up. When using the gun to jump, your jumps won't ever be consistent. I continuously fired the gun below my player and held down the jump button, and each jump was a different height. This could be an intentional mechanic based on how far away the last-fired bullet is, but it feels much more like random chance if that is the case. If it's not an intentional mechanic, then that is even worse. It shouldn't take a rocket scientist to realise that having jump height being inconsistent is an issue in a platformer game.

The gun isn't only used for jumping, it is also used to shoot some blocks to destroy them. This seems like a cool idea, however, it feels like more of a chore than a fun game mechanic. The blue blocks take multiple hits to destroy and when you need to destroy multiple to progress, it feels like the game artificially slowing things down to make it feel like the game is longer. I imagine in later levels that some blocks shouldn't be destroyed and you may need to shoot responsibly, but I got so bored of this game I never made it that far, if it exists. 

Finally, the art. The game has a pixel art style, and it doesn't execute it well. Lots of objects have inconsistent pixel sizes with each other. Instead of making larger versions of large blocks, they took one size of block and just scaled it up. This is just lazy and makes all the blocks look like they don't match up. On top of that, there are issues with layering allowing parts of the player to overlap weirdly with other blocks. And the worst part is that there are blocks that seem normal, but have no collision. This makes no sense. It doesn't add anything good to the game and makes it feel unfair.

In the current state,  there is a lot of random stutter in specific* locations, which is never a good sign for an adventure game, likely not a graphics problem, but a coding one. The Good: There are good bones of a good game under the issues. A good topic of choice, and interesting mechanics. 

The Bad: 
1. The UI requires more clicking than the idle clicker game I was playing just prior to this. I am legitimately worried about RSI if I get into this game too deeply. A few examples. Each pallet of up to hundreds of items needs to be manually loaded into pallets. There is no unlock-able palletizer at any time. Each piece of trash requires a separate click to pick up. I really like Simulator games like this. Games where I can just shut my brain off for a while, put on a video or some music or a podcast, and just relax. I have played and enjoyed a lot of games like this, which is why in the end, it is kind of a shame I cannot recommend this one. The gameplay loop, while simple and fun at the start, eventually becomes far more of a grind than I think is worth it, and the end game is just waiting around, which is awful and my main gripe.

You start the game and are introduced to how things will work. You will go to abandoned sites (and later on you can send NPC hirelings), you will pick up items that can be recycled (it is hard to miss them, they are the same 20 items repeated over and over in a world where you cannot interact with anything else), throw them in your truck, bring them back to base, sort them, and then either sell or process them. The more you process the items, the more money you get in the end; especially if you take contracts for certain items.

As you gain more money, three different tiers of processing machines are opened to you. The first level ones grind things up, the second level machines make basic blocks like plastic pellets, iron ingots, and raw paper, while the third level allows you to start picking and choosing some recycled items to make, like glass bottles, iron pipes, and newspapers. What is unfortunate about this game is just how quickly you can unlock all of these things, as well as every other upgrade. From carrying capacity, to hiring new staff, to getting robots; the game is over extremely quickly. I had nothing left to buy or do and was sitting on a huge pile of cash maybe about, 15 hours into the game? Less?

But what isn't over quickly, is processing items to the third level. Say you are like me and are a completionist and want to get the achievement for getting one million dollars. The best way to do this is to take contracts. For example: 30 newspapers and 40 glass jars, for about $8,000 (give or take). Alright, you feed the paper and glass into the shredders, and wait, because for every kilogram you collect it takes several seconds. Then those machines spit out the items into the next tier. Each one of these next machines takes two kilograms of items to process them into something new. So now you wait even longer. Finally, it spits out the product into the third machine and yeah, you guessed it, it takes even more of these items to make your final product. So now you wait EVEN LONGER, until eventually your 30 newspapers and 40 jars are done being spit out, so you can collect your money. During that time, you are doing nothing.

The start of the day is fun and busy. You can have eight drivers, each of who can go to a site to collect stuff on their own. That means if you hire the best level of secretary, you can generally get about 3 or 4 sites more for you to get to before the sun goes down. As you and everyone gets back, you can have two NPCs sort it all, and as they sort it you can start throwing things into the machines; and then as before.. you wait. You select contracts, throw down pallets, slowly collect your finished items onto them, and wait.

I have over 30 hours into this game, and I am only half way to making a million dollars. Normally I would not be upset about this. Often times the grind in these games is what is fun. I enjoy running through sites, collecting junk, pilfering old crates and discarded cash boxes, trying to get back before the NPCs do. It is the doing nothing and waiting for the machines to process everything afterwards that I cannot stand.

So, if you do go to buy this game then keep in mind what I said above. If you do get it, also be aware that it is extremely cheap looking, plays badly, has an uncountable number of spelling and grammar errors, can quickly give you a headache from looking at the painfully bright and colourful menus, and that it uses AI art for character portraits. In the end, I would not recommend this game, unless you can get it on a fantastic sale and don't mind only getting 20-30 hours out of it.

As a person with mild OCD this appealed to my desire to keep things clean.  It is a simple game involving visits to e.g. abandoned garages which are inexplicably littered with random items for recycling.  You do not drive your 1 truck it just appears there after a button press and the same in reverse when you have completed your rubbish pick.  Once you return to your depot you have a sorter which at first you operate by throwing items into the correct colour-coded crates for plastic, glass, metal, paper and wood.  You can buy basic machinery to process the materials into saleable products which can be sold in an online marketplace or to individual companies at a (negotiable) price.  The latter is more profitable.

As you progress through the game, you can buy more complex machinery which processes materials into more valuable products.  You can also employ sorters to do that job for you and unload your truck.  In addition you can hire up to 8 truck drivers who will carry out your instructions as to where you want them to go and will unload their own trucks into the sorter.  By this time you will have unlocked enough new destinations for them to go to.  This is helped by hiring a assistant to bid for contracts on your behalf - best assistant will offer you 8 contracts a day of varying bulk.  Prior to hiring the assistant you had to bid for contracts yourself on your own computer, which you can continue to do in tandem with the assistant. 

I found picking up the items on the premises quite tedious after a while so was quite happy to leave it to the hired help.  In order to make it a bit more interesting the devs have included some locked rooms which you can open with a lock pick (some have found this hard to use, I found using the left joystick on an XBox controller, pushing it into the forward position and slowly rotating to the left and right would produce a clicking sound indicating the right spot and then a press of the A button would open the door).  There are also chests which can be opened with a crowbar (on controller by A button presses) and contain a nice reward and tills which also require the lock pick but have a decent amount of money in.

Later in the game you can buy up to four robots to move your crates and finished products about.  You can also buy recycling bins which member of the public put items in, this will add a bit to your production capacity.  The production and storage areas can be substantially enlarged as you progress.

I managed to complete the game and get all the achievements in 59 hours.  I am pretty old so I expect young  hotshots could complete it more quickly than this.  I am a sucker for simulator-type games and enjoyed this one while it lasted.

Also the sorter is a long way from the truck park which means it takes the slow-walking hired truckers a long time to deliver the goods to the sorter such that I ended up running past them with the goods to speed things up.  You can only send them out once a day and by the time they have finished their go-slow deliveries it starts to get dark.  You do have a torch and you will need it.  The lighting in the production areas is particularly dim - I found I was operating the machinery a lot at night so this did not help.  Maybe the devs could add a few more lights or give the option to buy some.

An incredible experience with the best gameplay of any text-based adventure RPG I have found on PC. The UI and map provide seamless exploration and smooth gameplay. The game also includes quality music and ambiance, which puts it miles ahead of other choose your own adventure games on the market in terms of immersion. 

Even if you are new to a text-based adventure RPG I highly recommend trying out Bloodwood Dungeon, particularly if you enjoy a good story and dark fantasy.

If I could pick a "mixed" rating for this game, I would. Some of its glaring issues might be too much for certain players, especially those unfamiliar with old-school text-based RPGs.

The writing is decent for the most part - simple and to the point, but not overly expository, so it rarely overstays its welcome. There is some world-building, though it never goes very far or becomes particularly engaging on its own. What keeps you interested is more about what isn't being said - the mystery of it all - rather than the details presented outright. That intrigue is just enough to keep you going through the game's short ~2-hour runtime. 

Most quests boil down to thinly disguised fetch quests, with only one correct way to complete them. 

The music starts off fitting and atmospheric but quickly grows stale due to its simplicity and lack of variety.

I don’t have strong feelings about the AI-generated images. While the style suits the game's tone, many of them are difficult to appreciate. Character portraits are serviceable, but the scenery images are uninspired at best and distracting at worst, sometimes pulling me out of the experience rather than enhancing immersion.

The UI is functional, though not ideal. I spent 90%+ of my time reading a small text box in the top-left corner, which made playing on a large screen uncomfortable. Some layout adjustments would help.

The biggest issue by far is the combat system. It offers little in terms of interesting decision-making, mostly boiling down to clicking, watching rolls play out, and clicking again... and again... and again. It's overly random, boring to watch, and even worse to play - especially if you're forced to retry encounters multiple times.

And yet, despite all its obvious shortcomings (late-game combat being particularly frustrating), the game had just enough atmosphere to keep me playing. I finished it and enjoyed it - not because it's great, but because I was craving the kind of experience it attempts to offer.

All in all, it's dirt cheap, and it's clear some effort went into making it. If you're looking for a quick text-based RPG adventure in the vein of Bloodwood Dungeon, it might just be enjoyable enough for you too.

Debating a return.  Even took a break to clear my head to consider if I was missing something, but came back, and it's...just not there. Quit again after 10 min.  I'd watched a review of Dragon Ruins 2 and I think misled myself into thinking there was a bit more in this first game than there is.

The concept is appealing, but in practice it's just missing a spark for me.  

What I like:
-The idea of mapping while combat auto-resolves is a good concept for a dungeon crawler.

What it's missing:
-Something, like equipment drops to mix it up, or talent/attribute points at level. 
-Any real sense of flavor between the classes - if there's any difference at all between various comps/characters I'm just not seeing it

What I don't like:
-Gold is the bottleneck for pretty much everything the game actually has (level, gear upgrades, rez pots and teleport scrolls)
-XP stops accruing when you hit level until you buy the upgrade (albeit this is probably fine since for a long time you will be bottlenecked on gold anyway)
-As a result, it quickly reached a point where there was no point fighting enemies that didn't drop gold (wolves, etc.) and only fighting humanoids that did. The XP itself, as theoretically one of the game's two primary resources, was largely useless.
-The map design is possibly the worst dungeon layout I've ever seen. 

I think the last point is the dealbreaker for me - I could forgive the other shortcomings if it were fun toodling around or exploring, but navigating this dungeon layout just feels bad. It's haphazard at best, and at worst just intentionally obtuse to pad game time.

This game is short, simple, unvaried and almost wholly self-playing. There really isn't much here. It's mostly an exercise in game ideas for this subgenre (which seems to be what this developer mostly dabbles with, to be fair).

It has something though. A vibe. The art style and atmosphere are all kinds of rad. The responsive, simple, yet oddly satisfying gameplay has potential. It's a classic dungeon crawler in some sense, but almost plays like an idle game to some extent. Combat encounters are completely automatic. You just literally walk around until you need to retreat to heal in town, upgrade your monster murderers with the gold you got, and go back out there to murder again. That's it. It's very meditative. Less is more could very well be a thing here. It just needs something more to be fully realized. A few more variables. A bit more variation. And length. Still, the vibe is enough for me to recommend it to the right person.
