It really pains me to leave a negative review on an indie game, but given that it has similar price to a lot of really solid otome visual novels, I thought someone may appreciate a heads-up.

Non-spoilery TL;DR version: 
The story is... not good. It starts okay, and was enjoyable enough for the first hour or so, but then it started to feel like some very juvenile fanfiction really fast. Characters and events didn't make any sense, things were just happening for no reason, and MC was acting like three totally different people, with her thoughts and actions doing a complete 180 from how she was 10 minutes ago. I'm not sure how far along I was in the story, but I don't see any way it could possibly end up being something even remotely reasonable narrative-wise.

And now cue spoilery rant:
[spoiler]I went for Kasanov's route.
The story starts with MC and her squad of rangers on a scouting mission. We eventually get a bit of exposition and it seems there's some sort of military tension between MC's kingdom and elven kingdom, so they are ordered to capture an elf for interrogation. They catch Kasanov, who is indeed an elf, bring him in, and soon after we are told that unless he shares any valuable information he will be executed in 5 days.
MC is upset about killing defenceless prisoner like that (I mean, fair) and we get a bit weird countdown in the beginning of each day, that looks like you need to do something in order to save him, but the only thing the game lets you do is hanging out with your friends, and by the looks of it she just releases him regardless.
When Kasanov is released he suggests MC comes home with him to learn about what's actually going on. She has some doubts about abandoning her army duties and betraying her realm and her friends for about thirty seconds and agrees, after that suddenly all her friends - one of whom is a prince - appear and tag along, because apparently out of nowhere everyone is now dubious about the local politics to the point of deflection.
Starting from here MC more or less stops caring or paying any attention to her friends in favour of thirsting over Kasanov. I don't think she ever had a conversation not revolving around him from this point onwards.
They arrive to his kingdom, get captured by guards - including the prince, but no one seems to be even remotely interested. Everyone tries to figure out how to escape, apart from the MC who is like "fear not and sit tight my dudes, Kasanov, whom I known for a whole week and learned nothing about, promised to keep me safe, so there's literally zero reason to worry". Kasanov eventually comes to release them and reveals that he is a leader of the local group of rebels and plans a coup to overthrow current evil government and establish democracy. They all agree to help him, because I guess there's no way a cute elven boy that MC likes could not be fighting for the right cause, and him asking nicely is good enough reason to start a revolution and cause bloodshed without any context or knowledge of the current situation. Suddenly the king of MC's kingdom is also evil, so they agreed to go back and overthrow him as well after they are done here. Like there was zero build-up for that. They didn't seem especially happy with the king, but that's about it. In case you forgot, the prince is still there, and is also on board with some sudden light-hearted patricide.
MC is thirsting over Kasanov even more because she was pleased to learn that he's important and respected, and not just some rando.
They do the coup thing the very next day, and in the meantime MC promptly morphs into the Kasanov's lap dog with no agency of her own, and her contribution to the plot is mostly limited to fawning over him, telling people (including her friends) off for not being respectful and obedient enough, and complacently supporting Kasanov while he is killing people for being rude to him. She doesn't really seem to care about anything unless it prevents her from engaging in PDA with Kasanov at this point.
There was a moment where she hears some folks from the old government screaming and Kasanov laughing in the dungeons, and she's like "better go wait somewhere else, those cries of people being tortured are kinda killing the mood ", and later mentions that all of them supposedly were killed. Like, girl. You deflected your country's army because they wanted to execute an enemy's scout. Those pretty elven boys spin your moral compass like one hell of a magnet.
The whole coup thing is over in about 5 minutes, Kasanov seems more concerned about groping MC than any political stuff, MC seems pretty chuffed about the current state of affairs, and then there's a time skip for several months.
Nothing seems to change much after time skip apart from Kasanov by the looks of it being a sole ruler and decision maker in this fine newfound democracy, while still being preoccupied with groping MC. MC apparently also doesn't do much, follows Kasanov around, and relishes her status of military wife.
Then there was some kind of festival where Kasanov was very reluctant to peel himself off of MC to attend to his duties, and after a bit MC freaked out because he dared to speak to other people without continuously establishing that she is the most important person here. So she stormed off crying and contemplating their whole relationship because she had to sit and wait like everyone else while he was talking politics with someone.
At this point I gave up, and I have no idea what this story is even about.

It sounds like I'm just being mean and snarky about it, but, uhh, that is honestly close enough to how narrative goes, and all the parts of MC acting obnoxious are pretty much spelled out like this in her inner monologue.[/spoiler]

So, fun fact about the character of Slender Man: he is copyrighted, and naturally, Victor Surge (aka Eric Knudsen) is the copyright holder. Seeing as how he is not listed anywhere in the credits, I can only assume that the developers did not obtain permission to use the character in their game, hence them constantly referring to the titular antagonist as "The Faceless Man".

Other than that, it's just another Slender: The Eight Pages clone with the same jumpscare sound effect, a different map, a couple of interactive cutscenes, and for whatever reason, Blair Witch-style stick figures littered around the map. It does not earn the 6 dollar price tag at all, in my opinion, especially not with the two alternate modes, "Lost Memories" and "Hellmode". Spoilers on both modes below:

[spoiler]Lost Memories is the exact same game in the exact same map, with the only differences being that it seemingly takes place during daytime with a thick layer of fog, there is an extra line of dialogue once you collect all 8 notes, and there is a constant ambience of droning/banging noises which quickly becomes more annoying than unsettling.

Hellmode is the same game and same map yet again, with slightly less obnoxious ambience, and a thick red haze that makes it much more difficult to see. The only other difference is that once all 8 notes are collected,  a deep laugh is heard before abruptly returning to the main menu.
[/spoiler]

There also does not seem to be any difference in the aggression of Not-Slender-Man across any of the 3 game modes, and its aggression doesn't seem that high in the first place. You could likely go an entire playthrough without so much as seeing it.

The one thing I can somewhat praise this game on is level design. It is very easy to get lost in the forest where you search for notes, which is definitely a trait you want in a Slender map. The one criticism that I have is that there are several invisible walls in places that otherwise seem completely accessible, and constantly running into them can get irritating.

tl;dr, it's a cheap attempt at cashing in on Slender Man's popularity 10 years too late.

David Pateti is one of my best discoveries in recent years when it comes to retro horrors.

After the brilliant Terminal 81 and the great Mortisomem, he gave us another original game, which is Acre Crisis.
It is known that the game is inspired by Dino Crisis, but David does it in his own style.
Open world, survival elements, many types of weapons, outfits for the main character and additional game modes.

What I like in David's games is the multitude of different interesting mechanics.
And here we have a similar thing as in previous titles.

However, what I like most is the atmosphere and the story of the presented world, which is not shallow, but multi-threaded. I hope that we will learn the continuation of the plot, because it ended at an unexpected moment.

Here's a list of issues I encountered in the first ~1.5 hours of gameplay:
1. Clunky/lurchy movement. Not bad on its own but it sure doesn't help anything
2. One of the first enemy types runs straight at your ankles which is an issue because you can't aim straight down
3. When you kill an enemy the ragdoll seems to block your movement. This might also be the clunky movement or it could be:
4. every rock, tree, and slope is a major obstacle. The environment is very cluttered which exacerbates the movement issues especially when combined with:
5. There are invisible walls to stop you moving too far in the open forest. This is an issue when you are under pressure from:
6. 500 dinosaurs all the time. There are way too many dinosaurs. You kill a group of three and then you have five more bearing down on you. You kill them and there's another five. They go down easy enough, but there are too goddamn many. I saw dinosaurs fade into existence before my eyes in a place I just cleared out.
7. It seems like when you take damage it forces you out of the aiming state (problematic when fighting 500 dinosaurs).
8. There are no manual saves, only autosaves. It autosaves before long phone-calls and you don't get an objective pointer until after the call ends.

I think a lot of these problems would become non-issues by significantly reducing the spawn rate of dinosaurs. Suffocating under a sea of dinosaurs is almost a greater risk than being clawed to death. I wouldn't say it makes it unplayable, but it's not something I want to put up with.
I really wanted to like this game and I feel kind of bad giving a negative review after only 1.5 hours; maybe I'll give it another try later, but I can't call it a recommendable experience.

You play as a cowboy trying to become the king of Rockay City. The city map is divided into different colored areas that represent who controls them. You fight, kill, steal, and gradually take over these areas, eventually trying to control the entire city. The premise is there, but the execution is lacking. The main story is extremely shallow, the acting feels overly dramatic and the main character has absolutely no depth, charm, or strategy. I feel bad seeing Michael Rooker play dull. At one point, you can even bribe a gang leader to give up 1/4 of the map. Bosses are just faceless names with icons and don’t even get cut scenes. Meanwhile, there are lengthy cut scenes featuring a tough sheriff fully equipped sitting in an army chopper or his office, yet I never actually face him in-game, so why the emphasis on him?

Each mission takes 5-10 minutes and are incredibly repetitive. The FPS are sloppy, AI is terrible, games has bugs - In one early mission I was told to raid a bank vault. As I was trying to locate the control room, my two teammates somehow walked through walls and got stuck inside the vault. It was only when I set off a C4 to blow open the gate that my team of 4 finally reunited, finally not be overwhelmed by waves of police. Later in the game, my teammates would occasionally freeze up and doing nothing even I give orders.

Each time you level up you're given random items to choose one, but most of the rewards are skins for weapons and main character that are only usable in multiplayer modes. Why bother adding that in a solo game, especially when there's no decent weapons available?

I could go on listing the ridiculous design choices (like upgrading apartment), but I’ll stop here. I do not recommend this game.

Meh.  Not much strategy or depth to it even considering the sale price.  Just max the price without making the face frown and max the fish without causing fishing failures.  The pond ends up being all one fish of the highest level.  I'd give a middle review if that existed but between thumbs up or down it's a definite down.  

I could imagine adding some additional depth by making satisfaction not only dependent on price but also on finding the right balance of difficulty.  The customer might fish as usual but would not have maximum satisfaction unless they failed on one attempt or at least saw someone else fail while they were there.  Auto stocking would then have a choice of selecting a target number of fish in the pond to stock up to rather than just stocking the most expensive option.  Of course if the player is selling tickets at a loss that could more than make up for it being too easy and still yield a max rating.

I could also see setting the default price gained when a customer catches a fish to less than the cost to stock that fish.  We would then have to think a bit more about just letting them fish up everything easily.  Perhaps the stocked fish could grow a size if they survive a day and be worth a bit more and add more to difficulty.  Even if the customer does not actually catch it, just knowing a much higher value fish is somewhere in the pond that’s possible to catch with the provided rod would boost their satisfaction for a given price.

Satisfaction might then turn into more of a range of -2, -1, 0, +1, +2 dependent on multiple factors that have to be managed and thought about a bit more.  You could provide a difficulty slider if need be to adjust the price margins.  A simple loan system might be implemented to prevent game over from messing up once and finance the first few fish.

Sucks the joy out of the medium in my opinion, because you aren't really free to choose something in most situations, you just have to pick the 'right' answer, which will vary based on your build, but that sucks. I wish there were CYOA games like this where it was actually just roleplay (Picking the choice you want/the choice that you think fits your character as opposed to the choice the author thinks fits your build) even if there were less meaningful choices throughout the story.

I imagine the use of these stats is probably 'forced' on the creators by 'choice' or something along those lines, since I've only seen like one of these ever where it was rp and not stat based (forgot which one it was, but only had stats that tracked your decisions, they didn't change the outcomes of the choices or something.)

So yeah, pretty enjoyable vampire story to me, but it's in spite of the typical stat bs.

Wish choices were not succeed/fail a check but instead crossroads in the story no matter how minor or major where you see something a little different (even if it's just like a couple sentences that change on the next page) or a lot different.

Like I really wouldn't mind something that is 90% linear with just some neat minor little changes occasionally based on a choice here and there. I would 100% prefer that to the typical 'choice' type stats. Because they suck. lol

Love Undying was fab. A gorgeously told vampiric romance against the backdrop of victorian Cornwall. The writing is atmospheric and evocative, and I felt very quckly swept up in the roleplay. The subtle ways in which the game reinforces your choices and draws you into the world made for an imersive experience, and as the romance emerged it felt sweet and earned. The town of Boscawen and its characters are richly realised, and their struggles and conflicts, and the thoughtful choices you have to make about how to relate to them, invite a second look.

A good bargain for all those looking for a Vampire Novel/RPG hybrid with some decent replayability.

So many vampire stories these days don't take place in the Victorian era, and that this one  does makes it strangely fresh. And the decision to set it in the countryside is just a treat! The story is not groundbreaking by any means but you get a good amount of freedom to choose what kind of person/vampire you are.

This was definitely entertaining for me and will give it my Seal of Approval.

Love Undying is a dynamic narrative that possesses all the merits of an ardent romance and the bestial horror of an Anne Rice novel; both rhetorically sound and perfect in length, Lauren O’Donoghue composes a tale that is satisfactory to read, each decision influencing the story significantly. While some scenes are consistent among every path, your character’s identity greatly affects the flow of conversation and implicates the ease of subterfuge or persuasion. Beyond the stat-based mechanics and decision making, I appreciate the author’s attention to authentic romance and her desire to write purely ethical fiction; additionally, her inclusivity of varying identities was really lovely to see and I commend her efforts. Thank you so much for such an incredible experience!

Is ReSetna a full game? Yes, you can play the game from start to end-credits, but the game is bug ridden and has serious pacing issues. It does not feel properly playtested.

The story is mostly told through codex entries you pick up as you play the game. The in-game story is very minimal and, honestly, doesn't make a whole lot of sense. The entries are so fragmented, it's hard to make sense of it all until you collect a bunch. I honestly didn't even bother.

The game boasts 20+ hours on the store page. This is a lie. I beat the game in a little over 9 hours, and 1-2 of those hours were me attempting to complete an incredibly frustrating chase sequence that ended up just being an achievement and not something required to complete the game. I can't fathom getting another 11 hours out of this game, even if I tried to collect everything.

The combat needs a lot of work. Enemies do not die very fast, but are easily dealt with by dashing through them and attacking them from behind. The game starts out very slow. Enemies feel like damage sponges, especially the first boss. There's a parry button, but it locks you into a long counter-attack animation, and doesn't feel particularly worth it. One huge issue is that when you get hit, the game just stuns you. Were you mid-attack? Stun. Were you jumping? Stun and you fall to the ground. When fighting multiple enemies, particularly ones with projectiles, this gets incredibly frustrating as you end up getting stun locked if you try attacking or jumping away. 

Speaking of combat, the game has three weapons, but they do not feel like side grades. While each weapon has something somewhat unique about it, the damage never improves on the older weapons. Once I got the spear, I never used anything else. The game never requires the use of each weapon's unique properties, like the axe's ability to throw a projectile. This seems like a missed opportunity.

The game features some precision platforming elements, but good god can the controls be infuriating. As already mentioned, if you get hit while jumping, you lose all momentum and fall straight down. There is a warp ability that acts sort of like a grapple to floating nodes placed around the environment. It took me a long time to figure out that if you hold a direction while warping, the game kills your momentum. I couldn't figure out why I wasn't able to make it far enough until I realized if I didn't hold a direction, the game would properly launch me with momentum. Wall jumping is also very annoying. For some reason double jumping after jumping off a wall is delayed and very finicky.

ReSetna also suffers from some very weird pacing. The game starts out very typical. You explore. You find a boss. You get a power up. You unlock access to more areas. Then, all of a sudden, I unlocked several abilities in a row with no boss in between, unlocked some chip upgrades, all the weapons, and the game became a walk in the park. My health was larger, regenerated, and I came back from death. Usually in a Metroidvania you go through a loop of explore > boss > power up > explore > boss > power up, but past the very beginning of the game, they just throw everything at you and suddenly you're all-powerful.

Speaking of weird pacing, the game has awful breadcrumbing. There were two instances I was completely lost. One was a ladder that was barely visible in the top-right of the screen. I'm not the only one that had this issue, as I know at least two other people I've spoken with have missed this ladder. Another was a teleporter I apparently missed. Without it being displayed on the map, it was difficult to find. Typically in a Metroidvania, you go to areas with locked doors or rooms you haven't explored to find your way forward, but an unmarked teleporter left me exploring every nook and cranny for what I missed. I even missed an important vendor in the hub area for a while because it's a bit out of the way and the game never forces you to meet them.

Quests are poorly implemented. Some require items from around the map, but when you pick up said item it doesn't tell you what it is or does. There was an entire set of items I had no idea what they were for. When turning in the quest, I didn't even know what my reward was. No pop-up or anything. Items around the map are easy to miss. The lore items are literally a faint white glow on the ground. The game does a poor job of distinguishing some treasure from regular background objects until you get used to what they look like.

The game boasts 7 biomes offering unique experiences, but these barely change anything. The most unique area was the acid area, but past that each area's theme is...a color? I guess? This one's blue. This one is red. They don't offer anything unique like store page states. Lots of rooms are huge, empty spaces. Most biomes are just sterile, metallic areas with the corresponding color applied to it.

Some of the bosses were pretty neat, but once the game throws all the upgrades at you, they lack a challenge. Most of the bosses are after this point. The last "boss" is a joke, and super anticlimactic.

But lets talk about the bugs. Oh, the bugs. This game has bugs galore. From enemies spawning outside the combat zone, to text appearing and staying on your screen, to walls you can walk through, to respawn points not being properly places allowing you to skip areas, to treasure you can't loot, to an entire side-quest you can't complete because the NPC will not talk to you, and more. 

Simply put, this game is not ready for full release. It feels like a game that was only maybe a third complete, but they hurried and slapped the rest of the game together to call it complete. The game has clearly not be QAed properly. There are bugs galore and issues like getting stunned on hit that make the game feel awful to play.

Best of luck to the devs, but ReSetna offers very little new to the genre and is far from a polished product. They are supposedly fixing bugs and are aware of the bad combat feel, but I don't think that's going to fix the deep seated issue of game pacing that needs a complete overhaul of the game. With the game being at full release, I just don't see it happening. I can't recommend this game at all, especially in its current state.

[h1]Where Am I? What Did I Just Pick Up? What Does It Do? 🤔 [/h1]

Resetna is challenging, but not always in the right ways. Visually, it’s stunning, featuring a beautifully designed protagonist and a meticulously crafted world. The core combat mechanics are solid, and the upgrade system aligns with what you’d expect from a well-made Metroidvania. The developers’ effort is evident, and the game brims with potential.

However, Resetna struggles where it matters most—performance. Despite being seemingly perfect for the SteamDeck, it runs poorly, plagued by technical issues. Frozen maps, persistent menu overlays, clunky controls, and moments of uncertainty about what to do next all hinder the experience. What could have been a must-play is instead frustratingly rough around the edges.

[h2][b]Oops I Sharded Again! 📸[/b] [/h2]
Is anyone else accidentally creating shards when you simply try to use the down button to attack or is it just me? Have an option to turn off shards. Please.

Playing Resetna often feels like experiencing a work-in-progress rather than a polished game. One of the most baffling design choices is the complete lack of item notifications. Who decided not to tell players what they’ve picked up? Countless times, I grabbed something and had to dig through the inventory to figure out what it was—sometimes, I never even found out. I just shrugged and moved on, unsure of where I was headed until I stumbled upon something important by sheer luck. I’ve turned in a quest and was told I now had key 3 (had no idea how to even get that) to fight a boss but where was the key? Not in my inventory. I kept playing, died and once respawned at the save point a key was waiting there for me. 

One particularly frustrating moment involved backtracking aimlessly until I accidentally found a key. It wasn’t marked, indicated, or even visible—I only obtained it by randomly repeating the shutdown action at one of the terminals I had previously deactivated. Suddenly, I had a key! Where did it come from? Why was it invisible? Why did I have to repeat an old action to get it? And why wasn’t I told it was there? Who knows…

This highlights Resetna’s biggest flaw: its confusing approach to information. The game bombards you with excessive menu options while making vital details frustratingly inaccessible. Items and NPCs sometimes provide clues, but these are sparse, lack context, and often lead to more confusion. I see upgrade options for weapons, but what do they actually do? Are some weapons stronger than others? How can I tell?

[h2][i]Some Issues Holding Resetna Back:[/i][/h2]

[b]🔴 BUGS[/b] 
•	The options menu sometimes stays on screen even after closing it.
•	UI glitches frequently cause text to jumble into an unreadable mess.
•	The map occasionally freezes, leaving you stuck—unless you place and delete a shard, which somehow fixes it.
•	I’ve spawned into a full black screen more than once, requiring a reset.
•	I’ve walked through a door into a room that was loading and before the load finished I was being attacked by enemies DURING the load screen. I could hear it happening. Not good to walk into a room and get hit multiple times before the screen finishes loading. 


[b]⚔️ COMBAT[/b] 
•	Clunky and unresponsive, with hitboxes that feel slightly off.
•	Attack mechanics feel stiff—strangely, the sword seemed more fluid in the demo.
•	Enemy attacks are brutal early on, but once you upgrade weapons, the difficulty drops significantly.
•	However, weapon upgrades seem purely cosmetic—there’s little indication of actual damage differences.
•	Aerial enemies are especially frustrating; getting hit shouldn’t make you completely drop from the air, as it disrupts combat flow.

[b] 📦 FOUND ITEMS[/b] 
•	Players should be told what they’re picking up and what it does—basic information that’s bafflingly absent.
•	Some objects unexpectedly turn out to be NPCs that provide cryptic, unhelpful dialogue instead of useful direction.

[u] Final Thoughts:[/u] 
I really want to like Resetna, but right now, it’s a frustrating experience. I’ll give it another shot once patches come through, but as it stands, the game’s lack of clarity, poor UI design, and technical issues hold it back from being truly great. Please consider leaving better breadcrumbs to necessary upgrades and better highlight needed items. It's far too convoluted right now.

After spending a good amount of time with Resetna, I can confidently say it's a solid Metroidvania with great combat, rewarding exploration, and an incredible atmosphere. While it doesn’t revolutionize the genre, it delivers exactly what I was hoping for—tight gameplay, satisfying progression, and a world that pulls me in.

What I Loved:

Combat & Weapons: Having multiple weapons to switch between keeps combat fresh, and the upgrade system reminds me of the charm mechanics in Hollow Knight. The bosses are tough but feel fair, and I really enjoyed the variety in enemy encounters.

Exploration & Level Design: The game rewards curiosity, and I loved discovering secrets, upgrades, and lore as I progressed. The map was a lifesaver, though I wish quest markers were a bit more obvious.

Atmosphere & Visuals: The cyberpunk/post-apocalyptic setting is beautifully done. Every area feels distinct and immersive, with great environmental storytelling. As a sci-fi fan, this was right up my alley.

Music & Sound Design: The soundtrack is fantastic. It’s subtle when it needs to be, and the boss fight music really amps up the intensity. I’d love an even more pronounced sound effect for parrying.

Performance & Optimization: Runs smoothly, even on Steam Deck at max settings. Huge props for the optimization!

Classic Metroidvania Feel: The game sticks to the core elements of the genre—unlocking new abilities, backtracking to previously inaccessible areas, and strategic combat. It never felt tedious.

Issues & Frustrations:

Clunky Movement at Times: Some platforming sections feel a little off, and I had a few moments where jumps didn’t register as expected.

Hit Stun is Frustrating: Getting hit stops movement for a split second, which feels brutal in fast-paced fights. It made some encounters more frustrating than they needed to be.

Tutorial & UI Improvements Needed:

Hacking Mechanic Confusion: I didn’t fully grasp how hacking worked right away. A short tutorial prompt would help.

Quest Markers on Map: Would love for quest locations to stand out more.


Final Verdict:

I’d rate Resetna a strong 8-9/10 right now, with the potential to be even better after some polish. It’s one of the better Metroidvanias I’ve played recently, and I’d absolutely recommend it to fans of the genre. The combat, atmosphere, and level design are all top-notch, and with a few tweaks, it could be a masterpiece.

Would I recommend it?
✅ Absolutely! If you enjoy Metroidvania games, Resetna is definitely worth playing. It’s a fun, challenging, and visually stunning experience that I had a great time with. Huge props to the developer team who actually listents to audience and are working really hard to fix everything and balance it out.
I have a great time with ReSetna. I believe metroidavia fans will appreciate this game. :)

At the time of this review, there is a lot of room for improvement w.r.t certain aspects such as controls/feel, the starting weapon, some UI refinement, and the occasional bug. However, the foundations for an enjoyable gaming experience is there - and with active improvements in the works - this game can be a fine pickup for anyone who enjoyed the likes of Megaman/X/Zero, Dead Cells etc.

Some positives:
+ skill expression through varied combat: with many attack types (charge/directional/etc), many defensive tools (dodge/parry/shield), free weapon switching, and further upgrades by finding & slotting in chips
+ distinct enemies: they are all fairly easy to identify at a glance and usually have 2+ attacks in their moveset, always providing a baseline level of challenge
+ in-game "screenshot": presumably to keep track of environmental clues/storytelling without having to backtrack, so long as you remember to use it
+ chips upgrade system: a neat little tetris-esque minigame, refreshing departure from the usual inventory system in other games
+ level/backdrop design: while i've only seen around 4 zones so far, they all look and feel distinct with well-defined identities and their fair share of picturesque moments, should you pay attention to details in the foreground and background

Some negatives:
- punishing starting weapon: the axes have low damage, you need 2 directional hits to kill the numerous flying enemies in the starting zone; its short range forces you to jump to hit even low-flying enemies and increases the odds of you taking damage doing so; all the while not being fast enough compared to the other weapons to justify the downsides
- imperceptible/no invulnerability window: the player does not temporarily ignore damage when they take a hit (or for such a short time as to not matter), so you can easily lose a ton of health in a flash, especially when fighting multiple enemies + environmental hazards.
- inconsistent enemy stagger: some enemies (e.g. flying enemies in starting zone) do not stagger out of their attack animation when hit, leading to a lot of HP-trading especially when you're using the axes as you cannot kill them in one directional hit
- wonky animation timings: some attacks have a lot of animation lock, like the aerial directional attack, with no ability for the player to cancel out of the backswing until presumably when you unlock air dash (unsure if this exists, i have not gotten far enough but some environmental design suggests that it is unlockable). by itself this isn't a big problem, but combined with the lack of an invuln window makes some attacks incredibly risky to attempt. some other attacks ignore the base weapon speed/combo timing, such as the grounded up-swing firing off way too fast on the slower weapons.

A minor bug I found: some walls/corners can cause the player model glitch into a perpetual falling animation, presumably due to some miniscule gap in the terrain that the model can "fall" into but not actually move

Although there are certainly flaws as I've mentioned above, it appears the developer is aware of and actively working on many - if not all - of these issues and more. For that reason, I'd say give this game a chance, and check back often.

Resetna is the latest metroidvania from the Croatian studio Todays Games, and it has quickly earned a spot on my personal list of favorites in the genre. As a fan of metroidvania games and having played titles like Hollow Knight, the Metroid series, Blasphemous 1 & 2, and Prince of Persia: Lost Crown, I had high expectations for this game – and I can confidently say those expectations were met and even surpassed.

The game's story is intriguing, but I won’t spoil any details as I want players to experience the plot themselves. What I will say is that Resetna takes place in a vast, nonlinear world divided into seven distinct areas. This world expands as you progress, unlocking new abilities that allow access to previously unreachable zones. For metroidvania fans, this is a classic and essential feature, and it's flawlessly executed here.

One of the key strengths of Resetna is its incredibly precise combat system, which is central to the enjoyment of the game. The variety of weapons at your disposal allows for different approaches to combat, ranging from aggressive action to tactical strategy, with a special emphasis on the parry system – which is almost perfect. Successfully using the parry technique requires precise timing, and your success in combat often depends on how well you master this aspect.

When it comes to enemies, the game is filled with diverse types that keep you on your toes. Each of the seven areas presents different kinds of foes, and the variety of enemies ensures that the game remains fresh and unpredictable. But what really elevates Resetna to another level are the bosses – they’re undoubtedly the most thrilling part of the game. Many of them are incredibly challenging, requiring you to hone your skills and patience in order to defeat them. Even though some are quite tough, the sense of accomplishment when you finally overcome them is priceless.

In addition to combat, Resetna also features platforming elements that are both fun and challenging. At times, these sections of the game will test your precision, but their difficulty and the satisfaction of mastering them only add to the richness of the experience.

There’s no doubt that the atmosphere is what makes Resetna truly special. From the very first moments, you’ll notice how much effort has gone into creating a beautiful visual style, which, combined with the perfect dark sci-fi soundtrack, immerses you in an unforgettable atmosphere. Every detail in the world design contributes to the sense of being drawn into this dark, mysterious adventure.

Overall, Resetna is a true masterpiece in the metroidvania genre, offering everything fans of the genre could want – precise combat, challenging platforming, fantastic atmosphere, and a gripping story. For me, this is an experience I will definitely return to in the future, and I highly recommend it to anyone who loves metroidvanias.

Sync-move three gems at once to reach their target place, old idea enhanced by a few new mechanics, but terrible QoL and tedious levels make it a bad game.

[b]What is it:[/b] A puzzle game in which you have to move three gems on their target spots. All gems move as you push an arrow key, unless they are blocked by an obstacle. The difficulty is in finding the right walls to push against to separate the gems and guide them to their target spot. It’s an old idea, seen in many games, so what makes this one stand out? Other than the base mechanics of gems, walls and target spots, new mechanics include colored barriers that only let the same color gem through, one way teleporters, and a helper rock that can either move with the gems or stay in place, like a movable wall.

The gameplay is classic, the mechanics are interesting, and the levels are not that bad. Yet, I think the game is really lackluster, mainly because of terrible QoL, deliberate useless delays, and levels that are more tedious than clever.

From the start, there’s no menu or intro screen, you’re dumped right into the first tutorial level, then the first “temple room”. There’s no exit button, you can only close the game with Alt+F4. The only non-playing screen is a pause/settings/help dialog that shows up when pressing Esc, with a volume slider and a redundant mute toggle, a fullscreen switch and a resolution slider with no labels (which resolution is selected?) and instant change, so using the slider moves the whole thing under the cursor, making it really hard to control. The level select (temple room) is a bad gimmick, in order to open a level you have to actually play the game and maneuver the three gems into the right slot, which could be nice, I’m not against unique, immersive level selects, but it’s more annoying and cumbersome than interesting; trivial to do, but it takes many seconds out of your time when all you want is to play the next level. In a level, there’s no Undo, which is terrible in this type of game, one bad move and you have to either restart the whole thing or replay a lot of moves to get back to the previous state. Once you solve it, there’s a 4 seconds delay until it acknowledges your win, unless you have sound on and notice the congratulatory chime that plays. But between the moment you win and the moment it wipes the level, you can still move around, the first few times it did this I thought the game is broken and wouldn’t accept the solution. Then it starts a slow swipe down of the level, pause, swipe up back to the level select. And once you solve all the levels in a chapter, another slow and long animation happens, and yet another tedious maneuvering to get to the temple exit. I’m an impatient player, don’t waste my time with slow needless animations and interruptions! There’s no chapter select, except for the room selector room that you can reach when exiting the final temple room, and that one is badly done too: you can use it to get back to a previous room, but then you have to navigate through all the temple exits to reach it again.

And I said the level design is “not bad”, but that only covers the actual puzzles to solve, they are quite badly implemented. The game insists on having vertical levels, on a PC! There’s a lot of wasted space, to fit the narrow corridor that’s the actual puzzle, the level is padded with decorations, the elements are too small to properly fit, plus there’s the issue that the game tries to keep it’s pixel graphics crisp, which means that it only supports a few actual resolutions, padding to fit the screen, and on the Steam Deck it only uses 42% (!!!) of the actual screen, the rest is just black empty space. 42%! That makes it hard to see and ugly, on my 4K screen it’s nice and crisp and you can discern what those objects are, but on the Steam Deck it looks like fuzzy blobs of color, and it’s really hard to distinguish which is the gem, which is the target, and which are just colored walls. They’re all tiny blobs of color! And while the levels are unique and somewhat interesting, I prefer tight levels, with clever ideas in just enough space to fit the solution, but here the levels are too big, with plenty of space to just roam around, many of them with multiple solutions. Most of them weren’t clever, but tedious, the solution is obvious, but you have to execute many dozens of moves to move through the long corridors.

I was really looking forward to enjoying this game, but it was a real disappointment. It’s probably too late to fix this game, but a sequel could fix up a lot of the issues and be a success.

[b]How hard is it:[/b] Very easy to easy. Each chapter has 4-6 levels, with the last two a bit more difficult, but none takes more than 10 minutes to crack. I only had a bit of trouble with one level that required some thinking, the rest were just tedious work to move the gems closer to their spots one by one.

[b]How long is it:[/b] 30 levels in 6 chapters, 2-3 hours to finish. All levels in a chapter are unlocked, but opening the exit to the next chapter requires finishing all the levels in the current one.

[b]Level design:[/b] Meh. Good variety, none feels like a filler, but they are bigger than they need to be. I prefer tighter levels, more about thinking than making 100 moves just slowly getting the gems one by one where they need to be, but maybe that's just me.

[b]Quality:[/b] Quite bad. No undo, cumbersome level select without a quick way to open a level or select another chapter. Basic controls, and not rebindable. Barely any settings, and the ones it has are badly implemented. No cloud saving, a few progress achievements. Tedious navigation. No menu screen, no Quit button.

[b]Worth the price:[/b] No.

[b]Most positive aspect for me:[/b] A couple of interesting puzzles in each chapter.

[b]Most negative aspect for me:[/b] No undo.

[b]What would make it better:[/b] Undo! Add a home screen. Add a Quit button. Add a proper chapter select, accessible at all times from the home screen. Either have a plain level select, or make entering a level an actual challenge, right now it’s just tedious. Add a controller mapping for the Steam Deck, and make sure its resolution is properly supported. Make the resolution selection a dropdown menu with a list of supported resolutions, and remove the very low resolutions, the game is really unusable at those. Add cloud saving. Make it fast, shorten a lot all the transitions, and add a visual acknowledgement that the level is solved. Improve the graphics to better differentiate between gems, targets and walls, and between the teleporter entrance and exit.

As for the levels: turn them sideways, this is not a vertical phone game, make use of the longer width. Try to make them tighter, shorten corridors and walls where possible. Add more levels that require more thinking and better planning, the current ones are quite easy to brute force, focusing on one gem at a time. Remove the cruft, it’s OK to have decorations that make it look nicer, but don’t use walls for that.

10 hours into the game, for now, 1 stage away from beating it, I wouldn't recommend this game just yet.
Do I have skill issue? probably to a point, but I do want to share some perspective I've found over time;

The balance is pretty off. is it beatable? I think so. But it requires tremendous amount of luck.
The strategy, concept and story is refreshing, it's different than most Tower Defense games.

First 2-3 stages are fun and you can proceed pretty easily even without too much in-dept strategy. Game gets little complicated and needs much more thinking from stage 4.

From stage 5 though, you start to really need some luck. Because the objective of the stage has random-ness attached to it. Even with strategy you will have hard time getting through the stage. And that's where I have problem with the game and can't recommend it yet until it's been balanced.

Winning conditions in later stages + balance needed :
1. You will need to make sure Adventurer have minimum to no equipment from prior stages. Since equipment + high level adventurer just wipes out all your monsters, leading to no more gold + rolls to build your army to kill the adventurer. Which then he continues to get too strong for you to move on. Even 1 equipment added on top of prior stage equipment can lead to this non-ending cycle, beating this will be possible but very difficult. Equipment is often very pricey, pricey enough where if you were to miss ONE step, the victory is somewhat unattainable. Equipment is also not too strong on it's own, but once stacked, high leveled, angered, it is way too strong for you to recover.

2. Balance the adventurer's level, gear, experience, anger along with your monster placements, level of monster, along with items to maybe, just MAYBE win the stage. You can use strategy to balance all of this. Until you need a totem. which moves around randomly. Along with one of your monsters also moves around randomly. There is possibility to get an item to hold totem still, which is also randomly appears on selection, but requires insane amount of luck to get, which you don't get even through out the whole stage. And it's pricey. By the time you get the move, switch, shield even Rune magnet (totem holder), you may had to sacrifice enough monsters or gold to even strategize after ALMOST getting the win condition.

3. Win condition requirements are random, so you need luck to win. For example, on or after stage 5, you need to create certain monsters to move on. You need lots of Movement cards which doesn't show up easily, it's randomly spawned in selection with low chance. Than you need to hope to get shield, which is also random and hard to get, along with level up potions. Than, if than, you get the monster recipe complete, you still got to throw your hope and dreams in to Luck to even get the winning condition monster in the selection. Complete recipe does not equal complete recipe. You need luck to get the monster you need, and better hope that you have enough roll chances & gold left to get it. Oh by the way, you need to get totem after getting this monster. Which I've explained above how random it is to get the totem.

Final thoughts on strategy :
Most of the problem can be solve with plans and strategy; but without luck you can't really move on. As the stages progresses, these problems just get amplified. If you didn't have enough gold or made a mistake in early stages, adventurer is just too strong due to its equipment, where manageable game-play just becomes too reliant on luck to move on. Which can make you delete the save file and start again fresh, so you can make sure adventurer doesn't get equipment. 

You can buy many movement cards in the store before the stage begins, which you need gold and inventory slots for; which can also be double edge sword because you need gold and empty slots to get certain monsters and items to get winning conditions. And even when you have everything in line, if the game decides not to give you the monster you need on card selection, you are just out of luck. Because even after getting that monster, that monster has to die, which drops totem, the winning condition, which loves to randomly moves around the map. This leads you to needing lots of items and movement cards, even with Totem place holder (Rune magnet, hope you have gold and luck to get it spawned), to get the totem.

You have to balance luck and randomness while trying to prevent the adventurer to get equipment. And I keep emphasizing this because by the time you get recipe to get the monster and totem, the adventurer is already often high level enough to start taking on your strong monsters even without equipment. And let's hope you didn't let him get away with equipment from prior stages.

In conclusion, although there will be people beating this at this stage of development, which I wish I can play that well; But at this time I feel that game-play just relies too heavily in luck for a tower-defense style game. I think with some balance this will be more enjoyable to play.

The concept & story line is great. The strategy of having to balance the Level, Gear, Anger, Tile & placement management to tower-defense is new and refreshing to me personally. And would love to give another go at it later. But after getting stuck on randomness at second to last stage just got me little bit annoyed with game-play.

Tyga is a unique look into an alternate world where capitalism has failed us. I know, I know, you'll have to suspend your disbelief. I mean, raising the prices of a life saving drug by hundreds, even thousands of dollars? Companies having influence over laws and basic human rights? Such a thing would only be possible in a video game, and that's what makes Tyga so great. The radio really helps immerse you into the fictional world of Tyga, it utilizes different radio personalities ranging from engaging to just plain amusing. It's easy to forget you're on the job when the hosts get going, and perhaps that's the point. As the days go on though, you start to realize that there is more to this world than meets the eye. 

I very much enjoyed this game and the atmosphere it created. Though it's a little rough around the edges, you'll find that Tyga is a fun experience that reminds you what happens when greed eclipses community.

This might be okay if the game had an offline mode, but it doesn't. You need to run your computer the entire time the game is running. Worse, the game is a serious resource hog. Due to lack of interaction, lack of player choice, and extremely poor performance I can't recommend this. It might become good but right now it isn't.

One of crew is stressed out on the road, not an a problem we have a 6% chance of getting attacked nothing to worry about a 94% chance of success. Coming from Rack and Slay, this feels like the more skillful, less zany brother of the roguelike/lite pool games. Very clean and well executed, the myriad of trick shots required (or carefully planned power ups, if you're lucky and careful) combined with the random targeting of each card means that there's quite a nice skill ceiling to approach, and I believe this game makes it easy to come back and replay over and over.

A few annoyances/issues:
a) There are a few translation issues; the biggest one is calling the playing cards "Pokers" as if it was a noun, especially as one of the first things the player experiences, did not give me the right first impression, but luckily there's not much text involved. However...
b) I wish there were more/different power ups you could get; it seems like, if you simply play well up to a certain point, you will be able to get the powerups to make all cards in hand the same value and have the same success condition, which you can get down to a two turn cooldown. This is powerful, as the end game conditions can be mighty difficult to achieve; you can always get this by simply playing in a run for long enough. To that end, watering down the powerup pool with different things (hence tempting players/by pure luck, preventing players from just cheesing the end game) would be great. Regardless, it seems that one full run will allow you to get basically all the powerups, which feels a little boring. But the game is like $6 normally, so this would be quite a bit of a stretch anyway.

Otherwise, I think the core of this game is great, and it's worth asking price; at the time of writing, it's on a 50% sale! If you're a 2d pool fan, what are you reading this review for? Go buy this game!

Very neat little metroidvania if you don't mind some very repetitive backtracking due to the lack of markers on the map (Save rooms and Fast Travel rooms are marked though).  Another issue with the map is that it is segmented into different areas, and doesn't show you where and how these connect together.  

I rarely used the fast travel points because whenever I obtained a new ability I needed to re-check every single room, so using the fast travel to skip in and out of areas would have just made that process more confusing.  It would have been nice if ability-gates were marked on the map in this games' case.  I probably had to sweep through most rooms of the game almost 10 times because of this.

When you first start the game it is in portuguese.  You need to select "Opceon" on the title screen and then switch that to english.  Other than that, I didn't really encounter any jank or lack of polish.  1 bug that wasn't a major hindrence.

Combat is very simple.  It might look a little [i]beat 'em up[/i] in the trailer and it has a little bit of that, but mostly handles like any 8-bit platformer, except your swings keep enemies stun-locked.  

You'll acquire new items which boost your stats and level up by killing enemies for EXP, though the choices when you level up felt insignificant.  You'll probably just do as I did and pump the STR stat with maybe a few points into Item Drops.

I was worried I wouldn't like playing something this zoomed in as my experience with games like [b]Deedlit[/b] & [b]Dust: An Elysian Tale[/b] were quite miserable and it was in part due to that.  I was pleasantly surprised with [b]The Throne[/b] though.  Perhaps part of it was the neat visual style, but I also felt areas were interesting enough to keep me captivated.

Music isn't too bad, it helps add flavour to different areas.  If I'm being more critical; the underwater theme, while fitting and a nice change of tune is repetitive.  There's one tune that plays through too large of an area and gets repetitive as a result of this as well.

I think how open you are to repetitive backtracking is going to be the biggest deciding factor on whether this metroidvania is for you.  It feels a tiny bit like [b]Bloodstained: RotN[/b], if it were bite-sized and more retro, without all the cool spells.  I certainly enjoyed my time with it.  In fact I went as far as to 100% it, which I might be the first to do (0.1% achievement).

Exhibition of Speed is the odd case of a game which does hard things well and easy things poorly. The physics engine is clearly the star of the show, and for good reason; even just dragging your vehicle around with the cursor is plenty of fun. However, the game needs a lot of polish. *A lot.* I experienced frequent crashes with the native linux build which were *mostly* remedied by running proton instead. The menus felt sluggish compared to the world view- perhaps some sort of input delay? Unfortunately, my short play session involved little other than confusion. The node-based approach is not unlike a game engine's editor- this is fine, but the quality of life isn't there. For example, the best way to delete a node (at least as far as I can tell) is to click it and press your delete key; there is no delete button on the graphical element. I also could not find a settings menu, which didn't help me find the bind for using a follow cam if it exists at all. I know I have a lot of negative things to say, but the reason I'm bothering to say them is because this game seems like it's developing quickly and could easily become a great experience. For the asking price I really can't complain, especially given the highly technical interface is on full display in the screenshots.

As 3-DOF stereo glasses become mainstream the app is a must have. At the moment of writing required SBS-mode is available with the beta branch (i7-10870H, GTX-1660 it works flawlessly). 
I'm amazed by the amount of details contained in old scanned photographs. In addition to recognizing a particular remembered moment, I'm getting access to it's spatial constituents like rooms, tables, bodies, clothing which turns up my 'associative engine' the way flat pictures never did. 
The app also altered the way I interact with visual novels. I used to pay too much attention to text, but now when it's artistic surrounding literally pops out, it certainly gets its fair share of eye-time.
At the moment I run it on my gaming rig, but hopefully given that glasses won't actually require rendering large FOV and my primary use case is in static or artistically animated low FPS content a mini-PC or a laptop with decent integrated graphics (like radeon 680m) could provide for much more flexible scenario of use.

Anyway, Bauhaus Bonk is a one button game about controlling a constantly-spinning line by pressing a button to swap its pivot point, and your goal is to get to the exit of each level without bonking into anything. Sounds easy, but this game actually gets pretty tricky with some of its later levels, especially while attempting to gather all the collectables in each level! There's also various items to keep in mind, from colored eyes to change the color of the background (thus letting you move through walls of that color) to the dots that speed up or slow down your line, and even the ability to phase through walls. These, combined with levels that test your timing, precision, routing, etc. makes for a pretty engaging game!

Other than occasionally bonking into walls, you'll also be experiencing the "Bauhaus" part of Bauhaus Bonk with its visuals! Pretty sleek and abstract UI and levels, with the latter being shown off in a zoomed out view and within an art frame until you make your first move and start the level. Charming stuffs! The swing bop music is a nice fit too (and I've got one of the songs from the game stuck in my head as I write this review (specifically "Mr. Bonk"), aaaaaaaa)! Lastly, I wanna mention that it's cool that there's multiple leaderboards for every level! You can try to get to the end as fast as possible and/or factor in fewest amount of button presses taken and collecting all the collectables!

Bauhaus Bonk's a simple, tricky, and fun game! I imagine that it'll be a neat title for peeps that enjoy speedrunning, or perhaps it may turn you into a speedrunner yourself as you aim for better ranks/leaderboard positions. Perhaps you're a Kuru Kuru Kururin/Roundabout/Hyphen fan and wanna get in on some more stick-spinning action (even if the gameplay's different here). Or maybe you wanna see art come to life and traverse around it! Either way, this game's worth checking out!

Echoes of Mars is a lane-based tower defence game, think Plants vs Zombies. The first few stages have an interesting mechanic where structures are damaged by time and need repair, even without alien inflicted damage. This gives the resource management decision of choosing between build more or maintain existing.

After a few levels, you get access to newer structures that do not self-damage and the resource management comes a lot simpler.

The aliens you face don't really offer much variation between days (waves / rounds / levels), and the tower placement doesn't matter that much. As long as you have 5 generators and a few lowers in each lane, you'll have more resource than you can spend and end up spectating more than playing.

If the developer keeps working and changes up a few things, this could be a good casual tower defence game.
It’s worth turning off the in-game sounds and music, and sticking an album or podcast on to keep you company through the 50 levels.

A pensive, introspective, contemplative jaunt.

This is effectively a story about hyperrealities and odd human connections. It could be allegorical for many different things, depending on your mood, but that is at least the core. It's definitely an interesting thing, if a bit abstract. Moonless Moon does have a lot of style though. It has a very quizzical and philosophical vibe, detailing the odd experiences of the protagonist in her ability to move between worlds, and the small connections so made along the way. It broaches these topics more like a puzzling curiosity rather than a true story or philosophical discussion. Almost like the story itself, you're dipping your toe into this world however briefly, and it feels almost fleeting by design.

The actual design of the VN is also quite stylish backgrounds feature a bit of camera wobble and blur effects. The music is also quite nice, slow, contemplative, and chill, great for some proper mulling. There are even a few animated music videos, and while they're generally simple, they're fun to see, and give a nice book-ending to each arc of the story.

That being said, there are problems. Firstly, let's be blunt, the story is almost too vague. While I appreciated my time with it, because the story is so aloof and uncaring, it can seem a bit distant. Usually when a story covers abstract concepts - hyperrealities being at the top of that list - it usually grounds the imagery and allegories in concrete fundamentals so that the reader can understand them. But the protagonist themself doesn't truly understand this concept, and it seems like the game is disinterested in elaborating. Because of this, much of the story can feel obtuse, like it's broaching an interesting topic that ends right before you gather the point. It can leave you feeling wanting, almost as if the game had no point. Maybe that is the point: that our experiences are fleeting and that it's fine not to linger or think too deeply. But that seems a bit crass, and I don't like that interpretation, so for me, I was left wishing for something a little more.

There's also the "side-stories." The core story is between the main girls on the cover art, but there are a couple stories off to the side in different scenes. But the characters in these scenes aren't really relevant to the plot, and the ideas explored in the scene are generally extraneous to the main points the story is trying to get at, beyond sharing philosophies. That can make these portions feel like padding. While I don't think they are in themselves bad, I don't feel like they add much to the experience.

Then there's the design choices. All the characters only have one art-piece. They don't have reaction images and don't change design at all. What you see is what you get! And while the character designs are good, it's hard to take away the thought that you're just staring at some non-reactive PNGs. There's also the "riddle" segments. These segments have you looking for keywords in presented sentences, and then filling in the blanks of a sentence the game has provided you for solving. However, this doesn't really add anything to the experience. It was a nice change of pace from reading, but the mechanics of the riddles are very simple, and it doesn't feel like these were needed or relevant.

All in all, for something melancholic and meditative, this isn't so bad. It has a lot going for it. But just as this game alludes to fleeting worlds, this feels like a world I won't think on for too long. I was glad to explore it for the time it offered, but I have little reason to linger, preferring to visit other more complex, more interesting worlds elsewhere.

The game takes clues from classic action platformers on the NES. It's on the shorter end length-wise, being completable in an hour or so. You have infinite lives and checkpoints are dispersed at relatively reasonable intervals.

There's no options to speak of. The game starts windowed and you can change it to full screen. Controller supports works fine.

[h2]Controls[/h2]

Movement can feel sluggish. Especially initially the character can feel 'sticky' to control. It seems some inputs prevent other actions from being made, which might be caused by a lack of input buffering

For example, it can be difficult to perform a jump directly followed a landing crouched attack. If you try to inch yourself forward, you'll note that you're instead clearly forced to take a few steps forward. You seem to be locked into that running state, where it can even be difficult to crouch out of it at moment's notice - rather, you need to be in the particular part of the running animation to be able to cancel out of it. It's almost reminiscent of games with rotoscoped animations, where movement is extremely sluggish with overly detailed animations you can't cancel.

Your attacks have a pre-attack wind-up time as well as an attack delay after each. This can make swinging your weapon multiple times rather unsatisfactory and generally create a sense of slight unresponsiveness which is especially notable while doing air attacks.

It's as if you're playing with slight input delay so you can get used to it even if it doesn't feel great.

The sluggishness of attacking made me prefer jumping over enemies since it felt more responsive. It's unclear if this is intended as a tactic - albeit practically nonviable for certain stages, in others it felt like it might have undermined their difficulty since they mostly just consistent long lines of multihit enemies. This jumping tactic wasn't discouraged by any in-game mechanics, since enemies don't ever drop any pickups and there are no score points.

[h2]Inspirations?[/h2]

If you're looking for a Ninja Gaiden 1 NES type of experience, this isn't exaclty it - even though on the surface it can look similar due to movement, pick-ups, and such being familiar.

Given the numerous Castlevania 1 NES callbacks, the game seemed to try to position itself as a mechanical hybrid between Ninja Gaiden 1 and Castlevania 1. Namely, that the main character has capabilities similar to Ryu, but with some limitations of Simon. The issue to me seems to be that the delays of Simon's attacks feel perfectly in-tune with the weapon there being a whip; you throw the whip back before lashing it forward. The clear build-up and weight of the keyframes sells the attack process perfectly. When those delays are instead used for a quick katana slash, the animation isn't justifying it to the player.

I would have experimented with making the attack animation more pronounced, with greater emphasis on unsheathing and re-sheating as well as a clear 'pre-charging' state [i](ie. purely nonmechanical changes)[/i] - rather than keeping the subdued Ninja Gaiden quick slash.

[h2]Levels[/h2]

Stages are paced by the several checkpoints in them. Each checkpoint saves your current HP as you reach them and after dying you will be returned to the checkpoint with that saved HP amount. This means you can get yourself into an awkward position where you are one hit away from death and be forced to go through a gruelling gauntlet until you reach that next checkpoint. I think it would have made sense to have each checkpoint restore at least few points of HP before saving that HP value.

Stages involve few side routes you can take through them but they are barely worth mentioning. That aside, the actual stage design with the obstacles and enemy placements are probably the strongest aspect of design here. They for me were adequate enough to carry me through the whole game to its completion.

The infinite lives + all the checkpoints give a lot leeway here. While this makes it easier to push through whatever sketchy balancing present - it steers the game away from true retro-console / arcade experience and kinda gives me the sense of some lack of confidence in the level design [i](or perhaps the game overall)[/i], which to be fair might have been warranted in the sense that the game doesn't exactly feel finished as a development project.

I would say the level design has just enough 'unfairness' to keep it spicy enough to keep you interested. Pacing I suppose could have been better [i](say, some more natural times for player to 'breathe' from the intensity)[/i] and the limited enemy variance obviously limits design.

There's a later maze level that can create a sense dread considering just how terrifying these type of levels often tended to be in old-school games, but some rather clever design twist here makes it so that you certainly won't be dreading the labyrinth aspect of it that much once you have figured it out.

[h2]Boss design[/h2]

The bosses are perhaps the weakest part of the game's design - they barely feel like bosses at all and rather seem like they're just chilling around. They don't have any kind of an intro - they don't jump out of anywhere or awake in any manner but rather are already just walking around when you reach them. There isn't any type of a music change either, so at times you aren't even sure if the new creature you are slashing at is a boss at all.

Some of them can be defeated extremely quickly and with little effort - to the point where they don't even have time to attack you properly. The bosses don't seem to get particularly more difficult as you progress through to later stages, which can make them feel very disappointing mechanically instead of a climax to the stage.

[h2]Music[/h2]

It's bad and not easy on the ears - harsh, coarse and monotone. Often stage tracks give the sense of being a short loop even though they aren't because of just how repetitive they are.

As far as I could tell, the soundtrack in the trailer doesn't even appear in-game, not in any of the stages at least. I was hoping the game would have had music more in that vein in-game, but that regrettably wasn't the case.

[h2]Parting thoughts[/h2]

I got the sense of an awkward mix of retro and modern design elements, which are hard to pinpoint to any one particular aspect.

The game didn't feel to be particularly brim with creativity, with for example enemies being the likes of random animals [i](rabbits, rats, bats, etc)[/i], some animated plant life, and the usual demons and undead. With that and other factors such as backgrounds being mostly just solid blacks, the game gives a sense of being more of a well-honed prototype rather a truly finished game. For one, the game window's name seem to be "New Project", which is worth a chuckle. Bosses perpetuate this prototype-vibe perhaps the most due to feeling so nonchalant and like an afterthought as far as their presentation goes and just how easy they are to defeat.

As far as the story goes, I had to really think if there was any. I do faintly recall some sort of a starting cinematic that was so generic with some talk about a demon king that I think I spaced out. After that, I don't recall there being any references to a story. You got the classic Castlevania 1 NES -esque stage transition screens between each level but those don't give much of a narrrative.

On the pricing front, I got the game for some 4 bucks. I was rather trepid about purchasing it since it to me seemed more like a 2,5$ game that I would expect to being sale for around 2 dollars. This perception was only confirmed after having compleated it but since these type of games are up my alley, I wasn't bothered about getting it for that price.

I give it a lukewarm recommendation, since even though I feel it's slightly overpriced, the game was interesting enough to complete and there weren't any major hiccups - like I don't think I encountered any bugs whatsoever.

I do not like giving negative reviews, but given the technology behind this, its deserved. First off, its a very short story, my 31 minutes includes 8 minutes of the game, when I was called away from the computer and exited the game. There is no pause or save system, so i had to start again.
Its basically an artificial voice reading a story that sounds like the outline for a movie or a book. The characters are not fleshed out though some are named, and their activities are simply a case of "they did this", "they did that", "they knew this", they felt that". There is no tension to the story either in the narrative, or the voice narrating it. Its totally neutral. It certainly would not keep a young child happy if it was a bedtime story!
The final straw was when I had finished I was offered the option of starting over or leaving, and the quit button didn't work.
The art work is about what you expect, slightly distorted figures trooping through an undefined environment. More experienced gamers than I could probably name the games where these figures originated.
Its the second AI game I have played this month and has the same problem as the first. Its not convincing! There is no world in which to immerse yourself, no characters  to become interested in, and a rather boring story that has no details of the adventures the characters experience. Throw in the lack of a pause button or save, and you are stuck on your computer for the 25 minutes or so that it takes the AI voice to work its way through the story in a voice that lacks the subtle expressions and variations found in the voice of a human reader.
AI still has a long way to go before it can successfully take over the job of game creators.

There are plenty of visual novels out there about love or romance but I felt this one with sincerity. Even though the story implies that you are trading your heart to have everyone else’s, they didn’t turn this game into an opportunity to build a harem or appeal to sexuality to gain an audience. I'm not saying that I don't support polyamory and I'm not shaming one's sexual nature. After all, I'm a woman of my own wiles. What I am trying to say is that we have plenty of visual novels that cater to those preferences. It isn't easy for me to enjoy romance games because some can make me feel like I'm about to experience something comparable to a reality show, choosing between a bunch of people in a televised drama. Rather, this visual novel seemed to have us ask about who pays the price for the exchange our main character makes with the witch, what love is and how others define it from their own point of view. For me, it was also about how to love someone the way they deserve rather than how you might have wanted to love them or how you might have wanted them to love you.

The art is charming and unique in its own right. You know, too much color in my life usually causes me to quietly and internally spiral from over-stimulation to my eyes, but the pastels were so easy to look upon and scene transitions felt smooth. As for the story, the dialogue felt natural to read, even though the theme is fantasy. I never felt like there was too much information in the character backgrounds that could take us away from the main story, and I also never felt like I was left with questions about holes. I believe that you gain just enough insight about the main character to understand the life she lived. The music was fitting for the visuals presented; dreamy, eerie, pensive, serene. I couldn’t agree more with these sounds since even though the art is quite flowery, the theme should still be heavy to some degree in knowingly manipulating people’s lives.

I know that there are multiple pathways you can take to get the achievements, but I have to say that I wouldn’t change a thing from my first play-through. I tried to be as authentic as I could with my choices. Although perhaps I will go back later to appreciate the other outcomes that show us the consequences of one’s actions. Besides, I really did enjoy the art of this game and I’m sure I’ll like to see the other perspectives that other people could have made that would have differed from my own.

I noticed that the credits mention inspiration drawn from Hans Christian Anderson’s version– and original story– of The Little Mermaid. I’ve been grabbed by the heartstrings upon learning this because it was– and still is– one of my all time favorites. Though this game did not tell us that tale, the essence of sacrifices made for love ring the same. In this story, I sense the vulnerability of the other characters affected in the main character’s web that she hasn’t fully understood the weight of them being in, but you are left with the ability to help her see it through. Thank you, to the creators, for sharing this with us because I think I learned a little something about myself, too.

Somnifuge is a very unique, gritty, PSX inspired horror game. It’s not really survival horror, more of a psychological horror game with lots of puzzles, but it does have a survival horror “vibe”.

I was very excited for it, having played the demo only a week prior. It immediately reminded me of The Tartarus Key, another game that feels like survival horror despite being only puzzles. And to an extent that’s what I got, though I would say it’s a little more rough around the edges and WAY more “out there”.

The puzzles are good but sorta a mixed bag, generally challenging and fun but some feel a bit clunky. There’s no map, so sometimes navigating the mansion and the other ever changing environments was disorienting (and a little tedious). Often it’s intentional - the game definitely loves to disorient you and catch you off guard. But I think more often than not it was well designed, and definitely interesting.

The game had a very dream-like surreal logic to it. It kinda just went wherever it felt like. No clue what anything meant or what the context is, but it was certainly entertaining. If I had my way, I would’ve loved a bit more focus on puzzles (sometimes it felt a bit walking sim-esque), some polish and refinement, and a map. But it’s a unique game and anyone that likes dream-like psychological horror puzzle games DRIPPING in 90’s survival horror aesthetic - don’t miss this one.

A fun and unique take on roguelike deckbuilders.
It was a little tricky to pick up at first but once I understood the mechanics I enjoyed my time with it.
The idea of moving around on a grid and only getting to play one card a turn is an interesting one, and it makes it so battles feel more like puzzles to be solved than fights to win.
I also like that you can trick enemies into attacking each other which adds another layer of strategy to moving around the grid.
It was a little difficult at first but once you begin to learn enemy patterns and how to manipulate them into doing what you want enemies that used to seem tough become a lot more manageable.
There are a lot of different cards to get, and figuring out how best to use them and when can be a fun challenge. Some cards can feel a little weak but some other stronger ones will carry you a long way in the game so it balances out a bit.
My only real complaint is that you can sometimes get stuck in fights that are both impossible to win but also that you can keep yourself alive forever in too, usually the fights where enemies can either regenerate health or create new enemies. While these can sometimes be fun puzzles to solve sometimes you don't have the right cards to win and get stuck in an infinite loop, and personally I'd rather have the monster kill me and end the run than be stuck trading blows forever.
Overall though a fun and unique little game worth trying out! If you’ve enjoyed other roguelike deckbuilders and want to give something new a try then give Nunna a go.
