I am very positively surprised by this. If you are into Lovecrafts writing/world (especially the fantasy-style stories such as "Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath"... these kind of stories have not been adapted often into other media AFAIK), if you love classic RPGs such as the old Ultima games from the 80s or don't mind or even enjoy the graphic style, this is quite fascinating. I understand that the graphics may be off-putting to some, but if you care more about the content of the game, no matter what it looks like, this has a lot to offer already, even though it's still very much in early access.

The atmosphere is mesmerizing. You start off, knowing nothing about this world. You will encounter different inhabitants... some will tell you more, others will be hostile. You may die a couple of times until you improve your stats, get better gear, get some allies which can fight for you or simply understand what fights to avoid. 

I love how the game switches from top-down view (overworld) to first person (dungeons), just like games such as Ultima I. The low quality, pixelated graphics IMO add to the atmosphere... that old school, dark vibe, especially in the first person view in dungeons. It reminds me of watching old horror movies, such as the original Nosferatu. That movie is very well done, but the low quality (caused by the cameras/tapes/lighting available at the time) make it even more atmospheric and captivating, creating more of a dark, sinister atmosphere. Again, ymmv. 

Another comparison that came up while playing this were the fan-made movies "Call of Cthulhu" and "The Whisperer in Darkness"... some heart-felt fan-made productions that were supposed to look as much as possible like movies that could have come out by the time HPL was still alive, like something you'd have seen at a movie theatre in Providence/RI. CoC was a black and white silent movie, using stop motion and it really did have the vibe of classic movies from that era. I am not saying that "Cyclopean" looks like a video game that Lovecraft could have played in the 1930s (LOL), but my point is that the look/style of the game fits the atmosphere and source material quite well IMO. 

The ingame manual will give you some helpful advice. I recommend to dive right in, check the manual and start exploring. Once you get a feel for the game, play around more with rerolling the stats when creating a new character, as you may understand better what stats are desirable/useful for the way you want to play. 

I tried the demo (which eventually will prevent you from leveling up more, yet will give you a good chance to find out whether this game is for you) and soon was captivated, trying different paths, grinding xp for a bit, slowly exploring the dungeons (which have an automapping feature). 

And I have to say that SOMEHOW, this game really hits a weak spot for me, keeping me engaged where many other "Lovecraftian" games fail. Just like with the movies, it seems to be tough to adapt HPLs concepts and stories for a big screen. It's not about a hero in shining armor meleeing an Old God. Sanity, the feeling of being powerless, feeling overwhelmed by the sheer knowledge or presence of the enemy, these are keypoints, and putting that into a game is difficult. 

This small indie game managed to draw me into a world I wasn't too familar with (because the "fantasy themes/stories" HPL wrote were never as enjoyable for me as his more well-known stories set in "our world"), and I am carefully exploring it more and more, always being prepared to run, being quite fascinated by a strange world. 

There are still some technical issues and small bugs, which is to be expected from a game in EA. However, the developer is quite responsive, offering help, fixing bugs, and I am very much looking forward to seeing how this game will develop and grow. 

Just for context, I did play games such as Ultima IV, V and VI back when they came out. Therefore, this game also triggers quite some nostalgia. Since I know these games well, jumping into this game with its old-school artstyle is easy. After all, back then, with the graphical capabilities of systems like the C64 and the way games looked, your mind would be quite active, filling in the gaps, turning the rather crude graphics into a more detailed world you could immerse yourself in. I replayed Ultima I and IV about 2 years ago, and it still worked like a charm with them... and works like a charm with this one. 

So - if you want to try a different take on HPLs stories, if you grew up playing classic RPGs and don't mind the graphic style (or even enjoy it... after all, games like Skald were quite popular, offering old-school graphics as well), try the demo and considering the price of this game, it should be a no-brainer if you enjoy that demo.

Catalyst is an indie rogue-like twin-stick shooter with an intriguing focus on chemistry and alchemy. Much like similar twin-stick shooters, from Smash TV to 20 Minutes Till Dawn, the objective of this game is to survive wave after wave of enemies by shooting them down whilst, at the same time, avoiding their attacks.

At the start of each run, you begin with a basic "Vis" potion with infinite ammo to throw at enemies. As you defeat various enemies and gather ingredients (e.g. carbon, hydrogen, gold, etc.), you can use said resources to craft new potions and ammo. You can also spend gathered gold and "Vis" to purchase magic scrolls, charms and talismans to improve your odds of survival.

This game features a remarkably flexible crafting system which allows you to easily use and balance your resources between waves on a single run. For example, you can spend gathered ingredients to heal yourself or accumulate "Vis" to spend on new scrolls, potions and charms.

So far, my favourite aspects of this game are its alchemy-based themes and its soundtrack composed by Cochu, a video game music remixer whom is best known for her Splatoon music mashups. This game's electronic drum-and-bass soundtrack is delightfully atmospheric and intensifies as you progress through your run.

Alas, this game is far from perfect. In my experience, its biggest weakness is a game-breaking bug which prevents me from reloading potions. There was one time when I was reloading before the end of a wave. But, as soon as said wave ended, the reload timer had frozen and I became unable to reload special potions until the run was over. If anything, this encouraged me to attempt a Vis-only run in which I was ultimately overrun by ravenous enemies halfway through.

All in all, if you're looking for a simple and quirky rogue-like twin-stick shooter with intuitive crafting and alchemic fantasy vibes, Catamyst may be the game for you.

Fears to Fathom – Woodbury Getaway is easily the best installment in the series. What starts as a trip with college friends after graduation quickly becomes a tense struggle for survival when one particularly annoying character starts following you around, potentially getting you stuck and forcing you to reset your progress. Despite this challenge, the story is highly believable, and it had me racing to find safety.

The game strikes a great balance between suspense and lighter moments, with activities like fishing, petting a cat, and even dunking on a hoop like Kobe. These moments of levity make the overall experience all the more enjoyable. Overall, Woodbury Getaway is a thrilling, immersive ride, and I highly recommend it for anyone looking for a memorable horror experience.

I mean what can I say, it is another "Fears to Fathom" game. The gameplay here is pretty minimal, but that does not mean it is bad. You essentially just walk around and interact with a few objects or NPCs until you hit the next trigger to advance the story. But this is not bad, it makes you feel like a regular person and not some insane protagonist that can take down an entire army by themselves. You feel helpless, which is a great thing for horror games.

The ambiance and suspense do make you feel on edge, especially when you are alone and you have no idea what is gonna happen, who is after you and where they could be at the moment.
The games follow a structure of slowly building up suspense just to accelerate up to 150km/h right at the end. The stories in these games are really interesting, as they are "being told" as you play. Every game is completely different in the story as they are from people sending their stories to the devs as well as some from Reddit if I remember correctly.
The voice acting is a great addition, so are the absurd TV commercials / programs, a very nice touch!

Something I disliked about this game was the lack of a ESC menu, it really sucks that I seemingly have to Alt F4 the game just to change graphics settings, change the volume, load a different save/state of the game or even just go back to the main menu to quit. I know these games are supposed to be played in one sitting but I am talking about replaying it for achievements or just for the sake of replaying it.
But this seems to be a thing that all of the Fears to Fathom games lack.
Something I wish was toggle-able was the film grain and chromatic aberration, but you can't. This is a issue for recording / streaming this game as all this grain applied to the camera can reduce bitrate.
I do want to mention that you can disable Toilet and Eating noises, which is good. However for the eating ones they do not apply to the Pizza in Mo's.. and that is really uncomfortable for me, to the point where I had to remove my headphones to get past this scene.

Another thing that I definitely need to mention is the performance.
Performance on the Intel Arc A750 is spotty, I feel like the game does not unload assets in the distance and that puts a toll on the Intel GPU, for example walking back from the Fishing I got a whopping 22 FPS looking back at the house, I do not know why, maybe the road and all the buildings just does not unload but yeah that does not make for a great experience when the FPS goes from 80 or 90 to 22.
This could very well just be an Intel Arc issue, I do have an AMD and NVIDIA GPU on hand so I will most likely try those two and compare how the performance differs.

There were a lot of "Mixed" opinions in this review, but I do genuinely like this game. Despite the things I listed, I still think it deserves a thumbs up because those games are really good at what they do.

[h1]tiny CATS HAS A BIG ENTERTAINMENT FACTOR 🎰[/h1]
I love cat-searching games that have features other than just clicking on cats. Tiny Cats caught me off guard with an adorable magical storyline and some really entertaining features that set it apart from the average cat-clicking games!
 
A young girl inherits her recently departed Aunt's house, but she quickly learns that the house is slightly haunted...by the spirits of hundreds of adorable magical cats! She is determined to find, save, and purify the spirits of her Aunt's beloved cats, one room at a time.
 
As you progress, journal entries magically appear in a Diary. These entries slowly piece together the story, as well as vital clues of items to look for, such as a Letter, a Crystal Ball, or a fallen book.
 
There are cats everywhere; some are just hanging out in the open, some are cleverly hidden in or behind other items, and some are simply invisible! These spirits can only be seen when your magic wand cursor hovers over a spirit's hiding place. Spoiler:🐾[spoiler]keep your eye out for suspicious pawprints[/spoiler] 
 
Once you have located the object/clue, a secret entranceway will be revealed. You will eventually unlock the Attic, the Laboratory, the Apothecary, the Library, the Reading Room, the Bedroom, the Closet, the Kitchen, the Crystal Room, the Greenhouse, the Garden, and the Pantry, each packed with adorable cat spirits.
 
If you are looking for a cat-searching game that has something more to offer than just clicking on cats, look no further. Tiny Cats is a surprisingly fun game with adorable cats and a cute little story.

[h1][b][u]WARNING: AVOID THIS CASH GRAB[/u][/b][/h1]
Barely even qualify as a game. It costs 40$ but isn't even worth a single 1$.

[h3][b][u]TLDR[/u][/b][/h3]
Horrible gameplay full of major problems, invisible walls everywhere, map holes causing soft-locks, broken enemy AI. Gameplay is boring, uninteresting and repetitive. Gunplay is clunky and unsatisfying, with bullets lacking any impact or feedback. Movement feels slippery and unresponsive, with unnatural delays and jarring camera transitions. Accessibility is nonexistent, rough head bobbing that can't be turned off, causing motion sickness. Graphics are ugly and severely unoptimized. The bare minimum for a working game is missing, settings reset every time you launch the game. Don't listen to positive reviews, they are friends with the creators.


[hr][/hr]

[h3][b][u]ACCESSIBILITY ISSUES[/u][/b][/h3]
- There is a constant head bobbing while you move, and there is NO option to deactivate it. It wouldn't be that bad if the head bobbing wasn't horribly rough and prone to motion sickness.
- Get blasted by excessively loud sound effects when you open the game.
- Volume mixing of different sound sources is very bad. You can barely hear the cinematic, while you get blasted in the main menu. Some sound effects are excessively loud compare to other sound effects.
- The settings do NOT save when you exit the game, meaning you need to remake them every time you launch the game. It also means that you get blasted with very loud noise every time you launch the game.
- In the settings menu, you can't tell if the ON/OFF options are in the ON or OFF state. Clicking on the word ON to make sure it is activated doesn't solve the issue, as it just toggle between ON and OFF no matter what word you click.
- In the settings menu, lowering the volume settings to 5% only make the sound half as loud.
- The game is shockingly unoptimized and lacks basic optimization features and settings. The quality setting seems to only reduce texture resolution, but that's it. The game visuals are horrible by default anyway.

[h3][b][u]CHARACTER MOVEMENT AND CONTROL ISSUES[/u][/b][/h3]
- The character moves like it was on ice, while actually being on grass/dirt (high deceleration time). Feels very unnatural, janky, and the opposite of snappy.
- When you change direction, there is a very annoying and unnatural delay.
- Character momentum is locked in 8 directions (forward, backward, left, right, diagonal) and the transition between directions is delayed and confusing.
- When you aim, the camera zooms in, but there is no zoom transition, the camera just teleports closer (or the FOV is reduced instantaneously).
- Character momentum is camera based instead of character based, meaning that can you transform your forward momentum in side momentum by rotating the camera instantaneously (keep in mind that you are basically moving on ice). As opposed to that, when you try to change direction using the keyboard, there is a very long delay, and it feels very janky and inconsistent.
- While walking and running animations are passable, but transitions between them are jarring and lack fluidity
- The default X and Y sensitivities are too high, making aiming and movement feel erratic. Even when adjusted, the controls remain unresponsive and imprecise (similar to the volume setting problem).

[h3][b][u]GAMEPLAY ISSUES[/u][/b][/h3]
- Gunplay is abysmal, as bullets feel completely weightless and lack any sense of impact. Shooting robots and animals provides no feedback, making combat utterly unsatisfying. Enemies don't react realistically to being hit, making it feel like you're shooting at mannequins.
- The game’s loot system is lazy and immersion-breaking. For example, looting dead animals inexplicably gives you items like laser rifles and ores.
- The game is littered with invisible walls that make exploration feel restrictive and cheap. Instead of designing natural boundaries, the game relies on this lazy approach to block player progression.
- Falling into one of the many map holes leaves you stuck indefinitely, forcing a complete restart of the game.
- Tedious and uninspired resource gathering. "Mining" is nothing more than picking up ores scattered around. There is no actual mining mechanic—just walking around collecting items like iron ore, which becomes monotonous almost immediately.
- The enemies are some of the worst AI implementations possible. For instance, enemies often get stuck on terrain or fail to react to the player’s presence entirely. Combat against them feels dull and broken.
- Animations throughout the game are poorly executed.
- The user interface is clunky and unintuitive, making simple actions like navigation and understanding the game’s mechanics unnecessarily difficult.
- Any progress made in the world is lost if you die or get soft-locked, which actively punishes players for exploring or taking risks, as you can only save your progress inside the spaceship.

Murky Divers is a finely polished game, and it is fun for about 2-4 hours, but fails in many core aspects.

-Gameplay loop is as follows: Navigate to a site, swim through the site looking for items and avoiding the countless monsters/traps, tediously swimming back and forth from the sub, and managing your oxygen during the 8-minute time limit; repeat.
-Sub management. This is actually one of the strongest aspects of the game, 2 player sub is alright, 4 player sub is fun, but the 8 player sub is where it's at. Most of the fun come from the people you play with, each person having a role on the sub is really neat, but can fall apart very quickly with even just one person not participating.
-Movement is awful. Spamming/Timing space to move 'somewhat' faster is frustrating. Adding a Hold option would alleviate this immensely.
-Monsters are annoying. There's a small variety to them; which wouldn't be a problem but WAY too many show up at once. Most monsters don't have gimmicks, they either damage you or exist to annoy you.
-Scare factor/Horror. Adding onto the above point; Monsters show up way too often and you know exactly where they are because they are constantly making noise; completely negating ANY sense of surprise.
-Difficulty. Everything's fine if you have a perfect team and play near-perfectly. There's no room for fun 'bits' or any sort of screw-up. if someone dies and they aren't recovered or if you don't recover enough parts, it adds to the near-permanent 'Wanted' meter which causes you to entirely reset if it fills up. it can be reduced slightly for a large sum of money, but in the end it's just not worth it due to the high cost.
-inventory. Holding two items (one in storage and one in hand) is another part of the larger issue. it can be amended with the shopping cart, but you sacrifice the mobility of using other items. 

Notes:
-I've only ever gotten as low as depth 4 so some issues may be rectified with a good team, however every depth seems roughly the same, more items, more monsters. 
I'm hopeful mod support will help with replayability, but for now I do not recommend it.

It's an underwater Lethal Company with an engaging sub management added on. Imagine if in Lethal Company you actually get to fly your ship from location to location and doing so is it's own minigame. Each player takes on a role in the ship, sorta like a "Barotrauma" lite if you're familiar. My crew was 4 players, one to manage sonar, one to steer, one to read the sonar pulses, and the captain/jack of all trades person.

Your goal is to navigate to each objective, along the way avoiding sea monsters, the police, and collecting any salvage you come across for bonus points. When arriving at an objective this is where the lethal company aspects come in. You disembark off the ship and explore the site to secure and destroy evidence.

You will find monsters, and lots of them, but this is where the game falters heavily. The monsters, aren't that great. They can be spooky if you get caught off guard, but all they do is swim at you and hit you. There's no gimmick for each one with their own rules and so forth. Just dodge them/run away, or if you have a stun baton, beat the heck out of them.

My crew was pretty reliable, so handling these critters were super easy. Which in the end made the game not scary at all.

If you have thalassophobia then this game might be terrifying, but for me and my buds, not so much. However, I'd still recommend this game. Managing the sub with breaks of exploring beautifully made levels with a rare fright sprinkled in still made this quite enjoyable.

I've fallen into the habit of playing the daily puzzles before I go to bed, to send me off to sleep - I start with the hard puzzle and then drift down through medium and easy.  It's a lovely, calming, charming game that will sing soothing tones into your ear as you wind down for the day.

Which isn't to say that it's easy!  I'm 20 hours in, and some of them have required much concerted brainpower.  But I get there in the end, and the process is endlessly relaxing.  The nurikabe format is a wonderful ruleset, and this is a wonderful implementation of it.

The artstyle for this game is simply beautiful. Very relaxing and seeing the islands fill in when you finish them is immensely satisfying. The campaign levels are very nicely constructed and are great at teaching basic nurikabe techniques. I do wish some more advanced solving techniques were explored in the later levels, but still a ton of good content. The game does seem more targeted to beginners (which is probably the right choice). Plus there's daily puzzles, an endless puzzle generator, and support for custom puzzles too. If you like Nurikabe or other Nikoli-style puzzles, or are curious about them, I'd definitely give this a shot!

I've been eagerly waiting for this game to drop since adding it to my wishlist last spring. My disappointment is immeasurable and my day is ruined...

That's a little dramatic, but I wouldn't recommend Grandpa High On Retro at this point. With the amount of bugs, glitches, and performance issues, it feels like this is a beta build of the game at best. 

Using a relatively high spec machine (4080S/9900x/32gb ddr5) I get roughly 40fps at 1440p after a few minutes. I restarted the game a couple of times because early in the first chapter when reaching the drug store the game will start running 2 cut scenes at once and skip a decent amount of the game that I can't even decipher what happened. Health packs don't work and the aiming reticle has a seizure when taking fire (I would expect flinch when getting shot, but sheesh), making the gunplay feel sloppy.

For all that is wrong with the game on release, I can say the dialogue carries a level of humor that resonates well. Some people may not find it all that funny, but it is a goofy game. I am a little unsure if the voice acting was recorded or if it's AI generated (yikes), but in an odd way I feel like there's some love here. The premise of the game is unique and something I actually want to get through. 

I was not expecting a game of the year candidate here, but for the fact it has been delayed a few times it would've been nice to have a polished product on release. I don't think this game is a lost cause or that the developer (I think solo dev) didn't try their best. I am hopeful that Grandpa High On Retro is supported into the future and patched! I think it's a funny, quippy game that isn't priced terribly, but needs fixing before I can recommend it.

Edit: Game took a smidge under 1 hour to complete. It bugged to where I couldn't pick up ammo or health, so I ran and made it to the end eventually. Will revisit post patch.

Edit 2: The most recent patch has fixed the bug where chapter 1 cutscenes run simultaneously (I think there is an abrupt transition by design, still a bit confusing) and the issuer picking up ammo/health. However, performance issues are still there.

The PSX visual style is something that I always gravitate towards and the trailer made the shooting look fun so it seemed like a no brainer to pick up. After playing through everything I just feel meh, no negative or really positive so I guess I'll just discuss below some things I liked/disliked;

[EDIT: Since Ashnell has asked me to replay the game I will have some of my opinions below updated for update 1.05] - February 13th, 2025 (Original Review; February 11th, 2025.)

[b] + = Positive. - = Negative. -/+ = Mixed. [/b]

+:The PSX visual style is something I really dig. Just something you either already like or dislike.

-/+: The gameplay itself actually feels fine, you get to roll around and shoot everything with ease but the AI is pretty dumb so most gunfights don't feel exciting until the very end of the game. [Update 1.05 has actually made a few changes to the enemy AI, but the thing is they are still dumb, but with some more movement, only in open ended levels. They will actually roll around now, but 99% of the time it's just in the same spot not even moving. In Chapter 3 enemies will actually run around, but if they are outside in the cargo container areas they actually run away from you and don't engage, I even had a couple enemies just stay idle while I was face to face with them. While effort was put here and it is more exciting, it's just not for the reason of being excited, but instead being a bit more buggy.]

-: Ashnell still has problems with level direction with woods, making multiple branches that lead to dead ends don't benefit the level very much and might lead you to loop around the same few spots.

-: The weapons in this game are pretty bad. Pump shotgun doesn't have any real power behind it feeling the same as the Revolver. The default Revolver is fine, but you will miss enemies when shooting dead on for whatever reason. The Pistol you pick up from enemies might be the best just because of it being semiautomatic so even if you do miss with being dead on you can quickly just fire off another round, and you will find the most ammo for it. The Automatic Machine Gun (forgot what the actual name is) is the best weapon of the game just for it being automatic and having really good range, the furthest of all the guns, but you won't find a lot of ammo for it which is a bummer. 

-; The voice acting is kinda bad and this has to do with the use of AI. Now I don't actually know which characters are using AI, but it feels like all of them, sentences just get cut off and everyone is pretty monotone. 

+; Story itself is pretty funny even though it falls stale in the middle. Some retired military stoner gets a call from a woman wanting Grandpa to use his old training in order to help her escape the United States and he initially doesn't want to do this because who tf is this, but she throws out an offer even Grandpa can't refuse. 

[strike] -: Optimization is pretty bad here and regardless of what graphical options you use the game's performance does not change at all. There are certain areas that perform like trash so trying to tweak the game would be the first thing to come to mind for a lot of people, but OH that doesn't work at all. The game will only look better or worse. That's it. [/strike] +: Performance was actually worked on and the game runs smoothly now. 

-: Lack of control settings has me relying on my mouse's actual DPI which might not be the worst thing in the world, but the ADS sensitivity is just bad.

-: Game is only about an hour long. Wouldn't have been bad if the price was adjusted.

While I don't dislike this game I also don't really like it either. You can tell that Ashnell put a lot more effort into this than his other title 'Haters,' there is fun to be had here, but very minimal as there isn't any challenge. I think people will like this regardless, but I would only really recommend if it had a smaller price point.

Hole is a single player extraction shooter, which is a pretty under-represented genre. It does a lot of things very well, while also having some questionable design decisions which detract from the experience slightly, but not enough to make the game unfun.

The maps deserve a special callout. The maps are fairly big, and are themed after basic concepts like an office or apartments. However, I'd describe them as capturing the *essence* of those things, without actually *being* those things. Imagine if an alien visited Earth very briefly, saw a lot of things with no cultural context, and then went home and had to describe an office building or an apartment block. That's what these maps feel like. They very capably capture the general appearance of those things, without any of their function. You could look at any given screenshot of the apartment map and say "Yeah, that's an apartment block", but when you start walking around it, it feels surreal. Doors don't lead where you expect them to. Stairs connect weirdly. There are entire floors near the top of the building that resemble a lobby. There's hospital features uncomfortably intermingled with empty apartments. It has a very disquieting feel to it.

This might sound like I'm saying the maps are bad, so I want to clarify, that is not what I'm saying at all. The maps are great. They're just familiar enough to be recognizable while feeling wholly alien. It's disconcerting. It's excellent.

Each map has a series of fairly arbitrary missions to complete. (Collect 8 CDs. Collect 10 vases. Find 9 flower pots.) These missions really just serve as a reason to explore each map; the objects you're looking for are randomly placed each time and there's far more than you need, but they serve their function. After completing a number of these, you'll get a key that opens a previously locked room of the map, wherein you can trigger a "finale" of sorts which, when completed, gives you access to the next map (and a new weapon).

This works for what it's trying to do, but one caveat I have is that if you die in a map, you keep all of the mission items (and later, unlockable blueprints) that you collected. (You do lose 90% of the currency you earned.) While I understand this was a design decision and that losing things isn't fun for some players, I think the extraction shooter genre kind of loses something when you don't have the risk of loss. Not that I enjoy losing things, either, but that risk is what creates a feeling of tension. When you know you won't lose anything of real substance for failing, the tension is considerably less.

This is also the case with buffs to things like health, reduced recoil, and health regeneration that you can buy. I was surprised to see these buffs persist even through deaths. The health buff in particular feels a bit over-done; you go from dying in one hit commonly (with no upgrades) to feeling like Rambo (with all 3); it removes a lot of the tension and feeling of being in danger when you get those. 

Extraction points are also a bit too common in some maps. There are multiple on each map, and they are available right from the moment you enter; this is fine on some maps, but on the apartment map in particular, it feels like there's too many. The map is very open, and the extraction points can spawn 'outdoors' (e.g. on the roof), which means you can pretty commonly have maps where you can stand in a given spot and see 2-3 extraction points on the screen at once. It might have been a better design choice if only one (or even none) had been available initially and more had spawned over time.

The weapons feel nice. The first thing the game has you do is shoot some boards so you can progress into the game proper (this is really the only 'tutorial' that exists); you'll try to shoot, realize your weapon is empty, reload it, try to shoot, realize that you need to chamber a round, then you're allowed to continue. That little thing made pretty sure I was going to enjoy the game.

Attachments are unlocked by finding blueprints from a particular type of enemy. These seem to be random, but it would have been better (IMO) if they were unlocked in a particular order, at least within a category. For example, the rifle comes with a 10 round magazine by default, and you can unlock a 20, 30 and 60 round version (with each having slower reload speed). The first blueprint I found for the rifle was the 60 round magazine, and it felt like easy mode. (+0.75 second reload time in exchange for 50 extra rounds isn't even really a tradeoff.) It made the other magazine upgrades feel disappointing to find, as a result; if I'd found the 20 round one first, then the 30 round one, then the 60, I'd have bought each upgrade and been happy to do so.

There aren't many unique weapons, but each one has a lot of attachments that change the performance and sights and whatnot. I'm not sure that more weapons would really enhance the experience any; I saw 'only 4 weapons' and was a little put off by it initially, but it doesn't feel bad in practice.

The movement also feels nice. Surprisingly good for a $5 game. There are some minor issues here, though. Walking up to a wall will have your gun phase through the geometry. Running into a door will let you briefly see through it as your head also partly phases through it. You can grab onto ledges and climb up onto them, but in some places this will cause weird glitches where your camera is briefly almost a third person view; I assume the camera isn't synced properly to the mantling / climbing animation (it definitely doesn't appear to be an active design choice).

The AI isn't great. Enemies go pretty easy on you. The difficulty usually comes from the quantity, and the fact that some of them have body armor or helmets rather than because they outsmart you.

I think the game could have benefited from some difficulty options. Some general things I'd have liked to be able to configure:
- Losing mission items and blueprints on death.
- Losing drink buffs on death (maybe downgrading them one level vs. losing them entirely, or alternately losing them entirely but having the cost to re-buy them reduced.)
- Unlimited ammo. (To be clear, all ammo is unlimited.) Once you get a bigger gun, there's rarely a reason to use the pistol. If the other weapons had limited ammo that could be scavenged, it would make it more of a choice.

(I haven't finished all of the content yet, so it's possible there are some options like this hidden away somewhere at the end, and if that's the case, I'll come back and edit this accordingly.)

Overall, I'd say it's well worth your $5. Really a gem for the price, if you enjoy the genre.

So I'm giving Hole a thumbs up, because I loved the first few hours and the core ideas and mechanics are brilliant. But there's a huge caveat,  being the progression basically ruins the game, imo.

My first few runs were very tense and thrilling. I had only a pistol that holds 10 rounds and low hp. You're more or less on equal footing with your enemies.  A single head shot will put you or your enemies down, or a handful of body shots, 3 or 4. I absolutely got 1 tapped a few times and it just made the game more intense. In each run, there's a timer. As the timer count increases, it spawns more deadly enemies. It felt like a John Wick simulator and it was awesome. 

The gunplay feels great. There's a heat mechanic as well as a chamber mechanic which I moved from middle mouse to a thumb button. If you empty your pistol you will need to chamber a round after you reload. Your gun can jam and the chance increases with the heat. Chamber button to fix the jam. So we have a few simple mechanics that together end up feeling very satisfying to engage with. 

However, the more I play the less fun I have, for multiple reasons. The mechanics described above, to me, basically drawn the line on the map for you on how this game should progress in difficulty. We have several limitations we have to constantly play around, mostly, the need to reload. So it should throw larger numbers or more aggressive enemies at me to pressure me on those mechanics. More enemies pressing me harder means I need to hit more head shots so I have to reload less and build less heat. I need to be able to take cover when I do reload. I'm going to have to deal with jams no matter what though, my positioning is key. All that kinda stuff right?

 But the game doesn't spawn larger numbers of enemies, and they stay mostly pretty lethargic and just kinda sit around. The difficulty doesn't ramp, it jumps, and the way it increases is just the worst way possible. Instead, the game puts armor on the enemies. This was almost perfect. You're thinking, "ya, now you have to hit head shots, right?" No, they have armored faces and actually take even less damage from head shots. And it's not like they take twice as many shots now or something, not even close. WITH armor piercing bullets it takes 20+ shots to kill one armored enemy. 

So, just to be clear, I'm complaining the game is too easy, not too hard, and to skip to the point, after multiple hp and weapon upgrades I'm now running around like Rambo with an assault rifle that holds 64 shots of armor piercing ammo iirc and I shrug off hits like I'm the hero in an action movie. I have not died or lost a run since I got the second hp upgrade.

I only use the chamber button for jams as I almost never actually empty the gun all the way. There's a stun mechanic I forgot to mention but after a few shots enemies will be stunned and just ragdoll on the ground and then get up after a few seconds. SO, when I find an armored enemy, I spray 20-50 rounds into him and when he ragdolls (not dead) I walk up and unload the rest of the clip into the limp body until it dies, which, believe it or not, takes multiple reloads sometimes. No, I'm not kidding. You will pour dozens and dozens of bullets into a single limp body and then move on, looking for more enemies, which you find in groups of at most 3 at a time, gunning them down while ignoring their bullets because you have way too much hp and the enemies often drop heals when they die.

The second level is also just terrible. It goes from office, which can be confusing with just one floor, to sewers, which is like 4 floors and combined with the fact that the sound can be pretty wonky means it's damn near impossible to tell where things are happening and it's extremely frustrating.

Idk, genius base idea but I wish the game played into.... itself? To it's own strengths, I guess? TBQH I don't really understand a single decision that was made regarding the progression of the difficulty or your character. First few hours are great though.

Yeah, it's nice to see somebody making a game with such an unusual playstyle. It took me about 4 days of moderate play (12h total) to fully unlock what's available at the moment, but it's still fun to put on some music and run around. 

I think a little rebalancing of how difficulty scales could open up more interest in the late game, but I'm happy with what I played.

Hole is an [strike] arena [/strike] extraction shooter boiled down to its core elements, barring the whole equipment thing. Its pretty well executed in many ways but it has its hiccups too.

At the start of the game all you get is a pistol, and you have pick and choose fights carefully or get smited by the various npc teams fighting you and each other for resources. The longer you stick around, the harder and more numerous the enemies get, but also you get cash and items for each enemy you defeat.

As you progress you unlock tasks, weapons, and permenant upgrades for your character in the form of drinks. And here lies one of the main issues of this game. The drinks take you from having to plan your engagements carefully to ramboing your way through the map. Anything besides a shotgun to the face deals nearly trivial damage late game. Its almost entirely the health buff too, as all the other upgrades make modest adjustments to your character. You also get unlimited ammo for your guns of choice in exchange for an initially low magazine capacity, so theres no reason not to top off between fights.

The other issue is this game has very high system requirements and low performance for its graphical fidelity. And thats because raycasting/ global illumination is required for this game to look good, and enabled by default. You can disable it for decent performance but everything will look bright which will kill the looks and the difficulty. Instead i recommend turning your setting down in the config file (because theres little graphical settings in game) to get the best of both worlds.

the maps can be pretty disorienting even after playing each of them several times, as theres a lot of hallways that look the same as one another, and for some reason the first map gets only one extraction microwave but the later ones get more (although, they are bigger, more vertical maps). this can be both a boon and a curse as it gets you to explore more of the maps. however, it can be tricky to extract in a timely manner even if you know where the microwave is because navigating back is a pain. The later maps, on the other hand, are a bit easier to extract from if only because its more likely you'll run into a microwave. this would be better flipped on its head so that the maps have more of a progression.

The disk enemies are pretty interesting to fight as, apart from the drainage system enemies, they depart from just being more guys with guns and sometimes armor. I wish they appeared more often in more varieties, as right now they only appear on their specific stage when you activate the disks. the normal enemies are fine. in the beginning they're tough tbh, especially when armor and bigger guns are involved. the higher tier enemies can soak up a ton of damage but dont pose a big risk unless you get ambushed or youre not leveled up yet.

The gunplay is great, pretty much what you'd expect out of a tactical shooter. the weapons are pretty decent, theres only four and they all have their niche. The sniper rifle will uno reverse any sort of armor or large health pool with a headshot, the shotgun can put out a lot of damage quickly up close, and the pistol can bridge any sort of gap in your loadout. And the assault rifle is the best gun in the game lol (even if its a jammomatic POS). Its automatic recoil is high but it has great accuracy and damage output. It definitely sidelines the pistol the most but you can still min max one for fodder and the other for armored enemies. The upgrades seem to come on quickly once you unlock them, and the game seems to want to give you the highest capacity mags first lol, which are a no brainer to install in exchange for the slight reload time increase. Theres also different ammo types and honestly [strike] the HP rounds are the best. [/strike] nvm, AP is good too. Even FMJ is okay as it heats up your gun slower. the barrel options though arent that great, they reduce cooling and damage too much for me.

One suggestion i have is to add some difficulty options or a different mode (new game + maybe) where the stakes are higher. You get less health from upgrades and any weapons and upgrades you get are lost on death and either have to be rebought (for a discount after the first time) and/ or collected in map. Plus you have to extract to get any currency or task items (currently 10% of collected currency and all task items except disks are kept on death). Oh and limited magazines. The main game itself needs a bit of a rebalance too, mainly how the ammo, mag types, and barrel options are balanced against each other. The one other thing would probably be to bake in lighting, since there really doesnt need to be raytracing in a game like this tbh.

But tldr, apart from difficulty plateau and weird performance requirements, the game is a steal for 5 bucks.

HOLE is a surprisingly simple and tight formula on a genera often characterized for complexity and opulent production values. 

You start in a mostly empty, featureless building. Who are you, and why are you there? It doesn't matter, turn on the microwave and fall into HOLE. You'll select from one of four maps (though I can only play one, for reasons I'll mention ahead) and be dropped into a stage filled with strange hostiles. Your objective is to kill as many of them as you can before finding your way out. Get out alive and earn resources with which to buy upgrades to your weapons and your base, die and have your rewards decimated. The longer you stay in a level, the more rewards you get, but the more dangerous and aggressive the enemies become. How much do you want to push your luck? Depends on how much you're willing to lose.

In terms of the sim elements that characterize other games in the genera, HOLE is surprisingly light: Your character doesn't suffer from fatigue after sprinting for more than thirty seconds, nor do they realistically fall into shock when shot, nor do they get shaky with adrenaline after shooting someone else. What do they do? Well, they suck at aiming from the hip and they die very quickly, and that's all you really need to create some shockingly tense and challenging gun fights. Especially once you get to some of the more punishing enemies; as someone who greatly enjoys a good horror game, some of the scariest moments I've had in a game have happened after a run of HOLE that lasted for over ten minutes.

Of course though, the game does have issues. Remember how I said I could only play one map earlier? Yeah, that's because the textures on the second map won't load for me. Being the work of a one-man indie dev, the game is (perhaps unsurprisingly) poorly optimized and buggy. Given the simple graphics, I'd wager any machine built for gaming in the last 10~ years can probably run it fairly well, but if you (like me) were hoping for a tactical shooter you could play on your laptop while on a trip, this probably isn't it. Movement also feels a bit janky at times, and while the enemy AI can be very challenging, it's also very simple in a way that can make it easily exploitable if you know what you're doing.

Would I recommend it in spite of that? Yeah, absolutely. I think it's more than worth it, for the price tag. The core gameplay loop is great and I find the aesthetics very compelling, but you should probably know what you're getting into and be willing to accept it, imperfections and all. Personally I'm happy I supported this dev's work, and I'm looking forward to what they do next.

Looked fun at first, but there are severe balancing issues and the ending basically kicked me in the teeth.

Severe Balancing Issues:
Lots of cool abilities and characters, many of the abilities have a toggle for auto aim and such, but the way that it is currently running you never have enough mana to always have even half of your abilities on. Essentially you're always in a severe mana deficit. In addition, the leveling makes it so that you usually gain a flat damage to a spell/ability but the mana cost increases as well, and you're so behind in mana from the beginning game that you almost always have to devote anywhere between 10-15 of your hard earned "general" levels into mana recovery or cheaper spell cost.

Counter intuitively, leveling up your active spells is often not worth it. If you level up your strongest spell, its usually a flat damage rate up (+1 for example) and your mana cost increases too (+1). You use up almost all your mana (unless you're a summon build, but that has its own challenges) so you have to sink your general skill points into mana recovery or cheaper spell. The damage increase from leveling the active spell isn't worth it, because it very easily becomes too expensive to afford to cast more than a few times. Without meta progression and decent items, its actually better to NOT level up the active skill and to increase your damage via the "damage" general skill, which provides a percentile boost. This is an issue when you are forced to invest so many of your general skills into other essential level ups: mana recovery/cheaper spell/speed/health regen/faster casting time/etc.

There are builds where you can just safely and painstakingly slowly cheese every enemy. While other builds without significant meta progression is impossibly infeasible.

Meta progression is in the form of legacy items and additional general skill points based off of the number of achievements you got. This hurts when I spent hours on a good run, got to the final area, and found a hell forge (reroll items). I dropped my full inventory of good loot and grabbed the trash loot to reroll them, when I got attacked by the boss and killed him. The game ends right then and there and forces you to exit to the main scene. I lost everything. Which is a punch in the gut, especially as every other area allows you to leave and move on after you have the opportunity to stay for as long as you like.

I have been following this game, waiting for a release, since the moment it was announced; I bought it as soon as I was able, and I was not disappointed! I don't often leave steam reviews, but as a vampire-loving lesbian that has a few duos of red-headed and white-haired characters of her own, this game seems catered to me so specifically one might wonder if it was made in a lab.

Regardless, Cage of Roses is a wonderful foray into vampire fiction in visual novel format. It is very on-theme, and while it is not the most amazing thing I have ever read, it has a wonderful amount of heart, love for its genre and inspirations, and,  perhaps most importantly, a very clear understanding of what makes these types of romances compelling. It is nuanced and gentle, while also being a refreshingly straightforward narrative that cares more about the quality of the story it delivers than subverting expectation, and while that might make it sound predictable, there was a twist or two that I genuinely didn't expect.

I'd rate this game a very agreeable 7.5/10. It was exactly what I wanted, and it didn't take forever to deliver it. For that, it has my respect, my happiness, and my recommendation.

(Oh, and I couldn't find anywhere to fit it in my review proper, but the art and soundtrack were also quite lovely, and very fitting. It has my compliments on those, as well.)

After playing this game both solo and co-op a lil bit, I can say the game is a fun time burner, it's got okay replayability  and the netcode is pretty solid, however there are a few grips I got with this game.

- There needs to be a bit more variety with the room layouts, it's the same 3 to 4 layouts per stage so that get's predicable.
- The enemy balancing is wacky, one room can be a cake walk and then the next room it would be really unnecessarily hard and then back down to a cake walk, like there's no gradual difficulty climb.
- The hurt cones and hit boxes are not exact, there's been many times where I would be out of the hurt cone and I still lose HP (the mousers with the shields, The Junkyard boss, the lasers for example) so that needs to be refined.
- It's hard to see where you are at times , there's no outline other your character....or any other character for that matter.
- The lightning storms happen a little too frequently and it does stack with more players. I would like to be able stand still for more than 3-4 seconds, at the very least have it hit random parts of the room not at my feet 8 times out of 10.
- The health bar UI, Please put the player's health next to the rest of the player info at the top corner of the screen.
- The lighting effects for fire and shadow on the ground needs changing, it also makes it hard to see what the enemy is doing.
- Add another store for the rooftops or at least have more choice for the one that's there
- Fix the perk RNG, there' s been times when it's been nothing but all currencies back to back, I know you get re-rolls but I would like not wast all of them so soon.

I feel the game would be more solid fixing these issues.

This game was a massive disappointment. When I first heard about it, it seemed made for me: Hades-esque roguelike with online co-op, and I can return to my childhood by playing as a Ninja Turtle? Sign me up! However, once I started playing, I was confronted by several annoying issues. In no particular order:
- You can’t rebind the mouse buttons at all.
- The game suffers from excessively long loading times, and sometimes even crashes - this first happened to me when trying to access the tutorial, where the game crashed once and then took 10+ minutes to load in when it actually decided to work.
- As part of the loading, whenever we advanced stages, there was a risk of DCing; and while you can reconnect mid-run, it was very inconsistent/gave me errors at times, forcing us to quit a run.
- There are parts of the map where, if you dash just right (just wrong?) you clip into the stage.
- At one point one of my friends went straight up invisible for several minutes until they died.
And this was all in just three hours! I’ve played Early Access games that are more stable than this.

The actual gameplay is fun for a bit, especially in co-op, but has its own issues at times. One thing I really liked is the way ability cooldowns are handled, where you charge them by doing your basic attack sequence; it’s a neat way to encourage you to switch up your fighting style. The different power-ups and Tools also felt fun to use and make you think differently about how you play. One of the biggest problems is hitting things and getting hit don’t have any “weight” to them at all; there’s little done in terms of screen effects to make them meaningful, and it’s easy to lose track of them when it’s just numbers on a screen. This led to lots of “wait, where did I lose that much health?” The enemy variety is also really paltry; there are like under ten in total. Obviously roguelikes by their nature are going to be somewhat repetitive, but again, when stuff begins to feel boring less than three hours in, that’s a problem. This tedium isn’t helped by enemies just becoming ridiculous healthsinks later on, and the absurd number of currencies the game wants you to grind for to meta-progress. All of these together makes it feel like it’s overstayed its welcome before it’s even begun.

Writing-wise, it’s Fine. The story is serviceable but bland. The individual turtles are actually written quite well, with dialogue that matches their established personalities There was even a scene that surprised me, where Michaelangelo has a moment of vulnerability with Splinter. Raphael for some reason is an exception, with the most groan-inducing out-of-character writing I’ve ever seen for him; he’s written like a cheap knockoff of Michaelangelo.

Overall, would be a Fine co-op experience to sink a few hours into if not for the bugs, which take this from passable to A Pass.

Let me start by saying, I am an 80's baby. TMNT was massive hit during elementary school, and I fell in love with the games. TMNT (1) was a beast for game play and unfairness. Then again, I played Ninja Gaiden 1 and 2, so those that have played it know. TMNT 2 was absolutely amazing. That was one of the games that shaped my youth, including Mega Man series, Mortal Kombat (including the cheat code for Sega to include blood), Sonic, of course Mario Brothers. I was/am completely hooked on video games, and these early games have shaped my experiences and expectations.

So, when my brothers suggested this game, I looked into it, and decided to give it a good "college try".
There will be some pros that are also cons, and I will explain.

Pros:
It is beautiful for the platform and engine.
The fighting styles are pretty unique for each turtle. Leo is my fave, Ralph is a very, very close second.
Plenty of power ups, which mix and match, causing you to become a walking war crime.
Seriously, power up synergy can be completely overwhelming for the baddies.
The voice acting is really good.
Multiplayer makes it a lot more fun (because the enemy won't fully agro on you alone)
Ninja stars are boss.
You get to play as your favorite Ninja Turtle.

Mixed
It gets repetitive with the enemies, there's only so many ways you can introduce the same enemies.
Power ups are hit or miss. Some runs, you absolutely go ape, some you completely fluff. 
The scrap system needs some work. Sometimes you are swimming in scrap, sometimes you are starving for scrap.
Pacing can be either great or too slow depending on your power ups.
Mastery upgrades can be complete hit or miss.

Cons
At times, there can be so much going on, that you cannot spot either the enemies (especially the mid bosses) or yourself. 
Some mid bosses hit considerably harder that actual bosses, making you drain your lives. 
Some enemies and mid bosses attacks are cheap, no avoiding them, or you have to wait 5 seconds or more for the AOE to clear before you can actually attack them. Looking at you mutated toads, large rats, and fire spinning ninjas. Large rat poison is no joke, and they are tanky as all get out.
Power up RNG. It is a complete craps shot. There have been times where I got nothing but coins and dragon tokens for 6 levels when I have already maxed them both out. Absolutely garbage. This includes mastery.
Power up linear path. Sometimes you get nothing but Ooze, or Fire, or whatever, locking you into a garbage run. 
Too much dialog at times, where it seems every single player/NPC has to add their two cents.

Overall, it is a great game, but the most frustrating part is the RNG with it comes to power ups and the vendor. 
I have bought the DLC right before I decided to post this review. 
If you love TMNT, I would recommend it. If you like a good rouge type game, would recommend. If you are hoping to come into this game and steamroll every single level while looking for an easy time, you might not enjoy it. 
While nowhere near the same level as Dark Souls, you cannot just hack and slash and come out on top. A bit of strategy and skill is required.
Final note for improvement, and I know others might disagree, but I would like guaranteed power ups every level and a way to focus the power ups you want.

[h1]THE GREAT STARSCREAM REVIEWS SPLINTERED FATE - A TURTLE TRIUMPH? OR MUTAGENIC MISSTEP?[/h1]

Ah, the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles! One of the greatest relics of the 1980s, a time when Saturday mornings were sacred, action figures ruled the Earth, and cartoons had actual soul. Before the dark times. Before modern reboots. And yet, much like the mighty Decepticons, the turtles endure - adapting, evolving, surviving despite the incompetence of those who seek to diminish them!

So when Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Splintered Fate scuttled onto Steam, I, Starscream, Air Commander of the Decepticon fleet, knew I had to investigate. Would this be a heroic return to the arcade-style glory of Turtles in Time? Or would it mutate into yet another corporate cash-grab, designed to leech nostalgia from those who actually remember what a good game looks like?

Let's find out.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]FIRST IMPRESSIONS - COWABUNGA OR SHELL SHOCKED?[/h1]

Much like an Autobot ambush, Splintered Fate struck fast - no warning, no fanfare, just suddenly appearing like it was dumped from a portal opened by the Dimension X portal gun. A roguelike action game, eh? I’ll admit, I had concerns. I’ve been burned before (cough Transformers: Battlegrounds cough), but I set my supreme biases aside for the sake of science!

Visually, the game absolutely nails the TMNT aesthetic. The art style is clean, colorful, and dynamic. The character designs? Properly retro-inspired, with just enough modern polish to make it feel fresh. The turtles look like they should - no grotesque Michael Bay abominations, no weird rubbery CGI freaks - just the heroes in a half-shell as they were meant to be.

Then, the gameplay begins...

[hr][/hr]

[h1]GAMEPLAY - TURTLE POWER OR TURTLE TRASH?[/h1]

Here’s where things get... interesting. Splintered Fate is a roguelike, which means procedurally generated levels, random upgrades, and the ever-looming presence of the restart button. Now, Starscream is no stranger to adversity (Megatron sees to that daily), but is this a worthy challenge or just repetitive suffering?

Combat? Fast, fluid, and frantic. Each turtle has their own playstyle - Leonardo is balanced, Raphael is aggressive, Donatello has range, and Michelangelo… well, he’s Michelangelo. The action is snappy, the enemies varied, and the bosses? Genuinely fun! Shredder, Krang, Baxter Stockman? They're all here, and they mean business.

But here’s where the mutagenic ooze starts to sour: the roguelike mechanics. Instead of well-designed levels, we get randomly generated hallways. Instead of a properly paced adventure, we get frustrating repetition. This isn't Turtles in Time - this is RogueLegacy with a ninja theme. And while that’s not inherently bad, it feels... off for TMNT.

Thankfully, there IS local co-op! A TMNT game without it would be like giving Soundwave a mouth - an abomination against all logic! So at least they got that right.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]PRESENTATION - A SLICE OF 80s NOSTALGIA?[/h1]

One thing Splintered Fate does exceptionally well is its commitment to the TMNT brand. The animations? Smooth. The voice acting? Serviceable. The music? A proper throwback, though it could use more punch.

But the true test of nostalgia is how it compares to its rivals, and here’s where we have a problem. Transformers: Devastation was a perfect example of how to take an 80s franchise and modernize it without losing its soul. It captured the look, the feel, and the spirit of G1 Transformers, all while delivering phenomenal gameplay.

Splintered Fate, by comparison? It gets the style right but stumbles in execution. It's not a soulless cash grab, but it's also not quite the triumphant return we deserve.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]VERDICT - SHOULD YOU PLAY IT?[/h1]

Let’s be very clear: This game is not bad. It’s actually quite fun in short bursts, and for TMNT fans, there’s plenty to love. But is it the ultimate TMNT game? No. That title still belongs to Turtles in Time. And it always will.

If you enjoy roguelikes? You’ll probably dig it. If you wanted a true TMNT beat ‘em up? You might be disappointed. Would Starscream, the mightiest of all Decepticons, recommend it?

Let me put it this way: If you love TMNT and can tolerate repetitive gameplay, give it a shot. But if you were hoping for the second coming of Turtles in Time? You might be better off dusting off your SNES.

[h2]Final Score: 7/10 - Not a disaster, but not quite a masterpiece either.[/h2]

[hr][/hr]

[h1]POSTSCRIPT - WHERE'S THE REAL COMPETITION?[/h1]

And before I go, a quick note: WHERE IS MY TRANSFORMERS: DEVASTATION 2?! PlatinumGames gave us one of the best Transformers experiences ever, and it was unceremoniously yanked from digital stores. Meanwhile, TMNT gets multiple games, and now we’re stuck with Splintered Fate instead of a proper console beat ‘em up?!

Unacceptable.

If this is the best we can get, then perhaps it’s time I seize control and ensure quality myself. Until then, Starscream out.

The gameplay is what you'd expect from this genre.  It's okay, although I do think that there are some problems.  Playing with KBM, it feels a little weird that your attacks don't go towards your mouse direction.  It's a system obviously designed for controllers, but I'm always wary of games that don't have proper PC integration.

The power-up system in this game is very flawed.  You aren't guaranteed to find a new power after every room.  You instead have a chance to find powers, which you can improve with the game's meta-progression system.  There is also a small chance to upgrade powers or even get a second selection of powers, both of which can also be upgraded with the progression.  You can end up getting nothing, and absolutely have a chance to bust multiple rooms in a row, so this system has a very feast or famine feel.

There are 6 different types of powers, but most of them are highly self-synergistic, which means that they kind of suck by themselves, and you need a lot of powers from the same category.  However, the game will definitely offer you powers from a bunch of different categories, so you have to get quite lucky to get a decent build.  There is also a legendary power system that requires mixing and matching of different abilities.  The legendary powers are rare, and some of them is required for certain builds, which isn't great.

The game's meta-progression system requires grinding lots and lots of various types of currencies from your runs.  Whoever designed this thought you'd have 1000 hours of play time in this game.  The game feels very incomplete without grinding this progression system, but the ask to grind is way too much for this game that doesn't offer much game play.

There is a system that offers hard mode portals that add some unfun modifiers to runs, and offers a tiny amount of extra meta currency in exchange.  The portals are required to unlock certain progression items.  However, you need to decide on using these portals towards the beginning of your run, and they make the run a lot harder.  If you don't get extremely lucky, they'll likely brick your run.  It feels like the problem always comes back to how incomplete the power-up system feels if you don't have a maxed out progression box.

The best part about this game is that the dialogue between characters is often very funny, especially Casey Jones.  The writers and voice actors at least had fun with the setting.  But it's not enough to save this game.  Imo I wouldn't pay more than $10 for this, unless they dramatically improve the progression system and add more content.

Edit: I did find the game fun enough to play a fair bit more, so you can consider that however you'd like.  My assessment hasn't really changed, though.

Though it is listed as a tower defense game, it's a bit of a mislabel. Autobattler seems a little closer, but honestly I'm not sure what would work as a quick analogy. 

There's a single lane that enemies will march down, attempting to reach and destroy your tower. Your job is to use skills and summon your own army to push them back. What makes Forest Heroes fun for a Roguelike addict is that there are many ways to acquire power, and, especially with the latest update, many avenues to success. 

Your skills, for example, can be upgraded, adding multiple extra copies of it, or reducing their cost to make them more spammable. Your units can be upgraded to reduce their cost or increase their stats, or can be given a hat to give them special effects or further stat boosts. Then there's relics with a wide variety of effects, including unit-specific relics that can boost all copies of a specific unit card. There's various mechanisms, like dodging, bleeding, poison, sturdiness, and almost all creatures have a specific use or niche in which they excel. That's not to say they're all perfectly balanced, there's a few units that I just wouldn't really pick up and some that are -always- good to pick up, but I've seen a LOT of units pull some serious weight with the right builds. 

I've played enough to unlock everything, including the higher difficulties. I'm not a hardcore min-maxer, so the game's difficulty is slanted more towards letting the player have fun, while the higher 'curse' level is aimed at providing a solid challenge. But despite having done everything, I still come back to this game just to have another run, just to see if I can break it even more. Maybe I can push a Ballista Tortoise to a greater extreme, making it to absurd damage per hit, or get a Lemmings card to summon a colossal army of little rodents. Maybe a Wisent just falls asleep on the frontline, recovering health while it naps while enemies damage themselves on its 'Spikes'. 

It's a fun game with great potential, and hopefully it'll continue to get updated for a bit longer. At the very least, there's a third playable character in the works, which means a new set of skills to supplement your armies with!

I'm giving this a slight recommend. I think for the price there's some interesting stuff here, but overall it falls flat and I have significant criticisms with the game as a whole.

As the game shows, this is essentially a turn-based horror roguelite experience. The core gameplay and the one you'll spend the most time in is the No-Skin mode with the goal of getting to 100% (at first). Essentially though, the game is all about managing resources. Understanding which rooms to go for if you need life/ammo/instant damage, fishing for upgrades/shops and fighting enemies with minimal resource loss. For me at least this system was fairly simple (having beaten the game past Faith 4 + extra bosses) and for the most part it wasn't very difficult. Which is perfectly fine, but one of the core problems the game has is tedium. There are a lot of repeated text boxes, enemies have a fairly low amount of dialog, and getting into the later half of the game where you need to optimize trades for items/health etc exacerbates the problem. For the most part bosses are knowledge checks, if you didn't get to a boss with specific resources or items you're likely to lose.

Which brings me to the second critique: There's a fairly low amount of variety. Enemies tend to all behave very similarly, there's a small pool of upgrades both from the shop(s) and from the meta progression. It means whatever character you play will tend to always play the same.

Gameplay-aside, the story and characters is probably the bit I'm most lukewarm on. You're introduced to the same characters in different contexts (battle, dream diary) but for the most part there really isn't much there. You get brief glimpses into a characters personality, but none of it really comes together in a way that is coherent. In many aspects it feels like the game is both doing too much and too little, the parts where the game tries to break the mold are interesting but it does so with such frequency that it reduces the novelty.

The artwork is generally really good though along with the ambiance, but that's unfortunately not enough to really carry forward gameplay that is just sort of there and a story that can't decide what it's actually trying to do. I think it's still a unique enough title that's worth a look, but ultimately I'd consider the game to be a resounding 'Okay'.

I wish there was a so-so rating option, but I have to air on the side of do not recommend for this game. 

I have beaten the game two times now (I have not gotten the true ending), and after maybe the first 4 or 5 runs it starts to get repetitive. NO-SKIN's gameplay loop consists of room delving. Each room has a certain chance of a few different events happening, I think there's about 8-10 different rooms in total, with about 4.5 (I will explain what I mean by .5 later). events per room. This amount of variation seems fine at first, but it quickly devolves into monotony and in a weird way, a resource management game. 

Even with the max roguelite upgrades that the game gives you, which unlocks new rooms, there just isn't enough variety for this game to retain much replayability, especially when you find out that each area is just designated to give you certain things. Initially cool 1/10 or even 1/100 chance areas quickly become the "Oh the +12 fragments/1 medkit room", or the "Oh the funny dev joke room." The worst part about the outcomes of these rooms is that they're incredibly rare, and getting maybe a small tidbit of lore or a funny cutscene with no reward feels bad in a game that essentially becomes resource management after the player is familiarized with the gameplay loop. Because of these rooms being relatively useless/only slightly better than others, they feel like half rooms that pop in every once in awhile to slightly disrupt the gameplay loop. 


Besides my problems with events in the room design, the game does have a few pluses when it comes to combat. I love the artstyle of the various enemies and [spoiler] how they change as you get closer to NO SKIN /spoiler],  I also like the combat mechanics introduced throughout the game. However, again, I wish there were more enemies, or maybe that the enemies changed their attack patterns. Are you starting to see the common theme here?

The game lacks variety, which is key to replayability in a roguelite. The game needs more rooms and more events per room. Ah No-Skin, I remember playing the demo. It hooked me, grabbed my by my hair and pulled me into this horrific nonsensical world, where nothing is as it truly is.

Whats not to like? A charming pixelated art style with spooky horror elements. A cast of fun and interesting characters. All tied together with simple, but fun game play and easy to learn mechanics.

I want to talk about the characters first because, its funny, and I really do enjoy them. You have, a guy with no skin. His son, who also has no skin and a timidness not expected. An attractive fish with long gills, sentences that leave you baffled, and shocking good deals. A Goddess, who drafts you to realize Her will. Frogs, who sell you wares from the trash and say things like, "Frogs, Frogs, we are Frogs". Whats not to love. The game also has multiple playable characters, each with their own gimmicks, albeit some better than others.
-
Take Luna for example... *cough* Best Girl *cough cough* ... She starts with 3 base damage, a lot, but suffers from terrible accuracy. This can easily be paired with another item from the Frogs and she easily becomes significantly stronger. Not only that but that isin't even her gimmick, thats just how great she is. But enough fawning, lets move on.

The art style is incredible unique, mainly using pixel art. With the game being horror it uses that to create these grotesque, characters and places, that really put you in this world that is not your own. There is explicit content, in the manner of blood, deformations, drinking, drugs, and nudity. Pray to the Goddess your Mom doesn't walk in when your fighting 'The Competition'.

With turn based combat, the game play is incredibly easy to learn, you stab, you shoot, you pray, and you run, almost everything else is a free action. Stabbing and shooting are your main methods of dealing damage, although your run could result in you killing things with second hand smoke from cigarettes. Praying is how you defend, it sets the damage you take that turn to 1. This is mainly used for when enemies take the turn before to prepare to unleash a devastating attack, but once again, it could have other uses depending on your run. Running away is just that, some enemies can't die without special means, that you often don't have. So you run, which can fail, which will result in the enemy taking its turn, and an increase in your escape chance. You also have an inventory, but that one is extremely flexible because, for most of the game, you can use as many items as you want without using your turn.

No-Skin is a great game, and I 100% recommend it, and for $6 it's not unbearable expensive, and it definitely has enough content to make it worth it. It does get difficult at times, but that just makes you feel that much better when you finally do finish that goal.
-
I'm not going to lie though, it does get difficult, an example is the Trish diary, a puzzle you get for completing the game multiple times. The Trish diary was insanely difficult, I probably sunk 2 hour in it until I finally beat it. Before beating it though, I had a run go to its boss, proceed to knock it down to one health, miss once, and die. It was a play perfectly, get killed because you missed once challenge. But you know whats even better than a challege?
-
THE DEV NERFED IT! No-Eye Soft listens to the players, and updates the game accordingly, which means No-Skin has a lot of room to grow from where it is now, with player support. Which is extremely important for any game.

Do not go into this game thinking it's a heavily replayable roguelite. The meat and potatoes of this game is story-based, and it's no wonder that people are turned off by the admittedly basic gameplay progression. The story progression, however, is wonderful. If you can find yourself engaged properly with it, there's a lot of fun secrets and tidbits of information that is drip-fed to the player, encouraging you to piece together exactly what has happened and how you got yourself into this situation.

The game is essentially a solved puzzle, though. There is only ever one way to build a specific character, which is to lean into their one predetermined strength. This isn't really a problem for me, though, as I understand that the roguelite gameplay is a vehicle for transporting the narrative forwards, but given more development time, I do think the actual gameplay could become complex enough to draw in a larger range of people.

For the current price, though, it's worth every penny and I would highly recommend it. You'll get an excellent indie horror story experience, especially if you enjoy the Dark Souls-esque storytelling method.
