I would give this game a borderline "yes".
New player to the series, love the art style and the playstyle, choice making in the day and then some hands-on action at night.

Pros:
+ great art style
+ good gameplay loop, 3x decisions (with possible drawbacks) and then action at night
+ randomization adds replayability

Neutral:
= At first I thought this game is more combat based. But in fact this game is more looting based. You are encouraged to loot as much as you can when deploying at night while trying to repel zombie attacks. Your guys at first loot extremely slow so it can take minutes just watching them clear a box of supplies. I am sure in later stages it will pick up a bit more but I never got far.
= Game is really hard, even on easy. Buyers beware.

Cons:
- Lacks polish, e.g. no back or exit button when starting game, like I can't change my commander name once set, and you couldn't even see the box on the upper left corner at start. 

- Things are also not explained enough, at first I would thought at least each class has a weapon. But no, medics and engineer basically cannot fight unless you craft them a secondary weapon. This information was never told. 
Another example is turrets you built on maps does not use your ammo, but if you deploy your own turret it does. I had to find out the hard way because suddenly my rifleman had a fully upgraded gun with no ammo and then my turret is also stopped. And if your turret explode your noise meter will immediately become full and zombies will come pouring in. 
You will need several runs to slowly figure things out.

- Questionable designs
a. Too much randomization. You have 3 choices to make during the day, one is about rest, you can eat, heal, level up or craft gear for your characters, but this is randomized. Meaning that you might not get a chance to level up or craft at all. Nothing is certain. Same for the other two choices, you pick what to loot, where to go, etc. but it is all random. My game crashed during action once and I was set back to the beginning of the day, all the choices are different.
I think it is better to let the player choose directly at least for the rest bit so the choice feels more "tactical" than completely luck based.
What really baffles me is that even what you can craft are randomized. My engineer first had a secondary upgrade that is a barricade, my game crashed, I come back and later craft again the secondary upgrade is now a barbed wire. 

b. Collision. Oh man, characters in this game are huge, and if you have one guy standing in the doorway looting a box, your other guys will be unable to reach the other side unless you move the other character out of the way first. Sounds fine but when you have like 5 civilians blocking all the space it is borderline playable. 

c. No speed toggle. You can only choose to pause the game completely or play at normal speed. I would say during the heat of battle the game is indeed a bit too fast. But when you pause, you issue orders but you are not sure whether you ordered them correctly. You might have ordered your man to move when you wanted them to attack, and you would only find out when you unpause. If they have a slower speed setting then at least you can see you made a mistake and correct it immediately in slo-mo. In addition, during looting stage you have nothing to do apart from watching your man loot the boxes, if a speed up button is available the looting time can be shortened.

d. Survivors you found in stages will only fight and walk only, does not help you do other things. I find this really odd. At first I didn't know you can give them orders to walk (probably because at that time I haven't met the condition to recruit them yet). Then once I found out they can walk, I didn't know you had to exfil them as well for them to count. Because once your team is out you cannot control the survivor anymore. So the exfil order matters, make sure your survivor(s) are extracted BEFORE you last teammate. In a sense I would rather the survivors cannot be controlled at all and would run for the door once available, OR give us complete control to them like a squad member so they can help loot and can be the last one to leave.

e. Some bugs: achievements unlocking when I first start the game, saying I opened 10 doors but I just opened 1. Crashes mid game resetting the day's progress. Survivor rescued seems to be not tracking (unless you need to beat the game to actually "rescue" the survivors, but again it isn't explained)

===========
In conclusion, I find this game OK. I suck at it for sure but this game is also kinda working against you. If you like a tactical game where luck plays a major role, you will definitely enjoy this game. Also I want to mention the developer at this stage will only fix bugs and will not implement any QoL features. You can checkout their roadmap and find more information. They will only add more content/features if this game sells, a sensible choice, but buyers should know this as well.

I would recommend this game. I rather enjoy the gameplay loop. It keeps me engaged, it can be a challenge to manage time and resources, the RNG can be a real killer when you desperately want something. Its made in a way that if you enjoyed old flash games, you'll probably enjoy playing this. Give it a try, it has a demo. You might like it.

However some things to keep in mind.

1: This game is a rouge-lite, top down, real-time (with a pausing feature), tactical squad RTS.

2: It will not hold your hand, the game has a very bare bones tutorial compared to what the game has to offer, you will learn the mechanics of the game as you fail your runs. Ex). you will unlock more features and better starting gear from completing achievements (in-game)

3: Currently my biggest gripe is that the game seems to have an issue with reloading an autosave once you get to the later missions. It takes a solid few minutes to get the save to turn on but I did manage to get it to run again. I'm not sure as to why this is the case. I am not software inclined enough to know how to troubleshoot the issue. Perhaps others have run into this, maybe in a discord discussion or a steam forum. Food for thought. (Will update this out later if I can seem to get this fixed or it is fixed)

4: The graphics are perfectly pleasant, the only difficulty is with a specific enemy type, varying terrain, or overlapping textures. This will hide your characters, it would be rather nice if there was a faint outline of my characters if they were behind certain terrain features.

5: Pathfinding, it could use a little bit of work. By no means is it bad, there is simply a minor problem with units moving around each other or getting stuck. Units will not move out of the way, or clip through each other (as if sliding past another person) if you order another unit to get to a lootable crate or task them with movement. It will be best if you get used to moving each unit separately or in pairs of 2. They will get stuck on each other. The units understand they are blocking another units path because your unit will not attempt to move if they are to far away from a location, on the bigger maps, or if a group of units is blocking its pathway. The unit will simply stand still, which can, and will, most certainly get them killed.

6: The enemy will come at you in increasingly larger waves as you play and it will be up to you to find an escape route and loot as long as you dare. Waves start at 30 sec and you can increase the length between them with lucky pulls during your "planning phases" between missions.

7. Between controlling your units on missions is where you'll probably want to be as strategic as you can be, considering the in-between is randomized and luck based. Focus on maintaining your soldiers mental state and hunger more than their health. I have found it is much more beneficial to heal your units on map, at the beginning of the waves when you have some breathing room. 
                 -Unless you have antibiotics and/or a medic your units will never be healed. Antibiotics will always be used to heal your units regardless of whether they are used during your "planning phases" or during your tactical engagement phases with a doctor.

8: The game has bosses, you will need your wits to think of ways to kill them, I just wish they had a health bar so I could tell how much more i need to shoot them. Not a negative, I respect the decision. 

9: You will need to loot as much as possible, make no mistake. This game strives on you looting anything that isn't bolted down. You will loot incredibly slowly at first. Get yourself an engineer, and level that unit to be your loot monger. they are the best at it. They can also turn on power and other useful things.

Another amazing offering by 16 bit nights -- I particularly like this developer but I'll say the game stands on it's own merits (and faults) and my bias towards the Chromosome Evil Series (also by this developer) does not bias my review.

16 Bit Nights does what it has always done best -- make hard, challenging games that reward good decision making and punish harshly mistakes and poor strategic moves. When I first started playing this game I was afraid I'd pan it for being TOO punishing (a single zombie getting into grips with a player in your first playthroughs will often be lethal when the zombie genre is usually typified by how impotent a single zombie is without a horde of them behind it... so you have to dismiss what you THINK you know from other zombie games and treat WBC as it's own experience. 

Early playthroughs unlock perks and equipment that make later playthroughs easier, for one -- and once you develop your own strategy and playstyle where you (wisely) weigh risk and reward, the game really starts to shine. "Green" untrained soldiers ARE food for the undead, while veterans you've trained up can do miraculous heroic things. Working together, soldiers, medics and engineers all serve their own important roles, gathering research and rescuing survivors, repairing and building, and the business of fighting and killing the enemy. And looting. Lots of fun looting. 

The loot system consists of a variety of commodities: ammos, medicines, building and crafting materials, etc. These improve gear, effect map environments, restore/maintain your troops, etc. and learning how to best spend and save these commodities is critical to surviving the long haul of the campaign. Score a lot of food? make sure it lasts until the next big score. Train your soldiers in new skills or improve their equipment with the little time you have each day (and almost a dozen other things you can choose to spend your time) ... every decision counts, and while there is luck involved with many random events, it's your decisions and what you learn about the outcomes that enables you to make the best of what comes at you.

The game loop consists of you making numerous choices as you prep for a mission each day, then a move to a tactical site (you usually get 2 or 3 choices of places to go) and then your soldiers do a mission there then try to escape.. looting as they go. Sometimes you fight big monsters, sometimes it's the ever-dogging horde, sometimes escape is it's own goal. Enemies are diverse especially for a zombie game... they come in many flavors from slight differences in speed and strength, to supernatural abilities and monstrous bosses. 

The 16 bit world is hand drawn and lovingly made for people who can appreciate this, this alone is sheer bliss because the game is rocking your face with gameplay, not trying to stand on it's beauty alone... it is all style and substance. There is also a degree of replayability with different starting setups, scads of secrets to find, and different subtleties to a variety of things that seem generic at first (for example each soldier has it's own weapon specialties) 

The story that's being told is grim and desperate and feels rewarding to fight against and win against all odds. 

I'm just going to keep watching for what comes next from this developer.... because after Chromosome Evil 1 and 2, Welcome Back commander stole my heart all over again.

Gore, Tension, Triumph, Tactics -- this game has all of it in spades.

The plot revolves around how these five "hearts" interact and navigate the challenges of living together as a collective. The game unfolds with a series of choices that players must make, and these choices directly impact how the characters evolve and how their relationships change over time. Conflict, romance, friendship, and drama are ever-present, keeping players engaged as they try to understand and shape the dynamics between the five main characters.

Love is often romanticized as something eternal, something that endures despite time, circumstance, and change. But Five Hearts Under One Roof presents a different, more haunting perspective: that love is fragile, transient, and sometimes—despite our best efforts—imprisoning. It is not a game about passion so much as it is about the quiet, often painful ways love binds us, the spaces we create to hold it, and the inevitability of its passing.

At its core, Five Hearts Under One Roof is not just a story about relationships; it is a story about love’s impermanence and the way we try—sometimes desperately—to preserve it.

The setting is intimate, claustrophobic—a single house where five lives intertwine, their desires and emotions filling every room like echoes of a past that refuses to fade. The house itself is not just a physical space but a symbol of the relationships within it. Love, after all, is often built like a home: with walls that shelter and protect, but also confine.

Each of the five hearts beats with its own longing, its own fears. The game does not present love as a singular experience but as a spectrum—burning, yearning, suffocating, fading. And as you navigate the house, you begin to understand that love is not always freedom. Sometimes, it is a cage.

We fall in love believing that it will complete us, that it will hold us together. But Five Hearts Under One Roof slowly unravels this idea. Love, in its most intense form, is both the thing that connects us and the thing that isolates us. It is what makes us stay in places we have outgrown, what turns shared moments into chains we cannot break. The house is not just a home—it is a prison of emotions, of memories, of longing.

If Five Hearts Under One Roof has one undeniable truth, it is that love does not last forever. This is not a tragedy—it is simply the way of things. The game captures the impermanence of love not through grand heartbreaks, but through subtle moments: a glance not returned, a room once warm now feeling cold, a conversation that once flowed now stilted and forced.

There is a sadness in watching love fade, in feeling its presence turn into absence, but there is also something beautiful about it. The game does not ask you to fight against this truth—it asks you to accept it. Love is like light filtering through a window at dusk. For a moment, it bathes everything in warmth, in gold. And then, inevitably, the sun sets, and the light disappears.

This is what makes Five Hearts Under One Roof so devastatingly real. It understands that love is not just about presence, but about absence. That the ghost of love lingers long after it has left, haunting the places where it once lived.

Love is supposed to be liberating, but Five Hearts Under One Roof reminds us that it often isn’t. Instead, it becomes something we hold onto long after it has ceased to serve us, something we imprison ourselves within because we are afraid of what lies beyond it.

The five hearts in the house are not just lovers; they are captives. They stay, not always because they want to, but because they don’t know how to leave. Love is supposed to be a door, but more often than not, it becomes a locked room.

And yet, there is a quiet rebellion in recognizing this captivity. The game suggests that even in love’s constraints, there is a choice—to stay, to leave, to accept, to mourn. The house does not force you to escape, but it does make you aware of your own imprisonment. And sometimes, that awareness is enough.

Long after you step away from Five Hearts Under One Roof, it stays with you, like the echo of a conversation long finished, or the ghost of a touch now absent. It is not a game that ends so much as it is a game that fades, just like love itself.

And maybe that is the most powerful thing about it. It does not promise love that lasts forever, nor does it mourn love that does not. Instead, it captures the fleeting, fragile nature of love—its beauty, its tragedy, its inevitable passing. It reminds us that love is not something to be possessed, only something to be experienced, for however long it chooses to stay.

Final Rating: 9/10

I’m thrilled to support this game for its educational value, but when it comes to gameplay, it just doesn’t click for me.

On the positive side, it’s a decent refresher if you’ve taken physics courses before and want to brush up on your knowledge. But honestly, that’s about all I can praise.

While nearly half of the levels are fairly intuitive at first glance, some still rely heavily on trial and error. I get that this might be an intentional design choice, but it doesn’t feel satisfying—especially when I have pen and paper in hand. Personally, I prefer the sense of accomplishment that comes from solving a problem correctly on the first try.

Now, without giving away spoilers, I have to say I really dislike the design of the 1.5.0 test level. The first phase feels messy due to all the possible solutions caused by collisions, and it seems to lack the necessary constraints for a "perfect" solve. On top of that, the two input boxes appear simultaneously instead of sequentially, making it unnecessarily difficult to figure out what I’m supposed to do.

The font is another issue—it’s fine for short paragraphs but really strains the eyes for longer text or 3D elements.

As for the game's lore, the voiceover tries hard to make my exploration feel deep and thought-provoking, but honestly, it doesn’t land.

The game is also poor on sound design. One cannot even tweak certain volume in-game.

There are so many areas that could use more polish. Physics has a unique and captivating language, but this game just doesn’t make it fun enough for me to want to replay it—or even work on the LaTeX solutions I originally planned before diving in. That being said, with some more satisfying sound effects and clearer level designs, I might pick the game up again.

Yeah, I hate myself.
As a physics major junior student and also taking an educational course at the same time, I played this game during my winter vacation. (It's a pity that I still had to do math even on vacation, LMAO)
I like the game’s concept—you need to solve problems based on real-life figures, not just the “designed” ones. It took me some time to input the numbers into the calculator.
But I think this game could improve in some areas:

1. For people who know nothing about physics, it's a BIG challenge to understand the concept and solve the problems. Maybe the hints should have more scaffolding.
2. Some levels require concepts from previous levels, and I don't think these concepts are easy to memorize. For example, in 1.2.6 (Drag force), you need the concept of Buoyant force. Maybe it should be mentioned again in 1.2.6.
3. In the concept section, I think more text descriptions could make the concepts easier to understand.
4. There are some symbols I want to complain about: For vectors like x, v, a, F, etc., they should have arrows to represent the VECTOR.

But I still like the game! Can't wait for more updates!

If you're a fan of cooperative horror games that demand teamwork, strategic thinking, and immersive tension, UNDERWARD is a must-play. Developed by INTENSE, this game delivers a fresh and chilling experience, blending survival horror with procedural exploration in a dark and mysterious underground hospital ward.

Atmosphere & Visuals
From the moment you step into the abandoned facility, UNDERWARD sets the tone with eerie lighting, unsettling sound design, and an environment that feels alive with danger. Every shadow could be a threat, every hallway an unsettling mystery waiting to unfold. The developers have done a fantastic job crafting an immersive horror setting that keeps players on edge.

Gameplay & Mechanics
The core gameplay revolves around cooperative extraction, where players must safely transport monstrous test subjects while evading lurking dangers. The procedurally generated environments ensure that no two playthroughs feel the same, adding to the game's replayability. Communication and coordination are essential—one wrong move can spell disaster for the entire team.

While playing with friends is the ideal way to experience UNDERWARD, it also offers a satisfying challenge in solo mode, requiring careful planning and quick decision-making.

Underward is one of those games that creeps under your skin without you even realising it. The atmosphere is tense right from the start, and it doesn’t let up. I found myself looking over my shoulder while playing, which is always a sign of a good horror game. The sound design is on point – every little noise has you second-guessing if something’s lurking nearby.

What really stands out, though, is the lore. There’s a deep backstory to uncover here that really pulls you into the world. It’s not just jump scares – it’s that lingering sense of something being very wrong that keeps you hooked.

The setting is dark, twisted, and honestly, a little unsettling. There’s a sense of danger at every turn, and even when you think you’re safe, the game finds a way to surprise you. The story is pretty engaging too, with enough twists to keep you hooked. It’s the kind of game that makes you think, “Wait, what just happened?” more than once.

The enemies are creepy as heck, and there are definitely moments where your heart skips a beat. It’s a mix of psychological horror and survival, and it’s done really well. Not sure how many times I jumped or had to pause to take a breath!

If you’re into horror games that actually manage to make you feel uneasy while offering an interesting story to dig into, Under ward is definitely worth a shot. It’s solid, it’s scary, and it’s got me hooked with its dark lore.

REALLY IMPORTANT FEEDBACK FROM A DEV TO ANOTHER (MADE WITH LOVE)
OK, HEAR ME OUT. This game actually has a lot of potential and a really solid gameplay loop. BUT there are some crucial things that may or may not be heading in the right direction:
•	First of all, the way you get rid of monsters by throwing random objects at them sounds great on paper, but in practice, it feels a bit lame. I mean, it's not that bad, but it feels out of place to defeat a hellish aberration by trowing a cup at it or stopping an overwhelming monster with just some random trash. It’s maybe not ideeal, but ehhh... I dunno. It would be better to have some kind of real weapon to defend yourself. (Not an actual gun—that would be dumb in a noise-based game.) Maybe a crowbar, a knife, or something along those lines. Alternatively, make the enemies a real threat to the player—some could be unstoppable, meaning you can only slow them down but not kill them. That way, the "noise" mechanic would actually feel like a necessary tool for survival rather than just a gimmick. The player should feel like they're in real danger—after all, they're retrieving test subjects that were left behind for a reason.
•	Now, the nurses. (Oh, the nurses...) I'm gonna be honest—they make the game look like those sussy "virus-free games" you see on cracked game sites (At least, that’s how it feels here in the West—sorry!). 
•	The gacha system in a horror game is maybe not a good idea. (It doesn't even show what's inside the gacha.) For a horror game, this kind of mechanic just doesn't fit. Maybe a point-based shop would work better—just keep it simple.
•	The physics on some objects just "explode", but that really is a technical issue
•	For atmosphere, it would be great if some test subjects actually moved inside their test tubes, if the lights flickered in certain moments, or if the game just felt a bit more alive.
•	The enemies behavior needs some work.
There’s a lot that needs to be done to make this game a real thrill, but it's actually a pretty good one.
BUT if you really want to make something big, then take the mechanics you have, add some good monsters, expand the maps, throw in some good lore, and relaunch this as a fresh new game—even in Early Access if you like anyways, you have something big in hands. 
I heard the devs really care about this game, so I really hope this reaches them. If any of you see this, I’d love to hear your opinion—feel free to respond! And if at any point I came off as rude, I sincerely apologize.
As always, have a nice day! :)

So to start off, KOFXIII patch notes are poorly documented outside of the old SRK Wiki (and forums), which in of itself doesn't list everything in one comprehensive list, or is well organized. They're probably buried somewhere else on the internet, too. But the reason that KOFXIII Steam Edition exists is because it runs a later arcade patch version from the console KOFXIII (version 1.1), however these are very small changes, mostly fixes for specific stuff. What exactly, I'm not 100% sure so feel free to correct me if needed. Point is, console KOFXIII is different from PC KOFXIII since they're different patches. Hence, this is also why KOFXIII GM did not immediately come to PC, while it released for modern consoles instead. Which is where we already start to run into issues...

To put rollback into Steam Edition, they would effectively have to retrofit the netcode into a different game file from console's release. KOFXIII GM Steam Edition, if everyone else's anecdotes are to be believed, is not the latest arcade patch, but the console patch that we have had for all these years. Meaning they just lazily ported the console KOFXIII GM to PC, slapped an upgrade price onto it for $7, and called it a day. And you're paying for access to netcode that doesn't even work. Which, by the way, initially had a typo in its listing claiming that the $20 version was the upgrade pack, not the $7 listing.

When you boot up the game, it boots up in fullscreen at 720p. In 2025. And the settings claim it's set at 1080p, when it's not. It says 1080p for borderless window, which is the setting I wanted anyways, but the fact it didn't even boot up to my native resolution is ridiculous. As far as I can tell, the only difference from Steam Edition is the fact that GM has the rollback, the console patch instead of latest arcade patch, and is otherwise the exact same game. Which would be fine... if the netcode worked. Of what I played, I had maybe 3 smooth matches. Console KOFXIII is also scuffed, the netcode isn't good there, either, but at least they beta tested it first. This port never got a beta test and it released alongside the City of the Wolves beta test. "The Headliners" VS "Content Warning"

Headliners definitely has a lot better premise and setting.
It's not just a generic, spooky, creepypasta, lovecraftian plane where you goof off over and over again.
It's a lot more comparable to something like Cloverfield or Gantz.
It's in a very urban, big-city environment with friendly civilians and military running around, and that really sets it apart from something like Content Warning or Lethal Company.

However, The Headliners really needs video recording (or at least a few seconds of audio attached to each picture?) in order to pull ahead of Content Warning.
There's only so much fun that you can pull out of "Oooo, look at this picture of you in front of a monster! Lol" over and over and over again.
The videos that I've saved from playing Content Warning with a buddy are some of the most treasured and memorable moments I have on MP4.
The pics from Headliners?... I forget about them completely ten seconds after I see them.

It's a really good game, but it has the potential to completely stomp Content Warning and Lethal Company in 2025 if they choose their next updates very carefully.

Is Phasmophobia a little too scary for you to enjoy?
Is Lethal Company a little too involved to get a good lobby going?

If you answered yes to both of these questions, then I recommend you give this game a try. It's a little less mechanically dense than the games mentioned above, but with new maps and monsters on the way according to devs, there is likely to be more to keep you on your toes as the game continues development. The less cryptic nuance to the game makes it more approachable, and the lobby connections have been reasonably reliable.

[h1]👍2/5. Get It While It's Hot![/h1]
[h2]Little Rough Around the Edges, but Off To A Good Start.[/h2]

[h2]OVERALL[/h2]

The Headliners is fun, and I’m looking forward to seeing how the developers continue to improve the game. With further optimization, bug fixes, and the introduction of new features, there is certainly potential for this to be a party game I could recommend on more than a once-or-twice-off experience. At its $6–8 price point, it’s a solid choice for a casual night of fun.

[h2]THE GAME & FIRST IMPRESSIONS[/h2]
The Headliners is a proximity chat and "extraction-like" photography stealth game. The objective is to make it through all scenarios without your team getting killed, revisiting areas as needed until you reach a predetermined "photo quality quota." You and your team will buy upgrades to both improve photo quality and protect yourselves.

In our first playthrough, my group of four casually explored each area for roughly two hours until we all died. Ultimately, we found ourselves drawn to the role of news anchors, as the game doesn't provide a clear objective beyond scoring points for photographing anomalies.

[h2]WHAT'S GOOD[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Encounter Variety[/b] - From both outside and within buildings, there are a handful of creatures to run into, and the way to approach in snapping photos will take some quick reacting and strategy. You can work together as a team to try to lure them out, or set up one of your friends as victims to get a more engaging shot. The game will reward you for getting brutal photos when your friends are sacrificed too, so long as the entire party isn't dead. Just remember to grab their camera. They died for that [i]totally sick shot.[/i]

[*][b]Surprising Visual Moments[/b] - There’s plenty of action happening (though sometimes only in certain areas). Cars get flipped, things explode, and civilians are tossed around— like Will Smith’s encounter with the Octopus-Alien Baby in Men in Black. Overall, a lot of "HOLY CRAP" and "WHAT THE HECK JUST HAPPENED" moments.

[*][b]Stream Potential/Screwing Around[/b] - First and foremost, I think this game is targeted toward streamers and people who want to record moments in games with their friends. If you're someone who likes to roleplay and are looking for a "funny moments highlight reel" kind of game, this is a good fit.
[/list]

[h2]WHAT CAN BE IMPROVED[/h2]
[list]

[*][b]Overall Framerate Optimization[/b] - Our group's first impressions was going right into the graphics settings to: A. Turn off the uncapped frames B. Figure out what is causing lag in the downtown segments. Especially outside, the game can inexplicably drop to very low frames. At times, It seems the game can only try to push out 5 FPS on capable hardware, and then after a forced game crash through my playthrough, the framerate was much closer to the capped 60FPS I was aiming for.

[*][b]Content[/b] - For $6-8, There is a decent amount of content to play through the game a few times. However, I’d like to see additional objectives, highlighted areas, and side-quests as the game continues to develop. (See suggestions below.)

[*][b]"I'm Lost!"[/b] - Although the game includes walkie-talkies for communication, more tools for leaving breadcrumbs—such as flares, trails, or markers—would be beneficial. Our group had to circle the building multiple times to regroup, as many indoor areas look very similar.

[*][b]"Have we been here before?"[/b] - Because a lot of indoor areas look similar, It's hard to tell if the location we just went to is worth getting photos. It's also a little disappointing to see that the signage outside isn't always relevant to what building you're about to go into. (e.g. A TV Sale promotion above the door that leads into a hotel lobby)

[*][b]There's More Fun Outside[/b] - Some buildings just didn't have much going on. Adding a "Hot/Cold" meter to indicate nearby anomalies might help pinpoint areas with more action. Relying solely on audio cues led our group to repeatedly searching inside buildings, only to find that most of the excitement was happening outside.

[*][b]UI & Reminders:[/b] 
--[b]Emoting[/b] -  You can earn bonus points by performing emotes while a creature is in the shot. Our group discovered this mechanic late in the game due to the only hint being the signage in the lobby. An early, subtle reminder—or even making it a designated objective—would improve the experience.

--[b]Camera Locator[/b] Once a friend dies, they may have to talk to you beyond the grave (cheating in Discord) where their camera is. Whether it be an included feature or as an upgrade you can get in the shop,a tool to scan where dropped cameras are would be great. A reminder / confirmation "You have X cameras left behind" before getting into the chopper would also be helpful.
[/list]

[h2]Suggestions:[/h2]
[*][b]Themed "Here's the Scoop" Objectives[/b] - Right now the game is a bit aimless. It's just "get the best shots" and go. If these scenarios were a little more fleshed out, with a brief on what to expect after the first outbreak (free for all mode), the devs could make some interesting stories briefing what's happening and what photos the press execs want.

[*][b]"Wanted" Objectives[/b] - It could be fun to have missions to seek out different kinds of shot at different star-level ratings of difficulty

[*][b]News Anchor Mode[/b] - Alongside photos, I think it would be fun to have a more integrated film-crew segment that differentiates from what's been seen in CONTENT WARNING :such as a studio briefing, on-scene reporting, or interviews with civilians and creatures. After reaching quota, it could be fun to have a segment to report "positive" news, like sunshine up ahead on the forecast, or new puppies being born.

[*][b]Escort Missions[/b] - The civilians already seem to loosely follow players around inside. Though we are just press, It could be a fun bonus objective to help bring anyone in danger to safety, with the incentive of getting "interviews" from them for extra points after they're outside.

[*][b]More Integrated Traps[/b] - Bear trap are nice, but there isn't something to get better shots for every creature.

This game is a great time for the price, and will produce a lot of laughs with your friends. There are definitely some things I wish were different though, and some things that need some more attention. 

New York is in the midst of an alien invasion. You play as a journalist who's job is to take pictures of all the crazy things that are currently happening in the city. Each round, you have to get a certain amount of points, and you get points by taking pictures. You get 10 pictures with the default camera and the crazier the picture, the more points it's worth. For example, taking a picture of an alien is X number of points, and can be multiplied by different factors. I.E. if the alien is attacking a survivor, attacking you, or causing mayhem. You can also get points for "being brave" which just means getting super up close and personal with the monster. 

You can upgrade your equipment such as your camera (which lets you take more pictures, higher quality pictures, better zoom, or better flash). All in all, this all creates a very fun and entertaining experience. 

THE GOOD
- Lots of alien variety
- Decent amount of gear to choose from
- Game play produces a lot of funny situations
- I enjoyed being able to decide if i wanted to play safe and take pictures from rooftops, or get dangerous and go in close. 
- The game can get intense at times outside of the buildings, which is where huge aliens will spawn

THE BAD
Game play can get stale after 5-6 hours, and I believe this is caused by a few factors. 
- First off, the game is pretty easy after you figure out what kind of pictures need to be taken, and at a certain point you're just snapping a ton of pictures for easy points. 
- I like the point system to a degree, but it sucks when you get just shy of the required points. This forces you to do a mission for a trivial amount of points, and getting more points then is required doesn't seem to have any benefit (I could be wrong, but I didn't notice it giving me more money)
- There should be a difficulty setting. I think the game gets too easy because each time you hit the required amount of points you get all three of your lives back. Lives are lost each round you do not hit the required amount of points. So even if you do not make enough points one round, you have two more chances. After hitting the required points you get all three lives back. I would like to see a difficulty setting so that you get three lives and that is it, this would make each round feel more intense and force players to take riskier pictures. 
- I wish there were more meaningful upgrades. For example, the flashlight upgrade seems pretty pointless to me. 
- The amount of points for pictures needs to be more consistent. I've taken multiple pictures of an alien point blank and get less then 100 points for it. This makes it even a bigger gamble, as approaching the more dangerous monsters can be fruitless. 
- You cannot take pictures through transparent surfaces, as it will count as just taking a picture of glass, which counts as 0 points. 

This game is a lot of fun though, and does provide a good amount of fun for the price.

I just finished Far Cry 2004 and that made me curious about the “Russian Far Cry” which was recently re-released on Steam. While not really a fair comparison, I did find some similarities and familiar vibes. For starters, we’re in the tropical Pacific with bright colors and plenty of sunlight, and most levels that take place on islands (as opposed to ships) provide at least a small degree of player freedom when it comes to solving one’s objectives, but don’t expect the same semi-open areas as in Far Cry. Pirate Hunter is considerably more linear by comparison. By the very nature of the environment, the same applies to counter-piracy missions where we have to board cargo ships and free the hostages. Then again, the aircraft carrier level in FC, as well as all indoor levels really, weren’t any different, no?

Graphically, I thought Pirate Hunter looked a couple years older than it actually is, but it still created a convincing and immersive representation of the jungle. Lots of lush vegetation with sun rays shining through, leaves visually reacting to movement and gunfire and the developers even took the time to populate near-shore underwater environments with flora and fauna. Pirate Hunter also implements nVidia PhysX for pretty decent particle effects such as explosions and dust being thrown into the air, and a handful destructible objects like wooden huts. Made gunfights more exciting.

The AI wasn’t the exactly the most capable one around I’d say, but they did offer credible opposition and were more than willing to approach from multiple directions when possible and flush me out of cover with grenades. There’s no grenade indicator however. I think they also try to respect concealment behind vegetation for line-of-sight calculations. At least they didn’t feel like those overbearing, all-seeing hitscanners in Chrome or Chrome SpecForce, so that’s a plus. Though I do believe those pirates were unrealistically bullet-spongy on normal difficulty; they’re mostly rocking T-shirts yet can tank rifle fire like a champ.

Little to complain about in terms of player movement or gunplay. If you’ve played the original Far Cry, it all feels very similar except for the absence of prototype weapons. Sounded weighty too. The main difference is the addition of bullet time (all the rage back then!), called “adrenaline” here, which is a consumable item you pick up in the game world. Does precisely what you’d expect. Use it to rush a large group of enemies or overwhelm hostage guards before they can react. Killing more people in general or with the knife in particular gives a small bonus to bullet time duration.

Another area where Pirate Hunter differs from Far Cry is the addition of teammates. Most of the time, they’re an additional gun or two you can tell to hold position or follow you around. You can freely assume direct control of anyone. If anyone goes down, you can typically run over and revive them without penalty. By contrast, certain missions are broken down into multiple segments with one specific character each. Sniper shoots some dudes, then we phase back to the pointman, that sort of stuff. Also, there’s regenerating health only in Pirate Hunter.

In terms of the story, dare I say I found it more engaging than Far Cry? Most of the plot was relatively straightforward and sensible until the last quarter of the campaign… if we’re copying Far Cry, why don’t also drop the ball in terms of plot progression, right? Did Pirate Hunter really need boomer shooter-style bossfights which go completely against the mostly realistic setup of the rest of the game? Well, at least the game developers put a surprising amount of effort into those cut scenes and while I’m sure something was lost in the translation, hiring a decent script writer and a handful of passable English voice actors went a long way to made me not to immediately want to skip it all. Shame they couldn’t do the same for the mission briefing text because it’s truly laughable.

After you’re done with the story, you can go back and replay chapters for speedrunning or just to get a better score if you wish. There’s secondary as well as hidden objectives in most missions and some of them even unlock optional levels that didn’t feel like filler at all, surprisingly. However, I disliked the fact that hidden timers can occasionally pop up for certain objectives, so you’re going to fail and reload at least once.

On a technical level, Pirate Hunter liked to crash during level transitions. The game has frequent checkpoints and there’s also quicksaving, so no big problem. What was a problem is that at least for me, the game became progressively more unstable in later levels, to the point of barely being able to load into the final mission at all without everything graphical being horribly broken and unplayable! In general, heavy particle effects could crash the game and there were persistent lighting as well as shadow issues too. So in the end, I settled on three configurations, swapping as required for every single map: native rendering, through dgVoodoo2 or through DXVK. Otherwise I simply could have not finished the campaign.

Also don’t forget to install the WMV9 codec which is linked on the store page for cutscene playpack.

Overall, I came away pretty impressed by Pirate Hunter. I’ve played many low-budget titles of this era and PH is a lot more sophisticated and polished than most in my opinion. Very playable if it weren’t for major issues with stability, not a thrown-together mess either, as obviously a lot of effort and thought went into this piece of software. It’s a shame then that DIOsoft only ever released one game, right?

Painting-by-number meets minesweeper.

What I like:
+ The mouse controls work very well once you learn them.
+ Relaxing game
+ Having up to 4 colors adds an interesting layer to the "logic" puzzle of minesweeper
+ Drawing pictures helps a bit to counter the inherent problem of 'having to guess' that sometimes happen in minesweeper since you can 'guess' along the picture.
+ While the game seemed a bit expensive at first, I think the value is fair considering the amount of puzzles included.
+ Looking forward to seeing the completed museum !

What I don't like:
- The 'perfect' picture system feels out of place considering the 'cozy' theme, especially when you are forced to guess a color. This does not matter for small pictures but it's kinda frustrating to have to start over 30 minutes into a drawing.
- The choice of pictures are all over the place theme-wise. One second you are drawing a 'slime', the next a 'planetary rover'. This mitigates the advantage of drawing a picture since most of the time you don't really understand what you are drawing until the very end. Knowing the 'name' of the picture in advance would really help mitigate this.
- The 'classic mode' has all the problems of regular minesweeper with none of the advantages of drawing an actual picture.
- The 'custom mode' lacks features/tools to help convert an image into a puzzle. It will take 'software developer' level knowledge to make it work automatically and the alternative is the equivalent of completing a puzzle in reverse in a drawing tool, which kinda kills the idea of doing the puzzle in the first place. I would have preferred a tool to import an actual picture, followed by a 'cropping / resizing'  of the area to keep for the puzzle + an algorithm to keep only the lines.
- Would have liked having more music tracks

Technical points:
- The game menus do not support my widescreen monitor in fullscreen 3444x1440 (21:9 aspect ratio). I have to play the game in 'windowed' mode to compensate.
- It's not very clear that clicking 'Main Menu' in the middle of a puzzle will save that puzzle.
+ Game works fine under Nobara Linux using Proton compatibility.
+ No crash or performance slowdown.

Everything from the actual card game, to the soundtrack, to the art style oozes charm. Very glad I picked this up and I only wish I had more time to play it.

Really fun ccg that has an extremely interesting turn system where both players essentially share the same turn and one player passing forces the other to pass as well, which leads to a ton of depth and frequent decision making. Already shortly after the game's released in early access there's plenty of fun cards and strategies to make decks around, so I'm really looking forward to future updates when even more are added!

The game is SUPER unbalanced. This may as well be an actual sweaty TCG. When the game isn't based on real life tournaments and meta, there shouldn't be one correct deck, but in this game there is, it's Dark Fire and energy generating bugs, that's it. It get so boring and annoying, it feels like real TCGs I gave up on years ago.

From now on, unless the dev proves to be exceptional in terms of their responses, I will no longer be avoiding leaving negative reviews on EA products.

Why does this matter? Because now instead of carefully crafting feedback and leaving it in the discussion forums, only to be ignored by the dev and assaulted by other owners of the game going YEAH BUT I LIKED IT, I can just leave a thumbs down and not have to care about whether or not the dev is actually getting any value from my feedback. I can disallow comments on my reviews and only have to put up with clown stickers, and that's not nearly as bad.

To that end, this game sucks and I don't recommend buying it. It has barely any content for the price, a ton of the card 'designs' are just already existing sprites sloppily edited into a frame, the way cards display text is a mess, the game arbitrarily locks fun and advanced mechanics behind level barriers requiring you to effectively play baby mode until you get to late game and realize all the boring lvl 1 monsters in your deck aren't actually meant to be played, they're just there to smoosh together to make bigger and cooler things.

The UI and interface feel clunky and obtuse, the way mechanics are staggered makes certain strategies and colors/builds more powerful than others, and there are at least 3 unaddressed balance issues in game that result in either tier 0 decks or FTKs that make interaction meaningless. I would go into detail about what these are but the dev doesn't seem to care so why should I.

The end.

I am writing this review in hopes that the game developers will see it and perhaps take into account some suggestions. But also, this game is really a lot of fun!

1. Opening packs is GREAT! Dopamine hit every time. I do play with a MTG mod, so I can't say anything about the artwork per se, but it is so much fun to open up the cards and then sell them. 

2. Interactive customers is fantastic. Having the opportunity to trade directly with them is fun. I just wish I could offer them a different trade. I often don't have the card they are searching for, so I wish I had the opportunity to say I have a different card or perhaps to offer money for their card. The customers have some really good cards sometimes, so it sucks that I have to decline quite often. (And yes, I have opened over 1000 packs, so it's not like I lack cards in general)

3. The range of products is pretty great. Again, I do play with a mod, but the fact the mod is able to overlay the majority of the products speaks a lot to the variety. 

4. The shelving is pretty decent. I would honestly like to change the warehouse racks, though. Because of the variety of products, I need like 50 warehouse shelving units because I am only allowed to stock the same product boxes per shelf. I would change it so you could put different product boxes on the same shelves. It need only apply to the warehouse shelving unit to just help with the overflow of stock

5. Having workers is pretty cool. The fast cashier is amazing and I would love to have 10 of him. I have a gripe though with the restocking option for workers. The workers....don't really restock well. Yes, they grab the right product and put it on the shelves (and the speed depends on the worker). My issue is what happens AFTER they restock the shelf. They just drop the box on the floor instead of putting it away. Now, I thought this might be because I didn't have warehouse shelves, but even when I purchased warehouse shelves, I found the workers would not grab the product from those shelves to do the restocking, nor would they put the boxes away. This means I have to run around cleaning up after them--I might as well just restock the shelves myself. Along those same lines, the price setting option for workers isn't great. I'd like it if I could tell them to round UP, rather than to just round. I was losing out on money because the worker went around and set the prices to below market price with rounding down. I realize I could tell the worker to do a percentage above market price, but my customers have been finicky and complain when things are "too expensive" so it would be great to have an option to tell the worker to either round up or round down. 

6. The player tables are AMAZING. I have a good 16 tables in my shop. They actually make A LOT of money for my store. The trick is to make sure you are managing a specialized event every day. As your shop increases in level, special events unlock that you can then run at your store, making you even more money. My only issue I have with the tables are that NPCs sometimes sit at them and do nothing. And when end of day hits, I still have an NPC just sitting at the table, NOT MAKING ME MONEY. Something needs to change about that. The only way I can get them to leave is to hit q when facing the table, which makes the table move slightly, causing the NPC to get up and leave. I don't think the NPC needs to necessarily just leave at 9pm, but if there could be an interaction where you let them know it's closing time so they leave would actually be good. Because even turning the open sign to closed didn't make the NPCs leave.

7. I love that I am able to box up cards that are low value to just sell, which helps me go through the thousands of cards I have in my binder. I wish I could differentiate it a bit more. For example, boxing up cards that range from $.01 to $.51 is fine to sell at a certain price. But when I need to box up cards that range from $.51 to $1.00, I'd like if that box could be a separate price. You put 100 cards into each box. That could be $100 for me if I sold each $1 card separately. But I don't get a chance to because I have so many cards and try to sell the higher price ones first. So maybe it would be nice to not just box up 100 cards, but maybe be able to box up like 50 cards or 10 cards depending on the pricing of the cards and then they could be separate prices. 

8. I'm still trying to figure out how to get customers to buy my super expensive cards I have. I have one card that is market priced at over $16k. My customers have no problem purchasing cards up to like $3k, but I have noticed my $16k is just sitting there, not getting purchased. I didn't even put it above market price. My customers just keep saying that it is a fair price but that they are broke. I wonder if my shop level isn't high enough yet (currently level 36)? I want to get the achievement of being able to sell a $10k card. Maybe more hours will lead to that. Not sure. 

9. I wish there was a way to see profit throughout the day and not just when you hit enter to the end the day. Yes, you can see the money up in the righthand corner, but that is just the money you currently have, NOT the profit made for the day. It would be good to have a separate app on the phone that lets you see current profit for the day but also see past profits so you can compare easily to see if you are going up or down. It might also be good to see how much of each item has been sold over the course of the game. Yes, you can see the market price and see it's history as well, but your own store should have stats as well to look at during any time. It can really help you figure out which items you should have less of and what you should have more of

Overall, I still think this is a really fun game. I think it is even more fun with mods (like pokemon or MTG) because it helps spice up the items you can sell each game. I do highly recommend it.

An Addictive and Immersive TCG Shop Experience!

I'm genuinely impressed by how fun and engaging TCG Card Shop Simulator is! The entire vibe of running a trading card game shop, similar to a cozy comic book store, is incredibly inviting and downright addictive.

This game is all about collecting cards, developing your store, and fostering a TCG community with your shop at the center. While it's clear that the game utilizes base assets for the shop management system, the concept is well executed.

One area for improvement would be deepening the sense of a real community, making interactions more dynamic, charismatic, etc. increasing replayability. I'd love to see more flexibility in my options, allowing me to feel like I'm truly engaging with pseudo-real people and shaping the shop’s future in a more immersive way.

That said, this is a very nice game, and I highly recommend it. Congrats to the developer!

A slightly more relaxed shop simulator - I'm not running around like a headless chicken trying to stock shelves and order items but I still feel like I'm progressing steadily. I have to save for upgrades, but not for so long that it becomes frustrating, checkout is smooth enough that I'm still doing it myself 13 hours in, and it's genuinely exciting to open card packs! I'm also excited for the future since it looks like they plan to make the card game playable! The only critiques I have are pretty minor: some mechanics aren't explained very well (spraying cleaner, bundling cards), and the cards/dice/etc are in one app on your phone but board games etc are in a different one.

TCG Card Shop Simulator is an engaging and fun way to experience the fast-paced world of managing a trading card shop. As a fan of simulation games, I find the shop management mechanics particularly enjoyable. It’s satisfying to buy new stock, keep an eye on the market prices, and adjust the shop’s offerings to ensure maximum profitability. There’s a real sense of strategy in how you balance inventory and pricing, making each decision feel important.

The aesthetics of the game are quite pleasing, and the overall visual design adds to the charm of running a card shop. While the humanoid characters are functional, I think there's room for improvement here – hopefully, as the game’s budget allows for future updates, we might see more refined models and animations.

One of the best features in TCG Card Shop Simulator is the addition of licensed products, like Ultra Pro items. It’s a nice touch that adds authenticity to the experience, and I’m excited to see what other licensed products they’ll add down the line.

Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys simulation games. It offers a lot of fun, strategy, and room for growth, especially if you love the trading card scene. Looking forward to future updates!

Having played over 40 hours of this game in the space of a few short days, in my opinion this is one of the few titles that has me coming back time and time again for just one more pack opening or just one more day of trade in the store. Very fun, very addictive and very much up my street, being a trading card and collectible lover myself.

Tasked with opening, running, stocking and furnishing your own TCG shop, being able to watch your fledgling store slowly grow into a card and collectible empire over time is extremely satisfying. Keeping the shelves stocked and updated with the latest products, hosting TCG events for your customers, hiring (and sometimes firing) employees and even giving stinky patrons a good douse of deodorant are all key elements to growing your business, with a lot of fun and profit to be had along the way.

Being able to open packs for yourself and to either keep or sell the cards you pull is a huge feature of the game for me, and where the fun really lies. Either build your card albums with all of your prized pulls to satisfy your inner collector, or put your most expensive cardboard for sale in the store to accelerate your business growth. From time to time, a customer will come in to sell you a random card or offer a trade for a card you already have. Sometimes the juice isn't worth the squeeze, but other times you may be able to buy or trade for a card for much lower than market price and flip for a tidy profit.

With a good range of products to sell including card packs/boxes, dice and sleeves, figurines and even comic books, the game does a great job of making you feel like you are running a fun hobby store, but with only an £11 price tag instead of the many £1000s it would cost to open and operate in real life! The addition of official products such as Ultra PRO is also a really nice touch, and I hope more of these real life products are put into the game.

There are some improvements I feel the game could benefit from however. Although the game is fairly simple to play and the mechanics in general are quite approachable, I do wish the more managerial side of things was further fleshed out. Things such as automatic reordering of low stock, a deeper dive into the actual products sold and what customers are more interested in rather than a simple number of total products sold that day, an ability to see stock levels of your shop from a glance in the menu and to see historical sales data and trends to make better decisions for your store would be great additions to the game. I would also like to see the customer reviews being more accurate and descriptive, as on occasion I have been given a 1-star review due to a product not being in store, when in fact it was stocked on the shelves and ready to sell. None of these detract from my enjoyment of the game however, and I do understand that there are various mods out there to help facilitate these improvements and more.

Please also note that when purchasing cards from customers, be extra careful to enter the exact amount you are willing to pay, and not add another 0 or other number by accident. I have done this by mistake once, and overpaid for a card with no warning or safeguard to prevent this from happening. Definitely a lesson learned, but I made back the loss within the day so it wasn't too detrimental! This doesn't happen when you are giving change to customers or processing card payments however, as the game will tell you if you've given incorrect change or keyed the wrong amount into the card reader, so no worries on that front!

The game seems to be updated pretty regularly, with a roadmap currently outlined for future updates shown in-game. Exciting future updates include a playable version of the TCG within the game, a more extensive product range and various QoL improvements to make an already great game even better.

Zerkaa has a great playthrough of this game on his YouTube channel, as well as a prologue demo being available on Steam so you can try before you buy and get a feel for how fun and truly addicting this game is.

Fantastic stuff, I will likely be playing this for a good while longer, eagerly awaiting the roadmap additions to come to fruition. Probably the best £11 I've spent on a game the past few years. Highly recommended from a fellow TCG enthusiast!

This game CAN be quite fun and definitely has a ton of potential. But there are several issues I have with the game that lead me to be unable to recommend the game in its current state. Hopefully these can be fixed quickly as the game is otherwise incredibly fun with an interesting combination of progression systems.

The permanent rune-stone progression system has the potential to be a very fun way of specializing certain characters to have the stats you want, however the lack of permanent storage besides the active stones means it is often better to either pick general stats, or only focus on one character.

The spirit affinity system for relics means each run has an additional layer of build-crafting potential, with my only complain being that there doesn't seem to be a way to inspect the elemental status effects to see what they actually do.

[h3]Issues I have with the game(I will update this section as more issues come up, and others are fixed):[/h3]

1. I was able to fix this issue by switching to a different controller, however the original controller did not have any issues in other games.
    The game has a ton of trouble with reading inputs. Movement, attacks, dodges, directional attacks, any button press has somewhere between 25-50% chance to simply do nothing. This makes boss fights and chaotic rooms where you're dodging 4-5 AoE attacks impossible to complete without taking damage.


2. THIS ISSUE HAS BEEN RESOLVED BY AN UPDATE.
    Enemy's not dying fully. Some enemies will die and still be target-able by certain relics and skills. This is very obvious on purple hair(I forgot her name XD) where you can see the arcane stacks hovering around a empty squares where enemies used to be. This was originally a minor annoyance, however it caused me to be unable to progress past the [spoiler]cultist [/spoiler] boss as there were 3 copies of the boss left alive despite there being no more health bar, and no way to damage them.


3. The main quest? I have 2 quests that I discovered within 5 runs of starting the game. Both require me to talk to someone in the hub area. One NPC in the hub area says nothing when I talk to them. The other gives me the same dialogue each time with no progress.

The game has potential; it's fun, and challenging

This game is a seriously happy surprise. The three characters all play totally differently, and despite the fact the game really only has four directions and two buttons, it gets a ton of strategic depth as you level up your ability, find new artifacts, and learn how to beat down enemies.

The quickest way to imagine it: Necrodancer but you don't need to worry about the beat. Move as you need, dodge as you can, beat down as you wish. The abilities change things up quite a bit: a mage setting up explosions, a monk prepping a Yatyatatatatata attack, a knight getting bleed stacks in. 

And then you find a weapon that makes it so every attack you do does double damage... but to a random enemy in the room, so you go hide and beat on the golem while trying to dodge its attacks and kill everyone but him by luck. Or you get the Beat totem, a totem that has 500hp, and every hit you do to it hits every enemy in the room. Just gotta be careful to not break it, or it comes back with much less hp. 

Or maybe you find a hive of bees that go along with your attacks. There's a ton in here to find and upgrade, and I've barely scratched the surface. Highly recommended even at the early access stage, I can't wait to see where it goes with development.

The game is challenging but in a good way, still needs a lot of polish and work to become something really great.

The one thing that really doesn't make sense to me is some character's abilities.

One character's trait does DOT damage (bleed) but the bosses / enemies enter invincible states so often that DOT damage doesn't make sense considering how low the DOT ticks for.
 
Another character's trait requires you stand in place and let loose a barrage of attacks - but in a game where you're pretty much expected to be constantly on the move, this trait makes the absolute least sense. Would like to see a rework on these traits or new ones entirely as they're quite hard to play/build around.

Other than that - i'd say its worth the price tag.

A pretty good game for an early access one, so here are a few good and bad things about it:
Goods: 
- World building gives out massive Made in Abyss vibe, which is amusing. 
- Have "break the pot" kind of stuff from Zelda games, which is relaxing in a way.
- Characters have unique kits and level up branches. I'm sure devs will port more characters from their first game to this one over time, cannot wait to try them all.
- Roguelike system is niche (map generation, relics/artifacts, spirits), same as characters, artifacts will be ported here soon.
- Combat is literally the best thing so far: real time, interactive between your abilities and enemies'. 
- Permanent upgrades are generally good: runes are your "equipment" and they are random based, while stat-upgrades are farming based and linear.
- Beautiful pixel graphic. I gotta say, artistically this game is a gem of pixel on it own!
- Nice and pleasant songs and themes. Very engaging choice of sounds.
- Balanced difficulty, might lean on hard/DS side a bit: enemies' and bosses' attack patterns aren't simple but observable and learnable.

Bads:
- Game bugs (freeze character a bit when using active trait on cooldown, soft lock in some bosses scenarios which render them invincible, or invisible blocks that keep you in place... still counting and reporting them now). 
- It would be nice if players can have their own chest to store excessive runes which were forged from blacksmith, so players can switch them from time to time for different characters and builds.
- Movement and attack inputs might be a bit lagging for real time action combat, I'm already adapted to it, but this can be a problem for new players.
- Little content currently (lore, characters, artifacts, spirits' abilities, upgrades, runes' stats), might not scratch enough itch or persuade players to spend more time once they maxed out all permanent upgrades and clear all present stages. But hey, it is an early access game, so this might not be a problem in the end!

Au Revoir is an homage to old 3D point-and-click games while offering a terrifying glimpse into the future if Elon Musk's Neuralink actually worked.

Jokes aside, this game gives me vibes I haven't felt since playing Grim Fandango which is one of my favorite point-and-click games. You control Tristan who collects the synthetic brains of rich folk who have enough money to afford it then upload their consciousness into a new body and host. The game does a great job of illustrating the rather bleak and cyberpunk future in a rundown city controlled by a corporation. 

The puzzles are not difficult but still they challenge the player's observational skills as well as their reading comprehension. The game does not give hints at all in all honesty but at least the puzzles are intuitive enough for me personally. The majority of the time will be spent walking around the area to see what else needs to be done before the player can progress to a new location.

The game is pretty short and I am not kidding when I say that you will be walking a majority of the time which is not fine considering how SLOW the player moves. It suffers heavily from inconsistent sprinting and the weird camera changes that can be a bit disorienting. Other bugs include the player sometimes being able to walk through walls and doors such as at the apartment.

Other than all that, I recommend this game if you're in a mood for a short cyberpunk puzzle adventure. The atmosphere is what kept me in along with the story.

It is a short cheap cyberpunk adventure game that will give you a little entertainment but one that will leave you wanting for more. The puzzles are mostly simple and the interactions with the game world are very limited.

The premise is interesting- you work for a company that uploads people's consciousness to synthetic brains (for a price), but I never got super invested in it. I just didn't feel connected to the character I was playing as; I would have liked more of an introduction to him or a reason to care about him (or anyone in this world). 

Overall, I don't think the game fully clicked with me, but it's well made for what it is and I think the developers could expand on this concept and make something even better in the future :)

A game that by the end of it gets so difficult, I'm not sure if anyone can be "good" at the final boss.

To start off, this is less of a rhythm game than it might seem at first. There is definitely a strong rhythm component as all battles are to the beat that changes depending on the music, which depends on the enemy; however there is a lot of randomness to which button you need to press at any given time, meaning that even if there are charts present they're not really learnable in the traditional sense. This does turn up the difficulty, as every battle is essentially a sightread, and the further you go in the less time you have to react to the notes.

In short, it's more of a reflex game set to the rhythm. And it looks great.

Now the way you interact with battles is via a dungeon crawling wrap where you try and find the exit as you stumble into new enemies, which give you new loot to change up your loadout. True to the steam page, the gear you get is feasible even long after the level you get it, since its stats that change not the general power level. And I'm pretty sure I only managed to defeat the final boss thanks to a vitality chestplate that was amongst the earliest loot I got. But with such variation comes a lot of unexplained confusion.

I have no idea what half of the stats do. I vaguely comprehend that power level is how hard you hit, and that melee/ranged/magic powers, as well as slow/fast notes powers correspond to enemy weaknesses. Not quite sure how since it's hard to test different loadouts to compare the damage, but I vaguely understand it. But then there are the other effects: Vitality, Tank, Reflex, Fast. I think the first two correspond to health (how much you gain/lose) but no clue about the other two, or any more that might be on equipment I didn't use. There is a strong lack of explanation, and there isn't that much point in changing your loadout until freemode comes around. You don't know which enemy you're gonna face, so tinkering with your loadout only makes sense at the boss, and only once you fought it once and died. (and as a side-note, I only got 1/10 of the unique equipments that are meant to be dropped by bosses, though not sure if due to bad luck or low droprates)

And while on the topic of negative stuff, there have been a few softlocks where battle summary wouldn't appear after a won battle, or I couldn't move anywhere but up after dying to a boss. A bit annoying, but the game autosaves very frequently, so it was not a massive roadblock

Finally, the mechanics. Each boss introduces a new mechanic, which then gets used by all enemies in future levels. With the exception of the first boss, whose mechanic stays unique, and last boss, who doesn't have enemies after it. Due to that last one in particular I would've probably preferred if the mechanics were introduced at the start of a zone, and then the bosses were a final challenge, but that's just a matter of preference. What is important though, is that this causes a steady ramp up of difficulty, meaning that even when the input simplifies the game does not.


TL;DR is that this is a rhythm reflex title with a constantly increasing difficulty. It has some bugs and design flaws, but the gameplay is solid if you can keep up with the notes

I wish I had supported Criminal / Liminal Border on Steam (instead of the silly store Johren with their dumb DRM) a lot earlier. That way, I could’ve helped spread the word quicker on the platform about what I consider one of the most overlooked and underrated modern visual novels of all time.

That said, Liminal Border 3 / Criminal Border 3rd Offense is the third part of a four-episode series developed by Purplesoft (Amatsutsumi), written by Kazuki Fumi (9-nine, Kimagure Temptation), and illustrated by hentai artist Same Manma (I don't read her doujins, but it's impressive there's a female H-artist out there).

I already thought the first two episodes were basically perfect, taking advantage of the episodic VN format as best they could. The pacing was excellent from the start, with protag Itsuki accidentally creating a digital drug that causes intense horniness, leading him into a gritty psychological thriller involving the Yakuza and various parts of the underworld.

Despite all the dark stuff—gangs, drugs, and people potentially considering killing him—there’s a strong emotional core that has stood strong throughout: Itsuki’s character development from a loser nobody to someone willing to sell his soul for power, all for what he perceives as the greater good. The surprisingly wholesome bonds he forms in this dark, gritty drama drive his incredible character growth.

Criminal Border 1 and 2 were already near-perfect, balancing character building slice-of-life moments with hard-hitting drama at just the right times and with proper buildup.

But somehow, Criminal Border 3 blows the previous two episodes away—basically going from perfect to… even more perfect.

Sadly, I can't say more cuz spoilers. Let’s just say some real s*** goes down, and maybe Itsuki wasn't ready to pick a fight with certain people. But all it did was strengthen his resolve even more. And it helps that the heroine this chapter focuses on—Meryl—not only becomes one of his best allies but also gets the best character development of any heroine so far.

I can’t say anymore, but if/when Liminal Border 4 / Criminal Border Life Sentence (aka the final episode) gets translated, I will drop literally everything to read it. Even if the ending somehow disappoints, what’s been built up in Criminal Border 1-3 can’t be understated—the excellent cast, wholesome interactions, surprisingly down-to-earth setting, and amazing pacing.

Whether you decide to catch up now or wait for all four parts to be available in your language… I hope you support/read this series. It’s one of the best dark, gritty psychological thriller stories I’ve ever read.

With higher stakes than the previous parts, this third episode is thrill to read through, a constant fast pace keeps it consistently engaging.

Waiting (un)patiently for the last part.

What started as a pretty average episode, by the halfway it far surpassed anything done by the series so far. I was shocked, jaw open staring at the screen in disbelief. Kazuki Fumi has the biggest pair of nuts for doing this... and it WORKED. Just a complete shift in tone, and it just got real. Meryl was the focus of this part, and she has now become best girl. Criminal Border keeps getting better and better, raising the stakes, turning up the heat. And I'm all for it. It's just that good. I am already hooked and can't wait for Life Sentence.

A new game from William R. Fisher III, a honoured veteran of B-games, is a reimagining of his game that started a long (seven games!) series: The Last Half of Darkness. It is, in fact, its fourth incarnation, for the first time in 3-D with free movement.
The core gameplay is still exploration, looking for items and using them in proper places. It's not by any means a "walking simulator", unlike an average UE/Unity horror game, and it is certainly much more memorable than most of them, even if you've never played original game, and if you have, you might sometimes feel like you know for sure what items you need, but you don't know where they are this time. Pretty much everything from original is expanded and carefully brought to a more modern environment, while maintaining old-school B-movie feeling. There's some shooting action now, though, including one boss fight, but it's not that difficult even for me, and I'm bad at shooter games.
The game is made with lots of love and attention to details, and while original game and its previous versions were very imperfect in every way, this reimagining feels much more mature and solid. I haven't noticed any bugs, and all the bugs other players encounter get fixed less than in a day.
A must have for fans of classic horror adventure games and low-budget horror movies.
