A quick note about the game before the review: I played the original 1989 version in 1990 and fell in love with it. I had no idea this game was even coming. It came up in my discovery queue. This game will have you do a TON of backtracking. There is no hand holding, and also there is no map besides the outside area, which is also very basic. If these things are deal breakers for you, it's probably best to move on. If you don't mind these things, then onward we go!

This little indie game can tax your machine. Even with a 4090, a 12700k and 32MB DDR5 RAM, running this on cinematic settings at 4K could eat the frames at times. Overall I was at 90-110 most of the time, occasionally capping at 120 and dropping all the way down to 50 in a place or two (not that you need high frames for this game). The game can be completed on the first playthrough in roughly 3-5 hours. It took me nearly 6.5 due to having my brightness down and completely missing a door that I spent almost 45 minutes looking for. The story is expanded upon with the original, with more lore, combat and extra puzzles. It's fairly relaxing with tense moments. Combat is quite basic, but that's all it needs to be for this game.

The puzzles are all fairly simple, with an occasional moment where you might scratch your head for a minute or two. Some of the game can be completed in whatever order you choose but for the most part it will all lead you back to a linear path, so don't be afraid to go off and explore. Eventually you will find yourself where you need to be.

This game doesn't hold your hand. There are hints in the form of coins that you can find in game. You can use these coins at a certain location to get hints about what you should do next if you really feel stuck. Bullets for your gun are plentiful (and ultimately infinite if you know where to look) and certain other consumables will respawn at certain locations if you need them. Death works similar to the Tomb Raider games where you will be put back to the start of the area the game last saved, but any inventory items you picked up will remain with you, or any ammo/consumables you used will remain gone. Speaking of saving, you can save any time by hitting escape and forcing the game to autosave. It also autosaves any time you enter an area. The only thing I was disappointed in was the final area. I loved the final fight and the actual ending. It was somewhat frustrating to get around though due to having no map of the area. The final part of the game could really stand to have a map. Other than that, I have no complaints.

Overall I think this game was a steal for $15, especially if you loved the original game. It's a great way to spend 5 hours of your time. I highly recommend supporting the developer. If you're in the mood for a psychological horror game with a little bit of basic combat, you should look no further than this. Here's hoping we will see remakes of parts 2 and 3 as well. I've been a huge fan of the original Last Half of Darkness ever since I played it as a kid in the early 90s - so much so that I revisit it regularly. In many ways this remake remains true to its original, for better or worse. Fisher's games are often a little rough around the edges, but in a very charming kind of way. Playing the original game as a kid was the first time I realized that someONE has created this - not a big faceless company, but a person with a passion for video games, just like myself - an experience that this remake manages to faithfully recreate. This is part of the fun, and you will need to accept that in order to fully enjoy this game.

The cons, most of which I expected when I made the purchase:
* A few major graphical glitches and frame rate drops, especially noticeable in outdoor areas and on the Steam Deck. Human characters look a bit stiff. 
* Writing could be better; there are spelling errors, and that cringe inducing poetry is better left in the past
* Terrible voice acting 
* Gunplay - it doesn't add anything to the game; getting sprung by randomly appearing enemies while trying to solve puzzles is more frustrating than scary. Ditto for limiting flashlight batteries.

Pros:
* Visual design - this is where WRF excels. The mansion looks fantastic and exploration is fun and exciting.
* Atmosphere (or "eerie ambience", I should say) - this is is the reason I keep coming back to the original, and Fisher manages to recreate that feeling in a modern way.
* Works well as a remake - it feels like a new game but also familiar if you have played the original. 
* Simple but fun and effective puzzles.
* Passion project - what Fisher manages to accomplish as a solo developer is nothing short of impressive, and the fact that it is recognizable as a passion project makes it a deeply personal experience. The game just pulls you in with its rustic charm. 

If you are a fan of the original, you will get what you expect and you will very likely love it. If you are looking for a polished game with high production values, you might be better off checking out the likes of Outlast and Layers of Fear (both of which I'm sure Fisher drew inspiration from - and maybe they were inspired by his original?). If you are curious to find out what this incredibly unique franchise is all about you should definitely give this game a try.

Even in its Early Access phase, this game fails to deliver any value commensurate with its price. From the very beginning to the end, the game balance is severely flawed, making it virtually impossible to enjoy any aspect of gameplay.

* A message for the developers and my own reflections are included at the end of this review.

[h2]Expectations vs. Reality in a Movie Theater Management Simulator[/h2]
Movie Selection
Although the game is marketed as a movie theater management simulator, the option to choose which movie to screen is merely superficial. The films available are actually AI-generated content created by others, and the original credits remain intact. This lack of originality and disregard for creative ownership is a major drawback.

[h2]Hiring Staff and Delegating Tasks[/h2]
The concept of hiring staff to manage screenings and operations sounds promising at first. However, once you delegate these tasks, you as the player are left with nothing substantial to do other than watching a simulation. The interactive and engaging aspects are completely lost, reducing the experience to a monotonous series of automated tasks.

[h2]Lackluster Expansion and Repetitive 3D Graphics[/h2]

While there is a feature to expand your theater, the core gameplay itself barely changes. You’re just repeating the same dull tasks: assigning seats, selling snacks, cleaning, and dealing with troublesome customers. On top of that, scheduling essentially boils down to deciding how to fill a 14-hour daily slot. In the early stages, you’re stuck with three- or four-hour films that aren’t very popular, but before long, you can easily license far more popular one-hour films, so there’s virtually no strategic depth in planning your schedule.

I only watch around 70 movies a year myself, but I still think there were better ways to simplify this concept into a game. For example, rather than limiting movies to a single genre, they could’ve introduced multiple genres and given users different preferences. If all I want to do is run a money-making simulation, I might as well play a clicker game instead of something branded as a simulation game. There’s also an option to place arcade machines, but they just sit there unused.

The short animation of loading popcorn is the only thing that feels even slightly cute, and overall, the experience boils down to tedious routine work.

[h2]Additional Grievances[/h2]
[h3]Bizarre Beverage Skill Check[/h3]
The game includes a skill check related to beverages that seems tacked on without any meaningful integration, leaving one to question whether the developer even played the game themselves.

[h3]Tedious Cleaning Mechanics[/h3]
Cleaning is unnecessarily cumbersome as the dirt on the floors does not disappear with a long press; you have to click repeatedly, which only adds to the frustration.

[h3]Rigid Object Placement and Poor Quality[/h3]
Objects can only be placed in predetermined positions, stripping away any sense of creative freedom. The overall quality is so low that it feels as if a novice student, armed with generative AI and readily available online content, hastily assembled this crude simulation software.

[h3]Mostly Positive?[/h3]
Don’t be misled by the current user reviews. As of February 28, 2025, 83% of the 154 posted reviews are marked as positive, but the unlock rates for achievements that should be easily attainable in this game are only a few percent. For example, only 3.5% of players have earned the basic “Hire One Employee” achievement, and an ostensibly easy goal like “Achieve 100% Customer Satisfaction” also has a similarly low unlock rate.

Furthermore, the customer satisfaction score fluctuates wildly during film screenings. It appears that instead of calculating an average among everyone in the theater, the game uses the satisfaction of only those who have just finished watching a movie—likely a bug.

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]
In all honesty, it appears that the developers lack sufficient experience in actually playing and refining a game—or they are simply understaffed, leading to inadequate quality assurance. Having played a fair number of indie games, I can confidently say that this is not a game at all, but rather a shoddy simulation software produced by a small-scale company. For a price tag of around $10, there is no justifiable value here, especially when compared to the wealth of far more engaging titles available. Save your money and look elsewhere.

Cinema Simulator 2025 brings fresh innovation to the simulation genre, offering an exciting way to manage and design your own cinema. I was particularly impressed by the level of detail introduced through new mechanics and improvements.

Another great feature is the ability to customize the furniture inside different cinema halls. The options for arranging seating and interior design give players more creative freedom to personalize their theaters.

Additionally, the new gate-opening option is a smart improvement, providing better control over access and adding to the game’s realism.

Areas for Improvement
While the game offers many great features, there are some areas that could still be refined. A more immersive soundscape would enhance the overall cinematic experience. Also, minor technical optimizations and a smoother user interface would further improve gameplay.

Conclusion
Cinema Simulator 2025 is a promising title with fantastic new features that make cinema management more engaging and realistic. The customization options and improved ticket-handling system stand out as major strengths. If the developers continue refining the game with updates, it could become a true hidden gem for simulation fans.

This isn't a hard game like [b]Contra[/b] or [b]Metal Slug[/b], it is a military themed metroidvania very similar to [b]Blade Chimera[/b], [b]The Mummy Demastered[/b] and [b]Omega Strike[/b] (check those out if you enjoyed this).

You can't fire your weapon diagonally, only up and down.  You also can't hold down the fire button, you have to press each time.

The map is very primitive.  It's just comprised of blue squares.  You can at least see how rooms connect with each other.  Save points, shops and fast travel points are marked, but you need to use the map markers to keep track of spots that you want to revisit.  

The archaic map actually results in extending the playtime of the game quite a bit, because you have no idea which spots to revisit with your new powers as you acquire them.

You get different weapons and subweapons, the itemization is similar to what you get in the Castlevania metroidvanias.

The music was actually quite good, with 80's action movie vibes.

It can be a little tricky to 100% because it's easy to miss a few small things on the map.  There's a newgame+ after you beat the game which I haven't tried.

I wish I could recommend this game, because I love Metal Slug and I love Metroidvanias. 

This manages to botch both halves of that. As far as exploration goes, it is VERY tedious and level design is very sloppy. Backtracking is an absolute slog and after several hours of doing this, it's extremely tiring to go from one end of the map to the other, looking for the next route. You'll often find new areas only to be blocked because you're lacking an item for progression. Later, you gain that item and go back.. only to find you need a SECOND item to continue. You'll often unlock vehicle keys to give you access to cool mechs.. which you mostly just use for more traversal or pushing a block.

The weapons feel very weak and even fodder enemies require multiple rounds to go down. You never feel like you're becoming more powerful, even when you go back to old areas. And the game has SO many enemies in it per room that you will be forced to gun them down every time you cross it or you're going to be taking loads of damage. Similarly, boss fights often feel like they're too drawn out. You'll run through your entire stash of grenades and special weapon ammo only to get the boss down to, maybe, half health.

Guns of Fury is a 2D metroidvania that has been fused with elements of Run and Gun games such as Metal Slug. The moment to moment action is fantastic. It feels cathartic to mow down rows of standard enemies with a pulse rifle and the movement of the player character feels smooth and natural (for the most part). The boss battles against enemy soldiers and mechs are fittingly epic, though you cannot run through the bosses as easily as enemies, otherwise they will mow you down. You do have to be thoughtful and acrobatic during every boss encounter which are designed similar to Megaman bosses- well telegraphed attacks that hit like a truck. My favorite encounter (Mathias, round 2) actually felt like a dance by the time I learned the battle and felt incredible. Each biome is memorable, and the visuals overall are great. The addition of making a number of the elements of the environment destructible is a particularly inspired choice and brings back memories of Broforce. Additionally, one particular highlight of presentation that stands above the rest is the soundtrack. The music is all synthwave and has some of the catchiest tracks I have heard in ages (special note goes to themes for the foundry and sewer).  It took me about 12 hours to reach and defeat the final boss and it was a complete joy to get the first two endings (out of five).

While Guns of Fury does a lot of stuff right, it can use some quality of life features.  The biggest thing this game needs is some form of codex to track quests. For example, there is a quest around midgame that requires you to shoot upwards between two specific book cases in an archive across the map for the quest giver which I only encountered hours after I spoke to the quest giver- there was no way I was remembering that. Completing the game in terms of obtaining of all weapons/items is also difficult since the game does not tell you how many guns/offensive items/health upgrades/etc you have left and all obtainable items (regardless of upgrade type) all appear in the same green box. The map could also use some quality of life features. Maybe I have been spoiled by recent titles like Ender Magnolia and Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown, but the map in Guns of Fury is very basic. No different colors to denote different zones or objects of note- just colored rooms for save rooms/shops, no waypoint markers other than the ones you place. As a result it is markedly harder to recall specific rooms to revisit with new traversal abilities or items.  Playing through this game for the first clear was great, but my march towards 100% is feeling like a bit of a slog. 

I do not want to be too down on Guns of Fury. The moment to moment action feels fantastic and the bosses are incredible. Per the end credits, this game was made by just three people, which makes it a complete triumph in my book. Would buy anything the trio puts out next, day one. PLEASE follow up on the sequel hook in the credits. If you are looking for a fantastic and bombastic metroidvania and do not really care about completion, Guns of Fury is the game for you.

Guns of Fury is a game that takes the run-and-gun formula and mixes it with metroidvania. You go around shooting guns, throwing bombs and using melee weapons to defeat enemies and bosses along the way, acquiring new abilities that then give you access to other areas you couldn't access before. Along the way, you acquire new gear and upgrades to improve your character, with plenty of secrets to be found as well.

The story is as simple as it can be: you're a soldier-type hero that has to rescue a scientist after he invented a type of power cell to solve help the energy crisis before then being captured by an evil organization that want to use the power cell to power weapons. While it's definitely not the highest point of the game, it works well for its premise.

For the most part, the game is very fun to play. Movement is fluid and combat is fun and acquiring new weapons feels meaningful, helping dispatch enemies more easily. Combat encounters are also, for the most part, well balanced, sometimes increasing pressure on the player but at the same time not feeling overly hard either.

The main problem the game has is the level design, as it often feels like the game doesn't understand metroidvania progress. It often happens that you go to a new area after acquiring a new ability... And then you're immediately blocked by an area requiring another ability that you don't have, without any immediate reward, and this often feels frustrating.

Bosses are also a mixed bag: some aren't overly hard and feel just challenging enough, with the player being able to learn their patterns and use this to defeat them... While others feel overwhelmingly hard, as the boss moves around the area too fast while throwing attacks and limiting the player's movement with area-of-denial attacks.

There is also one other issue I had with the game, which is that there is an item that helps the player finds secrets... But it's a gear item, not an ability, so unless you spend a lot of time searching for secrets, you'll end up keeping this item equipped all the time, while you could have had other items equipped in that slot instead.

Despite its flaws, it's still a very fun game. It was very worth the wait.

The bosses come in both player sized, large, and giant room sized threats.
The secrets are really satisfying to find. Many are located in false walls, others rely on platforming, equipment, or ability upgrades to access. The interactivity in this regard had me wanting to 100% the map, which I am satisfied that I did. Sometimes there are ways to access secrets that use a specific interaction or mechanic once, this is okay but could be a little difficult to intuit, however experimenting and combing the scene for hints was part of the fun.

I write this review as an encouragement to the devs, even though I find the game deeply flawed, because I believe most of my issues are perfectible and can be adressed through fixes. It is my hope that with time this can become a true metroidvania classic, even though right now it fails at many critical aspects of the genre.

As it currently is, it is a rather great action platformer with good action feedback (chunky explosions!) and nice (if slightly sluggish) pixel art reminiscent of Metal Slug descendants such as CT Special Forces. Criss crossing through the various parts of the map shooting down enemies *feels* nice for the first few hours, and that's cool enough to experience on its own if that's what you're looking for.

Where it's currently struggling however is the map design and larger metroidvania features. The flow in the second half of the game aims for a more "open" feel, but the relative lack of direction and memorable visual cues means you're lost blindly bumping on each roadblock you pinned/remember until you find the correct one, with no significant cue as to where the correct path might be (and it's often further out of the way than it should). 
Secondly, while many upgrades and items are hidden through cool visual secrets and mechanical tricks, there is an *utter* lack of indication of where anything might be when sweeping for collection, a staple of the genre, apart from an equippable item that only shows upgrades tied to destructible/interactible bits (which is not all of them). The map system evokes GBA Castlevanias but is too large to function as they did at this scale (the lack of fast travel points is another issue, though can be justified by the economy requiring huge amounts of back and forth to collect enough money for all equipments), and even Super Metroid had indicators where items remained uncollected. In short: either a small map with no hints, or a larger map with, but the larger map here feels like uncomfortable padding.

Lastly, the equipment and upgrades are mostly inconsequential barring two or three clearly useful/OP ones - most should probably be turned into always active "passive" items to have any kind of use, but as it stands, many of the goodies found feel unrewarding as they're either weapon clones/downgrades, or utility tools that feel too situational to have any reasonable use.

I'm hoping for the game to be patched as none of these issues are fundamentally unfixable. I'm hoping this could become a new modern take on the genre - as it stands, it's a rough stone that still needs carving and polish to reveal the gem inside.

Guns of Fury really is what it looks like- A Metal Slug Metroidvania. It has its own identity so as not to be a simple clone, has good platforming and great gun-based gameplay. You earn the typical Metroidvania power-ups, such as double jump, slide, wall jump, etc, which then allow you to explore the map further. and even discover hidden weapons. Although some players have complained, the fact you can only shoot horizontally and vertically never became an issue for me in my 11+ hours to complete it as the level design is built around those limitations.

If I had to list some gripes, my biggest issues are that the game rarely tells you where you should be going next. So, unless you can remember an unreachable area that you now have a skill to traverse, you can be wandering around aimlessly for ages. This is more of an issue in the final third of the game as the map flows quite well until then. It's the backtracking to search for new areas to open which can be a problem. Also, it would be nice if the map showed what kind of blockage or direction a door is locked from so you don't backtrack all the way just to find you still cannot proceed. You can place markers on the map, but these are just coloured squares so don't mean much. Various icons to represent items, doors, etc, would help a lot with this.

Anyhoo, I enjoyed my time with Guns of Fury a lot. The level design was great, the enemies varied, the locations interesting and the bosses were fun without being too frustrating. Very much recommended!

The music makes this game. I would get excited upon reaching a new area JUST to hear a new banger.  The artist did a great job of marrying several music genres with the punchiness that makes a run-and-shoot game with frequent explosions feel all the more exciting.

Speaking of shooting and explosions, this game does a great job of mixing areas of reasonable challenge with areas of pure indulgence, where you walk forward blasting and everything just explodes and dies in front of you.  It's the same joy you get from a ridiculous 80s action movie.  The mech suits feel as over-powered as they should be.  Weapon variety is excellent, though the menu system for equipment changes and item use might feel a bit quaint for some.

Movement is good, though I found myself getting very mildly frustrated at certain quirks, like ducking and crawling for a moment before jumping down from a ledge.  Rare, but seemed to only happen at the worst moments, haha!  In general, you can't cancel out of certain movements as quickly and easily as I would prefer, but it was easy enough to adapt to.  There is a way to turn off individual abilities, so this was accounted for.  A smarter man than me will make use of this feature if they find themselves frustrated.

The story is as bare-bones as an 80s action flick should be.  It is enough to justify the carnage and explosions.  Though, it still managed to get me to start a new playthrough for revenge over a plot point.

There were parts where I got frustrated about being confused about progression, but once I figured it out, I would realize that the frustration was my fault.  Mostly it had to do with realizing that certain weapons were instruments of progression and they don't always make it obvious.

Great pixel art, great music, great explosions, fun fights, and an all-around good time.  This game is worth every penny.

Game is mostly based on Metal Slug, but has health/ammo upgrades similar to Metroid. There are no level up mechanic here, but there is an almost tacked on loot grinding aspect common in metroidvania genre.

General gameplay is good, controls are responsive, pixel art looks great, boss fights are challengin and fun, and the soundtrack is absolutely amazing. But the map layout seriously pours cold water on the overall experience. There are alot of backtracking involved, and the portal room locations leave ALOT to be desired (too few and in bad positions) which makes the process very tedious and un-fun.

Other aspects that I didn't like:
1. Most of the weapons are simply not that useful due to a combination of damage, ammo cost, fire rate, and projectile pattern issues. The plasma rifle ended up being my secondary 90% of the time, with the other 10% only when I needed other weapons for progression purposes. Similar deal with pistols and melee weapons, there are maybe 2 out of a dozen that are worth using, mostly because the different damage values simply didn't matter, as they didn't change the number of hits needed to kill mob enemies, so it's just a matter of using the faster weapon. There are definite quantity over quality issues here.

2. Interactive objects some times blend too well into the background and should be highlighted better. You can easily miss them if you aren't paying attention, which locks you out of progression.

3. Need more colors for map markers. There aren't enough of them for how often you'd want to use these, between marking weapon chest locations, door types (lv1 to lv4 keycards needed), progression requirements (double jump vs wall jump vs climbing, etc).

4. Other general QoL issues, like the metal detector really should be a passive skill instead of an equipment, just to cut down on amount of time spent in the menu instead of running and gunning.

Overall, I think this is probably a 7/10 game wrapped in the chassis of what could have been an 8/10 or even 9/10 game. I like Metal Slug so I can overlook alot of the downsides of the game, but I suppose not everyone can. I wish Steam had a neutral option instead of just like/dislike because that's my real though on this game.

Original:

I initially enjoyed Pantheon, as it evoked a sense of nostalgia reminiscent of my time with EverQuest. Many of the game’s characteristics—such as long leveling grinds, a strong emphasis on group play, and static mob camping—felt familiar and engaging.

Despite having invested 130 (120-ish of which were active hours) into the game and being an avid MMO enthusiast, I ultimately cannot recommend it. There are several key reasons for this.

First, the game leans too heavily on EverQuest-inspired mechanics without incorporating modern quality-of-life improvements or common enhancements seen in contemporary MMOs - I loved EQ. But if I wanted EQ, I'd go play EQ. Additionally, the community is moderated by individuals who appear more interested in wielding authority than fostering a positive and welcoming environment (It is a cesspool, which honestly most gaming Discords are). This has led to a rather toxic atmosphere. Furthermore, critical game updates and information are disseminated almost exclusively through Twitch streams, with little effort made to provide written summaries or official updates—something that should be standard practice, even with a small development team.

Under normal circumstances, I would still consider supporting and amplifying the game in its Early Access phase, as I generally appreciate the iterative development process. However, recent revelations regarding certain Game Masters (GMs) summoning rare spawns for a specific guild—under the pretense of benefiting "elite testers"—have raised serious concerns. Initially, these actions were denied (Directly by the guilty party), only to later be acknowledged (AFTER all the proof came out). The game director stated that such practices "should not be happening," yet other GM and community manager comments suggest that this behavior has been normalized.

What is most troubling is that, despite the implications of favoritism within a live environment that includes a functioning economy and competitive progression, the developers have shown no remorse. There has been no formal apology or transparent explanation regarding how this situation arose and how they plan to address it moving forward. Given that Pantheon is already a niche title with a relatively small player base, maintaining trust and fairness should be a top priority. And to get ahead of the 'knights', it being EA doesn't matter. It being wiped in 2 years, does not matter. The concept of "We should have a test server" is baked into service games 101. They chose to incentivize testers.

While I do not regret my initial investment in the game, I will not continue to engage with it unless the developers take full accountability, provide a clear explanation of what transpired, and take meaningful steps to rebuild trust within the community.

There's a lot to love here and I wish there was a neutral option but if its "yes or no" then the answer is no.
The game does well to evoke the nostalgia of the games of the late 90s / early 2000s but has brought the bad with the good in some cases.   Corpse running and XP loss on death are too punishing as implemented, particularly when its so very easy to die to bugs, misadventure, and what  "other people are doing."   The result is you've got a game where its not worth doing anything that's risky, because the penalty for failure is too harsh for the activity to be worth doing to begin with.

I logged a lot of hours in this game and got nearly every class to mid-teens in level to get a feel for them.  They all play very differently and the class system I think is well done, and there's good group synergy.  However, even on a server with maxed out population on every shard, actually finding a group (regardless of class, because I played them all, tank/healer/dps/cc)  could take hours.  Then 45 minutes for everyone to mobilize/travel/get where we are going due to no maps, no fast travel, etc.  Then 30 minutes in, the tank leaves, it all falls apart and you're back to looking for group for hours again.  I joined a guild, which helped a little, but still spent most of my evening either looking for a group, sat waiting for a group, sat waiting for a replacement when someone left, etc.

The issue is after about level 12, there's very little you can do on your own.  The few solo spots are overcamped on every shard by desperate players who only have a couple hours to play and don't want to spend it sat looking for group.  Its a group based game, and that's fine - but there's so many obstacles to actually making (and sticking with) a group that if you don't have hours to wait, it becomes don't bother.  And if you do get a good group, you feel obligated despite potential RL responsibilities or fatigue or whatever, to stick with that group for hours.  I even had people asking me for a time commitment before sending me a group invite.

Despite that, the game is fun, and I grit my teeth  and got a few characters to over level 20.  And this is where it just became unplayable.  The only potential "solo" content (if you want to call it that....) is a 30 minute at best speed walk to get down to the plains.  The stuff you can kill is interspersed with deep red insta-death mobs.  Ignoring the buggy, unity-pill-shaped mobs that aren't fully working or itemised and borked zone lines and whatnot, you could technically go down there and kill some stuff.  Of course, if you die, you've gotta spend 30 minutes at best speed just to get back and maybe get your corpse.  You could try to find a bindstone down there, but then its 30 minutes at best speed just to get back to civilization if by some miracle you manage to find a group.

I know the game wants to be old school and hard core.   But if you're going to make a game that makes grouping the main progression you need to make it easier for groups to get together.  I absolutely refuse to spend an hour just in travel time to get to an area that I can "sort of" fight in, knowing that the penalty for dying, lagging, finding something bugged, or actually trying to do something non-trivial and failing means I've got a 30 minute auto-run boredom return trip to get my corpse.  I put up with it for a while, but at later levels, the xp lost on top of it and going backwards, it just got to be too much.

Game absolutely needs fast travel, of my 400 hours played I estimate 3/4 of that was either walking some place or waiting for people to walk someplace to join a group.    I had a lot of fun at the lower levels where you could actually do stuff on your own while waiting for a group to happen but beyond that, nope.

This game presents some promising concepts for an old-school MMORPG, but several issues hinder the experience. The servers are divided into shards, and the lack of cross-shard LFG functionality makes it challenging to find groups, especially given the low player population. This issue is further exacerbated at lower levels, making it even harder to find a group.

The XP and grinding requirements are quite steep, with players needing to spend 6-10 hours in the same spot doing repetitive tasks with little reward. The absence of an auction system forces players to manually spam their items for sale, and the trade window doesn't display item stats, leaving you unsure of what you're receiving.

The lack of a map leaves players directionless, and the quests are vague, lengthy, and difficult to complete. Some class mechanics are not enjoyable and can feel limiting—for instance, as a Wizard, you spend 90% of your time sitting to regenerate mana.

The inventory and bank systems are cumbersome, requiring players to purchase bank boxes for extra storage and open each one individually every time they access the bank. There is no PvP, and boss respawn timers are excessively long, with higher-level players often camping the bosses.

The crafting system is poorly designed, and most classes need to find spell/skill scrolls from monster drops instead of training at a trainer. The loading screens between different zones detract from the MMORPG feel, and the combat system is clunky.

Given the current state of the game, by the time it's released in two years, the graphics may look outdated, resembling a game from the early 2000s. When you die, you drop your loot, which is more of a hassle than a challenge, as you need to find someone to summon your body. The XP loss from death can equate to 1-5 hours of grinding, which feels excessive given how easily you can die in the game. Even monsters well below your level can still pose a significant threat.

A part of me respects things like the lack of a map, but even a simple static map that lacks player location tracking and quest markers would be appreciated! I would kill for any sort of direction/guidance from these quest givers.

In regards to the professions, I cannot describe how disappointed  I was to have spent a good chunk of time gathering Jute and crafting various pieces in order to make my first armor upgrade, a Burlap Robe with a blue robe icon in the crafting menu, only to have it look EXACTLY like the generic leather/cloth chest piece my character started the game wearing. Nothing about my appearance changed. Right after, a random player ran up to the sewing table next to me wearing a blue robe, so that made it feel even worse. I was so excited to make my character look even [i]slightly[/i] different from default.

Continuing on character appearances, there's only a few hair styles and hair colors to select from when you create a character. Whatever race you pick has an unchangeable skin tone, face, etc. That means if you make a human, your only option is to be a white man/woman. I'm not saying there should be pronoun options and body sliders, but at the very least I feel like you should be able to play as a non-white Human after 10+ years of development on this game? I'm white, so I was fine, but this isn't the type of "old-school" I was expecting from a game released in 2024.

This game is rated "Very Positive" at the time of this review, so 80%+ of the reviewers seem to be doing perfectly fine with how the game is currently implemented. Maybe this game was made for EQ veterans specifically rather than those of us that played vanilla WoW and other older MMOs? Maybe I'm just too small brained? I feel like this game could remain true to being "old school" while also containing some very obvious QoL features without being too "hand-holdey."

Game looks like it could have been good someday, but has kneecapped itself with a few bad decisions.

-The failed kickstarter had a VIP status you could buy.  It gives access to hidden discord dev channels, special elevated customer service & for other subtle ways to make your game experience more smooth.  

-They plan to keep this VIP player system when the game is 1.0 released.  Do you think steam/new players are going to be ok knowing that they are officially lower tier than these people?

-Recently this came to a head when someone brought to light that high level dragons were being farmed by a VIP group on a live server, seemingly with direct dev assistance.    At first the community manager told them that it was normal & expected for VIP players to get such treatment.   Then when it started going viral, the community manager changed tone & threatened to ban the player for bringing this up.   In the end, the devs contradicted themselves multiple times but somehow found they did nothing wrong. 

-The game development is unfocused.  Item stacking doesn't work, but they are working on a PVP server? 

-Related to the last point, there is no road map.  No gradual milestones they are aiming for.  Where are they trying to be by end of the quarter?  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

-The patches are infrequent & are "two steps forward, one step back".   Latest example:  They updated the engine.  The water looks nicer, but it broke a bunch of stuff that was working before.

-Group only mobs.   Bad idea.  The chevron system needs to be fired into the sun.   Head first.


At the end of the day, this is just a video game & if it doesn't bring you joy, then move onto something that does, there are plenty of things in life that do.  
It was a fun nostalgic diversion for a bit.  & a few of the devs are genuinely passionate about the project, but this VIP player system is some amateur hour private server tier hogwash that should have been completely done away with the moment the kickstarter failed.  It will only continue to cause problems.

12 years. It's been in development for 12 years and none of the classes are even finished. There isn't even an auction / bazaar system. Google an image of what the cloth cap looks like when equipped. Go on, I dare you.

Then there's the design philosophy. There is a point at which "slow and dangerous" becomes "anti-engagement". There is a point at which "social game" becomes "you aren't able to play at all because there's only three people at your character level and none of them are LFG" or "there's only one camp at your level, and it's taken". Look at the server populations. Then look at the third party map website (yes, that's right, there is no map in-game, but players are already creating and hosting their own maps so the "immersion" of lacking basic UI in-game is completely pointless). Look at how many camps there are for a given level range. There is a point at which the profound lack of content is a damning indictment for a game that took more than a decade to create: compare the progress which similar projects have made. For crying out loud, private emulated EQ1 servers have created more custom content which is better balanced and more engaging to interact with. And, as a reminder, gameplay on those is literally automated to the point of being run in the background while the player is AFK...

After 12 years of development, Pantheon resembles Western Karana, with fewer things to do and (somehow) it's even uglier. And it even takes longer to run across, as if that was a good thing.

What have they done with more than a decade of time and millions of dollars? What have they done with it? Because it certainly was not spent to create this.

Very rough, but the bones are there for something special.  
The devs seem passionate but overwhelmed & unfocused.  I can't point to a single game system that is ready for release status.   Development needs to focus on something.  Anything.  Everything feels like a rough draft.  The rough draft of the novel looks good, show us one completed chapter.

What is left of the original community are the most ardent supporters or naysayers.  The community that has survived the 10 years of development is aggressively hostile towards anything they do not consider highly informed feedback.  Unfortunately, being highly informed is exceedingly challenging.

They recently(?) lost their communication manager & it shows.  They have a seemingly overwhelmed sarcastic discord mod that seems unaware that the game has had a big influx of new steam players that has not had 10 years to accept things like the two tier player privilege system.   If you want to keep informed about what is happening, then you will need to watch the multiple per week multi hour twitch streams by one of the dev leads.  You will also need to keep up with discord channels that zoom by & hope that the granular dev posts in the VIP players section are filtered down to the larger community.  

The official website is woefully out of date.  There is no up to date wiki.  There is a decent player run map website that is trying to flush itself out with item information ( shalazam ).  This lack of ingame information is oddly nostalgic of late 90s gaming.  Information is valuable.  Which is why the two tiered player privilege system they have in place is divisive. 

Steam buyers beware.
You will be a second class citizen in this game.   The game has been in development for around a decade & the devs have become 'friendly' with certain long term players/guilds.   They have established VIP guilds, special VIP only discord channels & advanced tester designations.  These VIP people are given access to information/tools/spawns.  When the newer community members found out, the devs removed the discord threads asking for clarification. Then dismissed the concerns.  We were told that never happened & it was a dev pretending to spawn rare mobs on the live servers.  Then we were told that if it did happen,  that it is perfectly normal because they have special VIP testers/guilds that help them.  The devs eventually investigated themselves & found they did nothing wrong.  

We have all witnessed private servers with larger communities than Pantheon collapse due to admins giving special privileges to their friends.   Yes, this is early access & will eventually be wiped, but these are unforced errors.  The fact that a dev had no problem openly putting themselves in a situation where impropriety could be assumed & the over the top mishandling of the situation by the community team is vexing.   The discord mods didn't need to hide all threads asking for clarification, but they did.  They released on steam, but didn't think steam players would mind that there is a two tier player privilege system?

I did not want to write a negative review, but the current direction the game is on will not lead to a successful launch.   My advice is transparency.   The current two tier player privilege system is opaque & leaves the larger community wondering what is going on behind closed doors.  Is it fair customers who bought the game years ago to continue to get special treatment?  Get special access to devs?  What else are they getting access to?  Are they going to continue to do this when the game goes live?  

I assume the kickstarter many years ago had a special funding tier that gave VIP access.   & if the game was still only a kickstarter funded game that would be fine.  But it is are not.  The kickstarter failed to fund the game until 1.0 release.  The Kickstarter bought special VIP privileges & VIP access need to be done away with.  

To be clear.  Even if the devs spawning rare mobs for their friends never happened & the response from the devs was even keeled & acceptable, a core problem is the two tier VIP access system.

The game is released to steam.   Its time for change.  Either everyone can be a VIP or nobody can.

The game only has ONE starting zone because it is the most popular, and you only spawn in the second starting zone if you pick Elves or get teleported there. I was informed by a player in the beginning that I could be teleported to Thronefast, but I wanted to explore the zone that my race started in. (I just thought that would be fun, but it wasn't at all.)

My first experience with this game was not good. I ran into several mobs I just couldn't attack because they Evaded everything due to being bugged out in their spawn point. 

I spent some time doing a bit of gathering, only seeing one or two players every now and then. (The majority of players are in the first starting zone as stated above.)

I dropped in blind, expecting an adventure based on the reviews I've seen here and news articles I've read. Only to realize I'd be on my own, and as I tried to explore on my own I started to realize the mess I had stepped into.. Most mobs that were my level were bugged, resources were very clearly scarce due to everyone having to gather all the same things, and most importantly there weren't really any players I could group with despite being on a server labeled to have a high population.

As I ventured through the forest and started to find higher level enemies, I had no choice but to turn back. That's fair. That's how it is in most MMO's, but then I saw a high level player boosting a low level player by killing the higher level mobs as they followed. Yet I didn't see a single player my level on my journey.

This instantly killed my idea of being able to find a group to venture into this area with. Since clearly this was a high population server, and there is people having to boost the low level characters through the area because there was literally nobody else that could be seen. Maybe they were there and we just hadn't run into each other, but I had already traveled far enough out to start to lose my direction, so I needed to turn back anyways.

I started to feel like my idea of adventure wasn't going to be offered by this game, so I caved and decided to watch a new player guide.... Even though I wanted to learn from playing the game/exploring as I went along through the world and met more people... (There were no people.)

After watching the guide I noticed that the mob grinding was all laid out for grinding at different level gaps. This made me start thinking the game is just too linear for me. Everyone seemed to be following the same path, killing the same mobs, and passing through the same zones over and over again to level. Yet if you don't follow this path, you can guarantee you'll be punished for it due to having less players to group up with and just being on your own in general. (I was under the impression this would be a grand social experience due to the hype I had read and heard in the reviews, news, & store page trailers....)

I requested a refund for the game, and will not be returning unless there are some major improvements as time goes on. I put in 119 minutes by a total accident, I was not paying attention to the time that closely. My poor experience with this world just so happened to only last that long. Lol. So that is the only reason I was lucky enough to request the refund with hopes of it being approved by Steam.

-

If you are unsure of this game and do decide to try it out. Don't pick Elves, and you'll probably have a better "first impression" than I did, but if you play Elves or get sorely unlucky on population for your server, be sure to monitor your time if you hope to get a refund if you get frustrated. I doubt anyone will actually read all of this, but if you did I hope it helps you understand why I do not think this game is worthy of a good review. 

I also really don't see where all the positive reviews are coming from either, but maybe I missed the hype train when it first released. Who knows. Anyways, good luck out there. <3

This game is not fun. I am an old school EverQuest, Ultima and mud fan so imagine my delight when a few months ago I saw a game that was supposed to be a revival of the old EverQuest formula. I paid my ticket price and got on the ride. I rolled three characters during my time, a warrior, a cleric and a wizard. Two started in Wild's End and my last one, the wizard, started in Throne Fast. The ride was not enjoyable. 

Starting with the technical aspects, the FPS in this game is horrible. I've got a solid rig (i7/3080ti) that handles other games without issue but this game just chugs along between 10 and 40 fps in the cities and very rarely up to 60 in the open areas. The input lag can get wild too. Expect to click abilities, vendors and corpses multiple times during high traffic playtimes. The animations are a glaring issue too. The character models are about as flexible as a lego figurine and the ability animations feel like they were ripped from EverQuest in 1999. Considering the current year, 2025, and the time spent developing the game (10+ years) I expected more in both optimization and graphical fidelity.

Onto the game play. Pantheon combat plays exactly like EverQuest with little to no variation from the formula. Find camp, pull monsters, rest and repeat. For casters the combat loops look like this: Stand up, cast spell, sit down. The cleric plays like a wow discipline priest but without the fun or ability to do meaningful damage. The warrior plays as you might expect: taunt mobs, take damage, wait for pulls. The game is not solo friendly or newbie friendly so most of my time was spent in groups of 2-5. The game play CAN pick up with a full functional group as you're able to tackle group-based content and higher level monster camps but more often than not it just slows down game play when you're waiting for a member to get a port or recover their corpse or you need to clear but the healer disconnected so you're stuck. Like EverQuest back in 1999, you can also expect wonky enemy pathing to regularly ruin your camp. Health bars and nameplates don't render until you're danger close and this results in easily preventable deaths. Running around in the pitch black dark is also a death sentence and with very few choices for players to increase their light radius or gain dark vision, you can expect to spend your nights waiting for day. There is no in-game map and considering the positioning system takes prior knowledge to use, you will spend an inordinate amount of time traveling, backtracking and using the ms paint Shalazam map. Leveling camps are highly contested and camps with loot are poopsock festivals. You can expect bored high level players to perma-camp and server hop all the best spawns.

I did not dive into tradeskills as they didn't look interesting or engaging. Resource nodes spawn in fixed points on the map and you can expect the valuable ones to be perma-camped or gated behind a camp full of group monsters. 

Last, the community. Most of the people I grouped with around Wild's End were helpful and willing to be patient with new players. That changed when I sent my cleric to thronefast and started grouping where 90% of the player base hangs out. I'm not exaggerating when I say I ran into salty poopsockers with every group I joined. If it wasn't some higher level player stealing our kills or camps, it was group members who were bickering over looting rights or where we should be going for better experience. There is no mechanic for distributing loot so expect to get ninja'd. You CAN switch off of free-for-all to round robin but I had several groups fall apart over which system to choose. Keep in mind, most of these people were not new and had several higher level characters they could easily use to farm or craft gear. 

The discord is a cesspool. Avoid at all costs. GMs are unprofessional, unable and unwilling to resolve conflicts between players. I wish I could recommend a guild to join but none of the ones I joined panned out. I ended up joining a large guild through the pantheon discord and it was a HUGE mistake. The toxic drama that is pervasive among private servers and old school MMOs is ratcheted up 100x in the pantheon guild scene and for no reason. There is nothing to actually compete for at high levels. With very few viable endgame camps or raid style content, higher level players just monopolize low level camps with good loot and with no mechanics (pvp/instancing/rules) to combat camp stealing, your group has to find another spot, switch servers or split up and go solo/duo. 

For a game that has already spent 10 years in the oven, there is zero chance this game releases in a state comparable to the old school MMOs it wants to emulate. Go play Project 1999 or Project Quarm instead.

This isn't the first time I've had fun with what I'd objectively call a bad game. It does give a very satisfying ancient MMO feeling, and there's a nice active playerbase. That said there's a lot of star-citizen esque fanboying in this community whenever complaints arise. "It's early access, why would you expect more than 20 of the 40 levels to have content?" type stuff. To which I'll say "Early access is just a marketing buzzword that has no real meaning, if you pay money for a product it's a released product".

But here are the major drawbacks I saw, and if they seem like deal killers for you wait for "release" (there's going to be a wipe on release) before picking it up:

The controls are... unique? You have rebindable hotkeys, but the bars they're on are locked meaning you can technically bind anything you want to any key, but they're visually locked in place to certain spots (grouped with other abilities of the same "type"). It's a really annoying hassle/workaround, meaning this system is effectively annoying for no real reason.

Macros are available... but only as a clicked button and not hotkeyable in any way...? This one baffles me.

Itemization and crafting are placeholders. Getting gear for the most part just makes you feel good about yourself, but doesn't have a particularly important impact on your performance outside melee classes getting their first major weapon upgrade. And crafting stuff (outside bags) are a massive grind to make for an incredibly minute bonus over looted items, made worse by the low impact of gear on stats. Guess it makes sense since we're not actually approaching endgame (20/40 is where it "stops"), and in other MMOs like this the first half of leveling rarely has meaningful gear in it.

It's weird that the disabled mastery system that's still visually there while only having 1/4th of the abilities with descriptions of their stats. Just seems really tacky to not disable it entirely but instead leaving this very rough looking leftover just sitting in the UI.
not worth the money and not worth your time. Estremely small mall content, very repetitive and boring.

First, I will say that the core gameplay captures the feel of old school MMOs very nicely, where instead of running through an instanced dungeon, you find a camp and pull mobs in to kill one at a time in the open world. For this reason alone I think the game has potential, and even though a negative rant follows, I will likely check back in in a year or two.

However.

This is an MMO in 2025. Here is a list of what them game does not have and some of these are not planned AFAIK:
- No mail
- No map
- No item linking
- No item rolling
- No auction house or bazaar mechanics whatsoever
- No item stacking (this means when you right click an item to put in your bank, it doesn't go into an existing stack)
- No way to move items between your characters on the same server
- No way to send tells to people without typing their entire name
- Cannot invite people in different zones to your group
- Does not tell you how much XP you earn for killing anything

Questionable design choices:
- Round robin group loot mechanics are extremely clunky
- Non-vendor crafting recipes are gated behind needing to camp chests
- Crafting in general is barely playable
- The night cycle is so dark you can barely do anything outside of a city
- You have to choose stats at the character creation screen when you have no idea what they do
- A small nitpick of my own, I played a tank that gets an ability giving a 10% parry buff at level 1, but you don't get the ability to parry at all until 10, I have no idea why they would do this

The social media community for this game is full of EQ old guards that want this game to be exactly like EQ without taking into consideration if it was good or bad design. Unfortunately, the developers seem to be on the same page as this community, and I personally believe for the worse. I will say that the majority of people I've interacted with in the game have been pleasant, so maybe this is just the anonymity of the internet at work.

I have to say it does have some of the EQ group vibes.

Sadly most of the things holding it back seem to be in an effort to make the game more hardcore. IMO though they are just bad attempts to remake the wheel. As EQ forced many to rage quit with it's basic mechanics. So I will just list the things I think that are holding it back.

1. Gate keeping. 
IMO most of the initial good reviews are people who have been buying packs and supporting this game financially for years. They are in so deep they probably even bought the game on Steam to give it a good review. That's great but it leads to them wanting their way only and feeling they have the right to shut others opinions down. It also seems to divide the community into those who know what works, where to get gear etc, and those who don't. Whom the gatekeepers often don't help. 

2. Strategic  Improvements.
Many new developers want to put their stamp on a new game. And this can lead to incredible new breakthroughs in game play. However this game seems to try to remake the wheel in an effort to make things more strategic. For instance every character has  triggers that allow other players to be more efficient at what they do. In practice however this just leads to many extra button pushes. which can often be pointless as if the other player type doesn't hit his button on time, the said ability is useless. Good luck seeing if the guy did it, as the mob will be covered in 20 debuffs/spells/abilities. For instance if a cleric hits his 8% reduction damage reduction on an enemy but the other player that can stack with that doesn't use his. You may end up with the tank getting his face kicked in. Which leads to the tank blaming the cleric. And the group splitting up. And this can happen with every class and sadly I have seen it happen. 

They also have made it where it's basically tank, healer, CC, dps.  If your not DPS this leads to many of the tank, healer, CC people stuck in chat asking for a group. As there are simply not enough groups that need them.  It can sometimes take hours to find a group. Which of course leads to not enough of them later on. Add to this you have multiple healer types, multiple tank types. While most groups only need one of each type. Which leads to more of them quitting as you level up. Which of course leads to groups needing said healers, tanks, cc later on. As there ends up being not enough to go around. Lack of groups also leads many DPS to be much longer in a group que. 

To make this worse those who know the game in and out level quickly. Others take their time. So the very small community is quickly split by huge level gaps. Those who want specific camps seem to go to other Shards. Which splits the people available for you to group with on your server. With just over 5k reviews. Imagine 5 servers, each split into 3 shards? Only 1/3 of your server is on at the time your playinjg. It can be tough finding a group no matter what role you are playing.

There is also the "strategic" reason for not having maps. Not having spell sets. Not having bind/gate spells. Which the gate keepers try to tell you is a feature, not a bug. 

3. Lack of mob viability. 
They have this weird thing where they have regular mobs and group mobs. Group mobs generally need a group to beat. This is very odd. As EQ had all mobs as group mobs. This made it very easy. Just con the mob, make sure you could beat it and get it. So if you didn't have a group, you could farm mats and xp while waiting. This game has a chevron icon on mobs that are group mobs. You can not beat them in most cases even if they are low con to you. 

The mixing of mobs types often leads to huge swaths of the map where you have grays who are not worth your effort. Maybe a mob or two your level, you can solo. Which leads to your running around the map, often running into group mobs out of no where and getting into an xp losing, body recovery situation.  Honestly it isn't marked,mapped, so you have to know where everything is. Eventually you learn. But it gets old.

4. Vision
The developers seemed obsessed with making it very hard to see.  You need a torch, thankfully they added a torch slot. But it is often night time, foggy, raining etc which means you can't see those group mobs you will run into. Racials are not in yet, so some races like Elves and Dwarves can't see in the dark yet. So it often feels like the guy is trying to blind you, or make your eyes sore while playing his game.

5. Crafting
Crafting seems solid. I love the way they get you into it early on. The gathering skills and quest make you solid money early on. You can easily craft your first set of armor and weapons. If you put in the time. But the flaw in the system seems you need other players to be online to buy the other mats made by other classes very quickly. So if no one is available in /auction chat to sell you the needed item to make your gear, your stuck. Since there is no auction house. You don't know appropriate prices and can get gouged really bad. If no one is on that makes the items you need. You can't make the gear you need. And the drops from mobs don't really drop gear a ton.  My cleric is level 17 and he still has not one piece of Plate Armor. That is the armor he is supposed to be wearing and is part of his kit. Supposedly part of his classes survivablity. Though gear seems to be like EQ and is more about the very rare stat buffs than the armor. I.E. wisdom/con gear bonuses are way more important to my clerics efficiency in groups. I.E. much better heals, buffs from those stats. Which is just made worse if your not getting the needed gear/stats.

6. The game can be good.
IMO the game could be much better. Especially for it's target audience. If it just stopped with the strategic and moronic things it is trying to add to the genre. While adding expected features that are expected by those who play MMO's. You know auction houses, maps, classes with bind/gate spells and abilities that make the game more social. Allowing saving spell sets, so you can set up your abilities quickly. Noting having to scroll through all of your abilities your group needs, and struggling to find it. Though I fear the current Gate Keepers and the cult that religiously guard the one developer saint of the game will lead it into a path of failure. 

I have played about 150 hours according to steam. I have tried all classes and class types available except for tanks. I usually play a healer in MMO'.s This games healers are okay IMO. Not great though. The other classes feel weaker than other MMO's. Because you often have to press so many buttons to achieve the same as other games. For instance the Summoner has to press one ability 3 times to set up up one attack. That's 4 button pushes for one attack. Pointless.

Sadly with the extra "strategic" extras it feels more like "Carpal Tunnel Syndrome" the game than EQ. When sadly without many of these extras, it could be a solid game.

Ultimately, even after having multiple public issues about unequal enforcement of rules - yet again today there are screenshots showing GMs running amok and 'interpreting' rules to favor certain players. To make things worse their dismissive tone when others have voiced concerns is the most disconcerting aspect of my issues with the game. 

Realistically this game would be great with new community management that enforces the rules in an equal manner - but who knows how likely that will be.

This is a review of where the game currently is and not where it will hopefully be. I want you, reader, to come into this informed so you'll know what you're getting into if you choose to try it. I wouldn't recommend anyone to plan to play this much higher than level 20. I do plan on returning to the game later to see improvements. 

Positives:
1. It's quite a fun experience from 1-20 
2. Visually it looks quite pleasing 
3. The team, Visionary Realms, is highly engaging especially on their Discord server
4. There are a lot of great ideas such as more variety of dungeons that you can see active progress on

Negatives
1. 20+ the exp gain slows dramatically. This makes deaths brutally more punishing especially when considering the next point
2. There just aren't enough people 20+ to get exp and when you do find those people they are very adverse to risk
3. In general there isn't a lot of finished content which is disheartening considering how long this has been in development. Yes, I know the founder passed away, funding wasn't strong in the beginning, and there have been many other challenges.
4. A lack of a high level roadmap is concerning. They used to do something like this in the past while it was in pre early access, but that isn't happening anymore.
4. Other issues primarily related to lack of content to keep one busy/entertained for more than a couple hundred hours.

So if you're looking to try it out and have fun for a bit -- go for it. But like with most MMOs I imagine you're trying to jump in and have a fun game to play for awhile. This isn't it. If you just want to check it out and support the dev to try and help get it off the ground, go for it! I certainly had a ton of fun for awhile.

The ability mechanics also clash with the slow grind exp rate. The constant use of abilities gets very tiresome after the 100th goblin for the night. Combat certainly has the difficulty of needing to be on your toes and use the right ability at the right time - mainly because basic group mobs can almost one shot with a single ability - but as a caster it takes away from the calculated use of spells/mana in the course of exping. Warriors have the exact same number of abilities on the LAS as Wizards, which makes everything feel the same with different roles.
Having group mobs and solo mobs are annoying and detract from immersion. Why is a human thug over here a group mob and over there it's a solo mob? Because we're in a theme park? I don't see the need for this and it just slows down development. 

The good:
The available game world they've made so far is the best designed I've seen for an MMO. Simply exploring is the most fun I've had in this game. The dungeon designs are AAA and challenging. Escaping from mobs by jumping off cliffs into the water is very satisfying.

A cute little souls-like with clear inspiration from the kingsfield series with an emphasis on slow meaningful combat encounters. There is no XP, so finding a new weapon usually means a new attack animation rather than raw damage.
Damage types are very important, with blunt damage breaking armour and slashing damage cutting off limbs.. but because they're bugs, cutting off a head doesn't automatically mean death, as they'll become more aggressive, but less accurate with their attacks.

I've only played up to the first dungeon with a friend, but this game can host a total of 4 players. There's still a LOT of branching pathways I didn't explore yet, and it seems every enemy can drop their gear, so it gives you something to farm for fashion as well as function.

The first major boss wasn't hard, but more like an obstacle course with various attacks to dodge while platforming up to its weak-spot.

Lastly, if you're normally scared off by the difficulty of these types of games, Flyknight is not very hard, you just have to play slower than you might be used to.. personally? I love what I've played so far. The game oozes with style and has a lot of unique ideas. This developer really knows how to capture the essence of a good souls-like, because I was roped in immediately.

I'll update my review as I get further.. maybe the game is secretly really short? But thankfully it's not very expensive, so while I hope it's got a few hours worth of content, I don't mind if it's short.

The combat system is slow, very simple, and becomes boring rapidly. The "limb-based combat" is limited. You can't lose limbs, and most enemies die too quickly after losing a limb anyway, rendering making them "do one attack less" pointless. There is nothing much else to it. You can't make enemies crawl without a leg for instance. And sometimes they can survive without a head, but that doesn't do anything. Steam page says "crush their head to deprive them of senses"? Now that is a plain lie. All enemies track and attack you headless, even archers.

Stamina is a huge problem that restricts you heavily and slows down the game to a crawl. For example, a successful parry can rob you of stamina completely, leaving you just standing around with no ability to counterattack, or even block other enemies. Everything requires stamina, even spells, which is bizarre to me. Spells have weight as well to slow you down even more, sometimes up to a huge number, like 15 weight for a spell. And when you're out of mana after 3 casts, it might as well be an extra couple of two-handed swords up your ass.

Fish on the other hand does not weight for some reason, but it doesn't do anything uniquely useful. It just gives you a small buff you never truly need. In fact, all items differ in looks and flat stats only. For example, there is no meaningful buffs on armor sets equipped completely, you just swap stats and weight around.

Most weapons are balanced around the same DPS. Slow weapons hit harder, weak weapons quicker, that's it. I have never felt the sense of progression the entire game. Rings, that have downsides or conditions, felt quite the opposite of progression. If you don't have armor set bonuses, the rings should be the core of your build. Let's say, you want to build a character that uses magic, so you choose to equip two rings for spells, only to find out that they cancel each other out.

In swamps I realized, that you don't really need to fight anyone except level bosses. You can just loot chests and move on. So I speedran past enemies. Didn't feel like fighting anyone at this point, most enemies feel the same to fight against anyway. In the third level I stopped looting all those barely useful items as well.

As soon as the story got me surprisingly hooked, the game ended abruptly.

Right now I would not recommend it. I hope this game improves, but merely additional content is not gonna cut it.

This game is inspired by early games such as King’s Field. In other words, think of a slower paced, first person Soulslike experience.

Map consists of three main areas to explore. Every location has many forks and different paths to take, which at times made me feel like I was missing out on something but in a good way. Thankfully the game let me go back and explore everything more thoroughly. It makes exploration feel more organic and non linear. Maps also have some verticality and a great sense of scale which make the areas fun to explore.

Don't expect traditional RPG leveling up mechanics. Its a bit more basic in that regard. Instead you get stronger the more you explore and discover loot. By finding better equipment to make you do more damage and take less of it from enemies.

If you decide to veer from the main path or go back to areas and explore them further, you’re going to find a number of useful items. Rings, armor pieces, and weapons. Each with unique stats with respective strengths and weaknesses. Magic spells, overhead weapons, swords spears, and bows. There is a nice selection of weapon types here and items with different status effects.

Combat utilizes a stamina bar. Which makes you more careful and methodical when you attack. Encounters are tense but still feel fair and challenging. Don’t expect it to be a difficult, death filled experience though. It’s not as hard as the games it’s inspired by. I believe I only died twice and I’m not the best at Soulslike games to begin with. Since the combat is a bit slower, it overall makes combat and spacing more manageable. 

Stamina regeneration is tied to armor and weapons equipped. This meant that in order for me to have stamina regenerate faster, I would have only one weapon equipped in my quick-slot bar at a time. Which was less fun for me in the long run, because I would have liked to quickly switch between weapons depending on the situation. But stamina regeneration is an important priority when it comes to every enemy encounter. So one weapon equipped at a time felt like a must. If not, combat encounters would feel a little too lethargic and plodding.

An overall short experience that will take you around 3 to 4 hours depending on your skill and how much exploration you want to do. I really enjoyed this length because the game doesn't overstay its welcome. I felt like it was the perfect length that complements its map and combat mechanics. It’s a fun, lovingly crafted experience well worth your time.

4.5/5

Well-priced and well-paced, FlyKnight delivers an adventure with minimal padding and a strong focus on exploration. The game adopts a more traditional first-person RPG approach, with a deliberately slow movement and attack speed. While this enhances the methodical nature of combat, the stamina system can feel somewhat restrictive, artificially slowing progress. However, players will adapt, though they won’t be speeding through the game.

One drawback is the limited player vision, an attempt to emulate early PlayStation aesthetics. This design choice doesn’t necessarily enhance the experience, making navigation feel unnecessarily constrained.

Combat is simple but effective. The ability to sever enemy limbs serves as a disarming mechanic, while beheading them causes lethal blood loss. Weapon variety plays a crucial role, as enemies have specific weaknesses. For example, armored insect-like foes require crushing weapons like maces to bypass their defenses. The diversity within weapon classes keeps progression engaging—finding a halberd with dual weapon types is a significant upgrade that encourages more strategic combat choices.

The game’s pacing is well-balanced, and cooperative multiplayer offers an optional way to experience the journey with friends or random online players. That said, playing solo is entirely viable.
