So yes, I’ve bought REVO on day one which is a practice I usually tend to avoid. There are patches, discounts and content updates waiting down the line and there is definitely no need to hurry myself into an early release. This time the situation was different though.  
 
See, I’ve been waiting for this game for approximately 30 years now. As a PC gamer, I’ve been a Virtua Fighter 2 kid. Tekkens flashed those colorful flares each time an attack connected. In comparison, VF2 felt real. The motion capture was breathtaking too. I still remember Shun performing his drunk kata in the intro somewhere around 1997. And I’ve spammed those cheap Lion combos long before Eddy Gordo (as well as a rather significant number of Eddy players) even came into existence.  Truth be told, VF2 was one of the few 3D games that would run - low details, no shadows, 320x200 - on my computer at the time and Toshiden kinda sucked. 

[h3] Round 1. [/h3]  

REVO is a 20-year-old game with a thin layer of polish on top. Consequently, the graphics are visibly dated. The models, shadows and textures (despite the upscaling) are unimpressive and the facial expressions on close-ups look awkward. The stages make a better impression. They are colorful and decently varied. Despite the age, it is visible that back in the day VF5 was not an unsightly game and the quality of the port is not terrible.  The music is also serviceable but nothing to particularly marvel at. Apart from the Shun’s stage track.

[h3] Round 2. [/h3]

The core game is tremendously enjoyable. Virtua Fighter’s mechanics are quirky and unique enough to stand out even in 2025. There is a satisfying feeling of momentum and weight present during the fights. The sound effects are very reminiscent of classic kung fu movies. The pace of the battles is breakneck, and the matches are concluded in seconds. There is much to be liked here.     

[h3] Ring out. [/h3]
 
There is absolutely no content for one-person, local game. VF5 was released back when the extensive story modes in fighting games were not yet a thing and consequently its single player offers only the training and arcade modes. In addition to that, on my first attempt, I finished arcade in 3 minutes and 15 seconds (the summarized timer of fights, excluding the short cut-scenes introducing the players is displayed). There is not even a single screen or animation following the completion of arcade and watching the ending credits (3:33 according to YouTube) takes longer than beating the game itself. And there’s not even one new single-player mode introduced for the current release. Not even a volleyball minigame.

I have no doubt that from the multiplayer perspective, VF5 is, at least for the fans, a worthy deal. It offers a reasonable roster of 19 characters, ranked matches and there is a tournament coming. I also realize the fact that it costs a fraction of what the other developers ask for a modern 3D fighter. It is not a modern fighter though. But on the other hand, it’s not a bad game either.

Consequently, I’ve had a difficult time deciding against giving REVO a recommendation. At it’s heart, Virtua Fighter is an unique and solid game, and furthermore the quality of Steam port is rather acceptable. Finally, hardly anyone will probably be buying this game with single player in their mind. And yet, I’ve felt that REVO deserved a finger down, I’ve just needed a justification. And you know what? SEGA obliged.

From what I was able to find online, the original VF5 had quite vast character customization options that now have been significantly trimmed down so that REVO could be introduced to Steam accompanied by day one costume DLCs. Moreover, the cost of all three packs surpasses the price of the base game. So, I guess I need to thank SEGA for solving this for me.

To sum up, perhaps I have approached this game with unrealistic expectations caused by my fond memories. It is also possible that I am judging REVO too harshly for the lack of even the most rudimentary story included. While I won’t be refunding, it is only for the old times’ sake that I want to have a VF game in my library. Still, as I finish writing this, I can’t fight the feeling that Virtua Fighter should have stayed exactly where it had been for the last ten years or so. A minigame for the Yakuza series. 

As always, do with this what you will and, as always 
[h3] Try to have a wonderful life. [/h3]

# Virtua Fighter 5 is a great game
This port is not.

It suffers from a prominent button remapping bug, terrible matchmaking, and false advertising on its Steam store page.

The matchmaking's the worst of it, as the game will give you a "good" connection that runs with 8 frames of rollback and is completely unplayable. If there's no functioning online, there's no reason to buy this version of the game.
Then the game's store description describes it as featuring (and I quote directly here):

`• Custom Combatants: Enter the ring with one of 19 playable characters. Master each of their unique fighting styles and customize them with distinctive costumes and items.`

There is absolutely no customization in the base game. It's locked to the DLC which is MORE EXPENSIVE than the base game itself. Absolutely criminal, Sega botched it.

This is, at the moment, the best 3D fighting game you can play anywhere. If you ended up feeling disappointed and a little burned out by the exceedingly agressive nature of Tekken 8 in its current state, this is where you want to be: Technical but not bloated, easy to pick up but endlessly challenging, elegant and easy to read. VF5 really is in a class of its own. 

There's basically no single-player content outside of a fairly robust training and tutorial mode, which I would normally consider a deal breaker, but this is clearly meant as a refresher before Virtua Fighter 6, and I couldn't be happier to have made the jump now. This is a fighting game that will actually make you better at fighting games.

Matchmaking and overall network quality were extremely rough on release, which is the main reason for the mixed reviews, but this has now been fixed and the current state of the netcode, while not amazing, feels adequate enough. Spend time in Room matches over ranked for the best experience.

Another point of contention is the fact that every single piece of cosmetics is locked behind DLCs. This is petty and kind of a shame, given that the game does have a robust character customization, but at least the base price is low enough as to remain reasonable even with DLCs added on top. The "Yakuza Series collaboration" and "Legendary" pack contain most of the cosmetics that You'll want.

Before I get to the review I do want to say the game runs perfectly on Steam Deck at around medium settings. Though if you are going to play on it do the right thing and get an ethernet dongle or the system dock.

Virtua Fighter 5 is an absolute classic fighting game that has been revised numerous times over the years. This latest version is functionally the kind of remake where new visuals are over top the original game code. Some of the aesthetic changes are controversial or not to my preference but the general vibe and art direction feels appropriate within the franchise. On top of that you have an all new balance patch which in my opinion has been fantastic and really freshened up the cast in satisfying ways.

The netcode was something I was very worried about with the rollback beta, but most of my concerns there were avoided in the final release. Despite the relatively low player count I have constant matches with different players and anything up to about 220 ping or so feels extremely playable to me. I have tested some lobby matches with friends who are on the complete opposite end of the planet and though there were some notable rollback frames in longer sessions it ran very smoothly overall. That is fantastic as even years from now when functionally no one is playing ranked anymore many of the room matches you find will continue to be playable. Though an update giving us more ping information alongside wifi indicators would be greatly appreciated.

If you are new to Virtua Fighter I can understand being a bit scared by the legacy and complexity of certain characters, but at a very base level the series is extremely approachable and much of the cast are 'button masher friendly'. As someone who has introduced the game to several friends over the years I can tell you that even very inexperienced fighting game players quickly learned the more nuanced aspects from very standard play. Because the fighting is pretty traditional and focused it is extremely uncommon for a move to look like it has visually unpredictable properties like many current fighting games. Training mode has just about any feature you could ever want, but if you do get stuck the VF series has tons of documentation for anything that may hold you up and the fanbase in general is very welcoming and ready to assist any player.

I do have a few complaints with this particular version of the game. Mainly the DLC is handled in a strange and confusing way. The vast majority of negative reviewers feel ripped off due to how poorly phrased the DLC packs are and I cannot help but agree. The base game functionally has no character customization, does not let you change the in-game soundtrack and lacks a ton of the extra stickers for reacting to matches in the lobbies. This is also on top of a ton of the customization options from Virtua Fighter 5 Final Showdown on Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 NOT making their way over to this newest release even if you get all of the DLC. There are a few new additions that were never in previous releases and ultimately this is just fluff, but it is unfortunate that this could not be the complete package of all things VF5.

All that said, I am nowhere close to a pro and never will be, but I have likely thousands of hours played across all versions of Virtua Fighter 5 and can see myself playing thousands more. This new version while lacking in some areas is my personal favorite release of the game and even if Virtua Fighter 6 ends up disappointing me I know I will always be able to comfortably continue playing this for the rest of my life.

Credit where it's due, VF5 is a classic and is such a wonderful game to come back to time and time again; having it accessible any means is always welcoming.
This particular iteration was made with the intention of porting over the game onto RGG's in house engine and it looks good, is well optimized, and is spurring up conversation in what to look forward to for the future of the franchise, or more specifically VF6.
So why all the negative reviews?

It was an originally a PS4 exclusive, but it was received more positively. If you just wanted the VF5 Ultimate Showdown experience with better presentation, easier access on newer hardware at the time, this was the way to do it. Unlike the initial release of VF5 for Xbox 360/PS3, the only single player content here is an arcade mode. This version, along with Final Showdown were made for fans who wanted an updated version of the game with an online focus to play competitively. For all intents and purposes, this was never being sold as a brand new release with extensive content. As much as I would love that, this release was more so intended to get people back into VF while also porting the most recent, and accessible versions of the game. That being said, I can understand why few people are annoyed with how this version may have been advertised, but it was never made out to be anything more than a newer revision of VF5 Ultimate Showdown. I think where my personal frustration resides is that despite the game already being a few years old with various sales, including the DLC, this release decided to make the DLC separate purchases again as opposed to making it part of the complete release. Is it necessary? No, you can play the game just fine without that content, and I imagine in time it'll be dirt cheap during a sale, but you'd think with how much time has passed, they would have just incorporated the DLC as part of this release instead of selling it separate for a total of $30 for all the sets, or $10 each. Annoying, but whatever. These are just minor aspects as to why people are mostly mad.

The major selling point of this release in particular, aside of finally being on another platform beyond the PS4, was rollback netcode. I was not part of the beta prior to this game's launch, but it seems very obvious that it was significantly more stable than it is now. It's extremely unfortunate, but the game can still be played normally offline, but also, you can go back to the original delay based netcode. It's tucked away in the settings and had they made this information more public, I'd imagine the outrage wouldn't be as bad as it has been, but alas that didn't pan out how it should. 

I originally debated on giving this a negative review, but the game is playable, the initial launch price is cut to $15 for people who JUST want to play the base game without the extra DLC costumes, there's worse things to spend that much money on. I imagine in time, the reviews will be significantly more positive once patches fix up the rollback netcode and people can enjoy this game online more conveniently. I think this launch was extremely clumsy and very on brand for SEGA, and I hate giving them passes when they mess up, but I think this was more of an unprecedented accident than anything else.

TL;DR the rollback online sucks, but you can use the original netcode to play significantly more stable matches, this is an online focused release of VF5, nothing more nothing less. It's cheap, it's fun, DLC being separate purchase again for an otherwise 4 year old game is annoying, but I expect discounts sooner than later down the line. Buy it at your own risk knowing all of the above.

After spending several hours with the game, I’m left with mixed impressions. It immediately reminds me of Street Fighter V’s initial launch—stripped down and lacking substantial content. The available modes are limited to Arcade, Online, Local Versus, and Practice, and that’s about it. Given its $19.99 price tag, the barebones nature isn’t a complete deal-breaker, but it does raise concerns about its long-term viability. I suspect this could be one of those fighting games where the community fizzles out within a few months. 

Even more frustrating is the lack of crossplay. In an era where even smaller fighting games are embracing cross-platform matchmaking, locking players into separate ecosystems is a step in the absolute wrong direction—especially for a niche franchise like Virtua Fighter. With an already limited player base, restricting matchmaking options only accelerates the risk of a dwindling online community.

[h2]Online Play & Connection Issues[/h2]
Matchmaking is fairly quick for now, and most matches have run smoothly for me. However, the internet connection indicator feels unreliable. I’ve encountered multiple instances where I accepted a match with a four-bar connection, only for the fight to start with severe lag—characters teleporting across the screen. While this hasn’t been a frequent issue, it has occurred enough times to be worth mentioning.

[h2]Gameplay & Appeal[/h2]
At its core, it’s still Virtua Fighter—a game built on solid fundamentals. If you’re a fan of neutral-based footsies and DEEP, methodical gameplay, you’ll likely find something to enjoy here. It’s impressive just how much depth the game achieves with only three buttons.

However, for casual players or those indifferent to the fighting game genre, this release is unlikely to change their minds.

My first ever fighting game (let alone my first ever video game) was Virtua Fighter 1 on my dad's PC back in late 90's or early 00's. Sentiment aside, Virtua Fighter 5: R.E.V.O. is a solid 3D fighting game, a nice throwback to the earlier styles of grounded martial arts before all the devil genes, super powers, and laser beams came around. This series introduced the first ever combo extension system, the "Bound" system that we're all so familiar with thanks to games such as Tekken incorporating it later. Suffice to say, this series is revolutionary. Thankfully, VF5: R.E.V.O. has retained much of the series' core fundamentals, allowing newcomers to learn about poking, sidestepping, parrying, and positioning better than most games in the genre.
The only constructive criticism I can give is the "lack" of everything. Lack of customization, lack of tutorial, lack of single player content, etc. However, with constant updates and added substance, I believe this game could become the side-game to Tekken we all craved. And I hope the new Virtua Fighter 6 will carry on this enthusiasm from both the players and the devs.

Let's start by saying there are 3 main reasons I somewhat enjoy playing Torque Drift 2, even if there are more consumer-friendly drift sims around: 

1. Graphics - Unreal Engine 5 has bad performance, yes. And I have a 4090. Graphically tho, looks stunning. Car materials, lights, models and environments are unmatched in this game compared to other games like CarX or even modded Assetto Corsa.
2. Licensed Parts & Cars - While there isn't a lot of content yet, you can find most cars and tracks you would expect from a drift game (as of February 2025, no european brands - except for a Lamborghini - unluckily).
In terms of tracks, there's a classic mountain touge, Long Beach, Daikoku (best rendition of Daikoku I've ever seen), Ebisu...
3. Destruction - While kinda basic, I think bumpers detaching from the vehicle really add to immersion when everything goes wrong and you wall-tap at high speeds.

Having said that, there are a few reasons Torque Drift 2 won't surpass Assetto Corsa and CarX; some choices made by the developers are honestly baffling.
At first, they implemented NFTs: every car, part, was an insanely priced NFT. How could they think this was a good idea? There's literally no reason I can think of where someone could like that and not avoid this game.
In the current version NFTs were luckily removed (I would've never bought this game otherwise), but their reputation is stained from that move and rightly so.
Like many other mostly-singleplayer games, Torque Drift 2 also suffers from the always-online formula. No internet connection, you can't play. When are they gonna realize this stuff drives people away from their games? Let's add to the fact that everything you buy (in-game and yes, currency can be bought with real money) is server-side. Some parts are available only on rotation: if you want that cool wheel, you gotta wait for it to be available. Digital fake products are made scarce for no reason at all.

Based on the fact that there's a solid base, and while excusing the fact that it's still lacking some content (like custom liveries, a driver model, a greater selection of events, vehicles, tracks, the forced HUD on display - really?) which are somehow forgivable for an early access title (which I don't really trust anymore), those anti-consumer tactics chosen by a relatively small studio (that really needed redemption after the NFTs fiasco) for a game which is already in its own niche I don't feel is deserving of a positive review.

I highly suggest taking a look at how Genki released TXR (early-access as well) and why it's been so succesful (right now the most played racing game surpassing in sales other AAA/AA releases).

[h1]The Slop Strikes Back[/h1]

Due to game reciving updates if anything in this review is [strike]striked off[/strike], that means it was changed.

Another six months passed since my man Arthur created his masterpiece [b]Supernatural[/b]. This time it's proudly announced that the game is now made by a WHOPPING 2 devs. So it's either double the quality or double the failure. Regardless, it's progress. Maybe around 5th game there is gonna be something worthy created by the crew, and here is why.

Dream Cage is yet another run-of-the-mill anomaly spotting game. And not the good one either. See I like to split anomaly games into two categories:

1) Fun ones where anomalies are there to disturb you and create a spectacle, so they are relatively easy to spot.
2) Boring bastard ones where change is barely noticeable unless you have a degree in pixel hunting.

Dream Cage tried to be a mix, which I find respectable, since for the most part it's not forcing you to find obnoxiously hidden or barely noticeable changes to progress the story [spoiler](unless you are going for the secret ending) [/spoiler] but anomalies are nothing special. They are not fun to find, they don't impress you, most of them don't disturb you and it feels more like a chore than anything. Surely it's a subjective take, I personally like more interactive games where I don't spend decades circling the environment trying to spot miniscule differences, but even the most patient person would go crazy.

Mainly because you have three restrictions. [b]Sanity, camera battery life and microphone threshold[/b]. Third only matters if you are a streamer. And comparing to two previous installment, it got worse. No more talking to the ghost. Make too much noise = death. And having things that hinder your progress so you don't just go through the game in half an hour is fine, but the way it's implemented is just terrible. You can see anomalies only if you use the camera, and when you use said camera it spends both your sanity and battery charge  [strike]unbelievable fast[/strike], especially so if you are scanning for anomalies. So you'll be forced to farm items before you even commit to proper investigation.

What items you might ask? Well, to keep yourself from kicking the bucket [b]you gotta pick up batteries and pills[/b] that spawn around the apartment, and it's so bizarre because items spawn right in front of you, just materializing with the glitch effect. This is somewhat justified with our protagonist having alzheimer's, but the sheer amount of stuff that can spawns is ridiculous. And you can't commit to mixed playstyle either, aka spot a few anomalies then go for items to replenish, because their spawn is random. Sometimes you need pills, it gives you batteries, or vice versa. Or sometimes it spawns nothing at all, so you either waiting or just taking an L and restarting the night. This time death has consequences. And talking about equipping, every time you pick up an item it plays out the same two unnecessary lengthy animations [strike]that cause motion sickness after a while[/strike]. This gets old incredibly quickly. I wish they would be as swift as in say Outlast.

You know what also gets old quickly? [b]Jumpscares[/b]. And some of them also affect your sanity. We are in 2025 and still receiving games where main scare factor is a thing going BOO loudly. So for majority of time you'll be walking around the apartment trying to remember dozens of things at once and waiting for items to spawn to keep playing the game while mildly annoyed by loud noises and tiring animations. 

The redeemable qualities are sound design that does it's job at building tension properly. Visuals are incredibly detailed and diverse thought the nights, and game seems to be running better than previous installments. Thanks you Unreal Engine 5. I'm glad we are on "quality over performance" ark. I love playing game in less than 60 fps and relying on upscalers or third party software like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/993090/Lossless_Scaling/] Lossless Scaling [/url]  to have playable frames. Where was I? Oh. Sleep paralysis sequences, they are well animated, tense and gruesome. Good reward for beating the night.[spoiler]hilariously enough tho, one of the best animations is spoiled to you right on store page, so it's even less things to see[/spoiler] And game' price. It's cheap, you buy it, beat it, and don't feel too bad if it doesn't hit the spot.

Dream Cage is a mix of anomaly hunt meets sleep paralysis simulator. You try to find anomalies in your apartment over the course of 5 days. Each day is a different time period in the main character's life. Each night you are tormented by different horrors as you suffer with sleep paralysis. You have to manage the battery in your camera (not sure why we have this tbh) and also your sanity, so you'll be on a constant hunt for batteries and medication while searching for anomalies and dodging ghosts.

Pros: - It looks great
- Great sound design
- Impressive animations
- Interesting story

Cons: - A few bugs in the current version. The microphone mechanic (yes the game listens to you) is kind of busted. I have a very quiet mic, so I had to turn the sensitivity up, but there is a big where if you turn it up past a certain point the "threshold" gets maxed out, so starting a game like this will result in nearly instant death. I also had a bug where a jumpscares animation froze the game. Another bug happened when I was reading a note and a jumpscare locked the text on screen.
- No pausing. Need to use the restroom? Too bad.
- The final day's anomalies are kind of disappointing. 

Overall I really enjoyed this game, and I think with a few more updates and bug squashing, it'll be a great game.

[h3]Overall (3/5):[/h3]
I played the other two games from this developer and was not expecting this one to be good since other ones were very poor. I think this one at least had a good concept and idea but unfortunately same as other ones had a poor gameplay mechanic, repetitive and boring jump scares, some annoying animations and bugs. Honestly I can't recommend this game since it has same issues as other ones and seems they just don't want to listen and improve. 

[h3]Graphics and Visuals (4/5):[/h3]
Same as other games from this developer this is the strongest aspect of their games, visuals are good with some good character animations. If you care about good looking game maybe it's good option for you. 

One negative thing is the overall darkness of the game specifically around sleep paralysis parts, I could barely see anything, in store page the animation is so bright but in game it was opposite and was not really fun. 

[h3]Gameplay and Mechanics (2/5):[/h3]
What you need to do in this game is basically collect battery, pills and find anomalies. It's very different than other two games. You need to be quiet and manage your sanity level with those pills. There are 5 levels with 10 anomalies in each and by finding at least 7 you can progress to next level. The most annoying part for me in this game was batteries and pills, every time you pick them up there is a long animation that you have to watch and you do this a lot, I mean like half of your gameplay is doing these. I understand that they added this for immersion but it didn't work honestly and became boring and annoying very fast.

The jump scares are just same with different ghosts. Every time one of them jumps at you when you open a door for example, the animations are all the same with just different character. In previous games they used lots of noise and loud sounds which after a while you get used to it and ignore it, same thing happens here. There are not a lot of spooky elements, just sounds and same cheap jump scares over and over. Really not scary at all.

Your sanity drops fast when using camera to find anomalies which I think was a good part of the game but if you learn the mechanic it can easily be avoided. You can easily finish the game around one hour. 

[h3]Storyline and Immersion (3/5): [/h3]
I believe story was better than previous games, as I said it had a good concept but unfortunately execution hold it back. Each level changes based on the character that game trying to tell story about which was good. There are some documents scattered around which tell more about story. 

Immersion is well done, each level is in same place but with different elements and layout, different noises and ghosts with related anomalies to that specific ghost.

[h3]Sound and Music (3/5): [/h3]
Sound effects was a huge part of this game, random noises can be heard throughout of each level which are related to that level and ghost. Some are really good some are really boring and repetitive. 

[h3]Performance, Bugs and User Experience (4/5): [/h3]
I didn't encounter any game breaking bugs but there were lots of animation bugs during my gameplay like for example I noticed a lot of animation issues when handling camera and pill, they float and get mixed together without showing hands.

Performance wise I limited my frame rate to 120 with 3090 and highest quality on 1440p resolution and hit it without any major issues. There were some occasional hiccups but nothing serious. 

[h3]Replayability (2/5): [/h3]
There is some replayability in this game if you want to get the true ending, you need to find all anomalies in each level plus reading all notes. But overall gameplay doesn't change and you have to play and see same thing.

Dream Cage is a fairly simple game. Innovation or special mechanics don't really apply here. I miss the ability to ask the ghost questions from the previous games this dev has made, BUT there's still some good to be found here. Maybe not at full price. I already got the good ending and once you figure out the tricks, the game is way too easy.

MISCONCEPTION CHECK

I see alot of reviews with wrong info. Let me alleviate some of that.
Q: The game stopped spawning items.
A: In some chapters, items no longer spawn concurrently. During play, I found that the last 2 chapters were most guilty of this. The first chapter makes you think that only the kitchen or maybe main area spawn items, but further in you will have to get items from other rooms too. If a battery spawns in the bathroom, kitchen batteries may not occur until the one there has been found. Some of the hiding places were admittedly difficult.

Q: Sound mechanic is only for streamers\is broken\kills you instantly.
A: No. On all accounts. If you turn the mic settings up higher, you'll get more out of it when playing alone. It does work but only for the defualt mic, so if you play with your mic on discord set to the headset and not your default, that may be why. It also does not kill you instantly. It simply force spawns the ghost and hyper increases the insanity meter. Simply duck behind something or close the nearest door. 70% of the time, you'll survive.

Q: Deaths are random/unfair/cheap.
A: Take more pills. Literally. if you always stay under 3/4 bars of insanity, the ghost just straight up doesn't spawn most of the time if at all. If you die and don't know why or how, then you didn't look through the camera at what was killing you. 

All that said, 6/10. Story is way more solid compared to previous games from this dev, but the mechanics and difficulty have gone down drastically. Many scares are jumpscares, and ghosts are only scary if you don't horde resources. Recommended because of the lower price point and the game at least being a functional product with somewhat fun anomaly hunting. 

GLITCHES 
Most are fixed, but I did find that some notes can soft lock the game when being re read in the same life. It doesn't set you back far enough to be a real issue though. Also, as of writing, you can just leave the camera on after it runs out of battery and farm pills to eat while holding it making you essentially never run out of battery. This does increase insanity drastically, though, so you won't rely on it later in game.

It's a great game overall. I thought it was fantastic that the anomalies were fairly balanced with how easy they were to find and how in your face they were (or weren't). There were plenty of jump scares that got me. I felt that the way the story was given as well as how it played out was perfect. Definitely worth playing a few times in order to get all of the achievements and reach both endings.

I feel a little bad saying this about what's a smaller indie game. But it feels like it's still Early Access and needs a ton more work and polish before it's worth buying. A few issues I had:
1. No controller support. Doing the sidescrolling Metroid action on planets is really bad with keyboard, and they should've known that anyone checking this game out on Steam is going to want to use a controller for that part.
2. Pretty bad physics/gameplay in the sidescrolling part of the game. Most games of this type give you better control over your movement in air. Particularly if you're jumping and moving backwards, the slow movement feels bad. Even if that's intentional, all it really does is give bad comparisons to other stuff in the genre.
3. Amateurish graphics. This is something that also really needs to be addressed. Everything looks like it was part of some free pixel art collection from an old Flash game with no sense of style. I'd expect the sprites in this game as placeholders, but again, it's not Early Access.
4. The UI needs a ton of work. There's no minimap to help you avoid constantly pausing to check your exploration, the big map itself gets loaded with icons that are hard to read, there's no feedback on how to open a few kinds of doors... I'd say this is at best 50% of the way to what a good, functional UI should be.

The bones are there to make something good, but right now it's way too flawed to recommend playing it. The build mode is great, though, so once they make it so it's actually fun to explore planets, this could be a fantastic game.

But trust me when I say that I wouldn't even want to play a newgrounds game in 2002 with controls this bad. The jumping feels terrible. The gunplay is awful. Nothing about this grabs me.

A game like this should have tight controls and combat to start with. You don't design this whole user-created ecosystem and THEN say that you'll make the movement enjoyable later, like StarLair does. 

If the controls were improved and tightened with more engaging combat, I would recommend this game. But I think it might be too late for the dev to change the controls. There's already a ton of user-generated content that is out there with the assumption that players have certain limitations. I just don't know how this game could ever be fixed. But hey, maybe I'll be surprised.

The whole game takes place inside a little fast food kiosk where you prepare foods such as hamburgers, hot dogs, pancakes, salads, fries, onion rings, eggs etc... 

As people come in to order their food they mention things about their daily lives, and a little mystery involving a serial killer is explored.

+ The actual gameplay is fun. The controls and layout of the kiosk is well thought out and preparing the food was never boring during the entire playthrough.
+ The story kept me hooked, I wanted to know who the killer was.
+ The atmosphere is immersive, with the rain hammering down and being stuck inside the small claustrophobic kiosk. 

- The ending is a bit of surprise, but also a letdown as well. it is too abrupt and low budget.
- The game uses text for dialog from the NPC characters. It would have been nice to hear some voices, even AI voices would have worked for more immersion.
- Could have used more horror elements and be more scary.
- I don't like how the knife was used, to cut things you have to "Throw" the knife.

Fast Paced, Frantic, and Fun.
Overall 7.5 / 10

The jumpscares in the demo were arguably better paced (especially with the turn around guy right after your first experience instead of right before). Absolutely worth the purchase, but please keep the original demo up.

the story is... okay. Nothing special but not bad either. The storytelling has weakened the story quite a bit. 
The story is mainly told through the customers, but too much “obvious” was told and repeated in other words that it couldn't really build any tension for me. In addition, halfway through the story you already knew how it would end, as the story is very simple.

The gameplay is very monotonous. A few things are added in the first few days, but it's basically always the same. Tthere are only 2 "jumpscares" that are repeated. I think some things could have been sped up to create more tension, which would also have improved the effect of the scares and even the game would have been shorter, the atmosphere could have been much better, which would have improved the whole game in my opinion. Leaving a positive review because I love supporting indie devs, and indie horror devs in particular.

HOWEVER

This is the full release version of a demo that released on itch.io in 2024. The demo was fantastic.
The full release leaves something to be desired as it:

1) costs money now
2) drags on much too long with too little change to the story.

The demo was about an hour and has the EXACT SAME story and events that the demo has - save for the ending where [spoiler] the killer attacks you with a knife versus using a present-bomb. [/spoiler] Because of this the demo felt much better paced, against the full release which is about 2.5hrs on its own with just very drawn-out food prep sections in between. Ultimately it was very unfulfilling, and the demo was the better play.

I am aware that there is an "Endless" and "Relaxing" mode, however I dont find the gameplay loop or food prep intuitive or fulfilling enough to play them.

The premise of this game is pretty simple and the story quite linear, you could easily speed-run and finish it within 30-40 minutes (Took me 60 and that was because I took a break in between and tried to immerse myself by restocking the shelves each day). There are also two endless modes, one which completely removes horror aspect for those that enjoy the cooking part which is pretty fun in it's own merit. 

It only lost 2 points because I think the story could've been a bit longer and had more depth, with different stories overlapping from different customers or varied jumpscares that weren't just a shadowy figure (ie. have the health inspector bang on the door and physically come in). The other issue that I encountered was that the map didn't clear after each day, some items you can drop into places which are not reachable and this meant they were just stuck there for the entire playthrough such as a salad that I managed to throw past a customer and it laid in the background whilst getting stinky over the days.  

Overall, pretty solid for the price and is genuine in it's marketing for what it offers.

Such a fun mix of cooking and horror in a game! This seemingly ordinary environment quickly turns into a nightmare as the protagonist must deal with terrifying and unexpected events. I really enjoyed it. 💙💙💙

I love the core mechanic that involves "immersive" food preparation. Think of an extended Arx Fatalis cooking system—you have to move around the kitchen, throw ingredients around in a goofy way, and I find it great! Even if the core mechanic starts to feel repetitive and boring around the middle of the game (which was about an hour in for me), you can still try to optimize and prepare orders as fast as possible.

As for the horror elements, there are a couple of jump scares. They did catch me off guard, but overall, the game has more of a thriller/uncanny vibe, which suits me better.

The story and characters feature some funny dialogues from time to time, although I wouldn’t say the story is very engaging. The biggest fun comes from the food preparation!

As a fan of short experiences and fresh mechanics, I totally recommend the game. You can feel that the developer put a lot of heart into it and did their best.

however it still feels like it doesnt have enough/still has more that it could offer. as examples for what *i* think could be added:
...intermission between nights, maybe going to your apartment and doing a routine before continuing. night of the living consumers esc. as an example, once you clock out of the shift, you have to grab your stuff in a locker or something and then leave the building, get in a car, and your tp'd to your apartment. (bonus points if you get to drive there and stuff inside your apartment is functional, allowing you to actually do whatever you want until you decide to go to bed. isnt this an immersive sim, after all?) an open map is discussed in a later point

...scary events are really repetitive, its just a shadow figure that appears in different spots, sometimes its more funny than scary to see a random shadow fall flat on the stove. i suggest subtler stuff like the the enviroment changing slightly to reward people who look closely, evidence of a physical presence of a person rather than spooky ghosts (that i dont think fits very well)

...a possible revamp of the story mode, with the current scale of the game i think its just about long enough but there's no sense of "who could it be" because its so blatantly obvious its that one guy. though, i did think the killer was going to turn out to be the 'victim's best friend' guy, but i was just slightly disappointed to see the killer was infact the most obvious suspect. it could use a sense of mystery, maybe some paranoia and clashing evidence that could point to anybody being the murderer. also "uncovering the mystery of what happened to the last worker" is more like listening to random people giving you exposition dumps rather than you doing any sort of personal investigating. (you could add these oppertunities in the previously mentioned intermissions?)

...im not sure how this would effect balancing, but cleaning processes could be added as a feature. maybe not something to enforce, but as an optional thing if people wanna keep things clean and tidy. for example, taking out the trash that you throw away to a garbage bin, mopping floors, cleaning windows (if any), cleaning tables and equipment. maybe cleaning the place would increase tip earnings from customers?

...in the chance that an intermission where you go to an apartment (or house) is added, you could add function to the earnings you get from serving people by allowing opportunities to buy stuff or upgrade stuff in your apartment for better quality of life. if your feeling spicy, maybe a feature to decorate said apartment with the furniture you buy, going from a mattress and a microwave or something to a good looking living space to your liking

...also in the chance that the same scenario is added, the ability to physically leave the building a drive home within a possible open map and go explore places (maybe to uncover the mystery of the killer and the previous worker). or just add whatever you want lmao

while these suggestions are quite ambitious especially because this doesnt seem to be the type of game to be much more than a small project, i quite like the game and think it could definitley be expanded upon. but hey, its your game, do what you want with it! i write this paragraph because i like the game and want to see it expand. either way, your choice, i support it!

I have beaten every limit time and unlocked most of the cars in the game.  Here are my observations:

- Moon-like gravity means your cars feel like they don't have suspension.
- Infinitely Rigid collision physics (your car will do flips if you touch a fence or a small dirt embankment)
- The road is so low poly in some cases that you can get high-centered ON THE TRACK.
- Flat levels have generous time limits, whereas the mountainous levels have extremely tight times for even the highest performance cars.
- You cannot use the handbrake option on controller. It seems to just switch your camera to rear-view.
- Pressing the left stick (which can happen often during tight corners) switches to a rear-facing camera and requires 4 more taps to switch between different cinematic cameras to get back to a normal camera.  This almost always ruins your whole run.
- No control customization, so you cannot fix the camera/handbrake issues.
- Menus require a mouse and cannot be navigated with a controller.
- Draw distance is shorter for trees than for checkpoints.
- Frame rate drops often, and the physics interpolation is rough.

All in all, what should be Zen is Quite Frusturating.

As a long time fan of both Rune Factory and Picross, the idea of this title excited me but ended up coming up short. Piczle Cross Rune Factory is a perfectly competent nonogram game but it does little-to-nothing with the IP and has its own issues even as a basic nonogram puzzler.

The trailers led me to believe this game would combine nonogram puzzle solving with features expected of Rune Factory, such as taming monsters and raising crops. In a way, this is the case, but the implementation is severely barebones and the game really is just a standard nonogram game with some visual bluster. Any features related to farm crops, monsters, and character equipment as seen in the trailers are purely decorational and have no relation to the core gameplay of puzzle solving. When I picked up this title I was hoping for even just a very basic background system such as planting crops and solving puzzles to pass time for them to grow, but the game has no extra features.

Utilization of the Rune Factory series IP was rather disappointing, as well. All 3D assets in this game appear to have been carried over from Rune Factory 5, so all iconography seen throughout the game really only represents that title, which was not quite as well received as the older games. As well, while some music plays and some characters are mentioned from outside of RF5, it only goes as far as the Rune Factory games currently on the market: Rune Factory 4 Special and Rune Factory 3 Special. This game is not a celebration of Rune Factory as a whole and as such contains no reference to 1, 2, Frontier, or Tides. This is a missed opportunity since although those games are admittedly much too old to pull 3D assets from, using the character designs for puzzles and using the music to play along to would have helped greatly in making this title feel more like a celebration made with care and less like an advertisement.

Piczle Cross Rune Factory has its problems as just a normal nonogram game as well:

Somehow, the controls with a mouse are totally foreign and strange feeling. This game really just does not behave itself while trying to control it with a mouse, which was disappointing as I was interested in having a nonogram game for PC. On Nintendo DS/3DS, the touch screen could be used very comfortably by dragging the stylus across several pieces, using a button to designate whether you were clearing or marking them. This game requires the pieces to be clicked one-by-one which feels very slow and awkward, and I unfortunately had to play the game with a controller instead. The gamepad controls do work well, but I would have preferred fluid mouse control. This could be done by dragging through tiles with left click to fill in or right click to mark.

The game features a "Challenge Mode" which tasks the player with solving each puzzle with an in-game timer, with mistakes subtracting from the time. Lazily, this timer is always set to one hour, no matter how basic the puzzle, which is an ungodly amount of time even for the more complex ones. Additionally, playing in Challenge Mode forcibly enables autocorrect to facilitate the time subtracting mechanic, regardless of your preference in the settings. This had the effect of using the mode actually actually making the game EASIER than my preferred settings, which is annoying to put up with for 50 rounds to unlock the Challenge Mode achievements.

To its credit, the game does have lots of puzzles to solve and also includes the colored nonograms. The puzzles are cute and there are a lot of gameplay options to facilitate newcomers that can be optionally disabled. However, the game mechanically is a very barebones nonogram experience with some issues even in doing that.

Enjoy this game.

The actual review: Sonar Scout is a straightforward game with fun, unique moment to moment gameplay and a strong theme that beautifully resonates through every aspect of the game. What starts out as a seemingly simple concept turns into a larger than expected journey through a variety of levels with a variety of submarines with their own gameplay. Sonar Scout has one simple idea, explore an underwater environment using your sonar to see. Your "pings" briefly make the landscape visible, during which time you must carefully navigate around the twists and turns of the underwater cave systems. 

The catch is, you have very limited uses of your ping, and a small health pool that depletes when you bump into the sides or make contact with one of the hostile creatures floating around the caves. At first this seems simple enough, with each beacon you activate helping to permanently paint the landscape in a short distance around it.

But this quickly gets trickier and trickier as these beacons are spread further apart, the landscapes get more complex, and more and more hostile creatures appear in the open spaces between them. This forces you to make efficient use of your battery and risk longer and longer jaunts in the dark, trying to keep the landscape in your memory as it fades to blackness on the screen.

A really welcome touch is that when you take damage you also get the effect of a sonar ping, meaning when you run out of battery you can sometimes navigate to safety using the last of your remaining health as a backup sonar ping. This leads to some extremely tense moments, crawling slowly through the caves trying desperately to get to safety.

The leader boards add a nice incentive to repeat the levels, getting quicker and more daring and trying to clear each stage in shorter and shorter times.

I've only played the first few stages right now but I'm already hooked and I'm looking forward to settling in to finish it.

Overview:
- You can sit still at a checkpoint/respawn, but not anywhere else in the game. You have to be constantly moving, or you will get respawned. This doesn't make any sense.

Note to all Devs: Do not start the first level of your game with a far checkpoint (if it has one), do not introduce new mechanics when the player has not even adjusted to the game, and finally, no first level should be longer than 20 minutes.

I like the quicker game playtime vs other survivors-likes, being able to hop in and out quickly makes it a more casual experience.

Also, while I haven't unlocked the entire map yet, I'm thinking I'm going to want even more levels than are currently in the game. Looks like there is going to be about 6 or so levels in the game, which at my current progression, I'm guessing the note on the store page about playtime is seeming like it will be pretty accurate as of the time of this review. 

All in all I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the genre, and I would even say that the pacing of this game might make it a better entry point to the genre than some of the other heavy hitters.

[h1]Warning[/h1]
I am a player who likes to try and solve games. If you're just looking to shut your brain off entirely, ignore this review as my focus is on gameplay systems and how they work. I also won't talk about the unfinished translation as parts of the game are not in English.

I will also slot in (see : x) to tell you that this idea is discussed properly in a later part of the review.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Initial Rambling [/h2]

Elements and Build is fundamentally a fun game that borrows ideas from autobattlers and tower defense games. It also manages to sneak in some original ideas through the tower combinations. However it's incredibly uncreative at a strategic level (see : strategic breakdown)  and was likely designed by somebody who wasn't very good at the afformentioned genres. (see : talent tree discussion)

What it does right is present a cute, approachable game for beginners who don't mind a slow early game grind to unlock the upgrades needed to consistently win. The towers that attack are fun to use and when you force a specific type of towers will grant bonuses that feel good to use. The levels are varied and fun, with novel ideas present across them, which makes for more variety in the gameplay.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Strategic Breakdown [/h2]

Want to know the secret to winning every time? Put your base in the corner and build a maze around it, using the corner walls to force enemies to a corner. Now once you've done that just pick any tower and stack whatever goes with that tower. You'll win every time once you have a few upgrades. Unfortunately that's the whole game. Once you realise this you'll no longer feel the need to play.

At no point do your choices beyond this matter thanks to the...

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Talent Tree [/h2]

Of the several meta systems (talent tree, equipment, base building) this one is by far the most game breaking and the worst in design. When designing a talent tree you want to feel that you're asking players to make a choice, but in this game you're expected to simply unlock every single node on the tree and become strong enough to overpower the game. Which is precisely what has happened for me. It's entirely impossible for me to die now in this game if I follow the afformentioned strategy. The solution however is a full rework of this system. Instead of buying upgrades that eventually lead you from being not quite strong enough to consistently win, to consistently winning. You should be given paths to go down with choices that make engaging gameplay changes that reward using different types of towers. Then allow players to freely change their choices between games and you'll have a system that can be balanced and give strong bonuses exclusively for varying playstyles.

With the current system however you're simply grinding the game until you can't lose. It feels like playing an RPG in the starting area and overlevelling so you never take damage and kill everything as they spawn.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Equipment [/h2]

This meta system is one you're less likely going to engage with. After finishing a level you're rewarded with equipment that you can equip for minor boosts going into the game. However it's not fully translated and from what I did understand I realised that it's too weak to make a significant different vs the talent tree. However you can sell the equipment to just buy points on the talent tree. This whole system exists just to funnel extra money into you for talents. It should be removed until the designers can find a functional use for it.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Starting Buildings [/h2]

Of all the meta systems this one is actually good. Your starting base can be augmented for a meaningful and quite dramatic change in the early game. I don't understand how to unlock these but I've unlocked quite a lot and they're incredibly fun to play with. This is by far the strongest and most positive gameplay decision you can make. This is like selecting your character. 

[hr][/hr]

[h2] What I'd change. [/h2]

Okay I'm sort of losing my trail of thought. Here is a list of what I'd do to dramatically improve this game, this is subjective but my focus is on engaging players at all skill levels.

1) Force flying enemies. When playing you can select what enemies you're against, players should always be forced to handle flying enemies at some point. It will reduce the effectiveness of hiding in the corner and doing nothing. Which allows you to play far greedier than you should.

2) Rework talent tree. Start with studying the old League of Legends masteries/modern runes + WoW talents to understand what small and large choices could look like. Play to different strengths a player may invest in across the game. Give talents that are viable most of the time and some that are only viable some of the time as it'll engage players when making decisions. Also make it an "account level", so you're not farming currency that can only be used in one system. (I have nothing to spend the currency on now.)

3) Remove the equipment system that is just used to get more currency.

4) Nerf all synergy bonuses when maxed out but buff the smaller bonuses to incentivise exploring the different bonuses together. As it stands you don't need to think, just stack 1 bonus.

[h2] Final Thoughts [/h2]

When it comes to gaming, I never really thought that [b]Webfishing[/b] would be a game I gravitated towards, as I myself never really like playing cozy games. But here we are with my review of [b]Webfishing[/b], a game that I enjoyed. The game is very simple but does have a rewarding progression system to keep the player invested. It also has a social aspect, something that I feel a lot of games have been missing for some time, so seeing it here is nice.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[list]
[*]Very fun and addictive gameplay
[*]Lots of ways to customize your character
[*]Being able to draw your very own sprays in the game
[*]Nice and charming art style
[/list]

[b]Cons[/b]
[list]
[*]Can get very repetitive after a certain amount of time
[/list]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
In [b]Webfishing[/b], you fish, that’s all that there is to the gameplay, the gameplay for the game is very simple but is also very rewarding to the player. It is fun and can be addicting to some players who like the idea of fishing and to those who like to be social. You can hold back your fishing rod to make the lure go further. When you catch a fish, you will be put into a minigame where you must hold the left mouse button down to catch the fish. However, there will also be times when you must click through a barrier to break it. If the red meter catches up to you or you don’t prompt the minigame, you will lose the fish you are trying to catch and the bait used.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3429997154
There are two different types of fish to catch, there are fresh water and saltwater fish, to catch them, you will have to go to the designated spot where they are located. But you can get access to certain lures that will give you the chance to catch salt or freshwater fish no matter the water you are using to fish with. There are also many different upgrades for you to get, you can even get a [b]fishing buddy[/b] that will catch fish for you. Fish can come in different rarities and sizes; you can sell the fish you catch for money and their prices do depend on the size and rarity they are.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3429998474
To get a higher quality fish, you must use a certain bait type that gives you the fish with those qualities. Your [b]fishing buddy[/b] can even catch higher-quality fish too when you put some upgrades into it as well. To get different bait types, upgrades, [b]fishing buddy[/b], cosmetics, etc, you will need money for all that.

There are lots of cosmetics for your character and you can change their appearance at any time, you can even change the type of animal they are as well. The customization options for the game are fantastic. There is even a way to draw your very own sprays into the game as well, I cannot draw. However, I can’t deny that some of these people have shown their creative side in the game, and I applaud them for that.

The only issue I have with [b]Webfishing[/b] is that the gameplay can get very repetitive. The gameplay loop doesn’t really change. You can use a metal detector to find things and play music for people, but that’s it—there's nothing else to do. Also, there is a hacker problem from what I hear. I have never encountered any hackers in the game, but some people have reported them appearing in the game.

[h1]Graphics and Performance[/h1]
The art style for [b]Webfishing[/b] is genuinely nice, it has a nice, charming art style that makes the world you explore like it’s outdoors, like a campsite sort of thing. I tested the game on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50, and 16 GB of RAM, I experienced no issues while playing but I did get one or two crashes. One other thing I should add is that sometimes names don’t load properly for at least 15-20 minutes and sometimes more. I have no idea if this is a bug or whatnot, but I thought it was worth pointing out for the game.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3429996095

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
[b]Webfishing[/b] is a very fun, casual game that I highly enjoyed. For 6.49 CDN, I think the game is worth the price. While I mentioned some of the problems in the game, I haven’t experienced any hacker problems or anything similar. Everyone’s experience with the game will be different, but I do recommend it for those who want to fish and chat with people.

The Good: It costs less than 2$, so it's probably cheaper than a McDonald's nuggets (depending on taxes and Big Mac index wherever you are). It's cheaper than most games in the genre which are in early success. 

The Bad: It feels about as much fun as a McDonald's nuggets, at the moment at least. I don't remember any real bugs, but the entire vibe feels extremely EA/ game-jam-like and a bit clunky. 

To be fair it has decent abilities, enemies, meta progression et al, but it definitely needs some iteration and polish:

1. The game needs window settings/ windowed mode (right now "settings" is only volume). The pixel graphics can seem a bit too large and in-your face even on small monitors. But hey some folks might like it. 

2. The arena (I could see only 1, but I honestly didn't play for long) feels way too cluttered. The style is 2D sprites but with an angled rather than top-down camera view, and the world is stuffed with trees, buildings et al, which irritatingly limit visibility and are a pain to navigate around. I don't know if that's supposed to be the metagame, but trying to get your character to sorta blindly move around isn't fun (for me at least) in a VS-like game. 

3. The boss-fights are interesting, but the constrained arena, make it a complete RNG machine. If you were lucky enough to be in a good location when the boss shows up you win. Otherwise you're in for a tough time. Also the boss mechanics might use a bit of work as well, to make it more skill, rather than luck based. 

I wanted to play the game for longer, but right now the graphics + the attention required to navigate the arena just gave me a headache. 

I would recommend giving it a try if you're crazy about VS-like games. Or give it a few months in case you don't like the first cut. The dev (solo I think), is committed to improving and adding more content to the game.

[h1]Listen Up Orphanians, My Husband Left Me[/h1]

[h2]Story[/h2]

The premise of the game is that there's an organization of magic, or Ley users who fight to keep the peace of the world of Orphania. Unfortunately, the leader's ex-wife, Soraya, succumbed to her lust for power and is now part of an evil cult of Ley sensitives who want to sell out the world to godhood-seeking Ley users from alternate universes. This is an interesting multiverse plot with a lot of potential, but the plot feels like an incomplete outline at times. The developer did add some new cutscenes and changes to existing cutscenes to fill in the gaps and fix inconsistencies, but some noticeable remaining gaps include:
- Hyusai suddenly [spoiler]learning the Symbol of the Order. This would make more sense if there was a cutscene where the party or Kiki informed the Doridenna monks of the Symbol, presumably as a backup plan in case the Leyans kill Devan[/spoiler].
- Vanja's romance with Devan would work better if they had more scenes prior to the Realm at War arc.
- On a similar note, Vanja [spoiler]being elected as queen of Siegburg feels somewhat forced, since she doesn't interact much with Siegburg after pitching the election idea. You could argue that the people would probably respect her for giving them a chance to vote unlike their previous tyrannical leader, but they don't really know her that well either[/spoiler].
- Belion [spoiler]is clearly a grifter who is manipulating Parcus and Soraya with his promise for a better world, but I think he should list more specifics about what problems he wants to fix [strike]like the price of eggs[/strike][/spoiler].

That said, I really like the post-credits scene that is obtained by doing all the sidequests and superbosses, [spoiler]since it implies that the party may have been unwitting pawns of Udur's villainous rival, who seemingly absorbs Udur's lingering power. I have a feeling this guy is going to be a tricky villain to overcome, since he knows how to play every faction to his advantage[/spoiler].

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

The combat system has you chain basic skills together in a long combo, and certain combinations will result in a powerful finisher, which often come with buffs and debuffs so that your character can multitask. You also have non-combo skills that simply cost ley, with some of them giving you an extra turn after everyone else's (and some enemies can use those too). However, you also have to be mindful of resources and plan around that. The list of finisher combinations can be rather long, so I wrote them down in a Google Doc for myself in case my characters are inflicted with berserk. For the most part, the game is balanced as long as you take advantage of the crafting system and update your gear as new recipes appear, which is also the primary way to learn new skills. The commercial version of the skill system makes it so that you don't learn all your skills at once and you must instead spend SP to learn them, which you only get upon leveling up. To compensate, the EXP rate in this version is higher, and you should be able to reach the level cap and learn every skill through normal leveling.

As for character meta, Devan and Gado are my favorites. Devan has good healing abilities and a powerful stat debuff finisher. Plus, you are kind of required to use him [spoiler]due to the Symbol of the Order[/spoiler]. Gado has decent attack options, lots of HP, and has chain finishers that apply group buffs, causing him to powercreep Leon. It's definitely a good thing [spoiler]Gado didn't follow his former friends in becoming a Leyan, or Orphania would be screwed[/spoiler].

The game has some block/ball pushing puzzles, and they can get pretty complicated towards the end of the game, to the point where they rival the Mystic Cave puzzles from Shadows of Adam. It got to the point where I found the superboss of the game to be a victory lap after beating the puzzle that guarded him. However, the commercial version of the game removed that puzzle, so that should make it easier to reach the superboss.

There is a collectible card game that I never completed due to the sheer difficulty of the tournament. Fortunately, it doesn't affect the story or combat, so if you're not into card games, you aren't required to play it.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]

7.7/10

A simple logic game, like minesweeper with colors, but the implementation is very unpolished.

[b]What is it:[/b] A logic puzzle game, in a grid where every other cell is a clue, you must figure out which one of the four possible colors the other cells must have. Every clue cell has four (or in the case of edge cells, three) colors inside, which indicate the colors of its direct neighbors. Starting with obvious clues like “4 yellow neighbors”, and combining clues with common neighbors and the already solved colors, you have to fill in the target cells with the right colors until the entire grid has been solved. Depending on how quickly you solved the level, you get between one and three stars. You do this in increasingly big grids, from 3x3 to 19x19, and then just replay the levels for as long as you want. Luckily the levels are randomly generated, so there is some replay value.

This is an interesting game idea, a simpler kind of minesweeper that doesn’t really involve numbers or all 8 neighbors, and would be good for a bit of relaxing puzzle time. But the implementation as it is right now needs a lot of work, and I cannot recommend it.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3329621765

The most critical bug is that levels fail to unlock. The first time I played this game, it just happened to 15x15, which was skipped and instead 17x17 was unlocked, with no way to play 15x15. But now I’m playing on a different device, and it so happens that no new levels unlock. I had to play 9x9 five or six times to get 11x11 to unlock, and now I don’t have the patience to see how long until 13x13 finally unlocks.

There is a tutorial explaining how to play the game, but it is crowded and poorly written, with typos and broken English, lots of things displayed on the screen, very small text, and even the wrong image next to the “this is the solution” text showing the unsolved puzzle instead of the solution.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3329622999

There are no settings other than a mute toggle. The game plays in a small 830x500, borderless, unresizable window, and on my 4k screen it literally takes just 5% of the screen! The text is barely legible, and the 19x19 grid is very hard to see without any way to zoom in.

The time is displayed in a weird way, “9:3” instead of “9:03”, and having the timer always present makes it stressful instead of relaxing to solve levels. Still, the time isn’t too strict, I can solve the levels with plenty of time to spare, but I’m a fast solver. If you re-solve a level with fewer stars than before, the level select screen only remembers the last solve, so you may lose stars.

The levels are rather easy, there’s almost always one or more obvious starting points, and once you solve a few cells, the rest are trivial to fill in. Once you have three known neighbors, the fourth one is obvious, which means that a new clue now has three known neighbors. In terms of complexity, I’d put this somewhere between color by number and minesweeper.

On the larger grids, it’s not just the cell size that stands in the way of comprehending what you see, but the fact that unsolved cells are also colored, so it takes a while to even find which cells you still need to solve.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3329623054

More proof of how unpolished the game is, the application is called “MainWindow” in the taskbar, and it only comes with a tiny app icon that doesn’t look good in the task switcher.

Overall, this could be a relaxing puzzle, but the implementation makes it frustrating instead.

One other thing to note, the developer doesn’t respond well to criticism, lashing out instead of trying to improve the game.

[b]How hard is it:[/b] Mostly trivial.

[b]How long is it:[/b] 9 grid sizes, must be solved in order, and sometimes they fail to unlock. Solving at least one of each size can be done in less than an hour.

[b]Quality:[/b] Very poor. No mid-level progress saving. Mouse only controls. No settings, and it does need a resizable window and a full screen toggle. Very poor accessibility, tiny cell size, no colorblind settings, hard to distinguish between clue and solution cells, or between solved and unsolved cells. No cloud saving, no achievements.

[b]Worth the price:[/b] Not in its current state, maybe if the developer improves it.

[b]Most positive aspect for me:[/b] Relaxing puzzle game.

[b]Most negative aspect for me:[/b] Hard to distinguish which cells still need solving, especially when they’re so tiny.

[b]What would make it better:[/b] Allow the window to be resized, and add a fullscreen toggle in the settings. Volume settings with sliders, not just a mute toggle. Mid level progress saving. Make sure new sizes unlock properly, or better, have all of them unlocked from the start. Add support for custom grid sizes. Add 2 and 6 color modes. Keyboard/controller support. Add a white mode. Instead of purple, make the unsolved cells black or white. Add some kind of colorblind mode, either different color themes, or patterns/symbols instead of colors. Allow zoom and pan. Add cloud saving and achievements. Add a setting to disable the timer.

Angles of Death reminds me of an old school arcade game, such as Asteroids, but with a tower defense overlay. Instead of a tower, though, the player must hold an ovoid sector of empty space. Using WASD controls, the player navigates a ship around this fixed area while adversaries--mostly the triangles referenced in the name, but also some other baddies and bosses--enter from the perimeter and chase the ship. These enemies deal damage by colliding with the player's craft, so they must be avoided. Meanwhile, the ship automatically spews an intermittent trail of damaging counter fire at the pursuers. The longer the player's craft survives, the more upgrades become available to buff the ship's defenses, augment its offensive capabilities, and tweak the rate at which various events, such as waves of opposition, occur. Through it all, destroyed adversaries occasionally drop gemstones that the player may collect and spend on various upgrades and tweaks that make surviving the onslaught easier and more interesting. The variety of perqs and ever growing intensity of attacks give the player an opportunity to experiment creatively with various combinations of upgrades, powers, and navigational finesse. The highest difficulty settings will definitely test the player's ability to thrive and survive. Angles of Death is a love letter to the earliest days of gaming.  Let me explain my thoughts on the game for you guys, to better understand my position.

You are allowed to choose 1 of 3 classes everytime you spawn.

First set your standard M4.....but with an 18 round magazine that fires in 3-4 round bursts and has the recoil of a .22 rather than an airsoft gun. It is also apparently a GBB or gas blow back, NOT an AEG or Automatic Electric Gearbox which is why they gave it the recoil they did, but still, too much recoil and why, of all the numbers, did you give it 18 BB magazines?! I have owned several GBB and AEG m4/ar platform airsoft guns, and have never seen a magazine hold less than 30'ish (you can always fit a few extra in and as the spring wears down, sometimes you can only get it too feed about 20 before it doesnt have enough strength in the magazine's feeding spring to actually feed the full 30, so the last 10 will be stuck in the magazine. 
You also get a gas blow back Glock 19(probably) for a sidearm(this is from a unique perk each class has, the first class replaces its knife with a sidearm), and a noise grenade. I have no issues with either and they both work as they should and simulate the airsoft version's accurately enough. Only thing I can think of is the magazine size for the Glock should be more than 10, and that it should have a much higher rate of fire. 

Both of the other options include their primary, a knife, and a grenade, so I will only be giving my thoughts on the primary and perk each class has.

Second option is an "KA 47" (why would you do that? The name Ak-47 is not trademarked and is common use so you can legally use it in anything you make to sell..) and an extra grenade perk. The KA47 has the same issue with recoil and magazine size that the m4 does, except instead of 18, this magazine holds 20 and the KA47 is fully automatic. Yet once again, they made it a gas blow back with too much recoil. Extra grenade perk is just that, you get 2 grenades instead of just 1. And a knife.

Third option is a mac10/11, and of all the guns, this is the only one that is an AEG. It also has an extremely low rate of fire and a 20 round magazine. Fortunately, it has no recoil! [h1] A Disappointing Zombie Shooter [/h1]

[i] I've reached the hospital, ready to clear the zombie threat. I start taking shots at the various zombies, and watch as they start to swarm me. As they get close I realize something terrible: I cannot shoot enemies right next to me, and I don't seem to have a melee attack. I die in seconds. [/i]

Doomsday Cleaner is a game that tries to offer short zombie killing experiences. You start by choosing your character and weapon (there are two identical assault rifles), and choosing the map. After loading in, you're told how many zombies there are and given an objective to kill them.

Pros:

-Shooting is okay: The guns seem to handle well, and fell somewhat decent as long as you keep them on semi-auto. On full auto, it's another story.

Cons:

-Feels like an asset flip: Game feels like someone found a base engine, some textures and models, and threw them together to sell. While most things look okay, the game just doesn't feel like much work has been put into it.

-Missing a LOT of features: As mentioned in my in-game example above, I died a few times due to not having a melee attack. That would be okay, except ammo is limited on maps and you can't shoot enemies that are right next to you. A lot of my game time was spent running away and quickly turning to fire one or two shots, hoping to take out the target. There are also no other weapons besides two assault rifles from what I could see.

-No replayability: The game has nothing to draw folks back. While there are higher difficulty levels, they just give the zombies more health and make them do more damage. Otherwise there's nothing to unlock, no leveling, no scoring system, etc.

Overall I can't recommend this game, even at $3 USD. There are a lot of titles out there with a lot to do for that amount, and you'd have a better time with those.
