Fun little minesweeper game that's cheap, but very hard (because of the enemies).

Pros:
+ Not expensive.
+ Unique take on the minesweeper formula by being a rogue-like, where the mines are monsters that will attack you when revealed and when you attack them (but you can ignore them and keep uncovering tiles). However you must correctly reveal or defeat all mines to progress.
+ Meta upgrades.
+ Not all maps are solvable, which normally is a bad thing but here it forces you to use items to either buff yourself or to uncover tiles for free. Otherwise a good player like me could beat all the levels and never uncover a single mine bypassing most of what makes this game unique.
+ An extremely handy feature is that if you click the tile when the nearby tiles are obviously a mine or clear, the game will automatically uncover/mark them all for you. Makes the game play a lot faster and more conveniently! But for more tricky situations that aren't obvious you still have to deduce yourself.

Cons:
- There are some level upgrades that are must haves, like restoring 5% health for every 30 uncovered tiles. Enemies hit hard and you can even die from a single one. Thus managing health is very difficult and annoying in this game until you get enough meta upgrades which takes a long time. So if you're unable to get that upgrade, you're probably going to have a bad time.
- Damage over time effects are very annoying and most enemies have them, and you won't always have been able to buy the cure. On the plus side the initial forest map sometimes offers a cure to its annoying hazard you can buy and it lasts that whole run.
- Unlocking new characters is pointless since they change little about how you play and your goal is to avoid triggering mines anyway.

I would consider myself a minesweeper enthusiast. I might even go so far to call myself a connoisseur of minesweeper. Not a single business day goes by where I don't open a new tab of minesweeper. I've even installed it as a personal web app on my work computer. Heck, maybe I'm a fanatic.

All of that is to say that this is the most inventive spin on minesweeper I have seen to date. Forget triangle mines, hex mines, and the fabled octamines - you now not only need to sweep mines, but build your character to survive further into the roguelite. Mines aren't instadeath - instead you have an opportunity to defeat the mine (monster) and continue on your quest. Between runs, upgrade your talents to earn more gold, runes, or increase your stats to build towards better runs in the future.

This is everything I thought minesweeper could never be and I've been waiting MONTHS for this to release. I sense a PIP in my near future, as my work productivity is about to plummet. Game of the Year in my book.

I love so much of what we're seeing from this game thus far, but it has some major issues baked pretty deep into its DNA.

The best thing about Witchfire is its premise, it's genuinely a gamechanger. It's a looter-shooter roguelite extraction-shooter amalgamation with free roaming levels, a lot of build customization, and an extremely satisfying core gameplay loop where the hardest challenges that levels have to offer are best done after doing all the easy challenges, but without strictly enforcing that so good players can really show off their skills and builds.

I especially have to give a round of applause to the curse mechanic, where you can effectively bait the witch into launching a curse against you to get a ton of juicy upgrades for a level's raid or boss. It creates unintentional high moments where you get caught off-guard by a curse and need to adapt, it creates intentional high moments where you feel like a mad genius for doing it on purpose and getting richly rewarded for your efforts, it's absolutely brilliant.

Witchfire really is something special, but what I find a bit problematic is that this outstanding high-level gameplay loop is complimented with a much more scrappy low-level gameplay loop, and I mostly don't mean that in a good way.

At the early stages of the game's progression the combat feels like fencing with guns, which is very fun and engaging. The enemies don't overwhelm you with enough projectiles to make sidestepping without dodging unviable, nor are the melee enemies so fast that they have to be dodged away from instead of letting you backpedal and shoot. Your offense is tempered with having highly limited ammo and long spell cooldowns, which plays into the gameplay loop where basic ammo drops become valuable loot.

Then, as the game gets harder, it starts throwing more and more aggressive enemies at you. At first it's knights that lock onto your position and jump at you. Those are actually quite fun since they're the only enemies that do something like this by this point, so they can be fun to dodge then counter.

However, the game ramps this up and up and up to the point where the only enemies that spawn are ones that fire projectiles with aggressive tracking, or launch pillars of silencing lightning that require dodging at the exact correct angle, or fire explosive poison balls that need to be shot out of the air (and by that I mean shot 20 times, not just once), or simply carpet bomb the cramped corridors of the later areas with enough explosives to render positioning almost pointless.

So what do you do? Dodge with perfect timing? Well beyond that being a difficult task in of itself, if even possible when facing off against a horde of 15 enemies, the stamina system has you in a chokehold. Almost every action you can take costs large amounts of stamina including basic stuff like jumping, sprinting, and a particularly baffling choice to make you lose stamina when getting hit, making rallying a bad situation nearly impossible.

The net result is that Witchfire feels like "A Game where You Cannot Defend Yourself". So how do you keep yourself alive in a game where you can't defend yourself? Equip the most laughably overpowered build you can muster, point the camera in the general direction of the enemies, and watch them all blow up before they can get an attack off. In particular the heavy spell Burning Stake almost-literally plays the game for you with its unending barrage of explosions that instantly nukes entire enemy encounters while fully recharging itself in the process. It's not even easy mode by that point, it's peaceful mode.

I want to see Witchfire's endgame (or midgame considering less than half the levels are out) better mimic what the early game manages to achieve by letting players bolster their defense while keeping a lid on their offense. The game as it is now severely lacks any push-and-pull during fights. You either push and instantly win or you pull and instantly lose, barely anything more interesting than that.

If I was making the game I'd probably do something along the lines of:
Make sprinting, single jumping, and taking damage cost no stamina
Make dodging go a shorter distance with more iframes (bit iffy on this one, but the long-distance dodge is very janky)
Remove the slow on losing stamina (the fact you have no stamina should be all the punishment needed)
Make empowered melees have no cooldown but require a chunk of stamina
Make spells have a cooldown in addition to needing charge
Make heavy spells not be able to charge while they're active so chaining them is much harder
Nerf the hell out of Burning Stake and buff Cursed Bell
And then maybe give all light spells multiple charges. That way players can cast a lot of light spells and only a few heavy spells.

I'm not going to pretend this would magically fix everything but I think something to that effect would make Witchfire more "Destiny meets Dark Souls extraction shooter roguelite" and less "Burning Stake 10,000,000 must die" especially since the latter invalidates how much effort the devs put into having enemies with interesting designs and animations.

I'll throw in one quick bonus: The equipment upgrade system isn't awful but it needs work. The game ask you to get hundreds of kills with a single weapon that isn't even maxed out. Already a problem in of itself but everything else you bring to a level can steal its kills. This incentivises you to farm fodder for an hour in the starting level or go to endgame areas and get your ass handed to you while trying to chip away at hordes of tough enemies with the worst gun in your arsenal.

Not a complete dealbreaker, especially when the loot is super cool and rewarding once upgraded, but still extremely tedious and unsatisfying. I think the idea is to get you accustomed to how a weapon works before you get to upgrade it to its full potential, but in practice this just doesn't work at all since upgrading weapons unlocks perks and not straight damage buffs. This means that the weapon at upgrade level 0 or 1 could be unbearable and stupid only for upgrade level 3 to fix everything. 

That's what happened for me with Midas, an assault rifle whose gimmick of overheating as it fires felt obnoxious to use. Then I reached upgrade level 3 and it unlocked a fast, damaging reload while overheated, and now the weapon feels perfect. The same thing goes for the sniper rifle All Seeing Eye, where the core gimmick of poison explosions on headshots doesn't exist until upgrade level 3. To put it all into perspective, both of these weapons each require 315 un-stolen kills to fully upgrade despite their gameplay being gimped before you've done this.

I don't know what specifically the fix for this is, but the devs should at least let us spend currency to bypass the challenge. Doing the challenge just doesn't contribute anything enriching to the experience, and I don't want what the developers have created with these cool weapons to be squandered just because it takes hours of grinding to actually get your collection of weapons ready to use.

Pros
The combat feels excellent, with highly satisfying visuals, impactful camera work, and impressive bullet effects.
The game environment is stunning, making exploration enjoyable.
The Gacha equipment system adds an exciting layer of progression.
Each weapon has unique effects, creating diverse and interesting gameplay styles.
I appreciate mechanics that punish mistakes, like the calamity bar increasing when taking risks or making errors—it adds an extra layer of challenge.
Overall, the game is solid, and I plan to keep playing.
Cons
The price feels too steep for the amount of content available. After 15 hours, I’ve completed all three levels and earned 17 out of 20 achievements. The game needs significantly more content to justify its cost.
The stamina system is overly punishing. Losing large amounts of stamina when hit makes later levels frustrating since you get hit frequently. Stamina is required for everything except walking, so escaping enemies becomes nearly impossible once you run out. You're left with two options: "spray and pray" or slowly walk away, hoping to survive. Worse, shooting and jumping prevent stamina regeneration, making the system feel overly restrictive. This is easily my least favourite mechanic in the game—it creates a frustrating loop that feels unfair rather than challenging.
While the visuals are excellent, they have a very distinct UE5 look. This isn’t necessarily bad, but as more games adopt this style, it starts feeling less unique. I prefer a more distinctive art direction.
Conclusion
Right now, I can’t recommend the game, mainly due to its high price relative to the content. The gameplay loop is enjoyable, but with such limited content, it becomes repetitive quickly—at least for me. If the game receives more content in the future, I might reconsider, but as it stands, it doesn’t feel like it offers enough value for the cost.

Often times when you hear a game is trying to take influence from several disparate genres you might expect the result to be a mess. When it comes to Witchfire, it just plain works. The guns are all unique and become more fun the more you use and upgrade them. Nothing in this game comes from just raw stat upgrades. When you level up your weapons, it's not just more damage, it is wholly unique and defining abilities. Similarly when you upgrade the Gnosis(the game's difficulty mechanic), it's not just the enemies becoming spongier and hitting harder directly, you get new enemy types, more events, the maps get more mechanics, etc

The game has great atmosphere with a subdued form of storytelling similar to the Souls series. The sound design is punchy. The weapons are cool and have diegetic design to convey their special traits. You feel badass when you're in the zone. The game design heavily skews and rewards aggression. Your spell cooldowns are based on kills. You have a Focus state which lets you dash to see a floating weak spot on enemies that will do a LONG and rewarding stun.

My one criticism would be that the Arcana (per-run buff system) mechanic can be a little hit-or-miss. Some of the perks you can get are clearly run defining but many, especially the elementals, can feel a little unclear. If you have ANY equipment that has some elemental property it lets the game offer you perks for that element but it's not always obvious how or if they actually interact. In the late game it's a little less problematic because you can kind of go all in on particular elemental builds but for a large part of my playtime I would be a little sad when I would get an Arcana for Elemental stuff. A small blemish on an otherwise exceptional game.

Really I can't overstate how well all these systems interact together, it feels very thoughtful and fun-forward. The game is obviously in early access and you can feel this mostly when it comes to the # of maps, but in terms of polish it's already up there. This game is like finding a hidden gem restaurant that you know will blow up once it gets traction. I'm excited for their future success but I'm more excited to sit down and start a run.

Preyers are men who committed unspeakable sins and now have magical powers, and are now deformed and nearly immortal. You kill enemies to earn the Game's titular currency "Witchfire" which you must spend to unlock certain aspects of gameplay, and to level up. The gameplay loop is simple, you choose a location to "expedition" to. You shoot enemies, collect witchfire, unlock "arcana" that affects your current run's gameplay (think perks from CoD), move on to objectives, kill enemies, collect witchfire, loot treasure, enter portal, and repeat. Gun play is fun and satisfying and the game is incredibly fun in quick 10-30 minute long sessions.

While the game is fun, its issues are glaring. There are only 3 maps, spell and weapon variety are lacking, often increased difficulty just means MORE enemies rather than any real challenge, TTK on enemies can be incredibly high, the health economy is broken, "Classes" are more like starter packs, and lack of content.

Let's hit these points:

- Maps
There are only 3 maps, and while they are fun to look at, their layout doesn't make for creative firefights. The maps feel like they're meant to be traversed rather than fought on. Because you revisit them so often in longer sessions it can get dull.

- Weps + Spells
Weapons and Spells are limited. You're allowed to choose 1 Demon (power) weapon of which only 3 are available, you're allowed to choose 2 weapons of which there are 14 available across 4 categories. Due to the Nature of the game there is a clear meta with only a handful of guns being viable. You can complete challenges by using the gun to upgrade the gun. There is less than 10 of each spell available.

- Difficulty
The game is challenging, that's what makes it fun. However, your most common deaths will often just be BS spawns. You'll be doing just great in a firefight only for 20 enemies who slow you down with their attacks randomly spawn behind you all at once. Progression in the game causes more enemies to spawn as well. TTK on most enemies is annoying, even basic enemies can take an entire mag at higher levels, and most of a mag on lower levels.

- Health Economy

Health is important in any rogue lite. However, upgrading your health does little, and healing takes forever. Because of the limited nature of the healing elixirs, one of the game's items becomes the de facto meta because of how much it enhances healing elixirs.

- Classes

Classes only determine your starting stats and Weapon. You get nothing extra by picking another class, leaving little reason for replay.

- Content

There's just a lack of content in the game. The story is phenomenal but is only spoon fed to you in tiny little bits. The maps are good looking but levels must be replayed constantly to invest in your character to advance. Gnosis (the primary angle in which to advance and unlock new content) punishes less skilled players by making the game even harder. Missions range from fetch quests, to the same level over and over again. 

We need new content to keep this game going.

A direct port of a 2018 Android game about rearranging marbles on a grid, semi-working and locked up behind a signup for another service.

[b]What is it:[/b] A logic game about moving marbles in a network of connected spots to get from an initial state to a target state.

There are different spots connected in a network, with marbles in almost all the nodes and only 3 gaps which you can use to move the marbles around. You can only move one marble to an adjacent, connected spot, if that target spot is free. There are 4 marbles of 4 colors, for a total of 16 marbles, and 19 spots in 3 concentric rings and 3 extra spots, one in the center and two in opposite corners, which are never part of the solution but can be used as buffers so you can more easily maneuver the other marbles, shifting them from one spot to another, one by one putting them in the right place. Doing this once is a nice puzzle, good for a little mental challenge, on par with solving a 15-puzzle.

There are three difficulty chapters, each with 20 different levels. The difference is that at the easy difficulty all three spare slots are free, at medium the center one is unusable, leaving just two spare slots, and at hard the two corner ones are unusable, with just one, the center, available as a gap. Other than having three, two, or just one gap to use, all 60 levels are the same, same number of marbles, same grid layout, just different target positions. Worse, the unavailable spots aren't completely unusable, they are just occupied by black marbles which you can still move, but doing that won't accomplish anything. The developers just didn't have to design a new board, or write more code to deal with the different board layout, they just added another marble to the starting position. Like I said above, doing this once is a nice puzzle, but doing it 60 times is boring. Its only appeal might be the same way solving a Rubik's Cube is appealing to some, not as a puzzle to solve, but as a challenge for solving it faster or more efficiently. And Goolee tries to be that, an alternative to speedcubing, tracking both the number of moves and the time taken to solve each level, and it even has worldwide leaderboards, and support for competition events. Except that these don't really work.

Let’s start with the standalone puzzle functionality. First thing you notice after starting this game you just bought with a lot of money is that instead of a Play button, there's a Demo button which lets you try the first 5 easy levels. Why is a fully paid for game offering you just a demo? Because in order to play the full game you must sign up for a PlayFab account. In case you don’t know, that's Microsoft’s (acquired by) alternative to Steam’s gaming services, including cloud saving and leaderboards. So yeah, to play this game, you must sign up for another service, even if you don’t plan on participating in worldwide competitions.

Once you decide to take the plunge and sign up, you can play the levels one by one, no jumping ahead. Technically you can unlock the medium/hard sets by using coins, but to get enough coins you have to complete all the previous levels, so it’s an useless alternative. Unless you decide to actually buy coins with real money, to unlock the content in the game which you already bought. Just 20/40 more of the same identical levels. Except that you can't actually do that, because the buying coins part is a dead feature from the mobile version of the game, which doesn't work in the Steam version because, duh, this is not an Android phone.

OK, fine, let's say you want to use the Android version to buy the coins, and it's a good thing that this game uses an external service that works across systems to save your progress, because you can continue playing on the phone, and lucky for you, the app is free in the Google Play Store, you don’t have to pay another 13 dollars/euros (plus tax) to get it on another device. (Huh, sidenote, if it's free on a phone, for which this game was made, so it probably works better with a finger than a mouse, why does it cost that much on Steam?). So you log in again with this PlayFab account to restore your progress, except that surprise, despite forcing you to use a third party cross-platform service, the devs forgot to actually implement the cross-platform progress sync…

OK, fine, forget about unlocking the harder levels, quicker, let's just play this and see how it is. Spoiler alert, it’s terrible. For a game that tries to enter the speedsolving scene, it has a lot of friction. To move a marble, you must click precisely on it, drag it over a directly adjacent spot, and unclick precisely over that spot. You cannot drag to a spot two connections over, and if you drag and drop just a little bit outside the target spot, the marble just jumps back to the starting cell. And no, it’s not better on a phone, it's worse since everything is smaller except the finger which is bigger than a mouse pointer. You can't speedsolve this when you have to carefully drag and drop each marble spot by spot. I tried to do series of steps quickly, but one mistake early on means that every subsequent step is wrong, and since there's no undo, now I have even more steps added to my counter and more time added to my timer… Slow and steady wins the race. Or in this case, rather slow and steady still loses the race, but at least it loses by less. Anyway, let's see how bad my score is, there's a World Ranking entry in the menu. Which shows an empty leaderboard. Did they not even implement the cross-platform leaderboards with this mandatory Microsoft-owned cross-platform service? I’m starting to believe that this external account that I had to sign up for was a little bit unnecessary.

But wait, what's this? Battle Of Mind? Sounds interesting, let's battle mind! Mind strong, me want battle mind! There’s a current challenge, a monthly challenge, and a special challenge, and techlympics. (Am I the only one who thinks these challenge names make no sense?) Except that trying to join any of these challenges requires both a secret code, and 100 gems. Gems? How do I get some of those? Oh, I can buy them. From the store. Which doesn't work because, again, this is not an Android phone, and they didn't bother to change the code to work with the Steam purchasing service. FYI, on Android 100 gems cost 1$, and 1000 gems cost 11$, so I guess this game is also testing if you're dumb enough to not not know simple math.

Are you familiar with Zawinski's Law of Software Envelopment? It states: Every program attempts to expand until it can read mail. Guess what, I received some emails in this game. One has the code for the monthly challenge, and one congratulates me for joining the challenge (I didn't) and rewards me with 100 coins and 5 gems! Except that there's no way to get these rewards out of the email.

[b]How hard is it:[/b] Easy.

[b]How long is it:[/b] 60 levels in 3 difficulty chapters, a few hours to solve each one at least once, must be solved in order.

[b]Level design:[/b] I have this bit in most of my reviews, but there's just one basic level… I guess, how’s the whole game idea? Might be OK as a physical puzzle to tinker with, but not that interesting.

[b]Quality:[/b] Terrible. One simple level repeated 60 times. Simple drag and drop controls, but very finicky. Basic graphics, badly chopped images for the marbles with no alpha blending and no AA, visible white pixels on the borders, and not even properly centered on the target spots. No settings other than one mute toggle. No cloud saving, no achievements, no workshop, no leaderboards. Broken features.

[b]Worth the price:[/b] No, and it dares to ask you to buy even more in-game currencies.

[b]Most positive aspect for me:[/b] A nice little puzzle you can practice a few times until you get the hang of it.

[b]Most negative aspect for me:[/b] I can’t pick just one!

Fun little hidden object game with it's own spin on the genre and pretty graphics to boot. 

Finding the objects is definitely on the easy side with only a couple causing me pause along the way. In some cases you do have to interact with something to get access to some of the items, but for the most part they are just found out in the open. 
The trickier side of the game is the loot stacking. A bit like playing Tetris except here you have all your found loot in an inventory on the right and then you have your final "sack" inventory on the left. Now the idea is to fit all the items in to the sack to be able to take them all with you. :) Every item has a certain shape (like blocks in Tetris), some can be combined and a few can even be used up, but for the most part you just have to arrange all of the loot to fit in the sack inventory. If you watched the trailer for the game, you already got the gist of it. I didn't have much trouble with the stacking until the last 5 levels. A few of the last levels did make me wish that I didn't have to complete the level to access the next level. But that's really the only - albeit minor - con for me in this game - that levels are locked until you complete the previous ones.

There are also a few collectible letters in the game - each granting an extra achievement aside from level achievements, so make sure to interact with any open face letter lying around. If it's a counting one it will trigger an achievement. But there are a few that aren't interactable though they look a lot like the "real" deal, so just try any that you come across along the way and you should get all achievements by the time you finish the game. But the game does have a level selection that you can access in the menu after hitting "Play", so you can always go back and recheck already completed levels in case you missed the letters the first time around. I do so appreciate a level/chapter selection option in games. 

All in all I very much enjoyed the game and would recommend it to anyone who tends to enjoy hidden object games or casual puzzle games, but do keep in mind that you'll likely spend more time on the stacking part than the actual finding objects part. I thought it was a nice change of pace from the usual mini-hogs though. :)

[h1]Hire a hot boyfriend!  For one hour.. [i]maybe[/i][/h1]

[i]Boyfriend For Hire[/i] is an animated narrative game with visual novel elements in that you click to move on the story and have the occasional decision to make which alters things slightly, but ultimately doesn't make any difference to the ending.

The game features six “chapters”, which, once seen, can be replayed sequentially or individually in any order you care to try.  Taking a leisurely, relaxed approach to progressing the game, each chapter will last up to, but not beyond, 10 minutes, giving the player a maximum of one hour's entertainment.

At the beginning of chapter 1, we join the MC, provisionally named Amy although you have the freedom to change this; being approached by the “cool girl” at her school, and also her frenemy, Christie, who wishes to play one-upmanship by pointing out that she has a new boyfriend who possesses all of the attributes any sensible girl could wish for.  Amy's friend defends her, stating that she also has a boyfriend; only for Christie to then challenge her to show him off at their upcoming club night.

This leads us into the discovery of the boyfriend for hire service, and after receiving pressure from her own mother to prioritise dating over her education (with mothers like this, no wonder society is going to pot), Amy decides to gamble on the service.

The brief story that follows is light and fluffy, and for the most part, I felt entertained as it unfurled; sporting a smirk every so often as teenage familiarities revealed themselves.

[h1]Positives[/h1]
- Amy has a choice of clothing every so often, and her sprite is seen in the chosen outfit for the remainder of the scene.
- The supporting musical accompaniment is jolly and fun initially, although it does become repetitive quite quickly.  The game [i]just about[/i] carries it off due its own brevity.
- The story, at least what is there, is lighthearted and aspects of it ring true to life of a teenager of dating age.
- The static sprites look story appropriate and quite pleasant, certainly representing the character ages accurately.  And the hired boyfriend is, well..  attractive.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
- Although the sprites look perfectly respectable when in position, they walk on and off screen, and the walking animations are, putting this nicely, fine for a cartoon made to entertain infants.  For the rest of us, they are stiff and awkward, and I started to feel a bit embarrassed about playing a character who moves like that.
- The text is available only in English, which makes the standard all the more disconcerting. No caption is unreadable, but the error count, notably in respect of English tense, is way too high for a story of this length.
- The user settings total a home button (back to the chapter select menu), and a sounds option. That's it.  You don't get a save, although, in fairness, it would be absurd to need one when you can select the chapter and you're going to max out at 10 minutes on any one of them.
- The “ending”.  I'll discuss this in a moment.
- The price.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
On first run through this game I was amused sufficiently to feel that I could ignore the language slips and dodgy animations for the cheap price of £2.57 and give it a “gentle” thumbs up (in other words, “get it if lighthearted and no drama suits your tastes”), but then I reached the last caption of chapter 6, and that immediately turned my view to a [i]cannot recommend[/i].
The problem is that the story doesn't finish, it just stops.  Imagine reading a novelette, that it has built up to the conclusion, you're looking forward to seeing how it ends..  a character makes a statement that leads the reader right into the finale, and the next words are “THE END”.
There, I just spoilered it for you.  Sorry about that.  Maybe.

The absence of a conclusion is a total mood killer, as unsatisfying as it could possibly get.
I also wish to point out my playing time, at 89 minutes, will look high and possibly have you questioning the max 1 hour statement I made initially.  This is because I originally played through two months before writing this review, and chose to quickly rerun the whole thing to refresh my memory of it.  Bear this average playing time in mind, because here comes the real kicker:

Two weeks before Christmas, they hiked the price!  In the UK, the full price is now £12.79, the original full price (which is also above fair value) was £4.29.  So, presumably because the game is not selling and the publisher wants a return on their efforts, they've imposed an increase of almost 300%!

I see on SteamDB that the highest number of concurrent players since release is one.  I am not surprised.  An absence of polishing before release, followed by an act of greed, has completely killed what could have been a cosy little one-evening narrative game.

Let it stay dead.  Your money is better spent elsewhere.

For years now I've tried games like Cities: Skylines, Sim City 4 and even the original Sim City SNES port but no city builder game ever really clicked with me until I got Tlatoani. I haven't been able to put it down since I bought it. Between my own fascination with the Aztec civilisation, the game's macro trade and city-state mechanics and the satisfying hierarchy of needs and resources I have been ensnared.

What I like most about this game is that it doesn't play itself. In games like Sim City and Cities: Skylines I feel as if the only real gameplay is min-maxing road layouts and grafting different district types onto that network; the playing god/ant farm appeal of watching little citizens go about their days doesn't appeal to me, I am a strategy game fan at heart, I like puzzles to solve, conniving and planning and that's exactly what Tlatoani provides: it gives you a toolkit, a nudge in the direction of what buildings synergize, who should live where, a pantheon of gods to appease and leaves you to work out the rest of the puzzle.

The Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan was an engineering marvel: the 'Venice of Mesoamerica' sat upon a lake on the site of modern day Mexico City and was the 4th largest city in the world. I had a big grin when I booted up the game and discovered that through land reclamation, canals and floating farms you can create an engineering marvel just like it. 

I won't claim to be a scholar or anything and making a good game matters more to me than authenticity but this game seems to give people like the Aztecs and the Maya more respect than popular culture does and makes a good effort to depict the kinds of staple crops and goods that were important to these city states and human sacrifice isn't overemphasised in-game with the Aztec temples and shrines treated as pillars of community and national celebration.

I haven't gotten far enough to fully experience them yet but the mechanics of opening trade routes with other cities and launching invasions to collect tribute are very intriguing.

I have only 3 complaints with this game so far, 2 of them I consider to be very minor but 1 of them is quite annoying and I hope to see it fixed soon.

1: Warfare - Everyone is saying similar stuff so I won't prattle on but warfare in this game isn't very deep or satisfying and invasions don't feel like much of a threat; I have been invaded at least 5 times so far and each was repelled by my initial, game-start contingent of guards.

2: Road Overlay - I would really like a road overlay added to the game. Symmetry is a tangible and rewarded factor of your city's layout in this game and I like to lay out my roads in a  way that facilitates this but there is no overlay that highlights them blue like when you mouse over a logistics building, this becomes a bit of a pain on maps with dense jungle... almost all of them.

3: (The Annoying one) Absent Build Menu Items - The most essential resources in founding and expanding your city-state in Tlatoani are Maize, Timber, Clay and Stone. For some reason, you will start a new save or generate a new map sometimes and the Clay Pit or the Quarry will be missing from your build menu necessitating expensive imports. I have tried building a road connection to areas where they can be harvested and rebooted the game but sometimes they are simply... gone, meaning I have to bin the city and start over. This can be really demoralising if you get a generation you really like.

This is the longest Steam review I have ever written so congratulations if you made it this far. If you are a potential buyer reading this then for £16 this game is very worth it, especially if you love the theme, just be sure to consult the developer's Steam guides and turn your colour settings to Vibrant in the game's options. If you are a developer reading this then I really hope you continue to work on the game and reach that 1.0 milestone, the potential here is massive and I can't imagine how awesome this game will be in future maybe with a Maya campaign and expansion too. Thank you for making this game and getting me into this genre which I previously failed to see the appeal of.

Overall, I'd 100% recommend this game! It's very cute and has nice vibes to it. There's a lot of subtle retro charm in the presentation and overall it's just a fun silly Halloween-themed experience, and for the price-point it's at it definitely has enough content. Lot's of enemy variety, nice artwork, and a cute story attached. Though, despite recommending this game as a fun retro-romp this isn't without it's faults - which I will list below. But I do just want to emphasize that despite me having these issues with the game it is overall a really nice experience and I DO recommend it.

The biggest issue to me is the inconsistent difficulty presented in the game. I really enjoyed the first 2 levels, they were very well-designed and has a good balance of the elements. The third level (the Graveyard/Cemetery) is where most of my gripes are. Unlike the first two levels the third one seemed to take the approach of 'make it harder like retro games' by just making it almost unfair in some areas instead of it being designed difficulty. Unlike the other levels where knowing the mechanics of the game and properly using them to your advantage was the key to completing it, the third one just comes out of nowhere with elements that you won't really be able to dodge or overcome unless you play through it again after dying. It becomes less of a showcase of your skill at the game and more of a memory game which was very, very frustrating and not in the fun retro way.

*Most* of my playtime on this game is on this third level, well over an hour was spent dying and restarting it, slowly figuring out how to deal with whatever random thing the game throws (sometimes literally, from off-screen) at me. I won't delve into spoiler territory but some standout points is one enemy that you actually cannot dodge without a specific powerup (that didn't even work two times I tried using it because the timing was slightly off) meaning I had to just brute-force it by hitting it and taking the damage. As well as one part near the end of the level where there's spikes placed in just the right way so that it comes out of nowhere near the end of an area you're supposed to move quickly through and insta-kills you.

I almost quit playing the game at this level simply because of how frustrating it was and unfair-feeling on first playthrough. It was genuinely just a game of keeping a mental note where 'x obstacle' was and hoping I didn't mess up anywhere in the stage. I'm glad I did stick through and eventually beat the level, not because beating it was satisfying (which is usually the draw for retro-styled games) but because the levels after that felt more like the first two! They were very well designed in most aspects and it felt fun to play through. I honestly don't know what happened with the design between all of the levels'  design and the third one.

This really is the biggest fault for me. The only other one I have an issue with is that after dying you have ~5 seconds to press continue before the game boots you back to the beginning. Allllllll the way back. That's a big part of this game, it's very arcade-ey in that regard and for the most part that's okay! But the '5 seconds to continue before restarting' bit me more than once and was just frustrating. The first time I tried playing I got to the graveyard and had to take a phone call only to miss the prompt and lose all my progress which wasn't fun.

In conclusion, despite some wonky difficulty 'curve' and potentially frustrating accidental progress deletion, I think this game is certainly worth checking out and is just a fun retro experience, despite some of the hiccups and bumps along the way.

I streamed this game to the end looking for diamonds in the rough in Steam's newly released section. I didn't realize it was an RPG maker game until about halfway through, thanks to the deliberately beautiful, surreal, bizarre claymation artstyle present throughout almost the entire game.

I am very conflicted about this game first and foremost. It is rife with somewhat obtuse design and enemy encounters, most of which is eventually straightened out and improved upon as you progress, and as your understanding of the combat  deepens. There is not a whole lot of mechanical depth in the game though- you do not get XP or even items to aid you in battle, most you find seem to do nothing at all. The story is also somewhat convoluted and hard to follow to a tee, but is still surprisingly captivating at times if you stick with it.

I love the art style in this game, it seems to be something the developer has been honing in on for a while, and I think he should pursue this further. While not a horror game, there's a very distinct disturbing vibe to a lot of the areas, and the atmosphere is just oozing out of the walls, especially in the lava/red lake areas.

Maybe it's because I was streaming, maybe it's because the writing and storytelling is intentionally murky, but I do sense that there's a strong story trying to break through the mold here, but I couldn't quite fully grasp all the themes at play and tie them together effectively, even after seeing the ending. 

This is frustrating because there's a lot of very sharp and deliberate imagery about the mind, the senses, religion, self fulfillment, and more, and lots of compelling scenes, but there seems to be something missing that glues it all together in a satisfying way. I really wanted to see something more deliberate in that sense, but again, maybe I just missed the point.

I wish on top of all of this, as much as I can given the scope of the developer being one person, that there was just more meat on the bone. More mechanics, items, enemies, more shake ups in boss design, music, etc. There is definitely a game and a story here, but it does feel like there's so much more that could be elaborated on without bloating it too much.

However, it didn't need those things to be an enjoyable time for me and my stream, which is why I'm recommending it to fans of obscure cult classic surreal RPGs, though this one definitely punches above its weight bracket and comes so tantalizingly close that I'm left wanting the developer to take their obviously unique mind and really apply some simple things that will exponentially enhance the experience. 

Combat is very simple at face value, revolving around determining what type of element an enemy is weak to, and which element they may attack with, to which you must block accordingly. If you choose wrong, and thanks to some of the more obfuscated hints in the game, you will, you take quite a staggering amount of damage, since it shouldn't be something you could mess up more than once or twice anyways.

Sometimes the mixed or obscure messaging causes a death which can be frustrating when you have to navigate back to said enemy, especially if you didn't rest at a save spot nearby.

Overall, if you like to peer inside the mind of devoted, creative people and their passion projects, or you just want to sink your teeth into an obscure RPG with a bizarrely enchanting story and world, I would recommend this game. I don't know how much my streaming of the game enhanced my enjoyment, and I tried to separate these things for this review.

[b]Tiny Pasture[/b] is an insanely cute idler that turns the space above your taskbar into a veritable menagerie.   Interacting with your adorable little pixel pets (or heartlessly selling them) awards coins, which can be used to purchase new animals, decorations, production items, and backgrounds.  I grew up with Tomagatchi and Neopets, so this was an easy buy... but it has a weird problem. 

[h3]What Works For Me[/h3]
✅ Progression seems to be balanced; in an hour, I've unlocked three animal types, established a steady income, and have no idea how I can ever possibly earn enough to unlock pandas.  

✅ Display options include window height, alignment, size, and scale.

✅ Transparent background allows you to see more of your workspace.  

✅ Did I mention how cute it is?  The corgi sploots.  The cats sleep. The red panda exists.  You also pet animals differently; I didn't know bunnies like chin scratches until this game.

[h3]What Doesn't Work For Me[/h3]
❎ It took me a minute to pinpoint this, but here's a problem I didn't have with games like [i]Rusty's Retirement[/i]: the animal sprites are [i]so[/i] forking cute and so big and so animated that I kept clicking on them or watching them instead of doing Very Important Work Thing™.  Where [i]Rusty's[/i] rewards you for looking away, [i]Tiny Pasture[/i] feeds you coins when you interact; sure, you'll gain more if you come back in ten minutes, but you could also get coins every few seconds.

Being someone who played a fair share of idle games and a few of this new genre started with "Rusty's retirement" (I didn't buy it but got all the achievement of the demo of that one). Tiny Pasture scratches the itch that Rusty's couldn't really do and that's why I recommend this game. 

I know that some people say that as an idler it requires much investment. Well as every idler I played the beginning is quite fast, you unlock a lot of new things quickly then you hit a wall after a while, sometimes a few hours of game. In Tiny Pasture to unlock things fast you can make your pets follow you to win money (Rusty has a similar trick with clicking). I would recommend to stay in the game at the beginning and only give a carrot per pet so it starts to grow and doesn't cost much. Then I switched to cheese and never gave more than cheese. I unlocked plants with berries on them and only after that unlocked the facility that feeds them. I never had a sick pet in 16 hours of gameplay.

So yes it is a game that requires your attention... until it doesn't. After a certain time you will hit the wall of "ok I unlocked everything but the rainbow pets" and that requires money my friend. A lot of it. I generally unlock one after 560 tries, sometimes much faster (fox on the first try), sometimes much after (I got my lama after more that 800 tries). I still have 5 rainbow pets to unlock so I'm now waiting (and writing a review in the maintime).

So what makes Tiny Pasture better than Rusty's or others of the genre? Well they combined the "cute idle game on the bottom of your screen" with "cute creatures to collect" and that makes it perfect in my eyes. 
Also you can resize the window and move it around the screen so that's a real plus on my side.

The first game was amazing, easily one of my favorites. This game is a massive step back in almost every singe facet. First, it is not a rougelike, as such, there is very little replay-ability. Instead of managing one character you now have 8, 7 of which are your subordinate legionaries who are all just awful in every way. While your main centurion is forced into brutally difficult battles against multiple foes, it's not an insurmountable job, he is often up to the task. Your subordinates are not and are equally placed into positions where they may need to fight several enemies at one, all of whom are phenomenally better than they are. This leads to an ultimate exercise in frustration as you just watch for 16 turns while you are fainted non-stop with no respite or counter and eventually brutally torn apart by angry Gauls. If you thought X-com had you playing against loaded dice this game takes it to the next level.  Secondly, progression is utterly broken. Your century does not ever seem to really improve or do so painfully slow and as such are never prepared for the various skill checks that occur throughout the game. There seems to be no incentive to ever try anything difficult or heroic unlike in the previous game as you are essentially guaranteed to fail. Given that there is no meta progression failure is permanent, meaning you are wholly at the mercy of heavily loaded 50 sided dice that will fuck you over without remorse. There is no option to fail and still reap some rewards in the form of having a slightly better character next time to help you incrementally improve and to eventually become the incarnation of Mars as was the case in the previous title. Here failure is painful, agonizing, without a purpose, and worse of all completely random. Thirdly, the new mechanics added to the game are overly complex and not explained at all. Fighting with a century is an interesting choice, though in execution it does not work. Simply being in control of a single soldier was far more straight forward and engaging. Again, here the dice rolls can and will fuck you. Did you manage to get a few good rolls on an attack phases and managed to kill a few Gauls leading to you completing your objectives? Well, don't think it was because you played smart and withdrew and advanced carefully, it was because you got lucky. Those same dice can do the same to you on the other side, killing multiple of your soldiers in one go because fuck you, the AI doesn't need to even bother with shifting its unit stance the way you do, they will always have a better disposition than you regardless. Another poorly implemented and explained mechanic. I was very excited to see this game on the store page given how much I enjoyed the first one and the setting is the perfect choice to follow up the 2nd Punic War and 2nd Macedonian War. However, I am truly disappointed with this sequel and cannot in good faith recommend it to anyone who was a fan of the first. I typically never leave reviews but this games was such a colossal disappointment that I felt compelled to write this wall of text to vent my frustrations. I hope that drastic changes and improvements are made as the game comes out of early access and if so I would be thrilled to give it another go, but in its current state it is truly not worth the migraine you will receive when trying to navigate the highly complex and poorly explained game mechanics while knowing all that separates you from victory of defeat is a dice roll.

Now I want to be clear about something immediately, 

If you loved Legionary's Life as much as I did, you absolutely should buy this game. That ten bucks can help support the dev and see that this game gets finished. With that said, 

I cannot currently recommend this game though. Not in it's early-access state. The big reason is lack of replayability, other reviews are much better about explaining it, but right now there's absolutely a *right* way to play, which hurts it's replay ability significantly. They need to add meta progresssion, and maybe add a couple degrees of randomness in the story telling. Right now, the game's more of a puzzle then a real game I feel, and a frustrating one that is too reliant on dice rolls.
Again, Alessandro Roberti nails it. I feel like I'm exactly this game's target audience. Overcomplicated, historically acurate text-based tactics and strategy. I love it.

I loved a legionnairs life, it was a 10/10 game for me. However, this game does not build upon the strenghts of the previous title. Rather it introduces more of the abstract dice rolling that people already did not like in legionnairs life, although in legionnairs life you could slowly and gradually improve your odds through meta progression, which made it exciting.

LL was fun because of the setting which was explained in sufficient detail but still easy to understand. In LL one really felt as a lowly soldier who could easily get taken out if one was not careful. The combat system was of average complexity but overall nice in my opinion. Dice rolls for checks were hidden in the background. Through meta progression you could slowly tip the favor to pass more and more checks, which also made it possible to discover more options and become a truly heroic legionnaire. This is what made LL great.

I love that the new game is still set in the Roman era. But other than that, it threw strenghts of the previous title over board. The story is written in such complexity and lenght that I stopped reading everything despite my interest in Roman history. Just the tribe's names were already so confusing and it did not feel like the story had any impact on my century. The dice rolls are now much more in the main spotlight than before. Combat is all rolls, which makes it just a number heavy game and totally takes out the fun behind it. Checks in the story are now fixed ability checks and if you don't train your troops fast enough, you won't pass them. Fixed checks also take out the exitment of off-combat storytelling because after a few playthroughs you know exactly wether you can pass them or not. Also, there seem to be fewer story decisions than in LL, which for me was one of the most fun parts. The base building minigame in its current state is very boring. Also, the fact that there is no meta progression really takes out one of the core strenghts of the previous title and my main motivation to replay the game so that I could reveal new story actions through a stronger character.

Suggestions for improvement:
- Bring back meta progression
- Hide the dice rolls. Rather show us what the dice rolls mean on the battlefield in terms of outcome.
- Please bring back the awesome story branches based on a check which is a mix of ability and dice roll (not fixed ability check)
- Add more story events during storytelling
- Rework mini game fort-building
- Rewrite the story in a way that is more broken down to what my character feels and sees and tell me less about politics (it's too much to read). I liked LL writing style a lot!

I will gladly review my recommendation during the course of further development, hope some things can still get changed :)

A very mixed bag.

Meta progression has been removed. This creates a "correct" way to play, and reduces replayability considerably compared to the first game. If you want to get the best outcomes and pass skill checks consistently be prepared to load a lot; sometimes up to a half hour back to adjust your training.

Fortuna is fickle but it appears to be just completely against you in this game. Even rolls where you are heavily favored you will lose quite routinely. You have to either roll with the punches and feel unfairly punished or reload until you finally pass something that, statistically, you should have passed the first try. I would have been perfectly happy if the combat system from A Legionary's Life was copy-pasted directly over with a few adjustments for formation bonuses. It was elegant, and although it also relied heavily on RNG it felt overall fair when you compared stats. The current combat system is adequate, just a bit bloated and convoluted in comparison. You could also strategically outlast superior opponents in order to eventually score a victory in the first. That aspect is sorely missing in this title - there is no way to actively eliminate fatigue and you both gain it at roughly the same pace, so essentially whoever has the better stats at match start is almost guaranteed to win. 

The concept of leading troops is great and feels like a natural next step from this first title. The writing is superb, and it is oozing with historical context. Play enough and you will genuinely feel responsible for the lives of your men. The story is not yet complete but what is there is definitely worth experiencing if you enjoy this time period.

Overall, despite the thumbs down, I hesitantly recommend. You will definitely get your worth out of the price - the question is how much you will enjoy that time. This title deserves some more time in the oven and I hope the developer will work on a bit of rebalancing. Even trying to optimize my approach I will often leave a play session feeling punished purely by bad dice rolls. If you're lucky you will have fun, if you're unlucky you will not - and that's a massive step down from the initial title where strategy prevailed, not blind luck.

Even after getting the hang of it and being able to rout most of the fights, they will take like 30-45 minutes to finish when you essentially won in the first 5. [b]I changed my review from negative to positive, because taking the role of a Roman centurion to this detail is way too much fun. The amount of RNG involved is genuinely infuriating. I wish I could focus more on the narrative and management aspects, which is what I was hoping for after playing the developer's last game, A Legionary's Life.

It has very wide dice rolls for any action in combat, which results in extremely varied potential outcomes for the same scenario, even despite the quality of your decisions. You and your opponent each roll a 50 sided die to modify your skills. When comparing it to the skill levels and modifiers the game has, this variety is extremely large and will result in lots of unfair moments. Someone else better suited to it may get deeper into the math, but to me it feels luck based to the extreme.

In narrative scenes, you have the exact opposite problem: absolute hard requirements of skills with no chance to succeed if you did not previously train to match the threshold exactly. You do not roll for this; you either have that much or you don't, which means you have to plan for this several hours prior while training. However, there is no way to know what skills will be focused on in the narrative while you are still training.

This is genuinely the worst of both worlds.

All of this could be okay if you could stop a campaign that wasn't going well, cash in some points, and then try again with a better start, like in Legionary's Life. However, this game has no meta progression at all. You will always have the same potential start. Sure, you can swap your starting stats around, but you will never have more to start with. If you change it around, you will just have different requirements to miss in the story. If this was the intended way to give the game replayability, I cannot imagine a more frustrating way to do it.

You play the role of a centurion with around 80 men under your command. After multiple in-game years of campaigning with the same men, I lead them through extremely tough battles, without ever losing a single one of them. I trained them from nothing to genuine legionnaires, while making sure to pick our fights well to ensure their survival. Granted, this game does a very good job of making you feel like you are actually responsible for them. I have been enjoying that a lot.

But then, out of nowhere, in a narrative skirmish event, some barbarians on a chariot did a fucking driveby and killed one of them with a javelin, simply because my men's ranged defense was 42 instead of the required 43. I am okay with losing some skill checks, but whenever I succeed absurd javelin checks, the enemy maybe loses a shield or stumbles a bit; while I lose to an enemy's javelin skill check, one of my men immediately dies?

This one was a narrative check, so it is completely fixed. I realized that the only way to avoid this outcome would be to redo the entire training phase several hours prior. This happened a few minutes before I started writing this review out of sheer frustration. This single event made me completely sick of the fixed skill threshold system, and I stopped playing for now.

I really want to like this game. I might still continue it. However, it demonstrates a baffling amount of disregard for the quality of your decisions. Instead, it relies too much on dice rolls to fake variety. XCOM gets memed on for bad RNG moments, but it has nothing on this game. There are only two ways I can see this game being enjoyable: either roll with the punches and lose your men to stupid things outside your control, or be prepared to reload old saves and redo hours of content just to match a fixed skill requirement to avoid disaster. I will see if I can make myself continue with either mindset later.

I'll start off with some of my gripes about the game. 

For starters, the game explains it's mechanics rather poorly. I have a hard time following what does what. Training is the most straightforward, followed by personal combat, but mass combat is so complex that I still don't understand what does what even after trying it several times. 

The game is rather RNG dependent, for personal combat again this isn't too bad, especially if you drilled your swordsmanship relentlessly. But it is really just a matter of almost pure luck when it comes to mass battle. Which can swing wildly on every attempt, even getting involved in a personal combat during the Threat phase is very dicey. This isn't helped that a lot of mass battles feels like your century is constantly fighting an uphill battle. The last two mass battles in the early access version is very difficult as well, and further penalized with a small stance penalty, requiring constant save-scumming to get even minimal victories. It is possible to rout and smash both formations with incredible luck though.

Money doesn't seem to serve too much of a purpose in the game, beyond buying ever so slightly better equipment. I also think you should be able to unequip certain equipment if you so choose, most notably the leg guards.

Lastly and this is my biggest gripe. Managing your fatigue in mass battle is very taxing, your centurion will always be the one who loses stamina at near twice the rate of everyone else in the legion. A lovely and charming simulator game that feels like a fairly faithful representation of Roman camp life and small-scale combat, but it could use some tutorial and QOL polish as it currently stands. It feels like it's a mostly-complete game, but there are definite rough patches, and elements of what feel like ongoing design struggles:

1. The use of a scale from 0 to 100 for the dice rolls, escalating costs for training skills higher, and the granular nature of training means it's very hard to actually feel the impact of training. A full 10 or 20 turn season of training focusing on sword skill might result in increasing sword skill by +5 for example. That is essentially something like a 5% increased chance for sword based skills to work for characters, and a small buff to formation combat outcomes. Haven't done the actual math, but the impact is on that kind of scale.

This feels like a case where the dev is trying to reward players for each additional point of training (vice using a scale like "beginner" to "master" or something), but the end result is that without clean, significant breakpoints, the result of training is hard to feel.

The use of so many skills pouring into the effect of the "sliding scale" of formation combat contributes to this too. For individual combat, you can at least train around using skills or strategies regarding a combination of skills. For formation combat, there's not really a "strategy" to train towards. 

The "Spearhead" and "Shield Push" buttons do add some variety and value, but it would be nice to have a lot more buttons like that which cause you to leverage different skiills and adopt different approaches.

2. The game can't quite decide if it wants to be a roguelite or a narrative game and some features are clearly incomplete - "directly appointed" centurions 'seem' to be just strictly worse than "promoted from the ranks" centurions since you lose opportunities to gain stats; if there's a reason to pick "directly appointed", it's not mentioned within the game. If it wants to be a rogeulite, the random camp events need to be more frequent and more impactful, and ideally there should be some element of metagame progression.  If it wants to be a narrative game, why can I archive runs? 

3. There's clearly an intention to incentivize smooth changes in commitment during formation combat. The penalty for rapid changes in commitment is far less punishing than the imbalance penalty. 

The fact that imbalance changes are applied twice per round and you can only change your posture once per round means that "per round" the costs are actually -4/-2/+2/+4/+6 per round. At a "permissible" range of +5 to -5, this means that the only way to avoid fairly catastrophic penalties are to never use the -4 or +6 options or to shift rapidly from one end of the spectrum to the other.

4. The design of determination and imbalance (and to a lesser extent, fatigue) resetting between phases of formation combat forces you into a sort of "lose-lose" situation with the AI during formation combat. If the AI is aggressive towards you initially, and you match that aggression, then at least in the early game it feels like you remain at neutral because you don't have any strong statistical advantages to leverage. If you use low commitment vs. the AI and then try to get aggressive when they overrun their imbalance, being behind on Determination increases the difficulty there pretty dramatically. If you remain at neutral, you don't really have the imbalance cap remaining to take advantage of the AI's overextension. I'm not sure what the solution is, but having determination be persistent between formation combat "pushes" or "lulls" would be a good experiment as I think that would allow for / encourage a strategy of clawing back that advantage after an initial push of AI aggression, and maintaining that advantage.

5. Showing the + modifier on skills during individual combat doesn't "feel" right. It doesn't really give a solid idea of the % chance of success. The opponent's skill is (for now) plainly visible, so there's no reason not to just show the % chance of success (or the % chance to hit and % chance to beat resistance, for skills where you have to do both). 

Feedback on smaller things that could use some improvement- 

1.Transparency on Campaign Season Length - The game is divided into "camping" and "campaigning" seasons, and it's not clear how long any campaigning season is going to last. There are clear flags for the length of the camping, there are flags for the length of a battle and even individual rounds within battles, but you're not clear if you're close to the end of a campaign or not. This makes it very hard to know how safe it is to commit to a battle.

2. Tutorial for Formation Combat - It would be very nice to get a tutorial eventually, or a lab / skirmish mode, where you could just play the formation combat to get an idea how it works. My general sense is there's a little too much randomness involved - I don't think you can control when notable legionaries are at the front or back, and it's very hard to send your Centurion to the back for more than a turn or two. Fatigue control on your centurion becomes very difficult, very quickly. You also run into the problem where a theoretically fair system becomes anti-player because each unit of AI you fight is only going to fight one formation combat with you, whereas you can fight multiple formation combats inside the same campaigning season without a chance to fully recover fatigue. "Imbalance" is also not super-transparent when you first start. It influences almost everything in formation combat, but the impact isn't really well-explained or viscearlly felt until you trip over it a few times. Until you are impacted by it, it's also not clear how immensely awful the last stage of fatigue is.

3. Lack of Tools to Influence Campaigning Season - I understand you're just a centurion inside a century, but you still have money, can potentially influence the legate of the legion as a whole, etc. Any ability to influence the campaigning season would do a lot to help with the issues above.

4. Transparency in Expectations - Any death in the century feels like a pretty big failure on my part. It would be nice if there were discussions / checkins for what the "expected" size of century is at the end of a battle, or periodically, so I don't freak out if I'm supposed to get my centry whittled down in a given battle.

At the time of this review, I've only put in about twenty minutes. I won't complain about the arcade loop being too short. No one complains about Donkey Kong only being four stages. I think the issue here is that it felt like a 30/70 split between actually playing the game and then waiting for your score to finish racking up. If there was some strategy involved on the level of other turn-based games, that might have worked, but this is primarily an action game. There is some strategy involved in the timing of releasing your player from the plane and when to deploy, but can it really factor into strategy when  your opponent might take two spaces in the time it takes you to finish landing on the one with the most points? Combined with waiting for items that help to give a combo to your score, landing on the biggest reward platform almost doesn't seem worth it.

I'm trying to think of any suggestions that could make the experience more enjoyable, but the time spent not playing is an issue embedded in the core of the game design. I'm at a loss, other than to suggest a single-player mode that could push the gimmicks further and demand more precision in drifting down to land, but that's a big ask. Sorry, barring any major future changes, I can't recommend this title.

EDIT: Now that I've taken time to mull it over, I think what could be done to improve the game's pacing is to give both of the players (or the player and the CPU) ten seconds to drop out from the plane. That way it can still be a race to the highest scoring platform. But instead of having another player go while one is waiting for the score to be tallied, it's done in rounds. Both players are only given four jumps per stage, anyway. So round 1, ten seconds to drop, whoever scored the best wins that round, the round ends when both players finish having their scores tallied. Then round 2, and so on.

I'm particular fond of these "Class of '83" arcade blasters from pixel games: Donut Dodo, Cash Cow DX & now Looney Landers! 

Looney Landers is clearly meant as a multiplayer arcade game but also works well in single player against a computer opponent. After a few hours, the AI becomes somewhat predictable but it still makes for a satisfying single player experience. Once you come up with some basic strategies, the AI opponent is not particularly challenging to beat score-wise. I have not yet been able to try multiplayer against a human (local PvP only) but assume it's insane and would cause friends to curse at each other. True to the description, the game is indeed fast-paced - each round is over in only 3 minutes! As usual for these kinds of games, you can also quickly restart by holding down a button on your controller. The scoring system is straight-forward, unlike many arcade games of the past, although there are a few mysteries and surprises that can be figured out after after playing and observing a few rounds.

Looney Landers is a fantastic short competitive sky diving arcade game with a throwback look and feel of the 1980's but gameplay and design that is rock solid for the modern era. I'm a big fan of this developer's games, and this is one takes a lot of the score-multiplying objectives of previous games like Donut Dodo and Cash Cow DX and uses it to provide a real skill challenge to get the best score. Very tough to do! But possible. Easy one button and joystick gameplay. 

Don't fumble a dive, don't die, get the star multiplier to carry your combo multiplier across levels, eat the bonus point objects. Chaotic and fun. The developer's intention to release further levels and gameplay modes is also great news. Worth buying regardless.

Perhaps the most fun SARL-S game yet! Looney Landers is all about minute control of your diver, and learning when to fall, deploy your parachute, and the bouncing physics is so rewarding. The steeper-than-usual learning curve leads to high skill expression after some hours, and the amount of control you have over your diver will start to be apparent. 

What might appear to be super random at first slowly becomes very consistent, and mastering the movement system and improving in-moment decision making will get you higher and higher scores. Having a CPU competitor at all times makes you always have to decide, should I go for the big score now? Or should I try to get some easier ones real quick before the CPU can get it? So many micro decisions per run, and I find it to be the perfect mix of random scenarios that skill can shine through.

For sure worth it!

Loony Landers is not successful.  It feels like the dev-team never "found the game" in what feels like a pile of ideas.  It does not come together.  I think they know that, too.  One of the first posts to the community-zone is a JPG that says "you have more control than you think!"  That's a band-aid to a big gameplay problem.

Because the gameplay... oh my.  The screen is crowded with wall-to-wall wacky-trash.  There's a clown, and teeth, and goofy shoes.  And spikes, which are not wacky by plenty deadly.  Your button opens the parachute, unless you are tumbling, and then it's a shield (???) of baffling purpose.

And there are always two parachuters... because in addition to all of the hazards, you are completing with the CPU.  The CPU is blue.  You are green.  I'm not colorblind, but oops, I'm looking at the wrong guy... and since the control you have is so limited, it even sometimes feels like you are controlling the other guy, when in fact, you're being dumped out of the plane and what the heck is all of this?

And once I figured out the gameplay loop... which seems to be "land on a bunch of arbitary platforms before the CPU player."  I can't interact with the CPU player, and there is so much chaos, you don't really feel like you're competing.  And the more points you score, the LONGER you must wait to play again - you are frozen as your score tallies (meanwhile the CPU claims another few platforms).  

I'm going to keep plugging away... there are moments of fun, maybe I haven't grokked it yet.  But again, it's an arcade game, things should be clear from the jump.  This is not the level of craft I expected from the team who made the other two games.

Меня, как его преданного подписчика  [spoiler]Хотя я не донатил, соррян конечно хд[/spoiler] заинтересовала эта новость и я ждал этой игры. Он провёл над её разработкой много времени и потратил на эту игру немало средств, и вот, он выпускает её в свет. Я купил игру пару дней назад, запускаю и пробую: вроде неплохо, меня обучают многим вещам (хотя да, ощущается, будто нагромождено много механик, в которых новичок может потеряться и запутаться, но признаю, это исправимо, если просто поиграть длительное время). Но когда дело доходит уже до самой игры...

Что ж, мой первый забег - я что-то кое-как понял из обучения (у меня всегда в играх плохо с пониманием обучения при помощи текста, поэтому мне пришлось разбираться что да как по ходу дела), и начал мешать героям дойти до меня. Ивенты и их исходы путали меня, политические ивенты мало на что влияли (я так и не понял, на что влияют отношения рас), максимум давали деньги или ману. Если говорить насчёт ивентов, то поначалу, новичку будет тяжело, ибо он не будет знать, за что какая кнопка отвечает (да, я знаю, что есть кнопка посмотреть за ману на что влияют выборы в ивентах, но ключевое, за ману, а мана тут играет немаловажную роль что в боях с героям, что в ивентах). К тому же, события ивентов не рандомизованы и если запомнить, что какая кнопка в каком ивенте даёт, то по сути, всегда будешь в выигрыше, а герои в просаке. Замечу так же, что не во всех ивентах имеется такая линейность, ибо например, где-то проходит проверка на твою удачу, но таких ивентов не то, чтобы много. 

По поводу исхода моего первого забега - я смог убить танка и мага, но лучница с 10 хп вывезла меня и я умер в самом конце. 

Второй забег тоже не увенчался успехом и когда запахло жареным, я просто вышел из игры, потому что мне подобное уже даже удовольствие не приносило.

Что по итогу раннего доступа (да, я играл в раннем доступе, поэтому у Сергея ещё есть возможность сделать работу над ошибками и прислушаться к коммьюнити, я всё же думаю он это сделает) - игра сейчас относительно линейная, задача именно что заключается в правильном выборе кнопок на ивентах (снижение максимального хп героев), а остальное играет маловажную роль, что портит общее впечатление об игре. 

Ладно, что-то я всё негатив, да негатив распускаю. Из плюсов игры: приятный саундтрек и арты, нарисованные вручную, чего сейчас почти не увидишь, ибо многие пользуются нейросетью, а она рисует мягко говоря не очень. В целом дизайн игры приятен глазу и видно, что Сергей сильно старался над игрой.

Если я где-то не прав, можете указать мне об этом в комментариях. На момент раннего доступа - оформляю возврат средств.

Like I can anticipate an enemy respawn to a point, and yet, sometimes this game will respawn 3 enemies right on top of you, and you are on a moving platform, and have to do 9 hits to 3 flying enemies in 2 seconds, which literally just kills you.

Very fun, short, simple game about shooting enemies and blasting yourself around as a frog. The visuals, sounds, music, and characters are all very fun and charming, and the overall gameplay loop is enjoyable as well.

There are a few frustrating aspects of the game, such as how quickly you run out of bullets if you're attempting to keep yourself in the air while shooting down enemies. The game also doesn't allow you to aim very far up, so when the owls are introduced it can be really annoying to try to take them out. They almost always spawn above where you can shoot, and because it's not immediately clear where they've spawned, it's easy for them to end up directly above you and kill you without any method of retaliation. If you do manage to shoot them when they're above you, you're almost guaranteed to propel yourself down into the water and leave yourself vulnerable. Landing in the water is also very frustrating, as it destroys all of your movement capabilities and is essentially a death sentence. I understand the point of the game is to stay airborne, but with the previously mentioned issues you're going to hit the water sometimes, and then the gameplay either slows to a crawl or you just die.

Overall, a fun little indie title that's definitely satisfying to get better at mechanically and complete! Just a few hiccups that keep it from perfection, but $5 is a reasonable price for the experience.
