The suspension on this car is *insane*, luckily so because the road ahead is bumpy.

The good:
+ 7 Very diverse, visually pleasing biomes/chapters of very decent length, my favorite being the tree-house & dessert highway.
+ Steering this bathtub buggy feels VERY nice, the grip very strong making steep climbs possible.
+ Lots of possible skips intended and non-intended.
+ 21 collectible items, most of them behind more difficult platforming challenges. Going for these can literally triple your playtrough time. They are optional and don't influence the ending.
+ Fair failure backups. The parachute mechanic when falling is a nice addition to "get back on track". Most of the times you can steer yourself safely on a lower section of the same "biome".... not always though, that what makes it a vital skill to learn.
+ Air-control. The way you rotate left/right mid-air is a great mechanic to adjust your angle on a small platform (jump up, pivot & land). An additional benefit is how you can align up your next jump by steering the body of the car towards the next jump before landing, it makes for GREAT flow. 

The bad (gonna go in-depth here, could be improved to make the game better)
- Parachute only opens up automatically and is at times hard to predict when it triggers. Numerous jumps are large enough that right before landing a regular jump, the chute opens right before landing, halting your air-speed and making you miss the jump because of it. Skill issue? maybe... but I prefer more control about when the chute opens. Being able to toggle the chute manually instead of (or in addition to) automatically would solve a lot of these problems. This could potentially trivialize some jumps, maybe some other solution is better. 

- wheel clipping into the terrain. rarely a dangerous issue, these glitches in the matrix correct themselves. But some jumps (especially in the final biome) are made substantially harder - unfairly so - because of wheels clipping into the terrain. As if the jumps were made with that bug in mind to make them harder. Those were my least favorite jumps because they relied more on physics engine luck then skill. 

- air-tumbles. You can adjust your left/right movement mid-air, but if your car is tumbling in any other rotational axis, you're screwed! And being upside down makes your left/right rotation mid-air useless. And easy fix for this would be to have the car always try to balance itself mid-air. Some jumps (mostly in the city) rely a lot on having luck with the air-tumbles to land correctly. It might look flashy when you pull off a nice 360 flip, but it's not worth the frustration of landing on a surface upside-down and having to pray to the physics engine to help you out.

Neutral/notes:
~ game took me 10 hours to finish the first time with 100% items
~ story is kinda forgettable. The levels have some thematic cohesion with the story but I never found myself "rooting" for the MC. The disconnect between some emotional beats mixed with insults when falling can be jarring and doesn't help the story.
~ Skins for your buggy can be selected at the start of each biome. But no new skins unlock as you go.
~ no bonus reward for getting all the items was meh, (no skin, just a steam-achievement)
~ Sometimes you get insulted when failing a jump, I'm fine with it, but I can imagine some people might dislike some of the more brutal ones. (I love em though) 
~ Somtimes these failure-lines get triggered even on successful jump for whatever reason, making it sound like story-progression dialogue instead. It's silly.
~ Misdirection like [spoiler]"the pipes"[/spoiler] are one of most funny moments in the game. Very meta, I love it.
~ References to [spoiler]Squid game[/spoiler] as platforming challenges are very fun.
~ When camera is forced close to the car, the body becomes invisible while the wheels stay visible, great game design. You can still see where you're going AND drive confidently knowing exactly where your wheels are. This mechanic is actually relied upon in a later section of the game.

Final verdict: 7.5/10
I can see the potential of it being a 9/10 if a few more things are fixed/improved (most importantly wheel clipping jumps).

This game is a real surprise, think of it as Musou + Hades. 

[i]The below impressions are based on my initial experience having reached the second area, so some of the gameplay specifics may be incorrect.[/i]

You select one of 100+ characters (though many of these will unlock as you play) and go through several short levels where you fight top down Musou battles, after each stage you select a new route with a specific power up reward, choose a new ally to join you or change your formation. After a few set stages you will face the boss of your area. There are four major areas in the game currently.

Once you finish a loop you can invest your earnings into upgrading from a giant skill tree, and your chosen character can also gain permanent improvements by reaching certain character levels during play. You will die, but every time you should come back stronger.

Gameplay is skill based, the game does not auto-attack like Vampire Survivors. You will have to frequently dodge clearly telegraphed attacks/projectiles - there is an i-frame system so dodging can be very satisfying during the harder boss battles.

You can recruit up to six allies per loop, they will each give you different skills or stat boosts. You will have to plan your approach carefully keeping in mind the character you are playing and how the new recruit compliments your current character, skills and other recruits.

The presentation is great, good voice acting, fantastic music - this is what you can expect from a Koei Tecmo release.

Koei Tecmo is on fire this year. This game is incredible, and I’m not even someone who typically enjoys roguelikes—though after playing this, I’ve definitely developed a taste for them. The more you play, the more fun and engaging it gets. The depth of theorycrafting and build experimentation far exceeds most games in the genre. With a massive roster of playable characters, solid graphics, and a great soundtrack, there’s a lot to love here.

At first, you’re going to get wrecked. You might even feel like the game is too hard or notice that Dynasty Warriors characters seem weaker than their Samurai Warriors counterparts—a familiar dynamic for fans of the Orochi series. Samurai Warriors characters, with their speed and agility, tend to have an easier time early on. If you’re struggling with a fresh save, try someone like Hattori Hanzo, prioritize speed upgrades, and ease yourself in. Then unlock Tadakatsu Honda and emphasize attack and defense or regen builds. The movelists and playstyles are nearly identical to the main Musou games, but as your account levels up (boosting universal stats like HP and attack power across the board), Dynasty Warriors characters become more viable. That said, some characters are solid from the start.

Character balance is a mixed bag. S-tier characters like Tadakatsu Honda, Lu Bu, and Keiji Maeda dominate, while others feel borderline unusable on a fresh account. Zhou Tai, for example, has strong single-target potential but struggles in most scenarios until the late game. If you want increased challenge and are skilled at games like these, pick one of these bums. 

All of this makes the game incredibly engaging. Experimenting with different characters and builds is part of the fun, and as you refine your skills, you’ll notice real progress. Eventually, you’ll reach a point where no bad build, poor RNG, or weaker character can stop you. Boss fights are pure knowledge checks—once you understand their patterns, even the final bosses feel easy to avoid. 

After completing the main game (six bosses), you unlock higher difficulty levels where enemies hit harder, have increased stats, and use different attack patterns. The replay value is insane—I’m 20 hours in, and I feel like I’ve barely scratched the surface. If you’re a completionist, there’s plenty to keep you busy.

I highly recommend this game. Even if you’re not into roguelikes, this one might just change your mind. It plays like a SHMUP fused with a roguelike and a Musou game—an addicting combination that’s hard to put down.

The gameplay is... okay? It's the standard musou controls with a cool idea that lets you collect and build effects and element depending on what warriors you pick to join you during your runs. In roguelite fashion, embers you have collected during your run can be used to permanently unlock other generals/some upgrades for future runs. Sounds fun no? But why isn't it?

Well here is where the negativity starts...
Why does the game look so damn fun in the trailer, but is it so boring when actually playing it? You have 4 worlds, 7 phases per world and then a boss. The thing is though....every phase looks like the same boring lazy thing. There is literally nothing memorable about it. It just looks like someone chewed up their dinner and spat it out.
Fill those with the usual hordes of enemies (which are decently fun to hack down), but boring 'elite' enemies with shield bars that do the same telegraphed actions that interrupt your gameplay, and respawn immediately after taking them down, so dont even bother killing them, just dodge, and focus on the loose mobs, do that 7 times in a row, and then fight the boss.........yea...about those bosses.

These bosses are the biggest damn damage spunges in the world. They can only be hurt after spending minutes taking their shield down. And then you get a short moment to damage them before they go up again and you have to repeat the whole thing again, hoping you dont have to do it a 3rd time. And now to that over and over and over again, with every run.

Pair that with a gamebreaking bug that plays the entire game in slowmotion for the duration of your missions while having the game set to 120 fps.

This game shouldve worked so well if they just put in the effort...but as far as it goes at the moment, it just does not feel satisfying to accomplish ANYTHING.

[b] More specific details about the game: [/b] 
The game is a pretty much a Musou / Warriors but played through a top down isometric perspective, together with some roguelite elements such as the concept of progressing further through increasing in difficulty and random rooms, getting random artefacts/item choices/companions/etc plus mixed with Auto-chess elements when it comes to mix-and-match of companion synergies/elements/tags to build up your power set and things that affect those synergies.

The in-game progression goes as a usual roguelite where you just start with nothing but your basic kit and as you go you will level up (stat increase and some health) and after bosses you get some artefacts (usual major item that gives you something good and sometimes also attached with some sort of penalty). 
The other aspect of in-run progression is that you will acquire companions, these are your major aspect of power since they act as attack summons (think a quick Tag attack from a Tag Fighting game) each with their type of attack plus each one also have their own Attributes such as their Faction, Warrior Type and possible associated Nature element which will contribute to increase your power on those Stats and they might have passives that increase synergy between those companions (e.g. +20% attack power for all companions that come from the Wei faction).

The meta progression through runs will be based on the heroes you use, they will retain the max level they reached in a run to contribute for the overall power level you have. Also the Soul resources you will naturally gain through each run and it will allow you to buy more formations (simply put a representation of a 2D military formation that can give diverse boosts to different elements), heroes to play with directly and also summon as companions in the game. As you unlock these they will also get you some small overall stats benefits to the entire team for unlocking these. 
Once you buy the entire roster and items you will be able to start saving to purchase Hero Weapons, which are simply an unlock of the secondary skill of each hero (you can also might be lucky and find at random these weapons through the runs but not only is random for the entire rooster it's also very rare to happen).

For a future sequel, it would be great if KOEI considers at least dual co-op, since for sure it would be very fun to have the option to play with a friend.

Yet another time that I wish Steam had a neutral rating. Warriors: Abyss isn't necessarily a "bad" game, but the issue it has is the comparative price to other roguelikes... If you're a massive fan of all things Warriors and you like roguelikes, sure this could be an amazing game where the niche it targets is you. However, the game plays like it was a rush to just throw something out there with very odd choices for the "upgrade" system true to every roguelike. New characters are fun, the formation system is a unique spin, and maybe there's more that I never saw. I refunded the game after a few runs simply because it read to me as: play a hero, earn currency for new hero, new hero feels relatively similar, play that one, get new heroes, nothing else intriguing about unlocking or changes. While this doesn't factor into my personal rating of the game, the skin bundle pricing is downright offensive. $100 if you want the three skin packs (4x the cost of the base game) and to my knowledge it's purely cosmetic. Again, I'm not sure who green-lighted the pricing structures behind this game, but it reads as a money grab more than "fun side project in the Warriors universe."
Ultimately, if this game was on sale or priced lower, I would be inclined to play it for a couple hours and have some fun, but at the current price point, I want a little more meat and a little more thought and care put into a game. The roguelike genre is becoming more and more saturated which means that we get a lot of hidden gems that pop up every now and then, games find it harder to stand out in this genre, and unfortunately, Warriors: Abyss is neither a gem nor truly holds it own. It's simply adequate.

Fun, but flawed.

This game wasn't on my radar at all, but it looked decent, so I picked it up. The gameplay loop is pretty simple, if you've played any Roguelite you'll know what's going on. Jump in, get as far as you can, die, power up in the meta progression (which I'll get on to in a second), then go back in. 

I think the meta progression feels the coolest part of the game, both unlocking passive boosts, playable characters, and allies as a three in one, and it's a fun way to use the Warriors characters and flavour. But there's no real picking paths to upgrade things, you can pick character X over character Y, but ultimately, you want to hit certain characters to unlock LV increases, and as things go on, you're just taking everything anyway.

Combat also feels fun, with the joy of classic Warriors games, in ploughing down scores of enemies, fitting in with the top down ARPG camera quite nicely. It feels more Vampire Survivors than Hades though, which is where the problems come in. Combat is pretty simple, two attack buttons, and various combos which match again the Warrior's games, but the characters feel similar, and most of the attack combinations end up being indistinguishable from each other. 

The flow of combat feels nice though, which is something, but a run though on one character doesn't feel that different to any other, and the nature of the in run progression causes the same issue, where while you can build in several different directions, the main difference is either the colour of the stuff you throw out, or some stat boosts which often feel underwhelming (besides making sure you always pick up the quick characters to get extra dodges, which feels pretty much essential). Comboing the right allies gives bigger boosts, but with quite a generous reroll system, it's not that hard to get who you want if you're picking the right path, so I didn't feel like I achieved anything by pulling these combinations together.

Boss fights are easy once you learn to take them patiently, assuming you picked up the aforementioned dodges, but some things (breaking the boss guard) seem inconsistent and arbitrary. I'm not sure if it's an issue with hitboxes, or underexplained mechanics, but something isn't right with them. Regular fights are fairly easy early game, but more of a challenge as you go, and the screen fills up with purple markers for you to avoid. There isn't a lot of variety in enemies, so I can see these getting stale over time, but for now, they still feel okay to me.

Ultimately, I'm going to be spending more time playing this game, and that's enough for me to recommend it. But I feel like it's a 6/10 game which could have been a 9/10 game if they put some more variety and work in to it, and were focused on making a great game. Unfortunately, as is always the way with KOEI TECMO games, instead they put time in to trying to charge triple the price of the base game so you can buy some shiny costumes (in a solo game!). Don't reward such practices and buy the DLC, but the base game itself is worth a punt if you're a fan of the genre, it's solid, and oddly satisfying, just like most Warriors games of old.

It's really fun. There's a lot of Hades influence (in gameplay terms; not much depth to the story though), a bit of Vampire Survivors and its successors, and of course plenty of good ol' fashioned Musou action.

The systems for building up your characters over a run are really fun, with a lot of room for thinking and variety, while still being easy to understand (well, once you start to actually understand the various terms involved; localization could have been better in a couple of spots there. There's a lot of content if you're interested in beating the game on the highest difficulty and/or with every character, though less so if you're not the type to keep coming back to a Roguelite in that way.

The only major thing I would change would be to let me play at the highest difficulty level unlocked on all my characters instead of having it tracked per character. There's so many of them that it would take a crazy amount of time to try to get all difficulties on all characters, and at a certain point, winning on NG+1 (which is the only one that does get unlocked for all characters) becomes more or less trivial. It would be great to skip that particular bit of grind.

Oh yeah, and those DLC prices are *insane*. It doesn't bother me as much as it should because I'm not really interested in any of the outfits they contain, but still, just skip that crap and buy the base game.

It says it is a "roguelite" and this is true to a certain extent. I would argue this feels more like old-school Gauntlet. Your objective is simple, kill things. Unlike gauntlet there's no exploration or anything like that. It's purely a game about smashing through waves of enemies, but what makes this exciting in this case is the character selection and the deeper character formation system.

Despite how it looks on the surface, the game is much more than simple flash and reused assets. Each character is truly unique with their own ability (which normally corresponds to their kingdom or says something about their personality), every character's movesets feel refined and impactful in ways that make DW8 look a little antiquated with its systems. With 100 characters from across the Dynasty and Samurai Warriors Franchise there is bound to be someone that you enjoy playing as. 

Beyond this every character you pick up through your run can make an impact on your choices. You can only choose six characters and only those six characters' secondary abilities, which can be run-changing, are activated. Their formation move is also added to your repertoire of attacks at the end of a power attack string. 

The game has a helpful "ease of use" when you go to choose your character, this tells you how capable they generally are of clearing the game. If a character has 1 Star for instance, they are quite challenging to clear a run with, this also creates a difficulty scaler separate from just higher or lower numbers (though the game does have that too). 

Overall it is fast paced, requires you to have some foresight about your overall plan for the run, (the bosses can be rather difficult without a good strategy to either bring down their shields or deal maximum damage while their shields are down.), and is just a blast to play through every run.

OMFG this game just hits my monkey brain in the right spots  XD  it was confusing AF at first, but after a few rounds I actually made it all the way to the 4th realm!! my literal 3rd run. I was just unlocking characters with the blue flame stuff at first and trying them out, but as I was playing it started clicking

So turns out you want to establish bonds with others as you go through the stages when possible. when you slot them into your template it will place their picture in the corresponding slot at the bottom of the screen while youre fighting. If you hold the mouse with the normal attack you will see it cycle through your slotted characters at the bottom and if you use heavy attack at that time, it will use that character like a "skill". 

Once you know that you can work on getting as many bonds as possible as you run, as well as whatever else you may need. Now easiest way to know what formations are the best is simply first, select a template. If you go to the templates you may have unlocked if you hover over them you can see in the bottom right how each might effect your DPS. Once you have a template selected, do the exact same thing with the characters you have bonded with. Simply place the ones in the slots that give you the highest numbers. If you have more than 5 or 6, you can click on one thats not slotted in and hover over the ones you have slotted in and then reference the DPS in the bottom again. You can also use the devils recommended, but I find once you understand it you can fine tune it even better

As far as ability points go, you will see them drop as you are playing. If you pick them up, try and focus on one attribute. Like you will see what looks like a meat bun on the ground. Those are ability/attribute points. Once you pick it up, choose the best one that corresponds to your character. If your character had an affinity for fire in the beginning then choose that. If there is no fire option, then select one that boosts skills. When you find another one, ALWAYS increase said points and dont mix it up too much

I hope that helps. I know its all confusing AF but reference this in your next run and your golden. This game is SOO much fun :) 9/10

An engaging, hard-to-put-down action Roguelite with the right level of complexity in decision-making and execution in combat. Different playable characters keep it fresh, although you'd need some serious patience to complete a run with each of them.
Some key points:
-The cast of characters are the core of everything here. Not only can you pick one to play as, but the characters you recruit become summons, offer passive effects, and grant levels on the upgrade paths. The last of those tends to be the first factor to consider, but once you get the hang of it, it's worth thinking about the interactions between characters to strengthen their summon attacks or unlock passives.
-Combat is pretty simple but well-designed. You have an evade with a cooldown, and dodge offset on the attack strings. Enemy attacks are often clearly visible and warned of in advance, but end up covering large areas of the screen. You can hit Musou as an invincible escape or to wipe out troublesome foes quickly. 
-Bosses can be hard to get the hang of, since you have to destroy their shield HP before doing damage, and it comes back, but eventually you can try to destroy them in one or two shields by pulling out all the stops with full summon and level 2 Musou.
-Speaking of that, meta-progression counts for a lot, especially early. That first boss is going to be rough the first few times. Even later, you'll always have the least power at that point in the run.

Anyway, no regrets at all paying $25. It's been a fixture on my Steam Deck for the past couple weeks.

I think they did a pretty good job interpreting the concept, but I think the reason it feels so "middling" to everyone is that it has a bit too much of a "matching minigame in a bigger game" feel rather than a set of mechanics that feel substantial enough for repeated gameplay.

To be honest, I feel like they should have more carefully considered the mechanics of the matching game aspect of the game independently of the turn-based battling rogue-like. The turn-based battles feel like an attempt to add "meat" to an otherwise overly simplistic matching game, but the matching game is literally the majority of moment-to-moment gameplay and it's easily the least fun/interesting part of the game. While there are difficulties that don't reveal the cards at the beginning of matches and there are some tagging mechanics that are similar to minesweeper, I think they missed an enormous opportunity in making a matching game into more of a puzzle rather than a rote memory game. I know that kinda upends what most of us expect from matching games, but my guess is that most gamers would appreciate a deeper experience on that end because simplistic matching games end up getting really boring really quickly.

Currently, I just try to match my best cards in my strategy and that even reduces the difficulty of matching by giving me clear targets to remember and focus on. I'd like to see something that forces me to think and develop new skills, similar to the way minesweeper trains you into learning its discovery methods as you get better. I just feel like the best version of this game avoids revealing all the cards at the outset for every difficulty and trains players to deduce matches using interesting mechanics that tie into the turn-based battle system.

I guarantee the devs that if they refine that level of depth in the matching game, they'll rapidly see a shift in the middling or negative reviews around replayability. A fun game consists of fun moment-to-moment gameplay, so that's where the maximization opportunities should be.

Pairs & Perils is a very neat game and cute concept, but requires a LOT of work from where it's currently at.

First thing I noticed is how exploitable this game is. You kind of have to force yourself to play fair in order to enjoy it. Using screen recordings, screenshots or even pen and paper could completely trivialise this game.

Second is what I'm gonna call "comboing" enemies. After 3 sets of cards have been played, 3 sets get redeployed that you can entirely see. It's VERY easy to memorise this new set and effectively combo enemies by just replaying the newly deployed cards over and over.

Thirdly is the uniqueness of each run. In this I'm including both card diversity and character powers. It's not very present. Each run, if you can get the Thief, Pause Time and any other decent card you can make every run an almost identical run. Most heroes' powers are completely useless, only exceptions being the alchemist, who you can get $2 per encounter from (equivalent of 1 upgraded thief kill) and the block character, who you can get a little bit of armour from. Items aren't very useful or good, with an example of one being "deal 1 damage to 2 random enemies". At the final encounter there's around 34 health between 3 enemies, and most of your cards (if they deal damage) will deal at least 2/3 damage to an enemy. Item design, character gimmicks and card diversity need a lot of work. 

So, where do we go from here. Something I'd like to see is cards not being replayed until your entire board (other than traps) is cleared, after which would also progress enemy attacks in order to prevent "comboing". Characters should have unique cards to start off with, E.G the wizard is the only one that can access the wizard card but buff the wizard substantially. Items don't feel impactful enough, I'd love to see them either being made stronger but harder to find, or maybe even coming with some drawbacks.

Overall, Pairs & Perils is super charming and a very unique idea. While I enjoyed it, and would recommend it, I don't believe it's worth it's current price in the current state, as I got 80% of the achievements in 1.6 hours. Would recommend waiting for either some kind of sale or major update if you're interested in this game.

Any review for NABI should be preceded with the warning: this is a game that is purposely designed to be so difficult that very few players will ever finish it. It's important that you're on board with that notion before going anywhere near it. (it's probably also worth mentioning that the game is very temperamental on SteamDeck IME, regularly hanging at 85% load-in. I've had the best luck by forcing it to boot using Proton Hotfix.)

That being said, I - typically a very volatile rage-gamer - don't find it as frustrating as one might have thought. Essentially, you play the titular Nabi, a cat attempting to ascend a hellish wall of doors in an endless void that (I believe) represents the afterlife. The game takes place in first-person, with Nabi's little ears and paws visible depending on the level of camera-tilt you've got going on, and occasional growls and trills accompanying your efforts. 

You aim using the mouse/joysticks, and jump forwards using the left mouse button. How far/high you jump is determined by the length of time you hold the button down: to edge forward, lightly tap it, and to leap, hold it down for a couple of seconds (you'll jump automatically if you hold it down too long). That's literally it for controls. You can look around while jumping, helping you to check whether you're on target...not that there's much you can do if you're not, as any misstep will send you plummeting into the void...and back to the start of the game.

Therein lies the challenge. You must ascend some 50 doors to "complete" the game, carefully gauging your jumps to land on any available ledges. The edge of doors, wooden shelves...they're all fair game, but they're fiendishly far apart and in short supply. It can be very difficult to tell which way you're supposed to be going, too, or what the devs intended you to be able to jump onto, all of which feeds the frustration potential. But it's also what makes the game masochistically addictive. The more time you spend developing your instinct for jumps (as there are literally no visual indicators or clues to show how far you will jump), the further you'll get, and the more do-able the next ledge will feel. I say this...I haven't made it to the first achievement (10 doors) yet...but I really want to!

So...what's behind those doors? Each one hides a hideous secret of some sort, a gruesome little horror vignette that you can observe before moving on...and they really are fascinating and unusual. Some early examples include a fairground tragedy, and a suicidal man. It's such a shame that the game's uncompromising difficulty will preclude so many players from ever seeing them all...still, I live in hope that the devs' next title will be a little more accessible, and that it will contain the same sorts of creepy little dioramas.

Naturally, because I'm not very good at it, I kind of wish there was some kind of concession for players like me: checkpoints, unlockable shortcuts so you don't have to start all over if you fall from a certain height etc. I do, however, respect the devs' decision not to compromise on their vision - and what they've created has kept me coming back over and over for another go. It helps that dying instantly reloads you back at the starting point, so there's no load screen adding insult to injury (as you're likely to die a LOT. A lot a lot).

TL:DR - Nabi is a brutally difficult, extraordinarily harsh little game to play...but it's also frightfully compelling. The visuals are vividly detailed; the rooms are creepy and unsettling; and the whole concept is mindbogglingly unique. For £1.69, even if you're on the fence, I think just buy it and give it a go - yes, it may prove far too annoying for you to persist with, but you may just find yourself a bit hooked on it, too!

The game does very much have that factorio feel about it. The game play though is anything but factorio like. the tech tree advancements are pretty much identical, so it gets boring very fast. everything you build has an exponential cost to it, so scaling up productions is painful and frustrating. 

To make it worse the storage space is minuscule compared to the costs of building or upgrading, yet everything costs more to produce in the higher tiers, which directly works against you, since again scaling production is exponential. I found there are also issues when building things, like if you try to copy&paste existing factory layouts, the game tends to try and fill the building requirements of the lower tier materials first on all buildings, which can result in a massive bottleneck where nothing is being produced and none of the buildings are getting finished, at least not in any reasonable amount of time.

there really should be no need for the exponential price of building, it just takes away from the core concept of a factory automation game type, where it's all about scaling production up as you go onward.

the game is also missing some quality of life features. for instance, you can after a few tech upgrades get an overview list of everything you are building or upgrading. the list lets you pause and resume all of it, but you cant control it on a building by building basis, which would help a fair bit in bottleneck situations, since you could pause everything and the unpause the most needed projects so they get done first, but sadly that's not a thing. the list also lets you move projects from the bottom of the list to the top, which i thought at first worked as a priority list, but that's not the case either, it works like that only on some things if you have enough items in storage, but not on everything, frankly i have no idea how it's deciding what to build first at this point, since it's not always even by the order you started building in.

Building: You can build individually or you can copy&paste entire factory builds, the game also lets you move one building at a time with drag and drop, but i feel like the developer missed on this part too. The devs could and perhaps should have let player move entire factory layouts around, they already had 90% of the required functions in the game, with the player being able to copy entire layouts and move one building, just combine them so we can move an entire layout. the reason it's super frustrating that you have to move every building one building at a time, is because as you advance in the tech tree, you get certain production bonuses if certain conditions are met. So, if you built an entire factory layout on grass, then you open a tech bonus that says "40% more production if placed on sand, while only touching at most 2 other tiles and the second day of the month was a Tuesday", so now you need to manually pick up and drag every factory of that type and drop it on a desert tile to get the production, this is a pain in the butt to do one by one and you continue to do it constantly moving forward.

Over all i feel this game would have been good if there was no exponential building costs, way more storage space and more player control on what gets done, in what order and when. but as it is now, i don't think the game fundamentally works as a factorio type game and i really cant recommend it.

As I particularly enjoy strategy games, I was determined to give this game a fair review, as I believe that a game's score shouldn't be influenced by other games, but rather how successfully the goal of the game is achieved.

The game gives really no instruction, rather throwing you into the main hub of the game where you can pick your modes and upgrade your monsters and dungeon. Included is also a rather engaging dungeon builder, where you must survive wave after wave, slowly building an impenetrable dungeon layout the likes akin to the Labyrinth of Greek myth.

I was so excited for this game, but in the end it really didn't live up to my expectations - it really does feel like a worse version of World of Horror. With the art, the gameplay, and the UI, I was definitely expecting them to be similar, but Terror Diversion really does feel like WoH with all the connective tissue shaved off.

There are a number of characters and mysteries to choose from, which is nice. Then you're given your WoH-style creepy scenarios to respond to, and there is some fun imagery and art here. However, this is also where things break down - roughly every second prompt is tied to the mystery you're working on, which is fine, but the rest of the prompts are random, which also makes them feel completely contextless. The prompts are also somewhat awkwardly written and lacking in detail, which makes that floating, unmoored-from-space feeling worse, and many of them don't have a branching decision to go with them. Instead, all you can do is, essentially, clicking "next". World of Horror has a map that you actively navigate, and the random events you encounter all work thematically with the locations you visit; in Terror Diversion, there is no map or choice at all involved in what flavour of event you get, which means there is also no level of strategy.

As a result, I found myself constantly wondering what the point was. Things were mostly just happening without me doing much more than clicking "next". I don't mind a horror vn, but this is clearly trying to be something else - and at the moment, it just isn't.

I've had Terror Diversion on my watch list for a long time. In the interim, I have been playing a mix of games in the point and click and choose your own adventure genre and I'm glad to have added this one to my collection. Terror Diversion draws inspiration from Junji Ito and has similarities to the game World of Horror without the combat involved. You choose between 4 characters with different starting stats (Strength, Dexterity, Charisma, Perception, Stamina, and Sanity) that will help increase the odds of successfully passing events throughout the 4 campaigns. Each campaign has 13 events in total with multiple endings. Some of these events involve doing a skill check against the corresponding stat you have or involve you selecting what you see is the best option to progress. In addition to passing certain events you may also have your stats increased or decreased as a result of your decisions. There is also unique events for each character and campaign. In it's current state it has no music, but I'm sure down the road there will be some added to increase immersion. I do hope the developer continues to add more scenarios, characters, and events to increase its replay value and allow for more decision making (multiple choice events rather than one choice events). I currently use my steam deck to play this and haven't had issues running it with the exception of some directional button issues on my end I think. Slimper is a wonderful homage to Jump King, borrowing the core gameplay loop of Nexile's controversial precision platformer while also earning its own identity through the inclusion of new mechanics. In particular, these are: 
- A jump strength indicator animation, which allows for high consistency in traversal strategies.
- A powerful wall jump ability that offers more diversity in traversal while also providing a means to reduce the impact of certain player mistakes.

Though slightly less polished, I believe this game has comparable quality of design to the other mainstream "Foddian" games I've tried, providing the same emotional rollercoaster resulting from cyclical success and defeat, the same bursts of relief & pride with each consistent room route learned, and the same sense of satisfaction upon eventual victory.

Regarding the artistic choices, I found the environmental design to be beautiful, possessing a surprising level of detail and with each different zone providing a distinct atmosphere, further improved by appropriately mellow music which shifts depending on the current area. Additionally, there are a few apparent stylistic nods to Celeste which did not go unappreciated.

Despite the praises, my main caveat for new players is that Slimper has a lack of punishment diversity in that the vast majority of individual missed jumps will bring you back to the same few rooms, which sometimes means falling down the majority of the map with one slip-up, whereas Jump King mostly confined this effect to its individual zones. However, due to Slimper's jump strength indicator animations, you are simply less likely to mess up any given jump once you know how to approach it, so in that regard, the difficulty balances out upon comparison.

I'm somewhat disappointed at this game's apparent fate of obscurity despite the level of effort that has gone into it and the fun it has provided me. I highly recommend any platformer fan gives it a chance considering its low price point, as I think the developer could use a little more support given the care put into this project. It is a worthy contribution to the genre.

[h1] Stylish Action Rogue-Like, but Very Early Access [/h1]

[i] The game oozes style, from the comic book style text pop ups, to the almost dance-like attacks. It's great to see the character just skate through the battlefield tearing enemies apart! [/i]

GwenBlade: Halloween is the Early Access new entry in the GwenBlade series. A hack-and-slash roguelike that focuses on stylish gameplay, the artist background of the developer quickly becomes apparent with the flashy visuals and cool character designs.

The game is great! Even at this stage of Early Access, but there are some caveats...

Pros:

-Smooth Gameplay: The game is super smooth and handles like a dream. Prompts are super responsive, and it feels amazing to carve your way through the battlefield with attacks, dodges, and jumps.

-Stylish as Hell: The game looks fantastic! While I realize this style might not be everyone's cup of tea, the game just oozes personality. It almost looks like an animated comic book with some of the design choices!

-Cool Powerups: While very limited for now, the current powerups really give you some oomph during a run. From mirage swords that fly towards your enemy, to a curse that deals high damage after a short time, you'll get lots to help you out!

Cons:

-VERY Early Access: This is probably the biggest make or break point for this title, at this time. While the dev plans to add more maps (biomes), weapons, enemies, and more, the game is very limited at this point. Right now the meta progression for the game does not appear to be fully implemented, as the vendor is there between runs but cannot be accessed. There's also currently only one weapon, one spell, a handful of enemies, a few powerups, and one map. For now, this almost comes across a bit more as a tech demo than a game. 

If you're okay buying a game for now that may be limited in what's available, definitely pick this up! The game plays great, and the dev is very active and regularly providing updates and interacting with the community. I'm all for supporting indie devs, and believe that if you're interested in this type of game, get in on the ground floor for a few bucks and watch it grow!

Updated 10/23/2024
The Dev reached out to me via email to explain the ending of the game and to also explain their intention with telling a story through this form of art.
For the sake of transparency I have included my response below:

Hello Paul,

Thank you so much for your email. As a streamer who plays many indie horrors that release on Steam I can greatly appreciate the work that goes into making these games and conveying powerful messages through this form of media. While I do see video games as a form of art, I can only imagine the difficulty it takes to not only develop the game, but to also tell the story you want to tell in a fluid way.

Unfortunately, I felt your game's story was a difficult one to process and understand for myself in the way it was told. I did appreciate the stylized choice of not including any text or voice overs to tell a story, and to rely solely on environments and gameplay to tell it instead, but when this happens it forces the player to interpret for themselves whatever it is they are experiencing. Although the game's description did mention it was inspired by liminal spaces, I was not expecting it to be a main focal point of the game. So having extremely long moments of absolutely nothing going on except walking to the next "event" almost immediately snuffed out my enjoyment and interest in what I was actually playing.

The game felt like it could be completed in half the time if the walking portions were simply removed. I was enjoying the game prior to the shopping mall portion, but that's when I started losing interest. What little substance I did get to experience in between these long moments of walking simply wasn't enough for me to justify the gameplay choice of endless walking. The graphics I did enjoy, as well as the moments with the camera, but, again, the game turning into a backrooms-style game with these transitions to random locations was abrutive enough that I lost sight of the story you were trying to tell. The transition to the concentration camp felt like it was included more for shock value than anything else. Deciding to include one of the most devastating genocides in human history as a brief moment in your game felt incredibly disingenuous to the suffrage of the Jewish people, and, to be honest, if we're on the same page of "video games as art", this truly awful moment of our human history deserves more meticulous attention and care than just to be included for a 5 minute portion of the game.

I want to stress that I am just one person and this is simply my opinion. While I do believe your intentions may have been good with the art you were trying to create, it simply was not for me and I walked away from the game with a different experience. I hope you can find solace in the other reviews that were left for your game that rated it positively.

Thank you again for reaching out. I wish you all the best with your future projects.

In a crowded gaming landscape filled with horror experiences, .redruM stands out as a bold and deeply engaging work. This psychological and cinematic horror game, created by a solo developer, thrusts you into the shoes of a crime scene photographer tasked with uncovering the identity of a killer through the lens of your camera.

The beauty of .redruM lies in its aesthetics of liminal spaces and unsettling environments. Every corner evokes a sense of disorientation and unease, as if reality itself is on the verge of collapse. While the themes of backrooms and liminal spaces are present, they are not taken literally; instead, the developer has skillfully adapted this aesthetic to create something unique and original. The meticulously crafted atmospheres transform the journey into an almost dreamlike experience, where the familiar becomes strange and the mundane turns disturbing.

The camera gameplay isn’t perfect, but it effectively encourages players to reflect on the few actions available in the game. This is not a title for everyone; it requires time and introspection. Each photo taken becomes an act of confronting the brutality of life and death. The violence serves a higher purpose: catharsis. Universal themes like death and loss weave together in a narrative that mirrors human fragility.

The game’s duration, around an hour, is perfect for an intimate and immersive experience. .redruM is not just a horror game; it’s a journey into the human psyche, an exploration of shattered aspirations and lost dreams. If you’re seeking an experience that challenges your perceptions and prompts reflection on what it means to be an artist today, .redruM is an unmissable title.

I love this kind of managerial game. It bears a lot of similarities with Tavern Master (which I like), both in graphics and in the basic gameplay, but it's a fully fledged game in and of its own, with a nicely fitting theme and with added complexity and challenges.

I like the approach with different restaurants with different cuisines (so far I've seen a salad bar, a French restaurant and a pizzeria; the fourth one is Japanese). Each level has concrete goals ("serve x dishes", "get x reputation", "be profitable for x months in a row"), which works well for me --- I typically don't thrive well in more sandboxey games. Each level also has its own constraints in terms of space and shape. Having said that, you can also just ignore the goals and do whatever you like, and/or keep playing after achieving all of them.

Managing staff adds a (small) layer of complexity, since each has different skills, traits and assignable tasks. However, you can train them by spending some money and time, to enhance their skills and unlock more possible tasks. Every now and then you find a(n almost) perfect employee.

I've played the game on medium difficulty so far, which poses a nice challenge financially. There are also easy and hard modes, for those who prefer a more casual or a more stressful experience, respectively.

I'm generally happy with the interface. As you can see in the screenshots, you get a quick overview of active orders and warnings about operations (idle staff, bottlenecks, lacking furniture, ...). I'd sometimes like more information: for example, there are events which prompt you to pick one of two ingredients to discount, where it'd be helpful to see the menu; or similarly with knowledge. Some warnings keep coming back, and I wish I could customise this a bit more; in particular, dish quality impacting my reputation, which I'm aware of but which clutters the interface by popping back up regularly after I dismiss it. I'm not too sure what ingredient knowledge does, but I also haven't tried to figure it out and there might be a tooltip explaining it. Staff will walk through sitting customers, queuing customers may stack, and in the third level my staff also walked through a particular table to take orders. Someone in the discussions forum suggested staff uniforms, which I really like. I'd like some global toggle to raise or lower all prices (by a flat amount or percentage). Having said that, all of these are minor comments, some of which I expect will be addressed in some QoL patch. None of them would be a reason for me not to recommend this game as it is.

All in all, I'm enjoying the game, and I heartily recommend it!

[h1] Do like big numbers? Do like so many flashy animations on screen that you don't know what's going on? This is the game for you [/h1]

[h3] Gameplay [/h3]

This game is unironically really fun for me. It's a blend of an ARPG and a CRPG. Where you have 5 party members you can control all at once, as your character levels up you earn something called "Skill Badges" that you can unlock more skills. One of the feature that I like about this game is the flexible customization within class restrictions. (i.g A character with a tank skills and gear, can just be swapped to a Melee DPS character with DPS kit in a heartbeat, or you want to have more elemental skills to trigger elemental combo, etc..).

As you play, you'll come across two types of exploration: via cards and a open maps. Each maps has a sequences of cards that you have to explore linearly by through one-by-one, and each maps has a card that let you to a open map that you can solve puzzle, and explore to obtains loot.

[h3] Story [/h3]

There is an interesting story to be told, if you can overlook the familiar JRPG trope: from nobody to world-saving god. You, the protagonist, are revived by the Chaos Goddess Melodia in a ditch. Melodia, an ancient goddess sealed in a ring, prompts your escape to the outside world. However, you are pursued by the Black Knight Asnida, who seemingly aims to prevent your escape with the ring. Initially, your goals are simple: explore, grow stronger, and discover how Melodia was sealed and why Asnida is pursuing you. As you explore, you meet more people, gain fame, and events escalate.

The game has some level of world building. There are explanation on how concept like souls work, what is chaos energy, what is entropy, etc... While it just a small details, it make you really appreciate the passion that went into this game

Each character you can play as (except You, the protagonist), has background story (and the 3 measurement for some reason, if it's a female character, don't ask). These are all really nice attention to details.

[h3] The Jank [/h3]

This game has [b] a lot [/b] of jank.

- The translation: The English translation is... servicable. There's a lot of translation errors, that often obscuring the nuances of the story and puzzle requirement, making thing harder than it suppose to be.

- Quest text sometimes is not very concise/unclear: Quest, at times, does not tell you where you need to go/what you need to do. (i.g A girl needs you to find her lamp, game doesn't tell you where to get it. I don't even remember where I got the lamp, I think it was me fishing in a pond somewhere to get it)

- The gameplay isn't responsive as titles like Path of Exile or Diablo. Skill execution varies, with some abilities being instant and others featuring noticeable wind-up and recovery animations, like that of Dark Souls. This may be an intentional design choice, but it can feel clunky.

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]

If you can look past the jank and translation errors, the core gameplay and the story are very fun to play and sit through. One man made this game, if you can over look the imperfection, there are fun to be have.

Ski Patrol manages to combine the fun sport of skiing with search and rescue into one package. The graphics, while not the greatest, still provide the game with a unique sense of charm. The focus clearly went into the technical aspects of the skiing movement, as that's where I believe this game shines. Words or footage alone can't do it justice; it's something you have to play to truly experience.

Regarding big critiques, I think Ski Patrol does fall flat when giving the player an engaging main objective to work toward. This is mainly (I think) due to the fact the "open world" part of the game is simply underdeveloped and lacking in the variety needed to keep the gameplay fresh and exciting. Things like having to repurchase disposable items for money multipliers, or having to ride lifts again and again I feel take up a lot of the total playtime and contribute to the gameplay loop growing stale and repetitive rather quickly.

In our contemporary world, one of sensationalist instant gratification experiences,  the indie game scene has always been a bearer of proper artistic improvisation, defying the established culture industry and pushing new boundaries to create new and emergent experiences.

Nowhere is this more obvious than in the horror genre, where the culture industry fails to grasp a very simple concept : the largest human fear is one of the unknown. Once you show us what the monster looks like, we can rationalize it, and it’s no longer scary. ‘If it bleeds, we can kill it.’ The more you rely on the viewer’s personal fears to fill in the gaps, the scarier the experience becomes. As Mies Van Der Rohe would say, ‘less is more.’

HANGAR 8 follows in suite, relying on a need to know basics and letting the player explore what exactly is going on, letting us with a silent protagonist and a ‘found-evidence’ storytelling mode, where we have to fill the gaps ourselves. 

This approach also extends to the gameplay and the overall atmosphere of the game, where the low-poly graphics enhance the overall feeling of existentialist dread and claustrophobia, instead of detracting from them. The focus is not on photorealistic graphics, but on the skilled use of light and shadow, which works regardless of context.

Only critique I might have is certain parts could provide player with a bit more feedback, but I’m on the fence as whether this is actually something to critique, as it completely fits with the aforementioned existentialist dread experience.

To summarize, a highly recommended indie jewel!

Claritas has a simple premise - make up a party from a variety of classes, try to synergize them properly for the challenges ahead, then get to it. You explore very simple square maps comprised of one terrain tile, covered with fog of war, which is exposed as you pass through it. You might find chests, random events, or the boss of the area. Defeating the boss nets you some items, including gems which are used for a variety of upgrades and crafting. There are random encounters, though there's usually only a couple of different foes per area. You can equip your characters with a variety of stat-boosting items to help specialize them or round out their defenses. Eventually you'll hit a wall that will either require you to grind or reconsider your party composition, skill set up and synergies. You can re-assign skill points as you desire for each character, and you can swap your party composition easily. The game also saves your progress with each class, so if you swap out a level 6 paladin and decide to swap him back in, he'll retain his levels.

Claritas is pure gameplay - there's no annoying story to get in the way, text boxes to mash through, or anything of the sort. Once you get through the tutorial, you're good to go. If you're looking for something to play where you basically just grind and that doesn't require involvement in plot or the like, this is it.

TL;DR Good incremental game, although it could to better with communicating things to the player

Universe Horizon does pretty well in terms of offering interesting gameplay mechanics, and unlocking them as you progress over time. It doesn't really feel overwhelming thanks to that. It is relatively short, although you may still need 10-20h to finish it, or more, depending on how actively you play. So it's definitely okay in terms of value.

The main issue this game has is lack of communicating relevant information. For example, it would really help to have some visual indicator for tabs where you unlocked new features - especially if you leave the game running for a while and you end up passing several milestones. I don't think you can go back to the previous map if you've progressed to the next higher level one so you can't read up what features they unlocked. So you just end up going through every tab individually to check if there's anything new, which gets annoying fast. I've definitely just missed some features occasionally because of this.

The game also isn't too great at communication number effects. Especially later when you unlock multiplier to certain resources, the producers of those resource still show you how much they produce without the multiplier, making it really difficult to actually figure out what a difference buying something makes. You'll just end up buying things more or less randomly, which isn't great and loosens up the feedback loop a bit.

The game also could handle the distance / speed units better. It starts out with kilometers and km/s, and progresses through Astronomical Units to light years. And the transition period is awkward, when for example your speed is displayed in AU/s but an upgrade still shows speed gain in km/s which just gives you absolutely no intuitive understanding of how relevant the km/s number is. And yes, the game does provide the conversion rate in the menu, but it's just really not user friendly having to manually convert the units in your head. I wish the game just moved to displaying all units as they are shown for your spacecraft, if its speed is measured in AU/s then have all upgrades and everything also display their effect in AU/s.

So. While the game could use some better communication, it's overall still pretty good though. It can get bit frustrating especially towards the later game, but personally could still enjoy the game anyway. Especially if you're looking for a shorter incremental, this one is definitely worth checking out.

Exo Wanderers is an exciting new arcade-style twin-stick shooter tank game. Earth is dying, and humanity's survival depends on finding a habitable planet in a nearby solar system. As an Exo Wanderer, you’re sent to explore a lush alien world, but you're not alone. Use your tank to defend your base from waves of aggressive aliens as you fight to secure a new home for humanity.

The gameplay is simple yet engaging: Destroy enemies and defend your base, all while collecting a mix of temporary and permanent upgrades. Build your tank to suit your playstyle with a variety of weapons, armor, and power-ups. There's also couch co-op for those lucky enough to have friends to team up with.

The tank mechanics are more arcade-focused than realistic, so don’t expect heavy simulation. While the story provides a solid backdrop, it's not the highlight of the experience. Voice acting is functional but unremarkable—serviceable for players who prefer not to read.

Visually, the game shines with a charming, cartoonish art style, and the world feels vibrant and full of character. The levels are creatively divided into stages, each with its own unique challenges and enemies. However, the gameplay could use some polish. While fun, aiming can sometimes feel unresponsive, and enemy AI is often unintelligent, with many enemies getting stuck or failing to actively hunt you down.

Despite these issues, Exo Wanderers has tons of potential. The casual, destruction-filled gameplay and customization options are a blast, and the game offers a lot of room for improvement in future updates. If you love tank games or twin-stick shooters and don’t mind the lack of hyper-realism, Exo Wanderers is worth checking out. I’m excited to see where it goes from here.

Nest is a fun little break of a game where you play a sniper holed up in a sniper's nest, taking out enemies in waves that increase in size each round, and keeping those enemies from getting close enough to throw grenades at your nest and kill you.

Pros: A fun idea. IMO very reasonably priced for what it's got. The game has a few challenge achievements that can definitely add some replayability.

Cons: Not a lot of variety: There appears to be only one enemy type, one gun, one map. Besides achievements, there's really not much that lends to replayability, as there's no leveling system, or unlocking of new maps, weapons, or enemies.

If the dev was asking for lots more for what's here, I'd probably avoid recommending the game. But for what it is? I'm personally of the opinion that Nest is worth $3 USD for a potential couple hours of playtime..

Here's every major thing I can tell that's wrong with this game:

1. The keyboard timing for wall jumps is way too precise. 
2. The keyboard timing for long jumps is also too precise.
3. The game is too short.
4. The game is too hard if you have one life, and too easy if you have three. 
5. The cutscenes for all the levels are the exact same thing.\
6. When typing words, no punctuation marks appear, even if KAngel says that there are punctuation marks in the word you're supposed to spell. (ex. haiiii :3 becomes haiiii3) The words are alphanumeric.
7. You have way too much time to type 3 characters.
8. I know this is a game about typing internet slang, but the typing feels completely unnatural. I failed three times on the final stage of the typing portion of the game, on words I could fairly easily type in a few seconds. This may be a skill issue, but it still feels too hard.
9. There are too many options for lives. At *most*, you should be able to choose between 1-9 lives and infinite lives. In reality, you can choose between every odd number between 1 and 31, and infinite lives.
10. You can choose infinite lives. I get that games should be accessible, but there are other ways to do it than making the game impossible to lose. If you're having such a bad day that you fail with 31 lives, then there are bigger problems in your life. 
11. This game has almost nothing to do with Needy Streamer Overload, besides the characters. This is coming from someone who has never played Needy Streamer Overload, so I shouldn't be able to tell there's anything wrong.

Finally, I have to say, even though I was overly critical of this game (and even though I could probably have made this myself in the coding platform Scratch, given a month and the art for the game), it isn't the worst thing on Steam. If you have 8 dollars, and you're genuinely excited for this game, don't let my criticism keep you from buying this. 

My only real problem is that this game feels rushed. If WSS Playgrounds had spent a few years on this game, like I presume they did with NSO, then it could have been great. But it simply isn't.

This is a visual novel with some investigative gameplay and some player choice, but the investigations are easy and there isn't really much of a challenge per se in terms of gameplay.

Rather, this is how a visual novel should ideally be, which has some interaction, but is mostly just an amazing example of tense and thrilling storytelling.  There were moments in the game that I had legitimate fear, and I had to remind myself I was playing a video game.  That is a feeling that I don't experience very often.

There are a number of plot twists that leave you guessing until the very end.  In my opinion, this game does have to be played to get the full experience.  Yes, you can watch a longplay, but I don't think it would give you the same experience.  The reason being, there are decisions that you make in the game that are influenced by your own personal opinions and judgment about the horrible situation you find yourself in, and the pacing of the game depends on how quickly you read the text and conduct the various investigations, which of course you would have no control over while watching a Youtube video.  By going at your own pace, you do become caught up in the rhythm of the storytelling, which has moments of pure dread in them that I think would be greatly diminished watching someone else play the game.

I think $16 is a bit high of a price for this game, but I have to admit that I had a lot of fun, and I spent 9 hours playing this game.  So I will say that I think I have gotten my money's worth out of the game.  Plus, the dev seems to be a cool guy.  

I don't usually like visual novels that much, but this one enraptured my attention from start to finish.  There is never a dull moment, and there are some comic relief moments so the game doesn't take itself too seriously.  But there are moments of true horror as well, and I was truly scared for a few brief moments, which I think must be difficult for a visual novel to achieve. 

Overall, I highly recommend this game.

[b]Then this is a game you should definitely give a try.[/b]
At this point in time, as a fresh EA release by a single Dev (if I'm not mistaken), it's definitely not as refined/polished or nice looking (uses AI art which might be off putting for some) as the games I listed above
But despite that, it's a decent game that provides A lot of entertainment, considering it's just Act 1 out of 4.

The game play is simple enough - you're the freshly minted King and have to juggle relations with 4 factions, which, as always, have different interest and will off you if you ignore them too much.
In addition to that you have 3 additional stats to keep in mind - Initiative (your currency for doing things), Health (if it gets too low your kingdom is doomed to die in agony from diarrhea or any other health complication) and Security (which seems to not play a big part in Act 1? Or maybe I never got it low enough to suffer consequences).

The game play is staple of the genre, each turn you have some events to choose from and multiple decisions to resolve each event. Based on that the stats mentioned above change and you either succeed with time or die trying.
BTW dying is a big part of the game, you'll die a lot, like all the 48 achievements currently available are different ways you "end" your game, most of which are by dying in some way.

Oh, almost forgot, you can also build buildings and hire people to work for your Kingdom, but except for a few specific choices the system, while an interesting addition, seems underutilized for now.

[b]Overall, as can be seen in the hours I spent in the game I got hooked and enjoyed it for the most part.[/b]
But it's definitely a hit or miss game, as in the beginning it's quite unforgiving (for example I died like 10 times in the first 2 hours and was considering refunding - lol), but choose to stay and am not regretting it.

So it won't be for everyone, but if you're interested in this typo of games, I suggest you give it a try, as one can get a decent view of what the game offers in the 2 hour refund window Steam provides and decide if they want to keep playing - [b]who knows, maybe you'll also get hooked.[/b]

Very positively surprised by how enjoyable the game is. It gets very difficult quite fast, and there is a lot going on in general, but ultimately it's fair and retrying is just one click of the spacebar way. Over my time playing through the game a patch came out to "make it easier" so the game is more lenient now (less health loss per mistake) but still fun.

There is an odd inclusion of a microtransaction/gatcha mechanic to unlock some extra particle effects, but it is very inconsequential, so you need not worry about it. Though I will state that it feels oddly balanced, as you need 200 coins to open a box (after you're out of rubies you get as a one-time reward for finishing a song) and coins are obtained through random play, at a rate of 1-2 coins per song. So you need to play for ~6 hours for a chance to get a platinum coin. Granted, once you get a coin you can get whichever cosmetic you want, but it still feels like a comparatively large amount of time, especially given the next point.

I think the biggest flaw of this game is its lack of replayability value. It's technically there since you can enable random seeds on all the songs, which keep the patterns but shuffle the spacial layout, but the game really doesn't try to encourage you to play more of it. I would love for the game to keep track of how well you did on each level, showing which ones you did deathless, and maybe even which you did hitless. Furthermore there could be great scorechasing potential by introducing a 'score mode' of sorts, where you get points depending on how close to each circle you are (and perhaps things like how much time you spend near a comet). No deaths, just points. Would make for a different-yet-similar mode of play, and would give people something to chase, since perfecting that score would be nigh impossible on harder tracks.

And speaking of dying and harder tracks, I do think there should be some invulnerability for a short time after dying, especially given the screen effects that happen. They can be very disorienting, and I think majority of the "game too difficult" complaints come partially from the fact that if you die once, you're very likely to lose another life shortly afterwards. Probably the only not fun thing is the game comboing you because you did a mistake in a tricky pattern.

Still, despite some of the above oddities/issues, the game was a blast to play. Took me just under 6 hours to finish challenge mode on all songs, though majority of them were pre-difficulty nerf, so they might've taken a bit longer than they would now. I definitely highly recommend this game though, so try out the demo and see if it's your cup of tea

Don't let the store page deceive you, as it makes this game look like just another mid RPG maker title, which it most definitely is not. 
Sol-Rui -after mini- is one of my favourite H games to date, breathing a lot of needed fresh air into steams anime RPG collection.

STORY
The story is damn near perfect for a lewd game, it's simple, it's horny, and it doesn't try to lore-dump about a fantasy city's entire history like many of the RPG maker titles available. 
To put it simply, you are trapped in a lewd game by a nefarious demon, and you get to choose whether you try your best to escape,or succumb to its temptations.

GAMEPLAY
You are presented with 4 doors, each of which containing a separate type of game entirely, your task is to clear all 4 without your corruption level hitting 100% (If you so choose.)
Door 1: A stealth type game set in a high school, delving further into the horror genre the deeper you go.
Door 2: A social RPG set in a stripclub, pleasing customers to raise your rank as a sex worker.
Door 3: A dungeon crawler type game set in a forest, utilising your typical JRPG battle system to defeat monsters.
Door 4: A mix of stealth and navigation puzzles to fight your way through a goblin camp.

LEWD STUFF
The Live 2D figure really helps bring this game to life, ensuring a very animated MC in every situation, with some of the more stand-out sexual encounters going for a more in-depth animation. 
All of which is very high quality, and covers a LOT of different themes and fetishes. 
The game also features a "remembrance" mode for those who wish to just watch the lewd scenes. This can be accessed quickly by trying to fight the main demon in the level select zone.

Overall a solid 10/10. Hope to see more like this.

It's a simple game based on a fun concept with underbaked execution.

It starts easy enough: you get a shovel and a yard, and you need to dig a hole. As you dig you find minerals, which you can sell to earn money. That money is then used to buy upgrades which help you dig faster or stay down in the hole longer.

For a digging game it's a shame that the digging itself is rather weak. Your shovel digs out a divot in the mesh in front of you, and only digs when there is material directly in your crosshair. In theory that's fine - why waste energy digging if there's nothing to dig? But in practice it means that unless you're perfect with your digging, you will end up with tiny bits of soil stuck in midair that will block your progress and can't be removed unless you perfectly aim at them. You'll often find them by taking fall damage after jumping in the hole and "landing" in midair on a speck of dirt.

To dig you click the left mouse button. There are no options to rebind this input, and no accessibility options. Holding down the mouse button does not continue to dig, so you have to spam the mouse button endlessly until you get one of the late game digging upgrades. Needless to say, clicking like crazy to move tiny piles of dirt gets old quick.

Speaking of upgrades, you have four pieces of equipment (your drill, inventory, battery, and jet pack) each with five upgrade tiers. Most people will max out their upgrades about an hour into the game, which is about as much time as you should expect to enjoy the experience. It would have been nice to have a more flushed out upgrade tree, or at least something else to spend your hard-earned dig money on.

Chonkers is an idle game. This should be obvious given the fact it's in the idle category, but I think a lot of the issues that plagued older reviews have been fixed or grossly exaggerated, because I'm not finding the game any harder than other idle games like Chillquarium or Cookie Clicker (which it's being compared to). 

The game clearly draws inspiration from Neko Atsume, which I LOVE as someone who whittled away at that game in my teens. You have a big room full of cats that you randomise by opening 'packs'. Some of these cats are rarer than others and will earn you more money, but the only penalty is to your time if you choose to pick a common one for aesthetic or collecting purposes. You use toys to level their exp faster (or not), you can click falling petals and chain them up to earn more money (or not), and the whole game is a rinse and repeat of choosing to either actively engage with it for faster rewards or leaving it running and checking in intermittently to rake in larger chunks.

"The cats don't do much." Well, yeah, they're cats. Real life cats sleep most of the day away, so that's not unusual. Other idle games have pulsing visual effects or creatures that just move around a virtual space, so I'm not too sure how much more active you want them to be in comparison to other games in the genre? It's no different to Neko Atsume. If anything, they're MORE animated by comparison, even when sleeping.

"The rewards are slow." Not compared to any other idle game??? You're not supposed to get all the rewards in two days. The point of an idle game is to leave it running while you sleep, work or do chores. You come back to it every couple of hours/days and reap your rewards. If you want something active, this game isn't for you. See: Idle game.

"There's micro transactions!" And if you want to sell the exp boosts the game give you, go right ahead? I think it's a bit misleading to imply there are micro-transactions in the way most of us understand micro-transactions or the game is a flagrant cash grab with exclusive furniture or cats. You can buy exp bonuses, golden rolls and other bits and bobs on the community marketplace that have been earned by other people simply playing the game. I'm not saying this is what other reviewers intended to say, but I wanted to clarify that for people who might be curious. Your choice to engage in the community marketplace hinges on your choice to make the game faster or collect rarer rewards quicker than others. That's it. You can leave the game running and achieve the same.

Overall, I really like it. If you like Neko Atsume, you'll like this game. If you like idle games and cats, you'll like this game. Give it a shot, I think you'll enjoy it!
