* The full breakdown (this is long, I'm so sorry but thanks in advance for reading):
Note: Leading with what I liked and my experiences so far then will add what I think could be improved upon (mostly just some QoL) then some ideas that might be neat to see.

I wanna say, I spent a long time just messing around in the demo and got to where I had basically all of tier 1 items unlocked for my first room and a couple things in the second room and enjoyed it a lot. I did eventually buy the game just a few days ago and have still enjoyed it, even more so actually since I have access to many more kitties now!

That said, you *will* absolutely see a bit of what looks like an insane price hike between the tier 1 items and tier 2, especially between rooms 1 and 2 (I do not have a 3rd room yet so cannot comment there). However, there is a *significant* increase in revenue once you start unlocking the 2nd tier of kitties (the ones just after the Moderately Sleepy tier, they'd 5k/5,000 each) so its actually not that bad. I went from making *maybe* 100k/24hrs in the demo only with ~50-55 tier one kitties, all tier items in room 1 unlocked and the tier 1 food + cardboard box in room 2 to making over 300k/24hrs at the time amount of cats once I had access to tier 2 kitties. Now with all tier 1 items in both rooms unlocked and access to tier 2 kitties, I'm currently getting about 550k/24hrs.

Chonker rates are pretty decent IMHO (In My [Honest/Humble] [Opinion/Onion]). Before I even purchased the game, I managed to get 6 Chonkers and they are SO ROTUND its great. I love them all. They do have a couple different positions and animations like the other levels of growth for the cats (minus the kittens who are relatively the same, more on that later) including the playing animations.

The daily tasks are *very* simple and easy to do (have game open for 1 hour + a random small task like refilling the food bowls 10 times in total) so it makes earning the XP boosters easy to obtain and if you do it for 7 days (not sure if it needs to be in a row or just done 7 times) you get a free kitty from the Golden Roll (I'd consider this high tier personally). XP boost is all that much but it can help a bit with leveling up the higher tier kitties (even just tier 2 has a *substantial* increase of XP required to become adults and reach level 5 compared to tier 1, but matches the revenue increases) and the rarer they are in those tiers as well.

That all said, here are a few QoL changes I think could benefit the game in the long haul (summary then elaboration):
* Stronger boost to XP from boosters *OR* Increase the XP gain when getting higher tier lanterns and toys.
Don't remove the boost just because someone swaps the item to a different one--let folks have their ideal decor/vibe room without punishment, basically. The XP earned/rate (excluding the boosters) is already calculated on a per room basis which makes sense and is great for longevity even with the aforementioned suggested change. The XP booster applying to all rooms is also great and shouldn't be changed there.

* Actually seeing the kitties when their awake on their own.
Personally, I haven't seen any of the cats being awake and doing things whether I had the lamps or not. I think it would be great for people to see the kitties up and stretching, playing with each other, grooming themselves, etc. when idling the game. This would also make it feel like the lamp actually does keep them awake longer or more often instead of them only being awake when the player interacts with them with the toy (either manually or with an auto-clicker) and help with longevity. Don't need to make them swap spots while looking at it, personally, I think just swapping rooms and letting them switch on their own like it currently does is fine ^^

* Adding a "sort by name" function to the cat list
Just something nice, so I can try to find a specific name of a cat I want to sell but can't remember what room it is and don't want to click through all the kitties to find them.

* Setting the kitty catalogue of owned cats to have the rooms as tabs
This is so there is less scrolling required to view what cats you have per room without having to go to that room and help minimize the overwhelming feeling when you get to having 30 cats per room and multiple rooms. This would also benefit from the sort by name function above.

Here are some things that I think would be nice to see but aren't really anything that I think would be necessary to enjoy the game:
* Same cat breed but different coloration / patterns to them, all equal chances to get them when getting a new cat or letting people pick the pattern after the kitten becomes an adult.
* More toy color options--so, different color skins for the toys purchased with no additional cost to acquire them in the game
* Seeing the kitties interact with the "distractions" on screen (but as an animation and not affect the ones the player can click on to help minimize any potential confusion)
* Since Space Cats are already a thing, maybe going ham and adding other fictional kitties could be nice. Some examples being Fae/Fairy Cats (cats with antennae and/or fairy wings), Mercats (cat upper bodies and fish-like lower bodies), Bug Cats (excluding butterflies since those would overlap with fae/fairy cats), and Seasonal Cats (as in, holiday or literal seasons inspired, please do NOT do exclusive cat events; so things like snow/winter/etc themed cats).

The papa's games are (unintentionally) wonderful deconstructions of the horrors of pyramid schemes.

We play as an inexperienced delivery boy/girl, that has to manage an [i]entire restaurant[/i] by themselves, as Louie goes to an 'adventure'; one in which we never see him return from. (he apparently forgot to hire other employees too.)

Most of the customers we meet are other unfortunate people who've also fallen into his schemes. You see, Throughout the series, "Papa Louie" repeatedly tricks unknowing fools into running his own restaurants, on the premise that he's "off on vacation" or that you've "won a raffle". Papa doesn't compensate either, as you have to [i]pay[/i] for upgrades in his bare-bones restaurants while on [b]starvation wages.[/b]

Papa Louie, while initially seeming like the capitalist dream, presents a harsh reality on the world of business. He's a corrupt pyramid scheme leader, the likes of which would make DisneyCorp blush.

The worst part of such a scenario is how he seemingly has created a cult of personality around him. He's international and seemingly has a lot of political sway. Any attempt to criticize him would probably be met in harsh silencing.

Mr Louie is the embodiment of how greed can corrupt man. While he have started with good intentions, and possibly wasn't lying the first time. He has slowly morphed into an unrecognizable monolith of consumerism and the pursuit of an endless fantasy of ownership that is [i]just[/i] ever-so slightly [b]unreachable[/b].

Tldr: Simple, short and sweet roguelike typing game with a couple interesting twists. Worth the money for typing enthusiasts!

Pros:
- simple but fitting animations/art. Keeps the screen clean in hectic moments
- chill soundtrack
- dynamic difficulty based on your initial performance (works really well, game felt challenging throughout all runs)
- a lot of run customization: choose dictionaries, average words per minute and word lengths
- after defending an attack wave, you switch from 'hammering your keyboard' to 'puzzling' giving you a brake if needed and requires you to think about a (mostly simplistic) strategy for a moment, giving the fame a nice twist

Cons:
- very short game length. The developer could add a few more stages to really enable you to play with build variety
- some upgrades seem to always be a better choice (looking at you, chainlightning!)
- a few more upgrade options would also be great

In summary: If you are a typing game enthusiast, or wish to improve your typing speed, I can recommend this game wholeheartedly. The many ways of customizing your run and the ability to let you see your current words per minute lets you track your progress while gunning down enemy spaceships

Underrated Gem with Potential:

The game’s main goal is straightforward: collect 10 balloons that randomly appear around the map while avoiding getting "bonk'd" by BOZO. It’s a simple concept, but one that could be expanded in exciting ways. For instance, adding objectives like completing tasks to restore power to the park and escape, or finding weapons to fight off clowns as a team, would add layers of depth and make it more engaging.

My friends and I tried this game on a whim during a stream and had a blast. The environment, which first caught my eye, is surprisingly aesthetic and mostly well-designed. In hard mode, clowns often pop up unexpectedly around corners, giving some good jump scares. The “pitch black” mode is especially eerie—seeing the clowns' glowing eyes in the dark adds a nice, creepy touch to the gameplay.

There are a few issues, though. The most notable bug is that after dying, players can leave and rejoin, which respawns them as a new player instead of reconnecting them as a dead one. The clowns also occasionally get stuck on objects around the map, though they usually re-aggro and free themselves. Another minor quirk is that sometimes clowns will “hard aggro” on a particular player, ignoring others even when they should have been "bonk’d". Also, the map includes a giant maze that often contains one or two balloons. While the idea of a maze with dead ends adds tension, its sheer size makes it feel more tedious than thrilling.

Despite these quirks, it’s a fun game to play with friends for a few hours, offering laughs and occasionally a good scare. For $6, it’s worth it, especially if you have a group that enjoys goofing around and laughing at some game jank. With additional polish, more game modes, and added objectives, this game could really become a gem!

Red Blue Cell is an old school inspired shoot 'em up that focuses on polarity.

Pretty much from the start you can see this game has such beautiful art. From the developer that created Ganablade, comes Red Blue Cell. This game is pretty simple if you’ve ever played a polarity game like Ikaruga, you’ll see that the game's mechanic revolves around you absorbing bullets that are similar to the color your ship can switch into. Besides that, You have your shoot button and special shot that can be built up by collecting mini gauges.

There's great difficulty options for those looking for a casual or more challenging experience. I got a 1cc from the retro mode they have which essentially removes the polarity part of the game and gives you the challenge of playing it like an old school shoot 'em up. Just raw dodge and muscle memory lol. If you’re someone that cares about score, there are hidden extra tokens that you must shoot and obtain similar to what a caravan shmup would do. Bosses even have what's called a “perfect kill” where if you remove all parts of the boss you will get more score and also more extends in exchange.

The game's length is typical for a shoot em up which is about 20-30 mins. The game is very generous by giving extends after obtaining a perfect kill. The music is pretty fitting for the old school theme and honestly, there's very little negative feedback I can say about this one. When you have time please give it a try. Using some assets is one thing; taking an FPS template, adding marketplace assets, and calling it a game is another. It’s buggy, ugly, and barely functional. I don’t want to hate too much, as I assume the developer is likely new or young. However, if I were the developer, I would delist Source Code and begin remaking and recreating the assets and code. Until then, do not purchase this game—even with the reduced price from $39.99 to $0.99.

[h1] A Horrendous Asset Flip [/h1]

[i] Ahh, a zombies mode. Or, rather, "Xombie" in this game. Is it absolute trash? Yes. Is it buggy as hell? Yes. Is it fun? No. [/i]

Calling Source Code a game is unfair to games, so I'll start by just saying that this is a horrible asset flip. The game tries to present itself as some kind of CoD killer, with a zombies mode, multiplayer, and all sorts of features, but it's so terribly done across the board. I get the feeling the dev priced this game at $40 USD to try and give the impression of quality, but it's absolutely not worth your time or money.

Pros:

It Looks Nice: It runs on UE5, so it does look decent.

Cons:

Everything: There is really nothing redeemable about this title. Not only is it clear it's an asset flip, given that the application name even references a multiplayer game template, but it's poorly optimized, what little needed to be added to maps to make it work wasn't done well, with oddly placed textures and oddities. Also, the trailers for the game are incredibly misleading. They give the impression of this title including some sort of epic storyline about World War III, but there is no story mode in this game. It's simply multiplayer (with or without bots) and a zombies mode.

Overall, avoid this game like the plague. Normally I'd possibly recommend an asset flip if it was just a few dollars and you could get some fun out of it, but it's obvious this dev is selling at a high price and utilizing mismarketing to try and convince folks it's a far more epic title than it actually is.

Update: After this review was posted, the dev has both cut the epic story trailer, and has now dropped the price to $0.99. Even at 99 cents, this game is still a waste of your time, so save your cash.

The visuals of the game are fairly good (although perhaps not by 2025 standards), but unfortunately the rest of the game lets it down. The models are pretty poor quality, the animation (especially facial animation) rigid and awkward, the voice acting almost non-existent (or is it just synthesized?). I don't feel like this game knows what it wants to be. The developers should have taken more time to figure out a consistent game design and tried to make perhaps something less ambitious.

Initially you are sent on a quest to essentially ransack the town, picking up valuable items to ... rebuild the town? If you just sell everything of value what's the point? Then I'm working in a cafe. I just earned $30000 or so selling valuable suitcases, now I'm only making $100 per shift at the cafe ... apparently from a Fanta, an energy drink and a single coffee. None of this makes sense.

What is the purpose? There is some sort of mystery but I'm stuck doing these meaningless chores, all the while being limited by an extremely short amount of time to do these things before I need to go back to my apartment and "sleep" to save my progress. I could probably have tolerated the jankiness of everything if I just knew what the heck I was meant to be doing and where things were going in this game.

There is a lot in this game to dislike.  There is no option to change the controls, unticking the subtitles box does not stop the subtitles being displayed, the voices are all computer-generated, and there was a bug where the options menu got stuck open and I had to restart the game in the intro (that goes on for way too long).  On top of that, the cafe parts are pretty repetitive and dull (which is, of course, fairly accurate).  

I have finally got to the point where I have given up, at least for the moment, because I am in the mine section, it requires a lot of crouching, and using WASD with Ctrl as the crouch button is absolutely killing my little finger. On top of that, there is a section where you need to jump up into a little cave area and the physics of game make this incredibly frustrating - I'm just hurling myself at the wall over and over again despite using the little crate to stand on as is, almost certainly, the idea.  I managed it once but died and I got bored and frustrated trying to do it over and over again.  That finally killed it for me. 
 
On top of all that, it is very irritating having to re-hire employees every day and to return to your apartment to save the game at the end of each day. 

But...

That said, it didn't stop me from playing the game fairly obsessively for the nearly 7 hours you can see above.  I paid 74p for the game so it has definitely been value for money.

The basic game loop is work in the cafe to make money, do a quest (that usually requires money, including, oddly enough clearing up rubbish in the town), repeat.  As you go round and round you slowly advance the story.  The game is set in the past by way of the main character's daughter looking through her dad's old VHS tapes.  In her time a pandemic is raging and the VHS tapes show a time just after a previous pandemic has ended where people are trying to get back to normality.  The whole thing is played as though looking through a camcorder which is a style you either like or you don't.  I'm not that fussed either way.  

I have marked this as a recommendation because, for all that I am complaining about it,  I did get drawn into it and it occupied a few mindless hours.  

If the controls could be altered this would go a long way to making this game more enjoyable to play.  I am an ESDF guy, I want space to be action, I want Z to be crouch, and I would really like there to be a crouch toggle if I can't have that so that I don't exacerbate my RSI and arthritis.  

If I had bought this game at full price I think that there is a very good chance that I would have refunded it but on sale, at the moment, it's definitely worth the money even of only for an afternoon's entertainment.

Breecell is a colorful falling piece puzzler in the vein of Puyo Puyo, Columns, and Dr. Mario.

In this game the player watches falling cells land into the play area and then clicks on specific cells to multiply them. Cells multiply in the direction indicated on their body.

The goal is to match 4 same-color cells in a 2x2 square, which also destroy any other same-color cells that might extend from the square. The game ends when the play area is completely filled with cells.

What separates Breecell from similar games is the inability to control the falling cells. Instead, the player must  take action on the cells in play, carefully choosing which ones to multiply.

I found out about this game from a Twitter post. I thought the art was appealing and I was attracted to the laboratory/research theme of the game.

As of this writing, there are 2 modes: an endless mode and a harder genkai mode with a smaller play area. 

The music is nice and the graphics are colorful. I see a lot of visual similarities to the Puyo Puyo Tetris series although for me personally Breecell looks and sounds a lot more appealing. 

Breecell is a great time and I think fans of the genre will enjoy the new twists it offers. A few extras or additional modes could really elevate it to the top of the genre but for the asking price I can't complain. There is a lot of potential here and I hope the developer continues with this series.

I bought this game on a whim just because it looked interesting and can say Breecell adds a twist to puzzle games that I have never experienced before. The cells will fall from the top of the screen and the only action you can perform on them at this point is to click on them which in turn forms more cells in the corresponding direction that is indicated on that cell. For example if the cell has a horizontal line and you click it, a new horizontal cell will form on the left and right of that cell.

The game comes with a tutorial to show you the ropes and it is highly recommended that new players do not skip it and play it the first time they pick up Breecell.  

Breecell is a fun game worth picking up if you are into puzzle games or looking for a game to nominate for the "Best Game You Suck At Award" because while I find it fun and like to play a quick round here and there, I do indeed suck at it.

Mister Antonio would like you to bring him balls, but only in a specific order. And what does Mister Antonio do with all the balls? Well, you’ll just have to find out for yourself.

[b]What is it:[/b] A sequence deduction game. On a small cluster of connected asteroids, several colored balls are spread around. You have to collect them in a specific order to satisfy Antonio the cat’s whims. Every time you pass by a ball, you automatically collect it and add it on top of the stack you're holding. The first few levels are easy, just decide if you go left or right around the asteroids, but a few more mechanics make it more challenging: there are clouds which sprinkle snow on all the balls you're carrying when going under them, trees that block going around all the way, a moose that kicks you and flips the stack of balls you're carrying, squirrels that steal the ball on the bottom and later put it back at the top. In essence, you have to build a stack by applying operations in the correct order.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3376834682

There are up to three connected asteroids, up to three target stacks, of up to six balls in each level, but never more than 9 balls in total. Overall, this is quite short and easy, with just 26 levels and short stacks to build. Still, like all of Bart’s games, this is a fun, relaxing game, with cute graphics and music. As with his other games, it’s also available on mobile devices, so it has very minimal QoL features, but it’s not just a direct port, it was adapted to fit better on a desktop.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3376835106

My biggest disappointment was that the game is too short. I expected to see 50 levels, as is typical in Bart’s games, only to see the credits when it was just getting interesting. Still, for the half hour of playtime it offers, it’s a fun time.

[b]How hard is it:[/b] Very easy to easy.

[b]How long is it:[/b] 26 levels, half an hour to an hour, levels must be solved in order, but there are hints available. Un/fortunately, the hints just offer the full solution move by move.

[b]Level design:[/b] OK, fairly distinct ideas, but there's not much to design with such simple mechanics and small levels.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3376836262

[b]Quality:[/b] Basic, but not that much more needed for such a simple game. No undo or fast restart, but levels are small enough not to mean too much work to start from scratch. Basic prev/next level select. Keyboard or controller, but not mouse, even though on mobile it works with just a finger. [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3376836720]Minimal settings[/url], just a fullscreen and a couple of sound toggles. No cloud saving, a few progress achievements. Fast and responsive, though a short unskippable intro is played every time you go back to the title page. Crashed a few times.

[b]Worth the price:[/b] Too short and simple for the full price, but I wanted to support the developer for his innovative ideas.

[b]Most positive aspect for me:[/b] Relaxing.

[b]Most negative aspect for me:[/b] Too short.

[b]What would make it better:[/b] More levels. Undo. A better level select. A quit button. Mouse controls. Colorblind mode. Cloud saving. Make the “A. Bart. Bonte. Game” intro skippable, or even better, don’t show it every time I open the title page. Add a controller button for showing hints.

This is a beautiful game that consists of three very different parts:
- Firstly, you have to deliver packages from one country to another while crossing as few borders as possible. If you find the route (or one of them) with the fewest hops, you get a star. With these stars, you automatically unlock higher levels with longer and more difficult routes. You can also use them to unlock other continents.
- As you deliver each package, you collect puzzle pieces along the way (you take photos of the area) by trying to drive over them with your delivery truck.
- In your photo albums, you can then put the collected puzzle pieces together to create beautiful (AI) paintings.

•	Finding the route
The game basically starts in Europe. I'm not sure if that's a good thing, because even for me as a European, finding the routes here is much more difficult than in the "Americas" (South and North America are combined into one continent in this game). You click your way through country by country and are always shown all the neighboring countries of the country you are currently in. This makes the game not particularly difficult from the start. It is then made even easier by the fact that you can go back step by step without penalty or simply start the route from the beginning. It is quite obvious that the aim of this game is not to push you to the limits of your abilities. Rather, it is about getting to know the world - at least the location of the many different countries in the world - a little better in a fun and entertaining way. And even if the game is designed more for children, this is something that could do us all good.
You reach the second level on each continent long before you have completed the tasks of the first level. This means that it is possible to tackle more difficult tasks early on if you are not challenged by the easy ones. Unfortunately, you do not get more stars for completing tasks at higher levels, nor do you get any other advantages in the game.
With just 15 stars you can buy the first additional continent. This is particularly suitable for all players who are not from Europe and therefore perhaps want to try out familiar terrain first. In addition to the Americas, Asia and Africa are available for this. Since Australia only consists of two countries (Australia and New Zealand), I think it is understandable that the developer did not add this.

•	"Photographing" (collecting the puzzle pieces)
Every time you successfully complete a task, you drive your van a short distance along a straight country road, on which a lot of jigsaw puzzle pieces are scattered around. You use the mouse to steer left and right to collect as many of them as possible. You don't need to pay attention to traffic rules, as fortunately there are no oncoming traffic or guard rails. You can shorten this sequence by right-clicking and thus receive a randomly determined number of puzzle pieces.
I think this part of the game only exists to explain the subsequent jigsaw puzzles. To be honest, I usually skip it with the autcollect function.

•	The photo albums
With autocollect you get between 15 and 23 pieces, if you collect them yourself, the result ranges across a much wider spectrum. The pieces usually belong to one of the next three puzzles in the album.
As soon as you have received at least 1 piece of a puzzle, you can open the puzzle in the album and try to connect the existing pieces. Of course, you can only finish it when you have all 64 pieces.
You gradually get a gallery of 18 pictures for each continent, each of which is typical of its continent in its own way.
Unfortunately, these are all AI-generated paintings, which to a large extent seem to serve already known clichés rather than actually showing the essence of the region in question and real existing architecture and landscape features.
I don't know to what extent it would have been feasible (and above all affordable) to obtain the rights to real photographs for this game. The educational approach of the game could only have benefited from this in any case.

•	Conclusion
The game's controls, rules and game principles are very easy to understand.
The entire presentation - the design, the fonts and icons - is soft and easy on the eyes and is therefore also well suited for children imo.
Finding out where so many countries you've heard of are and what other countries you've never heard of exist can be really exciting. But once you know, the game loses its excitement and quickly becomes repetitive. The appeal that remains is actually remembering the position of these countries and finding the "shortest" routes over and over again (which aren't always the shortest, since it's the number of borders that count, not the distance traveled).
This game is a pleasant and relaxing pastime that you can actually take back into real life. Later in the game, you can mostly decide freely whether you want to do puzzles or find routes, and which continent you want to play on.
I miss a freeplay mode a little and maybe the possibility to compete with others. The latter, of course, not online, but via an alternating multiplayer mode - perhaps even with up to four players.
As already mentioned above, I think it's a bit sad that instead of real photos of real buildings and real nature, only artificial imitations (albeit really pretty ones) made it into the game, and collecting the puzzle pieces seems a bit forced, but you can at least skip that.
All in all, I give the game a solid 8 out of 10.

TLDR; Have fun playing an escape room game of sorts with AI and don't take the horror label too seriously.

AI Asylum is more or less an escape room game, but it brings two things together that I love: AI and role play. I have sincerely longed for the opportunity to play more games with AI, so this appeals to me that I can enjoy one of my most cherished hobbies in writing narratives with them. This is a game that allows you to have conversations with AI who have different set personalities as patients in an asylum. I have concluded that the goal is to try to understand each personality as quickly as possible and speak to them in a way that will resonate with them in order to escape their room with your life. There is a gauge called “favor” that measures how the patient feels after each dialogue you submit, so you need to make sure you keep the scales tipped toward a positive perception of you and you might escape. I say might because you can earn a lot of favor, but still get murdered. I haven’t quite grasped if there is a reason for that yet, but I like the challenge to better exercise emotional intelligence. It can also be tricky if there is a personality you may not be sure how to approach, which I find intriguing and keeps me determined to understand their psyche. You only have so many rounds of replies you can give before it’s over, so I like that there might be pressure as you watch the countdown of tries you have left to talk. What is interesting is that you can say the same things to the AI on a new play-through, but it doesn’t necessarily mean that what worked the previous time will work in the next. To me, this means you can have a good amount of replay ability. 

The first type of play-through is where you can select from characters in the game’s story mode. You may be given a goal of extracting key pieces of information from them. Sometimes, you also need to look for items around the room to gather clues which may be in different places on another play-through. Those items can be shown to elicit responses from the characters, but the items may not have much of an impact if you haven’t dug for the dialogue that will cause the character to react. If you succeed in surviving, you’re graded on your dialogue, your favor level by the end of the play-through, whether you’ve extracted the information you were assigned to obtain, and how many items you located in the room.

The second type of play-through can be with characters you select that other players made. This is where I think it gets more interesting because there is an opportunity to delve into those personalities that other players have made. In my opinion, I see a strong potential here in players being able to contribute to the experience. When you create your own patient, you can select the appearance of the room they stay in from a few choices, the appearance of the character from several presets, give them a name, what they do, select several base characteristics for personality, condition needed for player to win, a short description for the patient directory that players can read, and a box that will allow about 2000 characters (spaces included) to give the AI a background story script to stick to. Players cannot see that background story information, so you don’t have to worry about any spoilers being given to the player. Just think about the different patients you could make with all of the various psychological behaviors one can have! This is what excites me and where I see most potential in this game, but if they want a user driven experience for its players, I hope they will find a way to allow players to customize the look of their patient and room to be as unique as the personality created.

However, as delighted as I was to find this game, it is rather bare bones in terms of world building and variety at its current stage. This goes for story, scenes, characters, and music. Currently, there are only about five rooms between the two story line characters you can chat with so far. Though I said that I hope they will add more character customization, some of the character presets you can choose from look like they just got back from a luau or Hawaiian vacation in their bathing suits, and another looks like a UFC contender. Maybe the character looks aren’t supposed to be very serious after all and could be fun in its own right, but this does seem conflicting with the horror theme. By the game description, I thought I was going to feel apprehensive, scared, and disturbed at once, but I must admit the game felt significantly lighter than I expected despite the suggestion of some dark themes. Then again, what feels scary to one person, might not be scary for another. The intro takes you through a condemned and decrepit building with ominous, suspenseful music, and blood on the walls. That precarious element seems to become dissolved by the more silly looking characters, or when one of the two story characters you speak with has a bedroom that suddenly looks fit for a princess. 

In the meantime, I’ve decided to reason with myself that modernization allowed patients to have dorms they could personalize. Maybe there is a reason for that, such as the idea that patients get special treatment for good behavior or they have special connections, so I may need to dig further somehow, but it hasn’t made sense to me yet in comparison to the rest of the sorry state the building. Perhaps there may need to be some context for the stark differences between those said rooms and the rest of the facility. I am otherwise ecstatic about character customization, so if they find a way to weave an explanation for those rooms and outfits, they could capitalize on this idea. Although consistency can be just as much of an issue as inconsistency if there is too much repetition. The music in the whole game so far seems to be only two tracks, one of which only plays when you are in a particular room of the five. The other track is what you will otherwise hear on loop at all times while playing from the startup of the game until you’re finished, so this may sound a bit redundant rather quickly.

I’m open to the twist of fantasy (such as the cat-girl, werewolf or ghost I saw) and I appreciate the element of science (whether it be some method of treatment or something being manufactured affecting patients) but wanted to know more about what elements of horror I was going to experience. In the past, people being treated in asylums were victims that suffered atrocities at the hands of the very people that were supposed to care for them. I know what happened before was from the lack of understanding about mental health compared to what we know today, but patients back then were subjected to horrible conditions. It probably would not be appropriate for me to describe them here. You can certainly do your own research to find out, but the asylums that began with noble intentions had become warehouses for the mentally ill where they were nearly forgotten by society. Show me more of the game's story that showcases a history of fear, misery, and despair incarnate, whispering from the creaks in the building’s foundation and writing on the walls. I want to learn more about the heart of the matter as to what caused the facility in the game to be abandoned and shut down, yet still functioning for those left behind. I am interested about the idea that started in this game and believe that so much can be done with it. Please know that my opinions or critiquing come from a place of admiration for the vision because I still had fun playing anyway. C:

At first glance this game caught my eye and looked really cool.  It reminded me of an old arcade machine that I remember playing as a kid. Sadly the game is filled with glitches and problems that clearly shows the ignorance and inexperience of this game developer.

The first thing I did was adjust the settings and checked the controller options. It was nice to see a large list of driving settings that could be adjusted but this is where things started off with some problems. I wanted to drive with a manual transmission and as soon as I got into the race,  it became impossible to drive because the developer apparently forgot that they configured the camera zoom and shift buttons to the same button on the controller.  Every time I wanted to shift up or down the camera wanted to zoom in or out. The fact that this was not tested is confounding.

I decided to switch back to automatic transmission and try another race. Things went alright this time but as soon as the race ended I paused the game and then suddenly the results screen was covered by the car gauges and the rest of the interface. 
I had to force close the game through the windows task manager because the interface covered the button to exit the race.

The game is 10 bucks and these are basic things that any racing game should not have issues with. On top of that the spotter over the radio is impossible to hear during the race because the engine sound is so loud. Speaking of which, the engines sound like my landscapers trying to start the lawn mower in the backyard and dont even sound like race cars. The car spotter is pretty much unintelligible and inaudible.

Lets talk about the games graphics. The cars look really good but the tracks are outdated and look like they came out of a mobile game. The shocking discrepancy in quality likely means that the developer purchased assets and mashed them together to put together an incomplete game.A quick search of the game engine's online marketplace confirms the bad news.  The developer has apparently used cheap asset packs to design large portions of this racing game. That was the final dagger to eliminate any remaining nostalgia I felt when seeing this game on the store.

The store page claims that this game will bring you back to the golden age of racing but instead it brings you back to the stone age of trying to overcome annoying glitches and bugs. I think the overall intention of this developer was good but the final product is something that you likely would find in an entry level programming class.  

Due to my experience with this game, I cannot in good faith recommend this game for ten bucks.

I have to be very upfront: the only reason I'm recommending is this is because Cannibal Interactive will give you exactly what is says on the tin with his games; Labyrinth of Wild Abyss: LayeRedux, if in fact a Labyrinth. However, there isn't any incentive to actually go through it.

I can only speak as someone who put in 15 minutes and got to level 5, if my brief is with the game is any indication of what rest of my time will be like then I gotta check out here. There's three critical issues with LayeRedux:

[*] There are no clear markers or apparent reason to the labyrinth layout, so the exits I did find were by pure chance.

[*]  The avatar(?)/character turns at 90 degree angles, similar to a dungeon crawler - at a *fixed speed* - but your movement is in real time, with sprinting giving you a significant speed boost. Given that there's no controller support, regardless of whether you use WASD, arrow keys, or numpad for movement, your fingers and wrist are ultimately going to wear out, preventing long play sessions. I'm guessing the movement vs turn speed was an intentional decision to heighten the feeling of powerlessness when trying to escape the monster(s), but it feels like playing Persona 1 while drunk, or King's Field 4 while wired.

[*] The description for the game says “Eyes on the walls may or may not alert the Monster to exactly where you are” and it's true. Since there's no way in-game to quickly to restart a level - I'm not counting F5 since it's built into RPM itself - or to access the options, I tried intentionally trying to finding the monster and actually found it hard. This could be a quirk of the earlier stages, but it contributed to the frustration I felt when trying to make any sort of progress.

 In short, it's not entertaining or engaging, but I like supporting attempts like this.

Going in completely blind, Ratshaker turned out to be an, interesting, experience. The game has a unique aesthetic, blending cartoonish visuals with horrific imagery that makes you screw your face in disgust as you explore a twisted house, with your only company being a rat you violently abuse throughout the game. The imagery in question at first glance comes across as corny and generic, but you later realise the scenes have a much deeper meaning with the ending presented to you, it really gets you thinking. The pixel overlay enhances the horror, as it makes certain models appear more detailed to the eyes. Scenes have great tension between them, despite the comedic remarks of the rat.

The main gameplay is pretty much a walking sim, but with a cartoony rat you can use to interact with items and reveal secrets by violently shaking and squeezing him, and is a very fun mechanic to toy with. He has a wide variety of dialogue and gargling sounds, so he never outstays his welcome. My only complaints with the game are the infrequent checkpoints, and the lack of direction in some areas, where it's easy to get lost if not paying attention.

I certainly enjoyed my time with Ratshaker, with its blend of horror and comedy, distinct visuals, and moment to moment rat shaking gameplay.

[h2]💭Introduction💭[/h2]

[i]RATSHAKER[/i] presents an experience that is unlike any other that I've experienced. It starts out in a seemingly peaceful and unassuming environment: a wheat field, an orange-hued sky, and a simple premise: shaking a rat. Beneath this absurd premise, however, is an unsettling journey through a house that has a deeply haunting atmosphere. As we descend through the house, the game's atmosphere grows heavier and heavier, despite the humorous, light-hearted quips from the rat throughout. Though [i]RATSHAKER[/i] doesn't rely on traditional jumpscares of what we may think of when we think horror, or the immediate threat of a creature around the corner, it instead decides to immerse the player in a story with visual storytelling that gradually reveals itself in disturbing ways that leave a lasting impact on the player.

[h2]✅The Good✅[/h2]

✅ [b] Noticeably excellent sound design [/b] – The voices that the player hears in their head about shaking the rat, the echoes of the rat's pain and laughter in the house, and the general environment in the game feels very high quality for a game that is about shaking a rat. It feels memorable and I enjoyed it. It was something where whenever I was just shaking the rat I was saying to myself, “Wait, was there a voice in the background that was just talking about shaking the rat?” It brought some levity to the otherwise grim environment. 

✅[b] Shifting atmosphere and tone of the game [/b] - The game initially starts out in a deceptively peaceful environment: in a wheat field with an orange glow of the sky, and your hand with a rat in it. There is a house before us and before even entering the house, the rat declares, almost mockingly, with a reference to Dante's Inferno, "Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here." At the time of the Rat's saying this, it feels silly and I dismissed it, but the aptness of the declaration of the rat becomes more apparent as we descend into a house that feels more and more claustrophobic the more we descend into it. 

✅ [b] Absurd and fresh Mechanics [/b] - To add to this, there is an element of oddness at the beginning of the game: an advertisement about getting rid of your problems by shaking a rat. While initially we do only shake a rat, it does end up being a key part of the game. The absurdity in integrating this as a core mechanic almost reminds me of the reload mechanic in [i]Cruelty Squad[/i]. (In [i]Cruelty Squad[/i], the player has to reload, but swing the mouse up and down in order to correctly reload the gun. It is a very unconventional way to reload a gun as far as expected game mechanics go. Typically one might reload a gun in a game with "R".)

✅ [b] A Narrative that reveals itself over time [/b] - While initially the game appears to only be about shaking a rat, there is a narrative that unfolds with some high quality visual storytelling over the entire length of the game. 

🟡 [b] Simple gameplay, deviating from traditional survival/psychological horror games [/b] - The gameplay of [i]RATSHAKER[/i] is condensed, simple, and the game relies on a dark atmosphere, immersion in the game, and excellent visual storytelling. While there may be an allure of the game due to its absurdity, and the clear direction for it being a horror game, those expecting a traditional horror game with direct threats like [i]Amnesia: The Dark Descent[/i], or [i]Outlast[/i] may find the slower pace of the game to differ from what we would expect from a horror game nowadays.

🟡 [b] A full playthrough of [i]RATSHAKER[/i] may be two hours or less [/b] - Even though you're potentially looking at [i]RATSHAKER[/i] for a fairly cheap price compared to most games, the themes of the game may encourage at least one more playthrough, especially if the player wants to get to the hidden ending of the game. 

❌[b]The ending is powerful, but leaves some questions open [/b]- While the final reveal of the game is fairly devastating and certainly recontextualizes all of the experiences the player has had up until this point, it might leave the player wishing for some more clarity on certain aspects with the story's resolution or pieces of the story that were unclear throughout. 

❌ [b] Lack of meaningful interactivity with the environment/story of the game [/b] - The game clearly thrives on its strong visual narrative, the haunting atmosphere, and the core game mechanic of shaking the rat while interacting with the environment. Despite this, the lack of variety and meaningful interaction with the environment, the characters, and the effects on the story may also leave you wishing for more interaction with the environment, story through in game actions, or even the rat itself. 

[h2]💭Conclusion💭[/h2]

[i]RATSHAKER[/i] has delivered a thought-provoking and atmospheric experience that blends surrealistic gameplay with grim visual storytelling elements. The strength of the game is the way that it is able to draw you in with the absurdity of the game but the inevitable claustrophobic world that ends up feeling haunting and introspective. However, the game's slower trod through the story and experience overall, the minimal interaction with the environment, and missing pieces for the story may leave players wanting more. 

For its strong efforts in a unique approach to visual storytelling as well as its memorable, haunting atmosphere, [i]RATSHAKER[/i] earns itself a light to strong 8 out of 10. An excellent experience.

Call me a silly billy, but when I first stumbled upon the elevator pitch for this game I was electrified. It reminded me of my primary take-away from RE7; the Bedroom DLC chapter, a side story that recontextualises the core game's setting into an escape room featuring a focal primary antagonist who'd regularly check in on you and assess the room to see if you've been making attempts to leave.
There's a Gun in the Office is about half an hour long, and a very cheap solo project, so I'd wholeheartedly recommend it. Plenty of things here I'd like to sing praise of, so please consider giving it a shot before I hand-wring away some of its magic!

_________

There's a Gun in the Office takes a somewhat different approach to what the RE7 DLC sets out to do, and one that I found orders of magnitude more effective. There's a loneliness here, the captor themselves is surprisingly downplayed to the point where you never actually see them directly - but their presence is always felt in numerous ways. Footsteps, a static void warping the player's perception around their physical presence, elevator dings and the sounds of doors unlocking. Rather than any spoken dialogue, the game is incredibly ambient in its sound design, focusing more on the muted realism of a lonely apartment - where noises you didn't make yourself cut through the stillness.

The puzzle design here is somewhat simplistic when you really get down to it, but that’s a very good thing here. We’re not rotating forks to cast the shadow of a snake head onto a wall here a-la RE7 - the focus is on a degree of mundane realism that helps sell the ordeal. Combing through shelves and cabinets for keys, learning what you can about the layout of the apartment before needing to retrace your steps as accurately as possible. Very effective at drumming up stress honestly! Retiring to my cell again at the end of the day before the fear hits me like a bolt of lightning… did I leave a door open? Did I put that key back where my captor left it? Because the captor is an absence rather than a presence, the fear becomes abstract. You’re left with a haunt that lets paranoia do most of the work, making you second-guess whether you’ve spun your plates effectively and truly covered your tracks. There’s something uniquely stressful about the fact that you’re always anticipating confrontation, but never actually seeing the person you’re hiding from. I‘m very keen on the subtle visual flourishes that lend to the unease, God knows why it messed me up that the skyline was randomly generated but the impermanence of it did Something to me.

If I had to complain, I do wish that the hallway didn’t have an updating map that tracks your interactions and mistakes - it gamifies things too much and deflates the primary source of anxiety in the game, that being the unknown. Knowing the full layout of the apartment feels a little strange, it’d be better if the day-end map only showed the rooms you’ve already discovered so far. I do think some harsher punishments for mistakes would have gone a long way, the captive throwing a few curveballs that make what becomes your routine a little more confusing or strenuous.

Reading the dev’s journey they’ve outlined in the Steam updates leading up to this game’s release is lovely, I truly believe they have every right to be very proud of what they’ve made here. They took it upon themselves to make something in their free time that I still think came out to be incredibly distinct. It’s a short, sharp experience that lingers, one of those rare small-scale games that knows exactly what it wants to be and delivers it with confidence.

I enjoy idle games, to an extent. They're a wave of newer games offering a persistent dopamine hit with a mix of consistent affirmations, consistent mechanics, and general consistency. The reason I use that word so frequently is that they're also very hit and miss for some people. They're not instant gratification, they require patience and a desire to push forward relentlessly. In a sense, they're actually a subconscious way for our brain to seek out progress in exchange for patience: Which, to reiterate, not a lot of people to have.

Addled Clicker is a Lovecraftian horror game which places you in a room where you can press a button over, and over, and over again. As you do so, a giant counter keeps track of how many times you press the button. Eventually, you may earn enough clicks to begin to purchase things from your local fish-headed gent. All of these items (except the final one) do exactly the same thing: Help pushing the button and adding onto your click counter. 

The more you press, and the more you linger around the button with the items, the more clicks you earn, but there eventually appear monsters which don't seem to be too friendly, and would like to eat your liver with some fava beans and a nice chianti. At the moment, the total number of monsters around the clicker are 3 in total. Note my wording there: The total number *around the clicker*. You can eventually find tools to help you navigate around the facility you're in, and find bits of lore, extra lives, and things that will make your run a bit easier, or even other monsters which also seem quite curious about the colour of your innards. 

Anyway, you're eventually given the choice to leave or stay, but through sheer compulsion more than anything else, and the desire to see what would happen, I stayed just to hit 9,999,999 and the ending was... about expected. Especially with the lore, etc. But I will say a tad underwhelming.

That said: I find Addled Clicker to be quite charming and unique. There's a lot here that is quite functional, fascinating and engaging, even if it's a game that can be beaten fairly shortly with drive and persistence. For a small game, it plays like one that's had a considerable amount of passion thrown in, and that's something to be admired. I died I think about 3 times in total, but the checkpoints and ability to keep items feels like it makes the game considerably more player-friendly. I appreciate this work. 7.5/10

Personally: I hate alien games if they're not Alien or Predator. That's just a personal preference. I don't like thinking that the ancient civilizations were "visited" by inter-dimensional beings in order to make the things that they made. As someone who is passionate about history and how civilizations were actually made and how they problem-solved issues, it's a bit of a slap in the face to attribute what humans did to other-worldly beings ie "better" and "more advanced" beings. I would have enjoyed the game a LOT more if there was a deeper dive into the death deities. Like maybe the Queen somehow disrespected Anubis and that's why her soul was trapped there. Maybe she was mad at Anubis and rebelled against him for taking her lover and that's why he cursed them both to haunt the halls of their tombs. 

There was a lot of potential and I think it's mostly just a cop-out to use aliens at this point. Not to mention it's low-key a little... Demeaning to human beings to say "you're too primitive to have the ability to make these amazing things, because Europeans couldn't do this, so you must have had help", when we know that people predating 2000 BCE were preforming brain surgery. 

But that's just my 2 cents. If you like alien themes, then you may like this. The other world concepts were beautifully done, despite my distaste for the alien theme. The details in that were just amazing.

I don't really see it having any re-play appeal at this time, but I may download it again to challenge myself.

[h1]My Goddess's Deck Has No Pathetic Cards[/h1]

[h2]Story[/h2]

There isn't much of a story here. Basically, your protagonist, Fatima, is the guardian priestess of a nation, Donerksela, and she must help them manage their resources in order to expand their population and increase her power. Sadly, we don't really get much more dialogue than that. Some of the choices can let you be more lenient when it comes to your citizens' workload, but that's about it. We also never learn what's up with the enemies that show up, but the last guardian apparently failed to defeat them. All we know is that once the final boss is defeated on week 90, your protagonist is able to become a goddess or maybe something worse depending on your alignment. Your alignment stat determines what your character will look like, but I have no idea if going for negative alignment significantly changes the story. It probably doesn't change much, since there's no cutscene for winning the game. Personally, I'd like to see how ascending to goddesshood affects Fatima's relationship with her citizens.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

As implied by the above section, the game is all about the resource management and card gameplay. You get a randomized board to build facilities on, and each tile has a preset type of facility you are allowed to build, but some cards allow you to override that restriction. Each facility also has durability that you have to look out for, though at high levels, you might not have to worry about that durability outside of friendly fire with your offensive cards. You generate a certain amount of resources each week depending on your facilities, so try to strike a balance so that you have every resource you need. However, to ensure you can't do a ton of stuff in one week, you have a set amount of EP that gets refilled each week.

But what exactly are you spending resources on? Food is spent to increase your population, wood is spent to increase your population cap, gold is spent on passives in the study menu, fuel is spent on repairs and manipulating your hand of cards, and ore is spent on facility upgrades. Passive skills in the study require almost all types of resources, and the nodes you can upgrade are randomized, though you can spend more resources to change a node to something else.

Enemies can inflict debuffs on you to slow down your resource production and they will also take up tiles on the map. Worse yet, they can attack your population, causing a game over if your population is wiped out. Because of this, you may want to store up some offensive cards while lowering the enemy spawn rate in the study menu. However, you still need some enemies to show up if you want to farm money for the shop. As for the bosses, which appear every 30 weeks, they have a lot of HP, clear all your resources, and deal massive population damage, but if you win, you get to pick a powerful relic to add a strong passive for the rest of the run. 

You can gain EXP and manipulate your alignment score to evolve Fatima into her next form. I'm not sure how this affects gameplay outside of aesthetics though. I think some transformations increase the number of card slots, which can help with stockpiling offensive cards. Evolution also unlocks the game animation speed setting in the options menu, but it feels wrong to hide such a feature behind game progress.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]

7/10

Once you get a hang of the mechanics, a casual run is fairly well-balanced, though the beginning of the game will be the hardest due to your lack of EP and card slots. Towards the end, you should have so many resources and passive buffs that you actually will feel like a goddess. Unfortunately, the game doesn't have much of a story and the translation is terrible, which makes it harder to learn from the tutorials and in-game manual. Maybe this would be better as a phone game considering how the gameplay loop works.

Dragon Ruins is a 4-man-party first-person grid-based dungeon crawler, a classic genre. This one is a very simple but effective entry in it. It's fun, but beating it requires you do the same dungeons over and over again and it's too simple to make repeat explorations of dungeons any fun. This was a pretty good 5 hour game, but an entirely boring 10 hour one. I really really want to give it a thumbs up here. But I really really can't recommend going to the effort of beating it.

The biggest interesting thing this game does is that battles are entirely automatic as you explore rooms. That's neat, and I like it. However, it's in your best interest to win any fight in any room instead of skipping past it for several reasons, so what ends up happening is that map exploration is very stop-and-go: You fill out your minimap, wait for the battle to finish, step through a door, and repeat. That's basically all exploration is; there's sometimes teleporters or traps but only occasionally, and that's it. The level design itself is very good, especially the early-game dungeons. The late-game maps get to be a bit of a samey space-filling curve. This is unfortunately compounded by the fact that you have to clear each dungeon 3-5 times to get all the story there and be prepared to move on. And when I finally defeated every dungeon every time the game had to offer? Nothing. The game could use a proper ending cinematic, or at least a "you won" screen.

The graphics are lovely, although they could have maybe used some more variety in the dungeon tilesets, maybe. I loved the enemy sprites, and I dearly wished some of the enemy sprites were available as player characters (I think the lizardmen and kobolds were cute, what can I say). The sound design and music were awesome. I give the soundtrack a thumbs-up at least.

In conclusion, I'd probably give Dragon Ruins III a try if it's expanded upon yet again. For a threequel, I'd hope they fix up some of the crust around game mechanics, throw away the concept of re-doing dungeons, add secrets to find or at least add more exciting interactable things on the maps, and figure out how to fix the stop-and-go combat problem that slowed down the game. A really cool core of a really cool game is here, and I'd like to see this stylish and simple-yet-effective game come into its own. A dragon can dream.

As a streamer and a longtime fan of alien-themed games, I was excited to dive into Last Sighting. The trailer promised an intriguing, suspenseful experience, but sadly, the actual gameplay was a major letdown. Here are the main issues that stood out to me:

Animations and Alien Interactions: The alien encounters are underwhelming and lack creativity. A single touch from the alien results in instant death, removing any chance for tension or strategy. The animations feel rushed and uninspired, failing to immerse the player in what could have been a thrilling experience.

Gameplay Mechanics: The stamina system is poorly implemented, depleting so quickly that it becomes more of a hindrance than a challenge. This severely limits exploration and interrupts the flow of gameplay. On top of that, the objectives are unclear, leaving players wandering around trying to figure out what to do next.

Audio and Voiceovers: The voiceovers frequently overlap, creating a chaotic and distracting experience. This feels like an oversight that could have been addressed with better testing and polish.

Graphics and Movement: The visuals are clunky, with environments that feel generic and unfinished. Character movement is awkward and unresponsive, which only adds to the frustration.

The best part of Last Sighting was, unfortunately, the trailer. It painted a picture of a game full of suspense and excitement, but the actual product fell far short. While the concept has a lot of potential, the execution feels rushed and incomplete.

As a fan of this genre, I truly wanted to enjoy this game, but it left me disappointed. It’s a shame, as with more care and attention, this could have been a standout experience. I will be requesting a refund, and I sincerely hope the developers address these issues to create the game that the trailer promised. pew pew.

[h1] Bottom line: [/h1]

This game has a very interesting premise, and a unique setting with a lot of potential, however, it is rough around the edges. Some small improvements to the User interface and a bit of polish could really make this game stand out.
As it stands, I like what I have played so far, and I am interested to see where it goes. 
Currently, at around $7, I think it is worth the price. 

[h2] Full review and feedback: [/h2]

The Basic Gameplay is as follows: 
You Travel between port towns and fish along the way. 
Once you dock you have several options:
You can sell your catch, buy supplies, upgrade your craft, hire sailors etc. 
You can also run small Sushi restaurant, hire cooks, serve customers, etc. 
Then you travel to the next town and repeat the process. 

It plays a bit like if you took the Sushi restaurant idea in Dave the Diver, but replaced the Diving mechanic with the Fishing in Dredge. Then stripped the them both down to just their core concepts.

Neither the Sushi restaurant, nor the Fishing are very complex, but the basic gameplay loop is simple enough to understand, and I think there is a lot of potential here.
The core concepts also leave a lot of room for future updates (New Fish, New Items, New Lures, Boat Upgrades, and so on).

[h2] Pros and Cons: [/h2]

[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Unique Setting (Place: Somewhere between what appears to be Korea and Japan. Time: Somewhere a few hundred years ago) 

[*] The Pixel Art looks nice and fits the setting.

[*] All the characters are cats, which gives the game a fun fantasy feeling.

[*] The combination of Fishing and Running a restaurant (restaurants plural?) is a fun and easy to understand concept, which reminds me a bit of Dave the Diver at a very very basic level.

[*] If the UI was made easier to understand, there is a lot of room to expand on the core concepts with (new fish, new items, new sushi dishes, new fishing rods, new crew, new cooks, new boat upgrades, and so on)

[*] This game was made by a Solo Developer, which is difficult enough, but they are also facing some absurdly difficult personal challenges (Just look at the Developer's Profile) and still managed to release a rather unique game. That is to be commended. 
[/list]

[b] Cons: [/b]
[list]

[*] There is NO Fishing Minigame. Fishing is performed simply by clicking the water repeatedly. 
There is NOT a mini game like in Dredge, or Stardew valley, or numerous other games. 
I think adding anything besides "click on water to Instantly get fish" would improve this game greatly. 

[*] The User Interface is a bit confusing. I understand the (+) Icon's are there to indicate what you can click on, but its not always intuitive what each thing does. Sometimes it opens a door, sometimes, it does nothing.

[*] Why when I have 6 fish in my ship can I not give them to the Chef who cooks that specific type of fish?

[*] Rowing seems automatic, I don't know what the power bar does or indicates beyond your speed, which you can't really control. 

[*] The Clock just tells the time. It does not appear to allow you to pause to look at the various menus, or to speed up the game at all. It is also not very clear what the different times mean. 
For Example: Does the restaurant close at 8pm? Can you only go fishing between 9am and 9pm? Who knows? The game doesn't really tell you. 
Without that information the clock isn't particularly helpful. 

[*] It took me a while to figure out how to sail to the next town. The first few times I sent the Ship "Sailing" and then I was stuck looking at the town with nothing to do, and no idea how to exit. Apparently you can launch the ship and have it run automatically? This wasn't entirely clear. I had to manually override the ship so that I could see the ship set sail. 

[*] Why do I have to pay money to spin a roulette wheel to Hire a Sushi Chef? But there's no minigame when it comes to the actual fishing? This seems strange to me.


These are all relatively minor complaints, but together they make it tricky to understand the User interface. 

The small guide helps a lot to improve understanding, however it appears that this was translated from another language, and could benefit from further review.

[b] Overall: An interesting game with a lot of potential. [/b]

This is a stunning masterpiece, where I would really have to try hard to come up with any ideas how to actually make it better. And maybe I would not come up with anything really.

The way how it is, is perfect actually. Perfect for me of course, I can understand that some fans actually managed to create their own "obsession" as much as some of our beloved characters in this piece - about a perfect ending or closure for this series, and then they got a bit frustrated, that the actual result differ from their expectation. I gotta admit, even I did not expect this turn of events regarding the Toko's daughter, but the way it's been handled seemed natural in the end, and probably it was the best possible outcome for all parties concerned. The characters got long awaited closure, as so did we, the readers.

When you finish the Last Episode (True ending or at least a Grand one), it's time to stay on the balcony during a nice chilly night and watch the stars in calm fashion for a while. That's how getting a closure in this trilogy feels - you will get some piece of mind and you will want to savor that moment for a bit.

I will try to pinpoint main pros and cons as I do in most of my reviews, however I am not sure if I can even come up with any cons for real.

Pros:

I read the "Shell" version on steam, so I did not actually read the original Kara no Shojo 3, thus I cannot compare the level of polishness between the two, however the steam version is extremely well polished. In comparison to KnS 1, where some misclicking during investigation could get you to a bad end etc., this version felt extremely well made. Map serves only for some fun interaction's now mostly, it's not tied to any important story flags. However the investigation decisions and conclusions now feel finally more "detective-like" for the first time in kns series I actually felt like you are doing some detective work a bit at least. Like you actually needed to use your head now and then. It's like during making this last piece Innocent Grey really matured and unraveled their full potential in every way - art, narration, gameplay, welp even the sex scenes matured.

Yes you heard me right. That's how a modern day vn should handle a sex scene. Just a bunch of CGs with a short text depicting smal details about the act, a bit of rugged breathing and possibly a small music emphasis to narrate the scene in either romantic direction or more erotic one. That's it, no stupid porn talk, no bullshit, no need to skip 30 minutes of degenerated nonsense.

It's probably tied to the main visible aspect of this vn and that's the heavy emphasis on art. KnS trilogy was always leaning in this direction, by having an artistic background for many characters or even murders, it's CGs, characters sprites and menu visuals were always one of the best in the visual novel field, at least for my taste, as that's always a bit subjective. But it always portrayed the world in a certain artsy, yet adult and slighty grim looking way. In the Last Episode, that art touch flowered fully and absolutely peaked. Characters sprites, the CGs, the paintings - everything looks almost like from a fairy tale. It feels handmade, like when a master artist just make a few strokes and suddenly you are looking at a masterfully made CG background, or well portraited character. I cannot stress enough how much I enjoyed going through this vn just within the visual aspects alone. It's overfowing with quality art, literally. From now on, all other visual novels will look like garbage, like a bunch of drunk high schoolers made them.

Narration and voice acting is great as always. There is no one so distinctive like Toko anymore (maybe Chie? Stella is also still pretty lit), however all characters are extremely well portrayed.

It felt to me that the story returned to it's roots within the KnS 1 a little bit. The vibe from the crime scenes felt more similar to it than in the second piece, intertwined neatly with the time jumps and different cases, just so all various branches can come together in the end to be closed. Some characters like Yaginuma got portraited in a more serious manner and the chemistry between all of them is pretty strong after the trilogy (basically tetralogy if you include Cartagra as well). I loved even the little jokes in the note here and there (about Uozumi's car for example).

Music was also perfected to fit the atmosphere. It's made in a way, that you know the tune from the previous titles, yet again it feels more matured, more artsy and more elegant.

To sum it up, I had almost no expectation from the third part, and was pleasantly surprised, how neatly it was made. I truly cannot find much to complain about. Also I liked how you uncovered always a bit of new information about the background of the crimes with each new playthrough up to third. I think you need 4 to 100% the game.

Possible small cons:

My elementary and middle school aged kids have played the JS version on tablets for hours as well, and this served as a very accessible introduction to rogue-like games for them. Limited number of choices, but lots of little decisions that influence the outcome of battles kept them engaged and understanding the core mechanics.

As with other rogue-like games, the fun is getting to know the meta and what to expect for power-ups and events, and using them to squeak-by and stay alive long enough to get some delightfully broken, or over-powered combos, and then decimate opponents ships, even passed the end of the game. (With the Bribe ability back on v1.0.3, my daughter first got passed level "infinity + 30" once and loved it).


On v1.1.6 I was able to get to over level "infinity + 185" dealing 1150+ damage per shot, but my son used the mouses scroll wheel and when the main choice buttons in the bottom right disappeared we couldn't figure out how to play anymore and had to throw the game. Later we figured out that hitting Enter brought them back.

Feedback to Antti on improvements to keep me coming back for more:
- Obviously, keep fixing bugs as you find them. This is not to say the game feels buggy at this point, I mean, I put the game under heavy strain in my  "infinity + 185" run and it kept functioning, which was amazing in itself! But there are some weird things that happen sometimes that probably come down to the order of the resolution. One small example, when you have a special "make another dice plated" and you click it, it sometimes re-plates one that was already plated.
- Clarify what Tinkerer abilities do and don't effect plated dice. "Cargo" sometimes seems to include plated dice and sometimes does not.
- Add make the end-game more worthwhile by adding some sort of unlock features, e.g., beating "infinity + 10" let's you chose a special hat at the start of a run which changes a core game mechanic, (off the top of my head) like every shot makes your dice pips go up in number, but when they would "go up" from 9 they instead pop and are destroyed.
- Excellent game, keep it up!

This came through my discovery queue as so many games do, and something made me stop and buy this one. And boy am I glad I did. This is the most enjoyably uncomfortable I have been in a game in a long time. Please stop reading the review and go buy this, some games have a sticker price that promises a lot, gameplay, puzzles, action and all the other usual suspects but not enough have you feeling something at the end, like right here. You can put a price on a game, but not how it makes you feel after playing and ten bucks is downright a steal for the amount of thinking it gives you to do. The value of some games come from when you're playing it, and for the lucky few (like right here man, go buy the damn game) the value comes from how long you think about it after. 

Sure, graphically it's a little same-y through the levels but have 𝙮𝙤𝙪 tried making a game? It's damn hard, and for every thirty unity asset flip all you can slop buffets out there, there's games like this, that leave you feeling like games as a medium still has some legs to it. I felt like a rat in a maze trying to comprehend the idea of cheese, and god damn was I scurrying around.

While the graphics are simple, the atmosphere it creates is genuinely fantastic, I've felt less dread playing big budget horror games that cost six times this price, and the simplicity really works with it, sometimes less is more and that's exactly what's going on here. The level design and general gameplay clearly draws inspiration from classic valve games a-la portal and the original half life, overlord poking fun at you and vent-crawling included.

The combat obviously isn't groundbreaking, (you did watch the trailer, right?) you're not going to snap your wrists off like it's a twitch shooter and you won't be slinging bullets like it's going out of style like in more modern boomer shooter-esque games, but it's engaging and fun and I don't think you could ask for anything else, there's a decent variety of enemies and enough weapons to not get sick of any as you go.

The soundtrack is sparse and saved for combat and setpeices, and using it like that adds to the previously mentioned atmosphere tenfold, no audio bugs or glitches either.

The controls are simple enough that you could probably play with one hand (hey, no judgement here) and you could probably run it on your smart fridge if you really wanted to.

I genuinely appreciate the effort behind OpenDraft, especially since it's rare to find software that offers offline privacy and no subscription model. However, in its current state, it doesn’t quite meet the needs for effective use, and I found myself returning to Masterplan, even though it’s no longer in development.

Here are some areas where I struggled:

- The overall controls aren’t intuitive. There are no shortcuts, and while the radial menu shows a symbol for the space key, pressing space doesn’t open it. Most functions are represented by pictograms, but some are misleading or too cryptic to understand.

- Textboxes are quite limited: they don’t have headers, can’t be resized, and only have one font that wasn’t to my taste. Additionally, I couldn’t open a second textbox despite following the pictogram’s instructions.

- Checkboxes are also restrictive since they can’t be resized. This limits text to about 20 characters per line, which felt very limiting.

- Navigating the canvas is cumbersome. When typing in a textbox, you can’t pan the canvas unless you switch back to the standard cursor, which has no shortcut.

- I couldn’t insert images, whether by Ctrl+V (as suggested by the pictogram), drag and drop, or even by clicking with the image cursor. Nothing worked.

- The drawing feature allows color selection, but erasing is limited to removing entire lines, which felt inconvenient.

- The grid feels impractical. The lines are too thick, and the textboxes don’t fit within the grid spaces - they overlap and don’t snap to the grid.

- I also didn’t quite understand the ambient sounds feature. Personally, if I want background noise or music, I’d prefer using YouTube or Spotify for more variety. However, that might just be my preference.

I really wanted to like OpenDraft, but it currently lacks too many basic features, and the existing ones felt a bit unpolished. In comparison, OpenDraft hindered my productivity rather than enhancing it. Although I appreciate the developer's effort and vision, I’ll be requesting a refund. At this point, I don’t have high hopes that the software will evolve to a point where I’d consider using it in the future, but I wish the developer all the best.
