[h1]Mega Bunny X [Eng and Pt-Br review][/h1]
Code Bunny is a small action game that should please anyone looking for a Mega Man-style game.
The game, however, has a more Gunvolt-like feel, as it has a scoring system based on maintaining a chain of hits, avoiding taking damage, not dying and finishing the stages as quickly as possible. Personally, I think this Gunvolt-like system is really cool and a real evolution of the classic Mega Man, as it allows the game to be played casually, if that's what the player wants, since the continues are infinite, or the person can focus on trying to get an S score in all the stages, thus increasing the replay factor.
Speaking of the replay factor, Code Bunny is interesting in this regard because it offers two playable characters, again, more similar to Gunvolt and his spin-off, Hazel whose weapon is used to mark enemies and then uses a type of insta dash attack (also used for more dynamic movement through the stages) and Axel who literally spins and bounces between enemies, a mechanic that I personally had never seen in any game. Here's a tip: try to start playing with Hazel, her gameplay is more intuitive and easy to pick up, but don't forget to check out Axel too, his gameplay is very dynamic and fun (but I also think it's more challenging).
The game is relatively easy, I believe that even the most casual players will play it focusing on at least maintaining a relatively high rank, much of the gameplay is focused on completing the stage quickly (similar to the Sonic games), which is quite fun given the game's mechanics. At the end there is always a boss, which are also easy, except for the last ones where the challenge increases a lot but they are still fair fights and not at all impossible.
The game's visuals are somewhat simplistic, but full of charisma, it may seem strange at first, but it is certainly one of the game's positive points. Each stage presents a new mechanic and tends to focus on it, but personally, I found the stages a bit short, the game itself is a bit short, but that's not a problem because the game is very fun and never gets boring and ends the plot perfectly. The plot was very well done, each character has a lot of charisma, the game's universe is very well developed and the conversations are pretty good. I would even say that the plot was too heavy and long for a game of this type, but that just shows how much the developer loves and dedicated himself to making the game.
[b][u]In the end, Code Bunny is a simple but very fluid game, with well-developed visuals, characters and mechanics that I recommend to all fans of Mega Man-style games.[/u][/b]

This game is quite the short and sweet experience. There's two different characters to play as; Hazel and Axel. Both characters play quite differently from each other despite playing through the same stages, and both characters have their own stories to go through, which I will not be spoiling here. It doesn't really matter in what order you go through the story; you could play as one character and then the other, or play through a stage with one and then play through it with the other, or whatever feels right to you.

Hazel's playstyle feels sort of like a cross between Kirin from Azure Striker Gunvolt 3 and Fox from Super Smash Bros. You have an MMZ style triple slash, but instead of having a dash or projectile weapon you have a projectile that tags enemies with lock on reticles which you can then zip over to for a rapid attack. The projectile isn't very spammable but you can tag multiple targets and as far as I can tell you will zip to them in the order you tagged them. You also have a parry move which allows you to both attack and avoid damage with good timing, and it can even tag enemies for you. Keep in mind that she has a karma system however, the more karma you build up the more damage you will take from enemies. Getting good with her is intensely satisfying, but she's also the more difficult character to do combat with.

The other character, Axel, feels like a cross between Sonic and Mega Man Zero. He's a much faster character who can spin to attack enemies and bounce off them and he can even do a sort of air dash move to cover distances. As long as you are spinning you won't be taking damage from enemies but be careful because Axel has a hard time maintaining spin on the ground and in most circumstances has a much harder time maintaining air time than Hazel.

It takes about an hour and a half to beat the story of one of the characters, so about 3 hours total to completely beat the story. There's also a sort of classic mode that allows you to play through without the story scenes, as well as a speedrunning mode. Because the game is so short, the difficulty picks up quite rapidly. Early stages will feel like a cakewalk and then not long after you are expected to have mastered your current character more thoroughly. Depending on how quick you are to learn, this may or may not be much of an issue for you to adapt to, however do not worry about it too much. You can retry as much as you need to until you succeed, so treat failures similarly to how you would in Hotline Miami; learn from your mistakes until you succeed rather than fretting over every failure. The game is very much designed around getting you back into the action as smoothly as possible after failure to make this as little jarring as possible.

As of the time of me writing this review the highest screen resolution setting as far as I'm aware is 1080p. If you have a screen with a larger resolution than this, I'd recommend using a program such as Lossless Scaling or something similar to play in fullscreen without blurry visuals. Aside from this, I've not had any gripes with performance, nor have I encountered any bugs or glitches.

This game is far from perfect, but certainly charming in its own way. Having two playable characters with a slightly different story certainly make replaying levels a bit more interesting, although I personally don't like Axel as much as Hazel due his weird energy system, which probably rewards playing competently while speed-running, but in a more casual playthough, using his abilities feels unreliable. Other than that though, the experience is pretty enjoyable, even if short.

Did 4 playthroughs total, 2 for each character, then S+'d bosses for both. The character mechanics are cool, and I can tell that the devs took inspiration from the Gunvolt or other Inti Creates games by combining movement and attacking (apparently they had Hazel's Ghost Crescent in the works before Kirin's Arc Chain was ever revealed, so that's a crazy coincidence). Ultimately I feel kinda midling on this. Playing it casually, it feels like nothing in the stages poses a real threat, bosses can be brute-forced into an S rank way too easily without really learning the boss, and the stages themselves are incredibly short. I feel like story cutscenes took up 3x more length than the actual gameplay, so my story mode runs left me feeling disappointed since the story itself didn't quite catch me.

Going for S+ rank stage runs where you can't get hit is probably where this game truly shines. Suddenly the short stage lengths are a blessing, and you start noticing how intricate the enemy placements are for getting you onto routes that'll get you to the goal quicker while giving you just enough time to find another enemy to keep your combo going, while learning what mechanics even give you a combo bonus. S+'ing bosses still didn't take too much practice since you have easy access to Armor and iFrames, so instead of "Where do I position myself to avoid this attack" it was "I just need to have a Tag/EX Gauge available", thus that itch for something more challenging still didn't really get scratched for me. The game is very much fine for what it does, I just wish there was some more meat to it before trying to hit the highest ranks, so I'd be down for whatever these devs have planned for the future.

CODE:Bunny is a fun and fast-paced action platformer with two main characters, Axel and Hazel, both of whom have very diverse and unique skillsets. I recommend starting with Axel as his kit makes the first-playthrough experience much easier, compared to Hazel, who is also very fun to play but her abilities and fighting style are a lot harder to master.

The game is relatively short, with there only being around 6 stages and an equal number of bosses. The stages are largely the same for both characters, with some differentiation in enemy placements to allow for the different ways both characters traverse levels. This would be a shame but there is enough replayability in going for S ranks on all of the stages and bosses, especially when looked at from a speedrunning perspective, which the game very kindly caters to with a dedicated speedrunning mode. The developers knew that this game will make for a gem of a speedrun experience for the people who take the time to dedicate to it.

It goes without saying that all of the art and spritework in this game is gorgeous, and all of the character designs are cute and endearing. There is also a story mode which adds more context for each of the stages, bosses and main characters which is great for people who want to enjoy more of the game's world and enjoy it at their own pace, rather than blitzing through the stages without the cutscenes in classic mode.

Overall very fun and enjoyable experience in a neat little package. Can't go wrong for the price on this one, especially if you're into platformers with cute art.

Hazel is sort of like Kirin from Gunvolt 3, with a similar mark & warp attack mechanic, albeit one which isn't used in the same way; here, you have an attack combo timer which depletes over time, and your aim is to get above the specified combo number at some point in the level while also finishing in the required time and avoiding taking hits or dying. The warp attack has forced momentum that takes a little getting used to, and will probably lead to you falling to your death or taking hits at first because it feels unintuitive. She also has a downwards attack in the air, which you will probably get used to using after every warp attack to get a second hit, and which raises you upwards you on a successful hit. Anyway, she's pretty fun, and it's very easy to get the S+ ranks for her.

Axel is more difficult. You can press a button to spin, which instantly gives you a speed boost and increases your momentum potential while in the state, while turning you into a moving hitbox. Unfortunately, I'm not so keen on his gameplay. I feel that the spin attack needs some work. For a start, there should be more feedback for when you are entering and exiting the spin state, and for while you are in the spin state too. The spin serves a platforming purpose, since its function of boosting your horizontal velocity is sort of dash-like, but if you are already in the spin state hitting the button only takes you out of the state; I would probably make the action of the spin button consistently boost your horizontal velocity (if your current horizontal velocity is below the boost amount) and activate the spin state, while finding some other input or mechanism for the player to exit the spin state. Additionally, the jump animation outside of the spin state is basically a slow version of the spin state animation, which is visually confusing.

The script is quite overbearing and you will probably end up skipping a lot of text. You could play it in the classic mode, without the story, but most people will be naturally inclined to see the story first, even if they end up skipping through it.

Later in the game on Axel's route, there is a boss with a special method of victory. It's very, very stupid, I'll just say that much. Have fun trying to figure it out until you get so frustrated you want to quit the game.

A few other minor criticisms:

- Action feedback could be a little greater, imo – the basic attack combos feel a little weak;
- Foreground and close background elements in the final level are too similar in colour & brightness;
- Levels and bosses have separate ranks, but only the level rank is displayed anywhere as far as I can tell, even when you fight the bosses on their own dedicated missions;
- Par time for levels should probably match precision with the player's time for clarity; and
- The fullscreen option in the display mode setting menu will display "Attack" instead, for some reason. (This is a silly, very minor thing, but it's a bug nonetheless.)

The game's length is short, but it's a fun way to spend a few hours and I don't regret buying it. Hazel's half is enjoyable and scratches an itch. I'd probably more readily recommend it if the price was lower, or if Axel felt better to play.

I say this because the level designs are very... hallway-like. That's the best way to explain it.  Levels can have gimmicks, but there isn't really enough to help them stand out. Finally got around to writing another review, hopefully I do this game justice, because I've been following it for quite some time before Steam release and have been impressed with what I had seen.
Basically, Code Bunny is one of many platformers you see everywhere, and for just 10 dollars, you get to play as two characters, extending the playtime to several hours on your first playthrough. And for those who are into score and time attacking, the game has a ranking system (from C to S+) and a speedrun mode, which you can sink your teeth into for extra playtime. When it comes to characters, we have:
- Axel: the technical of the two. Uses skating to navigate stages and defeat enemies. There's the standard combo attack, but you'll be often using the spin skill to bounce off enemies and fill your special gauge, which can either negate incoming damage or be used for special moves. Axel is difficult to master, but I still had some fun with him on my blind playthrough.
- Hazel: the execution master? If anyone here is familiar with Azure Striker Gunvolt 3, Hazel operates in a very similar manner to Kirin. You use your projectiles to mark enemies so you can teleport and slash them in proximity. Instead of the special gauge, Hazel has the Karma gauge, which builds up points as you deal damage to enemies and perform specific actions. If the Karma gauge depletes due to not hitting enemies long enough, your points deplete and start to affect Hazel's HP bar, making her more susceptible to incoming attacks, potentially oneshotting her, so you have to be both quick and careful when chaining enemies. Gameplay wise certainly a lot easier to master than Axel.
When it comes to cons, there's several odd moments I've encountered as Axel, namely that his spinning in the air sometimes goes too much out of control, or that it's practically impossible to reel him in the other direction if the situation calls for it, resulting in a decent chunk of deaths. Second to last stage has the teleporting hat gimmick that sometimes doesn't give you the necessary momentum to cross gaps or gain enough altitude to progress. I've also found the last stage to have an issue with checkpoint placement + the difficulty of distinguishing between solid tiles and background ones.
A few of the pros are the catchy chiptune soundtrack and pretty amazing stage pixel art. Having the option to converse with the other characters in-between missions also helps to break up the action into more manageable pieces.
Normally I'd try to avoid bashing another non-related game to praise the game I'm reviewing, but I feel like it needs to be said. Inti for me recently has been a huge mess in terms of their titles, and their most recent one, Divine Dynamo Flamefrit, is a major stinkeye for 7 dollars, considering you get at best 40 minutes of gameplay across 3 stages, with zero incentive to replay or buy the game separately from the Card-en-Ciel bundle. Meanwhile Code Bunny, for a first game from its developers, has done a pretty good job at providing enough grub for its price. 7.5/10 rating seems like a solid choice for me.

I can't tell you how many times I just avoided the "action" part of this action platformer, because of the Karma system in it. And then, on the bosses - unless you clear them perfectly - you're punished for doing well with how the Karma system makes it to where they can one-hit kill you if you slip up at the last second despite doing damn near perfect.

I've played through a ton of challenging action platformers before. Castlevania, Megaman, Ninja Gaiden, just to name a few. But those games kept me going, because there was a reward for doing well. This game? I quit, because I was tired of being punished by the game for doing well.

This is a thumbs up because I want the developer to keep trying. I think there's a good foundation here. That said, did I enjoy Code Bunny? No.

Code Bunny has two campaigns, each about an hour long, and each with different movement. They follow a lot of Zero / Sonic fundamentals, except for where they drop those fundamentals off a cliff. There's a plot, and the plot is... okay? It didn't feel better or worse than any other retro platformer, but it didn't feel like anything new either, and the short runtime *really* keeps the characters from getting much development.

The character I played, Axel, is like Sonic but unbalanced. His spindash makes him fully invincible, and it has only a fraction of endlag on landing, so you can just spindash into spindash and be a perpetual hurtbox made of immunity. Axel also regens health off of combos and can buffer a shield, in case being immune to all damage all of the time wasn't enough. For about 50 minutes of his 67 minute campaign, he is unkillable. For seventeen minutes---which is to say the final platforming stage with a bunch of random killplanes that you can't sightread, so you just have to die to them to learn that they're there---he dies every thirty seconds or so as you repeat the same sequence over and over again. The difficulty goes from a walk in a meadow to a spider in a toiletbowl INSTANTLY, and then immediately goes back to meadow walk for the final boss fight. I wouldn't mind if the game was consistently masocore, or if this level was difficult in a way that was fun or interesting to master, but this felt wildly obnoxious. My opinion on the game went from mildly positive to actual hatred, and it's difficult to keep this review objective in light of how much that level sucks.

There's also a kind of baffling moment in Axel's campaign where, during a boss fight, the way to win is to open the pause menu and select exit. This isn't telegraphed. You're told you're not supposed to fight, and you auto lose every time you score a win, but doing intuitive stuff like getting the boss down to low health and waiting or letting the big obvious clock hands in the back of the battle arena reach a certain position does nothing. Your average player will, at this point, quit out by clicking the big X at the top of the game window, which is a victory condition in the sense that you stop playing. I'm sure the devs could've hidden the win button in the sound options menu too, but why would the player look there either?

When the game isn't wasting your time, it's fine. Decent, technical platformer. The soundtrack has all the bleeps and bloops you'd expect of something that looks like it'd run on the NES. The art's legible. The levels are bug free. The game has levels, even if there's very few of them and they're all extremely short.

I want to see more from this developer, because I think the potential to make something fantastic is definitely there. CODE Bunny wasn't it for me, but I'd definitely check out a sequel.

Edit: The Hazel campaign is better, but also it's the exact same campaign so what I'm saying here is that the game feels like it was designed for Hazel and also Axel exists. Also, with the change between campaigns being basically just dialog, the game feels microscopically short. Ten dollars is an okay price to pay for this if you want to support the devs (this is worth doing, they can't make better games / stay alive if they don't have income,) but if you just want to play something at a price that feels fair on the wallet I'd wait for an 80% off before you try this one. [h1]A Beautiful Attempt That Falls Short of Its Potential[/h1]  

[b]TL;DR[/b]  
[b]While the game’s respect for Japanese calligraphy is admirable, its tedious mechanics, lack of features, and absence of audio ambiance make it frustrating rather than meditative. It’s an affordable, passion-driven effort but feels unfinished and unenjoyable. Traditional tools or more polished alternatives would likely offer a better experience.[/b]  

[hr]  

[H2]Introduction: A Flawed Tribute to Art[/H2]  
The idea of translating the mindful, meditative process of Japanese calligraphy into a game is fascinating. The developers clearly respect the craft, and their effort to make it accessible is commendable. Unfortunately, the execution falls flat, leaving a game that is more frustrating than calming and more tedious than inspiring.  

[hr]  

[H2]Main Hiragana/Katakana Mode: A Tedious Grind[/H2]  
In the main mode, you’re presented with a massive table of characters to practice. While this setup is ambitious, it’s hindered by poorly thought-out design choices:  
- [b]Awkward Camera Controls:[/b] Constantly adjusting sliders to pan and zoom around the table interrupts the flow of practice.  
- [b]Cumbersome Brush Mechanics:[/b] You need to manually recoat brushes with ink frequently, which, while realistic, feels unnecessary and tedious.  
- [b]Slow Erasing Process:[/b] The eraser is fixed to one size, making corrections slow and meticulous. This can be particularly frustrating when trying to fix small mistakes on a crowded table of characters.  

The combination of these factors makes what should be a meditative activity feel like an exhausting chore.  

[hr]  

[H2]Single-Character Modes: Stress Over Serenity[/H2]  
The single-character practice modes offer a simpler layout with one sheet of paper per character. However, this mode has its own problems:  
- [b]Punishing Errors:[/b] If you make a mistake, you have to scrap the entire sheet and wait for a new one. This is time-consuming and discouraging, especially for beginners.  
- [b]No Forgiveness:[/b] A simple undo function or a more forgiving system for small errors would alleviate much of the frustration.  

Instead of encouraging practice and improvement, this mode amplifies the stress of getting everything perfect on the first try.  

[hr]  

[H2]Audio: A Jarring Silence[/H2]  
One of the most glaring omissions in the game is the lack of music or soothing sounds to set the mood. Calligraphy is meant to be calming, and gentle background music or nature sounds could greatly enhance the atmosphere. Instead:  
- [b]Annoying Eraser Sound:[/b] The only sound is the abrasive, grating noise of the eraser, which quickly becomes jarring and unpleasant.  
- [b]A Missed Opportunity:[/b] The absence of relaxing audio makes the experience feel lifeless and stark, detracting from any sense of immersion.  

The game feels eerily quiet in a way that doesn’t evoke calm but rather highlights its unfinished state.  

[hr]  

[H2]What It Gets Right[/H2]  
Despite its flaws, the game has a few positive qualities:  
- [b]Affordable:[/b] Its low price makes it accessible to a wide audience.  
- [b]Respect for Calligraphy:[/b] The developers clearly have a passion for Japanese calligraphy, and their respect for the art form is evident.  
- [b]Unique Concept:[/b] Few games explore such a niche topic, which makes it stand out despite its shortcomings.  

[hr]  

[H2]What It Needs to Improve[/H2]  
For the game to live up to its potential, several changes are necessary:  
- [b]Better Camera Controls:[/b] Streamline navigation in the table mode to avoid constant interruptions.  
- [b]Flexible Erasing Options:[/b] Allow players to resize the eraser or undo small mistakes for faster corrections.  
- [b]Audio Enhancements:[/b] Add relaxing background music and sound effects to create a calming atmosphere.  
- [b]Undo Functionality:[/b] Introduce a simple undo feature to reduce the frustration of restarting.  
- [b]Customization and Accessibility:[/b] Include options for brush sensitivity, fullscreen mode, and other quality-of-life improvements.  

[hr]  

[H2]Pros and Cons[/H2]  

[b]Pros:[/b]  
- Very low price.  
- A unique and creative concept.  
- Passionate homage to the art of Japanese calligraphy.  

[b]Cons:[/b]  
- Cumbersome mechanics for navigation, brushwork, and erasing.  
- Overly punishing design, especially in single-character modes.  
- Lack of audio ambiance, with only an annoying eraser sound.  
- Missing essential features like undo, sensitivity settings, and accessibility options.  

[hr]  

[H2]Conclusion: Passion Isn’t Enough[/H2]  
This game is a heartfelt attempt to bring Japanese calligraphy into the digital realm, but its lack of polish, tedious mechanics, and jarring audio make it difficult to recommend. While I respect the developers’ vision and dedication, the game feels unfinished and more frustrating than relaxing.  

For those with boundless patience and a passion for calligraphy, there may be some value here. However, for most players, traditional tools or a more polished digital alternative will provide a far better experience.  

I’m glad this project exists, but it needs significant improvement to truly capture the beauty and mindfulness of Japanese calligraphy.

Molest is a refreshing and light-hearted experience that offers a perfect escape from the pressures of daily life. Set against a soothing, soft pink backdrop, the game exudes a calming atmosphere that immediately puts players at ease. The visuals are simple yet charming, creating an inviting environment where you can lose yourself in a world of soft colors and gentle sounds.
At its core, the gameplay is intuitive and easy to pick up, yet surprisingly engaging. Medals and coins—ranging from gold and silver to diamonds—rise from the bottom of the screen, and your goal is to quickly click and collect as many as you can. The pace is fast, and with the ticking time limit, there's a delightful sense of urgency that keeps you on your toes, challenging you to maximize your score within the given time frame.
The sound design enhances the experience, with crisp, pleasant sound effects that play with each successful collection. These little auditory rewards add a layer of satisfaction and fun, making each click feel rewarding. The background melody, light and lively, complements the game’s design, helping to create a relaxed yet motivating atmosphere.
What sets Molest apart is its ability to provide a simple yet gratifying sense of achievement. Whether you’re aiming to beat your own high score or simply enjoying the rhythm of collecting items, it’s easy to get lost in the game’s endless loop of rewards and challenges. The clean interface and minimal distractions ensure that you can focus entirely on the task at hand.
For those looking for a way to unwind or enjoy a casual gaming session, Molest delivers exactly that. It’s a charming, enjoyable game that doesn’t demand too much but offers a lot in return, allowing you to relax and test your skills in an unobtrusive yet fun environment. Absolutely love it, 10/10!

A really interesting little VN with some gorgeous art. Optimal conditions for a sacrifice is a bit hard to describe, since it's a very dream-like story which doesn't really adhere to standard narrative conventions. The story is about 'you', the sacrifice, attempting to win the archfey's heart. To successfully win her heart, you need to sacrifice parts of your body to three beautiful women who live in the forest (and you need to give each woman the right body part), before the archfey will take any interest in you. The archefey is fickle, however, and it may take a while before she'll deign to speak you.

This VN doesn't really have characters in the standard sense. You only get short scenes with each forest dweller, and your interactions with them are pretty limited to them asking for parts of your body and you being able to say yes or no. One of the forest dwellers constantly asks you questions, and another only talks in fish metaphors. The only character who has any real 'characterisation' is the archfay, but most of her dialoge is just musings about the nature of love, what it means to be loved, if there exists a love which can last forever... etc, etc.

This VN itself isn't really a story, either: it mostly seems to exist, like the archfay, to ponder the nature of love, and even its own purpose for existing (there's a part in the game where one character straight up asks you "so, what do you think the point of this game is?").

If you want a story with a clear beginning, middle, and end, and some well-defined characters, this really isn't the VN for you. I don't think this is a bad thing, however, as it's not trying to tell a conventional narative. This is a short, thought-provoking work which reads more like the writer's musings on romance and relationships than anything concrete, but I like it a lot regardless; for such a short game, there's a lot to dig your teeth into, and the presentation is gorgeous. The artwork makes this well worth the price tag, imo, despite the runtime being short (I can't imagine anybody spending more than 30 minutes on this).

This might be the sort of VN which would be good to stream, since it's short while being engaging. It asks a lot from the reader (especially the naga, whose scenes have a lot of choices in them), so it would provoke some interesting discussion if any Twitch streamers or YouTubers wanted to poke around at it. It's the sort of story you can read with a larger audience, or with a friend, since it's trying to create a dialogue with the reader.

It's a very unique experience as far as VNs go, and I would easily recommend it. I hope more people will find out about this gem of a game and give it a look!

[h1]A very unique and terrifying experience! Cabins can be scary even if they are not in the woods![/h1]

[i]Your job at the Cabin Factory is simple: inspect the cabins and decide on whether they’re haunted or not. If you do find any anomalies, get out…immediately.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
You play as an old lady, Greta, who works at The Cabin Factory, which specializes in building Hyper-Realistic Horror Cabins for use in theme parks and movies. Some of the cabins are supposedly haunted, so the company hires people to inspect them, ensuring they are safe to use.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Your task is to inspect the cabins that have been built to see if they are Haunted or Clear and then sort the cabins. You are told that if anything moves within the cabin, it is haunted. Some cabins contain large anomalies and some are harder to detect, and some cabins are Clear of course. You must successfully assess 8 cabins in a row to win the game. However, there are many more anomalies than this, so keep playing again and again!

[h2]Environment & Scares[/h2]
All cabins are built the same. But the contents of the cabins vary. For example, one time you enter the cabin there may be a man sitting at the kitchen table, and the next time you enter he may be standing outside the window. This does not mean that it is haunted, only if someone or something moves from their original position of the original layout of that specific cabin. I think they have done a very good job with the variety of layouts and all the scares they contain. It is a very creepy atmosphere in this game, and I don't want to spoil any of the scares.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
The game looks really good and the people inside the cabin are very creepy. The sound design is also very good. This game is so well designed that it made the hair on my body stand up and sent shivers down my spine.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
This is a very good horror game and unlike anything I’ve played before. A very creepy experience where you have to spot the difference. The game is relatively short. It can take as little as 30 minutes to complete a round if you are quick and guess correctly every time. But to get the full scope of the game with all the anomalies you will need to play for about 2 hours. I can't really think of anything to complain about. Maybe that it would be cool with more cabins that are built differently. I strongly recommend this game!

[h2]Rating: 9/10[/h2]
Very short (what do you expect for $3?), but fun if you enjoy "spot the difference" type games. The mechanics are simple—walk around, check for signs of haunting, report.

Having played almost everything in this genre, including exit 8, platform 8, shinkansen 0, ten bells, and stairway 7;

I can confidently state that The Cabin Factory is the best of them all. 

Despite the tiny setting and slow speed, it effectively creates horror in ways that the others can't match. This is primarily thanks to its unique twist on the formula. You aren't simply trying to find anomalies, but "haunted" cabins, the difference being whether or not something moves.  Meaning that you can have cabins containing anomalies, which are still perfectly safe.

This is played to great effect, as you are constantly on the lookout not for anything out of place, but for anything moving. And this focus on mobile threat detection means you are constantly blindsided by anomalies which are interesting, enthralling, and startling. Sometimes you see an anomaly just as you go in, but you can't just turn back, because you've got to go in and see whether or not anything will move. This prevents the endless paranoia of the genre from getting boring, by letting you know something is at stake this time

Compared to other things in the genre, it also features a higher quantity of threats,that you have to maneuvre around and flee from, which are always sudden and terrifying experiences.

This is BY FAR the worst "anomaly" game I have ever played.

First, the game tells you to search each cabin for "hauntings". They describe the "hauntings" as "anything that moves inside the cabin". 

Okay, so apparently that means that, if you enter the cabin, normally you'd see a portrait of a woman, & this time, the woman in the portrait is missing & is in a different place, that isn't a haunting. 
If the man sitting at the table is gone, & is instead hovering menacingly outside of the window, not a haunting.
Everything in the cabin is stuck to the ceiling? Not a haunting.

Okay, I get that. Technically, even though those are CLEARLY HAUNTINGS, the game is saying to basically look for Poltergeist activity.

So why, then, when I go through the ENTIRE CABIN TOP TO BOTTOM, SEE NO MOVEMENT, DOES THE GAME SAY I'M WRONG FOR CLICKING "CLEAR"???

I had a theory that the game was specifically rigged against the player, so I started an experiment.

I went to the 2 buttons, Danger & Clear. 
I clicked 500 times randomly. Sometimes, I clicked one button 20 times in a row, sometimes I clicked back & forth, but you wont believe this:

What is apparently a 50/50 chance to "be right" when randomly clicking, I only clicked the correct button 30 times out of 500. 
There were times where I clicked Danger or Clear 20 times in a row & was wrong TWENTY TIMES IN A ROW. Then, as soon as I switched buttons, I would be wrong 8 more times in a row. This happened multiple times.

There is absolutely no way in any concievable situation that flipping a coin 500 times would result in 470 of those landing on Tails. 

I am 100% convinced that, even when the Cabin is "clear of movement", the game will still count it as "Danger".

There was even one time when I was teleported to the cabin on fire, literally the CABIN WAS ON FIRE, & when I clicked Danger, I was wrong. There was apparently no danger at all, even though I was literally teleported into a blazing inferno full of ghosts.

What constitutes a "haunting" is so vague & undefined, that you can literally have people disappear out of photos, have dark figures watching you from the window, have the room randomly fill with gigantic stuffed animals, hell once I was even blocked in by the ghost girl, & that STILL didn't count as a "haunting".

I did this experiment with a few friends present, & they were also baffled at the 470/500 misses, & one of those friends is a Mathematics major. He explained that, even though coins aren't technically always 50/50 odds, the odds of getting it wrong 470 out of 500 times is absolutely astronomical, & in that experiment, I was unable to ever get more than 2 correct guesses in a row. It didn't matter if I alternated, clicked the same button, randomly clicked, I was never once able to get more than 2 correct in a row. & keep in mind, there were times when I clicked TWENTY TIMES on the SAME BUTTON & was wrong TWENTY TIMES IN A ROW. So, according to the game, there were times where there were TWENTY CABINS IN A ROW that were Clear of any hauntings? or adversely, TWENTY CABINS IN A ROW that weren't clear of danger & were haunted? Bullshit. Absolute bullshit.

Oh, & one more thing: several times when entering the cabin, I would see a small diorama of the cabin itself & I would then be locked inside of the cabin. Okay. Nothing I tried would get the door to open. Every single time that happened, I would tell my friends to pay attention to what happens next: the MOMENT I approach the diorama, the screen would go red & INSTANTLY kill me. No, I don't mean "it killed me because I didn't move". I mean I touched the diorama & immediately turned & ran for the door, & didn't make it more than a single step before dying & losing my progress. Fun!

The last "anomaly" game I played, The Exit 8, was so much more user-friendly. The idea was to look for ANYTHING out of place each time you walked through, as in, if a sign was upside down, or if the man suddenly didn't have the phone he usually had, that counted as an "anomaly". How ridiculous is it that the cabin changes every single time, but the game arbitrarily decides if those changes count as "hauntings" or not? There were literally times where the cabin would be changed, I would click "Danger", & lose, then the cabin would be exactly the same way as before, but this time when I clicked "Clear", there was danger & I would lose again.

I am fully convinced, after hours of scientific research, testing, & gameplay, that this game is 100% rigged against the player, forcing them to basically take a leap of faith every single time they choose a button. Nothing is defined, anything can or wont be a "haunting", & the base area you're supposed to look for changes in was constantly changing, but those changes don't count as changes. It's maddening.

This game is absolutely horrible in every way & was a totally miserable experience.

If I could refund this game, I would. 

Do not, I repeat DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME unless you want to tear your hair out from the game constantly giving you the middle finger & trying to trick you. Whoever developed this game needs to be banned from releasing anything else after this atrocity.

That’s where I come in. It’s my job to make sure these..oddly familiar..cabins are all free from haunted entities. Creepy is fine, perfect in fact; green button. Outright bizarre? Still acceptable. Green button. The second I see something moving; red button. Haunted. Rejected. Disposed of.

I enter this particular cabin; everything seems normal. Too normal. But..that’s kind of the point. Normal is normal. I search upstairs, Hans is in his place. Back downstairs, father is..father is missing. A shadow flashes across the window as he stalks across the back of the house. I need to make it to the front door before he cuts off my escape.

I run across the cabin to the front door, father’s footsteps louder and louder on the boards outside. I slam through the front door and down the porch as his massive hand narrowly misses my shoulder. If he’d caught me, he would have killed me. My supervisors watch over me but from such a distance that they’d be mere witnesses to the carnage.

I dash over to the console and slam the red button down.
Haunted.
Reject.
Dispose.

I turn to see father’s face curled into a hateful snarl as he and the cabin are whisked away to god-knows-where.

[h2]You should know: This game has a good, compelling antagonist route.[/h2] Those aren't exactly common in this genre so if you like the sound of that, grab this game.

Overall, I found this game charming, albeit with some hit-and-miss elements. This game does a really good job of putting its [b]fun, refreshing lineup of outcasts in the spotlight.[/b] Seriously, the blind guy who cusses like a sailor is probably the most "normal" of them all. Despite their circumstances, [u]the characters are pretty believable[/u] even with the setting being primarily fantasy, and it's easy to root for them! The main leads really lean on their semi-dysfunctional teamwork to get things done, and [u]there's no melodrama.[/u] If you like your protagonist to be proactive, you're also in luck. 

The art is really varied and lively, and I think the steam page undersells some of its CGs, which tend to look nice and dynamic. There are more CGs than some full-budget titles, with attention being given to moments other game developers wouldn't have bothered with! There's also some pretty decent action scenes; I'm usually not a fan of them, but they're competently done here. Depending on your route there will be several new scenes, making it pretty replayable. Just check out how long I played the game at the top of the review!

The main downside with this title is that [u]the plot slows down/draws itself out at times, specifically during the "autumn village" section.[/u] Again, the game is pretty detailed; it gives the characters a lot of opportunities to shine and display their personalities, but maybe to a fault? Your mileage may vary, as I have a lower tolerance of slice-of-life stuff. That said, the drawn out portions are usually setting you up for the final confrontations as well as the final route, and the game does a good job at hinting that "something is wrong™". I put the game down and picked it back up later only to realize I had taken a break right as things got good.


Disclaimer: There's appropriate splashes of actual dark/horror elements here, which I found interesting. You shouldn't find it off-putting unless you're [i]really[/i] sensitive, but I figured ya'll deserve a heads up. 

This is a solid indie romance title and while imo it isn't in my top 3, [b]I do think this game is memorable and worth buying. Especially if you're already familiar with indie titles in this genre![/b]

If you like the idea of a troupe of goofy misfits experiencing a "hero's journey" type story with a rewarding final route, and you are willing to put up with a (on the surface) generic world setting with lopsided (but worthwhile) pacing, grab it. The final route is worth the price alone.

Goo Goo Grapplers is my game of the year, and here's why:

Narrative:

Johnson Grappler's story of redemption is second perhaps only to Arthur Morgan's. During the ~60 hour campaign, you truly get to know Mr. Grappler not only as a Goo Goo Grappler, but as a father, husband, and capable desperado with a heart of gold. The segment in which he faces off against Dark Grappler, his evil alter-ego born of his distorted desires that manifested during the Tangiers crisis of 1969, in which he lost his long-time partner to a gang of renegade radical Jainists, is an unbelievable story beat that seems capable of only coming from the minds of legends like JRR Tolkien or Kentaro Miura. Yet it was neither of these literary geniuses who blessed us with such palpable and moving fiction. It was Both Good Productions. I highly recommend choosing the neutral-good ending, at least for your first playthrough. I'm currently working on the pure good ending, and I'm not sure if I can bring myself to ever finish any of the evil endings. Samuel L. Jackson's performance as Hytham Grappleton is quite gripping as well.


Graphics:

The 16-bit art style harkens back to classics such as Super Metroid and Drilldozer. The thematically rich environments are incredibly immersive, and almost make you forget you're looking at pixel art with the amount of detail on display.

Gameplay:

The campaign offers a good demonstration of what fun there is to be had, but the mechanics really shine through in multiplayer. Movement is challenging yet responsive. Power-ups are useful yet require apt skill. But most crucially, the gameplay is easy to learn, yet hard to master. The best type of game there is.

Sound / Music:

Featuring an original score by John Williams in collaboration with Caused By Carelessness (Who still owe me a physical copy of their album "Get Better"), the only games I can think of with a better soundtrack would be Super Smash Bros. and Guitar Hero 3. [b] 2025/01/18 EDIT: [/b] I am changing this to a positive review, although I have several critiques of the game. However, I don't want the negative review to affect the sales of a solo dev indie game that is clearly a labor of love and has a lot of care put into it.

[u] Original Review: [/u]

I really want to give this a positive review because it has so much potential, but it is pretty hard to justify a positive review 5 hours into the game. I am currently at Level 11 and can see the upgrades up until Level 14 so my review is based on all upgrades that are currently visible to me.

Positives:
+ Interesting concept
+ Cute pixel art
+ Relaxing Music
+ Kitties at Level 10 are cute
+ Really promising game with a lot of potential, but falls a bit short in execution.

Negatives:
- Not a "fully idle" game like the description claims. There is ZERO automation. You still have to manually restock and the restocking cycle is dependent on how advanced the level of items you sell are.
- No functionality to auto purchase items, autocraft, or make these features less tedious to complete.
- Advanced equipment crafting is a pain to navigate. Rather than listing every variation of an equipment (eg, +1, +2, +3, +4) in the same list, it would make more sense to be able to set the Enhancement level on each equipment type itself (eg, Copper, Iron, etc) or add collapsible submenus for Advanced crafting.
- The % crafting chance for advanced equipment, even with upgrades is abysmal and there is no incentive to pursue this if you really want to idle since you also have to manually craft everything with a fairly high percent fail rate for higher tier upgrades.
- Material vending machines are interesting as a concept, but falls a bit short since it is heavily reliant on the kitties you send on explorations. 

Issues:
- Cannot rescale window when dragged to a secondary monitor, the drop down just completely disappears. You have to drag it back to your primary monitor to rescale it.
- Smallest you can rescale the window to is 1176 x 664. This may not be an issue for some, but on a 27" vertical secondary monitor, part of the smallest resolution window clips into my primary monitor.

There are a lot of interesting or promising ideas presented in the game, but the execution does not feel fuly thought out. If some of these items get updated in the future, I would be happy to revisit the game and change my review.

I had been following the creation of this game for a few years, since the Oric was the first computer I own (at 4!) and seeing what this was set to achieve on such a humble machine was enough for me to buy the game.
Still, I expected not to like it: I had never heard of the original game (a bad omen) and well, this would just be an early text adventure game, just with added graphics.

But I was wrong, the game is good and it is fun! Not goofy fun like Monkey Island but fun because of the game design - and that I'm not sure was the same in the original game.

The fact a game is capped at 2 hours is actually genius. You know you will probably not play more than 2 hours so you can plan for it, and when you see the time running out you are forced to think quicker and try out things out of despair.

The achievements - which I normally hate - are somewhat meaningful here since they do add some replay value (I'm still missing some so I'm not done with the game) and when you fail (cause you will) but realize you've collect some new ones, it feels like a proper reward.

The score is also a nice thing to have, and it's complete with an old-school high score screen (I guess we say "leader board" nowadays). It's a good enough reason to keep searching for things to unlock even when you feel it might not relate to the intrigue.

Which is another nice thing about the game, even though the scenes are limited, there are extra and at times useless interactions that actually bring a bit of life to the environment, and all this has a written or illustrated response - a luxury given the system.

So yeah, if you had an Oric, go for it, if you like text adventure games, go for it, if you have a thing for point & click adventure - which the game is not - I'd suggest you go for it anyway because you may enjoy this different brand of adventure more than you think.

My thumbs-up comes with a lot of caveats as I'll get into, but overall, this re-release does its job of providing a functional game and extras along with it. However, I find the page's claim that the bugs have been fixed to be suspect since this version has crashed and freezed on me a little more often than the emulated version I played a few years ago, and I've got the same setup and I'm following the same steps as I did before. From what I've played so far, it hasn't been too bad yet, but I would definitely recommend saving your progress very frequently, and don't forget to make multiple saves cause it's possible to softlock yourself if you go the wrong way. The audio mixing is still pretty awful, but since the source code was lost long ago, it's understandable that they seem to have been unable to go in and make changes or provide subtitles. 
As for the extras, they range from pretty cool to shouldn't be here. One extra in particular, the game guide, was blatantly plagiarized from an old walkthrough of DG from the website Balmoral Software, and I was hoping the Steam version would remove it, but they didn't. I didn't even see an acknowledgement of Balmoral in the guide itself or in the readme document. If only Epic Games Store would let you review games, then I would've mentioned it on that page. I think it's pretty scummy to plagiarize something so much, and the funny thing is one of the biggest changes the "new" guide makes besides the presentation is removing any instances of the guy who wrote the Balmoral walkthrough insulting DG. 
Otherwise, the extras are pretty good, though I think there could have been a little more done with them. The "art book" is rather short with a lot of filler text that doesn't directly have to do with the game. The strange thing is that I know there's more artwork out there that could have been put in here, but for reasons I've never been able to find out, these have never been made public yet. The artwork that IS in the book is very nice, though. 
The original manual has been included, which is nice since it could be hard to track down a scan of it before. The two best extras are the original pitch document that gives more insight into the beginnings of the game's development and includes more art that helps make up for the "art book"'s slack, and extensive notes from Harry Horse himself about Diary of a Plagiarist, the volumes he wrote in the 80's that were the genesis of Drowned God's story. It's very good to have these notes because it's probably the most amount of information we'll ever get about Diary of a Plagiarist, since Harry was never able to get the books back.
In all, if you're interested enough in Drowned God's story that you would like to see these extras, then by all means, get this version, especially since it's a lot cheaper than the Epic version which still charges 25 bucks. However, if you don't particularly care about learning any behind-the-scenes stuff, then you could probably skip getting this version.

Paranormal Night Shift may be the best Observation Duty-like game I've ever seen, and I've seen dozens. It treads new ground in the genre, introducing features that have been sorely lacking elsewhere. 

The mechanics are simple and fluid, requiring you to click anomalies instead of fumbling through a clunky interface like most games in the genre. The framing story is engaging and fun, which is especially notable in a predominantly story-free genre. The "big" anomalies are vitally tied to the location and lore, not just random weirdness. When anomalies have built up to the point of near-failure, the game actually gives you clear indication that you need to get your butt in gear. Instead of the locations remaining identical throughout the story, they subtly change each night, introducing a different but realistic challenge. On occasion, the gameplay even gets a pleasantly surprising changeup.

Oh, and it's scary as heck.

That said, though, it's difficult. Some anomalies seem a little too tricky, such as when a small item changes color. Apart from that, though, the only criticism I have is that I wish there were more locations, to extend this delightful experience.

Full disclosure: I am absolutely terrible at games like this, but I love watching streamers play them. I primarily bought Paranormal Night Shift to support the developer and to be able to recommend it, because it certainly deserves to be one of the stars of the Observation Duty genre.

I'm pretty surprised this game isn't picking up much traction yet. The price probably has a lot to do with it. I don't think most people are really willing to risk spending over $10 on an indie horror game that isn't either really hyped, has positive reviews, or is from a dev with a proven track record. I took the risk though, and I'm happy I did. This was quite enjoyable. It had a decent story, and had a pretty creepy aesthetic most of the time. It took me almost 4 hours to complete, but I was goofing off streaming at the same time, so it could be beaten quite a bit faster I'd imagine. I did have a few issues. I got stuck where I wasn't supposed to be a few times. One of those times I had to restart from the checkpoint. Luckily I was basically stuck at the checkpoint, so I didn't suffer much there. Admittedly, I was purposefully trying to jump where I obviously shouldn't have been. It also isn't the most optimized game. It started off running really great, but by time I got to chapter 4 I think, I had fallen down to 20fps. The surprising thing about that was it was almost ok at that framerate with 2x frame generation on. I'm usually much more sensitive to lower frame rates, but it always felt smoother that other games at the same fps, by a  lot actually. I won't go into too much detail about the gameplay, but I personally liked it a lot. It was far more challenging than this dev's last game, but still pretty easy in a good way, at least for me. 
I'm really happy I played it, and only have two real complaints- the performance and the price. And performance wise, I was easily able to get the frame rate way up by just changing one setting that didn't make the game look any worse, but I do like to crank all my settings up because I have a pretty powerful PC and should have no problem playing a game like this maxed out at 4K. This is just another of the poorly optimized Horror Engine games we are plagued with, not really worse than average, and even better in some regards. The price however, it's a bit steep. It would be nice to see it dropped by $5. I doubt it will happen, and I understand the dev wants compensated for the time he put into making this, but the indie horror market is cutthroat. Some of the best indie horror games ever are this price or less. On the other hand, it's not like it's an outrageous price, and I don't feel cheated by it. Really, it's the combination of the two. If it was either cheaper OR optimized better, I could swallow the other issue much easier.

This was a strange, horrific experience. Kumamawashi looks like an innocuous children's game but is full of sinister level designs and elements that are just downright broken and got me soft locked several times, taking me probably 15 hours to finally complete.  Yet something compelled me to keep playing it, perhaps a combination of the nostalgic graphics and music and addictively simple puzzle element designed to lure you in and then enrage you not unlike the bear you play as in the story. 

A girl offers a bear an apple in the woods before being kidnapped by a witch and he must go through fifty floors of twisting, rotating platforms to save her. If you decide to play this game, note two things: 

1. Set the stamina in the options to max, the game considers this "easy" but it's actually the only way some areas can be completed. 

2. Make sure you collect every power up on each level of the tower before you proceed to the next floor. 

If you do this then the game will still be extremely frustrating but playable. You basically just rotate the floor pieces as the bear moves and try to guide him to the exit, but as you progress the game starts having branching paths and giving powerups that you MUST collect to fully complete the game. At times you must adjust your speed but you can only do this at the save orb you reach that restores your stamina. If you have the wrong speed set you might not know until you are near the exit and have to restart because you ran out of stamina. If you set the speed fast at all times you will still need to restart because the bear will move too quickly for you to be able to rotate some of the platforms. Later on the max speed is insane as the bear will fly across the map before you even have a chance to react to it. There are also "enemies" which must be killed in "fights" which are essentially just button timing minigames where you try to kill them while losing as little stamina as possible. This adds an interesting puzzle element because you sometimes want to take a path where you avoid fights or fight just the weaker enemies to survive.

Even though it was insanely frustrating having to restart because I missed a necessary powerup, I still really enjoyed this game and the challenge it posed. The music sounds like something from a 90s JRPG but in childlike music box mode, and the graphics are just beautiful. Unfortunately there's only one tileset the entire game uses and no environmental decorations so it starts to get repetitive later on. That and sometimes you will get lost because the game reuses some puzzles. Some puzzles are clever and others are just filler for you to pass through. This isn't a VERY good game, but it's good enough to recommend. The ending came as a total surprise and felt absolutely bizarre compared to everything that came before it. The devs could easily make this game more playable with just a few lines of code by letting the player teleport between orbs. This would reduce unnecessary backtracking and let the player go back to the floors where the powerups needed to complete the game are located.

I ended up writing a positive review, though I was kinda on the fence and, if possible, it would have been a neutral one.
There are indeed several good points about this visual novel but at the same time I found myself disappointed after I finished it.

I enjoyed the first half quite a bit, as the "phantom thief" plot combined with girls' love is fresh and interesting; the writing is also good and the art is very cute.
The second half though, while it's not bad on its own and is still interesting if the "phantom thief" theme is what you are mainly interested in, completely forgets about the romantic part, as you get the POV of other characters and some backstory.
While the Epilogue does return to Desiree's POV, her relationship with Irina is again basically forgotten until the very last second, when the game delivers a quick and unsatisfying ending, where the best thing we get is [spoiler] a peck on the cheek and the hint of a possible future relationship that can only be a long-distance one, considering their jobs [/spoiler].

So in the end I'd recommend this VN to people who are mainly interested in the phantom thief story (which is pretty good) rather than the GL aspect (or at least be aware that the romance is a relatively small part of the game, is mostly platonic/subtexty, and its ending is rather unsatisfying).

If you have played their spooky dwellers games before you’ll find it easier to get going but it could be a bit overwhelming/confusing if you haven’t as there really aren’t any simple tutorial levels, although there are instructions. There is an excellent book at the top if you forget game mechanics but be prepared to take 10 mins at the beginning to get the hang of it. 

I was feeling lazy and played this mostly on relaxed so can’t say how challenging it would be on the other settings (I think it would be especially on harder setting) but what I loved was that it wasn’t a mindless game nor was this too much thinking but just the ‘goldilocks’ fun keep you engaged.

This game looks like it was made by somebody with experience, but on a shoestring budget and on very TIGHT deadline.

It is very short and very small in scope, but definitely does NOT feel like some lowest-effort trash pushed along the line of least resistance.

The premise is simple - aliens disguised as humans are taking over the country, and that's why you - simple man just fired from his job - have to walk through few random places and kill everybody on your way.

It starts pretty rough. You and your boys (a bunch of copy-pasted worker models) protest in front of your workplace. Then a group of masked henchmen (copy-pasted masked bandits) tries to squash the protest by beating up everybody. You fight them with your fists and search up the building looking for the boss.

Then in the next level, you visit the office, only to find that there's no work for you and get attacked again. The game doesn't bother to explain why YOU are getting attacked all the time, while other people just stand around.

Later on, you are pushed through the biggest hits of FPS level design. :D

Sewer level - check, warehouse level - heck, underground garage - check, construction site - check. 

For my taste, they could've shoved in some WW2 bunkers and abandoned factories, just to make it a complete package. :)

For the first 20 minutes, you have to use your fists and a rusty pipe (which is, imo a lot when the whole game can be finished in 1 hour). The melee 'system' is absolutely basic; it works like an extremely short-range gun. You beat up two versions of copy-pasted aggressive civilian characters and find the special glasses on a random pile of trash.

These glasses are THE gimmick of this game. You put them on, and you can see the real (alien) heads of the enemies. That's only a cosmetic change; enemies act exactly the same regardless if you see their real form or not.

Also - some enemies stay human even if you put on the glasses, which means they are just normal people... that for some reason decided to side with the aliens and attack you furiously? Hmmm...

There's only 3 or 4 places when you have to put the glasses on to progress - it will reveal a teleport to the next level or door hidden in the wall.

And that's the whole gimmick. It's not that deep. 

Shooting is as basic as it can be; as you progress, you find new guns: revolver, shotgun, SMG, and alien laser. All have alt fire when you press RMB, but all feel pretty stiff and generic to use.

Enemies aren't very bullet spongey, but the game definitely rewards headshots. Not only do you save bullets that way, but you can also admire a pretty neat effect of the enemy's head exploding into pieces. For sure that's a highlight of the game's combat system. :) 

I appreciate that every level brings new enemy models - especially female androids stole my heart. <3 

Visually, it is... not that bad. :)

3D assets are surprisingly well made and coated with some pretty sharp textures. The devs had rather meager asset libraries, so each level was produced with the 'make more with less' approach. But it doesn't feel repetitive or boring; before you get bored, you're already jumping to the next lvl. Little animations when you pull the lever or open the sewer manhole show that somebody really cared about this game despite all budget and time constraints.

To sum it all up - it's nothing special, but also not utter garbage. Imo it sits in the category of 'this ain't much, but it's honest work'. The game doesn't pretend to be anything more than a low-budget shooter with a funny gimmick - and I like it. It doesn't try to waste your time with pretentious metaphors about life and death and sense of life. For a few $ it's a quite ok deal.

I haven't played the game yet, but if you're on Linux (I'm using Linux Mint) you NEED to play this game outside of Steam through something like Lutris or Bottles, as running it through Steam with Proton crashes the game on startup because of a missing dependency, Nvidia physX. 

I tried installing physX in my steam "bottle" by changing the name of the executable to the one of the Nvidia physX driver, installing it, then changing the executable back to Metathrone, but it doesn't work and the installer just says that I have "a newer version of physX installed on my system". Just doesn't work in this instance through Steam. Anyways, to get the game running on Linux, create a new Bottle with the "Soda" Runner. Then install Nvidia physX version 9.10.0513 in that Bottle (no idea if this works on AMD cards). Then, since this game is DRM-free, copy the files of the game from Steam to your newly created Bottle. Puzzle Machine is a brilliant little game that packs a lot into its compact package. 
It’s essentially four games in one, each offering a unique twist on logic puzzles. 

The first mode, inspired by the classic zebra or Einstein puzzles, eases you into the gameplay with straightforward matching tasks. But the real challenge—and fun—comes with the Knight, Pirate, and Spy puzzles. These modes take the concept to the next level, introducing positional logic where you have to consider not just what’s being said but also who’s saying it and where they’re positioned. It’s a fresh mechanic that keeps your brain working overtime.

The game’s minimalistic graphics are functional yet appealing. They provide just enough visual clarity to focus on the puzzles without being distracting. The clean interface is a testament to the game’s design philosophy: simplicity over flash, letting the puzzles shine as the main attraction.

Sound design is minimal, with almost no sound effects, but the game does feature a variety of music tracks. The tracks are hit or miss—some are quirky and might not suit everyone’s taste—but thankfully, you can skip them with a press of the spacebar or turn them off entirely.

The difficulty progression is spot-on. Early puzzles are almost relaxing, but as you move through the levels, the game ramps up, and you’ll find yourself pausing to rethink strategies. With a large library of premade puzzles, the replayability is high. You can pick it up for a quick session or dive into a challenging streak whenever you want. It’s not the type of game to binge for hours, but it’s perfect for casual and consistent play.

Overall, Puzzle Machine is an absolute steal for its price. You’re getting four distinct puzzle modes, a well-thought-out progression curve, and a game that genuinely respects your time and intellect. 
If you’re a fan of logic puzzles or just love a good mental challenge, this game is a clear recommendation.

First Impressions
- No system options at all on the title screen. Not even sound volume options.
- Graphics/mapping look lovely for a retro title
- Nice music so far
- Not able to dash in interior places but able to dash in exterior areas is...an odd design choice
- Not able to save anywhere except on the world map/save points is definitely retro, but not in a good way. Saving anywhere benefits the player and is a QOL improvement this game needs.
- Wasn't aware that this had a silent protagonist. Not a dealbreaker for me as I'm used to them from past retro titles, just wasn't expecting it.
- Party wiped from the first two battles. Missing attacks irking me to no end. Trying to grind in the early going is way too tough already. Medium to high difficulty is stated on the Steam page, but the enemies hit too fast and too hard in the early game when you're trying to level grind. It feels more like artificial difficulty due to unbalanced battles than it does anything else, but that could just be me.
- I think this game isn't for me.

Overall first impressions are that this is definitely a very retro title that appears well put-together so far, though it's in need of some quality of life modern improvements like saving anywhere and system options (at least implement volume options). I also think it's way too difficult, especially in the very early game when trying to level grind. Even in difficult RPGs, there's a balancing curve to combat where in the beginning you start off relatively easy. Not so in this game. You're thrown into the difficulty right off the bat.

I like games that are challenging, but not arbitrarily difficult for the sake of it. I also enjoy grinding, but when I'm not even given the chance to without using up my limited, available stockpile of items, then it feels unbalanced to me. This game is for those who enjoy high difficulty without some, I think, necessary quality-of-life improvements. This is a solid RPG so far without any bells and whistles of modern RPGs. 

I'll be refunding this one, but I do encourage others to give it a go. It looks like something solid with the presentation, but just not for me. So, despite my criticisms, I'll give this game a recommendation, but only because there's a lot here that's solid. I also think that, for the right person, it could be a lot of fun.

The game is fairly short, but this means it never becomes tedious, and you're always making some kind of progress towards your goal of upgrading your campsite and/or gear. Progress is smooth, and never feels tiring. You're always improving and after two or three trips into the dungeon, you're going to upgrade or unlock something new.

There are many QoL features as well, like a goblin that allows you to convert materials into others, which means that you can still farm items you don't need, and it won't be a waste of time. This is greatly appreciated and a welcome breath of fresh air.

The enemies are fun, and I like all the different variations to their attacks and types. Some will attack you, some will use magic, and others will protect themselves. The snail, my favourite of the enemies, is basically a DPS check; once it reaches you. it explodes and deals tremendous damage, but you can survive if you're healthy enough.

The ending is also really cute, and made me chuckle. The game is well worth your time if you're looking for something light, casual, and addicting. Absolutely, check it out.

Dungeon Rummage is a quick, fun little game that doesn't overstay its welcome. If you're looking for a couple of hours of gaming, it's worth giving a try. The power progression is satisfying, and the bosses are difficult enough to ensure the game doesn't feel too easy. The addition of a merchant NPC to trade one kind of resource for another stops the game from becoming too grindy, so that your camp and equipment upgrades never seem to take too long to get, but nor do they come too quickly.

The dungeons themselves are fairly straight forward, but the random appearance of bonus areas with extra resources give them just enough of a change that it doesn't become too repetitive repeating the dungeon for resources (that and the balance of how you gain resources is great to begin with).

I would also like to see more of the semi-random events like rare enemy spawns, secret rooms, etc. as it can get a tad repetitive traversing the same areas multiple times. Dungeon Rummage - Survival may be a smaller game (a few hours of playtime, good for the price) but it is definitely not for the faint of heart.

Upper dungeon floors serve as an gentle introduction, allowing players to familiarize themselves with the mechanics without feeling overwhelmed. As you progress deeper into the dungeon, the challenge increases. Enemies become more formidable, and resource management becomes crucial. And the end of each floor is a boss you must defeat in order to proceed, so you'll want to make sure you're prepared to throw everything at them.

Players need to strategically gather materials and upgrade their camp to enhance stats, craft potions, and prepare for tougher enemies. You will not make it through the dungeon on your first, or even your fifth attempt, you have to work your way up in power with new weapons, armor, and consumables.

Overall, Dungeon Rummage - Survival strikes a balance between accessibility and challenge. It's designed to be a relaxing experience, but it still requires thoughtful planning and strategy, especially in the later stages. This makes it suitable for both casual players looking for a laid-back diversion and those seeking a bit more challenge.

A surreal and dreamlike exploration of The Troubles in Ireland. With powerful symbolism—such as political prison camps and the Red Hand of Ulster—Benign Land offers a trippy, unsettling perspective on a history that is too often overlooked. With wonderful and unnerving audio.

I really enjoyed this immersive experience. The visuals and the soundscape are mesmerizing, and the controls are elegant. Knowing it was originally part of a larger exposition provides a bit of needed context. It made me think deeper about the scenes presented here - silent, solemn landscapes that offer an impressive sense of place.

Initially these environments are almost timeless, more mythical than real. But at some point the scenery becomes much more relatable, and at the same time oppressing. History looms over you, humbled visitor, wordlessly asking you profound questions.

Definitely one of the more artistic experiences on Steam. Recommended.

I just want to post a review with my impressions so far because this game still has 0 reviews and I am immediately enjoying the game after picking it up during the 30% sale.

TL:DR Conclusion copied to the top:
Overall I easily recommend this game. If you come across it and you think the game-play or aesthetic look cool but the lack of reviews is stopping you then please don't let that stop you. I think this game is great and I am glad that I decided to pick it up and be the first to leave a review. This is a small indie game and I can just tell that care was taken in the making of this game which makes it quite charming.

At the time of writing this review I have played about 45 minutes so far. I came across this game and was drawn to the aesthetic and the unique concept for the game-play. So far I have played the first 3 "levels" each of which has been a fairly long spree of puzzles introducing the mechanics and adding new dials to mess with. It looks to me like there are about 9 levels in total plus a practice mode and an endless mode with endlessly generated puzzles. After the first 3 levels I have only been introduced to about 1/3 of the adjustable dials on the remote which means puzzles are going to get about 3 times more complex and difficult as the game progresses. The trailer footage gives a good idea of what the game-play is like so I am not going to talk about that much. All this is to say I think the amount of content seems really good for what this game is and what the price of the game is.

I really like the aesthetic. The rendering style, environments in the background, music, and robot characters make for a very retro Sci-Fi vibe that I am very into.
