I am updating the review to reflect the first patch, the devs fixed most of the issues that I had with animation, text reading, and save points, so I don't think you will find it as contentious as in my original review. On a subjective note, even though the game has a lot of interesting ideas with the psychological effects, it does not handle sound effects and certain aesthetic elements as well as it could, that said, for a $5 indie survival horror, I think the game is in a decent state now. Takes about 2 to 3 hours to finish with no hints.

Admittedly a big part of the game was backtracking, the main area is abnormally large, very lengthy runs just to check every area, and then try to figure out if you missed anything. Initially I was going to say that the areas were way too big, but at the same time it kinda reminded me of the original Silent Hill a bit, the farm area had some nice long camera angles which I liked, the main issue is that you didn't gate the roads enough, as well as the camera often pointing right at the character, making it hard to see the direction. There are basically only 2 main locations in this game, as well as some psychological locations in between, the first one is somewhat open for exploration, it's kinda like a big circle and you have to figure out the order. The puzzles were not very hard overall, however because of the size of the farm, putting the hints together could be challenging, but for the most part the puzzles are straightforward once you have the items.

The visuals is something that I felt was not bad, but also sporadic with detail and quality, sometimes the game felt very cheap looking, but occasionally you had some neat looking areas, even that nice spinning effect inside of the mill which I assume could be the Silent Hill reference. The big farm area actually looked decent, and when the camera wasn't being a *****. I didn't mind exploring it. The caves were a bit more simple looking, it felt like you were taking Qs from Silent Hill with the visibility distance, not as good obviously, but I felt like you at least tried to capture that feeling, somewhat decently.

There is limited combat as well as some "resource management", it won't really impact your experience a lot as the game is pretty easy overall, the enemies are very basic, and you can kinda stand your ground, sometimes move back a little, but I like some of the death animations. I don't have too much to say in regards to the narrative, I like that you added a lot of psychological effects and it worked well enough for a small game, it's just that overall suspense of the game wasn't as heavy as a few similar titles.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

+ There were a few moments with the locations that I really enjoyed, yea the overall consistency wasn't great, but the few times you get those long shots and a few angles in the structures, the game didn't look bad. It often reminded me of Silent HIll, not with the same attention to detail, and the game usually didn't have as much texture as I wanted, but overall, not bad for an indie game, I have seen a lot worse.

+ The puzzles were relatively intuitive, aside from just having too much distance between them, the only one that annoyed me a little was a random death in the corn, yea there is a clue for it, but you might get there before you find it.

+ The story and vibes were decent overall, it's nothing special to be honest, but at least there were several attempts to create psychological depth to the narrative, I just didn't really like the font of the text. Some of the scenery like the graves part and the totem were adding to the mood, even if the music was a little off sometimes.

+ Actually a couple of nicely made cutscenes as well

[h1] Feedback (outdated): [/h1]

- Usually when you rotate in these game the character kinda walks in place if you know what I mean, but you didn't have any animation for that, which I think breaks the immersion a little, I think RE1 had it, so why not use like a shorter version of the walk animations to have it on a rotation as well, just so the character does not look like solid asset. Also I thought the rotation was a little slow. 

- So the way you save in this game, you lite the lanterns kinda like using the ink ribbons, but at the start of the game, it creates a checkpoint before the chase, and if you die in a corn field before finding the save location, it feels frustrating because you are reset to that point before the clock puzzle. Why not put another checkpoint after the chase or before the chase 

- Navigating the farm was a bit frustrating for 2 reasons. First, you will be hugging the walls to make sure you find everything, but you didn't gate the locations enough, so you can kinda find a lot of bad camera angles. The camera also often points in a way where you can't see where you going, especially if you backtrack.

- I would add a little text after placing the dynamite, that it's still missing the line. It said use the plunger before I even crafted the line.

- For the pages, I think it should default to right side of the page after pressing a button. Maybe you had 2 for each side, but I think it will confuse players trying to press through them. I was not a fan of the font for the text personally. You could also color code hints maybe

- I feel like you should make all of the monster noises louder, including the "Trapper". Even if you hit them, I think they should make more screams. Music choices were not always great, I think the chase could use something more intense for example.

First of all i wanna say thanks to the developer of this game. Figure Skating is a sport i love and as we all know there isnt out there any game about this amazing sport.

This game is simulation style, so it tends to simulate the real life sport, which for me is a really good ideia. So what does this means exactly? It means that you cannot go full russian girl jumping quad after quad after quad. Jokes aside, its pretty much this, jumping a quad with a woman is pretty hard, and the same thing goes to the triple axel.

Since this is a game probably the biggest question is going to be: is the gameplay good? Well, yes, the gameplay is really good and simulation like. You have to gain speed, you have to control your stamina, you have to be careful and not jump into the barriers, you have to plan your own program. The physics of the game are pretty good aswell. But be careful, this game might not be a good experience without a controller (xbox, or playstation), but if you have one you are good to go. 

The graphics of this game are nothing special of course, but its not bad at all. Since this is an indie game there isnt much the developer can do. The outfits that you unlock in the game are ok, it could use some work, but overall its decent, but its something that can be upgraded in the future. The customization of the game in general is pretty decent. Its not something you gonna lose to much time in it anyway.

Now about the programs, either short or free skate. Im gonna tell you the best thing that this game has, and it was a brilliant move by the developer. You can upload any music you want, so you can skate to anything you want. (When i saw this update i bought the game immediately). For example im trying to replicate the Mone Chiba free skate from this season. (I wanted to do the Valieva Bolero free skate, but since its hard jumping quads i gave up lol). All you need to upload the music you want is an mp3 file, so for that go to youtube, choose the music you want, google youtube mp3 converter, copy the link and boom you can skate to your own program or replicate a program from any skater.

About the jumps, well. There are some jumps that are pretty hard for me, such as, the 3A with a woman, most of the time i cant get the timing right, and usually it goes underrotated or i have a fall. But i can do a 4Toe quite easily, which is kinda weird, but maybe its just my timing is better with the 4Toe. This is something the game doesnt really explain in the tutorial. In fact i thing the game could use a better tutorial, that explains how the componentes work, and how the jumps work with the orange circle that you can catch (the speed boost). I have learned this because i saw the videos of the developer on youtube, where he explains the game better. 

When you finish the program, lets say i just did the short program at the worlds. So i got a good score, i just did 68. The first girl just did 78, and this is a thing i hate, i cannot see what she did. I wanna see her program, her jumps, her spins, her step sequence, and the GOE she got on every element. 

Also when you finish the program you can see that the components come from musical jumps (jumps in the right timing to the music) and from the actions you do (its the circles you collect in the right timing aswell), well my question is: what about the composition, presentation and skating skills?? This was something i found very odd not to have, but i understand it might be difficult to put this in the game, so maybe thats why its not there.

Again when you finish the program you also have the technical score, of course, you get a message there saying GOE, and it shows a number, i think this is the average GOE of the program i guess. But this should show the GOE for every element that i just did.

This game is hard, its not easy to win the worlds, you gotta score more than 220 to win with a woman, this may be something many people will not enjoy, personally i like it, since its realistic. 

This game doesnt really have a career mode, so you start at a very basic competition where nobody scores much, then you move on to another competition, where they score a bit more but nothing special. Then you can go to the first grand prix assigment, and here they score quite a lot, its not easy to win. Then after the first grand prix assigment you get the second one. And guess what happens if you do well in both these grand prix? Yes, you go to the grand prix final. Which is gonna be quite difficult to win a gold. After this you have the worlds, if you finish top 3 there you then have the final competition that is called legends cup. And thats it. So this here could use some updates for sure, cause the game feels very simple. The developer added the european championship and the four continents, but its only a challenge, you cannot compete in them, since the game doesnt have a nationality system.

I have no ideia if this game is gonna get more updates in the future, i really hope so, because there is a lot of potential in this amazing game / project. 

Now final toughts, since this review is pretty long already. 
Should you get this game? If you are a figure skating fan like me, and know what the sport is about, sure, you should, and you will enjoy this a lot. 
Now lets say you are someone that only watches this sport when its olympic season, well, i dont think you will like this at all, since you need to have basic knowledge of the sport to understand how it works.

A premium modern beat em up in the making.  The combat, technically and mechanically, is supreme in regards to offensive and defensive options available, and execution of those options.  I really have a sweet spot for beat em ups that do a good job incorporating fighting game mechanics.  The pixel art is sublime as well and has so much character to it.  

There is so much to explore, whether it be the character skill trees, builds, upgrades, and the map itself, leaving so much up to the players choices.  I could tell within the first thirty minutes of playtime that the devs have a plan, and a vision for this game, all the while incorporating elements from excellent beat em ups, fighting games, and other genres in modern gaming.  Even the ally AI is pretty good (I got carried through a couple levels by AI lol).  

It's games like WB that show what early access is really supposed to be used for, and that is games with a rich fundamental base that can only improve over time while maintaining a solid standard of quality.  I intend to pick up this game on as many platforms I can to show support.  Amazing stuff, great work so far.  Bravo on releasing a early access game that doesn't feel under-cooked.

This game is really cool, although it's very clear that it's on early access and needs a lot of polish and content updates. It's really similar to Valdis story actually, in that it's a high skillcap action rpg that rewards you for mechanical mastery and system knowledge, but that is also super unforgiving at first. I personally prefer Gilroy because he has a double jump, an airdash, a wavedash, and really freeform air combos, but most of the characters have something cool about them and you'll likely find someone you really like.
The game's designs are also really cool, the protagonists look really unique, and the bosses are super crazy and memorable too, the regular enemies are surprisingly original too, with designs that look really different from what you'd expect from a fantasy game.
While the game's story isn't as developed as Valdis, i still find the lore tidbits to be really interesting, and it's really cool seeing returning characters and/or elements.
I usually don't like action rpgs because i feel like the rpg part takes away from the action, but i find that like it's predecessor, this game has a really good mix of both, and that it's generally synergistic between both systems.

I have some issues with the game tho, mainly that the difficulty curve is really awkward, that the game is designed around npc partners and that the game is balanced around enemies having long-lasting super armor.
The way the difficulty works, the game gets harder for each stage you complete, but also for each time you die, so if you find a difficulty wall, it's only gonna get harder and may eventually get to a stage where it might as well be unclearable because the enemy scales harder than you do. Meanwhile, if you get a smooth early game, the game stays easy and you can steamroll it before it gets hard. This makes for a very swingy game where you're either winning pretty decisively or struggling a lot.

The game has an option to give you an npc partner and to put it briefly, most of the mechanics, from the money, the revive system, the difficulty, etc. are balanced around said partner, i find the game to be more fun and challenging solo, but it's clear it's not balanced around that so it feels a bit awkward, i believe the dev is working on this but it's an issue at the moment.

Lastly, all bosses and most elite enemies are balanced around having super armor that also blocks damage, so a good amount of your playtime is gonna be hitting enemies that aren't staggered by your attacks, there are also enemies that only get staggered after you do a parry (an attack after a perfect block) and this feels super lame cause you have to wait for the enemies to do something and can't be proactive. That said, the game is actually designed around the armor, and the enemies usually have enough of a windup for you to see they are preparing an attack for you to respond, and you can actually combo them after you break the armor so it's a lot better than a lot of other action games in that regard.

Lastly, most beat em ups have the issue of "why play this when you could play Fight n Rage", i think this game's action is well executed enough, and has enough other elements to make it different that it's really worth playing, and i find myself booting it up when i wanna aircombo and wavedash everywhere as Gilroy.

[b][i]Digseum[/i][/b] is a nice, short incremental game that is all about digging up artifacts to be able to present in your museum.  This is [b]not[/b] an idle game, however!  All of the gameplay is active and overall, I found the concept to be very pleasing and enjoyable.  The gameplay itself would probably get too mundane over time, but with a game as short as this, that doesn't matter because you should be able to 100% this game in around three hours of play time.  Every new mechanic that gets introduced is pretty well balanced and helps to make this game a nice short trip. 

Pros:
+Overall premise and concept is pleasing and enjoyable
+Overall gameplay loop is also pleasing and enjoyable
+The game is short and sweet and the mechanics help to make this game pleasing and enjoyable

Cons:
-The game is short and sweet.

If you are expecting an idle game, [b]don't[/b] buy this game, but if you are expecting a short and sweet, as well as pleasing and enjoyable little excursion, then this is a game that I would [b]highly recommend[/b].

Arcade racers are one of those golden genres for me like shmups, beat 'em ups, and RTS where if someone makes a new one, I will be there checking it out ASAP. So I was quite interested when this dropped on Steam at the end of December, but its $20 pricetag was too high to consider for a complete unknown with very few reviews. Just a month later it dropped to $10 and $5 on sale, and you bet, I'll spend a fiver to take a chance on new arcade racer.

On the positive side, this game is really built out with many tracks, cars, car upgrade items, and race modes. There's a lot here and it feels enjoyably old school in that way, back when games used to be mostly single player focused. Also, it looks pretty good. Sure, I guess you could classify these graphics something around the level of "high end mobile gaming," but that's fine. They won't dazzle you but look just fine on a 4K screen.

The downside, unfortunately, is the driving physics themselves, which is the one thing you really have to get right. Now, they're not *terrible*, but there's two flaws to them that stop this game from being legit good and instead keep it in mediocre territory.

First is the braking system. Whether regular brake or handbrake, both are dramatic and don't work like you'd expect. The regular brake stops your momentum almost completely no matter how fast you're going, and the handbrake jerks the car wildly. And not in a powerslide manner as you'd expect, but again it sends your car to a halt and when combined with your steering into a turn, you can suddenly go from, say, a 2 o'clock direction to 10 o'clock in the blink of an eye. That just doesn't work, it's unusable. As you can see in my video above, I started off at first trying to use the brakes around corners and constantly crashed into walls and finished last. It's in later races when I learned to not use brakes *at all* and just let off the gas for corners and then I was consistently finishing 1st.

The other problem with the driving physics, which isn't as dramatic as the braking problem, is the cars don't have enough weight. Well, at least the starter car doesn't, perhaps others do. When you crash into a wall your car doesn't just sit there like it should, it bounces back, and often in a different direction than it was originally facing. This makes those occasional crashes and spinouts that much more difficult because sometimes you'll end up facing in the wrong direction entirely.

But the developers of this game already gave the controller system a fix a couple weeks after the game came out, so who knows, maybe they'll continue to tweak it. Because if they alleviated those two issues, for me this would turn a mediocre game to an actual good one. 6/10

Disclaimer: This review contains heavy spoilers for the game. Do not read if you want to keep the plot a surprise.

Intro:

I first played this short, yet spellbinding visual novel in its first Game Jam version back in October. This version is mostly the same, aside from occasional cosmetic changes. I wanted to wait until I finished this recent version to review it, so here I am! I think this gripping feminist thriller needs more love, and I’m going to write about why I loved it so much! So, now let’s get into my overall thoughts and conclude after that.

Overall Thoughts:

The setting of 1900s England is very convincing, with great attention given to the look, feel, and manner of speaking the characters express themselves in. And sadly, the way Alma is treated by everyone feels very realistic and shows how much misogyny existed in that time period, and still does now… The setup with her being sent to a cottage for “hysteria” feels historically accurate and exactly how others would use that against her. And her futile attempts to get others to believe the strange messages she sees on the leaves is sad and shows just how hard it is for women to be believed by men. The eventual reveal of the Neighbour and the Boy is utterly brilliant and I didn’t see it coming at all. Once again, Borealis chose to keep this in reality, and not diving into delusions or fantasy like I half-expected. And Alma’s resolve is well-earned and easy to root for as the player.

While there aren’t many characters, they are all interesting and serve to effectively enhance Alma’s journey and motivations. Alma herself is likeable and sympathetic, with her unfairly being treated when she’s just trying to live her life the way she wants. Her development into rebellion and solving the conflict herself is rewarding and a good example of empowerment. I also like how you might doubt her senses at first, but come to quickly believe in and cheer for her. Mrs. Miller is cold, but wants to please Alma’s father deep down. She is a good obstacle and foil to Alma, and shows how other women can also contribute to the patriarchy and be someone’s obstacle and caretaker at the same time. The Neighbour is the perfect villain for this story, and the most frightening of any of Borealis’s games so far. His cruelty towards his own son and evil actions towards women make him terrifying and a good symbol of the privilege men get in that time period. His predator-like mannerisms are scary as well. And I love the fact that the villain of the story is a realistic person like him, I think he’s far more scary than any monster could possibly be… And the Boy is a sad and tragic figure that is the perfect motivation for Alma and the player to reach the end. He could also act as a symbol of the pure people facing the violence of the patriarchy. Him being the secret messenger retroactively makes the previous leaves so sad and scarily real.

There aren’t many choices in the game, only a few. But they all affect the ending you get, so they matter a lot. Bad Ending 1, where Alma tells Mrs. Miller everything, is the most sad yet possibly most realistic outcome for Alma, and really shows the stigma against mental health as well. Bad Ending 2, where Alma sneaks into the Neighbour’s house during the day is a good and tense path that shows more of the Neighbour and the Boy, and what their interactions are like. The brutality of it is also shocking, which makes Alma’s fate sad, since she tried to resist and died for it… However, the Good Ending is satisfying and really showcases Alma’s bravery and agency. The tense rescue at night is unnerving, and I actually got scared when the Neighbour started chasing them. Using the plants as a cover was smart and thematically clever, along with the happy and well-earned epilogue.

The art is on par with True Colours. The character sprites look gorgeous and are fitting of the era. The backgrounds are beautiful and memorable. Sadly, there’s only one CG (the image at the Good Ending that’s the same on the game’s banner), and it’s my sole criticism of this game. I wish there were at least 2 or 3 more, since I wanted to see more of this world, but I understand that this made for a Game Jam, and I still enjoy everything. And it might be because of the shorter length, but the partial voice acting, especially on Alma and the Neighbour, really enhance the experience greatly and make the tense moments all the more anxiety-inducing. It’s so well done. And the music and sound effects are top notch. I love the small, yet very effective amount of music. It’s all old-fashioned and really captures the feeling of being alone in the country, with the more creepy music really grabbing my attention. I wish I could listen to it separately from the game… And the sound effects are used masterfully, with certain moments, like the Neighbour’s cottage door throwing open or the garden shears hitting the ground really putting me on edge and presenting itself so amazingly! It’s one of the highlights of the game.

There are other things I like. Such as the tension leading up to the Boy reveal that is so uneasy and mysterious, and makes you really want to see what happens next. This would make a good thriller movie. I also like how no one came to save Alma at the last second, her resolving the conflict on her own makes the message have more integrity. And the pacing is so good! I was gripped from beginning to end the whole time and never lost interest. There was never a dull moment and everything felt natural, with suspense being there the entire time. This is so good, especially for a game made in such a short time frame.

Conclusion:

All that being said, this game is very well made and its story and characters are so fresh and interesting. It truly is a feminist tale wrapped in a Victorian thriller that truly sells you on its terror. And like the last two, Borealis positively portrays mental health and has an uplifting ending message, something that is very nice to still see. The music and art are nice with its overall tone. You could argue that the price is too high for its 1-2 hour length, but it’s important to remember that this was only made in a few weeks for a contest. It’s well polished for that, and it’s not expensive. At least you can keep it forever, and replay it anytime you want. So, if you like strong women and mysterious thrillers, definitely check this out!

Personally, I love this a lot and it shows why Borealis is one of my favorite game developers. It made me terrified and happy for its main character to succeed, and really shows how important it is for women to be represented as capable. It’s a shame once again that few people have played it, since women empowerment stories are quite rare and this is an unusual setting for a visual novel… Still, I loved it and I’m glad I could share my thoughts. To end this, I’ll just say: never give up and fight back against oppression, and do what’s right, no matter the cost!

Beyond Citadel is a combat shooter that doesn’t seem to fully understand what it wants to be. Is it a philosophical thriller about the survival of humanity, an ultra-violent action game with manual reload mechanics, or a military training simulator for girls in lingerie? The game was created by a Japanese developer who was clearly inspired by Evangelion, Doom, Wolfenstein, and, apparently, a bunch of other cool stuff thrown in for good measure.

The gameplay is the main reason to dive into this. The shooting feels fantastic: every gun has a satisfyingly heavy kick, many have alternate fire modes, and the pistol with a grenade launcher attachment is an absolute standout. But there’s a catch: the reloading system takes realism to a whole new level. If you’re using a machine gun, you’ll need to open the feed tray, remove the old belt, insert a new one, close it, and rack the bolt—only then are you ready to fire again. At first, this feels cool, but when you’re surrounded by hordes of enemies and fumbling with your weapon’s mechanics, the excitement quickly turns into quiet panic.

The game does have a story, but it’s presented in such a fragmented and chaotic way that even if you understand English, piecing it together feels like a low-priority task. And who needs it when you’re surrounded by cyber-waifus and tons of violence? There’s plenty of bloodshed here, but if it’s too much, you can turn it off—apparently for the more sensitive souls who accidentally downloaded this game thinking it was something cute.

The level design seems interesting at first but starts to feel repetitive over time. Initially, you think, “Wow, these locations are massive!” But after a couple of hours, you’re just sprinting through them like a mad courier, trying to find keys and power cells to finish the level as quickly as possible. Occasionally, you’re entertained by different mechanics like piloting mechs or helicopters, but most of the time, you’re busy slicing through enemies and stocking up on supplies from merchants.

And, of course, the big question: why is there so much fanservice? Why are all the girls in armor that covers, at most, 10% of their bodies? Why do the enemies look like they’re dressed for a fashion show rather than combat? And why are you, the protagonist, fighting in your underwear? No one knows, but the developer decided it was necessary, so here we are.

Overall, Beyond Citadel is a strange but oddly cool shooter. It delivers satisfying gunplay but wears you down with repetitive level design. It tries to tell a story, but you quickly forget what it’s even about. It gives you intense combat but occasionally reminds you that you’re also a part-time gunsmith. Is it worth playing? If you’re into a dark cyberpunk world with hardcore shooting and questionable character design choices—definitely.

A quality retro shooter with very detailed and rather complex gun mechanics and related movement and combat systems that would be pretty advanced for even a modern shooter. While there are some rough edges in production, those 'charms' are overshadowed by how addictive and engaging the gameplay actually is. 

As it should be apparent the game is saturated with suggestive and sensual imagery, mixed with rather ambitious religious themes and metaphors, all drenched with overwhelmingly grotesque, engagingly gratuitous gore. All of the enemies in the game are women. The enemies can and will be absolutely butchered and blown to pieces by all the weapons in the player's arsenal. The game shows all of this in stylized, explicit detail. This is a rather deliberate but particular combination you have to be willing to wade through (I guess there are some gore settings I haven't looked at). But truth be told, in terms of what the game exposes you to, there's nothing here that mainstream anime like Evangelion, Ghost in the Shell, and others hasn't already shown. And the ultraviolence and gore in gameplay is on par with other shooters of this type (Though I think the gore is rendered with levels of detail well beyond the norm, the complexity matches the level of detail of other things in the game.) 

So while there's some discussion to be had about motivations and intentions behind choosing to present this particular content in this way, after the first 30 minutes or so we will have descended well past the shock value of it all and will be focused on the gameplay. 

At the end of the day the star of the show for this game is, as I started with, the really compelling gun mechanics and overall combat. Projectiles have trajectory and speed. Needing to use multiple clicks to unload, reload, top up, cock, and aim the weapons is extremely satisfying once the initial learning curve is handled. Having to manage magazines and not throw them away is something that seems like it would be a real pain but in actuality is just a matter of discipline that becomes second nature. While it seems like this complexity should hurt the gunplay, in reality It really gives each weapon a lot of personality and will have the player constantly switching weapons to suit the situation in ways that I haven't experienced in an FPS in a while. A lot of guns can get 1 hit kill headshots on typical mobs, for example, but due to how they reload and how they handle there's often a lot of reason to switch from shotgun to pistol or pistol to SMG or SMG to battleaxe all within a single encounter. 

The other thing to talk about is map design, it's very retro and classic, and all rather abstract. A lot of it reminds me of my time with Nightmare Reaper, yet with even less thematic cohesion and detail. A few places and setpiece stages really feel like real places and are quite grand at that, but most maps are literally just floating fortress mazes with no intent to even try to be anything other than an interesting gameplay space. That's fine. The map design has some rough spots but by and large I have enjoyed all of the maps. With only a few exceptions I haven't had to do a lot of back-tracking after clearing the stage. Another thing is that due to how the game is built, maps are often exceedingly open ended for a retro-shooter. You sometimes will feel that you're climbing your way out of the map where you can cheese enemies, but for sure the dev has anticipated all of this. You simply have a lot of options. 

As far as the story, it's there, there is some interesting lore and nice NPC encounters. It ends up being rather somber and moody, far more engaging that I went in expecting given how sortof almost haphazardly things are laid out in the actual game world. I won't get into any of it here but the text is sufficiently well written and engaging that I tried to pay attention despite it not being the sort of story I generally would care about. At the same time I never felt bad or like I was missing vital context if I didn't quite get all what was going on and just kept moving forward. It actually does a good job of establishing a lot of context for why the game is what it is if you do pay attention. It didn't have to be as detailed as it is. But it doesn't drown the player with reams of diary entries or other logs either, so I appreciate that. 

Overall, 8/10 FPS as I played it. I want to see more from this creator and I would like to see other game devs take note of some of these systems.

[h2]Gameplay & Difficulty[/h2]
Coming fresh off Wolfenstein 2, Beyond Citadel's shooter gameplay was much more to my taste. Its strength is that it's not so much a test of dexterity and twitch reflexes, but resource management, positioning and conservation. In twitch shooters, any enemy can kill you in an instant, but the best counter-strategy will be to just kill them faster. In Beyond Citadel, you can tank hits from almost any enemy, but over the whole level your mistakes will add up and send you to a game over.

At least, this is how the game plays out until you accumulate most of the upgrades and a big stockpile of extra lives, where upon much of the tension dilutes and the game becomes significantly easy, only avoiding becoming trivial thanks to the huge enemy roster, requiring a varied use of your arsenal. The cherry on the cake is how the last chapter introduces a wallrun mechanic, which is rendered moot by the Xeta rifle's grappling hook introduced earlier that lets you skip the wallrun obstacle course and every other outdoor area in the chapter.

[h2]Gun controls[/h2]
I really appreciated the detailed gun controls. They're in a sweet spot where they're tricky but still intuitive and forgiving. The result is that you feel clever and more masterful when you use your guns well, and the tension when reloading and the importance of positioning is amplified. I think they still could have gone further with the constraints though, like no auto magazine refilling. With how I played the game, I never needed more than one spare magazine.

[h2]Visuals[/h2]
My first impression of the visuals is that they were a bit too lo-fi—the environments especially featuring a lot of tiling textures and very primitive lighting, but it grew on me. There were quite a few stunning bits of scenery and some really extraordinary level design (and some stinkers too, however)

[h2]Narrative & Vibe[/h2]
The way the story was drip fed via dialogues and loading screen tips was very effective. It made me feel like I was piecing everything together and really gave me room to imagine what this world and its history were like outside of the missions.

The religious elements elevate the vibe of the game quite a lot. The themes of sacrifice and persecution are felt throughout the game, from the Martyr's story down to the lore of individual enemies, and even in the horrific results of combat, where your mutilated foes gasp their final breaths. Beyond Citadel renders a unique vibe of brutality, melancholy and devotion unlike any I've experienced before.

The game appears to be a standard retro shooter with echoes of Marathon at first glance, but it soon reveals mechanics that make it a far more tactical affair than the usual lighting fast jump/strafe/shoot offerings. Most notable is how each gun handles differently in terms of how reloading works - for example when you empty a handgun magazine you must first eject the magazine, load a new one and rack the slide as 3 separate actions. While this may sound a bit much, it adds a significant amount of additional engagement to the moment to moment gameplay and the guns I've used so far feel distinct and satisfying to use. There are simplified modes that make the guns handle more like a standard FPS but as the main USP it's worth at least attempting to engage with it - it soon becomes second nature and feels really cool. "Tactical retro shooter" is lazy shorthand for what this game offers but if that sounds like something you would enjoy, I recommend you give Beyond Citadel a whirl.

The ammo and magazine management places a lot of responsibility in the player's hand. The game's trust that the player will develop muscle memory to execute multi-button reloads and un-jamming actions sucks the player into this more tactical sequel. [i]Beyond Citadel's[/i] mechanics add much needed complexity to the genre. These features feel obtuse at first blush, but the game guides players along, pitting the them against easy enemies and bosses in the beginning, and steadily raises the difficulty each act to push the player's skillset further.

The hardest difficulty is punishing, but the cryo checkpoint system evens it out. There are more NPC characters, used to restock valuable resources, and a new perk system to customize your build. Already, this feels like an experience worth replaying. Add to that the developer's regular patch schedule, and player can expect a truly impressive, fine-tuned experience.

Even if the aesthetics live outside your niche, I fully recommend this for any and all, retro and current FPS fans.

Beneath the blood and guts, [b]Beyond[/b] Citadel is an apt name for an expansion upon the original's unique style. Boasting more weapons, new abilities, and over three dozen enemy types across over fifty levels, the world of Citadel has much to offer provided you can successfully acclimate to (or reconfigure) the game.

Your first gun, for example, is a .50 cal lever-action cavalry carbine which may be the perfect introductory weapon since it feeds the first new detail to the player, provided they allow it - manually cycling the action. In BC, you can rack the charging handle of every weapon manually, be it to chamber a new round, clear jams, or even simply eject cartridges to empty the weapon. It's neat to pick up the live rounds again and put them back in the pool and a neat way to add flavor to something that you normally autopilot through.

Bolt actions, pump shotguns, lever actions, and reload animations are practically mandated pauses in shooting where you wait for an animation to finish, but if you allow it, Beyond Citadel puts them into your hands. Instead of hitting R and sprinting around an arena while the animation plays, suddenly it's on you to actually load the gun. Suddenly it's on you to remember how to unjam the weapon, or to chamber the next round, or to be mindful about your spare mags. It's optional, but it's got a way of connecting you to your guns.

It's also got a way of encouraging you to use more weapons. Rush through your reloads, waste your spare mags, never retrieve them, and suddenly you have more ammo than you have mags. Eventually you might have to remove a magazine, wait for it to refill, and [i]then[/i] reload the gun - and you might not have time to wait. That, or you'll have used that gun so heavily non-stop, never repairing it, and it'll just flat-out break, exploding in your hands.

Granular weapon handling is a peculiar thing to have in a game like Citadel, yet strange as it was, I felt like it worked really well and find it hard to picture the game without it. Detailed gun mechanics are consistent with the detailed art and gore of Citadel, which need no reintroduction. It's unique, yet natural, and even in a sense as it applies to retro gaming which, in their own ways, often had some strange level of granularity or depth to them.

Beyond Citadel is like when you order a pizza with all the wrong toppings. It's a tactical first person shooter with an on-the-spectrum like focus on firearm operation for it's fictional, holy, post-apocalyptic anime weapons , the basis of which is all for the most part based on actual ballistic weapons. This means that not only to you have to maintain these space guns (this is actually isn't that involved) but each gun has to be operated differently based on it's feeding mechanism. Open bolt belt fed guns need to be charged as do magazine fed guns (IF there isn't a bullet in the chamber), shotguns need to be pumped. and bolts need to be cycled etc. The guns can fail to extract and need to be un-jammed. Enemies have to be led at a distance. You have to account for bullet drop at long, long distance.  All this seemingly at odds with a Doom Eternal like, RPG-lite system that gives you double-dashes and speed upgrades - but some how it works and feels rewarding once you get into the swing of things.

All this behind an, at some points, questionably translated religious, post-apocalyptic anime backdrop. The anime art style...this is kind of tricky to put into words...when they're 'chilling at home' and not fighting is quite crude and clashes kind of hard with everything else that is happening in the world, but when everybody is suited up and fighting to death on the battlefield everything works quite well, and there is some really sick sprite work on offer.  The particles exploding around everywhere as high calibre rounds pierce armor and flesh sending sparks and blood in the air to reveal a torn apart anime girl...is strange - but like in a good way.

I'm rambling here, if you're not sold - i'll just say; this is worth 20 bucks just to experience something totally unhinged from one dude, that had no outside editing at any point.  I'd love to see this guy working with a musical composer/ sound team on the next one.

Beyond Citadel is the sequel to 2020’s The Citadel, a doom-esque FPS shooter with 2.5D graphics, a surprisingly deep weapon mechanic system, and an uncomfortable affinity for anime girls.  You play as The Martyr, the last resort of the Seven Angels, guardians of humankind, that is led by a mysterious signal to overthrow the seven Trumpeters of the Apocalypse.  It’s your job to save the world from impending doom, and boy howdy will you have the tools to do so.

Beyond Citadel basks in its love for its weaponry.  There are over 2 dozen weapons to choose from and each feels like it's been given a level of care often rescinded in other titles.  While it takes some time to get used to it, the eject-reload-cock button combo of each gun really heightens the tension and visceral feel of each weapon, whether it be slapping in shotgun shells and pumping for your next kill or releasing a mag quickly to pull a freshly loaded one into your assault rifle, to sliding spent cartridges out of your .50 cal Whalegun after each shot.  There’s a lot of time and effort put into this and it shows on every shot fired.

Guns in this world, much like everything around you, can be put into disarray and you’ll have to handle deterioration of your guns after extended use.  Certain enemies will drop repair pieces to help keep your guns in tip-top shape, but eventually you’ll deal with a jam, which is violently fixed by frantically cocking your weapon to get the jam out.  The first few times this happens in a fight, you’re terrified because it’s not in your mental rhythm of slinging rounds, but your foes don’t care and you better fix it quickly or swap weapons.  

While the guns feel good, the movement is right on par, making the gameplay loop of Beyond Citadel enjoyably refreshing and rewarding.  DOOM fans of old will be very used to the style of movement, which holds double jumps, double dashes, and corner peeking.  Firefights are fast and frantic, and a frenetic pace is commonplace amongst the near 40 levels to traverse through.  For some players, a great gameplay loop is all that is needed to enjoy themselves, but I would be remiss if I didn’t note just about everything else that is going on in Beyond Citadel, because there is a whole bag of mixed emotions to go along with everything nice said above.

I’ve seen the term “gooner shooter” being thrown around amongst forums regarding Beyond Citadel and I hate that I can’t think of a better term.  The Martyr is, well, scantily clad to say the least, entering combat with about as much thread to tie a couple shoes together.  I refuse to elaborate on the secret art you can find in each level, but just know art pieces like Interrogation 1 and 2 just weren't for me.  Your enemies, coated in much more armor than you, are anime girls all the same and you’ll know what they look like due to the hyper-violence Beyond Citadel instills in every bullet.  Headshots will blow through helmets, leaving rolled back eyes in crumbled messes after blood-curdling screams and gurgles.  Shots to the chest will leave enemies on the ground weakly palpitating for their last breaths until they succumb to their wounds or you instill Rule #2 from Zombieland.  Shots to the stomach will leave enemies trying to keep their intestines from flooding out while trying desperately to get final shots at you before dying.

It’s…unnerving, uncomfortable, and slightly perverse in its detail.  You are dealing with the fact that it’s you or them, but in no case did I ever feel great when killing any of these enemies knowing it’s been coded and developed for me to hear exactly how bad getting hit by any of these guns can be.  When you die, you have instances where you’re ripped in half and your last moments are seeing the bottom half of your body ripped from you, insides oozed out for the enemies to continue beating on your soon-to-be-corpse.  Seeing the gore and viscera with long-dead eyes staring back at me from heads separated from their spine and their internal remains spewed across the cold floor did not make me feel well.  It’s not a slight on the game, but if that is what it wanted: it certainly did its job.

There are some fun instances of level design, especially when corridors get tight and snap shooting is necessary to leave with a clean bill of health.  But Beyond Citadel will open its levels to great lengths, and the bigger the level the worse the experience I had.  A lot of your time will be spent avoiding enemy fire to get close enough to use the weapons you can or want, and this is done naturally in other levels at a much better pace.  These later, bigger levels suffer from extending level length by succumbing you to the “find 4 to proceed” trope that no level benefits from and serves only as an obstacle to add more enemies in front of you or drag your face across every inch of the level to find the one switch you’re missing.  Some levels have multiple rooms that will increase some levels by 10-20 minutes which feels like an eternity.

Beyond Citadel also suffers from a lack of cohesion between levels.  There is clearly a lot the developer wanted to do with this game, but the whiplash between levels in a specific zone feels disjointed.  There’s no real reason as to why certain levels couldn’t all be meshed together in a single zone but you’ll go from claustrophobic corridor corner shooting with a shotgun to play peek-a-boo with snipers and mortars in wide open spaces to city-spanning mech levels against hundreds of enemies.  Playing to a specific mechanic or leaning into a certain style of area could allow certain weapons to flourish or give the player an opportunity to focus on a specific obstacle and master it; you could blend all these mechanics into later levels to allow the progression of the player to shine against a tough-built level, but none of this is really brought to fruition.

But nothing disappoints more than the final zone and in turn, the ending of Beyond Citadel.  Once you have disposed of what in all intents and purposes felt like the final boss, you are then fed into a final “Epilogue” zone that is twice as long as any zone you’ve played, is built entirely to be a platforming section and instills a wallrunning mechanic that is built specific for these stages only.  Why this wasn’t just slotted before the final boss confuses me still as I write this and felt like cut content that the developer just did not want to give up on, but again: cohesiveness and disjointedness throughout the game rears its ugly head.  Once this is done, the plot-specific pieces to the puzzle are slotted in, you’re greeted with a final-final boss that really isn’t, and then you’re put in a final room to choose between one of two options.  The second option isn’t really…explained?  You’re given a choice between two outcomes, but only one outcome is highlighted to do, so the illusion of choice is gone as it points to Option A like a Call of Duty campaign.  Once you do either ending, the game just…ends?  You’re given a line of text and the game returns to the Title.

There is the opportunity to do a New Game+ and explore the EX levels that are unlocked after each Zone clearance, but after 13 hours I had more than had my fill.  I hate that Beyond Citadel provides some of the snappiest and satisfying gunplay I’ve played in years as it’s surrounded by lack of cohesiveness, stability, proper decision-making, and questionable artistic choices.  There’s a fine chance that the vision Doekuramori had for Beyond Citadel was not made for tastes like mine, but turning off the Gore and avoiding having to look over your shoulder when you find a collectible doesn’t remove the abhorrent exterior surrounding a promising love for gunplay and the weapons included.

The game has a solid enough gameplay loop but the issue is that the game front-loads the management.
You will receive fixed parts/shelving per level, you cannot buy more, cannot redesign a large amount of it, many of the counters and desks have a lot of padding/spacing preventing overlap, but resulting in what feels like larger gaps. Especially with the lack of a guide/grid system for lining up shelving across from other shelves.

The gameplay is heavily focused on 'management in the moment', with each desk being it's own component, with a computer designed for a singular task. As someone who has worked in libraries, you check in and out books in the same area usually, at best having two counters at the same desk to help pace the influx. I would love some more strategy and reason to place value on having a sorting order for books, including customers putting books back in the wrong spot while browsing and any number of complications.

This means there is a lack of actual organisation and management. Say goodbye to most of your actual book ordering attempts, you get random extra books in the middle of the day instead of say; ordering in book-packs or any number of logistics based parts of running a library. Your best bet is throwing similar genres in with each other, because all other more involved types of organisation are meaningless when you are under such a time crunch.

I'd much prefer if you had to order in books depending on the flavour of the day/week and then work around the fact you might have too many of one genre and needing to figure out how to store them, while keeping them accessible in case they are requested.

Again, the game has promise and has a solid start, I plan to come back to it once the Devs have had time to develop features, but as it stands the game is entirely front-loaded, with no back-room management, logistics or organisation, consider it's current state closer to a rush/party game, than a store management simulator.

I can't remember the last time I played an 8-bit game, but this one certainly reignited the joy I felt when I used to play them. The story and art draw you in, compelling you to explore at your own pace. Meanwhile, the combat challenges you to refine your skills in reactionary battles that grow tougher the further you go. And don’t even get me started on the music! I had my fair share of losses and moments where I needed a break, but with some rest and a soundtrack that fueled me, I came back stronger, focused on the prize, and ready to launch a volley of counterattacks to claim my victory. 
Reaching the end, whether you beat the game or aim to platinum it, the rewards make the journey worthwhile. There's a deep sense of satisfaction amid the rush of adrenaline, but you'll have to experience that for yourself to truly understand. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with this game, and now, I invite you to strap in and venture into the world of S.C.C. Rusted. What a fun take on a classic! I was a little overwhelmed at first but I quickly realized it's the same old minesweeper, just with some added spice only made possible by the bizarre nature of hyperbolic planes!  I'm excited to get to know all the different settings and geometries!

Main takeaways: 
 - If you are a fan of minesweeper, you will get a lot of mileage out of this game!
 - There are a couple bugs that distracted from my experience.
 - 8 geometry options: 6 different hyperbolic tiled fields plus 2 normal tiled fields (including the classic square)
 - 2 presets of logic difficulty (Easy and Hard)
 - 6 different field sizes for each geometry

Some highlights: 
 - The game felt really fresh: the mind-bending sensation of moving around the hyperbolic fields hasn't gone away!
 - It's really improved my appreciation and understanding of hyperbolic space! (Emphasis on "improved." It still hurts my head lol)
 - The weird geometries opens up the mines to be exposed to a different number of tiles than would be possible in euclidean geometries.  I love that I can play a game of minesweeper where a heptagon tiles the plane!
 - I liked that there were so many different options I could play around with!
 - I appreciated the tutorials for some of the mechanics.
 - The different themes were fun.
 - It was fun that normal square tiled and hexagon tiled options were available to play as well. It was interesting to compare how game-play changes in a hyperbolic vs euclidean plane

Some critiques:
 - The app's response and adaptation to different window sizes on my PC was a little weird.  There was strange stretching and squashing of letters, buttons covering up different parts of my score, and text not properly responding to field orientation.
 - I may have missed it but I would love to be able to see my best times recorded for each geometry, size and difficulty level.

Again, I'm loving this fresh take on minesweeper! Thanks!

After playing The Corn Maze from Wild Wizard Studios I found that it serves as a remarkable homage to the basic but scary horror games from the past. If you ever played the classic Slenderman game, The Corn Maze serves as a spiritual successor to Slender: The Eight Pages by combining elements of tension, exploration, and survival mechanics into an intense horror experience.

The premise is straightforward but effective: The dark and creepy corn maze traps you as you navigate with just your flashlight's dim light. Your goal? Survive by gathering batteries and compasses to escape the maze while evading the threatening blue cone-headed creatures that pursue you from the shadows. The combination of sound design and restricted visibility creates intense suspense which keeps you constantly on edge while each path in the maze presents a chance for a thrilling confrontation.

I had the pleasure of meeting the solo developer behind Wild Wizard Studios at Vincon 2025, and it’s inspiring to see such a passionate creator already launching games on Steam. As a solo developer Wild Wizard Studios has created The Corn Maze which stands as a remarkable accomplishment and they are developing Fry Day which puts players in control of an old farmer battling waves of angry chickens in a top-down shooter experience. My preview of Fry Day revealed that it will be an arcade-style experience that blends humor with intense action.

The Corn Maze comes highly recommended to anyone who loves indie horror games. The Corn Maze demonstrates how simple concepts can produce exceptional horror experiences when properly executed. I can't wait to see what new projects Wild Wizard Studios develops!

[h1]Comentario Analítico: "Queen of Treasure Isle"[/h1]

Queen of Treasure Isle es un excelente Metroidvania estrenado a modo de Acceso Anticipado el 20 de Enero del 2025 de la mano de [b]gobou[/b], por quien conservo una gran estima por cuán significativo es su trabajo para quienes amamos Yume Nikki.

Es un juego excéntrico y fuertemente inspirado en un clásico de la NES llamado Altantis no Nazo.

Carece totalmente de textos, provocando que tanto los tutoriales como los debloqueables y el argumento se vea reducido a meras imágenes, lo que puede dificultar entender la finalidad de algunos objetos pero que así mismo aporta a la mística de ir descubriendo el juego y su historia poco a poco y por nuestra cuenta.

Tal y como si de un espeleólogo se tratase, es el jugador quien debe descifrar al escenario por medio de minúsculas pistas visuales que lo premian por saber iterar con las herramientas proporcionadas, y no hablo de descubrir secretos, hablo de encontrar rutas ocultas pero a su vez vitales para progresar, muy a La-Mulana. No es para nada intuitivo, cada rincón es un rompecabezas y se requiere de una mente alerta y vista aguda para encontrar caminos ocultos que pueden acabar por dotarte de un inservible coleccionable o un objeto clave.

Está planteado para ser rejugado y revisitado, y quienes lo estamos experimentando en las fechas tempranas a su estreno nos encontramos con un listado de Guias en Steam totalmente vacío. En YouTube no hay un solo canal que haya subido el juego completo, el usuario que más lejos llegó y documentó por medio de videos soy yo, seguido de un sujeto que apenas superó unas cuantas zonas antes de abandonarlo. Ahora mismo somos entre 5 y 10 gatos locos los únicos que nos comunicamos mediante las discusiones de Steam para intercambiar información respecto a rutas, objetos y jefes, tan es así que hay aspectos de los que aún no tenemos total constancia, véase el sistema de amistad entre el jugador y las brujas o el contenido del NG+.

Y ya que estamos; hoy mismo mientras jugaba se publicó una actualización para solucionar un par de conflictos de los que pocas horas antes me había quejado en las discusiones. ¡Me adjudico total responsabilidad de haber incentivado ese parche! Entre varias cosas, introdujeron Check Points en la sección más dífícil del juego apenas horas después de habérmela pasado sin éstos.

Podrá parecer que estoy reduciendo sus méritos a la condicional de ser reciente y desconocido, pero no es así; Queen of Treasure Isle sabe hacer entender al jugador que debe conservarse atento, y aún si estuviera repleto de guías seguiría siendo un excelente título.

[b]¿En conclusión?[/b] Mi madre me dio la vida y [b]gobou[/b] las ganas de vivirla.

[b]Edit:[/b] Me tomé el tiempo de escribir su primer guía, acá la adjunto para cualquier interesado.

[i]Cats Visiting Christmas Town[/i] is a fun hidden object game filled with Christmas charm and kitties to find across 5 festive maps. 

[h2][u]Gameplay & Features[/u][/h2]

Settings include; audio controls, language, vibration (on or off) and a reset game option. 

If you wish to put your game into windowed mode, put [i]-screen-width 1920 -screen-height 1080[/i] (or a resolution of your choice) under properties in the games Steam library page under launch options and relaunch the game. Then after relaunch just hit alt+enter for it to resize. 

[u]Highlights[/u]

* Relaxed or timed mode available
* Artwork is hand-drawn (a nice touch over all the AI games) that is cute and festive
* 5 festive maps for you to enjoy
* Most of the achievements are easy except the timed ones
* The cats purr when you are near one and meow when you click on them 
* Soundtrack is festive and Christmas-y
* Hint system with rechargeable hints  
* Most of the cats are easy to find as the map in not interactive, no cats hidden behind or in objects

[h2][u]Overall Experience[/u][/h2]

I think this game is charming and I really enjoyed the other game also made by [i]AGE Zero[/i] called Tiny Cats. I am not a fan of timed achievements so those are a bit of a shortcoming for me as I play these games for a relaxing experience but for some the timed mode is a highlight. 

I tried the timed mode and got by all the levels and while doable it was honestly not overly enjoyable. Just frustrating. They only give you 3 minutes, if they rounded it up to 5 then it would not be as stressful. Also do not rely on the purrs to find the cats, it just tells you a cat is in the vicinity but is not highly accurate. 

Still the price is nice and the artwork is adorable. All the cats look like cats and none are just a tail sticking up or squiggles. For those versed in this genre you know what I mean when I say this. A festive find to keep the Christmas spirit rolling in the new year. 🐈

As an Aruban who has spent the last couple years working in Casinos, I had to check this game out. If nothing else, to look for inaccuracies or misrepresentation. I think they did surprisingly well, although there was less actual casino related content than I'd expected. I have several notes.

1. Mention of Weisswurst. My German aunt traumatized me with these as a kid when we visited. A delicacy, we were told. A special treat. Truly traditional cuisine. I was the only one in my family who couldn't stomach them. Every time with those awful white sausages. I'm not saying they're the reason I haven't visited Germany in 20+ years, but they certainly don't help.

2.  $17 for two cocktails? Not in the tourism district, I can tell you that for sure.

3. During the restaurant scene, one of the characters orders "Keshi Yena Ravioli." Now, first off, it's misspelled as "Kenshi" in the game, but there's no 'n' in keshi. Starting this game, I decided immediately I would bring up keshi yena in my review, if the game didn't mention it. You did. Good on you. Gold star for research. Local dish that's way better than it sounds (I know, the list of ingredients sounds a little weird) and, although the ravioli bit isn't traditional, solid choice. Btw, "keshi yena" literally translates to "stuffed cheese" although that's not really relevant to the game.

4. Whomever came up with the Dutch names for this game was clearly being a cheeky bugger. The Hairy Beaver casino is one thing, but Femke's surname being "Moffenhoer" is fucking wild. I won't spoil the surprise of what that means; partially because I'm worried Steam would remove my review.

5. Elena is stated to work at the Casino near Royal Plaza Mall and says she started her shift at 4AM. Obviously, the Harige Bever isn't real, but the casino near Royal Plaza is the only one on the island with 24 hour tables where a dealer shift starting at 4AM would be possible. Either staggering coincidence or the writer really knows their Aruban casinos.

6. When the protagonists are discussing how to launder their money, they bring up 'structuring deposits' and buying art and it made me feel like the person who wrote this has had to sit through the same mandatory anti-money laundering courses I've sat through at work. Only thing missing was mention of nuclear arms proliferation. God only knows why the government thinks anybody would be trying to fund nuclear arms proliferation on Aruba, but we have to learn about it every 6 months. Settling on jewelry (and knowing about all the jewelers on main street) is... well... I ain't saying nothing, but... you know... rumors exist. Alleged rumors.

7. Gerhard mentions he doesn't understand what the old men in the local bar are saying, but we don't actually get any dialogue from those old men. This would've been a good moment for some cheeky Papiamento (the local language) to be thrown in. Nobody would understand it anyway. Well, almost nobody.

8. There's just one thing that felt really unrealistic: Femke looks up her old contacts on the island after a year and manages to stay under the radar. Nah, no way. People talk here. You show up again after a year and visit one old friend, half the island knows you're here by the end of the day.

All in all, pretty fun visual novel. I think the third(?) I've played by Little Black Book and I always got the impression they did their homework about the places and people they feature in their games. Can't speak for the UK parts of the game, but the Aruba knowledge was surprisingly accurate.

** DISCLAIMER: While I am not financially tied to this game this review comes with a personal bias in which I think the developers behind this game are great people. With that, I will try to be as honest as possible in my review. **

Summary:
A great pickup for its price if you like experimenting with class combinations and min-maxing your damage output engine to see "number go up" while being able to ignore some of the rougher edges with regards to polish and in-game clarity.

Review:
Gnaw & Order is a rogue-like auto-battler that excels in its replay-ability by exploring interesting systems via rats armed to the teeth with abilities that burst and explode light a fiery wasteland V8 (or V16 after enough upgrades). You start slow and steady learning the mechanics through text explanations and gameplay as you're introduced to all of the available rat classes right out of the gate. Each rat you find can combine with rats of the same class to unlock their next tier that includes an additional skill tree. This essentially gives each rat x 3 skill trees to explore which is around 30 classes to level into. Items will drop that you can equip, sell or combine, and tokens will allow you to open packs that include said items or gear abilities that can eventually combined to improve other abilities. There's even a stock market that you can monitor to sell your equipment at the opportune moment. If that sounds like a lot, that's because it is as these systems can be a tad overwhelming at times. While I found myself greatly enjoying the ability to experiment and uncover synergies, I had many unanswered questions about my damage output, visual clarity regarding the abilities that were triggering and other keywords that were presented via text in abilities. The developers have been able to include clarity over the course of the recent patches, but even after my time playing, there's a lot to be desired there. At times the engine will stop visualizing the abilities that trigger and the numbers flying in front of the enemies can't help you identify what character is doing damage or what those numbers are when things really snowball. This can also greatly hinder someone who is curious and wants to dive deep into the genuinely interesting mechanics and synergies included in Gnaw & Order.

Visually, the game plays to it strengths and provides a lot of UI-embedded feedback vs many onscreen animations. The setting is clear and enticing to get you going, but a lot of the creatures of the wasteland and the main rat characters themselves seem very loosely tied together as there is no story to uncover beyond flavor text given at the beginning and the bad guy waiting for you at a later wave (to avoid spoilers). With respect to sound and music design, the bare minimums are there, but unfortunately the soundtrack gets old quickly after a run or two. Audio feedback while navigating menus and during combat are solid.

Lastly, I genuinely mean this when I say, this game has so much potential and I would recommend you give a shot if you have $5 and a few hours to kill after work. I found myself addicted to figuring out how to deal as much damage as possible. Whether I'm building my favorite "Money Crit" build with the Entrepreneur, Gambler, and Mechanic or a wacky "Fire + Poison + Drug Addict(!?)" build, I'm still trying to find ways to combine all of these abilities into a perfect storm and watch the enemies' health bars pop like balloons wave after wave. If you can get past the rough edges, the lack of clarity, and trust your guts on how the abilities work, I guarantee you'll have a good time with this game.

I'm sad that my review is the first one, because this is a very good psychological horror game and I had quite a bit of fun with it. The exploration-based gameplay and the mysterious plot are intriguing, while the artstyle and the sound design create a compelling atmosphere.

You are (almost) alone in a big mansion and have to piece together hints, both physical and supernatural, through exploration and puzzle-solving, to understand what happened to Lydia and her family. 
I appreciated how you are given complete freedom to explore from the beginning, you can wander through the many many rooms as you wish and can solve the puzzles in any order.

There is a permadeath element (though it's not present in the easy mode), as you have to restart if the monster catches you, but it's not as oppressing as other stalker enemies in most horror games, since most of the time you'll be able to see the monster when you enter a room and just find another route. 
Even if it sees you and you can't find a hiding place, there's a "last chance" system where you and it throw a dice and if you win you can continue escaping. Exploration (and memorizing the mansion layout) is important because you can find several items that give you a permanent boost to speed, stamina and to the luck you need for the dice throwing. 

There are also several cool little touches and hidden secrets (even a retro fantasy shmup you can play within the game) which are further proof of how the game was developed with care and passion.

(Last edited: Fish Clicker Update)

First, you need to know that there's a free version of the game, and this is the remake of that. Both are the same game at its core. Look at the vids and screenshots of both games; they showcase actual game content, so you can see what to expect.

For those who have played the original (free) version, I'm going to point out what's different in the remake by splitting it into three categories: [b]changes, new content, and scrapped content[/b]. I've 100%-ed both games, so I'm confident I've seen most of the content (if not everything) that both games are offering.

[b]Changes:[/b]

- Recast leans more towards the incremental aspect of the game compared to the original (which kinda feels more like an idler). This means making money by leaving the game completely unattended is much harder. It's still a side activity game; you just need to click in more frequently now.
- The Pavilion DLC is now a part of the base game with a new multiplier system to increase the reward.
- Rebalancing of various item costs and effects. Imo most of them are good, but YMMV.
- Some things have been renamed. For example, the Swedish Fish.
- Baits have been changed into only a single kind; it lets you catch items in large numbers.
- You can now eat every fish and spread the upgrade points to any available stat of your liking.
- The Hatchery now lets you customize three slots instead of two (it only keeps the sun fish slot as non-customizable).
- Improved Fight mode with the newly introduced fishing gear and drop rate system.
- The Swimmer no longer has a health system nor obstacles to kill you, so it's easier to farm. But the bar is smaller, and you can no longer phase through the sides to reach the opposite ends.
- Changes on the visuals in general. Recast is running on Godot while the original is on Unity, so a lot of readjustments were made. If you think Recast is kinda lacking in the sprite department, that's because the dev said the sprite artists had moved on to bigger jobs. If you think the font is smaller or outright unreadable, the dev is currently looking at the issue. If you think there's a lot of empty spaces in some areas and too much clutter in other areas, well... Imho the visuals are mostly a downgrade from the original, but again, YMMV.
- The Fish Clicker is back with new passive trinket system. It still relies on limited events.

[b]New content:[/b]

- New offline resource gain feature by the means of a net, which is upgradeable in the Workshop.
- New endgame map and mechanics to sink your resources into, plus a new NPC. Check the vid and the screenshots.
- New collection tracker and some lore (or "flavor texts" according to the dev).
- New title system to replace your fisher name.
- Boosts: temporary power-ups that will speed up your timer.
- Lootboxes in the Market! No, it won't cost you real money (you're already paying for this game). They contain resources to help with your progress.
- More achievements than the original.
- A new feature related to the black orb (won't spoil).
- Supposedly a better save system (I don't see the difference from the old one, though).

[b]Scrapped content:[/b]

[strike]- The Fish Clicker.[/strike] It's added now.
- That little shell-hunting game.
- That little bit with Sam.
- The Abyss (you know what it is if you've 100%-ed the original).

Now, my [u]personal[/u] verdict.

Do I think this remake is an improvement of the original? Yes.
Do I recommend this game? Yes.
Do I prefer this version more than the original? Sadly, no. Not because it's bad, just a personal preference.

Pacifish Recast is a well-made incremental game and definitely performs better as that kind of game than the original. Just like the original, it's a fun game to keep as a side activity when doing something else. The reason why I prefer the original over Recast is because I was looking for an idle game when I picked up the original Pacifish. The original is a better idler, visually better, and I have access to the scrapped content, which I actually like (not the Fish Clicker, though; sorry, clicker lovers). [Edit: The Fish Clicker is now in Recast. My opinion about it is still unchanged.] Obviously, the issue lies in my personal taste and not the remake.

So if you want more automation/idler, play the original.
If you want more incrementals play Recast.
If you enjoy the work of this dev and just wanna support him because he's just a chill dude and willing to listen to feedback, consider buying whatever he has to offer.

You got yourself a hub town and you got yourself some dungeon delving, go out and grind. So far it has been a lovely experience, especially at the price point. The graphics are done in a voxel style which I've always been a big fan of so if you like the charm that has to offer you'll be on board. So far my only request to the dev would be to please put an auto-battle feature. The combat reminds me of a Dragon Quest or Earthbound and I think it could really help the whole of the time spent, since grinding is so needed to have a feature such as that. If you enjoyed Boot Hill Heroes, if you enjoyed Wild Arms this is a unique opportunity to pick up something else that has that same panache but with its own twists. The game is somewhat like billiards, but with obstacles such as spikes that are eager to shred your ball on its way to the hole. However, sinking the ball into a hole doesn’t mean victory—it’s just one step in a journey through a labyrinth of interconnected holes you must navigate with a limited number of lives. And the labyrinth isn’t small, by the way—here’s how it looks when zoomed out: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3421552764

Luckily, there are checkpoint holes, and you can find health kits along the way to restore your ball’s durability. If things get too tough, you can use a hint that sketches a trajectory for your ball, like this: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3421552994

But these hints don’t always solve the problem. Even if you align the shot pixel-perfectly, there’s no guarantee the ball will follow the path. On top of that, moving mechanisms, shifting platforms, and magnets that alter the ball’s trajectory can throw you off. It’s the kind of game that really makes you rack your brain! And trust me—it’s totally worth the money!

I think those who are fans of Vampire survivors or similar titles will probably get quite a bit of enjoyment out of it.

Scary World is a very focused Bullet Heaven in the spirit of Vampire Survivors.

A wall of lava drives you ever to the right on the game's single map. Your goal: To power up enough before it forces you to fight the boss that awaits at the end. If you defeat it, a portal opens that takes you back to the map's beginning, now with stronger enemies. If you play defensively from here, you'll soon have beaten the "official" objective of surviving for 10 minutes.

The game explains little of its mechanics, and so it highly rewards you for paying attention to and learning them (e.g. bonuses you trigger), as well as the map's layout.

The streamlined design makes Scary World feel very unique in a saturated genre.


Late disclaimer: I have only beaten the minimal challenge of surviving for 10 minutes a couple of times, and only on the lowest difficulty. 
The game may well expand past that point. I can't say if I would like that better or worse.

Still cutting my teeth with it, but if you're remotely familiar with the style of Vampire Survivors, you can see 2.5 hours being a decent chunk of time for these types of games.

In current state, I do not recommend it.

It wants to be different which I respect, but in doing so it removes essential elements that are needed in games like this:

- re-roll option(s) for items.
- unique passives.
- some form of a small leveling system for each character.

The game in it current state is unbalanced and where I should feel pretty strong with a Level 5+ item; it does nothing at all different to make me feel like I'm causing an impact.

A small game that has a lot to offer. I really liked the retro style but with an innovative twist, with some elements that catch the eye and are very pleasing overall.

Especially the early stages of the game can seem a bit difficult and punishing, but I think it's quite usual for a roguelike. 

As far as I've seen to date I only point out a slight general balancing problem. In the moment that I'm writing the game has only the English language, but it remains enjoyable having little text.

I close with a special mention for the atmosphere, which between game rhythm, musical accompaniment and settings I find really well done.

The Rogue of Nexus, if experienced for what it is, can offer hours of fun (I would like to say lighthearted but I assure you it's not). A pleasant discovery at the right price.
