So my PS3 stopped working a while ago and one of the games I had was this little indie game that was published by Sqaure Enix. I remember it was good but thought the flash game of it was better(Which I don’t think you can play anymore) and I even gotten the graphic novel of it cause I liked the art of it. Too bad the story just stops after the city and doesn’t conclude the whole mystery man thing. Wanting to play it again, I got it on Steam so lets see if it’s good?
Story:

One night, a garbage truck dumps a little girl on a peninsula where she is founded and adopted by an Octopus named Blister who finds her clothes, builds her a house and names her Scarygirl. Lately she starts having dreams of a strange man and finds a Guru Bunny under her house who tells her the answers are in a place called Bad City.

And that’s all the plot from the book we’re getting as the actual plot of this game is that the forest is dying and Scarygirl looks for the Tree of Knowledge for answers.

If you never “read” the book, you probably won’t mind the story that’s presented here. But if you have, then some story bits may leave you confused or annoyed . First is that we have to help Tree of Knowledge or the forest would die. Problem is that in the book he was a villain who was going eat Scarygirl before Blister kills him.

The second was the placement of the sewer level cause in the book, she meets a giant in the sewer who gives her a helmet to breath underwater. We don’t get this helmet until after the ocean level which makes no sense for both story and gameplay.  Don’t see why we could just go through the gate to the city normally and do Bad City first and save the sewers for later.

And finally, that mystery man in her dreams is never properly explained. We meet the guy at the end of the game, but the reason he appears in Scarygirl’s dream doesn’t come up. Instead we have to make a deal with him which leads to a different ending and a toy being unlocked in the shop. And since there are three endings, you need to do the last level three times to buy the last few extra toys.

I think it would’ve been better if they just stuck to finding out who the mystery man was cause that was the interesting plot hook. Not finding out why the tress are dying.

Also there was a pair of DLC levels on consoles about Scarygirl getting possessed by a ghost but they weren’t on Steam.
Gameplay:

Ever played Earthworm Jim? The basic controls are similar to that game with using your tentacle arm to swing with hooks and hover to slow down your descent. That’s where the similarities end as instead of shooting things, it’s a 2D beat-em up with combos, block and maybe counter if timed well, a grab for stunned enemies and even a rage mode that can kill almost everything in a few seconds. There’s even a few swimming sections and they aren’t too bad either.

Combat is simple enough for the most part with some simple combos and enemies that have a gimmick or two like giving you poison or flying around. Sure you are forced into combat a few spaces but it only gets annoying later when enemies with more health start showing up, but sometimes you can just use your rage mode to clean everything up.

Until we get to Guards. These are one of the worst, most annoying enemies I have ever faced and they are almost everywhere in the second half of the game. These blue jerks have long swords, spears, etc, have lots of health and can block you. In fact they are the only enemies that block your attack in the entire game. And if you think you could just hover over them and attack them from behind, they’ll hit you in the air so that’s out. If this was to encourage me to engage in the combat more, it failed as I was never thought how to guard break and I just spammed the combo that summons a bunch of tentacles from the ground since it has some reach.

Levels are the simple get to the end variety, though it since there’s no exit sign or anything, some level might feel like they just end. There some bull-crap in some levels like not having the air helmet for the underwater level or the instant death traffic in the city, but those are few mainly towards the end of the game and very early in those levels. To help, you find gems in every level that you can use in shops to buy new moves, hooks with their own buffs like longer glides or slower attacks for more damage, and little figures to display in the tree-house. Though you might want to hold off getting the figures until after beating the game as playing normally, you’ll barely have enough to buy all the moves or even all the hooks.

Though if I can address a nitpick I have, it’s the odd pacing of the bosses as well as the final boss itself. Now for the first two worlds, it seems fine. Got three levels per world and a boss at the end. Then we do world 3 and there’s no boss. World 4 is normal but World 5 has it’s boss on level 2(which is followed by my least favorite level since it’s nothing but forced combat in a small space with some of the more annoying enemies), world 6 is another world with no boss then in the final world, the second level is just a boss fight while the final level has a half-assed boss rush since it’s just the 1 and 5 bosses as well as the most boring boss fight in the game. Not with the guy who appears in Scarygirl’s dreams, who the level is named after and is shown riding a sort of mech suit in one level. But a random enemy spawning machine that doesn’t even look that good. So no final battle against the main villain.
Presentation:

Music is more ambient than anything, but some of the tunes do have a nice melody to them and one or two might get stuck in your head.

The art looks really good.  It may be 2D but it’s taking advantage of it’s 3D graphics with it’s camera views and the pathway twisting and turning. And even bland locations like dark woods and sewers look lovely. I don’t know how to explain the character art. I absolutely love it with with it’s skeleton vultures, beggars that look like robot armadillos, octopuses wearing mask and snakes with owl heads. If there’s one reason to play this game, it’s to see the art.
Verdict:

It’s got gorgeous art and some decent platforming, but the odd story decisions, late game combat and the final boss hold it back.

[b][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/202750/Alan_Wakes_American_Nightmare/]Alan Wake's American Nightmare[/url][/b] is an excellent continuation of [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/108710/Alan_Wake/]Alan Wake[/url], taking place two years after the original game. Alan is still trapped in the Dark Place beneath Cauldron Lake, struggling to escape.

In this installment, the game unfolds like an episode of Night Springs, the fictional TV show from the original game. One night, while Alan's friend and manager, Barry, sleeps, an episode written and starring Alan airs. As you guide Alan through the bizarre events of Night Springs, you'll also confront his doppelganger and worst enemy, Mr. Scratch.

The game is relatively short but packed with fun. It features three main levels to explore that are bound in a time loop, alongside ten [i]Fight Till Dawn[/i] arcade-style challenges where you fight waves of The Taken until sunrise. The game is more action-oriented than its predecessor, but fits perfectly as a third special episode of Alan Wake and is an enjoyment to play!

I played and completed [b]Alan Wake's American Nightmare[/b] on the [URL=https://store.steampowered.com/steamdeck/]Steam Deck[/url], and I highly recommend it to all fans of the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/108710/Alan_Wake/]Alan Wake[/url] series - [i]just be sure to play the original game and its two special episodes first, or it won't make sense![/i]

This is a neutral review. 

Binary Domain is a mediocre sci fi shooter/action game where you have to save the world from over zealous AI. So the story is ok. The characters and dialogue are ok but nothing memorable. I liked how you can upgrade not only your gear ( main weapon, resistances, gadgets ) but also the gear of the companions. 

It's not precise to define this game as FPS only. It's actually a hybrid between a shooter and an action game (Prince of Persia style). There are parts of the game where it plays like a classic FPS, and parts where you have to pass certain scripted action sequences. The game is non stop action. It never has a dull moment, so yes it's adrenalinic, but it's also frustrating. Why frustrating? 

Because this is a console port. Binary Domain was primarily made for XBOX and Playstation, and later for PC. Combat, game mechanics and everything else are clearly optimized for consoles and for a game controler, and NOT for keyboard and mouse. That fact brings many little problems that are frustrating but luckily do not prevent game completion. Examples: 
- the key buttons for sprinting and for taking cover is the same. Often when I would have to flee from a difficult enemy the main character would take cover over and over instead of running away from danger. Often it would mean defeat and re-loading. 
- the key buttons for the special power and for reloading weapon is the same. That means everytime you want to use your special power the main character reloads the weapon, which consumes ammo very quickly. And ammo is limited of course. 
- Some times in the scripted action sequences it wasn't clear what I had to do to pass them. The game didn't make clear enough what buttons to use ( it showed some strange symbols, maybe for game controllers ), so I would often frantically button mash until I would understand what is required of me. So the game mechanics and controls are poor, archaic. 
- there is a fight when you are in control of a goliath robot and have to repel enemies that come from all sides. They didn't optimize mouse sensitivity well so it was very slow to turn the cannon 360 degrees. So I had to retry until I was able to find the right sequence of turning left or right in order to kill enemies before they killed me. 
Those are just a few examples or how this game is not optimized for a PC. 

I liked the game in the beginning, then when you hit midgame it practically becomes a non stop boss fight. Some boss fights are objectively hard and frustrating. They revolve around targetting the only weak spot the bosses have. And since the bosses move around quickly it's not easy to hit those spots ( and minions do spawn contantly ). There was especially one incredibly brutal boss fight that nearly made me quit the game. So I went to youtube to see the only way it can be done. 

I also didn't like how the game experiments with voice commands. The companions from time to time ask you questions and the game expects you to answer vocally. But voice recognition wasn't implemented properly. You can switch to key button replies but it also doesn't work well, and you have limited time to answer. If you fail to answer you lose influence with companions, and influence is important story wise. You also lose influence if you accidentally shoot them - and that happened often, not because of my mistakes, but because they would often stand and run between me and the enemies. Also they get angry and decrease "faith" in you randomly if you don't play fights perfectly enough, which annoyed me. 

To conclude, it's fun but also full of little frustrating imperfections due to it being a console port. It's also a little ridiculous how they blatantly copied many elements of Mass Effect 1.

[b]Sophie’s Choice[/b]

Games are great, I love them all, from hard core strategy through to frantic FPS action, but if I had to pick my least favorite genre.... well... it’s like asking a parent who their least favorite child is, it’s not an easy question to answer and you’ll almost certainly get the generic “I love them all equally”  reply.

That’s the easy way out; the problem is that it almost certainly isn’t true.


[b]Gaming Bones[/b]

Deep down we know the answer, even if we don’t want to admit it to ourselves, but I’ll be brave, I’m going to take a stand for absolute honesty.

My least favourite genre is probably the puzzler, that’s not to say that I haven’t sunk plenty of hours into playing them over the years, but they just don’t grab me like other genres do.

They’re just too shallow, too casual, they’re fine for killing time on my phone or tablet during a commute but when I’m at home and looking for a gaming fix  it’s rare that you’ll find me sitting in front of my PC playing Peggle or Tetris.

That’s not to say that I don’t enjoy puzzlers, but when I’ve got the gaming itch and enough time to indulge it properly, I like a little more meat on my gaming bones.


[b]Monster Connoisseur[/b]

Monster movies are great; I love them all, from werewolves and vampires through to undersea kraken and outer space aliens, but if I had to pick my absolute favourite movie monster genre, it’d have to be zombies

I’ve exposed myself to so much zombie culture over the years that I can’t walk through a shopping centre or mall without thoughts of Dawn of the Dead playing through my mind.

Could the undead break through those glass doors? How long would the cakes and cookies in Starbucks stave off my hunger?  Would I really be lucky enough to be in a mall when the zombie apocalypse strikes?

These are the sorts of questions that keep me up at night but rarely do I have the same thoughts about other supernatural beasties.       If I’m out at night and there’s a full moon, I don’t check my pockets for silver bullets.
On the rare occasion that I’ve seen a bat, I don’t reach for the crucifix and the garlic.

Werewolves and Vampires don’t stalk my waking thoughts but zombies...  the “what if” of the undead apocalypse is always there, shambling beneath the surface of my mind.... but enough of my problems...


[b]Apathetic Fanatic[/b]

Seemingly random questions at the start of reviews are great, but why am I sharing my aversion to puzzle games and my unhealthy zombie obsession?
It’s because these particular personal preferences have presented me with a dilemma.
You see  I’m about to play through a game called “Containment”, a zombie themed puzzler which means I should both love it and be completely disinterested at the same time...  


[b]Survival Flavour[/b]

Containment certainly takes an interesting twist on the puzzle genre, instead of having colourful gems, blocks, fruits etc. to play with, here your puzzle pieces are zombies and survivors.
The survivors themselves come in various different flavours from chainsaw wielding punks to gun toting cops.
Each level presents you with a block of these survivors and some zombies mixed in for good measure. If you do nothing the zombies will infect the survivors around them, turning them into zombies too!

This encourages you to play through quickly, spend too much time mulling over your decisions and your group of survivors will turn into a shambling horde, so expect some frantic and rushed decision making as you play.


[b]Shuffle Around[/b]

The game mechanic itself is a fairly simple one, you swap the positions of the different survivors by clicking on them, and your goal is to reposition the survivors in such a way that a zombie is surrounded by the same survivor type.

So if you’ve got a zombie that already has a couple of redneck survivors standing next to it, you’d quickly want to scan the closest survivors for more rednecks, if there are some close by, you’d start clicking on them to slide them into position around the zombie.
As soon as our red necked buddies have the walker surrounded, they’ll take it down.
That’s one less to worry about, time to move on to the next.
It’s a simple rinse and repeat formula that makes this, like most other puzzle games, quick to learn, initially addictive but ultimately a little repetitive.


[b]Touches[/b]

There are lots of nice touches in Containment.
Different survivors have different attack animations when they take down a zombie, it’s a fairly simple thing, but this variation really does add to the experience, you’ll find yourself looking forward to taking a zombie out with a group of survivors you haven’t “experienced” yet.

When you complete a level, instead of the screen fading to black then loading in the next challenge, the camera will move away from your last victory and rush through the city until it focuses on the next group of survivors waiting for your point and click salvation.


[b]Migraine Free[/b]

With regards to the aesthetics, it’s refreshing to play a puzzler that isn’t all bright primary coloured eye candy and flashing lights.
Containment knows its setting and has a palette appropriate for its post apocalyptic theme.
Everything is pretty good looking too in its own top down, mostly static kind of way.


[b]This isn’t just any puzzle game...[/b]

This is a refreshing entry into the genre and one which I enjoyed a lot more than I thought I would.
It avoids the migraine inducing bright cheeriness which infects most other puzzlers, it’s gritty, it gives a nice “end times” vibe and if you’re in the mood it can be genuinely fun to play.

Is it the sort of game that will make me want to rush through my working day to get back home and play?

No, puzzle games don’t do that for me, too shallow, remember, but it is a fun distraction in short bursts and one which I’ll definitely load up again.


[b]This is a post apocalyptic puzzle game.[/b]

If puzzle "match up" games are your thing and you’re looking for something a little different in the genre, then Containment should fit the bill.
It’s a stylish, quick hit, post apocalyptic puzzler and there aren’t many games you can say that about!

Containment: The Zombie Puzzler - Short-lived Fun

Containment: The Zombie Puzzler offers a unique twist on the puzzle genre with its zombie-themed gameplay. However, my experience with the game left me wanting more, resulting in a lackluster 2/5 rating. While it provides a brief burst of entertainment, it quickly loses its appeal and fails to incentivize continued play.

One of the most disappointing aspects of Containment: The Zombie Puzzler is its short length. I managed to complete the entire game within a mere 30 minutes, which left me feeling unsatisfied and underwhelmed. The lack of content and depth prevented me from fully immersing myself in the game and exploring its potential.

Moreover, the game did not provide enough motivation for me to continue playing beyond the initial completion. The absence of compelling achievements or unlockables diminished the replay value significantly. It felt like there was no reason to invest more time into the game once the initial objective was achieved.

While the core puzzle mechanics in Containment: The Zombie Puzzler are engaging initially, they quickly become repetitive and lack the necessary complexity to keep players engaged in the long run. The lack of variety in puzzle types and the absence of new challenges hindered the overall experience. It failed to evolve and offer new surprises to keep me hooked.

Visually, Containment: The Zombie Puzzler adopts a simple and minimalist art style. While it may be appealing to some players, it does little to captivate or impress. The sound design is equally unremarkable, lacking the impact and immersion that could have enhanced the gameplay experience.

In conclusion, Containment: The Zombie Puzzler offers a brief burst of puzzle-solving fun but falls short in terms of content, replay value, and overall depth. Its short length and lack of incentive to continue playing hinder its potential for prolonged enjoyment. While it may serve as a casual distraction for a short while, it fails to provide a truly captivating and engaging experience.

This is a really fun puzzle game. It's basically a block-matching game. Zombies and citizens are in a grid. To kill the zombies, you you need to swap citizens among cells until you surround the zombies with people of a single color. If you take too many turns, the zombies spread to neighboring cells. You'll also occasionally get attacked from the sides of the grid. You have a variety of special weapons - sniper rifle, grenades, air strikes, gas masks (which create wild card citizens that serve as all colors), and others. The game is not hard, and the campaign is short (~2-3 hours), but the levels are randomized so there is plenty of replay. There is also a survival mode, though it is just like the campaign but without the ability to continue on if you lose (you have to start over in survival mode, but can replay a level in campaign mode). I wish the game got a bit tougher on later levels, or for a way to increase the difficulty, but the game is quite a lot of fun as is. Overall, a really nice and fun game. I highly recommend it.

Conclusion: ⚖️
The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav has a lot of promise with its rich setting and intriguing story, but it ultimately fails to maintain momentum. While it’s decent, it doesn’t offer enough new or exciting to make it stand out in the crowded adventure game space.

Max Payne 3, developed by Rockstar Studios and released in 2012, brings the iconic character of Max Payne back for another dark, gritty adventure filled with slow-motion gunplay, brooding storytelling, and complex character dynamics. While the game received widespread praise for its gameplay improvements and engaging story, it also faced some criticisms, particularly for its departure from the series' original setting and tone. Here’s a detailed review of why Max Payne 3 remains a standout title, despite a few flaws.

What Works
🎮 Engaging, Mature Storytelling
One of the core strengths of Max Payne 3 is its compelling narrative. Max is no longer the young, troubled cop of the past. Now a washed-up, broken man living in São Paulo, Brazil, he’s hired as a bodyguard for a wealthy family embroiled in a dangerous world of crime and corruption. The writing is sharp, and the voice acting (with James McCaffrey returning as Max Payne) does an excellent job of conveying Max’s despair and cynicism. The story is deeply emotional, offering insights into Max’s troubled past, while also keeping players on edge with unpredictable twists and high-stakes action.

💥 Outstanding Combat and Bullet Time Mechanics
The bullet time mechanic that Max Payne is famous for returns in Max Payne 3 with more refined controls and spectacular visuals. The gunplay feels more fluid than ever, with intense shootouts that are made even more thrilling by the slow-motion effects. The wide variety of weapons, from pistols to shotguns and assault rifles, coupled with the ability to dive into gunfights with acrobatic moves, gives the game a dynamic and exhilarating combat system.

🌎 Immersive Environments and Graphics
While the game moves away from the snowy streets of New York, the environments in São Paulo are just as detailed and atmospheric. The game captures the gritty, urban setting with impressive visuals, whether you're navigating the favelas, mansions, or seedy nightclubs. Rockstar Studios does a great job of making every locale feel rich and lived-in, adding to the overall atmosphere of Max Payne 3. The cinematics blend seamlessly with gameplay, making you feel like you're playing through a film.

🎮 Smooth, Polished Gameplay
With Rockstar’s involvement, the game benefitted from high-quality game mechanics and smooth integration of narrative and gameplay. The controls are tight, and the pacing of the action sequences is excellent, with a perfect balance between quiet moments and intense firefights. Whether you're using a cover system or performing an intense bullet-time dive, the gameplay feels responsive and satisfying.

What Doesn’t Work
❌ Shift in Tone and Setting
One of the most divisive aspects of Max Payne 3 is its departure from the New York City setting. The shift to São Paulo changes the feel of the game, removing much of the iconic film noir atmosphere that made the first two games stand out. While the new setting is immersive in its own right, some long-time fans felt that the game's gritty, urban landscape lost some of the charm of its predecessors, which had a more cold, noir-inspired tone.

❌ Linear Level Design
Although the story and combat are top-notch, Max Payne 3 is relatively linear in terms of level design. Some players felt that the game’s focus on scripted moments, narrow corridors, and restricted paths made it feel somewhat less free than the more open-world experiences Rockstar is known for. While this doesn’t ruin the game, it’s a small downside for those hoping for more freedom in exploration.

❌ Occasional Repetitiveness
While the action sequences are varied and exciting, there are moments in the game where the combat can start to feel repetitive. Many of the levels consist of clearing areas full of enemies, and while the game offers several ways to approach combat, the structure of the gameplay can sometimes feel formulaic.

Conclusion
Max Payne 3 is an excellent game that builds upon its predecessors by improving the mechanics and delivering a gripping, dark narrative. The character of Max Payne is as tortured and complex as ever, and the combat mechanics are as exciting as they come. While the shift in setting and tone might disappoint some, Max Payne 3 still succeeds in delivering a memorable and intense experience. The game’s cinematic presentation, combined with the stunning action and emotional depth, makes it a standout title that’s well worth playing for fans of the series and newcomers alike.

[h1]Review[/h1] 
I have played the original games. So, its quite a surprise that after such a long time that rockstar had announced a third game in the Max Payne franchise where the main protagonist suddenly becomes bald and its set in South America. That is an absolutely radical move against the identity of the originals and is usually just a sign for disappointment.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Its hard to find a game that took the franchises gameplay and improved it in every aspect in a sequel. Not only can you dodge in every direction, but also stay and move a lot on the ground. Bullet time is a bit overpowered as you can use it any time during dodging, although standing up takes a while which makes positioning one of the most important parts of the game, aside fast reaction time and going for headshots.
Due to the way the dodges and bullet times are included, the gameplay not only is fun but also in itself a cinematic experience. The biggest drawback of the game, which actually can be so annoying that it can kill the replay value is the lack of a proper skip button for cutscenes. There are mods to fix this although not being ideal. Otherwise, the replay value is high for special modes, time attack, high scores, challenges and so on and so forth.

The games levels very a lot, with multiple different interesting set pieces that also add to the gameplay or change it up. Even something like shooting outside of a vehicle never gets stale due to different set pieces and context it provides.

Your character can die easily but so can enemies. My biggest criticism of the previous games was that you could die in a second from full health. Here you don’t have to spam quicksave because the health system works much better. You can find painkillers which regenerate your health. Alternatively, if you don’t use it and have no health left, your character will drop to the ground and you can shoot the person who downed you. If you accomplish this, your character will stand up with half hp left.

Luckily the dream sequences in the previous game are gone. I never liked those much.
There is even a multiplayer mode which has made slow motion work in a pvp setting. Although there aren’t many playing anymore and its balancing is questionable, it can increase playtime.

[u]Story[/u]
A more complex story although being not that personal. This causes the stakes to be not that interesting. The biggest twist for me was that the buildup to being betrayed came by a different person that you neither remember much after discovering it nor care about due to this. The story is eventful although less about the main stories plot but rather through the perspective and experiences from the main character. I’m still impressed on the very witty and sometimes stupid on purpose writing coupled with the ironic main character who takes a job in a Brazil while never bothering to learn any Portuguese whatsoever. 

[u]Sound[/u]
A variety of unique and distinctive tracks with combat sound effects that adds to a unique memorable experience. Every level has a distinct track which gives it a completely different feel than the level already provides. I specially like the voice acting from the protagonist as its better than it ever was.

[u]Graphics[/u]
Its incredible how much quality you can get in a game when you have a studio with an enormous budget and the focus on a single player experience. The game came out over 10 years ago and the graphics are so good it could have been a few years ago. Everything can be thorn to pieces, especially environments but bullets have an impact on enemies too, although not being to the point that you can shoots of limbs and have gore. 

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
One of the best single player third person action shooters. It provides a decent story, different set piece after set piece in its level structure, satisfying gunplay with a bullet time feature that stands out and is well implemented into the gameplay. A third instalment into a franchise that does almost everything better while also staying true to its identity even while making moves that would make it seem that it did the opposite. This is a true sequel that almost makes you feel like Max Payne.

Max Payne 3 is a brutal, stylish, and cinematic third-person shooter that delivers intense gunplay, a gripping neo-noir story, and some of Rockstar’s best action sequences. However, while it excels in combat and presentation, it also struggles with pacing, linearity, and a departure from the franchise’s classic noir roots, making it a divisive entry among long-time fans.

The shooting mechanics are top-tier. Gunfights are visceral, fast-paced, and satisfyingly weighty, with Rockstar’s signature attention to detail making every bullet impact feel devastating. The Bullet Time system is as fluid and exhilarating as ever, allowing for cinematic slow-motion gunfights that never get old. The physics-driven enemy reactions and destructible environments make every shootout feel dynamic and cinematic.

The game’s story and presentation are a mixed bag. On one hand, Max’s descent into self-destruction, complete with his gritty internal monologue and alcohol-fueled cynicism, feels authentic and well-written. The game’s stylized visuals, with glitch effects and distorted transitions, enhance the paranoia and psychological distress Max experiences. On the other hand, the narrative direction—moving away from the New York noir aesthetic into a glossy, Michael Mann-style crime thriller set in Brazil—feels like a departure from the franchise’s roots. While the story is solid, it lacks the tragic, poetic atmosphere that made the first two Max Payne games so iconic.

Another drawback is the game’s structure. Unlike the semi-open level designs of its predecessors, Max Payne 3 is extremely linear, with long, unskippable cutscenes that often interrupt the action. While the cinematics are beautifully crafted, they sometimes take too much control away from the player, making the game feel more like an interactive movie than a pure shooter.

That said, Max Payne 3 is still a fantastic action game. The combat is incredibly satisfying, the set pieces are thrilling, and the presentation is top-notch. It may not be the classic noir experience that fans expected, but as a stylish, cinematic shooter, it delivers some of the best gunplay in the genre.

MP3, Max Payne as a whole, has been a big part of why i love video games. Everything from it's gritty presentation, beautiful combat, James McCaffrey's amazing voice (Rest in peace, legend), and of course the protagonist himself; Max. Max is a character, not good or bad, he is simply gray; he tries to do good but what i love about this series is how real it is, reality isn't saving everyone or triumphing over the evil, no, reality is grasping at the straws, the inability to see the clues at the right moment, living in a world bigger and better or worse than you and that's what Max Payne does best. Especially 3. But let's not get ahead of ourselves and criticize, or praise, this game for what it is.

First of all, the combat. Absolute 10/10. The controls are really responsive and feel great. Maybe i miss the speed of Max Payne 2 a bit, but the "precision" of this game's combat is waaay better imo. I want to put the emphasis on the word precision as i think it really defines this games overall movement and combat. One minor nitpick is sometimes walls and Max have a weird interaction where he puts his weapon towards the air. Other than that everything; the shootdodge, bullet-time, bullet projectories, enemies reacting to wounds and ragdolling, they are all done professionally and Rockstar and everyone behind this game deserve infinite praise.

The story. Well i think it is a good story. It is bigger than Max and really disturbing at times and i think these are great things in a Max Payne story. The characters are good, many of them memorable and feel real. Cutscenes and camera angles are great, the voice acting is top-notch, and i love that we experience the story from Max's eyes and we can only know as much as he knows, but maybe we can make out more details than he is able to do. At times, Max really does feel like a "dumb gr*ngo" and i think this is intentional and totally fine; his inability to piece everything together at the right time, as i've said before, feels authentic and realistic. Max isn't Batman, and detective work is not something Sherlock Holmes would've make you believe it is. Life, and the past is, well let me quote from Max Payne 2; "The past is a puzzle; like a broken mirror, as you piece it together, yout cut yourself, your image keeps shifting, and you shift with it." Having mentioned Max Payne 2, i think it is high time i talked about my gripe with this story. Well to keep it short, those who'd played 2 would know, Max came to terms with his initial loss in the first game at the end of the second game, but in 3 we see him still as a mess. This may be intentional; showing us a broken man like Max can't ever escape from his past nor his future. If interpreted like this, it makes sense. Or it can be that Rockstar were lazy, just wanted to continue the story of Payne and just went ahead with it without considering the end of 2.  But even if this is the case, it is still a well-written story. I don't think there are plot holes anywhere; maybe Max could've been killed in a few cases [spoiler] like in the police station with Becker and Victor [/spoiler] but other than that i think that everything is conveyed subtlely but also understandably.

In other areas, this games graphics are gorgeous, i encountered 2 or 3 visual bugs where the entire floor disappeared, textures didn't load but that could be an issue caused by me. The game runs smooth with no frame drops. Sometimes in certain areas enemies are hard to spot and it is hard to ascertain from where you are getting shot at.

The soundtrack is 10/10. I discovered HEALTH thanks to this game and they did an amazing job with this game. [spoiler ]The part where you're in the cemetery with Passos and DEAD plays, and you hear Max's child's crying or when you are in the airport and TEARS begins, such an epic OST [/spoiler] . 

So all in all, if you haven't played this masterpiece yet, play it. Play the entire trilogy. There is nothing else like it, and other from Remedy's upcoming remakes, there probably never will be a game and protagonist like Max Payne. Rest in peace, James McCaffrey.

Simply put, I think Max Payne 3 is a contender for best Third-Person-Shooter ever. Personally, I can't think of anything that can beat it. Over a decade ago, this game was released to some negativity, because they exchanged the rainsoaked scenery of New York for the sunny Sao Paolo (I remember, that I shunned the game myself at first for that reason alone...), but the sun may be shining, yet Max Payne is still as dark as you remember. This game is off-the-charts brutal. 

What makes Max Payne such a joy to play? On the surface it's a third-person shooter with cover mechanics and a bullet time feature that allows you to pick off enemies. The basics are simple, but actually the game is rather challenging, because Max himself can't really take many hits before going down. That means that the game constantly forces you to be efficient. The gunfights feel almost believable, even if just one guy is going to end up mowing down about a thousand mercenaries with heavy weapons all on his own. Also really cool is how the enemies try to flank, put down cover-fire and push forward, so you can never feel too safe covering behind walls. 

While all of this is going on, the graphics, while dated, are still very pleasant to look at, especially since you can really thrash the rooms throughout the gunfights. The story is pretty engaging and still hits that noir vibe I liked from the first two games. Max is also very funny in this one - tragic, bitter, yet funny. Good one-liners throughout!

The only downside to this game is the constant interruptions of cutscenes: It is meant to be a cinematic experience, but in some missions - especially in the beginning - there is a lot of downtime. Most of the scenes are either action-packed or funny, so it's not terrible, but when replaying the story mode or going for the challenge-modes, it can get a bit annoying. Some of the cutscenes you just can't skip. Gives you an incentive not to blunder your attempts, I guess...
Also annoying: Rockstar Launcher, but it is to be expected unfortunately.

I feel like a heretic saying this but it has to be said, Max Payne 3 is the best of the trilogy.

There I said it, yes the game isn’t the work of the original devs, Remedy. However, the 10 or almost ten years of evolution of third-person shooters, and storytelling make it a by far better game than the first or second. 

How should I start? Well, gameplay wise its much better. The camera is now set to one side (so Max himself never gets in the way of your aim). The ability to hug cover is a thing by pressing the Q key when near walls. Bullet time, the key feature of the first two games is still here, but it's now not a requirement to survive every encounter. Shoot dodge is also retooled and now results on you lying on the deck whenever you finish it. Oh and you also look like a total muppet when you dive into a wall. Health also has a rework, yes max still loses health like crazy when shot, but losing it all now sends you into a ‘knockdown’ state, if you can quickly shoot the dude that got you can get back up at the cost of painkiller bottle (effectively making them extra lives). 

Oh and AI has an upgrade as well, badies no longer rush you like in the first to. Now they have some self-preservation skills, and will take cover and try to do things like flank you. However, they are manageable even later in the game when they have things like body armour. 

It’s just a more enjoyable experience, to be frank.

Oh and graphically it just looks good, even 10+ years later. It’s last of the line of games from the xbox 360, PS3 era when PC games were also starting to look nicer. Environments are bright for the most part detailed and rich. Models and animation look good, and even by today's standards, the organic destruction that can happen looks lovely when big gunfights start up.

Story wise I feel it’s better as well. Yes I know that’s dunking on Sam Lake a bit. However Max Payne 3 feels more grounded in every respect. This time Max is washed up now ex-cop following the events of the last game, and doing bodyguard work for a stupidly rich family in Sao paulo Brazil. Of course, Max Payne hasn’t got the best track records of keeping people under his watch, well alive, nothing helped by his drink and drug-fueled depression. Gone are themes about super soldier serums, and grand over-the-top conspiracies, and in are more grounded things like drugs, gang crime, kidnapping, human trafficking, and corrupt paramilitary police, oh and maybe a spot of betrayal. It's actually a good story (maybe save for a slight hiccup with the overall scheme). Yes some have moaned about the switch from the comic panels to in-game engine cutscenes, but I found them better.

Also credit to the writers, Max’s depression and addiction is actually well presented and believable. As someone who suffers badly from the former, it actually hit as being somewhat relatable.

The only real downer is the visual effects that come with the cutscenes, more earlier in the game. It’s emulating things from the film ‘Man on Fire’ (a film I haven’t seen but told is what inspired the idea). It shows the alcoholic and drugged-up haze of Max’s mental state early in the game, and it clears as he sobers up during the course of the game. Yes, it's an artistic choice, but I can see how it could make some people actually nauseated. 

In short, yes as I said the third is the best in the series, heck its one of the best, and most underrated third-person shooters ever. The only other downer is the use of that annoying Rockstar social club nonsense that acts as extra DRM for the game (yes its crashy, and stupid given that it caused the game not to start on at least one occasion when it couldn’t connect to the servers). However look past that, and this game is one of the essential GOAT’s.

The basic premise should be apparent enough from the store page- navigate MC Escher inspired environments full of impossible shapes by rotating the stage, effectively manipulating the direction of gravity.
Subsequent chapters introduce new mechanics that add new layers of complication to the puzzles. These mechanics aren't always obvious in their function, however, and the game relies on the design of their introductory levels to explain them, rather than any overt tutorialization. This strategy was not always effective, in my experience.
The majority of the puzzles presented a stimulating challenge to me. The interactions between the player character and items, and the mind-bending geometry of the levels sometimes presents so many variables it becomes impossible to track them all completely. In these cases the puzzle becomes more of a process of elimination- figuring out which moves will fail the level, which are dead ends that don't actually change the situation. This appears to be intended, with the "inverter" achievements rewarding players who are able to go from beginning to end in certain levels without wasting any moves. Although I typically didn't mind these levels, some might find them frustrating.
The second half of the game consists of "mirrored" versions of the levels from the first half, with identical (albeit flipped) basic structures, but certain elements like spawn locations, keys, obstacles, etc. altered to present a new challenge. Many of these mirrored levels are rather subversive, requiring you to break the game's conventions and exploit behaviors which would otherwise appear to be unintended.
Some of the game's challenges require precise control of a sort the game isn't built for, which can be quite aggravating, and though some secrets should be reasonably apparent to the keen-eyed, others require actions you would normally have no reason to take, and have little in the way of hints to point the way.
The game has a story, after a fashion. It isn't direct, providing a bit of dialogue upon completion of each chapter and requiring the player to fill in the gaps, but I didn't find it too hard to reach what I believe is a complete understanding of it.
All in all, the bridge is very unique. It's great value for its sale price, and I found it quite enjoyable on balance, but I can understand why it isn't the most highly rated.

Serious Sam 2, released in 2005 by Croteam, is the fourth installment in the Serious Sam series. Unlike its predecessors, this game shifted to a more cartoony and lighthearted style, moving away from the hyper-realistic graphics of the first games. Though it maintains the series’ signature action-packed gameplay, its visual style, tone, and some of its gameplay mechanics divide opinions among fans.

What Works Well?
💥 Classic Chaos
True to the series' roots, Serious Sam 2 delivers unrelenting action, with players facing waves of enemies in fast-paced, explosive encounters. The action remains intense and addictive, with a focus on high-body-count shootouts that keep you constantly on the move.

🎯 Expansive Arsenal
The game offers an impressive range of weapons, from the classic shotgun to more exotic choices like the laser gun and rocket launcher. Each weapon adds a new layer of fun to the chaos, making the combat feel dynamic and enjoyable.

🌍 Vibrant Environments
The visual shift to cartoony and vibrant settings helped give the game its unique flavor. While this style is not for everyone, many players enjoy the bright, colorful environments, which stand in contrast to the darker, more serious tone of the original games.

What Could Be Better?
❌ Repetitive Gameplay
Though the fast-paced action is fun at first, some players feel the game can get repetitive over time. The wave-based combat and limited variety of encounters can lead to a sense of monotony once the initial excitement wears off. The lack of significant gameplay variety can make it feel like more of the same.

❌ Cartoony Tone
While the shift to a more lighthearted, cartoonish aesthetic was a bold choice, it alienated some long-time fans of the series. The humor and visuals are very different from the grittier and more serious tone of the earlier games, which some felt didn’t fit the Serious Sam franchise's core identity.

❌ AI and Level Design
Some players found that the AI and level design were not as engaging as in previous entries. The enemy AI can sometimes feel predictable and lacking depth, while the levels often feel like empty arenas with minimal challenges besides surviving the onslaught.

Conclusion
Serious Sam 2 is a fun and action-packed shooter for those who enjoy arcade-style combat. While the change in tone and visuals was a daring departure, it doesn’t fully capture the essence of what made the earlier Serious Sam games so beloved. The repetitive nature and lack of depth in the gameplay hurt its long-term appeal, but it still offers plenty of mindless fun for fans of high-speed shooting action.

If you miss the old days of Duke Nukem 3D and Shadow Warrior, Serious Sam-II is the way to go. Despite its shameless obsession with spoofing Duke Nukem Forever, Serious Sam-II is a worthy sequel to a very fun game. The action is even more frantic than before and the enemies are tougher, and to handle them, you need to chuck grenades simultaneously while firing away the primary weapon, which is a very welcome and innovative addition to gameplay. The level design is brilliant and very creative and even more beautiful than in the first game. You really gotta love how you are rewarded with an amusing cutscene each time you finish a level. This is the direct sequel to the first Serious Sam game, which was divided into two halves, being The First Encounter and The Second Encounter. It picks up basically right where the last game(s) left off, so it's recommended you play those first, but this does stand well enough on its own. 

Overall, I liked the aesthetics and level design of this game better - levels are much shorter, creating more natural breaks in gameplay, and the environments are much more diverse. There are plenty of entertainingly silly cutscenes, and the humor from the first game is dialed up WAY past 11 (probably to about 15 or so, if I had to estimate). Each boss fight mixes up the regular run-and-gun gameplay by introducing some new, temporary gameplay mechanic, which was fun, for the most part. Enemy and weapon variety is pretty much identical from the first game(s), but this entry adds vehicles and gun emplacements, which are fun to use. The BEST part of this game is the duel-wielding system, where you can mix-and-match ANY two guns and fire them independently of each other! That was a blast, and never got old.

The biggest problem with this game is that it suffers from the same problem the first game(s) did: too many enemies. No, I don't mean that the game is too difficult because it throws too many enemies at you at once for you to be able to handle - in fact, it's closer to the exact opposite. It throws a ton of enemies at you at once, and each time, there is that initial rush where the player goes "okay, I have to keep moving, figure out what enemy types are spawning, where they're coming from, what weapons would be most effective," etc., and it is very fun to figure this all out on the fly and adjust to it. The problem is, once you've done that, once you've settled into that ballet, ideally it would last for a minute or two and then either give you a chance to breathe and wind down, or mix it up and force you to adapt again. What ends up happening more often than not is it just keeps going. The exact same enemy types keep coming at you, for minutes on end, with no variance. This happens most often in what amounts to perfectly square, flat arenas with little to no obstacles or cover. And what happens most often is it just gets boring. The game is at its best when you're forced to keep moving forward, making your way through tight level design, killing everything thrown at you, and when you need to take a breather you can just stop moving forward for a second. It's at its worst when you're stuck in a small, boring box, and you have to kill 500 of the same enemy before you can do anything else. There was one part in the final level where I had to basically stand in the exact same spot for what felt like 5 minutes straight, killing individual enemies that spawned one at a time, right in front of me, none of which posed any real threat to me. I honestly got so frustrated and bored with it that I considered quitting, but I knew I wasn't far from beating the game and wanted to finish it.

That big paragraph sounds harsh, and it is in a way, but overall, I still do recommend this game. It was a lot of fun when it wasn't frustratingly boring, and the wackiness of it had me laughing out loud at times, and in disbelief at times.

The enemies! Disregard my mention of the enemies in the negatives. Sure, they look wackier and silly, but they are a really creative and unique set of enemies. Oh, and no space monkeys, which is a super plus in my book.

When I picked up the plasma rifle for the first time, the gunfights suddenly felt better. The more weapons I collected and learnt to use, the better the gunfights felt. Though, it never fully reaches the satisfying feeling from the other games.

Some early stages feel too cramped, but it gets better. On planet Kleer, it almost feels like a proper Serious Sam game here and there, and environments keep getting more and more impressive, imo. They did an excellent job with the environments and atmosphere, and scattering stupid jokes here and there. Traps and secrets are, of course, plentiful! It's a serious sam game, after all.

The wacky story and silly humor made me laugh out loud at properly funny moments (e.g. the chicken machine). However, most of it made me cringe. But there's a certain charm to it. As I was playing further, I started looking forwards to the next cutscene. I wanted to see how cringy it would be. To see if they could lower the bar for humor even lower.

And.... Yes, they did. They kept lowering it, and lowering it. And I started laughing more and more at the sheer stupidity of this story, the bad transitions, the obvious plot holes, the desperate attempts at comedy. Some moments were probably very funny in the writers head, then came out nothing like they imagined, but it still made it to production. I mean this as a weird compliment, as I was thoroughly amused. I both disliked the wacky style and loved it at the same time. Not sure how to describe it better without spoilers.

Playing this was certainly one the experiences of a lifetime. If your sense of humor requires quality, then this game will annoy you a lot (which is also very funny). If you enjoy Serious Sam, then you'll find enjoyment in this wacky, unique and creative installment in the Serious series.

I thoroughly enjoyed playing Call of Juarez: Gunslinger. The story is straightforward and enjoyable, weaving a narrative that keeps you engaged without overcomplicating things. The game's structure is simple yet not trivial, offering a gameplay experience that's accessible but still rewarding.

While it's not a masterpiece, Gunslinger is a game that you can play with pleasure. The Western setting is evocatively recreated, with an atmosphere that feels authentic despite the limited technical resources at the developers' disposal. The art direction and environmental design do a commendable job of transporting you to the Wild West, making up for what the game lacks in graphical fidelity.

The mechanics, particularly the gunplay and the unique ability to slow down time for precision shots, add a layer of depth to what could have been a basic shooter. The storytelling, delivered through the unreliable narration of the protagonist, adds a charming twist to the traditional linear narrative, enhancing the replay value as you uncover different layers of the truth.

Overall, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a solid entry in the genre that doesn't pretend to be more than it is but delivers fun and satisfaction in spades. I give it a 7/10.

If you have bought this title, and are having issues with reading the manual. For some reason, the manual is not accessible via the right hand menu in the library. So you will have to google steam powered + confrontation manual to get it.

There are no loot drops what so ever. You can only upgrade armor and weapons via weapon stands. Which are located sporadically around the various maps. Other upgrades include glyphs, which are obtained via plinths a giant magic rock.

Main Screen - On the campaign menu there is an Additional Content button, but when selecting it. There is nothing listed, and I cannot find anything regarding additional content.

The main menu is located right at the bottom of the screen. Where you can access options, switching profile and quiting the game. It looks out of place on the main screen, compared to the other buttons. Which have a UI element to them.

Gameplay
Naration - The naration feels like the old pen and paper DM, explaining things to you. Other than that it is uninspired.

User Interface - In game with the party interface it does look nice and clean. Though the minimap is rather lackluster, even worse when bringing up the full map. You cannot zoom into the map. Though it does leave white dots showing where you have been on the map. It does seem out of place compared to the rest of the UI.

Character Panels - Pressing I gives you the character panel, which shows you their attributes, skills, armor etc.. One gripe is it does not include all of the stats. Which are on a seperate panel pressing O. So you will not be able to see when increasing attributes what they are improving. The tooltips on attributes do specify what they improve. Also their class should be on the panel as well.

Skills and Armor - I would have liked a way to respec my characters, this feature is in Aarklash: Legacy. So I can make the party I want, with the builds I want. 

Healing - Some characters have a heal over time. Others have an aoe heal. There is the option of using bandages to heal. But you can only use them on other characters, not on yourself. Frustration can set in when due to pathing you cannot reach the character you want to bandage.

Codex - Only accessible in the main menu, and not while you are playing the game. Also they have missed adding lore and character biographies to the character entries. Character entries only have a visual model of the character, plus a list of their abilities. In Aarklash: Legacy you are able to examine enemy units and their abilities.

Combat - Rushing blindly into rooms, will definitely get your party killed in this game. Some fights do take some strategy on what to focus on, what to crowd control. Line of sight, and pulling groups away from patrols. So you do not end up in some crazy cluster frak wipe, when a party member gets feared. Combat is mainly pausing, chaining some commands, such as move here, attack this, use this ability for each party member. Unpause then watch the fight unfold, pause and reissue commands when required.

Multiplayer - I have not tried multiplayer, but according to the forums and how this title was recieved. Do not expect any.

A $5 mobile-looking action game based around a rotational momentum gimmick where you grapple to little points, rotate around them and try to predict and launch yourself at the right arc to collect gems in curve, hunt switches, get to better points and evade death. There's also some competitive grappling vs evil budget design enemies where passing through their grapple rope cuts it and you need to constantly reposition and regrapple to limit their options for recovery without falling yourself. Surprisingly despite the first impression the art design and voice-overs give this is a pretty competent $5 game.

No story. Uggo the Barbarian clears levels. Everything is limited to a single screen so level designs are pretty limited but Rotastic has the momentum-based gameplay down solidly. Although it takes some getting used to and newer gamers may find things to be random and unfair I found that I could mostly get where I wanted to go after playing for about thirty minutes. There's a lot of levels, they can be cleared in a few quick hours and the game has an emphasis on clearing levels as quickly as possible while getting the most points and mixing in little tricks like loops, mid-air stalls and dramatic drops. It's a perfect arcade set-up and good game for seeking mastery if you try it and it sinks its teeth into you. I found clearing the levels pretty agreeable, often having fun though the limitations of the map design does make them repetitive about 4 worlds in. There are a few interesting gimmicks with new tiles but they show up rarely and more would be welcome. Some gimmicks are also teeth-pullingly bad like trying to hit multiple switches in a row on a timer, or hitting a switch that opens a path for 5 seconds but has to be reset after another 15 spent waiting because the trap is covering most of the entry but isn't quiiiiite done resetting yet. Switch hunt levels basically made me groan every time and the actual sequential switch hitting parts feel like out of place laziness considering the surprising bit of passion in the rest of the game.

The graphics are better than I expected from how genuinely ugly the base character designs are. It's a crude, often gory little ugly fantasy aesthetic like Castle Crashers, though the actual background art and the smooth linework makes everything work pretty well somehow. The game sorely needs an option for sound adjustment along the lines of Music, Sounds and Voices. It's a shame, the Rotastic Guy gives a good performance and sounds like he is having a great time but hearing the same lines over and over again is probably one of the ironic punishments in Hell. The music is the hidden star of the show: nothing mind-blowing here but a bunch of surprisingly catchy and pleasant tunes. 

Speaking of hidden shine the multiplayer is surprisingly good? Not genre-defining or anything and limited to local only but Rotastic has a pretty fair and consistent set of rules that lends itself to spontaneous, frantic back and forths and loud fun. At least if you can convince other people to play Rotastic with you. But I can't miss tipping my hat to the devs for doing good work here. It is a little too easy to just camp a node and let yourself rotate out to the minimum distance and wait for AI enemies to suicide trying to approach you but eh, forgivable. It at least makes things doable in the single player mode when you fight the AI who can have pretty ridiculous reflexes and speed and make the competitive jewel grabbing levels a chore.

I probably got this for less than a $1 in a Humble Bundle but I have to give credit where it is due: Rotastic is a good budget title.

Rotastic is an ancient game from 2012.  It's a whopping 12 years old at the time of this review.  The game lacks support for the typical features of modern gaming PCs, hasn't been modernised or updated to run smoothly on contemporary machines.  The game looks and feels dated.  Despite this lack of modernisation, it carries a pretty high price tag for such an old game.  This seems to have be lingering on Steam with an inflated price to try profit from abandonware.

The game itself is a very shallow and simple action reflexes game where you have a simple grappling hook and you must attach/detach it from various points while you swing around it endlessly.  You can lengthen or shorten the grapple and attach/detatch as you need, and you need to time everything right to swing between the nodes and collect all the gems on the way.  Basically if this was made today it would have been a mobile app instead of slightly worsening the entire Steam catalogue by appearing here. 

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.

The game features simple, cartoony 2D graphics, of the type you normally expect to see in low effort mobile apps.  3D graphics programming does require a degree of skill and competence and unfortunately not all developers have the budget or talent to deliver this, despite 3D graphics cards hitting the mainstream in the 1990's.  Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, left handed gamers or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.  

PC gamers will be insulted by the presence of console peasant children's toy controller prompts, despite this being on PC.  Developers should try to be aware which platform they're developing for.

This looks a lot like it was designed for consoles, but released on Steam instead by mistake.  While this is on PC, it has all the hallmarks and deficiencies of a console game, from the clunkier than needed control scheme to the less than cutting edge graphics.  There's 10's of thousands of PC games on Steam, and PC gamers deserve only the best.  This might not appeal to many gamers due to the lack of PC-centric design.  It's unclear why this never made it to the video game console appliances it seems to have been designed for.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 11 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 100,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Rotastic is relatively expensive for an abandonware nostalgia gouge, at $5 USD, and it's not worth it.  The game is just too old, hasn't been modernised.  And as the old saying goes, you can't go home again.

For comparison, the $5 asking price for this game could get you games like "Torchlight", "Killing Floor 2" or "Deus Ex: Human Revolution".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

Dishonored is one of the first games I've really immersed myself into the story. From the continuity of the world-building to the small little secrets only a handful of players bother to sniff out, you can really tell the developers and writers poured their hearts into the game.

[b][i]May contain minor spoilers below[/i][/b]

[u][b]Story-telling, Atmosphere, and Replayability.[/b][/u]
The game starts in the city of Dunwall where a pandemic is rampant and witchcraft lurks in the shadows, both feared by those witnessing, and dismissed by the skeptics, this is where your choices influence the outcome of the world. With blood on your hands, the pandemic worsens and you start to notice the subtle shifts of your surroundings like the city's decay, your allies behaviors, and the environmental well-being of Dunwall's inhabitants. While keeping your hands clean would pave way for a more hopeful outcome.
Of course, the best aspect about the game's story-telling is that it lets the player realize and see for themselves the consequences of what they chose to do, rather than explicitly presenting the changes and hand-holding the player experience. While the changes unfold subtly throughout the journey, the ending lays bare how horrible, (or virtuous) of a person you are.
This adds to the game's replayability since most players would miss the small, subtle details in their first playthrough. And there's also achievements for the completionists, and two endings for those who wonder just how much weight their choices truly bear.

[u][b]Gameplay and Mechanics[/b][/u]
As someone who leans more into the casual gamer side, I'd say the controls and the amount of control you're given is intuitive. Though there are some game mechanics that makes it feels a little sluggish at times, but that could also just be myself being bad at the game.
As much as I love the magic system, I found some flaws with it. To unlock and upgrade more advanced magics you'd need to collect items as per usual for any other games but for Dishonored, the items needed to collect are hidden away, needing time and meticulous searching to obtain every single one. And as most players could carry on without it, they leave it behind, resulting in them not experiencing the magic system to the fullest by the end of the game. You could argue that the items are always hinted at but even then, you'd need time, and not everyone is going to invest a few more hours just to experience a bit more of the game that's cool but ultimately not important.

To sum it up, I highly recommend it! I can't really compare it to other stealth games due to this one being my very first, but I really love it that I kept coming back throughout the years to play again. And a lot of the times I discovered new secrets, easter eggs, and short interactions between NPCs that I didn't catch even with 80+ hours into it.

Dark and dreary, this stealth/assassination game provides an excellent story-driven experience in a world rife with rampant whaling, dark magic, and plague rats. Government corruption and power struggles are the soup du jour here, but rather than force you to sit through the ins and outs of political banter, the meat of the story experience hinges on you interrogating your role as the silent protagonist assassin. Should be killing your targets or dealing with them in non-lethal ways? Can you even manage that? Why even bother? It's poignant stuff if you take the time to invest your thoughts in it.

Gameplay-wise, movement and combat feel pretty good overall, and the game often gives you sprawling environments with lots of shadows to hide in so you can plan your stealthy actions accordingly. Just don't be surprised when your plans abruptly backfire due to being spotted by awkward enemy behavior or an unforeseen level hazard. There's no real punishment for being a sloppy assassin, and the end-of-mission report on your "chaos level" provides a good incentive to replay the game again in the future.

All in all, solid game, definitely worth a second run in the future!

P.S. Rest in peace, art director Viktor Antonov. You did incredible work in this game, and you were taken from this world too soon.

MISSIONS
The game is segmented into missions where you infiltrate an area of the rat plagued town, find runes find coins, and stealth your way to the end character of the mission, and return to the home base Pub for the next part of the story.  The missions can be replayed with different strategies to pass the same area.  You quickly gain powers such as Dark Vision, Blink warping, jumping higher, more ammo, or the ability to possess an animal.

COMBAT WEAK, FRUSTRATING AI
Although the powers you gain are useful, they are greatly diminished in practical combat because the enemy AI alert system is too quick.  One wrong move by you and the enemies have a hive mind and rush you from everywhere, and almost all your powers go out the window.  Yeah you can fight a few enemies in hand to hand combat but not a bunch at once. You can try to warp or slow motion, but your magic power during combat is used up so quickly.  Therefore this game is not an action game to react and take down enemies but a game you need to reload and try to quietly take down a few enemies at a time using a Stealth approach.

STEALTH
The stealth gameplay is a similar style to Arkham Batman games how you use dark vision to see enemies through walls, warp up on ledges, and plant traps. In some ways you have more freedom to move and jump, but some of the early missions have a lot less places to hide or to perch, and you lack powers, so they are not as fun. As the game progresses the levels are better designed with multiple paths, and elevations, and you can be more methodical to take out the enemies in the area.  I enjoyed crawling under floors, dropping from above, using sleep darts, or luring multiple enemies to hit them with a few grenades.  The second half of the game design placed the enemies more strategically and it had a few engaging mechanical puzzles to add to the variety.

STORY HELPS INTENSIFY THE GAME
The game feels best by the second half when the story gets a bit more intense and you anticipate saving a character or hunting down an enemy, and this drives you past a lot of the shortcomings of the combat. The atmospheric creativity builds with a beautiful Ballroom and Mansion, dark Disposal Trains, and inventive enemies like Tall Boys enhance the world creation.

FINAL
Dishonored 1 was not always fun and some areas felt tedious, but some of the later large areas had engaging stealth parts.   The story was fine, but why does the Boat guy friend suddenly mortally despise me ?

A Masterclass in Stealth and Player Freedom

Dishonored is one of the best stealth games I’ve ever played. What sets it apart is the sheer amount of choice given to the player—not just in how you navigate each mission but also in how you neutralize your targets. Whether you prefer to stick to the shadows, eliminating no one, or carve a bloody path through Dunwall, the game adapts seamlessly to your playstyle.

The level design is phenomenal, offering multiple routes to every objective. You’re never forced down a single path, and creative use of Blink (teleportation) and other abilities lets you approach challenges in ways that feel uniquely yours. Every encounter is a puzzle with multiple solutions, and that freedom makes every mission deeply rewarding.

The game's atmosphere is another highlight. The art style is dark, gloomy, and stylized in a way that perfectly captures the plague-ridden, oppressive world of Dunwall. It doesn’t just look like a city in ruin—it feels like one. The grimy streets, the eerie lighting, and the sickly, exaggerated character designs all reinforce that suffocating sense of decay. It’s as if the world itself is sick, mirroring the corruption of the ruling elite.

My only real complaint is the lack of an in-mission stats tab. As someone who plays on the hardest difficulty, striving for a true ghost run with zero kills, not being able to check whether I’ve been detected in real time was frustrating. I had to constantly reload checkpoints because I wasn’t sure if an enemy had noticed me or not. Given how fast I teleport around, sometimes I wouldn’t even realize I’d been spotted until the mission ended. A simple stats screen mid-mission would have made a world of difference.

Despite that, Dishonored remains a must-play for stealth fans. The combination of fluid movement, rewarding level design, and deep player agency makes it a truly special experience. If you love games that let you tackle challenges your way, this is one you shouldn’t miss.
